The Histories

by Herodotus

c. 430 BC 2026

This is an AI modernization of The Histories into contemporary English. The original is available from Standard Ebooks. Also available as an epub.

Editor's Introduction

Herodotus came from Halicarnassus, a Greek city on the coast of what is now Turkey and at that time part of the Persian empire. He wrote around 430 BC, fifty years after the war his book builds toward. His purpose is in his first sentence: to set down what he had found out, so that great deeds would not fade with time, and above all so that the reason the Greeks and the Persians fought each other would be preserved. Nobody had written a book like it before. Cicero called him the father of history and the name stuck.

He takes his time getting to the war. Book One is mostly about Croesus of Lydia, a rich king who misread an oracle and lost his kingdom to the Persians. Book Two is Egypt from end to end — the Nile, the pyramids, mummification, the crocodile, the priests and what they eat. Book Four is Scythia and Libya: burial mounds, scalps used as hand towels, a people said to turn into wolves for a few days every year. Then the Persians move west, the Greek cities of Asia revolt, Darius sends an army that is beaten at Marathon in 490 BC, and ten years later his son Xerxes comes with everything he has. The nine books are named after the Muses, a tidy piece of work by later editors rather than by Herodotus.

The digressions are the book, not an interruption of it, and the reason is his method. He collects. He tells you who told him a story, gives you two or three versions when he has them, and says plainly when he does not believe what he has just written down — his rule is that he is obliged to report what people say and not obliged to believe it. Thucydides, writing a generation later about a war he had fought in, worked the opposite way: he composed the speeches himself and stated a method at the start. That history is in this collection too, and the two men together are where the whole business of writing history comes from.

What most readers come for is in Books Seven to Nine. Xerxes has the Hellespont whipped for wrecking his bridges. Three hundred Spartans hold the pass at Thermopylae. The Greek fleet fights in the narrows at Salamis while the king watches from the foot of a hill on the shore, and the following summer the armies meet at Plataea. Herodotus is at his best there and he is still the same man who wanted to know how they embalm a cat.

This edition is the complete work, all nine books and every digression, modernized from G. C. Macaulay's English translation of 1890. His section numbers are kept, so any passage can be found in another edition, and his distances and weights are given in miles, feet and pounds, except where he is doing arithmetic with his own units.

Book One: Clio

Chapter 1: The First Wrongs, Gyges and Candaules, Arion, and Solon's Visit to Croesus

This is the account of the inquiry of Herodotus of Halicarnassus, set down so that the deeds of men may not be forgotten with time, and so that the great and marvelous works done by Greeks and non-Greeks alike may not lose their fame; and above all, so that the reason they went to war with each other may be remembered.

1. The Persians who know their history say that the Phoenicians started the quarrel. The Phoenicians, they say, came from the sea the Greeks call the Erythraean, the Persian Gulf, to our sea, the Mediterranean. They settled in the land where they still live today, and right away they took to making long voyages. They carried Egyptian and Assyrian goods to many places, and one of the places they came to was Argos. At that time Argos was in every way the leading city of the country now called Greece. So the Phoenicians arrived at Argos and began to sell off their cargo. On the fifth or sixth day after they arrived, when nearly all their goods were sold, a large crowd of women came down to the shore, and among them was the king's daughter. Her name, and the Greeks agree on this, was Io, the daughter of Inachus. The women were standing near the stern of the ship, buying whatever wares they liked best, when suddenly the Phoenicians passed the word to one another and rushed at them. Most of the women ran off and got away, but Io and some others were seized. The Phoenicians put them on board and sailed off at once for Egypt.

2. That, according to the Persians, is how Io came to Egypt; here they do not agree with the Greeks. And this, they say, was the first wrong. After this, they say, some Greeks (they can't say which people) put in at Tyre in Phoenicia and carried off the king's daughter Europa. These would presumably have been Cretans. That made them even for the first injury. But after this, they say, it was the Greeks who committed the second wrong. They sailed in a warship, the Argo of Jason and his crew, to Aea in Colchis, on the river Phasis at the far eastern end of the Black Sea, and when they had finished the other business they came for, they carried off the king's daughter Medea. The king of Colchis sent a herald to Greece to demand compensation for the kidnapping and to ask for his daughter back. But the Greeks answered that since the non-Greeks (the "barbarians," as the Greeks called anyone whose language was not Greek) had paid them no compensation for kidnapping Io of Argos, they would pay the non-Greeks none for this one.

3. In the next generation after this, they say, Alexander the son of Priam, the prince of Troy also called Paris, heard of these things and decided to get himself a wife from Greece by force. He was quite sure he would never have to pay for this wrong, since the Greeks had not paid for theirs. So he carried off Helen, the wife of Menelaus of Sparta. The Greeks decided first to send messengers to demand her back and to ask compensation for the kidnapping. When they made this demand, the other side threw the kidnapping of Medea back at them: the Greeks now wanted compensation from others, they said, though they had paid none themselves and had refused to hand the girl back when asked.

4. Up to this point, they say, it was only a matter of women being carried off on both sides. But after this the Greeks were very much to blame, because they started the fighting: they invaded Asia before the non-Greeks ever invaded Europe. Now, in the Persians' judgment, carrying off women by force is the act of wrongdoers, but making a great business of revenge for it is the act of fools; the sensible thing is to pay no attention once the women are gone, since obviously they would never be carried off if they did not want to go. And the Persians say that they, the people of Asia, made nothing of it when their women were carried off, but that the Greeks, for the sake of one woman from Sparta, gathered a great army, came to Asia, and destroyed the kingdom of Priam. From that time on, they say, they have always regarded the Greeks as their enemies. For the Persians claim Asia and the non-Greek peoples who live there as their own, while they consider Europe and the Greeks to be a separate world.

5. That is how the Persians say it happened, and they trace the start of their hostility to the Greeks back to the taking of Troy. But about Io the Phoenicians do not tell the story the way the Persians do. They deny that they took her to Egypt by force. They say instead that while they were at Argos she slept with the captain of their ship, and when she found she was pregnant she was ashamed to tell her parents, so she sailed away with the Phoenicians of her own free will, so as not to be found out. Those are the stories the Persians and the Phoenicians each tell. I am not going to say that these things happened one way or the other. Instead I will point out the man who, to my own knowledge, first began to wrong the Greeks, and then I will go on with my story, covering the cities of men, small and great alike. For most of the cities that were great long ago have become small, and the ones that were great in my own time used to be small. So, since I know that human prosperity never stays in one place for long, I will give both kinds their due.

6. Croesus was a Lydian by birth, the son of Alyattes, and ruler of the nations on this side of the river Halys. That river flows up from the south between the Syrians and the Paphlagonians and empties northward into the sea called the Euxine, the Black Sea. Croesus was the first non-Greek we know of who conquered some of the Greeks and made them pay tribute, while he won others over as friends. The ones he conquered were the Ionians, the Aeolians, and the Dorians who live in Asia; the ones he made his friends were the Spartans. Before Croesus' reign all the Greeks were free. The raid of the Cimmerians, a nomad people from north of the Black Sea, which struck Ionia before Croesus' time, was not a conquest of the cities, only a plundering expedition.

7. Now this is how the throne, which had belonged to the Heraclids, passed to Croesus' family, the Mermnads. Candaules, whom the Greeks call Myrsilus, was ruler of Sardis and a descendant of Alcaeus son of Heracles. Agron son of Ninus son of Belus son of Alcaeus was the first of the Heraclids to become king of Sardis, and Candaules son of Myrsus was the last. The kings who ruled this land before Agron were descended from Lydus son of Atys, after whom this whole people came to be called Lydians; before that they were called Meonians. The Heraclids, descended from Heracles and a slave girl of Iardanus, took over the government from these earlier kings; it was entrusted to them because of an oracle. They reigned for twenty-two generations, five hundred and five years, handing the power down from father to son, until the time of Candaules son of Myrsus.

8. This Candaules fell passionately in love with his own wife, and being in love, he was convinced that she was by far the most beautiful woman in the world. Believing this, he used to talk to Gyges son of Dascylus, the one among his bodyguards he liked best. He shared his most important business with Gyges, and he also used to praise his wife's beauty to him, far beyond all measure. Not long after, since disaster was fated to fall on Candaules, he said this to Gyges: "Gyges, I don't think you believe me when I tell you how beautiful my wife is. People's ears are less trusting than their eyes. So find a way to see her naked." Gyges cried out and said: "Master, what a foolish thing to say, telling me to look at my mistress naked! When a woman takes off her clothes, she takes off her modesty with them. Men worked out long ago the good sayings we ought to learn from, and one of them is this: each man should look at what is his own. I do believe she is the most beautiful of all women, and I beg you not to ask me to do what is wrong."

9. With words like these he resisted, afraid that some harm would come to him from it. But the king answered him: "Don't worry, Gyges, and don't be afraid, either of me, that I'm saying this to test you, or of my wife, that she might do you some harm. I will arrange it from the start so that she won't even know you have seen her. I'll put you in the room where we sleep, behind the open door. After I go in, my wife will come to bed too. There is a chair near the entrance of the room, and she will lay her clothes on it as she takes them off one by one. That way you will be able to look at her at your leisure. Then, when she walks from the chair to the bed and her back is to you, make sure she doesn't see you as you slip out through the door."

10. Since there was no way out, Gyges agreed. When Candaules thought it was time for bed, he led Gyges to the bedroom, and right after that his wife came in too. Gyges watched her come in and lay down her clothes. When her back was turned to him as she went to the bed, he slipped out of his hiding place and started to leave. But as he went out, the woman caught sight of him. She understood what her husband had done. She did not cry out, though she felt the shame of it, and she acted as if she had noticed nothing, because she meant to take revenge on Candaules. For among the Lydians, as among most other non-Greek peoples, it is a disgrace even for a man to be seen naked.

11. So for the moment she kept quiet, as I said, and gave no sign. But as soon as day came, she got ready the servants she knew were most loyal to her, and then sent for Gyges. He had no idea she knew anything of what had happened, and he came when she called, since he was used to going whenever the queen sent for him. When Gyges arrived, the woman said to him: "Gyges, two roads lie open to you now, and I give you the choice of which you will take. Either you kill Candaules and have both me and the kingdom of Lydia, or you must be killed yourself, here and now, so that you never again obey Candaules in everything and see what you should not. Either he must die, the man who planned this, or you must, the man who looked at me naked and did what is not allowed." For a while Gyges was stunned by what she said. Then he began to beg her not to force him to make such a choice. But he could not move her, and he saw that he truly had to choose: kill his master, or be killed by others himself. He chose to live. Then he asked her: "Since you are forcing me to kill my master against my will, tell me how we are going to attack him." She answered: "The attack will come from the same place where he showed me naked. We will attack him while he sleeps."

12. So they made their plan, and when night came (Gyges was not allowed to leave, and there was no escape for him: either he must be killed or Candaules must), he followed the woman to the bedroom. She gave him a dagger and hid him behind that very same door. Later, while Candaules was asleep, Gyges crept up to him and killed him, and so he won both the wife and the kingdom. The poet Archilochus of Paros, who lived at about that time, also mentioned Gyges in a poem in iambic verse.

13. Gyges won the kingdom, though, and was made secure in it, by the oracle at Delphi. The Lydians were furious about what had been done to Candaules and took up arms. But Gyges' followers and the rest of the Lydians came to an agreement: if the oracle declared that Gyges was to be king of the Lydians, he would be king; if not, he would give the power back to the descendants of Heracles. The oracle gave its answer, and so Gyges became king. Yet the Pythia, Apollo's priestess at Delphi who speaks his oracles, also said this: that vengeance for the Heraclids would come upon Gyges' descendants in the fifth generation. The Lydians and their kings paid no attention to this prophecy until it actually came true.

14. So the Mermnads drove out the Heraclids and took the throne. When Gyges became king he sent a great many offerings to Delphi. Of all the silver offerings at Delphi, more are his than anyone else's. Besides the silver he gave an enormous amount of gold, and in particular one gift more worth mentioning than the rest: six golden mixing bowls, the great bowls the Greeks mixed their wine and water in, which stand there as his offering. They weigh thirty talents, something like 1,700 pounds (the talent is a weight as well as a sum of money, and a talent of silver, about fifty-seven pounds of it, is a fortune). The bowls stand in the treasury of the Corinthians, though in truth this treasury does not belong to the people of Corinth but to Cypselus son of Aetion. This Gyges was the first non-Greek we know of to dedicate offerings at Delphi, except only Midas son of Gordias, king of Phrygia, who dedicated the royal throne he used to sit on when he judged cases in public. The throne is well worth seeing, and it stands in the same place as Gyges' bowls. The people of Delphi call the gold and silver Gyges dedicated "Gygian," after the man who gave it.

As soon as he became king, Gyges also led an army against Miletus and Smyrna, and he took the lower town of Colophon. But he did no other great deed in his reign, which lasted thirty-eight years, so we will pass him by with no more than has already been said.

15. Now I will speak of Ardys son of Gyges, who became king after him. Ardys took Priene and invaded the territory of Miletus. While he was ruling at Sardis, the Cimmerians, driven from their homes by the nomad Scythians, came into Asia and took Sardis, all except the citadel.

16. After Ardys had been king for forty-nine years, his son Sadyattes succeeded him and reigned twelve years, and after him came Alyattes. Alyattes made war on Cyaxares, the descendant of Deioces, and on the Medes. He drove the Cimmerians out of Asia, he took Smyrna, which had been founded from Colophon, and he invaded the territory of Clazomenae. From there he did not come back the way he wanted to, but with heavy losses. During his reign, though, he did other things very much worth mentioning, as follows.

17. He made war on Miletus, a war he had inherited from his father. This is how he used to invade their land and besiege Miletus. Whenever the crops in the fields were ripe, he would lead an army into their territory, marching to the music of pipes and harps and flutes, both low-pitched and high-pitched. When he came into the land of Miletus, he did not knock down the houses out in the countryside, or set fire to them, or tear off their doors; he left them standing as they were. But he destroyed the trees and the crops in the fields, and then went back the way he had come. The Milesians controlled the sea, so there was no point in his army trying to blockade them. And he left the houses standing so that the Milesians would have places to live while they sowed and worked the land, and so that their labor would give him something to destroy whenever he invaded.

18. He kept up this war against them for eleven years, and in the course of those years the Milesians suffered two great defeats: once in a battle at Limenion in their own territory, and again on the plain of the Maeander River. For six of the eleven years Sadyattes son of Ardys was still king of the Lydians, and he was the one who invaded Milesian land at those times of year; for it was this Sadyattes who started the war. For the five years that followed those first six, the war was carried on by Alyattes son of Sadyattes, who inherited it from his father (as I said before) and threw himself into it hard. None of the Ionians helped the Milesians carry the burden of this war except the people of Chios. The Chians came to their aid to repay a favor in kind, because the Milesians had earlier helped the Chians all through their war with the people of Erythrae.

19. Then in the twelfth year of the war, while the Lydian army was burning the standing grain, this happened. As soon as the grain caught fire, a strong wind drove the flames onto the temple of Athena called Athena of Assesus, and the temple caught fire and burned to the ground. At the time nobody thought anything of it. But later, after the army had gone back to Sardis, Alyattes fell sick. His illness dragged on, so he sent messengers to consult the oracle at Delphi, either because someone advised him to or because he himself thought it best to send and ask the god about his illness. But when the messengers reached Delphi, the Pythia said she would give them no answer until they had rebuilt the temple of Athena they had burned at Assesus in the territory of Miletus.

20. This much I know from what the people of Delphi told me. But the Milesians add to it that Periander son of Cypselus, who was a close guest-friend of Thrasybulus, then the tyrant of Miletus (a tyrant being a man who has seized sole power outside the law, not necessarily a cruel one), heard of the oracle given to Alyattes. Periander sent a messenger to tell Thrasybulus, so that he would know about it ahead of time and could plan whatever the situation required. That is the story the Milesians tell.

21. When this answer was reported to Alyattes, he sent a herald to Miletus at once, wanting to make a truce with Thrasybulus and the Milesians for as long as it took him to build the temple. So the envoy was on his way to Miletus. Meanwhile Thrasybulus, who had been told the whole story in advance and knew what Alyattes intended to do, came up with this trick. He gathered into the marketplace all the food that could be found in the city, both his own and what belonged to private citizens, and he announced to the Milesians that when he gave the signal they were all to start drinking and celebrating together.

22. Thrasybulus did this and gave this order so that the herald from Sardis would see a huge quantity of food piled up carelessly and the people feasting, and would report it to Alyattes. And that is just what happened. The herald saw all this, delivered to Thrasybulus the message the king of Lydia had given him, and went back to Sardis; and the peace that followed came about, as I am told, for this reason alone. Alyattes believed there was a severe famine in Miletus and that the people had been worn down to the depths of misery, and when the herald came back from Miletus he heard the opposite of what he had expected. After this the two sides made peace, on terms that they would be guest-friends and allies to each other. Alyattes built two temples to Athena at Assesus instead of one, and he recovered from his illness. That is how things went in the war Alyattes waged against the Milesians and Thrasybulus.

23. As for Periander, the man who told Thrasybulus about the oracle, he was the son of Cypselus and tyrant of Corinth. The Corinthians say (and the people of Lesbos agree with them) that a very great wonder happened in his lifetime: Arion of Methymna was carried ashore at Taenarum on the back of a dolphin. This Arion was a lyre-player second to none of his day, and the first, as far as we know, to compose a dithyramb, the choral hymn to Dionysus; he gave it that name and trained a chorus to perform it at Corinth.

24. This Arion, they say, spent most of his time at Periander's court, but he got the urge to sail to Italy and Sicily. There he made a great deal of money, and then he wanted to go back to Corinth. So he set out from Taras, in southern Italy, and since he trusted Corinthians more than anyone else, he hired a ship with a Corinthian crew. Out on the open sea, the story goes, the crew plotted to throw Arion overboard and keep his money. He found out about it and begged them, offering them his money and asking them to let him live. But he could not persuade them. The men taking him told him either to kill himself, so that he could have a burial on land, or to jump into the sea at once. Driven into this corner, Arion begged them, since that was their decision, to let him stand on the deck in his full singer's costume and sing, and he promised to kill himself after he had sung. They were delighted at the thought of hearing the best singer in the world, and they moved back from the stern to the middle of the ship. He put on his full costume, took up his lyre, stood on the deck, and performed the Orthian strain, a high, ringing hymn. When the song was over he threw himself into the sea just as he was, costume and all. The crew sailed on to Corinth. But a dolphin, they say, took Arion on its back and carried him ashore at Taenarum. When he reached land he went on to Corinth, still in his costume, and when he got there he told the whole story. Periander did not believe him. He kept Arion under guard and would not let him go anywhere, while he kept a careful lookout for the men who had carried him. When they arrived, Periander called them in and asked whether they had any news of Arion. They said he was safe and well in Italy, and that they had left him doing nicely at Taras. At that moment Arion suddenly appeared in front of them, looking just as he had when he jumped from the ship. They were so astonished that, when they were questioned, they could no longer deny it. That is the story the Corinthians and the people of Lesbos both tell, and at Taenarum there is an offering of Arion's, not very large: a bronze figure of a man riding on a dolphin.

25. After waging this war against the Milesians, Alyattes the Lydian eventually died, having reigned fifty-seven years. When he recovered from his illness, this king had dedicated an offering at Delphi, the second of his family to do so: a great silver mixing bowl with a stand of welded iron. The stand is a sight worth seeing above all the offerings at Delphi. It is the work of Glaucus of Chios, the first man in the world to discover the art of welding iron.

26. After Alyattes died, his son Croesus inherited the kingdom at the age of thirty-five. As I said, he fought against the Greeks, and the first of them he attacked were the Ephesians. When he besieged them, the Ephesians dedicated their city to Artemis by tying a rope from her temple to the city wall. The distance between the old city, which was the one under siege then, and the temple is about 4,200 feet, a little under a mile. These were the first Greeks Croesus attacked, but afterward he did the same to the other Ionian and Aeolian cities, one by one, accusing them of one thing or another. Where he could find serious grounds he brought serious charges; against some of them he charged only trivial offenses.

27. When the Greeks in Asia had been conquered and made to pay tribute, he planned next to build ships and attack the islanders. When everything was ready for the shipbuilding, they say that Bias of Priene came to Sardis (or, according to another version, Pittacus of Mytilene). Croesus asked him whether there was any news from Greece, and his answer put an end to the shipbuilding. "My king," he said, "the islanders are hiring 10,000 cavalry, and they mean to march on Sardis and fight you." Croesus thought he was telling the truth and said: "If only the gods would put it into the islanders' heads to come against the sons of the Lydians on horseback!" The other answered: "My king, I can see you are eager to catch the islanders on horseback on the mainland, and it is natural you should want that. But what do you think the islanders want? Ever since they heard you were going to build ships against them, what have they been praying for except to catch the Lydians at sea, so they can take revenge on you for the Greeks on the mainland whom you hold as slaves?" Croesus, they say, was delighted with this ending, and he took the advice, since he thought it was well said. He stopped building ships, and instead he made a treaty of friendship with the Ionians who lived on the islands.

28. As time went on, nearly all the peoples on this side of the river Halys were conquered. Except for the Cilicians and the Lycians, Croesus conquered every nation there and kept it under his rule: the Lydians, Phrygians, Mysians, Mariandynians, Chalybians, Paphlagonians, the Thracians both Thynian and Bithynian, the Carians, Ionians, Dorians, Aeolians and Pamphylians.

29. Once these had been conquered, and while Croesus was still adding to his Lydian empire, all the wise men of Greece who happened to be alive at the time came to Sardis, which was then at the height of its wealth, each brought there by his own reasons. One of them was Solon the Athenian. Solon had made laws for the Athenians at their request, and then he left home for ten years. He sailed off saying that he wanted to see the world, but really it was so that he would not be forced to repeal any of the laws he had made. The Athenians could not repeal them on their own, because they had bound themselves by solemn oaths to live for ten years under whatever laws Solon gave them.

30. So for this reason, and to see the world, Solon left home and visited Amasis, the king of Egypt, and then Croesus at Sardis. When he arrived, Croesus welcomed him as a guest in the royal palace. Then, on the third or fourth day, on Croesus' orders his servants took Solon around to see his treasuries and showed him everything, how great and splendid it all was. When Solon had looked at all of it and examined it as he pleased, Croesus asked him: "My Athenian friend, we have heard a great deal about you, both about your wisdom and about your travels: how you have gone through many lands to see them, in your search for wisdom. So now I have a great wish to ask you whether, of all the people you have seen, there is anyone you think is the happiest of all." He asked this because he thought he himself was the happiest man in the world. But Solon did not flatter him at all; he told the truth. "Yes, my king," he said: "Tellus the Athenian." Croesus was amazed at this and demanded: "Why do you judge Tellus to be the happiest?" Solon said: "First, Tellus lived when his city was prospering, and he had fine, good sons, and he saw children born to every one of them, and all of them lived to grow up. Second, he was well off by our standards, and at the end of his life he had a most glorious death. When the Athenians fought a battle at Eleusis against their neighbors, he brought up help, routed the enemy, and died there the finest of deaths. The Athenians gave him a public burial on the spot where he fell, and paid him great honor."

31. When Solon had stirred up Croesus with the story of Tellus and all the ways in which he had been happy, the king asked again whom he had seen who deserved second place after him. He was sure that he would at least get second place. But Solon answered: "Cleobis and Biton. They were from Argos, and they had enough to live on, and on top of that they had the bodily strength I am about to describe. Both of them had won prizes at the games, and this story is also told about them. There was a festival of Hera at Argos, and their mother absolutely had to be driven to the temple in a cart. But the oxen did not come back from the field in time. So the young men, with no time for anything else, put themselves under the yoke and pulled the cart themselves, with their mother riding in it. They pulled it for about five miles, and brought it to the temple. When they had done this, and the whole gathered crowd had seen them do it, their lives came to the best of ends; and in this the god showed that for a human being it is better to die than to live. The men of Argos stood around them praising the young men's strength, and the women of Argos praised the mother for having such sons. Their mother was overjoyed, both at what they had done and at the praise it won. She stood in front of the goddess's statue and prayed that she would give her sons Cleobis and Biton, who had honored her so greatly, the best gift a human being can receive. After this prayer, when they had sacrificed and feasted, the young men lay down to sleep in the temple itself, and they never got up again; that was the end that held them. The Argives had statues made of them and dedicated them at Delphi, because they had shown themselves to be the best of men."

32. So Solon gave these two second place for happiness. Croesus was angry, and said: "My Athenian friend, do you think so little of our prosperity that you rank us below even ordinary private citizens?" Solon answered: "Croesus, you are asking about human life, and you are asking someone who knows very well that heaven is jealous and loves to throw things into confusion. In a long lifetime a man gets to see many things he would rather not see, and to suffer many things he would rather not suffer. I set the limit of a man's life at seventy years. Those seventy years add up to 25,200 days, not counting any extra months. But if every other year is made a month longer, so that the seasons come around at the right time of year, there will be 35 extra months in those seventy years, and those months make 1,050 days. Of all these days, 26,250 in the seventy years, not one brings anything at all like what another brings. So you see, Croesus, a human being is nothing but chance. As for you, I can see that you are very rich and king over many people. But what you asked me about, I cannot call you yet, not until I learn that you have brought your life to a good end. The very rich man is not one bit happier than the man who has only enough for each day, unless his luck stays with him and he ends his life well, with all his good things still around him. Many very rich men are unhappy, while many with only modest means are lucky. In fact the rich man who is unhappy has only two advantages over the poor man who is lucky, while the lucky man has many over the rich man who is unhappy. The rich man is better able to satisfy his desires, and better able to bear a great disaster if one falls on him. But the other has the advantage of him in these ways. True, he cannot satisfy his desires or bear a disaster as well as the rich man can, but his good luck keeps those things away from him. He is sound in body, free of disease, untouched by suffering, the father of fine children, and good-looking himself. And if on top of all this he ends his life well, then he is the one you are looking for, the one who deserves to be called happy. But until he is dead, hold back: do not call him happy yet, only lucky. Now, no mere human being can have all these things at once. Just as no single country can supply everything it needs for itself, but has one thing and lacks another, and the country that has the most is the best, so it is with a man: no one person is complete in himself. He has one thing and lacks another. But whoever keeps the greatest number of these good things to the end, and then dies a gracious death, that man, my king, I think deserves the name. In everything, though, we have to look at the end, and see how it turns out at the last. For heaven gives many people a glimpse of happiness, and then tears them up by the roots and throws them down."

33. That is what Solon said, and he did not please Croesus. Croesus sent him away and thought nothing of him; he decided Solon was a complete fool, a man who ignored the good things in front of him and told people to look at the end of everything.

Chapter 2: The Son of Croesus, the Testing of the Oracles, and Athens under Pisistratus

34. After Solon had gone, a great retribution from heaven fell on Croesus, probably because he had judged himself the happiest of all men. First a dream came and stood over him as he slept, and it showed him the truth about the evils that were about to happen to his son. Croesus had two sons. One of them was disabled, since he was deaf and unable to speak. The other far surpassed the young men of his own age in everything, and his name was Atys. About this Atys, then, the dream told Croesus that he would lose him, struck by an iron spear-point. When Croesus woke up and thought the matter over, he was terrified by the dream. First he found his son a wife. Then, although the young man had been in the habit of leading the Lydian armies, Croesus no longer sent him out anywhere on any such business. And he had the javelins and lances and every other weapon men use for fighting taken out of the men's quarters and piled up in the inner storerooms, for fear that something hanging on the wall might fall down on his son.

35. While Croesus was busy with his son's wedding, a man arrived at Sardis who was under a misfortune and whose hands were not clean of blood. He was a Phrygian by birth and of the royal family. This man came to Croesus' house and, following the custom of that country, asked to be purified of the killing, and Croesus purified him. (The Lydian way of purifying a man is almost the same as the Greek one.) When Croesus had done what custom required, he asked the man where he came from and who he was. "Stranger," he said, "who are you? From what part of Phrygia have you come to sit as a suppliant at my hearth? And what man or woman did you kill?" The man answered: "My king, I am the son of Gordias son of Midas, and my name is Adrastus. I killed my own brother without meaning to. That is why I am here: my father drove me out and stripped me of everything I had." Croesus answered: "You happen to come from a family who are our friends, and you have come to friends. As long as you stay in our country you will want for nothing. And you will find it best for yourself to bear this misfortune as lightly as you can." So Adrastus made his home with Croesus.

36. During this time a monstrous boar appeared on Mount Olympus in Mysia. It came down from that mountain and ravaged the fields of the Mysians. The Mysians went out against it many times, but they could do it no harm; instead it did harm to them. So at last messengers from the Mysians came to Croesus and said: "My king, a monstrous boar has appeared in our country and is destroying our fields. We are eager to kill it, but we can't. So now we ask you to send your son with us, and a picked band of young men with dogs, so that we can rid our land of it." That was their request. But Croesus remembered what the dream had said, and he answered them: "As for my son, don't mention him again in this matter. I will not send him with you, since he has just been married and that is what concerns him now. But I will send picked men of the Lydians with you, and my whole pack of hunting dogs, and I will order those who go to do everything they can to help you rid your land of the beast."

37. That was his answer. The Mysians were satisfied with it, but just then Croesus' son came in, having heard what the Mysians had asked. When Croesus said that he would not send his son with them, the young man said: "Father, in the past the finest and noblest part was ours: to go out again and again to war and to the hunt and to win a good name. But now you have shut me out of both, though you have never seen any cowardice or lack of spirit in me. How am I supposed to show my face now when I walk to and from the marketplace? What sort of man will the citizens think I am? What sort of man will my new wife think I am? What kind of husband will she think she has been married to? So either let me go to the hunt, or give me reasons and persuade me that things are better for me the way they are now."

38. Croesus answered: "My son, I am not doing this because I have seen any cowardice in you, or anything else unworthy. It is because a vision came and stood by me in a dream as I slept, and told me that you would die young, and that you would be killed by an iron spear-point. Because of this vision I hurried on your marriage, and because of it I now refuse to send you on this business. I am watching over you, to see if I can somehow steal you from your fate at least for as long as I live. For you are, as it happens, my only son: the other one I do not count, since he is deaf."

39. The young man answered: "Father, after a vision like that, no one could blame you for watching over me. But there is something you don't understand, a point in the dream whose meaning you have missed, and it is only right that I explain it to you. You say the dream told you I would die by an iron spear-point. But what hands does a boar have? What iron spear-point is there for you to be afraid of? If the dream had told you I would die by a tusk, or by anything else like that, then you would be right to do what you are doing. But it said 'by a spear-point.' So since our fight will not be against men, let me go."

40. Croesus answered: "My son, you have partly won me over with what you say about the dream. Since you have persuaded me, I will change my mind and let you go to the hunt."

41. Having said this, Croesus sent for Adrastus the Phrygian, and when he came Croesus said to him: "Adrastus, when you were struck by a terrible misfortune (and I do not hold it against you), I purified you, and I took you into my house and have paid for everything you need. Now, since you received kindness from me first, you owe me kindness in return. So I ask you to be the guardian of my son as he goes out to the hunt, in case some wicked robbers come upon you on the road to do you harm. And besides, you ought to go where you can win fame by your deeds yourself. It is your inheritance from your fathers to do so, and you have the strength for it too."

42. Adrastus answered: "My king, if it were not for this I would not be going to any contest of courage like this one. In the first place, it is not right for a man who has suffered such a misfortune as mine to seek the company of men his age who are prospering. In the second place, I have no wish to, and for many reasons I would have kept away. But now, since you urge me and I ought to please you (for I owe you kindness in return), I am ready to do it. So you may expect your son, whom you tell me to guard, to come home to you unharmed, as far as it depends on his guardian to keep him safe."

43. After Adrastus had answered Croesus with words like these, they set out, supplied with picked young men and with dogs. When they reached Mount Olympus they tracked the animal down. They found it, took their stand around it in a circle, and began hurling their spears at it. Then the guest, the man who had been purified of killing, whose name was Adrastus, threw his spear at the boar, missed it, and hit Croesus' son. So the young man was struck by the spear-point and fulfilled what the dream had foretold. Someone ran to tell Croesus what had happened, and when he reached Sardis he told him about the fight and about his son's fate.

44. Croesus was terribly shaken by his son's death, and he took it all the harder because his son had been killed by the very man he himself had purified of killing. Overwhelmed by the disaster, he called on Zeus the Purifier, calling him to witness what he had suffered at the hands of his guest. He called on the same god as Protector of Suppliants and as Guardian of Friendship too. He called him Protector of Suppliants because when he took the guest into his house he had, without knowing it, been sheltering his son's killer; and Guardian of Friendship because he had sent the man as a guardian and found him his worst enemy.

45. After this the Lydians arrived carrying the body, and behind it came the killer. He took his stand in front of the body and gave himself up to Croesus. He held out his hands and begged the king to kill him over the body. He spoke of his earlier misfortune, and said that now, on top of it, he had destroyed the man who had purified him of it, and that life was no longer worth living for him. When Croesus heard this he took pity on Adrastus, even though he was suffering so great a sorrow of his own, and said to him: "My friend, I have already had from you all the justice I am owed, since you condemn yourself to death. You are not the cause of this disaster, except in so far as you were its instrument, against your will. The cause is one of the gods, I suppose, the same one who warned me long ago of what was going to happen." So Croesus buried his son with proper rites. But Adrastus son of Gordias son of Midas, the man who had killed his own brother and had now killed the son of the man who purified him, waited until everyone had gone and the tomb was quiet. Then, knowing himself to be the most unfortunate of all the men he had ever heard of, he killed himself on the grave.

46. For two years after the loss of his son Croesus sat quietly in mourning. But after that, two things made Croesus put an end to his mourning: the overthrow of the rule of Astyages son of Cyaxares by Cyrus son of Cambyses, and the growing greatness of the Persians. Now he began to think how he might cut short the power of the Persians, if he could find any way, while it was still growing and before they became great.

With this plan in mind he set out at once to test the oracles, both the Greek ones and the one in Libya (as the Greeks call Africa). He sent messengers in different directions: some to Delphi, some to Abae in Phocis, some to Dodona. Some were sent to the shrine of the hero Amphiaraus and to the shrine of Trophonius, and others to Branchidae in the territory of Miletus. These are the Greek oracles Croesus sent to for prophecies. Others he sent to ask at the shrine of Ammon in Libya. He was sending the messengers out to test the oracles and to find out what they really knew. Then, if they turned out to know the truth, he would send a second time to ask whether he should go to war against the Persians.

47. He gave the Lydians he sent to test the oracles these instructions. Starting from the day they set out from Sardis, they were to count the days, and on the hundredth day they were to consult the oracles. They were to ask what Croesus son of Alyattes, king of the Lydians, happened to be doing at that moment. Whatever each oracle answered, they were to have it written down and bring it back to him. What the other oracles answered nobody reports. But at Delphi, the moment the Lydians entered the temple to consult the god and asked the question they had been told to ask, the Pythia spoke these words in hexameter verse:

	I know the number of the grains of sand and the measure of the sea;
	I understand the mute, and I hear the one who does not speak.
	There has come to my senses the smell of a hard-shelled tortoise
	boiling in a bronze cauldron, with the flesh of a lamb mixed in;
	bronze lies beneath it, and bronze is laid over it like a cloak.

48. When the Pythia had spoken this oracle, the Lydians had the prophecy written down and went straight back to Sardis. When the others who had been sent around arrived with the answers of the oracles, Croesus unrolled the writings one by one and looked them over. At first none of them pleased him. But when he heard the one from Delphi, he immediately bowed in worship to the god and accepted the answer. He decided that the oracle at Delphi was the only true one, because it had found out what he himself had been doing. For after he had sent his messengers out to the various oracles to consult the gods, he kept the appointed day carefully in mind and came up with this trick. He thought of something it would be impossible for anyone to discover or to guess: he cut up a tortoise and a lamb and boiled them together himself in a bronze cauldron, with a bronze lid on top.

49. That, then, was the answer Croesus received from Delphi. As for the answer of Amphiaraus, I cannot say what he told the Lydians after they had performed the customary rites at his temple. There is no record of it, any more than of the others, except that Croesus believed that his oracle was a true one too.

50. After this Croesus tried to win the favor of the god at Delphi with great sacrifices. Of every kind of animal fit for sacrifice he offered three thousand. He heaped up couches plated with gold and silver, cups of gold, and purple robes and tunics, and made a great pyre of them and burned it, hoping this would win the god even more to the Lydians' side. And he proclaimed that every Lydian should sacrifice whatever he had. When he had finished the sacrifice, he melted down a vast quantity of gold and cast it into ingots, each eighteen inches long, nine inches wide and three inches high. There were one hundred and seventeen of them. Four were of pure gold, weighing two and a half talents each (about 140 pounds apiece). The others were of gold mixed with silver, weighing two talents each (about 115 pounds). He also had a lion made of pure gold, weighing ten talents (about 570 pounds). When the temple at Delphi burned down, this lion fell off the ingots, since it had been set on top of them. It now stands in the treasury of the Corinthians and weighs six and a half talents (about 370 pounds), because three and a half talents (about 200 pounds) of it melted away.

51. When Croesus had finished all these things he sent them to Delphi, and these other gifts along with them. There were two enormous mixing bowls, one of gold and the other of silver. The gold one stood on the right as you enter the temple and the silver one on the left. These too were moved after the temple burned down. The gold bowl now stands in the treasury of the people of Clazomenae, and it weighs eight and a half talents and twelve pounds more (close to 500 pounds in all). The silver one stands in the corner of the temple's front hall. It holds six hundred amphoras, about 6,000 gallons, and the Delphians fill it with wine at the feast of the Theophania. The people of Delphi say it is the work of Theodorus of Samos, and I think they are right, because the workmanship is clearly out of the ordinary. Croesus also sent four silver wine jars, which stand in the treasury of the Corinthians, and two basins for holy water, one of gold and the other of silver. The gold one is inscribed "From the Spartans," and the Spartans say it is their offering. But they are not right about that. This one too is from Croesus, but one of the Delphians wrote the inscription on it because he wanted to please the Spartans. I know his name, but I will not mention it. The statue of a boy through whose hand the water flows is from the Spartans, but neither of the basins is. Croesus sent many other offerings with these that were not specially marked out. Among them are some round silver castings, and also a gold figure of a woman four and a half feet tall, which the Delphians say is a statue of Croesus' baker. Croesus also dedicated the necklaces from his wife's neck and her belts.

52. Those are the things he sent to Delphi. To Amphiaraus, having heard of his courage and of his terrible fate (he was the seer who rode against Thebes and was swallowed up by the earth), Croesus dedicated a shield made entirely of gold, and a spear all of solid gold, the shaft as well as both points. Both of these were still there in my own time, at Thebes, in the temple of Ismenian Apollo.

53. Croesus told the Lydians who were to carry these gifts to the temples to ask the oracles another question as well: should Croesus go to war against the Persians, and if so, should he add an army of allies to his own? When the Lydians reached the places they had been sent to and had dedicated the offerings, they consulted the oracles and said: "Croesus, king of the Lydians and of other nations, believes that yours are the only true oracles in the world. He has given you gifts worthy of your discoveries, and now he asks you whether he should go to war against the Persians, and if so, whether he should add an army of men to his own as allies." That was their question, and the answers of both oracles agreed. Both told Croesus that if he went to war against the Persians, he would destroy a great empire. And they advised him to find out which Greeks were the most powerful and make them his friends.

54. When the answers were brought back and Croesus heard them, he was delighted with the oracles. Fully expecting to destroy the kingdom of Cyrus, he sent to Pytho (the old name for Delphi) once again. He found out how many men of Delphi there were and gave each of them two gold staters. In return the Delphians gave Croesus and the Lydians the right to consult the oracle first, freedom from all fees, and front seats at the games. They also gave them a privilege for all time: any of them who wished could become a citizen of Delphi.

55. After making these presents to the men of Delphi, Croesus consulted the oracle a third time. Once he had learned that the oracle told the truth, he used it again and again. This time he asked whether his kingdom would last a long time. The Pythia gave him this answer:

	But when the day comes that a mule is king of the Medes,
	then, soft-footed Lydian, run by the pebbly Hermus;
	run and do not stay, and do not be ashamed to be called a coward.

56. When these lines reached him, Croesus was more pleased with them than with all the rest. He supposed that a mule would never rule the Medes in place of a man, and that he and his descendants would therefore never lose their power. After this he set about finding out which of the Greeks he should count as the most powerful and win over as his friends. When he looked into it, he found that the Spartans and the Athenians were the leaders, the Spartans of the Dorian people and the Athenians of the Ionian. These were the two most distinguished peoples in ancient times: the Ionians were originally Pelasgian (from the people who lived in Greece before the Greeks), and the Dorians Greek. The Ionian people never moved from their land in any direction. The Dorian people, on the other hand, were great wanderers. In the reign of Deucalion they lived in Phthiotis. In the time of Dorus son of Hellen they lived in the land below Mount Ossa and Mount Olympus, which is called Histiaeotis. When the sons of Cadmus drove them out of Histiaeotis, they settled in the Pindus mountains and were called Macednians. From there they moved again to Dryopis, and from Dryopis they came at last to the Peloponnese, where they began to be called Dorians.

57. What language the Pelasgians used to speak I can't say for certain. But if we must judge by the Pelasgians who are still left, we can draw a conclusion. There are the Pelasgians of the city of Creston, above the Tyrrhenians, who were once neighbors of the people now called Dorians and lived at that time in the land now called Thessaliotis. There are the Pelasgians who settled at Placia and Scylace on the Hellespont, who had earlier lived alongside the Athenians. And there are the people of the various other towns that really are Pelasgian, though they have lost the name. If we must judge by these, the Pelasgians used to speak a non-Greek language. So if the whole Pelasgian people was like these, then the people of Attica, being Pelasgian, must have unlearned their language at the same time as they changed and became Greek. For the people of Creston do not speak the same language as any of their neighbors, and neither do the people of Placia; but they speak the same language as each other. This proves that they still keep the form of language they brought with them when they moved to these places.

58. As for the Greek people, it seems clear to me that they have always used the same language since they first began. They split off from the Pelasgian people and were weak at first. But from that small beginning they have grown into the great number of peoples we see today, chiefly because many non-Greek peoples have joined them. And I think it is also true of the Pelasgian people that as long as they remained non-Greek, they never grew much.

59. Of these peoples, then, Croesus learned that the Athenians were held down and torn apart by faction under Pisistratus son of Hippocrates, who was tyrant of Athens at that time. A great wonder had happened to Hippocrates when, as a private citizen, he went to watch the Olympic games. After he had offered sacrifice, the cauldrons standing on the hearth, full of meat and water, boiled over without any fire under them. Chilon the Spartan happened to be there and saw the wonder. He advised Hippocrates, first, not to take a wife into his house to bear him children; second, if he had one already, to send her away; and if he happened to have a son, to disown him. Hippocrates, they say, would not take Chilon's advice, and afterward this Pisistratus was born to him. At Athens there was a feud between the people of the coast and the people of the plain. Megacles son of Alcmaeon led the coast faction, and Lycurgus son of Aristolaides led the faction of the plain. Pisistratus, aiming at tyranny for himself, raised a third party. He gathered supporters, called himself the leader of the hill-country men, and came up with this trick. He wounded himself and his mules, and then drove his cart into the marketplace as though he had just escaped from his enemies, who, he claimed, had tried to kill him as he was driving out to the country. He asked the people to give him a bodyguard. Before this he had won a reputation as a commander in the war against the Megarians, when he captured Nisaea and did other great services. The Athenian people were taken in and gave him a band of men picked from the citizens. They became not his spearmen but his club-bearers, because they followed him around carrying wooden clubs. These men rose up with Pisistratus and seized the Acropolis. After that Pisistratus ruled the Athenians. He did not upset the existing officials or change the old laws. He ran the city under the constitution that was already in place, and he governed it fairly and well.

60. But not long after this the followers of Megacles and those of Lycurgus joined forces and drove him out. That was how Pisistratus took Athens the first time, and how he lost power before it had taken firm root. But the men who had driven him out soon fell to feuding with one another again. Harassed by the party strife, Megacles sent a message to Pisistratus asking whether he would take his daughter as his wife, on condition that he would become tyrant. Pisistratus accepted the offer and agreed to the terms. Then, to bring him back, they worked out the silliest scheme ever practiced, as I think, by far. After all, the Greeks had been set apart from non-Greeks long ago as the cleverer people, further removed from foolish simplicity; and this was done among the Athenians, who are counted the first of the Greeks in intelligence. In the village of Paeania there was a woman named Phya. She was almost six feet tall (four cubits less three finger-widths), and good-looking as well. They dressed this woman in a full suit of armor, put her up in a chariot, and showed her the pose that would make her look most like the part. Then they drove to the city. They had sent heralds running ahead, and when the heralds reached the city they said what they had been told to say: "Athenians, welcome Pisistratus with goodwill. Athena herself has honored him above all men and is bringing him home to her Acropolis." So the heralds went all over the place saying this. At once a report spread to the villages of the countryside that Athena was bringing Pisistratus back, and meanwhile the people in the city, convinced that the woman was the goddess herself, were worshipping this human being and welcoming Pisistratus.

61. Having got back the tyranny in this way, Pisistratus married Megacles' daughter, as he had agreed with Megacles. But he already had sons who were grown men, and the descendants of Alcmaeon were said to be under a curse. Since he did not want to have children by his new wife, he had sex with her in an unnatural way. At first the woman kept this to herself, but later she told her mother, whether because her mother asked or not I cannot say, and the mother told her husband Megacles. Megacles was furious that Pisistratus had dishonored him, and in his anger he immediately went and made up his quarrel with the men of the other faction. When Pisistratus learned what was being done against him, he left the country altogether and went to Eretria, where he talked things over with his sons. Hippias' advice won out: they should try to win back the tyranny. So they began to collect gifts of money from the cities that owed them favors. Many gave large sums, but the Thebans gave more money than all the rest. Then, to make a long story short, time passed, and at last everything was ready for their return. Some Argives came from the Peloponnese as hired soldiers, and a man of Naxos named Lygdamis had come to them of his own accord and showed great zeal in supplying both money and men.

62. So they set out from Eretria and came back after ten years. The first place they seized in Attica was Marathon. While they were camped there, their supporters from the city came to join them, and others streamed in from the villages, people who preferred tyranny to freedom. So these were gathering. As for the Athenians in the city, they had thought nothing of it as long as Pisistratus was collecting money, and nothing of it even after he took Marathon. But when they heard that he was marching from Marathon toward the city, they went out to stop him. So they were marching out in full force to fight the returning exiles. Meanwhile Pisistratus' forces had set out from Marathon toward the city, and the two armies met at the temple of Athena Pallenis, where they camped facing each other. Then, guided by the gods, Amphilytus the Acarnanian, a seer, came to Pisistratus. He came up to him and spoke an oracle in hexameter verse:

	The cast is made, and the net is spread out wide;
	the tunnies will dart through it in the moonlit night.

63. He spoke this oracle under divine inspiration. Pisistratus understood it, said he accepted the prophecy, and led his army against the enemy. The Athenians from the city were busy with their morning meal just then, and after eating some of them had turned to dice and others to sleep. Pisistratus' forces fell on them and routed them. As they fled, Pisistratus came up with a very clever plan to keep the Athenians from gathering together again and to keep them scattered. He put his sons on horseback and sent them on ahead. They caught up with the men who were running away and said what Pisistratus had told them to say: that they should not be afraid, and that each man should go home.

64. The Athenians did just that. So Pisistratus took Athens for the third time, and this time he rooted his tyranny firmly. He did it with many hired foreign soldiers and with a large income of money, which came partly from Attica itself and partly from the region around the river Strymon. He also took as hostages the sons of the Athenians who had stayed and had not fled at once, and put them on Naxos; for Pisistratus had conquered Naxos too in war and handed it over to Lygdamis. Besides this, he purified the island of Delos as the oracles commanded. This is how he purified it: as far as one could see from the temple, he dug up all the dead who were buried in that area and moved them to another part of Delos. So Pisistratus was tyrant of Athens. Of the Athenians, some had fallen in the battle, and others had gone into exile from their native land with the sons of Alcmaeon.

Chapter 3: Sparta, the War of Croesus with Cyrus, and the Fall of Sardis

65. That was the state of things Croesus heard was going on among the Athenians at this time. About the Spartans, he heard that they had come through great troubles and had now got the upper hand over the Tegeans in their war. For back when Leon and Hegesicles were kings of Sparta, the Spartans had done well in all their other wars, but had met with disaster in just one: the war they fought against the men of Tegea, a city in Arcadia, their neighbor to the north. What is more, in the times before this, the Spartans had had the worst laws of almost any people in Greece, both in their dealings among themselves and in that they would have nothing to do with strangers. And this is how they changed over to good government. Lycurgus, a Spartan who was highly respected, came to the oracle at Delphi, and as soon as he entered the inner hall of the temple, the Pythia said this:

	"You have come, Lycurgus, to my rich temple,
	dear to Zeus and to all who live in the halls of Olympus.
	Shall I call you a god or a man? My prophet's voice is in doubt,
	god or man; but rather a god, I think, Lycurgus."

66. Some people say that, on top of this, the Pythia also laid out for him the whole system of government the Spartans have now. But the Spartans themselves say that Lycurgus brought it from Crete, when he became guardian of his nephew Leobotes, who was king of the Spartans. As soon as he became guardian, he changed all the laws then in force, and he made sure that nobody broke the new ones he set up. After this Lycurgus organized their military life: the sworn bands called enomoties, the companies of thirty, and the common meals where the men ate together. Besides this he set up the ephors, the five officials elected each year, and the Council of Elders. With these changes the Spartans came to have good laws. When Lycurgus died they built a temple to him, and they still honor him greatly. So, as you would expect in a fertile land with a good number of men living in it, they shot up at once and grew prosperous. Then sitting still was no longer enough for them. They thought they were stronger than the Arcadians, so they asked the oracle at Delphi about conquering the whole of Arcadia. The Pythia answered them like this:

	"You ask me for Arcadia. You ask a great deal; I will not give it.
	There are many men in Arcadia, tough men who live on acorns,
	and they will stop you. But I do not grudge you everything:
	I will give you Tegea, to dance on with stamping feet,
	and her fair plain, to measure out with a line and divide."

When the Spartans heard this report, they left the rest of the Arcadians alone and marched against the Tegeans, carrying chains with them. They trusted a deceptive oracle and expected to make slaves of the men of Tegea. But they were beaten in the fight, and the ones who were taken alive were put to work wearing the very chains they had brought with them, "measuring out with a line" the plain of the Tegeans after all. Those chains they had been bound with were still kept at Tegea in my own time, hanging around the temple of Athena Alea.

67. So in that earlier war, I say, they kept fighting the Tegeans and kept losing. But in Croesus' time, when Anaxandrides and Ariston were kings at Sparta, the Spartans had at last come out on top in the war, and this is how it happened. Since they were always being beaten by the men of Tegea, they sent messengers to consult the oracle at Delphi and asked which god they should win over in order to defeat the Tegeans. The Pythia answered that they must bring home to their own land the bones of Orestes son of Agamemnon. But they could not find Orestes' grave, so they sent again to ask the god where Orestes lay buried. When the messengers asked this, the priestess said:

	"There is a Tegea in the land of Arcadia, built on level ground,
	where two winds blow, driven by hard force together,
	and there is blow and answering blow, and trouble laid on trouble.
	There the son of Agamemnon lies in the life-giving earth.
	Bring him home with you, and you will be master of Tegea."

When the Spartans heard this, they were still just as far from finding the grave, though they searched everywhere, until Lichas, one of the Spartans called "Well-doers," discovered it. The "Well-doers" are the oldest citizens leaving the ranks of the "Horsemen," the king's guard of young men, five of them each year. During the year in which they leave the "Horsemen," they are bound to let the Spartan state send them, without a break, wherever it needs them.

68. Lichas was one of these men, and he found the grave in Tegea by a mix of luck and cleverness. At that time there was a truce and the two sides had dealings with each other, and he had come into a smithy in Tegea and was watching iron being worked. He was amazed at what he saw being done. The smith noticed how amazed he was, stopped working, and said: "Well, my Spartan friend, if you had seen what I once saw, you would really have something to marvel at, since you marvel so much now at ironwork. I wanted to dig a well in this yard, and as I was digging I came upon a coffin ten and a half feet long. I didn't believe there had ever been men bigger than the men of today, so I opened it, and I saw that the body was as long as the coffin. I measured it, and then I filled the earth back in over it." So the smith told him what he had seen. Lichas thought over what he had been told and guessed that this was Orestes, as the oracle had said. He reasoned it out like this. The smith had two bellows, and Lichas concluded that these were the two winds; the anvil and the hammer were the blow and the answering blow; and the iron being worked was the trouble laid on trouble, since, he thought, iron was discovered to be an evil for mankind. Having worked this out, he went back to Sparta and told the Spartans the whole thing. They then brought a trumped-up charge against him and drove him into exile. So he came to Tegea, told the smith about his bad luck, and tried to rent the yard from him. At first the smith would not let him have it, but in the end Lichas talked him into it, and he moved in. Then he dug up the grave, gathered up the bones, and took them away to Sparta. From that time on, whenever the two sides tested each other in battle, the Spartans had much the better of the war. And by now they had also conquered most of the rest of the Peloponnese.

69. So Croesus learned all this, and he sent messengers to Sparta with gifts, to ask for an alliance, after telling them exactly what to say. When they arrived, they said: "Croesus, king of the Lydians and of other nations, has sent us here, and this is his message: 'Spartans, the god told me in an oracle to make the Greek my friend. Now I am told that you are the leaders of Greece. So, as the oracle says, I invite you to be my friends and allies, with no trickery and no deceit.'" That was Croesus' message to the Spartans through his messengers. The Spartans had heard about the oracle given to Croesus themselves, and they were glad the Lydians had come, and they swore oaths of friendship and alliance. They were also bound to Croesus by some favors he had done them before this. The Spartans had sent to Sardis to buy gold, which they meant to use for the statue of Apollo that now stands on Mount Thornax in Laconia, and when they asked to buy it, Croesus gave it to them as a gift.

70. That was one reason the Spartans accepted the alliance; the other was that he had chosen them as his friends over all the other Greeks. Not only were they ready to answer his call themselves, they also had a bronze mixing bowl made, covered with figures around the outside of the rim and big enough to hold three hundred amphoras, about 3,000 gallons. They sent it off, wanting to give it to Croesus as a gift in return. This bowl never reached Sardis, and two stories are told about why. The Spartans say that when the bowl was on its way to Sardis and came off the island of Samos, the Samians heard about it, sailed out in warships, and seized it. But the Samians themselves say that the Spartans who were carrying the bowl found they were too late: they heard that Sardis had fallen and Croesus was a prisoner, so they sold the bowl on Samos. Some private citizens bought it, they say, and dedicated it in the temple of Hera. And it is likely that the men who sold it said, when they got back to Sparta, that the Samians had robbed them of it.

71. So that is what happened with the mixing bowl. Meanwhile Croesus, who had mistaken the meaning of the oracle, was preparing to invade Cappadocia, expecting to overthrow Cyrus and the power of the Persians. While he was getting ready to march against the Persians, one of the Lydians gave him some advice. This man had been thought wise even before, but because of what he said now he won a very great name for wisdom among the Lydians. His name was Sandanis, and this is what he said: "My king, you are getting ready to march against men who wear trousers of leather, and the rest of their clothes are leather too. They eat not what they want but what they can get, because the land they live in is rough. What is more, they don't drink wine; they drink water. They have no figs for dessert, or anything else that is good. Now, if you beat them, what will you take from them, since they have nothing? But if you are beaten, think how many good things you will lose. Once they have had a taste of our good things, they will hold on to them tight, and there will be no driving them away. For my part, I thank the gods that they don't put it into the Persians' heads to march against the Lydians." That was his speech, but he did not persuade Croesus. And it is true that before the Persians conquered the Lydians they had no luxuries and nothing good at all.

72. The Greeks call the Cappadocians Syrians. Before the Persians came to power, these Syrians were subjects of the Medes, but at this time they were subjects of Cyrus. For the border between the Median empire and the Lydian was the river Halys. The Halys flows down from the mountains of Armenia through the land of the Cilicians. As it flows on, it has the Matienians on its right and the Phrygians on the other side. Then, passing by these and turning north, it marks the border with the Cappadocian Syrians on one side and the Paphlagonians on the left. In this way the river Halys cuts off from the rest of Asia almost all of its lower part, by a line running from the sea opposite Cyprus to the Black Sea. This stretch of land is the neck of the whole peninsula, and the distance across it is a five days' journey for a man traveling light.

73. Croesus was marching into Cappadocia for these reasons. First, he wanted to add the land to what he already had. But above all he trusted the oracle, and he wanted to punish Cyrus on behalf of Astyages. For Cyrus son of Cambyses had conquered Astyages and was holding him prisoner, and Astyages, the king of the Medes, was Croesus' brother-in-law. This is how he had become Croesus' brother-in-law. A horde of nomad Scythians, who had quarreled with the rest of their people, left and took refuge in the land of the Medes. At that time the ruler of the Medes was Cyaxares son of Phraortes son of Deioces. At first he treated these Scythians well, since they had come to him asking for protection. He thought very highly of them, and he handed some boys over to them to learn their language and the art of archery. As time went on, the Scythians would go out hunting all the time and always bring something back. Then once it happened that they caught nothing. When they came back empty-handed, Cyaxares (who was not, as he showed on this occasion, a man of the best temper) treated them very harshly and insulted them. After this treatment from Cyaxares, the Scythians felt they had been shamed. So they made a plan: they would kill one of the boys they were teaching and cut him up, prepare his flesh the way they used to prepare wild game, and bring it to Cyaxares as if it were game from the hunt. Once they had given it to him, they meant to get away as fast as they could to Alyattes son of Sadyattes at Sardis. And that is what was done. Cyaxares and the guests who ate at his table tasted that meat, and the Scythians, having done this, went to Alyattes and asked for his protection.

74. After this, since Alyattes would not hand the Scythians over when Cyaxares demanded them, war broke out between the Lydians and the Medes and went on for five years. In those years the Medes often beat the Lydians and the Lydians often beat the Medes, and among other battles they even fought one at night. They were still at war, and evenly matched, when in the sixth year a battle took place in which, after the fighting had begun, the day suddenly turned into night. Thales of Miletus had predicted this change in the day to the Ionians, naming as its limit the very year in which it actually happened. When the Lydians and the Medes saw night come on in place of day, they stopped fighting, and both sides became much more eager to make peace. The men who brought about the peace between them were Syennesis the Cilician and Labynetus the Babylonian. They were the ones who pressed them to swear an oath, and they arranged an exchange of marriages: they decided that Alyattes should give his daughter Aryenis to Astyages son of Cyaxares, since without some strong bond to hold them, agreements tend not to hold firm. These nations swear oaths with the same ceremonies as the Greeks, but in addition they cut the skin of their arms and lick up each other's blood.

75. This was the Astyages, then, the father of Cyrus' mother, whom Cyrus had conquered and taken prisoner, for a reason I will explain later in my history. This was the grievance Croesus had against Cyrus when he sent to the oracles to ask whether he should march against the Persians. And when a deceptive answer came back, he marched into the Persians' territory, thinking the answer was in his favor. When Croesus reached the river Halys, he took his army across, in my own account, by the bridges that were there. But according to the story most Greeks tell, Thales of Miletus got the army across for him. When Croesus was at a loss how to get his army over the river (for, they add, the bridges that are there now did not yet exist at that time), Thales, who was there with the army, made the river, which was flowing on the army's left, flow on its right as well. He did it like this, they say. Starting upstream of the camp, he dug a deep channel and curved it around like a crescent moon, so that the river would be turned out of its old bed into the channel, flow around behind the camp where it was pitched, and, once past the camp, fall back into its old bed. So as soon as the river was split in two, both branches could be waded. Some even say that the old bed of the river dried up completely. But I don't accept this story as true, because how did they cross the river on the way back?

76. When Croesus had crossed over with his army, he came to the place in Cappadocia called Pteria. Pteria is the strongest place in this region, and it lies roughly in line with the city of Sinope on the Black Sea. There he made camp and laid waste the farms of the Syrians. He also took the Pterians' city and sold its people as slaves, and he took all the towns around it too, and he drove the Syrians from their homes, though they had done him no wrong. Meanwhile Cyrus had gathered his own army, picked up in addition everyone who lived in the lands along the way, and was coming to meet Croesus. But before he set out with his army, he had sent heralds to the Ionians and tried to persuade them to revolt from Croesus; the Ionians would not do it. Then, when Cyrus had arrived and camped facing Croesus, the two sides tested their strength against each other in the land of Pteria. The fighting was hard, and many fell on both sides. In the end night came on, and they parted with neither side the winner.

77. That is how the two armies fought it out. Croesus blamed his own army for its size, since the army he fought with was far smaller than Cyrus'. Being unhappy with it for this reason, when Cyrus made no attempt to attack him the next day, he marched back to Sardis. He meant to call on the Egyptians to help him, according to the oath they had sworn, since he had made an alliance with Amasis, king of Egypt, even before his alliance with the Spartans. He meant to summon the Babylonians as well, since he had made an alliance with them too, and Labynetus was ruler of the Babylonians at that time. And he meant to send word to the Spartans to come at a set time. Once he had gathered all these together along with his own army, his plan was to let the winter pass and then march against the Persians at the start of spring. With this in mind, as soon as he reached Sardis he began sending heralds to each of his allies, telling them to gather at Sardis in the fifth month from then. But the army he had with him, the one that had fought the Persians, which was made up of hired soldiers, he dismissed and sent away completely. He never expected that Cyrus, after fighting such an even battle with him, would march on Sardis after all.

78. While Croesus was making these plans, the outskirts of the city suddenly filled up with snakes. When the snakes appeared, the horses left off grazing in their pastures and kept going there and eating them. When Croesus saw this, he believed it was an omen, as indeed it was.
