So he sent messengers at once to the Telmessians, who interpret omens. The messengers he sent to consult them got there and learned from the Telmessians what the omen meant, but they never managed to report the answer to Croesus. For before they sailed back to Sardis, Croesus had been taken prisoner. The Telmessians' verdict was this: Croesus should expect an army speaking a foreign language to invade his land, and when it came it would conquer the people who lived there. For the snake, they said, is born of the land, while the horse is an enemy and a stranger. That was the answer the men of Telmessus gave Croesus when he was already a prisoner, though they did not yet know anything of what had happened to Sardis or to Croesus himself.

79. But Cyrus, as soon as Croesus marched away after the battle in Pteria, learned that Croesus meant to disband his army once he had marched off. He thought it over and decided that the best thing for him was to march to Sardis as fast as he could, before the Lydians' strength could be gathered together again. Once he had decided this, he did it without delay. He led his army into Lydia so fast that he himself was the first to bring Croesus the news that he was coming. Croesus was now in a desperate position, since things had turned out the exact opposite of what he expected. Even so, he led the Lydians out to battle. At that time there was no nation in Asia braver or tougher in battle than the Lydians. They fought on horseback, carrying long spears, and they were excellent horsemen.

80. The armies met on the plain in front of the city of Sardis. It is a wide, open plain, with rivers running through it, especially the Hyllus, which all rush down to join the largest of them, the Hermus. The Hermus flows from the mountain sacred to the Mother goddess, called Dindymene, and runs out into the sea near the city of Phocaea. When Cyrus saw the Lydians lining up for battle, he was afraid of their cavalry, and on the advice of Harpagus, a Mede, he did this. He gathered together all the camels that were traveling with his army carrying food and baggage. He took off their loads and put men on them, equipped as cavalry. When he had fitted them out, he ordered them to go in front of the rest of the army, toward Croesus' horsemen. He ordered the infantry to follow behind the camels, and behind the infantry he placed all his cavalry. When all his men were in their places, he gave them orders to spare none of the Lydians, but to kill everyone who got in their way; only Croesus himself they were not to kill, not even if he fought back when they caught him. Those were his orders. He set the camels facing the horsemen for this reason: horses are afraid of camels and cannot stand either the sight of them or their smell. That was why the trick had been thought up, so that Croesus' cavalry would be useless, the very force with which the Lydian king expected to win the most glory. And when they came together for battle, as soon as the horses smelled the camels and saw them, they wheeled around and bolted, and all Croesus' hopes came to nothing at once. Even so, the Lydians did not turn cowards. When they saw what was happening, they jumped down from their horses and fought the Persians on foot. In the end, after many had fallen on both sides, the Lydians turned and fled. They were driven back inside the walls of their citadel and besieged there by the Persians.

81. So the Persians laid siege to them. But Croesus, thinking the siege would last a long time, sent more messengers from the citadel to his allies. The first messengers had gone around to tell them to gather at Sardis in the fifth month. But these he was sending to ask them to come to his help as fast as they could, because Croesus was under siege.

82. He sent to his other allies, and he sent to Sparta as well. But the Spartans too, as it happened, had a quarrel of their own on their hands at that very moment, with the Argives, over the district called Thyrea. This Thyrea was part of the Argives' territory, but the Spartans had cut it off and taken it for themselves. At that time the whole region to the west, as far down as Cape Malea, belonged to the Argives, both the land on the mainland and the island of Cythera and the other islands. When the Argives came out to save their territory from being cut away from them, the two sides met to talk and agreed that three hundred men from each side would fight, and whichever side won that fight would have the disputed land. They also agreed that the main body of each army would go back to its own country and not stay to watch the contest. They were afraid that if the armies were there, one side, seeing its own men losing, would come up to help them. When they had made this agreement, the armies withdrew, and the chosen men from both sides were left behind and fought each other. They fought and turned out to be evenly matched. In the end, out of six hundred men, only three were left: Alcenor and Chromius on the Argive side, and Othryades on the Spartan side. These three were still alive when night came on. The two Argives, thinking they had won, ran off to Argos. But the Spartan Othryades stripped the armor from the Argive dead, carried it to his own camp, and stayed at his post. The next day both sides came back to find out the result. For a while each claimed the victory. One side said more of their men had survived. The other side said those men had run away, while their own man had stood his ground and stripped the bodies of the other side's dead. In the end the argument led them to fall on each other and start fighting, and after many had fallen on both sides, the Spartans won. After this the Argives cut their hair short, though before this they had been required by law to wear it long. They made a law, with a curse on anyone who broke it, that from then on no Argive man would grow his hair long, and no Argive woman would wear gold jewelry, until they had won back Thyrea. The Spartans made the opposite law for themselves: from that time on they would wear their hair long, though before that they had not. And they say that Othryades, the one man left alive out of the three hundred, was ashamed to go back to Sparta when all his comrades had been killed, and killed himself there at Thyrea.

83. That was the state of things at Sparta when the herald from Sardis arrived to ask them to help Croesus, who was under siege. Even so, in spite of their own troubles, as soon as they heard the herald's news they were eager to go to his help. But when they had finished their preparations and their ships were ready, another message came, reporting that the Lydians' citadel had fallen and Croesus had been taken prisoner. Then, and only then, they gave up the effort, grieving over what had happened as a great disaster.

84. This is how Sardis was taken. On the fourteenth day after Croesus came under siege, Cyrus sent horsemen around to every part of his army to announce that he would give rewards to the first man to climb the wall. After this the army made an attempt, and it failed. When all the rest had given up the attack, a Mardian named Hyroeades tried to climb up on one side of the citadel where no guard had been posted. Nobody was afraid the citadel would ever be taken from that side, because there it is a sheer cliff and cannot be attacked. This was also the only part of the wall around which Meles, who had been king of Sardis in earlier times, had not carried the lion that his concubine bore him. The Telmessians had ruled that if the lion were carried around the wall, Sardis would never be captured. So Meles carried it around the rest of the wall, the parts of the citadel where the fortress could be attacked, but he skipped this part, since it was a sheer cliff and could not be attacked. This is the part of the city that faces toward Mount Tmolus. Now the day before, this Mardian Hyroeades had seen one of the Lydians climb down on that side of the citadel to fetch his helmet, which had rolled down from above, and pick it up. He noticed this and turned it over in his mind. So he climbed up himself, first of all, and other Persians came up after him. Then many more made their way up, and so Sardis was finally taken, and the whole city was plundered.

85. Meanwhile this is what happened to Croesus himself. He had a son, whom I mentioned earlier, who was a decent enough young man in other ways but could not speak. In his earlier days of good fortune, Croesus had done everything he could for him. Among the other things he tried, he had also sent messengers to Delphi to ask about him. And the Pythia told him this:

	"Lydian, lord of many, Croesus, so blind to what is fated,
	do not wish to hear in your halls that longed-for voice,
	the voice of your son. It would be far better for you to be without it,
	for the first day he speaks will be a day of disaster."

Now as the citadel was being taken, one of the Persians, not knowing who Croesus was, was about to kill him. Croesus saw him coming, but he did not care, because of the disaster that had fallen on him; it made no difference to him whether he was struck down and killed. But when this son who could not speak saw the Persian coming at him, fear and grief broke open his voice, and he said: "Man, do not kill Croesus!" That was the first time the son ever spoke, and from then on he could speak for the rest of his life.

Chapter 4: Croesus on the Pyre, the Customs of Lydia, and the Rise of the Medes

86. So the Persians took Sardis and captured Croesus himself. He had reigned fourteen years and had been under siege fourteen days, and he had fulfilled the oracle: he had brought his own great empire to an end. The Persians who had taken him brought him before Cyrus. Cyrus had a great pyre built and made Croesus climb up onto it, bound in chains, and with him twice seven sons of Lydians. Perhaps he meant to offer them to some god as the first fruits of his victory, or perhaps he wanted to fulfill a vow. Or perhaps he had heard that Croesus was a man who feared the gods, and made him climb onto the pyre because he wanted to find out whether any of the divine powers would save him from being burned alive. That, they say, is what Cyrus did. But as Croesus stood on the pyre, in all his misery, he remembered the saying of Solon: how Solon had said, as if inspired by heaven, that no one who is still alive may be called happy. When this thought came to him, they say, he sighed deeply and groaned aloud after a long silence, and three times he spoke the name "Solon." Cyrus heard this and told the interpreters to ask Croesus who this person was that he was calling on, and they came near and asked him. For a while, it is said, Croesus kept silent when they asked. But at last, when they pressed him, he said: "A man I would have given a great fortune to have every ruler talk with." Since this answer was unclear, they asked again what he meant. They kept pressing and gave him no peace, so he told them how Solon, an Athenian, had once come to him, looked over all his wealth, and made light of it, saying such and such. He told them how everything had turned out for him just as Solon had said, though Solon had not been speaking about Croesus in particular so much as about the whole human race, and especially about those who think themselves happy. While Croesus was telling them this, the pyre had already been lit, and its outer edges were burning. Then, they say, Cyrus heard from the interpreters what Croesus had said and changed his mind. He reflected that he too was only a man, and that he was handing another man over to the fire alive, a man who had once been no less fortunate than himself. Besides, he feared retribution, and he reflected that nothing human beings possess is secure. So, they say, he ordered his men to put out the fire as quickly as they could, and to bring Croesus and the others down from the pyre. But for all their efforts, they could no longer get the flames under control.

87. Then, as the Lydians tell it, when Croesus learned that Cyrus had changed his mind, and saw that everyone was trying to put out the fire but could no longer hold it back, he cried out to Apollo. If any gift of his had ever pleased the god, he begged, let the god come now and rescue him from the evil that was upon him. So he called on the god in tears, and suddenly, they say, out of a clear, calm sky clouds gathered and a storm broke. Rain came down in a violent torrent, and the pyre was put out. Then Cyrus, seeing that Croesus was a good man and dear to the gods, had him brought down from the pyre and asked him: "Croesus, who on earth persuaded you to march against my land and become my enemy instead of my friend?" Croesus said: "My king, I did it, to your good fortune and to my own misfortune. And the one to blame for it was the god of the Greeks, who urged me to march with my army. No one is so foolish as to choose war over peace: in peace sons bury their fathers, but in war fathers bury their sons. But I suppose it pleased the gods that things should turn out this way."

88. That is what he said. Cyrus had his chains taken off, sat him down beside himself, and treated him with great respect. Cyrus himself and everyone around him looked at Croesus with wonder. Croesus sat lost in thought and said nothing. But after a while he turned and saw the Persians plundering the Lydians' city, and he said: "My king, should I tell you what is on my mind, or should I keep quiet, in my present condition?" Cyrus told him to speak freely and say whatever he liked. So Croesus asked him: "What is this great crowd of men doing so eagerly?" Cyrus said: "They are plundering your city and carrying off your wealth." Croesus answered: "It is not my city they are plundering, and not my wealth they are carrying off. None of these things belongs to me anymore. It is your wealth they are carrying and driving away."

89. What Croesus said troubled Cyrus. He sent everyone else away and asked Croesus what he saw in all this that Cyrus ought to act on. Croesus said: "Since the gods have given me to you as your slave, I think it right, if I see anything that others do not, to point it out to you. The Persians are proud and unruly by nature, and they are poor. So if you let them carry off great wealth as plunder and keep it, here is what you can expect: whoever gets hold of the biggest share will rise up in rebellion against you. So, if what I say pleases you, do this. Post spearmen of your guard at every gate. Have them take the goods away from the men carrying them out of the city, and tell them that a tenth of it has to be set aside for Zeus first. That way they will not hate you for taking the things from them by force, and they will let them go willingly, admitting to themselves that you are doing what is just."

90. Cyrus was delighted beyond measure when he heard this, because he thought Croesus' advice was good. He praised him warmly and ordered the spearmen of his guard to do what Croesus had advised. Then he said to Croesus: "Croesus, since you are ready, like the king you are, to do good deeds and speak good words, ask me for a gift, anything you want, and you shall have it at once." Croesus said: "Master, you will please me most if you let me send these chains to the god of the Greeks, whom I honored more than any other god, and ask him whether it is his custom to deceive those who treat him well." Cyrus asked him what charge he had against the god, to make such a request. So Croesus went back over the whole story for him: what he had intended, the answers of the oracles, and above all his offerings, and how the prophecy had urged him to march against the Persians. And as he told it, he came back again to his request that he be allowed to put this reproach to the god. Cyrus laughed and said: "You shall have this from me, Croesus, and anything else you ever ask me for." When he heard this, Croesus sent some Lydians to Delphi. He told them to lay the chains on the threshold of the temple and ask the god whether he was not ashamed of having urged Croesus with his prophecies to march against the Persians, persuading him that he would put an end to Cyrus' empire. And they were to show the chains and say that these were the first fruits of the spoils Croesus had won from it. This was what they were to ask, and also whether it was the custom of the gods of the Greeks to be ungrateful.

91. When the Lydians arrived and said what they had been told to say, the Pythia, it is said, answered them like this: "Not even a god can escape what is fated. Croesus has paid for the crime of his ancestor five generations back. That man was one of the spearmen of the Heraclids; he followed a woman's treacherous plan, killed his master, and took his royal office, which was not his by right. Loxias (that is, Apollo) was eager for the disaster of Sardis to fall on Croesus' sons rather than on Croesus himself, but he could not turn the Fates aside from their course. Whatever they allowed, he accomplished, and gave to Croesus as a gift. He put off the taking of Sardis for three years, and Croesus should know that he was captured three years later than the time fated for him. Second, he came to his rescue when he was about to be burned. As for the oracle, Croesus has no good grounds for complaint. Loxias told him beforehand that if he marched against the Persians he would destroy a great empire. When he heard that, if he had wanted to plan wisely, he should have sent and asked whether the god meant his own empire or Cyrus'. But since he did not understand what was said, and did not ask again, let him admit that he himself is to blame for what followed. And when he consulted the oracle for the last time, Loxias told him what he told him about a mule, and he did not understand that either. Cyrus was that mule. He was born of parents of two different peoples, his mother of nobler birth than his father. She was a Mede, the daughter of Astyages king of the Medes; but he was a Persian, one of a people subject to the Medes, and though he was beneath her in every way, he was the husband of his own royal mistress." That was the Pythia's answer to the Lydians. They brought it back to Sardis and repeated it to Croesus, and when he heard it he admitted that the fault was his own and not the god's. So that is how it went with the empire of Croesus and the first conquest of Ionia.

92. There are many other offerings of Croesus in Greece besides the ones I have mentioned. First, at Thebes in Boeotia there is a golden tripod, which he dedicated to Ismenian Apollo. Then at Ephesus there are the golden cows and most of the columns of the temple. And in the temple of Athena Pronaea, Athena of the Forecourt, at Delphi there is a large golden shield. These were still there in my own time, but others of his offerings have been lost. And his offerings at Branchidae, the shrine of the Milesians, were, as I am told, equal in weight and similar to those at Delphi. Now the offerings he sent to Delphi and to the shrine of Amphiaraus he dedicated from his own property, as the first fruits of the wealth he inherited from his father. But the other offerings came from the fortune of a man who was his enemy. Before Croesus became king, this man had stirred up a faction against him and had joined in trying to make Pantaleon ruler of the Lydians. Pantaleon was a son of Alyattes and Croesus' brother, but not by the same mother: Croesus was born to Alyattes by a Carian woman, and Pantaleon by an Ionian. When Croesus had taken possession of the kingdom, which his father gave him, he put to death the man who had opposed him by dragging him over a carding comb, a board set with iron spikes for combing wool. And the man's property, which he had vowed even before then to dedicate, he offered in the way I have described to the shrines I have named. So much for his offerings.

93. As for wonders worth writing about, Lydia has few compared with other lands, apart from the gold dust that washes down from Mount Tmolus. But it has one work to show that is far larger than any other, except only those in Egypt and Babylon. This is the tomb of Alyattes, Croesus' father. Its base is made of great stones, and the rest of it is a mound of heaped-up earth. It was built with contributions from the tradesmen, the craftsmen, and the girls who worked there as prostitutes. Down to my own time there were still five boundary stones standing on top of the tomb, with inscriptions carved on them recording how much of the work each group had done. When it was measured, the girls' share turned out to be the largest. For in Lydia the daughters of the common people all work as prostitutes, to earn their own dowries, and they keep at it until they marry; and the girls choose their own husbands. The circuit of the tomb is about 3,800 feet, nearly three-quarters of a mile, and its width is 1,300 feet. Next to the tomb is a large lake, which the Lydians say never runs dry, and it is called the Lake of Gyges. That is what this tomb is like.

94. The Lydians have very nearly the same customs as the Greeks, except that they make their daughters prostitutes. They were the first people we know of to strike and use coins of gold and silver, and they were also the first shopkeepers. The Lydians themselves say that the games now played among them and among the Greeks were their invention too. They say these were invented at the same time as they sent out colonists to Tyrrhenia, the land of the Etruscans in Italy, and this is the story they tell about them. In the reign of their king Atys son of Manes there was a severe famine all over Lydia. For a while the Lydians went on putting up with it. But when it did not stop, they looked for remedies, and different people came up with different ideas. That was when, they say, they discovered how to play dice and knucklebones and ball, and all the other games except draughts (the Lydians do not claim to have discovered that one). They invented these games as a way of dealing with the famine, and this is how they used them. On one day they would play games the whole time, so as not to feel the lack of food, and on the next they stopped playing and ate. They went on like this for eighteen years. But the hardship did not let up; it grew worse and worse. So their king divided the whole Lydian people into two halves and drew lots to decide which half would stay and which would leave the country. He put himself in charge of the half that drew the lot to stay, and his son in charge of the half that was leaving. His son's name was Tyrrhenus. So the half that drew the lot to leave went down to the sea at Smyrna. There they built ships, loaded into them all the goods they could carry, and sailed away to look for a living and a land to live in. They passed many peoples, until at last they came to the land of the Ombricans, in Italy. There they founded cities, and they live there to this day. They changed their name and stopped calling themselves Lydians; they took their name from the king's son who had led them out, and called themselves Tyrrhenians after him.

So the Lydians had been made subject to the Persians, as I have said.

95. After this, my history goes on to ask who this Cyrus was who destroyed the empire of Croesus, and how the Persians came to be the leaders of Asia. I shall follow the account of certain Persians, those who do not want to glorify the story of Cyrus but to tell what actually happened; it is their account I shall write. But I could also give the story in three other versions. The Assyrians ruled Upper Asia for five hundred and twenty years, and the first to revolt from them were the Medes. They fought the Assyrians for their freedom and proved themselves brave men; so they threw off the yoke of slavery and were set free. After them the other nations did the same as the Medes. But when all the peoples on the mainland were independent in this way, they came back under the rule of tyrants, and this is how it happened.

96. There was a clever man among the Medes named Deioces, the son of Phraortes. Deioces set his heart on becoming sole ruler, and this is what he did. The Medes lived in scattered villages. Deioces was already well thought of in his own village, and now he set himself to deal justly, much more than before and with greater zeal. He did this even though there was great lawlessness all over Media, and even though he knew that injustice is always at war with justice. The Medes of his village saw how he behaved and chose him as their judge. And since he was aiming at power, he was honest and fair, and by acting this way he won no small praise from his fellow villagers. So much so that people in the other villages heard that Deioces was the one man who judged cases rightly. Before this they had always suffered from unjust verdicts, so when they heard about him, they too gladly came to Deioces to have their disputes settled. In the end they would trust their cases to no one else.

97. More and more people kept coming to him, because they learned that his verdicts matched the truth. When Deioces saw that everything was being brought to him, he refused to sit any longer in the public place where he used to sit and hear cases, and said that he would judge no more. It did him no good, he said, to neglect his own affairs and spend all day judging his neighbors' disputes. So robbery and lawlessness spread through the villages, much worse than before, and the Medes gathered in one place and talked over among themselves the state they were in. And I suppose it was Deioces' friends who did most of the talking, saying something like this: "We can't go on living in this country the way things are. So let us set up a king from among ourselves. Then the country will be well governed, and we ourselves can get on with our work and not be ruined by lawlessness." With words like these they persuaded themselves to have a king.

98. When they then put the question of whom they should make king, Deioces was put forward and praised by everyone, until at last they agreed that he should be their king. He told them to build him a palace worthy of a king and to give him a bodyguard of spearmen for his protection. The Medes did so. They built him a large, strong palace in the part of the country he named, and they let him pick spearmen from among all the Medes. Once he had power over them, he made the Medes build a single fortified city and devote their attention to it, caring less about the other towns. The Medes obeyed him in this too, and he built large, strong walls, the ones now called Ecbatana, set in rings one inside another. The walls are designed so that each ring rises above the one outside it by the height of its battlements and no more. The lay of the land, I suppose, helps this to some extent, since the city stands on a hill; but it was done much more by design, since there are seven rings in all. Inside the innermost ring are the royal palace and the treasuries. The largest of these walls is about as long as the wall around Athens. The battlements of the first ring are white, of the second black, of the third crimson, of the fourth blue, and of the fifth red. So the battlements of all the rings are painted in different colors, and of the last two, the battlements of one are plated with silver and of the other with gold.

99. So Deioces built these walls for himself and around his own palace, and he ordered the people to live outside the wall. When everything was built, Deioces was the first to lay down these rules of royal conduct: no one was to come into the king's presence, but everyone was to deal with him through messengers; no one was to see the king; and besides, it was improper to laugh or spit in his presence, and this last applied to everyone without exception. He surrounded himself with all this ceremony so that the men of his own age, who had grown up with him and were of no lesser family and no less courage than he, would not see him and resent him and plot against him. If they never saw him, he thought, they would believe he was a different kind of being from themselves.

100. Once he had set these things in order and made himself secure in his rule as tyrant, he was strict in upholding justice. People would write down their cases and send them in to him, and he would decide the cases sent in and send them back out. That was how he handled the judging of cases. He also arranged things so that if he heard that anyone was behaving outrageously, he would send for him and punish him as each offense deserved. And he had watchers and listeners all over the land he ruled.

101. So Deioces united the Median people alone, and ruled over them. The tribes of the Medes are these: the Busae, the Paretacenians, the Struchates, the Arizantians, the Budians, and the Magi. That is how many tribes the Medes have.

102. Deioces' son was Phraortes. When Deioces died, after a reign of fifty-three years, Phraortes took the power in his turn. Once he had it, he was not content to rule the Medes alone. He marched against the Persians, attacked them before anyone else, and made them the first to be subject to the Medes. After this, ruling two nations, both of them strong, he set about conquering Asia, going from one people to the next. At last he marched against the Assyrians, the Assyrians who lived at Nineveh. They had once ruled the whole of Asia, but at that time they had been left without support, since their allies had revolted from them, though at home they were still doing well enough. Phraortes marched against these Assyrians, and he himself was killed, after reigning twenty-two years, and most of his army was destroyed.

103. When Phraortes' life had come to its end, the power passed to Cyaxares, son of Phraortes, son of Deioces. This king, they say, was much more warlike than his forefathers. He was the first to organize the men of Asia into separate units; that is, he was the first to separate the spearmen, the archers, and the horsemen from one another, since before that they had all been mixed together without any order. It was he who fought the Lydians on the day the daylight turned to night in the middle of the battle, and who brought under his rule the whole of Asia beyond the river Halys. He gathered all his subjects and marched against Nineveh, to avenge his father and also because he wanted to conquer that city. He fought a battle with the Assyrians and defeated them. But while he was besieging Nineveh, a great army of Scythians came down on him, led by Madyas son of Protohyas, king of the Scythians. They had invaded Asia after driving the Cimmerians out of Europe, and they had come into the land of Media chasing the Cimmerians as they fled.

104. From Lake Maeotis, the Sea of Azov, to the river Phasis and the land of the Colchians is a thirty-day journey for a traveler with no baggage. From Colchis it is not far to cross over into Media. There is only one people in between, the Saspeirians, and once you are past them you are in Media. But the Scythians did not make their invasion by this route. They turned off it and took the upper road, which is much longer, keeping the Caucasus Mountains on their right. Then the Medes fought the Scythians and were beaten in the battle. They lost their power, and the Scythians took control of all Asia.

105. From there the Scythians went on to invade Egypt. When they were in the part of Syria called Palestine, Psammetichus king of Egypt came to meet them, and with gifts and pleading he turned them from their purpose, so that they went no farther. As they were on their way back, they came to the city of Ascalon in Syria. Most of the Scythians passed through without doing any harm, but a few who had stayed behind plundered the temple of Aphrodite Urania, Heavenly Aphrodite. This temple, as I find by inquiry, is the oldest of all the temples of this goddess. The temple in Cyprus was founded from it, as the people of Cyprus themselves say, and the one on Cythera was founded by Phoenicians who came from this part of Syria. The Scythians who had plundered the temple at Ascalon, and their descendants forever after, were struck by the goddess with a disease that made them women instead of men. The Scythians say that this is the reason they suffer from the disease, and that this is why visitors to Scythia can see there, to this day, the condition of the men the Scythians call Enarees.

106. So for twenty-eight years the Scythians ruled Asia, and through their violence and recklessness everything was ruined. Besides demanding from each people the tribute they had laid on it, they rode around apart from the tribute and seized by force whatever each tribe had. Then Cyaxares and the Medes invited most of them to a banquet, got them drunk, and killed them. So the Medes won back their power and ruled the same peoples as before. They also took Nineveh (how it was taken I shall explain in another history), and they made the Assyrians subject to them, all except the land of Babylon.

Chapter 5: The Birth of Cyrus and the Fall of Astyages

107. After this Cyaxares died. He had reigned forty years, counting the years when the Scythians ruled, and his son Astyages took over the kingdom from him. Astyages had a daughter, whom he named Mandane. One night he dreamed that so much water flowed from her that it filled his city and flooded the whole of Asia besides. He handed this dream over to those of the Magi who interpreted dreams, and when they told him exactly what it meant, point by point, he was afraid. So later, when Mandane was old enough to marry, he would not give her to any of the Medes who were his equals in rank, because he feared the vision. Instead he gave her to a Persian named Cambyses. He found Cambyses to be of good family and quiet temperament, and he counted him far below a Mede of middling rank.

108. In the first year of Mandane's marriage to Cambyses, Astyages saw a second vision. He dreamed that a vine grew out of his daughter's womb, and that this vine spread over the whole of Asia. After he had seen this and laid it before the dream interpreters, he sent for his daughter, who was now pregnant, to come home from the land of the Persians. When she arrived he kept her under guard, because he meant to destroy whatever child she bore: the Magi who interpreted his dreams had told him that his daughter's child would become king in his place. To guard against this, when Cyrus was born, Astyages called in Harpagus. Harpagus was a close relative of his, the Mede he trusted above all others, and the man he had put in charge of all his affairs. Astyages said to him: "Harpagus, do not neglect in any way the task I am about to give you. Do not betray me, and do not take up anyone else's interests in place of mine, or you will bring ruin on yourself afterwards. Take the child Mandane has borne, carry it to your house, and kill it. After that, bury it any way you like." Harpagus answered: "My king, never in all the time past have you seen me give you any offense, and I mean to watch myself in the time to come as well, so that I never do you wrong. If it is your pleasure that this be done, then it is my duty to carry out your service properly."

109. That was his answer. The child was handed over to him, already dressed for death, and Harpagus went home weeping and told his wife everything Astyages had said. She asked him: "So what do you mean to do now?" And he answered: "Not what Astyages ordered. Not even if he goes still further out of his mind, and grows madder than he is now, will I go along with his wishes or serve him in a murder like this. There are many reasons why I will not kill the child. First, he is my own kin. Then, Astyages is old and has no son. And if, after he is dead, the power passes on with my hand in this, won't the greatest of dangers be waiting for me then? For my own safety this child has to die, but one of Astyages' people must be the one who kills him, not one of mine."

110. So he spoke, and at once he sent a messenger to one of Astyages' herdsmen, a man he knew grazed his herds on the pastures best suited to his purpose, in mountains thick with wild beasts. The man's name was Mitradates, and his wife was a slave like himself. Her name was Cyno in Greek and Spaco in the Median language, because the Medes call a female dog spaca, which in Greek is kyna. This herdsman kept his pastures on the foothills of the mountains north of Ecbatana, toward the North Wind and the Black Sea. Here, in the direction of the Saspeirians, the land of the Medes is high, mountainous and thickly forested; the rest of Media is all flat plain. So the herdsman came in great haste, since he had been summoned urgently, and Harpagus said to him: "Astyages orders you to take this child and leave it on the most desolate part of the mountains, so that it will die as quickly as possible. And he told me to tell you this: if you do not kill it, but save it from death in any way at all, he will put you to death in the most terrible way there is. I have been appointed to see that the child is exposed."

111. When the herdsman had heard this, he picked up the child, went back the way he had come, and reached his home. Now his wife, as it happened, had been expecting her baby any day, and by some chance of heaven she gave birth just then, while the herdsman was away in the city. Each of them was worried about the other. He was afraid for his wife in childbirth, and she was afraid because Harpagus had sent for her husband, which he had never done before. So as soon as he came back and stood before her, she, seeing him again when she had hardly hoped to, spoke first and asked why Harpagus had sent for him so urgently. He said: "Wife, when I got to the city I saw and heard something I wish I had never seen, and I wish it had never happened to our masters. The whole house of Harpagus was full of weeping. I was astonished and went inside, and as soon as I went in I saw a baby lying there in the open, gasping and screaming, dressed in gold jewelry and embroidered clothes. When Harpagus saw me he told me to pick up the child at once and carry it away and leave it on the part of the mountains most full of wild beasts. He said it was Astyages who had given me this job, and he made a lot of threats against me if I failed to do it. So I picked it up and carried it off. I thought it was the child of one of the household slaves, because I could never have guessed where it really came from. But I wondered to see it dressed in gold and fine clothes, and I wondered too that they were openly weeping for it in Harpagus' house. Then right away, on the road, I learned the whole story from the servant who came with me out of the city and handed me the baby. It is really the son of Mandane, Astyages' daughter, and of Cambyses son of Cyrus, and Astyages has ordered it killed. And here it is."

112. As he said this, the herdsman uncovered the baby and showed it to her. When she saw how big and beautiful the child was, she burst into tears, clung to her husband's knees, and begged him not to expose it, whatever happened. But he said he could not do anything else. Harpagus would be sending men back and forth to check that it was done, and he himself would die a miserable death if he failed to do it. When she could not persuade her husband after all, the wife said: "Since I can't persuade you not to expose it, then do this, if a child really has to be seen lying out there. I have had a baby too, but it was born dead. Take that one and expose it, and let us raise the child of Astyages' daughter as our own. That way you will not be caught wronging our masters, and we will not have done badly for ourselves either: the dead child will get a royal burial, and the living one will not lose his life."

113. The herdsman thought that, things being as they were, his wife was right, and he did as she said at once. The child he had brought home to be put to death he handed to his wife. His own child, the dead one, he took and put in the chest he had carried the other in. He dressed it in all the other child's finery, carried it to the most desolate part of the mountains, and left it there. On the third day after the child had been exposed, the herdsman left one of his under-herdsmen to keep watch and went to the city. At Harpagus' house he said he was ready to show the child's dead body. Harpagus sent the most trusted of his bodyguards, and through them he saw the herdsman's child and had it buried. So that child was buried; and the boy who was later called Cyrus was taken in by the herdsman's wife, who brought him up, giving him some other name, no doubt, not Cyrus.

114. When the boy was ten years old, something happened that revealed who he was. He was playing in the village where the cattle sheds were, playing, as I say, in the road with other boys his age. In their game the boys chose as their king this boy who was known as the herdsman's son. He assigned some of them to build palaces and others to be his bodyguards; one of them, no doubt, he made the King's Eye, and to another he gave the job of carrying messages, handing out a task to each. Now one of the boys playing with them, the son of Artembares, a man of standing among the Medes, would not do what Cyrus told him. So Cyrus ordered the other boys to seize him, and when they obeyed, he gave the boy very rough treatment and had him whipped. As soon as the boy was let go, he was all the angrier because he felt he had been treated so far beneath his dignity. He went down to the city and complained to his father about what Cyrus had done to him. He did not call him Cyrus, of course, since that was not yet his name, but "the son of Astyages' herdsman." In the heat of his anger Artembares went straight to Astyages, taking the boy with him. He said he had been treated in a way no one should be, and told the king: "My king, this is how we have been insulted by your slave, the son of a herdsman." And he showed him his son's shoulders.

115. When Astyages had heard and seen this, he wanted to punish the boy to satisfy Artembares' honor, so he sent for the herdsman and his son. When both were there, Astyages looked at Cyrus and said: "You, the son of a man as lowly as this, dared to treat the son of this man, who is first in my favor, with such disgraceful insult?" Cyrus answered: "Master, I was right to do it to him. The boys of the village, and he was one of them, made me their king in their game, because I seemed to them the best fitted for it. Now the other boys did what I told them, but this one disobeyed and paid no attention, until at last he got the punishment he deserved. So if I deserve to suffer anything for that, here I am."

116. As the boy was speaking, Astyages began to recognize him. The features of his face seemed like his own, and his answer seemed rather too free for a herdsman's son, and the time of the exposure seemed to match the boy's age. Struck with amazement at all this, he was speechless for a while. When at last, with difficulty, he had recovered himself, he wanted to send Artembares away so that he could get the herdsman alone and question him. So he said: "Artembares, I will deal with this so that you and your son will have no cause for complaint." With that he dismissed Artembares, and at Astyages' command the servants took Cyrus inside. When the herdsman was left alone with him, Astyages, now alone with the man, asked him where he had gotten the boy and who had handed him over. The herdsman said the boy was his own son, and that his mother was still living with him as his wife. Astyages told him he was ill-advised to want to be brought to the worst extremity, and as he said this he signaled to his bodyguards to seize him. So as he was being led off to be tortured, the herdsman told the story as it really was. He began at the beginning and went through all of it, telling the truth, and at the end he begged the king to pardon him.

117. Now that the herdsman had told the truth, Astyages cared less about him. But he was extremely angry with Harpagus, and ordered his bodyguards to summon him. When Harpagus came, Astyages asked him: "Harpagus, by what death did you kill the child I handed over to you, the child born of my daughter?" Harpagus saw that the herdsman was in the palace, so he did not turn to any false story, in case he should be refuted and caught out. Instead he said: "My king, as soon as I received the child, I thought hard about how I could do what you wanted, and how, without offending against your command, I might still not be guilty of murder against your daughter and against you yourself. So this is what I did. I called this herdsman and handed the child over to him. I told him first that it was you who ordered him to kill it, and in this at least I did not lie, because you did give that order. I handed it over, as I say, to this man, and told him to leave it on a desolate mountain and to stay by it and watch until it died, and I threatened him with every kind of punishment if he failed to carry this out. When he had done what he was ordered and the child was dead, I sent the most trusted of my eunuchs, and through them I saw it and had it buried. That, my king, is how it happened, and that was the death the child died."

118. So Harpagus told the truth. Astyages hid the anger he felt against him for what had happened. First he told the whole story back to Harpagus just as he had heard it from the herdsman. Then, when he had gone through it all, he ended by saying that the child was alive and that what had happened was all for the best. "For," he went on, "I was very troubled by what had been done to this child, and I did not take it lightly that I had fallen out with my daughter. So, since our luck has changed so happily, first send your son to keep company with the boy who has just arrived, and then come and dine with me yourself. I mean to offer a sacrifice of thanks for the boy's rescue to the gods to whom that honor belongs."

119. When Harpagus heard this, he bowed low before the king. He thought it a great thing that his offense had turned out so well for him, and that he had been invited to dinner on such a lucky occasion besides, and so he went home. As soon as he got there he sent off his son, his only son, a boy of about thirteen, telling him to go to Astyages' palace and do whatever the king commanded. And he himself, overjoyed, told his wife what had happened to him. But when Harpagus' son arrived, Astyages cut his throat and cut him apart limb by limb. He had some of the flesh roasted and some boiled, had it all prepared for eating, and kept it ready. When it was time for dinner and the other guests had arrived, Harpagus among them, tables loaded with mutton were set before the other guests and before Astyages himself. But before Harpagus was set the flesh of his own son, all of it except the head, the hands and the feet. These were put aside in a covered basket. When Harpagus seemed to have eaten his fill, Astyages asked him whether he had enjoyed the meal. Harpagus said he had enjoyed it very much. Then the men who had been given their orders brought him his son's head, hands and feet under a cover, stood beside him, and told him to uncover them and take whatever he liked. Harpagus did as he was told and lifted the cover, and he saw what was left of his son. Seeing it, he did not lose his self-control but kept himself in hand. Astyages asked him whether he knew what animal's flesh he had been eating. He said he knew, and that whatever the king did was pleasing to him. With that answer he picked up what was left of the flesh and went home. After that, I suppose, he meant to gather all the remains together and bury them.

120. That was the penalty Astyages laid on Harpagus. As for Cyrus, he thought it over and summoned the same Magi who had interpreted his dream in the way I have described. When they came, Astyages asked them how they had interpreted his vision, and they gave the same answer as before: the child would have become king if he had lived and not died first. He answered them: "The child is alive, not dead. While he was living in the country, the boys of the village made him their king, and he did everything that real kings do. He ruled, he appointed bodyguards and doorkeepers and message-bearers and all the rest, each to his place. So what do you think all this points to?" The Magi said: "If the child is alive and has been king already, without anyone planning it, then take heart and rest easy about him, because he will not rule a second time. Some even of our oracles have come to very little in the end, and what comes from dreams, at any rate, often turns out to mean something trivial." Astyages answered: "I too, Magi, am strongly inclined to think so: since the boy has been called king, the dream has been fulfilled, and he is no longer any danger to me. All the same, think it over carefully and advise me what will be safest both for my house and for yourselves." To this the Magi replied: "My king, it matters a great deal to us as well that your rule should stand firm. Otherwise it passes to foreigners, coming round to this boy, who is a Persian, and we, who are Medes, will be made slaves and count for nothing in the eyes of the Persians, since we are of a different race. But as long as you are established as our king, being one of our own people, we have our share of power and receive great honors from you. So we have every reason to look after you and your rule. If we saw anything in this to be afraid of, we would tell you everything in advance. But since the dream has come out in something trivial, we ourselves are confident, and we urge you to be confident too. As for this boy, send him out of your sight, away to the Persians and to his parents."

121. When he heard this Astyages was glad. He called Cyrus and said to him: "My boy, because of a dream that has not come true I did you a wrong, but by your own destiny you are still alive. So go now, and go in peace, to the land of the Persians, and I will send men with you to escort you. When you get there you will find a father and a mother of a very different kind from Mitradates the herdsman and his wife."

122. With these words Astyages sent Cyrus away. When he reached the house of Cambyses, his parents took him in. And when they learned who he was, they welcomed him warmly, since they had been quite sure that their son had died right after he was born. They asked him how he had survived. He told them that until now he had not known, but had been completely mistaken; on the way, however, he had learned his whole story. He had been quite sure he was the son of Astyages' herdsman, but since the journey from the city began he had heard everything from the men escorting him. He told them he had been raised by the herdsman's wife, and he kept praising her the whole time, so that Cyno was the main person in everything he said. His parents took up this name from him. And so that the Persians would think their son had been saved in a more miraculous way, they spread the story that Cyrus, when he was exposed, had been nursed by a female dog. That is where that story comes from.

123. As Cyrus grew up into a man, he was the bravest and best loved of all those of his age. Harpagus set about making a friend of him and kept sending him gifts, because he wanted to take revenge on Astyages. He could not see how punishment could come to Astyages from himself, a man with no power of his own; but when he saw Cyrus growing up, he tried to make him his ally, seeing a likeness between what Cyrus had suffered and what he had suffered himself. And even before this he had made some progress. Since Astyages was harsh toward the Medes, Harpagus had gone to the leading Medes one by one and persuaded them that they must make Cyrus their leader and put an end to Astyages' reign. When he had done this and everything was ready, Harpagus wanted to reveal his plan to Cyrus, who was living among the Persians. Since the roads were watched, he had no other way to do it, so he came up with this scheme. He got a hare ready and slit open its belly without pulling out any of the fur. Into it, just as it was, he put a letter in which he had written what he had decided. Then he sewed up the hare's belly again, gave some nets to the most trusted of his servants, as if he were a hunter, and sent him off to the land of the Persians. He told him by word of mouth to give the hare to Cyrus, and to tell him at the same time to cut it open with his own hands and to let no one else be there when he did it.

124. This was carried out, and Cyrus took the hare and cut it open. He found the letter inside, took it out, and read it. This is what it said: "Son of Cambyses, the gods watch over you; otherwise you would never have come to such good fortune. So take revenge on Astyages, your murderer. As far as his will goes, you are dead; it is by the care of the gods, and by mine, that you are alive. I think you learned long ago, from first to last, how things happened to you, and also what I have suffered at Astyages' hands because I did not kill you but gave you to the herdsman. Now, if you will take my advice, you will rule all the land Astyages now rules. Persuade the Persians to revolt and march against the Medes. Whether I am appointed to lead the army against you, or some other of the leading Medes, you have what you want, because these will be the first to turn on Astyages, desert him, come over to your side, and try to bring him down. So know that here, at least, everything is ready. Do this, then, and do it quickly."

125. When Cyrus heard this, he began to think about the cleverest way to persuade the Persians to revolt. After thinking it over, he found that this was the most suitable way, and this is what he actually did. First he wrote what he wanted on a sheet of paper, and he called an assembly of the Persians. Then he unrolled the paper and, reading from it, announced that Astyages had appointed him commander of the Persians. "And now, Persians," he went on, "I order each of you to come to me with a sickle." That was the order Cyrus gave. (The Persians are made up of many tribes. Some of them Cyrus gathered together and persuaded to revolt from the Medes: the tribes on which all the other Persians depend, namely the Pasargadae, the Maraphians and the Maspians. Of these the Pasargadae are the noblest, and the Achaemenids, the clan from which the Perseid kings come, are one of their families. The other Persian tribes are these: the Panthaliaeans, the Derusiaeans and the Germanians, who are all farmers; and the rest are nomads, namely the Daans, the Mardians, the Dropicans and the Sagartians.)

126. There was a certain stretch of Persian land overgrown with thorns, about two miles or a little more on each side. When they had all come with what they had been told to bring, Cyrus ordered them to clear this land for farming in a single day. When the Persians had finished the job set them, he told them to come back the next day, bathed and clean. Meanwhile Cyrus gathered in one place all his father's flocks of goats and sheep and his herds of cattle, slaughtered them, and got them ready to entertain the whole Persian host, along with wine and the most agreeable foods besides. When the Persians came the next day, he had them recline in a meadow and gave them a feast. After they had finished eating, Cyrus asked them which they liked better, what they had had the day before or what they had now. They said there was a great difference between the two: the day before had brought them nothing but hardship, and this day nothing but good things. Cyrus took up what they had said and laid bare his whole plan. "Men of Persia," he said, "this is how things stand with you. If you will do as I say, you will have these good things and ten thousand others, with no slave's labor at all. But if you will not do as I say, you will have countless labors like yesterday's. So do as I say, and make yourselves free. I believe I was born by some providence of heaven to take this work in hand, and I don't think you are worse men than the Medes, either in other things or in war. Since that is how things are, revolt from Astyages at once."

127. So the Persians, having found a leader, were glad to try to free themselves, since they had long resented being ruled by the Medes. When Astyages heard what Cyrus was doing, he sent a messenger to summon him. Cyrus told the messenger to report to Astyages that he would be with him sooner than Astyages himself would like. When he heard this, Astyages armed all the Medes, and, blinded by heaven, he appointed Harpagus to command the army, forgetting what he had done to him. When the Medes marched out and engaged the Persians, some of them, those who had not been let in on the plot, kept on fighting. Others went over to the Persians. But most of them deliberately held back and ran away.

128. So the Median army was shamefully scattered. As soon as Astyages heard of it, he said, threatening Cyrus: "Even so, Cyrus will not get away unpunished." With these words he first impaled the Magi who interpreted dreams, the ones who had persuaded him to let Cyrus go. Then he armed the Medes who had been left behind in the city, the young men and the old. He led these out, gave battle to the Persians, and was beaten. Astyages himself was taken alive, and he lost the Medes he had led out as well.

129. When Astyages was a prisoner, Harpagus came and stood beside him, gloating over him and taunting him. Among the other things he said to wound him, he asked him in particular how he liked being a slave instead of a king, meaning that dinner at which Astyages had served him the flesh of his own son. Astyages looked at him and asked in return whether he claimed what Cyrus had done as his own work. Harpagus said that since he had written the letter, the deed was rightly his. Then Astyages told him he was at once the stupidest and the most unjust of men. The stupidest, because when he could have become king himself, as he could have if what had now been done was really his doing, he had handed the supreme power to someone else. The most unjust, because on account of that dinner he had made the Medes slaves. If he really had to give the kingdom to someone else and not keep it himself, it would have been more just to give this prize to one of the Medes rather than to one of the Persians. As it was, the Medes, who had done nothing wrong, had become slaves instead of masters, and the Persians, who used to be the Medes' slaves, had now become their masters.

130. So Astyages, after reigning thirty-five years, was brought down in this way. Because of his cruelty the Medes bowed under the yoke of the Persians, after they had ruled Asia above the river Halys for one hundred and twenty-eight years, not counting the time when the Scythians ruled. Later on, however, they regretted having done this, and they revolted from Darius; but after revolting they were brought under again, beaten in a battle. At this time, then, in the reign of Astyages, the Persians under Cyrus rose up against the Medes, and from then on they were the rulers of Asia. As for Astyages, Cyrus did him no further harm, but kept him at his own court until he died. That is how Cyrus was born and raised and became king. After this he conquered Croesus, who, as I said earlier, was the one who started the quarrel; and once he had conquered him, he became ruler of all Asia.

Chapter 6: The Customs of the Persians, the Greeks of Asia, and the Revolt of Pactyes

131. These are the customs the Persians follow, as far as I know them. They do not think it right to set up statues of the gods, or temples, or altars. In fact they say that people who do these things are fools. The reason, as it seems to me, is that they do not believe the gods have human form, as the Greeks do. Their custom is to go up to the highest mountains and offer sacrifices to Zeus there, and the whole circle of the sky is what they call Zeus. They also sacrifice to the Sun and the Moon and the Earth, to Fire and to Water and to the Winds. These are the only gods they have sacrificed to from the very beginning. But they have also learned to sacrifice to Aphrodite Urania, and they learned it from the Assyrians and the Arabians. The Assyrians call Aphrodite Mylitta, the Arabians call her Alitta, and the Persians call her Mitra.

132. Now this is the way the Persians are accustomed to sacrifice to the gods I have named. They build no altars and they light no fire. When they mean to sacrifice, they use no libation, no music of the pipe, no garlands and no barley-meal for sprinkling. Instead, when a man wants to sacrifice to any one of the gods, he leads the animal to a clean place, one free of any pollution, and calls on the god, usually with a wreath of myrtle wound around his tiara, the soft cap the Persians wear. The man who sacrifices is not allowed to pray for good things for himself alone. He prays that all will be well with all the Persians and with the king, since he himself is of course counted among all the Persians. When he has cut the victim up into pieces and boiled the meat, he spreads out a bed of the freshest grass, clover above all, and lays all the pieces of meat on it right away. Once he has laid them out in order, a Magus, one of the Magi, the Persian priestly caste, stands beside them and chants a song over them about the birth of the gods (that, they say, is what their chant is), since it is against their law to sacrifice without a Magus. Then, after waiting a short time, the man who made the sacrifice carries the meat away and uses it for whatever he likes.

133. Of all the days of the year, each of them most honors the day he was born. On that day he thinks it right to serve a bigger feast than on other days. At this feast the richer Persians set on the table an ox or a horse or a camel or a donkey, roasted whole in an oven, while the poor set out smaller animals, cooked the same way. They eat few main dishes but many desserts, and these are not served all at once but one after another. That is why the Persians say that the Greeks get up from dinner still hungry: after dinner the Greeks are served nothing worth mentioning in the way of dessert, whereas if they were served a good dessert they would not stop eating so soon. The Persians are very fond of wine. It is not allowed for a man to vomit or to urinate in front of anyone else, and that is how they guard against these things. It is also their custom to discuss their most important business while they are drinking heavily. Whatever they decide in that discussion, the master of the house where they happen to be meeting puts before them again the next day, when they are sober. If they still like the decision when they are sober, they act on it; if they do not, they drop it. And whatever they discuss first when they are sober, they consider again when they are drunk.

134. When they meet each other in the street, you can tell whether the two who meet are of equal rank, because instead of greeting each other with words, equals kiss each other on the mouth. If one of them is a little lower in rank than the other, they kiss on the cheek. If one is of much humbler birth than the other, he throws himself down on the ground before him and bows in worship. After themselves, they honor most the nations that live nearest to them, then the ones that live next nearest, and so on, giving honor in proportion to distance. They honor least the people who live farthest away from them, since they think that they themselves are by far the best of all human beings in every way, that others have a share of merit in the proportion I have just described, and that those who live farthest from them are the worst. Under the rule of the Medes the different nations also governed one another by the same rule the Persians follow in giving honor. The Medes ruled over all of them, and directly over those who lived nearest to them; these in turn ruled over their own neighbors, and those again over the nations next to them. So the Median people extended their power step by step, from ruling directly to ruling through others.

135. The Persians take up foreign customs more readily than anyone else in the world. They wear Median clothes, because they think them better-looking than their own, and in war they wear the Egyptian breastplate. They also take up every kind of luxury as soon as they hear of it, and in particular they have learned from the Greeks to have sex with boys. Each of them marries several lawful wives, and they keep many more concubines besides.

136. Next to being brave in battle, the mark of a real man is to be able to show many sons, and every year the king sends gifts to the man who has the most, since they think that numbers are strength. They educate their sons from the age of five to the age of twenty in three things only: riding, shooting with the bow, and telling the truth. Before a boy is five he never comes into his father's sight, but lives with the women. This is done so that if the child dies while he is being raised, his death will cause his father no grief.

137. I approve of this custom of theirs, and also of the next one I am going to mention. The king himself does not put anyone to death for a single offense, and no other Persian does any harm that cannot be undone to any of his own servants for a single offense either. Only if he weighs things up and finds that the wrongs are more numerous and greater than the services does he let his anger loose. They also say that no one has ever killed his own father or mother. Whenever anything of that kind has been done, they say, it will always turn out on inquiry that the killer was a changeling or the child of adultery. For it is not reasonable, they say, that a true parent should be killed by his own son.

138. Whatever they are not allowed to do, they are not allowed even to talk about. The most shameful thing of all, in their view, is to tell a lie, and the next most shameful is to owe money. They have many reasons for this, but the chief one is that a man who owes money, they say, is bound to tell lies sometimes too. Any citizen who has leprosy, or the disease that turns the skin white, may not enter a city or mix with the other Persians. They say he has these diseases because he has sinned against the Sun in some way. A foreigner who catches these diseases is driven out of the country altogether in many parts of it, and so are white doves, which they charge with the same offense. They never urinate or spit into a river, and they do not wash their hands in one or let anyone else do these things. They hold rivers in very great reverence.

139. Something else is also true of them, which the Persians themselves have never noticed, but I have. Their names, which describe their bodies or their high position, all end in the same letter: the letter the Dorians call san and the Ionians call sigma, our s. If you look into it, you will find that every Persian name ends in this letter. Not some in this one and others in other letters, but all alike.

140. All this I can say for certain from my own knowledge. But what follows about their dead is told as a secret mystery and not openly: that the body of a Persian man is not buried until it has been torn by a bird or a dog. (I know for certain that the Magi do this, because they do it openly.) Be that as it may, the Persians coat the body in wax and then bury it in the ground. The Magi are very different from other men, and from the priests in Egypt in particular. The Egyptian priests make it a point of purity to kill nothing alive except the animals they sacrifice. But the Magi kill every kind of creature with their own hands, except dogs and human beings. They even make a great point of it, killing ants and snakes and every other creature that crawls or flies. As for this custom, let it stay as it was established from the beginning. Now I will go back to my earlier story.

141. As soon as the Lydians had been conquered by the Persians, the Ionians and the Aeolians sent messengers to Cyrus at Sardis. They wanted to be his subjects on the same terms as they had been subjects of Croesus. When Cyrus heard what they proposed, he told them a fable. A piper, he said, saw some fish in the sea and played his pipe to them, thinking they would come out onto the land. When his hopes came to nothing, he took a casting net, caught a great many of the fish in it, and hauled them out of the water. And when he saw them jumping about, he said to the fish: "You can stop dancing now. You wouldn't come out and dance before, when I piped to you." Cyrus told the Ionians and Aeolians this fable for a reason. Earlier, when Cyrus himself had sent a messenger asking the Ionians to revolt from Croesus, they had refused; and now, when the conquest was over, they were ready to obey Cyrus. So he spoke to them in anger. When the Ionians heard this answer brought back to their cities, each of them built a wall around itself, and they met together at the Panionium, the shrine of all the Ionians, all except the people of Miletus. With the Milesians alone Cyrus had sworn a treaty on the same terms the Lydians had granted them. The rest of the Ionians decided together to send messengers to Sparta, to ask the Spartans to help the Ionians.

142. These Ionians, the ones the Panionium belongs to, happen to have built their cities in the finest climate and the best seasons of any people we know. For no land, whether north of Ionia or south of it, east of it or west, does as well as Ionia itself. The lands in one direction suffer from cold and wet, and those in the other from heat and drought. These Ionians do not all speak the same language; they have four different dialects. The southernmost of their cities is Miletus, and next to it come Myus and Priene. These were settled in Caria, and they speak the same dialect as each other. The following cities are in Lydia: Ephesus, Colophon, Lebedus, Teos, Clazomenae and Phocaea. These cities speak nothing like the ones I just mentioned, but they agree with one another. There are three more Ionian cities left. Two of them are on islands, Samos and Chios, and one, Erythrae, is built on the mainland. The people of Chios and Erythrae speak the same dialect, but the Samians have one all their own. So that makes four separate dialects.

143. Of these Ionians, then, the Milesians were sheltered from danger, since they had sworn a treaty. The islanders had nothing to fear, because the Phoenicians were not yet subjects of the Persians, and the Persians themselves were not seafarers. Now these twelve cities had split off from the rest of the Ionians for no other reason than this. The whole Greek nation was weak at that time, but of all its peoples the Ionians were by far the weakest and the least regarded; apart from Athens they did not have a single city of any importance. The other Ionians, and the Athenians among them, avoided the name and did not want to be called Ionians; even now, I notice, most of them seem ashamed of it. But these twelve cities took pride in the name. They set up a temple of their own, which they named the Panionium, and they decided not to let any other Ionians share in it. (Nor did any others ask to share in it, except the people of Smyrna.)

144. In the same way, the Dorians of the district that is now called the Five Cities, though it used to be called the Six Cities, take care not to admit any of the neighboring Dorians to their temple at Triopium. They even shut out those of their own number who break the temple's rules. For example, at the games of Triopian Apollo they used to give bronze tripods as prizes to the winners, and the rule was that the winners must not carry them out of the temple, but must dedicate them to the god then and there. Then there was a man from Halicarnassus named Agasicles. When he won, he paid no attention to this rule. He carried the tripod off to his own house and hung it up there on a nail. For this the other five cities, Lindus, Ialysus and Camirus, Cos and Cnidus, shut the sixth city, Halicarnassus, out of any share in the temple.

145. That was the penalty they laid on the Halicarnassians. As for the Ionians, I think the reason they made themselves twelve cities and would not take any more into their league is this. When they lived in the Peloponnese, they were divided into twelve parts, just as the Achaeans, who drove the Ionians out, are divided into twelve parts now. Starting from the side nearest Sicyon, first comes Pellene, then Aegira, and Aegae, which has the river Crathis, a river that never runs dry (the river of the same name in Italy was named after it), and Bura, and Helice, where the Ionians fled for refuge when the Achaeans beat them in battle, and Aegium, and Rhypes, and Patrae, and Pharae, and Olenus, where the great river Peirus is, and Dyme, and Tritaea, the only one of them that lies inland. These are now the twelve divisions of the Achaeans, and in the old days they were the divisions of the Ionians.

146. That is why the Ionians, too, made themselves twelve cities. For it would be sheer folly to say that these are any more Ionian than the other Ionians, or that they come of any nobler descent. A large part of them are Abantians from Euboea, who do not even share the name of Ionia. Minyans of Orchomenus are mixed in with them, and Cadmeans, and Dryopians, and Phocians who broke away from their own state, and Molossians, and Pelasgians from Arcadia, and Dorians from Epidaurus, and many other peoples besides. And those who set out to found their colonies from the Prytaneum, the town hall of Athens, and who think themselves the noblest-born of the Ionians, brought no women with them to their new home. Instead they took Carian women, after killing their parents. Because of this slaughter the women made a rule for themselves, bound one another by oaths to keep it, and passed it on to their daughters: they would never eat with their husbands, and no wife would ever call her own husband by his name. The reason was that these men had killed their fathers and husbands and children, and then, after doing that, had taken them as wives. This happened at Miletus.

147. Some of them, too, chose Lycian kings to rule them, descendants of Glaucus and Hippolochus, while others were ruled by Cauconians from Pylos, descendants of Codrus son of Melanthus, and others again by kings from both families together. Still, since these twelve cities cling to the name more than the other Ionians, let them be called, if they like, the Ionians of truly pure descent. But in fact all are Ionians who are descended from Athens and keep the festival of the Apaturia. And all of them keep it except the people of Ephesus and Colophon. These alone of all the Ionians do not keep the Apaturia, and their reason is a certain murder.

148. The Panionium is a holy place on the north side of Mycale, set apart by the common agreement of the Ionians for Poseidon of Helice. Mycale is a headland of the mainland that runs out westward toward Samos. The Ionians used to gather there from their cities and hold a festival they called the Panionia. (And not only the festivals of the Ionians but those of all the Greeks alike follow the same rule: their names all end in the same letter, just like the names of the Persians.)

Those, then, are the Ionian cities.

149. The cities of Aeolia are these: Cyme, which is called Phriconis, Larisa, Neonteichus, Temnus, Cilla, Notium, Aegiroessa, Pitane, Aegaeae, Myrina and Gryneia. These are the ancient cities of the Aeolians, eleven in number, since one of them, Smyrna, was taken away from them by the Ionians. For these cities, the ones on the mainland, used to number twelve as well. These Aeolians happened to settle in a land that is more fertile than Ionia but does not have as good a climate.

150. This is how the Aeolians lost Smyrna. Some men of Colophon had lost out in a struggle between factions and been driven from their city, and the people of Smyrna took them in as refugees. Later these Colophonian exiles waited for a time when the people of Smyrna were holding a festival for Dionysus outside the walls. Then they shut the gates against them and took the city for themselves. After this, when all the Aeolians came to the rescue, the two sides made an agreement: the Ionians would hand over everything that could be carried away, and on that condition the Aeolians would give up Smyrna. When the people of Smyrna had done this, the other eleven cities divided them among themselves and made them their own citizens.

151. These, then, are the Aeolian cities on the mainland, apart from those on Mount Ida, which are separate from the rest. As for those on the islands, there are five on Lesbos. The sixth city on Lesbos, Arisba, was enslaved by the people of Methymna, even though its citizens were of the same blood as they were. There is one city on Tenedos, and another in what are called the Hundred Isles. Now the people of Lesbos and Tenedos, like the Ionians who lived on islands, had nothing to fear. But the rest of the cities agreed together to follow the Ionians wherever they led.

152. When the messengers from the Ionians and Aeolians reached Sparta (for all this was done in a hurry), they chose a Phocaean named Pythermus to speak for all of them. He put on a purple cloak, so that as many Spartans as possible would hear about it and come to listen. Then he was brought before the assembly, and he made a long speech asking the Spartans to help them. But the Spartans would not listen to him. On the contrary, they decided not to help the Ionians. So the messengers went away. But even though they had sent the Ionians' messengers away, the Spartans still sent some men off in a fifty-oared ship, to find out, as I suppose, how things stood with Cyrus and with Ionia. When these men reached Phocaea, they sent the most respected man among them, whose name was Lacrines, to Sardis, to give Cyrus the Spartans' message: he was to do no harm to any city in Greece, because they would not allow it.

153. When the herald had said this, Cyrus is said to have asked the Greeks he had with him who these Spartans were, and how many of them there were, that they dared make such a declaration to him. When he heard their answer, he said to the Spartan herald: "I have never yet been afraid of men like these, who have a place set aside in the middle of their city where they get together and cheat each other with false oaths. If I stay healthy, they will have their own troubles to talk about, and not the troubles of the Ionians." Cyrus threw out these words as an insult to all the Greeks, because they have marketplaces and buy and sell in them. The Persians themselves do not use markets, and they have no marketplace at all. After this Cyrus put Sardis in the charge of a Persian named Tabalus, and gave a Lydian named Pactyes the job of looking after the gold of Croesus and of the other Lydians. Then he marched off himself to Ecbatana, taking Croesus with him, and for the moment took no account of the Ionians. For Babylon still stood in his way, and so did the Bactrian nation, the Sacae and the Egyptians. He meant to lead the campaigns against these himself, and to send some other general against the Ionians.

154. But when Cyrus had marched away from Sardis, Pactyes led the Lydians in a revolt against Tabalus and against Cyrus.
