He went down to the coast, and since he had all the gold that had been in Sardis, he hired mercenaries and persuaded the people of the coast to march with him. So he marched on Sardis and besieged Tabalus, who had shut himself up in the citadel.

155. Cyrus heard about this on his march, and he said to Croesus: "Croesus, where will all this end? It looks as if the Lydians will never stop making trouble for me and having trouble themselves. I wonder whether it would be best to sell them all as slaves. As it is, I think I have acted like a man who kills the father and then spares the sons. That is just what I have done: I took you prisoner, and I am carrying you away, you who were much more than a father to the Lydians, and I handed the Lydians back their city. And after that, can I be surprised that they have revolted from me?" That is how he said what was on his mind. But Croesus was afraid that Cyrus would destroy Sardis, and he answered: "My king, what you say is reasonable. But do not give way to your anger completely, and do not destroy an ancient city that is innocent both of what happened before and of what is happening now. As for what happened before, I did it, and I carry the consequences on my own head. As for what is happening now, the wrongdoer is Pactyes, the man you put in charge of Sardis, so let him pay the penalty. But pardon the Lydians, and give them these orders, so that they will not revolt or be a danger to you. Send word forbidding them to own weapons of war. Tell them instead to wear tunics under their cloaks and soft high boots on their feet, and order them to teach their sons to play the lyre and the harp and to keep shops. Soon, my king, you will see that they have become women instead of men, and there will be no fear that they will revolt from you."

156. Croesus suggested this to him because he saw that it was better for the Lydians than being made slaves and sold. He knew that if he did not offer a good enough reason, he would not persuade Cyrus to change his mind. And he was afraid that at some later time, if the Lydians escaped the present danger, they might revolt from the Persians and be destroyed. Cyrus was very pleased with the suggestion. His anger cooled, and he said he agreed with Croesus' advice. Then he called for Mazares, a Mede, and ordered him to proclaim to the Lydians what Croesus had suggested. He also ordered him to sell as slaves all the others who had joined the Lydians in the march on Sardis, and above all, whatever it took, to bring Pactyes himself to Cyrus alive.

157. Cyrus gave these orders on the road and then marched on to the Persians' homeland. But when Pactyes heard that an army was coming to fight him, he was terrified and fled at once to Cyme. Then Mazares the Mede marched on Sardis with a part of Cyrus' army. He no longer found Pactyes or his followers at Sardis, so first he forced the Lydians to carry out Cyrus' orders, and by his orders the Lydians changed their whole way of life. After this Mazares sent messengers to Cyme, ordering the people to hand over Pactyes. The people of Cyme decided to refer the question of what to do to the god at Branchidae. There was an oracle there, set up long ago, which all the Ionians and Aeolians used to consult. The place is in the territory of Miletus, above the harbor of Panormus.

158. So the people of Cyme sent messengers to Branchidae to consult the god, and they asked what they should do about Pactyes in order to please the gods. When they asked, the answer they were given was that they should hand Pactyes over to the Persians. When they heard this answer reported, the people of Cyme were ready to hand him over. But when most of the people were ready to do it, Aristodicus son of Heraclides, a man of standing among the citizens, stopped them. He did not trust the answer, and he thought the messengers who had gone to consult the oracle were not telling the truth. In the end other messengers were sent to the oracle to ask a second time about Pactyes, and Aristodicus was one of them.

159. When they reached Branchidae, Aristodicus stepped forward from the others and put this question to the oracle: "Lord, Pactyes the Lydian came to us as a suppliant, asking for protection, running from a violent death at the hands of the Persians. The Persians are demanding him, and they order the people of Cyme to give him up. But although we are afraid of the power of the Persians, we have not yet dared to hand the suppliant over to them, not until your advice is made clear to us, telling us which of the two things we ought to do." That was his question, but the god gave them the same answer again, telling them to hand Pactyes over to the Persians. At this Aristodicus deliberately did the following. He went all around the temple, destroying the nests of the sparrows and of all the other kinds of birds that had hatched their young on the temple. While he was doing this, it is said, a voice came out of the inner shrine, speaking to Aristodicus: "You most wicked of men, how dare you do this? Are you dragging my suppliants by force out of my temple?" And Aristodicus, they say, was not at a loss at all, and answered: "Lord, is this how you come to the help of your own suppliants, while you tell the people of Cyme to hand over theirs?" And the god answered him again: "Yes, I do tell you to, so that you will be destroyed all the sooner for your wickedness, and so that you will never again come to the oracle to ask about handing over suppliants."

160. When the people of Cyme heard this reply reported, they did not want to be destroyed for handing him over, or to be besieged for keeping him. So they sent him away to Mytilene. But when Mazares sent messages to the Mytilenians, they got ready to hand Pactyes over for a price. What the price was I can't say for certain, because the deal was never completed. For when the people of Cyme learned what the Mytilenians were doing, they sent a ship to Lesbos and carried Pactyes off to Chios. There he was dragged by force out of the temple of Athena Poliuchus, Athena Guardian of the City, by the Chians, and handed over. The Chians handed him over and got Atarneus in return (Atarneus is a district of Mysia, opposite Lesbos). So the Persians took charge of Pactyes and kept him under guard, meaning to bring him before Cyrus. And for a long time afterward, none of the Chians would use barley grown in this district of Atarneus for sprinkling at a sacrifice to any god, or bake sacrificial cakes from the grain that grew there. Everything the land produced was kept out of every kind of sacred rite.

161. So the Chians had handed over Pactyes. After this Mazares marched against those who had joined in besieging Tabalus. First he enslaved the people of Priene. Then he overran the whole plain of the Maeander, letting his army plunder it, and he did the same to Magnesia. And right after this he fell sick and died.

Chapter 7: Harpagus Conquers Ionia, and Cyrus Takes Babylon

162. After Mazares died, Harpagus came down to take his place in command. He too was a Mede by birth. He was the man whom Astyages, king of the Medes, had served that lawless banquet, and who had helped to give the kingdom to Cyrus. Now Cyrus appointed him commander, and he came to Ionia and began taking the cities by building up mounds of earth against them. Whenever he had shut a people up inside their walls, he would pile up mounds against the walls and take the city by storm. The first city in Ionia he attacked was Phocaea.

163. These Phocaeans were the first of the Greeks to make long sea voyages. It was they who discovered the Adriatic, and Tyrrhenia, and Iberia, and Tartessus, out past the Strait of Gibraltar. They did not sail in round-hulled merchant ships but in fifty-oared galleys. They came to Tartessus and made friends with the king of the Tartessians, whose name was Arganthonius. He ruled the Tartessians for eighty years and lived to be a hundred and twenty in all. The Phocaeans became such close friends with this man that first he invited them to leave Ionia and settle anywhere they liked in his own country. When he could not persuade them to do that, and later heard from them how the power of the Mede was growing, he gave them money to build a wall around their city. He gave it without stinting, for the wall runs a good mile or more around, and it is built entirely of large stones closely fitted together.

164. That is how the Phocaeans' wall came to be built. Harpagus marched his army against them and laid siege to the city. At the same time he made them an offer: he would be satisfied, he said, if the Phocaeans would just pull down one battlement of their wall and dedicate one single house to the king. But the Phocaeans hated the thought of slavery. They said they wanted one day to think the matter over, and after that they would give their answer, and they asked him to pull his army back from the wall while they deliberated. Harpagus said he knew perfectly well what they meant to do, but all the same he would let them deliberate. So, while Harpagus had his army pulled back from the wall, the Phocaeans dragged their fifty-oared galleys down to the sea. They put on board their children and women and all their movable goods. They also loaded the statues from the temples and the other offerings, all except the ones made of bronze or stone and the paintings; everything else went into the ships. Then they embarked themselves and sailed for Chios. The Persians took possession of Phocaea, a city empty of its people.

165. As for the Phocaeans, they asked the people of Chios to sell them the islands called the Oenussae, but the Chians would not. They were afraid the islands would become a center of trade and their own island would be shut out of it. So the Phocaeans set out for Cyrnus, the island of Corsica. Twenty years before this, following an oracle, they had founded a city on Cyrnus called Alalia. (By this time Arganthonius was dead.) But before setting out for Cyrnus they first sailed back to Phocaea and slaughtered the Persian garrison that Harpagus had left in charge of the city. When they had done this, they laid a solemn curse on any of their number who stayed behind from the voyage. They also sank a lump of iron in the sea and swore that they would not come back to Phocaea until that lump rose to the surface again. But as they were setting off for Cyrnus, more than half the citizens were seized with such longing and regret for their city and their homeland that they broke their oath and sailed back to Phocaea. Those who still kept the oath weighed anchor from the Oenussae islands and sailed away.

166. When they reached Cyrnus, they lived there for five years alongside the settlers who had come before them, and they built temples there. But they kept plundering the property of all their neighbors. So the Tyrrhenians and the Carthaginians (from Carthage, the Phoenician colony in North Africa) made an agreement and sailed against them, each with sixty ships. The Phocaeans manned their own ships, sixty in all, and went out to meet the enemy in what is called the Sardinian Sea. When they met in the sea battle, the Phocaeans won a kind of Cadmean victory, the kind that ruins the winner too: forty of their ships were destroyed, and the remaining twenty were put out of action, their rams bent aside. So they sailed into Alalia, took on board their children and women and as much of their other property as their ships could carry, left Cyrnus behind, and sailed to Rhegium.

167. As for the crews of the ships that were destroyed, the Carthaginians and Tyrrhenians captured by far the greater number of them. They brought them ashore and stoned them to death. After this the people of Agylla found that every living thing that passed the spot where the stoned Phocaeans lay became twisted, or crippled, or paralyzed: sheep and goats, pack animals and human beings alike. So the people of Agylla sent to Delphi, wanting to make amends for the offense. The Pythia told them to do what the people of Agylla still do today: they offer great sacrifices to the dead men and hold athletic games and horse races in their honor at that place. That was the fate of those Phocaeans. But the ones who took refuge at Rhegium set out from there and took possession of the city in the land of Oenotria that is now called Hyele. They founded it after learning from a man of Poseidonia that the Pythia's answer had meant them to found a shrine to Cyrnus, who was a hero, and not to found a settlement on the island of Cyrnus.

168. That is what happened at Phocaea in Ionia. The people of Teos did almost the same thing. As soon as Harpagus took their wall with a mound, they boarded their ships and sailed straight off to Thrace. There they founded the city of Abdera. Timesius of Clazomenae had founded it before them, but he got no good of it: the Thracians drove him out. Now he is honored as a hero by the Teans in Abdera.

169. These were the only Ionians who left their native cities rather than live in subjection. The other Ionians, except the Milesians, did fight Harpagus just as those who left had done, and they proved themselves brave men, each fighting for his own city. But when they were beaten and their cities taken, they all stayed where they were and did what they were ordered to do. The Milesians, as I said before, had made a sworn agreement with Cyrus himself and stayed out of it. So Ionia was enslaved for the second time. And when Harpagus had conquered the Ionians on the mainland, the Ionians who lived on the islands were so frightened by all this that they surrendered to Cyrus.

170. The Ionians had been badly treated, but they still kept holding their assemblies at the Panionium, as before. I am told that Bias of Priene gave the Ionians a piece of advice there, a most useful one, and if they had followed it they might have been the most prosperous of all the Greeks. He urged the Ionians to set out together in one common fleet, sail to Sardinia, and there found a single city for all Ionians. That way, he said, they would escape slavery and prosper, living on the largest of all islands and ruling over others. But if they stayed in Ionia, he said, he could not see how they would ever be free again. That was Bias of Priene's advice, given after the Ionians had been ruined. But good advice had also been given before Ionia's ruin, by Thales of Miletus, whose family was Phoenician by descent. He advised the Ionians to have one single seat of government and to put it at Teos, since Teos, he said, was at the center of Ionia. The other cities would go on being lived in as before, but would count as if they were only districts of one state.

These, then, were the plans these two men put before them.

171. Harpagus, having subdued Ionia, marched against the Carians and the Caunians and the Lycians, taking Ionians and Aeolians along to help him. The Carians had come to the mainland from the islands. Long ago they had been subjects of Minos, king of Crete, and were called Leleges. They lived on the islands and paid no tribute, as far back as I can find out by hearsay; but whenever Minos asked, they manned his ships for him. And since Minos conquered a great deal of land and was lucky in his wars, the Carians were in his day by far the most famous of all nations. They also produced three inventions that the Greeks took up. The Carians were the ones who started the fashion of fastening crests on helmets and of putting emblems on shields. They were also the first to put handles on their shields. Until then everyone who carried a shield carried it without a handle, steering it with a leather strap slung around the neck and over the left shoulder. Then, a long time afterward, the Dorians and Ionians drove the Carians out of the islands, and that is how they came to the mainland. That is how the Cretans tell the story of the Carians. The Carians themselves do not agree. They believe they have lived on the mainland from the beginning and have always gone by the same name they have now. As evidence they point to an ancient temple of Carian Zeus at Mylasa, which the Mysians and the Lydians share with them as kindred peoples, since they say Lydus and Mysus were brothers of Car. These peoples share the temple, but those of other races who have come to speak the same language as the Carians have no share in it.

172. In my opinion, though, it is the Caunians who have lived there from the beginning, even though they say themselves that they came from Crete. They have come to resemble the Carians in language, or else the Carians have come to resemble the Caunians; I can't say for certain which. But in their customs they are very different from all other people, the Carians included. For example, the finest thing in the world, to their way of thinking, is to gather in large groups for drinking, by age or by friendship, men, women and children alike. Again, they once set up temples to foreign gods, but afterward changed their minds and decided to worship only their own native gods. So all the young men of Caunus put on their armor and marched as far as the borders of the Calyndians, striking at the air with their spears and saying that they were driving the foreign gods out of the country. Those are the customs these people have.

173. The Lycians, on the other hand, came originally from Crete, for in ancient times all of Crete was held by non-Greeks. The two sons of Europa, Sarpedon and Minos, quarreled in Crete over who should be king. Minos won the struggle between their factions and drove out Sarpedon and his supporters. Once expelled, they came to the land of Milyas in Asia. (The land the Lycians live in now was called Milyas in the old days, and the Milyans were then called Solymi.) While Sarpedon reigned over them, they went by the name they had brought with them, which is still what their neighbors call the Lycians today: Termilae. But then Lycus son of Pandion came from Athens to the land of the Termilae and to Sarpedon, after he too had been driven out, by his brother Aegeus. From this Lycus, in time, they came to be called Lycians. Their customs are partly Cretan and partly Carian. But they have one custom all their own, which no other people shares: they take their names from their mothers and not from their fathers. If you ask a Lycian who he is, he will give you his mother's family, and list his mother's mother and her mothers before her. And if a woman who is a citizen marries a slave, her children are counted as nobly born. But if a man who is a citizen, even the first man among them, takes a slave as his wife or his concubine, his children have no citizen rights.

174. The Carians were conquered by Harpagus without doing anything brilliant, and so were the Greeks who live in that country. Among these, besides others, are the people of Cnidus, settlers from Sparta. Their land runs out into the sea; it is the region called Triopium, which begins at the peninsula of Bybassus. All of Cnidus except a small strip is washed by the sea: on the north side it is bounded by the Gulf of Ceramus, and on the south by the sea off Syme and Rhodes. So, while Harpagus was conquering Ionia, the Cnidians began to dig through this small strip, which is about half a mile across, wanting to make their land an island. Everything inside the isthmus was theirs, since the isthmus they were digging across is exactly where Cnidian territory ends on the mainland side. A great many men were at work on it. But it became clear that the workmen were getting hurt far more than you would expect, and in a way that seemed more than natural, in various parts of their bodies and especially in their eyes, whenever the rock was broken up. So they sent men to the oracle at Delphi to ask what was causing the trouble. And the Pythia, as the Cnidians themselves say, gave them this answer, in the three-beat iambic verse:

	Do not wall off the isthmus with towers, and do not dig it through;
	had Zeus wanted your land to be an island, he would have made it one.

When the Pythia had given this oracle, the Cnidians not only stopped digging but surrendered to Harpagus without a fight when he came against them with his army.

175. There were also the Pedasians, who lived inland in the hill country above Halicarnassus. Whenever something bad is about to happen to them or their neighbors, the priestess of Athena there grows a long beard. This has happened to them three times. They were the only people anywhere in Caria who held out against Harpagus for any length of time. They gave him more trouble than anyone else, having fortified a mountain called Lida.

176. In time the Pedasians were conquered. When Harpagus marched his army into the plain of Xanthus, the Lycians came out against him and fought, a few against many, and gave proof of great courage. But they were beaten and shut up inside their city. Then they gathered their wives and children, their property and their servants into the citadel and set fire to it, so that the whole citadel went up in flames. When they had done this, they swore terrible oaths to one another, went out against the enemy, and were killed fighting, all the men of Xanthus. Of the Xanthians who now claim to be Lycians, most are newcomers from abroad, except for eighty households. Those eighty households happened to be away from home at the time, and so they survived. That is how Harpagus took Xanthus, and he took Caunus in much the same way, since the Caunians for the most part did as the Lycians had done.

177. So Harpagus was conquering the coastal regions of Asia, while Cyrus himself was doing the same in the interior, subduing every nation and passing over none. Most of these campaigns I will pass over in silence. But I will tell about the ones that gave him the most trouble and are most worth telling.

178. When Cyrus had brought all the rest of the mainland under his rule, he set about attacking the Assyrians. Assyria has many other great cities, of course, but the most famous and the strongest, where the seat of the kingdom had been set up after Nineveh was destroyed, was Babylon. And this is what kind of city it was. It lies in a great plain, and it is square, each side about thirteen and a half miles long, so that the whole circuit of the city comes to about fifty-four miles. That is the size of the city of Babylon, and it was more magnificent than any other city we know of. First, a moat runs all around it, deep and wide and full of water. Then comes a wall fifty royal cubits thick, about eighty feet, and two hundred cubits, some three hundred feet, high. The royal cubit, by the way, is three finger-widths longer than the ordinary cubit: about twenty inches against eighteen.

179. I must also explain what they did with the earth that came out of the moat, and how the wall was built. As they dug the moat, they made the earth they carried out of it into bricks. When they had molded enough bricks, they baked them in kilns. Then, using hot asphalt for mortar and laying in mats of woven reeds every thirty courses of brick, they built first the sides of the moat and then the wall itself in the same way. Along the top of the wall, at the edges, they built one-story chambers facing each other, and between the rows of chambers they left room to drive a four-horse chariot. All the way around the wall there are a hundred gates, all of bronze, with posts and lintels of bronze as well. There is another city eight days' journey from Babylon, called Is. There is a small river there, also called Is, which flows into the Euphrates. Along with its water, this river Is throws up great quantities of lumps of asphalt, and that is where the asphalt for the wall of Babylon came from.

180. That is how Babylon was walled. The city is in two halves, because a river called the Euphrates runs through the middle of it. It flows from the land of the Armenians, a large, deep, fast river, and empties into the Persian Gulf. On each side, the wall is carried down at its corners to the river, and from there a return wall of baked brick runs along each bank like a rampart. The city itself is full of houses three and four stories high. Its streets run in straight lines, including the cross streets that lead down to the river. At the end of each street there was a gate in the rampart along the river, as many gates as there were streets, and these were bronze too, and opened, like the streets, onto the river itself.

181. This wall I have described is like a breastplate for the city, and inside it another wall runs around, not much weaker for defense than the first but enclosing a smaller space. In the middle of each half of the city stood a building. In one was the king's palace, huge and strongly walled all around. In the other was the temple of Zeus Belus, with bronze gates. This still existed in my time, a square measuring 1,200 feet each way. In the middle of the temple grounds a solid tower is built, 600 feet long and 600 feet wide. On top of this tower stands a second tower, and on that a third, and so on up to eight towers. A ramp has been built winding around the outside of all the towers to climb them. About halfway up there is a landing with seats, where people going up sit down and rest. On top of the last tower there is a large shrine, and in the shrine a large couch is set, richly covered, with a golden table beside it. No statue has been set up there, and no human being spends the night there except one woman of the country, whichever woman the god chooses from all the women. So say the Chaldeans, who are the priests of this god.

182. These same men also say, though I do not believe them, that the god himself often comes to the shrine and rests on the couch. The same thing happens, according to the Egyptians, in Egyptian Thebes, where a woman also sleeps in the temple of Theban Zeus (both these women are said to have nothing to do with men). It happens too with the prophetess of the god at Patara in Lycia, whenever there is one, for there is not always an oracle there; but whenever there is one, she is shut up at night in the temple, inside the shrine.

183. In the temple at Babylon there is also another shrine lower down, with a great seated statue of Zeus made of gold. Beside it stands a large golden table, and his footstool and throne are gold as well. According to the Chaldeans, these things were made from eight hundred talents' weight of gold, about 45,000 pounds. Outside this shrine is a golden altar. There is also another, very large altar, where full-grown animals are sacrificed; on the golden altar it is forbidden to sacrifice anything but young animals still at the breast. On the larger altar, too, the Chaldeans burn a thousand talents' weight of frankincense, about 57,000 pounds, every year at the festival of this god. In those days, in the reign of Cyrus, there was also still standing in the sacred grounds a statue eighteen feet high, of solid gold. I did not see it myself; I am reporting what the Chaldeans say. Darius son of Hystaspes had designs on this statue but did not dare to take it. Xerxes son of Darius did take it, and he killed the priest who told him not to touch it. That is how magnificently this temple is furnished, and there are also many private offerings in it.

184. Babylon had many other rulers, whom I will mention in my Assyrian history, and who improved its walls and temples. Two of them were women. The first, called Semiramis, lived five generations before the other. She built embankments across the plain that are well worth seeing; before that, the river used to flood the whole plain like a sea.

185. The queen who came after her was called Nitocris, and she was wiser than the one who had reigned before. In the first place, she left monuments behind her, which I will describe. Then, seeing that the empire of the Medes was great and restless, and that it had taken many cities, Nineveh among them, she took every precaution against it that she could. First, the river Euphrates, which flows through the middle of their city: before her time it ran straight, but by digging channels upstream she made it so winding that it actually passes the same village in Assyria three times on its way. The village the Euphrates comes to is called Ardericca. Even today, people traveling from our sea, the Mediterranean, to Babylon, as they sail down the Euphrates, arrive at this same village three times, on three different days. That is one thing she did. She also built up an embankment along each bank of the river, amazing for its size and height. And a long way upstream from Babylon she dug a basin for a lake, running alongside the river at a short distance from it. She dug it deep enough everywhere to reach water, and made it so large that its circuit measured about forty-seven miles. The earth dug out of it she used up by piling it into the embankments along the river. When the basin was dug, she brought stones and lined it all around with a stone wall. She did both these things, making the river wind and turning the excavation into a marsh, so that the river would run more slowly with its force broken on its many bends, so that the voyage to Babylon would be a winding one, and so that after the voyage would come a long way around the lake. She carried out these works in the part of the country where the approach to it lay, on the shortest road from Media, so that the Medes could not mix with her people and find out about her affairs.

186. These were the defenses she threw around her city from deep in the country. Along with them she made another improvement that grew out of the same work. The city was in two halves, with the river between them. Under the earlier rulers, anyone who wanted to cross from one half to the other had to go over by boat, which, I imagine, was a nuisance. She took care of this too. While she was digging the basin for the lake, she got this other monument out of the same work. She had very long stones cut, and when the stones were ready and the basin dug, she turned the whole stream of the river into the place she had dug. While the basin was filling with water, the old riverbed dried out. In the meantime she lined the banks of the river with baked brick where it runs through the city, the same way as the wall, and also the steps leading down from the small gates to the river. Then, at about the middle of the city, as far as I can judge, she built a bridge out of the stones she had had quarried, binding the stones together with iron and lead. Across the top she laid squared timbers, which stayed in place during the day, and the people of Babylon used them to cross over. But at night they took the timbers away, for this reason: so that people would not cross back and forth at night and rob one another. When the excavation had been turned into a lake full of river water and the bridge had been finished, she led the Euphrates back out of the lake into its old bed. So the excavation, turned into a marsh, was thought to have served a good purpose, and the people of the city had been given a bridge.

187. This same queen also set the following trap. Over the gate of the city that more people passed through than any other, she had a tomb built for herself, right on top of the gate. On the tomb she had these words carved: "If any king of Babylon after me runs short of money, let him open my tomb and take as much as he wants. But let him not open it for any other reason, unless he is truly in need; for that will not turn out well." The tomb stayed undisturbed until the kingdom came to Darius. But Darius thought it outrageous not to make any use of this gate, and outrageous too, when money was lying there and the money itself was inviting him to take it, not to take it. The reason he would make no use of the gate was that he would have had a corpse over his head as he drove through. So he opened the tomb, and found not money but the corpse, and these words: "If you had not been so greedy for money and so shamelessly grasping, you would not have broken open the resting places of the dead."

188. That, they say, is the kind of woman this queen was. And it was her son, who had the same name as his father, Labynetus, and was ruler of the Assyrians, against whom Cyrus was now marching. When the Great King goes to war, he goes well supplied from home with food for his table and with cattle. He also takes water with him from the river Choaspes, which flows past Susa; this is the only river whose water the king will drink. A great many four-wheeled wagons drawn by mules carry a supply of this Choaspes water, boiled, in silver jars, and follow him wherever he marches.

189. On his way to Babylon, Cyrus came to the river Gyndes. Its springs are in the mountains of the Matienians, and it flows through the land of the Dardanians and into another river, the Tigris, which flows past the city of Opis and out into the Persian Gulf. Cyrus was trying to cross the Gyndes, a river big enough for boats, when one of his sacred white horses, full of spirit and high-handed, went into the river and tried to cross. The current swept it under and carried it away at once. Cyrus was furious with the river for this insolence, and he threatened to make it so weak that from then on even women would be able to cross it easily without wetting their knees. After making this threat, he broke off his march on Babylon and divided his army in two. Then he stretched out lines and marked out straight channels, a hundred and eighty on each bank of the Gyndes, running off in every direction, and he lined up his army along them and ordered them to dig. With so many men working, the job did get done, but they spent the whole summer at it.

190. When Cyrus had taken his revenge on the river Gyndes by splitting it into three hundred and sixty channels, and the next spring was just beginning, he finally went on with his advance on Babylon. The Babylonians had marched out of their city and were waiting for him. When he came near the city, the Babylonians gave battle, were beaten, and were shut up inside their city. But they had known well even before this that Cyrus was not one to sit still, and they had seen him attack every nation alike, so they had brought in provisions in advance for a great many years. So while they thought nothing of the siege, Cyrus did not know what to do, for a long time passed and he was getting nowhere.

191. So, whether someone else suggested it to him when he was at a loss, or whether he saw for himself what he should do, this is what he did. He posted the main body of his army where the river flows into the city, and another division behind the city, where the river flows out of it. He gave his army orders that as soon as they saw the river had become shallow enough to wade, they should go into the city that way. Having posted them like this and given them these orders, he himself marched off with the part of his army that was no use for fighting. When he came to the lake, Cyrus did the same things the queen of Babylon had done with the river and the lake. He led the river off through a channel into the lake, which was by then a marsh, and so the old riverbed became fordable as the water sank. When this had been done, the Persians who had been posted for this very purpose went into Babylon along the bed of the Euphrates, now that the stream had sunk to about the middle of a man's thigh. Now, if the Babylonians had known about this beforehand or had noticed what Cyrus was doing, they would have let the Persians into the city and then destroyed them miserably. For if they had shut all the gates leading down to the river and stood on the ramparts along the banks themselves, they would have caught them as if in a fish trap. But as it was, the Persians came on them unexpectedly. And because the city is so big, as the people who live there say, after the outer parts of the city had been captured, the Babylonians living in the middle had no idea they had been captured. They happened to be holding a festival, and they went on dancing and celebrating all that while, until they learned the truth all too well.

That is how Babylon was taken the first time.

192. How great the resources of the Babylonians are I will show by many other proofs, and among them by this one. Apart from the regular tribute, the whole land the Great King rules is divided into portions to supply him and his army with food. Now, there are twelve months in the year. For four of them he is supplied by the territory of Babylon, and for the other eight by all the rest of Asia put together. So the Assyrian land, in resources, amounts to a third of all Asia. And the governorship of this territory, which the Persians call a satrapy, is by far the best of all the governorships. When Tritantaechmes son of Artabazus held this province from the king, a full artaba of silver came in to him every single day. (The artaba is a Persian measure, about 1 2/3 bushels; it holds three Attic choenixes, about three quarts, more than the Attic medimnus.) As his own private property in this province, apart from his warhorses, he kept eight hundred stallions and sixteen thousand mares, each stallion serving twenty mares. And he kept so many Indian hounds that four large villages in the plain were let off all other taxes and assigned instead to feed the hounds.

Chapter 8: The Land and Customs of Babylon, and the Death of Cyrus

193. That was the wealth that belonged to the ruler of Babylon. Now the land of the Assyrians gets very little rain. That little is enough to nourish the roots of the grain, but the crop is ripened and the ear grows full by watering from the river. This is not done, as in Egypt, by the river itself rising over the fields; here the crop is watered by hand or with swing-buckets. For the whole Babylonian country, like Egypt, is cut up by channels. The largest of these channels is navigable for ships, and it runs toward the point where the sun rises in winter, from the Euphrates to another river, the Tigris, on whose bank the city of Nineveh stood. Of all the lands we know, this is by far the best for growing grain. As for trees, it does not even try to grow them, neither fig nor vine nor olive. But for grain it is so good that it returns as much as two hundred times what was sown on average, and when it does its very best it yields three hundred times. The leaves of the wheat and barley there grow a full three inches wide. As for millet and sesame, I know for myself how tall a plant they grow into, but I will not record it, because I am well aware that even what I have already said about the crops has been enough to make people who have never been to Babylonia disbelieve me. They use no olive oil, only oil they make from sesame seed. Date palms grow all over the plain, most of them bearing fruit, and from the dates they make food, wine and honey. They tend these palms the same way people tend fig trees. In particular they take the fruit of the palms the Greeks call "male palms" and tie it onto the date-bearing palms, so that the gall wasp can get into the date and ripen it, and so that the fruit of the palm does not drop off. For the male palm carries gall wasps in its fruit, just as the wild fig does.

194. But the greatest wonder of all in that country, after the city itself, to my mind, is the one I am about to describe. Their boats, I mean the ones that go down the river to Babylon, are round and made entirely of leather. They cut willow in the land of the Armenians, who live upstream of the Assyrians, and make ribs out of it. Around the ribs they stretch hides, which serve as an outer covering, a hull. They do not broaden out a stern or draw the bow together to a point; they make the boats round, like a shield. Then they pack the whole boat with straw, load it with cargo, and let it float down the river. Mostly these boats carry down casks of palm wood full of wine. The boat is steered by two oars and two men standing upright: the man inside pulls his oar while the man outside pushes his. Some of these boats are built very large and some smaller; the largest of them carry as much as five thousand talents' weight, something like 140 tons. In each boat there is a live donkey, and in the larger ones several. So when they have finished the voyage to Babylon and disposed of their cargo, they auction off the ribs of the boat and all the straw, but they load the hides onto their donkeys and drive them off to Armenia. For it is simply impossible to sail up the river, because the current is so swift, and that is why they make their boats of hides and not of timber. Then, when they have come back to the land of the Armenians, driving their donkeys with them, they build more boats in the same way.

195. So much for their boats. Here is how they dress. They wear a linen tunic that reaches to the feet, over it another tunic of wool, and over that a white cloak wrapped around them. Their shoes are of a local style, rather like the slippers worn in Boeotia. They wear their hair long and tie bands around their heads, and they rub perfume all over their bodies. Each man has a seal and a hand-carved staff, and on every staff a design is carved: an apple, a rose, a lily, an eagle or something else. For it is not their custom to carry a staff without a design on it.

196. That is how they equip themselves. Their established customs are as follows. The wisest of them, in my opinion, is this one, which I am told the Eneti in Illyria also have. Once a year, in every village, it used to be done like this. When the girls reached the age for marriage, they gathered them all together and brought them as a group to one place, and a crowd of men stood around them. The auctioneer had each girl stand up in turn and put her up for sale. He started with the best-looking of all. Then, when she had been sold for a large sum of money, he would put up the next best-looking after her. They were sold to be married. All the rich Babylonians who were ready to marry would bid against one another for the most beautiful girls. But the ordinary men who were ready to marry had no need of good looks; they would take money along with a plainer girl. For when the auctioneer had finished selling the best-looking girls, he would stand up the least attractive one, or any who was crippled in some way, and announce her for sale, asking who would take her in marriage for the least amount of gold. She went to the man who was willing to accept the smallest sum. The gold came from the sale of the good-looking girls, so the beautiful ones provided dowries for the plain and the crippled. No man was allowed to marry off his own daughter to whomever he pleased, and no buyer was allowed to take a girl away without a guarantee. He had to put up guarantors that he would marry her before he could take her away, and if the couple did not get along, the law said he had to pay the money back. Anyone who wanted to could also come from another village and buy. This, then, was their finest custom. But it no longer exists in our time. Lately they have hit upon another way of doing things, so that the men will not mistreat the girls or take them off to another city. Ever since they were conquered and were oppressed and ruined, every man of the common people who has nothing to live on puts his daughters to work as prostitutes.

197. Next in wisdom after that is this other custom of theirs. They carry their sick out into the marketplace, since they make no use of doctors. People come up to the sick man and give him advice about his illness, if they have ever had anything like what he has themselves, or seen someone else who had it. They come up and advise him and recommend whatever treatment cured them of a similar illness, or cured someone else they saw. And no one is allowed to walk past the sick man in silence without asking what illness he has.

198. They bury their dead in honey, and their ways of mourning are similar to those in Egypt. Whenever a Babylonian man has had sex with his wife, he sits beside burning incense, and his wife does the same on the other side. In the morning they both wash, for they will not touch any vessel until they have washed. The Arabians do the same in this matter.

199. The most shameful of the Babylonians' customs is this. Every woman of the country must, once in her life, sit in the sacred precinct of Aphrodite and have sex with a stranger. Many women who are too proud to mix with the rest, because their wealth makes them arrogant, drive to the temple in covered carriages drawn by pairs of horses and take their places there, with a large crowd of servants following them. But most do it this way. In the sacred enclosure of Aphrodite great numbers of women sit with a wreath of cord around their heads; some are arriving and others leaving. Straight passageways run between the women in every direction, and the strangers walk along them and make their choice. Once a woman has taken her seat there, she does not go home again until one of the strangers has thrown a silver coin into her lap and had sex with her outside the temple. When he throws the coin he must say only these words: "I call on you in the name of the goddess Mylitta." Mylitta is the Assyrians' name for Aphrodite. The coin may be of any value. Whatever it is, she will not refuse it, for that is not lawful for her, since the act makes the coin sacred. She goes with the first man who throws a coin, and rejects no one. After that she goes home, having done her duty to the goddess, and from then on you could not offer her a gift big enough to win her. So the women who are tall and beautiful are soon released, but the plain ones stay there a long time, unable to fulfill the law; some of them stay as long as three or four years. In some parts of Cyprus, too, there is a custom like this one.

200. Those, then, are the established customs of the Babylonians. There are also three tribes among them that eat nothing but fish. When they have caught the fish and dried them in the sun, this is what they do: they throw them into brine, then pound them with pestles and strain them through fine cloth. They eat them either kneaded into a soft cake or baked like bread, as each one likes.

201. When Cyrus had conquered this nation too, he wanted to bring the Massagetae under his rule. This nation is said to be both large and warlike. They live toward the east, where the sun rises, beyond the river Araxes and opposite the Issedonians. Some also say that this nation is Scythian.

202. Some say the Araxes is larger than the Danube (which the Greeks call the Ister) and others that it is smaller. They say there are many islands in it about the size of Lesbos, and that people live on them who in summer eat roots of every kind, which they dig up. They have also found certain fruits on trees good to eat, and they store these up, it is said, in the season when they are ripe and live on them in the winter. It is also said that they have found other trees with a fruit of a special kind. They gather in groups in one place, light a fire, sit around it in a circle, and throw some of this fruit onto the fire. They breathe in the smell of the fruit as it burns and get drunk on the scent, as the Greeks get drunk on wine. The more fruit is thrown on, the drunker they get, until at last they get up to dance and start to sing. That, it is said, is how they live. As for the river Araxes, it flows from the land of the Matieni, the same place the Gyndes flows from, the river Cyrus divided into three hundred and sixty channels. It empties through forty mouths, and all of these but one end in swamps and shallow pools. They say that men live among these marshes who eat raw fish and usually dress in sealskins. But the one remaining mouth of the Araxes flows in a clear channel into the Caspian Sea.

203. The Caspian Sea is a sea on its own, not connected with the other sea. For the whole sea that the Greeks sail, and the sea beyond the Pillars of Heracles (the strait at the western end of the Mediterranean) that is called the Atlantic, and the Erythraean Sea, the Indian Ocean, are in fact all one. But the Caspian is separate and lies apart by itself. Its length is a voyage of fifteen days for a rowed ship, and its breadth, at its broadest, a voyage of eight days. Along its western side runs the Caucasus, the largest of all mountain ranges in extent and the highest. Many different peoples live in the Caucasus, mostly on the wild food of the forests. Among them, it is said, there are trees whose leaves have a special property: they pound them and mix them with water, and with this they paint figures on their clothes. The figures do not wash out, but wear out along with the wool, as if they had been woven into it from the start. And people say these tribes have sex in the open, like cattle.

204. So on the west of the sea called the Caspian, the Caucasus is the boundary, while to the east, toward the rising sun, comes a plain that stretches as far as the eye can see. The Massagetae hold a large part of this great plain, and it was against them that Cyrus was now eager to march. There were many strong reasons urging him on. The first was his birth, that is, the belief that he was something more than an ordinary mortal. The next was the good fortune he had had in his wars, for wherever Cyrus marched, no nation could escape him.

205. The ruler of the Massagetae was a woman, who had become queen after her husband's death, and her name was Tomyris. Cyrus sent to her and courted her, pretending he wanted to marry her. But Tomyris understood that it was not her he was courting but the kingdom of the Massagetae, and she turned down his advances. After this, since trickery got him nowhere, Cyrus marched to the Araxes and began an open campaign against the Massagetae. He built bridges of boats across the river for his army to cross, and put up towers on the boats that were to carry them over.

206. While he was busy with this work, Tomyris sent a herald with this message: "King of the Medes, stop pushing ahead with the work you are pushing ahead with now. You cannot know whether it will turn out to your advantage in the end. Stop, I tell you, and be king over your own people, and put up with seeing us rule the people we rule. But I know you will not want to take this advice, since you would choose anything rather than stay at peace. So if you are so very eager to try your strength against the Massagetae, come on: give up the labor of yoking the river's banks together. We will first withdraw a three days' journey from the river, and then you cross over into our land. Or if you would rather receive us in your land, do the same thing yourself." When Cyrus heard this, he called together the leading men of the Persians and, once they were gathered, put the matter before them for discussion, asking their advice on which of the two he should do. Their opinions all agreed: they told him to let Tomyris and her army come into his own country.

207. But Croesus the Lydian, who was there, found fault with this opinion and declared the opposite view. He said: "My king, I told you before that since Zeus had handed me over to you, I would do all I could to turn aside any fall I saw coming toward your house. And my sufferings, bitter as they have been, have taught me wisdom. If you think you are immortal, and that the army you command is immortal too, there is no point in my telling you what I think. But if you have realized that you are a mortal man yourself, and that the men you command are mortal too, then learn this first: human affairs turn on a wheel, and as it turns it does not let the same people be fortunate forever. So I hold an opinion on the matter before us that is the opposite of theirs. If we agree to let the enemy into our land, this is the danger for you. If you are beaten, you will lose your whole empire besides, because it is clear that if the Massagetae win, they will not turn back and run home; they will march on the provinces of your empire. On the other hand, if you win, your victory will not be as complete as if you had beaten the Massagetae after crossing into their land and then chased them as they fled. For I will set the same argument against the other side and say that once you have won, you will march straight on the kingdom of Tomyris. And besides all that, it would be a disgrace, not to be borne, for Cyrus son of Cambyses to give way to a woman and retreat from her land. So my advice is that we cross over, go forward from the crossing as far as they fall back, and then try to get the better of them like this. The Massagetae, I am told, have no experience of the good things Persians enjoy, and they have never had any great luxuries. So slaughter cattle without stinting, cook the meat, and lay out a feast for these men in our camp. Provide bowls of unmixed wine without stinting too, and food of every kind. When you have done that, leave behind the weakest part of your army and let the rest start to fall back from the camp toward the river. For unless I am mistaken, when they see all those good things they will fall on the feast, and after that it will be up to us to show what we can do."

208. Those were the two opposing opinions. Cyrus dropped the first one and chose Croesus' plan. He told Tomyris to withdraw, since he meant to cross over to her. She withdrew, as she had promised at first. But Cyrus put Croesus in the hands of his son Cambyses, to whom he meant to leave the kingdom, and strictly charged him to honor Croesus and treat him well if the crossing against the Massagetae should go badly. After giving these orders and sending the two of them away to Persia, he crossed the river himself with his army.

209. When he had crossed the Araxes and night had fallen, he had a dream as he slept in the land of the Massagetae. In his sleep Cyrus seemed to see the eldest of the sons of Hystaspes with wings on his shoulders, and with one of them he overshadowed Asia and with the other Europe. Now Hystaspes son of Arsames was a man of the Achaemenid clan, and his eldest son was Darius, who was then, I suppose, a young man of about twenty. He had been left behind in Persia, since he was not yet old enough to go to war. So when Cyrus woke up, he thought the dream over, and since it seemed to him to mean something important, he called Hystaspes, took him aside alone, and said: "Hystaspes, your son has been caught plotting against me and my throne. I will tell you how I know this for certain. The gods watch over me and show me in advance every danger that threatens me. Last night as I slept I saw the eldest of your sons with wings on his shoulders, and with one of them he overshadowed Asia and with the other Europe. Going by this dream, there is no way he is not plotting against me. So go back to Persia by the quickest road, and make sure that when I return there after conquering these lands, you bring your son before me to be questioned."

210. Cyrus said this because he thought Darius was plotting against him. But in fact the divine powers were showing him in advance that he was fated to die there and that his kingdom was going to pass to Darius. Hystaspes answered him like this: "My king, heaven forbid there should be any Persian born who would plot against you, and if there is one, I pray he dies as quickly as possible. For you made the Persians free men instead of slaves, and rulers of all nations instead of subjects of others. And if a dream tells you that my son is planning a rebellion against you, I hand him over to you to do with as you please."

211. With that answer Hystaspes crossed back over the Araxes and set off for Persia to keep watch over his son Darius for Cyrus. Cyrus, meanwhile, went forward a day's march from the Araxes, as Croesus had suggested. After this, Cyrus and the best part of the Persian army marched back to the Araxes, leaving behind the men unfit to fight. Then a third of the army of the Massagetae attacked and began killing the men Cyrus had left behind, who put up some resistance. When they had overcome their enemies and saw the feast laid out, they lay down and ate, and when they were stuffed with food and wine they fell asleep. Then the Persians came down on them. They killed many, and took even more prisoner than they killed. Among the prisoners was the son of Queen Tomyris, who was leading the army of the Massagetae; his name was Spargapises.

212. When she heard what had happened to her army and to her son, she sent a herald to Cyrus with this message: "Cyrus, you who can never get enough of blood, do not be puffed up by what has happened. It was the fruit of the vine that did it, the wine you fill yourselves with until you go mad, so that as the wine goes down into your bodies, ugly words come floating up. It was by setting a trap, I tell you, with a drug like that, that you beat my son, and not by courage in battle. So now take the advice I give you, and it is good advice. Give me back my son and leave this land unpunished, having triumphed over a third of the army of the Massagetae. If you will not, I swear to you by the Sun, the lord of the Massagetae, that I will give you your fill of blood, greedy for it as you are."

213. When this message was brought to Cyrus, he paid no attention to it. As for Spargapises, the son of Queen Tomyris, when the wine wore off and he understood how bad his situation was, he begged Cyrus to have his chains taken off, and Cyrus granted it. But as soon as he was free and had the use of his hands, he killed himself.

214. That was how he died. Tomyris, since Cyrus would not listen to her, gathered all her forces and fought a battle with him. Of all the battles ever fought between non-Greeks, I judge this one to have been the fiercest, and I am told it went like this. First, it is said, they stood at a distance and shot arrows at each other. Then, when their arrows were all used up, they charged and fought hand to hand with spears and daggers. They went on fighting like this for a long time, and neither side would run. But in the end the Massagetae won. Most of the Persian army was destroyed on the spot, and Cyrus himself died there, after reigning twenty-nine years in all. Then Tomyris filled a skin bag with human blood and had the Persian dead searched for Cyrus' body. When she found it, she pushed his head down into the skin, and as she defiled the corpse she said: "I am alive and I have beaten you in battle, and yet you destroyed me by taking my son through trickery. But I will give you your fill of blood, as I threatened." Many stories are told about the end of Cyrus' life, but this one I have told seems to me the most believable.

215. As for the Massagetae, they dress like the Scythians and live like them too. Some of them are horsemen and some do not ride (they follow both ways), and there are archers among them as well as spearmen. It is their custom to carry battle-axes. For everything they use either gold or bronze. For spear points, arrowheads and battle-axes they use bronze, but they decorate their headdresses, belts and the straps they wear around their armpits with gold. In the same way, they put bronze breastplates on their horses' chests, but use gold on their bridles, bits and cheek-pieces. They use no iron or silver at all, because there is none in their country, but they have gold and bronze in plenty.

216. These are their customs. Each man marries a wife, but they share their wives in common. The Greeks say the Scythians do this, but in fact it is not the Scythians who do it but the Massagetae: whenever a man of the Massagetae wants a woman, he hangs his quiver up in front of her wagon and has sex with her freely. They set no fixed limit to a man's life. But when a man grows very old, his closest relatives all come together and kill him as a sacrifice, along with some cattle, and then they boil the meat and feast on it. They consider this the happiest end. A man who has died of disease they do not eat; they bury him in the ground and count it a misfortune that he did not live to be sacrificed. They sow no crops but live on cattle and fish, which they get in plenty from the river Araxes, and they are milk drinkers. The only god they worship is the Sun, and they sacrifice horses to him. The idea behind the sacrifice is this: to the swiftest of the gods they give the swiftest of all mortal things.

Book Two: Euterpe

Chapter 9: The Oldest People, and the Land and River of Egypt

1. When Cyrus came to the end of his life, Cambyses took over the royal power after him. He was the son of Cyrus and of Cassandane, the daughter of Pharnaspes. She had died before Cyrus did, and Cyrus had mourned her deeply himself and had also ordered all the peoples he ruled to go into mourning for her. Cambyses, then, the son of this woman and of Cyrus, looked on the Ionians and the Aeolians as slaves he had inherited from his father. He began to march an army against Egypt, and as his helpers he took with him not only the other nations he ruled but also those of the Greeks who were under his power.

2. Now before Psammetichus became their king, the Egyptians used to believe that they were the first of all people to come into being. But ever since Psammetichus became king and wanted to know which people really had come first, they have believed that the Phrygians came into being before them, though they themselves came before everyone else. Psammetichus had not been able to find any way of learning, by asking questions, who the first people were, so he came up with a scheme. He took two newborn children belonging to ordinary people and gave them to a shepherd to raise among his flocks. He told him how they were to be raised: no one was to say a single word in their presence; they were to lie by themselves in a room where no one could come in; at the proper times he was to bring goats to them; and when he had filled them up with milk, he was to do whatever else they needed. Psammetichus did this, and gave the shepherd these orders, because he wanted to hear what word the children would burst out with first, once they had stopped their meaningless crying. And that is just what happened. After two years had passed, with the shepherd carrying on in this way, one day he opened the door and went in, and both children fell down in front of him, stretched out their hands, and said the word "bekos." At first, when he heard this, the shepherd kept quiet about it. But the word came again and again whenever he visited them and looked after them, which he did constantly. So at last he told his master about it, and at the king's command he brought the children before him. Psammetichus heard the word himself, and then he began to inquire which nation of men called anything "bekos." In the course of his inquiries he found that it was the Phrygians' word for bread. In this way, and on the strength of this evidence, the Egyptians came to admit that the Phrygians were an older people than they were.

3. That this is how it happened I heard from the priests of Hephaestus at Memphis. The Greeks, though, tell many other silly stories, and one of them is that Psammetichus cut out the tongues of certain women and then had the children live with these women.

So much, then, for what they told me about the raising of the children. But I heard other things too at Memphis, when I talked with the priests of Hephaestus. I also went to Thebes and to Heliopolis for this very reason: I wanted to know whether the priests in those places would agree with the account of the priests at Memphis, since the men of Heliopolis are said to be the most learned in history of all the Egyptians. As for the stories I heard about the gods, I am not eager to tell them in full. I will only mention their names, because I think all people know equally little about such things. Whatever I do record about them I will record only because the course of my story forces me to.

4. But about human affairs the priests all agreed with one another. They said the Egyptians were the first people on earth to discover the course of the year, dividing it into twelve parts to make up the whole. They said they found this out from the stars. And in my opinion they calculate more wisely than the Greeks do. The Greeks throw in an extra month every other year to keep the seasons in line, while the Egyptians count twelve months of thirty days each and then add five days every year beyond that number, and so the circle of their seasons comes round to the same point it started from. They also said that the Egyptians were the first to use names for the twelve gods, and that the Greeks took the practice over from them; and that they were the first to give the gods altars and statues and temples, and the first to carve figures in stone. For most of these things they showed me actual proof that it was so. They said, too, that the first man to become king of Egypt was Min. In his time, they said, all of Egypt except the district of Thebes was a swamp, and none of the land that now lies below Lake Moeris was above water then. That lake is a seven days' voyage up the river from the sea.

5. And I thought what they said about the land was right. For it is plain to anyone who sees it, even if he has not heard it beforehand, as long as he has any sense, that the Egypt that Greek ships sail to is land the Egyptians have been given as an addition: it is a gift of the river. The same is true of the country above this lake for a distance of three days' sail, though they did not go on to say anything of the kind about it. That too is another example of the same thing. For this is what the land of Egypt is like. First, when you are still approaching it by ship and are a day's run from land, if you let down a sounding line you will bring up mud, and you will find yourself in sixty-six feet of water. This much shows that the land is being built out forward into the sea.

6. Second, there is Egypt itself. Its length along the sea is sixty schoeni, taking Egypt, as we define it, to stretch from the Gulf of Plinthine to Lake Serbonis, along which Mount Casius runs. It is from this lake that the sixty schoeni are measured. For people who have little land measure their country in fathoms (a fathom is six feet); those who are less poor in land, in stades (a stade is six hundred feet); those who have a lot of land, in parasangs; and those who have land in great abundance, in schoeni. A parasang equals thirty stades, about three and a third miles, and a schoenus, which is an Egyptian measure, equals sixty stades, about six and two-thirds miles. So the coastline of Egypt would be 3,600 stades long, about four hundred miles.

7. From there inland as far as Heliopolis, Egypt is broad. The land is all flat, without springs, and made of mud. The road inland from the sea up to Heliopolis is about the same length as the road from the altar of the twelve gods at Athens to Pisa and the temple of Olympian Zeus. If you worked it out, you would find that the difference between these two roads is very small, no more than a mile and two-thirds. The road from Athens to Pisa falls short of about 167 miles by that much, while the road from the sea to Heliopolis comes to the full 167.

8. From Heliopolis on up, though, Egypt is narrow. On one side a range of mountains belonging to Arabia runs alongside it, stretching from the north toward the south, where the noonday sun and the south wind are, and running on upward without a break to the sea called the Erythraean, the Indian Ocean. In this range are the stone quarries that were used to cut the stone for the pyramids at Memphis. On this side, then, the mountains end where I said, and then they turn back. Where the range is widest, as I was told, it is a two months' journey across from east to west, and its eastern edges are said to produce frankincense. That is what this mountain range is like. On the Libyan side of Egypt another range stretches out, rocky and covered in sand. The pyramids are in this range, and it runs in the same direction as the part of the Arabian mountains that goes toward the south. So, from Heliopolis on, the land that belongs to Egypt is no longer very wide. For about four days' sail up the river, Egypt proper is narrow. The land between the mountain ranges I have mentioned is level plain, but where it is narrowest it did not seem to me to be more than about twenty-two miles across, from the Arabian mountains to the ones called the Libyan. After this Egypt widens out again.

9. That is what this land is like. From Heliopolis to Thebes is a nine days' voyage up the river, and the distance is about 540 miles, or eighty-one schoeni. If you add up these measurements of Egypt, the result is as follows. I have already shown that the distance along the sea comes to about four hundred miles. Now I will tell you the distance inland from the sea to Thebes: it is about 680 miles. And from Thebes to the city called Elephantine is another two hundred miles.

10. As for most of this land I have been describing, I too thought, just as the priests said, that it had been won by the Egyptians as an addition. It was clear to me that the space between the mountain ranges I mentioned, the ones above the city of Memphis, was once a gulf of the sea. It was like the country around Troy and Teuthrania and Ephesus and the plain of the Maeander, if I may compare small things with great. And small those places are by comparison, since none of the rivers that piled up the soil in those regions deserves to be compared in volume with even one of the mouths of the Nile, and the Nile has five mouths. There are other rivers too, not at all equal to the Nile in size, that have done great things. I could name several, and above all the Achelous, which flows through Acarnania and out into the sea and has already turned half of the Echinades islands into mainland.

11. Now in Arabia, not far from Egypt, there is a gulf that runs in from the sea called the Erythraean. It is very long and narrow, as I am about to explain. As for its length, someone setting out from its innermost point to sail out through it into the open sea would spend forty days on the voyage, rowing. As for its width, where the gulf is broadest it is half a day's sail across. And it has a tide that ebbs and flows every day. I believe Egypt was once another gulf just like this one. The one ran in from the northern sea, the Mediterranean, toward Ethiopia. The other, the Arabian Gulf that I am describing, our Red Sea, ran from the south toward Syria. The two gulfs bored inland until their ends almost met, passing alongside each other with only a little space left between them. So if the Nile were to turn aside and flow into this Arabian Gulf, what would stop the river from filling that gulf up with silt as it kept on flowing, within twenty thousand years at any rate? For my part, I think it would be filled up within ten thousand. So in all the ages that passed before I was born, why should a gulf even much bigger than this one not have been filled up by a river so great and so hard-working?

12. So as for Egypt, I believe the people who say that this is how things are, and I am also strongly convinced of it myself. I have seen that Egypt juts out into the sea farther than the land on either side of it. Shells are found on its mountains. A crust of salt forms on the surface of the ground, so that even the pyramids are being eaten away by it. And of all the mountains of Egypt, the range above Memphis is the only one that has sand. Besides this, I notice that Egypt is not like the land of Arabia that borders it, nor like Libya, nor like Syria (it is Syrians who live in the parts of Arabia along the sea). Its soil is black and crumbles easily, because it really is mud and silt brought down from Ethiopia by the river. The soil of Libya, as we know, is reddish and rather sandy, while the soil of Arabia and Syria is more clay and rock.

13. The priests also gave me strong evidence about this land. In the reign of King Moeris, they said, whenever the river rose at least twelve feet it watered Egypt below Memphis. And when I heard this from the priests, not yet nine hundred years had passed since Moeris died. Now, though, unless the river rises twenty-four feet, or twenty-two and a half at the very least, it does not spread over the land. I think too that if that land keeps on growing in height at this rate, and keeps on increasing in area in the same way, then the Egyptians who live below Lake Moeris, especially in the region called the Delta, will suffer for all time to come, once the Nile no longer floods their land, the very thing they themselves said would one day happen to the Greeks. For when they heard that the whole land of the Greeks is watered by rain and not by rivers as theirs is, they said that someday the Greeks would be cheated of a great hope and would suffer terribly from famine. What this saying means is that if the god does not send them rain, but lets a drought go on for a long time, the Greeks will be wiped out by hunger, since in fact they have no other source of water to save them except Zeus alone.

14. That was a fair thing for the Egyptians to say about the Greeks. But now let me explain how things stand with the Egyptians themselves. If, as I said before, their land below Memphis (for this is the land that is growing) keeps on rising at the same rate as in the past, then certainly the Egyptians who live there will go hungry, since their land gets no rain and the river will not be able to spread over their fields. It is true, though, that at present they gather the fruits of the earth with less work than any other people, and with less work than the rest of the Egyptians too. They don't have to labor at breaking up furrows with a plow, or hoeing, or any of the other jobs that other people do to raise a crop. Instead, when the river has risen of its own accord and watered their fields, and after watering them has gone down again, each man sows his own field and turns pigs loose on it. When the pigs have trampled the seed into the ground, he waits for the harvest. Then he has the pigs thresh the grain, and so he gathers it in.

15. Suppose we wanted to follow the opinion of the Ionians about Egypt. They say that the Delta alone is Egypt. They count its coastline as running from what is called the Watchtower of Perseus to the fish-salting works of Pelusium, a distance of forty schoeni, about 267 miles, and they count it as reaching inland as far as the city of Cercasorus, where the Nile divides and runs to Pelusium and to Canopus. The rest of Egypt they assign partly to Libya and partly to Arabia. If, I say, we followed this account, we would be declaring that in earlier times the Egyptians had no land to live in at all. For, as we have seen, their Delta at least is land laid down by the river, and it has appeared only lately, so to speak, as the Egyptians themselves say and as I believe. So if at first there was no land for them to live in, why did they waste their effort trying to prove that they had come into being before all other people? They had no need to test the children to see what language they would speak first. But I do not believe that the Egyptians came into being at the same time as what the Ionians call the Delta. I believe they have always existed, ever since the human race came into being, and that as their land moved forward, many of them stayed behind in their first homes while many others gradually came down into the lower country. At any rate it is certain that in old times Thebes was called Egypt, and the distance around Thebes measures about 680 miles.

16. If our judgment on these matters is right, then the Ionians' opinion about Egypt is not sound. But if the Ionians' judgment is right, then I say that neither the Greeks nor the Ionians themselves know how to count. They say that the whole earth is made up of three parts, Europe, Asia and Libya. But by that reckoning they ought to count the Delta of Egypt as a fourth, since it belongs neither to Asia nor to Libya. For by their reckoning it cannot be the river Nile that divides Asia from Libya. The Nile splits at the point of the Delta and flows around it on both sides, and so this land would lie between Asia and Libya.

17. So we set aside the opinion of the Ionians and give a judgment of our own on this question as well. Egypt, we say, is all the land where Egyptians live, just as Cilicia is the land where Cilicians live and Assyria the land where Assyrians live. And we know of no boundary between Asia and Libya, properly speaking, except the borders of Egypt. But if we adopt the opinion the Greeks generally hold, we must suppose that the whole of Egypt, starting from the Cataract and the city of Elephantine, is split in two and so takes a share of both names, one side belonging to Libya and the other to Asia. For from the Cataract onward the Nile flows to the sea cutting Egypt down the middle. As far as the city of Cercasorus the Nile flows in a single stream, but from that city on it splits three ways. One branch, called the Pelusian mouth, turns east. The second branch heads west, and this is called the Canopic mouth. But the branch that runs straight on goes like this: when the river, flowing downward, comes to the point of the Delta, it cuts through the middle of the Delta and so runs out to the sea. This branch carries a share of the river's water that is neither the smallest nor the least famous, and it is called the Sebennytic mouth. There are also two other mouths that split off from the Sebennytic and run to the sea, and these are called the Saitic and the Mendesian. The Bolbitinic and Bucolic mouths, on the other hand, are not natural; they were dug.

18. The answer given by the oracle of Ammon, out in the Libyan desert, also bears out my opinion that Egypt is as large as I make it out to be in my account. And I heard about this answer only after I had formed my own opinion about Egypt. The people of the cities of Marea and Apis, who live in the part of Egypt that borders on Libya, believed that they themselves were Libyans and not Egyptians. They also found the rules of the Egyptian religion a burden, because they did not want to be forbidden to eat beef. So they sent to Ammon, saying that they had nothing in common with the Egyptians, since they lived outside the Delta and agreed with them about nothing, and they said they wanted to be allowed to eat everything without restriction. But the god would not allow them to do so. He said that Egypt was all the land that the Nile spread over and watered, and that Egyptians were all those who lived below the city of Elephantine and drank from that river. That was the answer the oracle gave them about this.

19. And when the Nile is in flood, it spreads not only over the Delta but also over parts of the land called Libyan and the land called Arabian, sometimes as far as two days' journey on each side, and at times even more than this, or at times less.

As for the nature of the river, I could not learn anything about it, either from the priests or from anyone else. And I was especially eager to learn from them about these things: why the Nile comes down rising in volume for a hundred days, starting from the summer solstice, and then, when it has reached that number of days, turns back and goes down again, its stream failing, so that it stays low all through the winter until the summer solstice comes round again.
