I could not get any explanation of any of this from the Egyptians, when I asked them what power the Nile has that makes it behave the opposite way from other rivers. I also asked because I wanted to know, besides what I have just said, why it is the only river that sends out no breezes blowing off it.

20. However, some Greeks who wanted to make a name for themselves for cleverness have explained this water in three different ways. Two of these I do not think worth even talking about, except to point out what they are. One of them says that the Etesian winds, the steady north winds of summer, are what make the river rise, by keeping the Nile from flowing out into the sea. But the Etesian winds often fail, and the Nile still does its usual work. Besides, if these winds were the cause, then all the other rivers that flow against the Etesian winds should have been affected in the same way as the Nile, and even more so, since they are smaller and push against the winds with a weaker current. But there are many such rivers in Syria and many in Libya too, and none of them behaves at all like the Nile.

21. The second explanation is even more ignorant than the one I have mentioned, and more of a marvel to tell. It says that the river does these things because it flows from the Ocean, and that the Ocean flows around the whole earth.

22. The third explanation sounds by far the most convincing, but it is the most mistaken of all. In fact it has no more truth in it than the others. It claims that the Nile flows from melting snow, when in fact it flows out of Libya through the middle of the Ethiopians and so comes out into Egypt. So how could it flow from snow, when it flows from the hottest places to cooler ones? Most of the facts are enough to convince a man, at least one who is capable of reasoning about such things, that it is not at all likely to flow from snow. The first and greatest piece of evidence is the winds, which blow hot from those regions. The second is that the land never has rain or frost, whereas after snow falls, rain must come within five days; so if it snowed in those parts, it would rain there. The third piece of evidence is the people who live there, who are dark-skinned because of the burning heat. On top of that, kites and swallows stay there all year round and never leave the country, and cranes fleeing the cold weather that comes on in the region of Scythia come regularly to these parts to spend the winter. So if it snowed even a little in the land the Nile flows through and where it rises, none of these things would happen, as the facts force us to admit.

23. As for the man who talked about the Ocean, he has carried his story off into the unknown, and so there is no need to refute him. For my part, I know of no river called Ocean. I think Homer, or one of the poets before him, invented the name and brought it into his poetry.

24. But if, after finding fault with the opinions others have put forward, I must give an opinion of my own on these puzzling questions, I will say what I think is the reason the Nile rises in summer. In the winter the Sun is driven out of his old path through the sky by the storm winds, and he comes to the upper parts of Libya. To put it as briefly as possible, that is the whole explanation. For whatever country this god comes closest to and stands directly over, that country, it is reasonable to suppose, is the most in need of water, and its own rivers dry up the most.

25. But to explain it at greater length, it works like this. As the Sun passes over the upper parts of Libya, this is what he does. The air in those parts is always clear and the land is always warm, since there are no cold winds, and so as he passes through it the Sun does just what he usually does in summer, when he travels through the middle of the sky. That is, he draws the water up to himself, and when he has drawn it up he drives it away to the upper parts of the country, and the winds catch it up, scatter it, and turn it into rain. So it is natural that the winds that blow from this region, the south and southwest winds, should be by far the rainiest of all winds. I think, though, that the Sun does not send away from himself all the water he draws each year from the Nile, but keeps some of it with him. Then, when the winter grows milder, the Sun goes back again to the middle of the sky, and from then on he draws water equally from all rivers. In the meantime, though, these other rivers flow full, because a great deal of rainwater mixes with them, since their country gets rain then and is full of torrents. In summer, however, they are weak, because the rain fails them and the Sun is drawing on them as well. But the Nile, the only river that gets no rain and is drawn on by the Sun all winter, naturally flows during that time with much less than its proper volume, much less than in summer. For in summer it is drawn on equally with all the other waters, but in winter it carries the burden alone. So I believe that the Sun is the cause of all this.

26. The Sun is also, in my opinion, the reason the air in those parts is dry, since he dries it out by scorching his path through the sky. So in the upper parts of Libya it is always summer. But suppose the stations of the seasons had been switched around. Suppose that where the north wind and winter now stand in the sky, there stood the south wind and the noonday, and where the south wind now stands, there stood the north. If that were so, then the Sun, driven out of the middle of the sky by winter and the north wind, would go to the upper parts of Europe, just as he now comes to the upper parts of Libya. And as he passed over the whole of Europe, I believe he would do to the Danube what he now does to the Nile.

27. As for the breeze, and why none blows off the river, my opinion is that nothing would naturally blow from very hot places, and that a breeze usually blows from something cold.

28. Let these things be, then, as they are and as they were from the beginning. But as for the sources of the Nile, not one of the Egyptians or Libyans or Greeks who talked with me claimed to know anything about them, except the scribe who kept the sacred treasury of Athena in the city of Sais in Egypt. And even this man seemed to me to be joking when he said he knew for certain. Here is what he said. There were two mountains with sharply pointed peaks, standing between the city of Syene, in the district of Thebes, and Elephantine. The names of the mountains were Crophi and Mophi. From between these two mountains, he said, flowed the springs of the Nile, which were bottomless. Half of the water flowed to Egypt and the north, and the other half to Ethiopia and the south. As for the springs being bottomless, he said that Psammetichus, king of Egypt, had put this to the test. He had a rope twisted many thousands of fathoms long, tens of thousands of feet, and let it down there, and it found no bottom. By this the scribe gave me to understand (if what he told me was really true) that there were powerful whirlpools there and a current flowing back on itself, and that because the water was dashing against the mountains, the sounding line could not get to the bottom when it was let down.

29. I was not able to learn anything about this from anyone else. But I learned as much as follows by the most careful inquiry, going as far as the city of Elephantine and seeing for myself, and from there on gathering what I know by hearsay. As you go up the river from the city of Elephantine, the country climbs steeply. So here you have to tie ropes to both sides of the boat, the way you would harness an ox, and make your way on like that. If the rope breaks, the boat is gone at once, swept away by the force of the current. This stretch takes about four days to sail through. In this part the Nile winds like the river Maeander, and the distance you have to travel in this way is twelve schoeni, about eighty miles. Then you come to a level plain, where the Nile flows around an island called Tachompso. (In the country above Elephantine, Ethiopians begin to live right away; they hold half of the island, and Egyptians the other half.) Next to this island there is a great lake, with nomad Ethiopian tribes living all around it. When you have sailed across this, you come to the stream of the Nile again, which flows into the lake. After this you get out and travel overland for forty days, because sharp rocks stick up out of the water in the Nile and there are many reefs, so that no boat can get through. Then, after you have crossed this country in the forty days I mentioned, you get on board another boat and sail for twelve days, and after that you come to a great city called Meroe. This city is said to be the mother city of all the other Ethiopians. The people who live there worship Zeus and Dionysus alone of the gods, and honor them greatly. They have an oracle of Zeus established there, and they go to war whenever this god commands them through his prophecies, and wherever he commands them to go.

30. Sailing on from this city, you will come to the "Deserters" in the same length of time again as it took you to get from Elephantine to the mother city of the Ethiopians. The name of these "Deserters" is the Asmach, and this word means, in Greek, "those who stand on the king's left hand." They were 240,000 Egyptians of the warrior class who revolted and went over to the Ethiopians, and this is why. In the reign of Psammetichus garrisons were posted: one at the city of Elephantine against the Ethiopians, another at Daphnae of Pelusium against the Arabians and Assyrians, and another at Marea against Libya. Even in my own time the Persians keep their garrisons posted in the same way as they were in the reign of Psammetichus, since the Persians have outposts both at Elephantine and at Daphnae. Now the Egyptians I am speaking of had been on guard duty for three years, and no one had come to relieve them. So they talked it over among themselves, agreed on a plan, revolted from Psammetichus all together, and set off for Ethiopia. When he heard this, Psammetichus went after them. When he caught up with them, he pleaded with them at length and tried to persuade them not to abandon the gods of their country and their children and wives. At that, the story goes, one of them pointed to his genitals and said that wherever these were, there they would have both children and wives. When they reached Ethiopia, they put themselves at the service of the king of the Ethiopians, and he rewarded them like this. There were certain Ethiopians who had quarreled with him, and he told the Egyptians to drive these people out and live in their land. And since these men settled among the Ethiopians, the Ethiopians have become gentler in their ways, having learned the customs of the Egyptians.

31. So, besides the part of its course that lies in Egypt, the Nile is known as far as a four months' journey by river and land. That is how many months you find, if you count them up, are spent in going from Elephantine to these "Deserters." And there the river flows from the west, from the setting of the sun. But what lies beyond that, no one can say for sure, because that country is desert on account of the burning heat.

32. This much, though, I heard from some men of Cyrene. They told me they had gone to the oracle of Ammon and had talked with Etearchus, king of the Ammonians. After talking about other things, it happened, they got onto the subject of the Nile, and how no one knew its sources. And Etearchus told them that once some men of the Nasamonians had come to him. (This is a Libyan people that lives in the Syrtis and in the land a short way to the east of the Syrtis.) When the Nasamonians arrived, he asked them whether they could tell him anything more than he knew about the desert parts of Libya. They told him that there had been among them some sons of chief men, unruly young fellows. When they grew up, these young men came up with various wild schemes, and among other things they chose five of their number by lot to go and look at the deserts of Libya, and see whether they could discover more than those who had explored the farthest before them. For along the part of Libya that lies on the northern sea, from Egypt as far as Cape Soloeis, which is the farthest point of Libya, Libyans live all along the whole coast, many peoples of them, except for what the Greeks and Phoenicians hold. But in the upper parts, above the seacoast and above the peoples whose land comes down to the sea, Libya is full of wild beasts. And beyond the land of wild beasts it is all sand, terribly waterless and utterly desert. So these young men (the Nasamonians said), sent off by their companions well supplied with water and food, first went through the inhabited country. When they had passed through that, they came to the country of wild beasts, and after that they crossed the desert, traveling westward, toward the west wind. They crossed a great stretch of sand over many days, and at last they saw trees growing on a level plain. They went up to them and began to pick the fruit that was on the trees. But just as they started picking it, some small men came at them, men shorter than average, and seized them and carried them off. The Nasamonians could not understand a word these people said, and their captors could not understand a word of the Nasamonians' speech either. They led them (so the story went) through enormous swamps, and after crossing these they came to a city where all the men were the same size as their captors and dark-skinned. Past the city flowed a great river, running from the west toward the sunrise, and crocodiles could be seen in it.

33. So much for the account of Etearchus the Ammonian, except to add that, as the men of Cyrene told me, he said that the Nasamonians got home safely, and that the people they had come to were all sorcerers. Etearchus guessed that this river flowing past the city was the Nile, and reason compels us to think so too. For the Nile flows out of Libya and cuts Libya through the middle. And as I guess, judging what is unknown by what can be seen, it starts as far from its mouth as the Danube does from its own. For the Danube begins among the Celts and at the city of Pyrene, and runs so as to divide Europe down the middle. (The Celts live beyond the Pillars of Heracles and border on the Cynesians, who live farthest west of all the peoples who make their homes in Europe.) And the Danube ends, after running through the whole of Europe, by flowing into the Black Sea at the place where the Milesians have their colony of Istria.

34. Now the Danube, since it flows through inhabited land, is known from the reports of many people. But no one can give an account of the sources of the Nile, because the part of Libya it flows through is uninhabited desert. About its course, though, I have told as much as it was possible to learn by the most careful inquiry, and it runs out into Egypt. Now Egypt lies roughly opposite the mountain country of Cilicia. From there to Sinope on the Black Sea is a five days' journey in a straight line for a man traveling light. And Sinope lies opposite the place where the Danube runs out into the sea. So I think that the Nile crosses the whole of Libya and is equal in length to the Danube.

So much for the Nile, then.

Chapter 10: The Upside-Down Customs of Egypt, and Its Gods

35. I am going to talk about Egypt at length, though, because it has more wonders than any other country, and more works to show than any land, works too great for words. That is why I will say more about it.

The Egyptians have a climate unlike any other, and a river that behaves differently from every other river. To match them, they have set up manners and customs that are the opposite of other people's in almost everything. Among them the women go to market and do the trading, while the men stay at home and weave. Other people weave by pushing the weft upward; the Egyptians push it downward. The men carry loads on their heads, the women on their shoulders. The women urinate standing up, the men squatting down. They relieve themselves indoors and eat outside in the streets, and they give this reason for it: things that are shameful but necessary should be done in private, and things that are not shameful should be done in public. No woman serves as priest of any god or goddess; men are the priests of all of them, male and female alike. Sons are not obliged in any way to support their parents if they don't want to, but daughters are forced to, however unwilling they may be.

36. In other lands the priests of the gods wear their hair long; in Egypt they shave their heads. Among other people the custom in mourning is for those closest to the dead to cut their hair short; but the Egyptians, when someone dies, let the hair grow long, both on the head and on the chin, after being clean-shaven before. Other people keep their daily living separate from their animals; the Egyptians live together with theirs. Other people live on wheat and barley, but for any Egyptian to live on these is a great disgrace; they make their bread from a grain called olyra, which some call spelt. They knead dough with their feet and clay with their hands, and they pick up dung with their hands too. Other men leave their genitals as nature made them, except those who have learned otherwise from the Egyptians; the Egyptians practice circumcision. As for clothing, each man wears two garments, each woman only one. Other people fasten the rings and ropes of the sails on the outside of the ship; the Egyptians fasten them on the inside. Finally, in writing letters and in counting with pebbles, the Greeks move the hand from left to right, but the Egyptians move it from right to left; and while they do this, they say that it is they who go the right way and the Greeks who go the wrong way. They use two kinds of writing, one called sacred and the other common.

37. They are religious to excess, more than any other people, and here are some of their customs. They drink from bronze cups and scour them out every day; not just some of them do this, but all. They wear linen clothes, always freshly washed, and they make a special point of this. They circumcise themselves for the sake of cleanliness, preferring to be clean rather than good-looking. The priests shave their whole bodies every other day, so that no louse or any other unclean thing may get on them while they serve the gods. The priests wear only linen clothes and sandals made of papyrus; they are not allowed to wear any other clothing or any other sandals. They wash in cold water twice a day and twice again every night, and they perform other religious rites that are practically countless. They also enjoy quite a few good things. They do not use up or spend anything of their own: sacred bread is baked for them, each of them gets a large supply of beef and goose meat every day, and they are given wine made from grapes as well. But they are not allowed to taste fish. The Egyptians do not sow beans in their land at all, and any beans that do grow there they will neither eat raw nor cook to eat. In fact the priests cannot even stand to look at them, believing beans to be an unclean kind of vegetable. Each god has not just one priest but many, and one of them is the high priest; and whenever a priest dies, his son takes his place.

38. They believe that bulls belong to Epaphus, and because of him they test them in this way. If the priest sees even a single black hair on the animal, he judges it not clean for sacrifice. One priest, appointed for the purpose, examines all this, both with the animal standing up and with it lying on its back. He pulls out its tongue as well, to see whether it is clean as far as the prescribed marks go, which I will describe in another part of my history. He also looks at the hairs of the tail to see whether they grow in the natural way. If the animal is clean in all these respects, he marks it with a strip of papyrus wound around the horns. Then he smears sealing clay on it and presses his signet ring into it, and after that they lead the animal away. Anyone who sacrifices an animal that has not been sealed is punished by death.

39. That is how the animal is tested, and this is how they sacrifice it. They lead the sealed animal to the altar where they are going to sacrifice, and light a fire. Then they pour wine over the altar so that it runs down onto the victim, call on the god, and cut its throat; and after cutting its throat they cut off its head. They skin the body. Over the head they first pronounce many curses, and then, if they have a market with Greek traders living among them, they carry it to the marketplace and sell it; if they have no Greeks among them, they throw it into the river. The curse they pronounce over the heads is a prayer that if any evil is about to fall on the people offering the sacrifice, or on Egypt as a whole, it may fall on this head instead. Now, as regards the heads of sacrificed animals and the pouring of wine over them, all Egyptians follow the same customs for all their sacrifices alike, and because of this custom no Egyptian will eat the head of this or of any other kind of animal.

40. But the way of taking out the victims' entrails and burning them differs from one sacrifice to another. I will describe the sacrifice to the goddess they consider the greatest of all, in whose honor they hold their greatest festival. When they have skinned the bull and pronounced the curse, they take out the whole of its lower entrails but leave the upper entrails and the fat inside the body. They cut off the legs, the end of the loin, the shoulders and the neck. When this is done, they stuff the rest of the carcass with consecrated loaves, honey, raisins, figs, frankincense, myrrh and every other kind of spice. Once it is filled, they burn it as an offering, pouring a great quantity of oil over it. They fast before they sacrifice, and while the offerings are burning they all beat their breasts in mourning. When they have finished beating themselves, they set out what is left of the sacrifice as a feast.

41. So all the Egyptians sacrifice clean bulls, both full-grown animals and calves. They are not allowed to sacrifice cows, which are sacred to Isis. The image of Isis is of a woman with cow's horns, just as the Greeks picture Io, and all Egyptians alike revere cows far more than any other kind of livestock. For this reason no Egyptian, man or woman, would kiss a Greek man on the mouth, or use a Greek's knife, or his roasting spits, or his cooking pot, or taste the meat even of a clean animal if it has been cut with a Greek knife. Cattle that die are buried this way. The cows they throw into the river. The bulls each town buries in its own outskirts, with one horn, or sometimes both, sticking up out of the ground to mark the spot. When the bodies have rotted and the appointed time comes round, a boat arrives at each city from the island called Prosopitis. This island is in the Delta, and it is about sixty miles around. On the island of Prosopitis there are many cities, and one of them is the city the boats come from to collect the bones of the cattle. Its name is Atarbechis, and it has a holy temple of Aphrodite. Many people go out from this city in all directions, some to one city and some to another. They dig up the bones of the cattle, carry them off, and all bury them together in a single place. They bury their other livestock, when it dies, in the same way as the cattle, because the same law covers those animals too; and they do not kill them either.

42. Now everyone who has a temple of Theban Zeus or who belongs to the district of Thebes sacrifices goats and refuses to sacrifice sheep. This is because not all Egyptians worship the same gods equally. The only exceptions are Isis and Osiris, who they say is Dionysus: these two they all worship alike. But those who have a temple of Mendes, or who belong to the Mendesian district, refuse to sacrifice goats and sacrifice sheep. The Thebans, and those who follow their example in keeping away from sheep, say the custom was established among them for this reason. Heracles, they say, very much wanted to see Zeus, and Zeus did not want to be seen by him. In the end, when Heracles kept begging, Zeus thought of a trick. He skinned a ram, cut off its head and held it in front of his face, put on the fleece, and showed himself to Heracles that way. That is why the Egyptians make their image of Zeus with a ram's face. The Ammonians do the same, following their example; they are settlers from both Egypt and Ethiopia, and they speak a language that is a mixture of the two. In my opinion the Ammonians also took their name from this god, because the Egyptians call Zeus Amun. So the Thebans do not sacrifice rams but hold them sacred, for this reason. On one day a year, however, at the festival of Zeus, they cut up and skin a single ram in the same way, and dress the image of Zeus in its fleece, and then they bring another image, of Heracles, up to it. When this is done, everyone in the temple beats his breast in mourning for the ram, and then they bury it in a sacred tomb.

43. About Heracles, I heard it said that he was one of the twelve gods. But of the other Heracles, the one the Greeks know, I could not hear anything anywhere in Egypt. There is plenty of evidence that the Egyptians did not take the name of Heracles from the Greeks, but that the Greeks took it from the Egyptians (I mean those Greeks who gave the name Heracles to the son of Amphitryon). The chief proof is this: the parents of this Heracles, Amphitryon and Alcmene, were both of Egyptian descent. Then too, the Egyptians say they do not know the names of Poseidon or of the Dioscuri, Castor and Polydeuces, the twin sons of Tyndareus, and these have not been accepted among their gods. Yet if they had taken the name of any god from the Greeks, these are the ones they would most naturally have remembered, assuming that in those days, as now, some Greeks made voyages and were seafaring people. I believe they were, and my judgment forces me to think so. So the Egyptians would have learned the names of these gods even sooner than the name of Heracles. In fact, though, Heracles is a very ancient Egyptian god. As they say themselves, it is 17,000 years from the time when the twelve gods, of whom they count Heracles as one, were born of the eight gods, down to the beginning of the reign of Amasis.

44. I wanted to learn something certain about these matters if I could, so I also made a voyage to Tyre in Phoenicia, since I heard there was a holy temple of Heracles there. I saw that it was richly furnished with many offerings, and in particular there were two pillars in it, one of pure gold and the other of emerald, so big that it shone at night. I got into conversation with the priests of the god and asked them how long it had been since their temple was built. I found that they too disagreed with the Greeks. They said that the temple of the god was built at the same time Tyre was founded, and that it had been 2,300 years since their people first settled at Tyre. I also saw at Tyre another temple of Heracles, the one called the Thasian. I went to Thasos as well, and there I found a temple of Heracles built by the Phoenicians, who had sailed out in search of Europa and had settled Thasos. And all this happened a good five generations before Heracles the son of Amphitryon was born in Greece. So my inquiries clearly show that Heracles is an ancient god. I think the Greeks who have built two temples of Heracles act most correctly: to one Heracles they sacrifice as an immortal god, under the title Olympian, and to the other they make offerings for the dead, as to a hero.

45. The Greeks tell many stories without thinking them through, and one especially silly one is the tale they tell about Heracles. They say that when he came to Egypt, the Egyptians put garlands on him and led him out in procession to sacrifice him to Zeus. For a while he kept quiet; but when they were starting to sacrifice him at the altar, he turned to his strength and killed them all. For my part I think that when the Greeks tell this story they know nothing at all about the nature and customs of the Egyptians. How could people who are not allowed to sacrifice even animals, except pigs, bulls and bull calves (the clean ones) and geese, how could they sacrifice human beings? Besides, how could Heracles, being only one person, and a man at that (as they claim), possibly kill tens of thousands? Having said this much on the subject, I pray that both gods and heroes may look kindly on what I have said.

46. Now the reason why the Egyptians I mentioned do not sacrifice goats, female or male, is this. The Mendesians count Pan as one of the eight gods, and they say these eight gods came into being before the twelve. Their painters and sculptors paint and carve the figure of Pan just as the Greeks do, with a goat's face and legs. They do not think he really looks like that; they think he is like the other gods. But why they represent him in this form I would rather not say. The Mendesians revere all goats, the males more than the females, and the goatherds too are held in greater honor than other herdsmen. One goat in particular is revered, and when he dies there is great mourning throughout the whole Mendesian district. In the Egyptian language both the goat and Pan are called Mendes. And in my own lifetime a wonder happened in that district: a he-goat had sex with a woman in public, and this was done so that everyone could see it.

47. The Egyptians regard the pig as an unclean animal. To begin with, if one of them brushes against a pig in passing, he goes to the river and plunges in at once, clothes and all. Then too, swineherds, even though they are native Egyptians, are the only people who may not enter any temple in Egypt. Nobody is willing to give his daughter in marriage to one of them or to take a wife from among them, so the swineherds marry among themselves, giving their daughters to each other and taking each other's. Now the Egyptians do not think it right to sacrifice pigs to any of the other gods; but to the Moon and to Dionysus alone they sacrifice pigs, at the same time, on the same full moon, and then they eat the meat. The Egyptians tell a story about why they hate pigs at all their other festivals but sacrifice them at this one. I know the story, but it is not a proper one for me to tell. The sacrifice of pigs to the Moon is done like this. When the priest has killed the victim, he puts together the tip of the tail, the spleen and the caul, the fatty membrane around the gut, and covers them with all the fat from around the animal's belly, and then he burns them as an offering. The rest of the meat they eat on the day of the full moon on which they made the sacrifice; on any later day they will not taste it. The poor among them, because they have so little, shape pigs out of dough, bake them, and offer these as their sacrifice.

48. For Dionysus, on the eve of the festival, each man kills a pig by cutting its throat in front of his own door, and then gives the pig back to the swineherd who sold it to him, for him to take away again. The rest of the festival of Dionysus the Egyptians celebrate in almost every way as the Greeks do, except for the choral dances. But instead of the phallus, the carved penis the Greeks carry in procession, they have invented something else: figures about eighteen inches high, worked by strings, which women carry around the villages. The figure's penis is made to move, and it is not much smaller than the rest of the body. A flute player goes in front, and the women follow, singing the praises of Dionysus. As for why the figure has a penis larger than nature and why it moves that one part of the body and no other, there is a sacred story told about it.

49. Now I think that Melampus son of Amytheon was not ignorant of this sacrifice but knew it well. For Melampus is the one who first introduced to the Greeks the name of Dionysus, the way of sacrificing to him and the procession of the phallus. Strictly speaking, he did not reveal the whole of it when he made it known; the wise men who came after him explained it more fully. But it was Melampus who taught about the phallus that is carried in procession for Dionysus, and it is from him that the Greeks learned to do what they do. So I say that Melampus, a clever man, worked out an art of prophecy for himself, and having learned many things from Egypt, he taught them to the Greeks, among them the rites of Dionysus, changing a few details. I will not say that what is done in the god's worship in Egypt and what is done among the Greeks just happened to turn out the same by accident: if so, the rites would be in keeping with Greek worship and not a recent import. Nor will I say that the Egyptians took this or any other custom from the Greeks. But I think it most likely that Melampus learned about Dionysus from Cadmus of Tyre and from those who came with him from Phoenicia to the land we now call Boeotia.

50. In fact, the names of almost all the gods came to Greece from Egypt. My inquiries tell me it is true that they came from non-Greeks, and I think it most likely they came from Egypt. For apart from Poseidon and the Dioscuri, as I said before, and Hera, Hestia (goddess of the hearth), Themis, the Charites (the Graces) and the Nereids (the sea nymphs), the Egyptians have always had the names of all the other gods in their country. What I say here is what the Egyptians themselves believe. As for the gods whose names they claim not to know, I think these were named by the Pelasgians, except for Poseidon. The Greeks learned about this god from the Libyans, because no people except the Libyans have had the name of Poseidon from the beginning and have always honored him. The Egyptians, I may add, have no custom of worshiping heroes at all.

51. So the Greeks adopted these customs, and others I will mention later, from the Egyptians. But making the statues of Hermes with the phallus, as they do, is something they learned not from the Egyptians but from the Pelasgians. The Athenians were the first Greeks to take up the custom, and the rest learned it from them. For it was just when the Athenians were starting to be counted as Greeks that the Pelasgians came to live with them in their land, and that is exactly why they began to be counted as Greeks. Anyone who has been initiated into the mysteries of the Cabeiri, which the Samothracians perform and which they received from the Pelasgians, knows what I mean. For these same Pelasgians who came to live with the Athenians had lived in Samothrace before that, and it was from them that the Samothracians received their mysteries. So the Athenians were the first Greeks to make statues of Hermes with the phallus, having learned it from the Pelasgians. The Pelasgians told a sacred story about it, which is revealed in the mysteries at Samothrace.

52. In the old days the Pelasgians used to make all their sacrifices with prayers to the gods, as I know from what I heard at Dodona, but they gave none of them a title or a name, because they had not yet heard any. They called them "theoi," gods, from the idea that they had "set" (thentes) all things in order and so held the sharing out of everything. Then, after a long time had passed, they learned the names of the gods from Egypt, all except Dionysus, whose name they learned much later. Some time after that, the Pelasgians consulted the oracle at Dodona about the names. This oracle is considered the most ancient of all the oracles among the Greeks, and at that time it was the only one. So when the Pelasgians asked the oracle at Dodona whether they should adopt the names that had come from foreigners, the oracle told them to use them. From then on they sacrificed using the names of the gods, and later the Greeks received them from the Pelasgians.

53. But where each of the gods came from, or whether they had all always existed, and what they looked like, the Greeks did not know until the other day, so to speak, or the day before. For I believe Hesiod and Homer lived four hundred years before my time and no more, and they are the ones who composed the Greeks' account of the gods' births, gave the gods their titles, divided up their honors and their skills, and described their forms. The poets who are said to have lived before these two were really, in my opinion, later than they. The first part of what I have said comes from the priestesses at Dodona; the last part, about Hesiod and Homer, is my own.

54. About the oracles, both the one in Greece and the one in Libya, the Egyptians tell this story. The priests of Theban Zeus told me that two women who served in the temple had been carried off from Thebes by Phoenicians. They had heard, they said, that one of the women was sold into Libya and the other to the Greeks, and that these were the women who first founded oracles among those peoples. I asked them how they knew this story so exactly, and they answered that the priests had made a great search for these women and had not been able to find them, but that afterward they had heard this story about them, the one they were telling me.

55. That is what I heard from the priests at Thebes. What follows is what the prophetesses of Dodona say. They say that two black doves flew from Thebes in Egypt, and one of them came to Libya and the other to their own land. This one settled on an oak tree and spoke in a human voice, saying that an oracle of Zeus must be founded there. The people believed that the message came from the gods, and so they founded one. The dove that went to the Libyans, they say, told the Libyans to found an oracle of Ammon, and this too is an oracle of Zeus. The priestesses of Dodona told me these things. The eldest of them was named Promeneia, the next Timarete, and the youngest Nicandra; and the other people of Dodona who served at the temple told the same story.

56. But my own opinion about it is this. If the Phoenicians really did carry off the consecrated women and sell one into Libya and the other into Greece, then I suppose that this second woman was sold, in the country now called Greece but formerly called Pelasgia, into the land of the Thesprotians. Then, while she was a slave there, she set up a shrine of Zeus under a real oak tree. That would be natural: having served in the sanctuary of Zeus at Thebes, she would remember him in the place she had come to. After this, once she understood the Greek language, she founded an oracle. And she reported, I suppose, that her sister had been sold into Libya by the same Phoenicians who had sold her.

57. I also think the people of Dodona called the women doves because they were foreigners, and because they seemed to them to make sounds like birds. After a while, they say, the dove spoke in a human voice: that is, when the woman began to speak so that they could understand her. As long as she spoke a foreign language, she seemed to them to be making sounds like a bird. For if it really had been a dove, how could it speak with a human voice? And in saying that the dove was black, they show that the woman was Egyptian. As it happens, the ways of giving oracles at Thebes in Egypt and at Dodona are very much alike. The art of prophecy from sacrificed victims came from Egypt too.

58. It is also true that the Egyptians were the first people to hold religious festivals, processions and solemn approaches to the temples, and that the Greeks learned these from them. My evidence for this is that the Egyptian festivals have been held since very ancient times, while the Greek ones were introduced only recently.

59. The Egyptians hold their festivals not once a year but many times. The chief one, held with the greatest zeal and devotion, is at the city of Bubastis, for Artemis. The second is at Busiris, for Isis. In this city there is a very great temple of Isis, and the city stands in the middle of the Delta of Egypt; Isis, in the Greek language, is Demeter. Third, they hold a festival at the city of Sais for Athena; fourth, at Heliopolis for the Sun, Helios; fifth, at the city of Buto in honor of Leto; and sixth, at the city of Papremis for Ares.

60. Now, when they are going to the city of Bubastis, this is what they do. Men and women sail together, a great crowd of both in every boat. Some of the women have rattles and shake them, some of the men play the flute the whole way, and the rest, women and men, sing and clap their hands. As they sail, whenever they come opposite some city along the way, they bring the boat close to shore. Some of the women keep on doing what I have described; others shout and jeer at the women of that city; some dance; and some stand up and pull up their skirts. They do this at every city along the riverbank. When they reach Bubastis, they hold a festival with great sacrifices, and more grape wine is drunk at this festival than in all the rest of the year. The people who gather here every year, so the locals say, number as many as 700,000 men and women, not counting children.

61. That is how it is done there. How they celebrate the festival of Isis at the city of Busiris I have already told. As I said, after the sacrifice they all beat their breasts in mourning, men and women together, many tens of thousands of people. But for whom they beat themselves, religion does not allow me to say. All the Carians who live in Egypt do this even more than the Egyptians themselves, since they also cut their foreheads with knives; and this shows that they are foreigners and not Egyptians.

62. When they gather at the city of Sais for their sacrifices, on a certain night they all light a great many lamps in the open air around their houses. The lamps are saucers filled with salt and oil mixed together, with the wick floating on top, and they burn all night long. The festival is called Lychnocaia, the Lighting of the Lamps. And those Egyptians who have not come to this gathering keep the night of the festival too, and they all light lamps as well, so that the lamps are lit not only in Sais but all over Egypt. As for the reason why this night is given light and honor, there is a sacred story told about that.

63. At Heliopolis and Buto they gather every year and only sacrifice. But at Papremis they sacrifice and worship as they do elsewhere, and besides that, when the sun is starting to go down, a few of the priests busy themselves with the image of the god, while most of them stand at the entrance of the temple holding wooden clubs. Opposite them stand more than a thousand other men, who are there to fulfill vows, and these all carry wooden staves too, and stand in a body. The image is in a small wooden shrine covered with gold, and on the day before, they carry it out to another sacred building. The few priests who were left with the image pull a four-wheeled cart carrying the shrine and the image inside it. The other priests, standing in the gateway, try to stop it from coming in, and the men under vows come to the god's help and strike them, while the priests defend themselves. Then there is a hard fight with staves, and they break each other's heads. I think many of them actually die of their wounds, though the Egyptians told me that nobody died. The local people say that they established this festival for the following reason. The mother of Ares, they say, used to live in this temple. Ares had been raised away from her, and when he grew up he came there wanting to visit his mother. But the attendants of his mother's temple, who had never seen him before, would not let him in and kept him out. So he brought men from another city to help him, roughed up the temple attendants, and went in to see his mother. That, they say, is how this exchange of blows became the custom at Ares' festival.

64. The Egyptians were the first to make it a religious rule not to have sex with women in temples, and not to enter a temple after being with a woman without bathing first. Almost all other people except the Egyptians and the Greeks have sex in temples and go into a temple after being with a woman without bathing, because they think there is no difference in this between people and animals. They say they see animals and all kinds of birds mating in the temples and in the sacred precincts of the gods; and if this did not please the god, the animals would not do it.

Chapter 11: Sacred Animals, Embalming, and Life along the Nile

65. That is how these other peoples defend what they do, though I for my part do not accept it. But the Egyptians are extremely careful in their religious observances, both in other matters that concern the sacred rites and in the ones I am about to describe. Egypt borders on Libya, but it does not have a great many wild animals. Those it does have are all, every one of them, held sacred by the Egyptians, some living alongside people and others not. But if I were to say why the sacred animals have been dedicated in this way, I would find myself talking about the gods, which is the subject I most want to avoid; and whatever I have actually said that touches on it lightly, I said only because I had no choice. As for these animals, the custom is this. Certain Egyptians, both men and women, have been appointed to provide the food for each kind of animal separately, and the office passes down from father to son. The people in the various cities fulfill their vows to these animals in this way. When a man makes a vow to the god the animal belongs to, he shaves his children's heads, either the whole head or a half or a third of it. Then he weighs the hair on a scale against silver, and whatever it weighs, he gives that much silver to the woman who looks after the animals. She cuts up fish of the same value and feeds it to them. That is how food has been arranged for their keep. If anyone kills one of these animals on purpose, the penalty is death; if he kills one by accident, he pays whatever penalty the priests decide. But anyone who kills an ibis or a hawk, whether on purpose or by accident, must die.

66. There are a great many animals that live with people, and there would be many more if it were not for what happens to the cats. When the females have had kittens, they no longer go to the males, and the males, who want to mate with them, cannot. So the males have worked out a trick. They take the kittens away from the females, by force or by stealth, and kill them (though they do not eat them after killing them). The females, robbed of their young and wanting more, then come back to the males, since the cat is an animal that loves its young. And when a fire breaks out, something strange, almost supernatural, takes hold of the cats. The Egyptians stand around at intervals keeping watch on the cats and take no trouble to put out the fire, but the cats slip through or leap over the men and jump into the flames. When this happens, the Egyptians go into deep mourning. In any house where a cat has died a natural death, everyone who lives there shaves off their eyebrows, and only their eyebrows. But in a house where a dog has died, they shave their whole body and their head as well.

67. When cats die they are carried to sacred buildings in the city of Bubastis, where they are embalmed and buried. Dogs are buried by each people in their own city, in sacred tombs, and ichneumons (a kind of mongoose) are buried in just the same way as dogs. Shrews and hawks, however, are carried off to the city of Buto, and ibises to Hermopolis. Bears, which are rare there, and wolves, which are not much bigger than foxes, they bury on the spot where they find them lying.

68. The nature of the crocodile is as follows. During the four coldest months of winter it eats nothing. It has four feet and lives both on land and in water: it lays its eggs and hatches them on land, and it spends most of the day on dry ground, but the whole night in the river, because the water is actually warmer than the open air under a clear sky and the dew. Of all the living creatures we know of, this one grows from the smallest beginning to the greatest size. The eggs it lays are not much bigger than goose eggs, and the newly hatched young one is in proportion to the egg; but as it grows it reaches as much as twenty-five feet long, and sometimes even more. It has eyes like a pig's and large teeth like tusks, in proportion to the size of its body. Unlike every other animal, it grows no tongue. Nor does it move its lower jaw: it brings the upper jaw down onto the lower, and in this too it is unlike every other animal. It also has strong claws, and a scaly hide on its back that cannot be pierced. It is blind in the water, but in the air its sight is very sharp. Since it lives in the water, the inside of its mouth is always full of leeches. All other birds and animals run from it, but the trochilus is at peace with it, because the crocodile gets some good from her. When the crocodile has come out of the water onto land and opened its mouth (it usually does this facing the west wind), the trochilus goes into its mouth and gulps down the leeches. The crocodile is glad of the help and does the trochilus no harm.

69. To some of the Egyptians crocodiles are sacred; others do not hold them sacred at all but, on the contrary, treat them as enemies. The people around Thebes and around Lake Moeris consider them very sacred indeed. Each of these two peoples keeps one particular crocodile, chosen out of all the rest and trained to be tame. They hang earrings of glass and gold in its ears and put bracelets around its front feet. They give it special food and sacrificial offerings and treat it as well as they possibly can while it lives, and when it dies they embalm it and bury it in a sacred tomb. But the people around the city of Elephantine actually eat crocodiles, since they do not consider them sacred. Their name for them is not "crocodiles" but "champsae." It was the Ionians who called them crocodiles, comparing their shape to the lizards in their own country that live in stone walls, which they call crocodiles.

70. There are many different ways of catching them. I will describe the one that seems to me most worth telling. A man baits a hook with a pig's back and lets it out into the middle of the river, while he himself stands on the bank holding a live young pig, which he beats. The crocodile hears its squeals and heads toward the sound, and when it comes on the pig's back it swallows it. Then the men pull. When it has been dragged out onto land, the first thing the hunter does is plaster its eyes shut with mud. Once he has done that, he can master it very easily; but if he does not, he has a great deal of trouble.

71. The hippopotamus, the "river horse," is sacred in the district of Papremis, but not to the rest of the Egyptians. This is what it looks like. It has four feet and split hooves like an ox. It has a snub nose and a mane like a horse, and it shows tusk-like teeth. It has a horse's tail and a horse's voice, and it is as big as the biggest ox. Its hide is so extremely thick that once it is dried, it is used to make javelin shafts.

72. There are also otters in the river, which they consider sacred. Among fish they consider sacred the one called the lepidotus, and also the eel; these, they say, are sacred to the Nile. Among birds, the fox-goose is sacred.

73. There is another sacred bird too, called the phoenix. I have never seen one myself, except in paintings, because it comes to them very rarely: once every five hundred years, so the people of Heliopolis say. They say it comes regularly when its father dies. If it looks like the paintings, then this is its size and appearance: some of its feathers are the color of gold and others are red, and in outline and size it is very much like an eagle. They say this bird does something that I cannot believe. It sets out from Arabia, they say, carrying its father to the temple of the Sun (Helios), all plastered up in myrrh, and buries him in the temple of the Sun. This is how it carries him. First it shapes an egg out of myrrh, as big as it can carry. Then it tries carrying it. When it has tested it enough, it hollows out the egg and puts its father inside, and it plasters over with more myrrh the part of the egg it hollowed out to put him in. With the father inside, they say, the egg weighs exactly what it weighed before. After plastering it up, the bird carries the whole thing to Egypt, to the temple of the Sun. That, they say, is what this bird does.

74. Around Thebes there are also sacred snakes, which are not at all harmful to people. They are small, and have two horns growing from the top of the head. When they die, they are buried in the temple of Zeus, because they are sacred, they say, to that god.

75. There is also a place in Arabia, lying roughly opposite the city of Buto, where I went to ask about the winged serpents. When I got there I saw bones and spines of serpents in such enormous quantities that it is impossible to give the number. There were heaps of spines, some large, some smaller, and others smaller still, and there were a great many of these heaps. The place where the spines lie scattered on the ground is something like an entrance from a narrow mountain pass into a great plain, and this plain adjoins the plain of Egypt. The story goes that at the beginning of spring winged serpents fly from Arabia toward Egypt, and the birds called ibises meet them at the entrance to this country and do not let the serpents pass, but kill them. It is because of this deed, say the Arabians, that the ibis has come to be greatly honored by the Egyptians; and the Egyptians themselves also agree that this is why they honor these birds.

76. This is what the ibis looks like. It is jet black all over, with legs like a crane's and a strongly hooked beak, and it is about the size of a rail. That is the appearance of the black kind, the ones that fight the serpents. There are two distinct kinds of ibis, however, and the other kind, the ones that crowd most around people's feet, have a bare head and a bare throat all the way down. Their feathers are white except on the head and neck and the tips of the wings and the rump; in all the parts I have mentioned they are jet black. In their legs and the shape of their head they look like the other kind. As for the serpent, it looks like a water snake. It has wings without feathers, very much like a bat's wings. Let that be enough about sacred animals.

77. As for the Egyptians themselves, those who live in the farming part of Egypt cultivate memory more than any other people, and are by far the most learned in history of all the peoples I have come across. This is how they live. For three days in a row every month they purge themselves, seeking health through emetics and enemas, because they think that all the diseases people get come from the food they eat. In fact, the Egyptians are, for other reasons as well, the healthiest of all people after the Libyans. In my opinion this is because of their climate, since their seasons do not change; for it is changes in things generally, and above all changes in the seasons, that are most likely to bring on disease. As for their diet, it is this. They eat bread, making loaves out of spelt, which they call cyllestis. They regularly drink a wine made from barley, because they have no vines in their country. Some of their fish they dry in the sun and eat raw; others they eat cured in brine. Of birds, they eat quails, ducks and small birds raw, after first curing them in salt. Everything else they have in the way of birds or fish, apart from the ones they have set aside as sacred, they eat roasted or boiled.

78. At the dinner parties of the rich, when the meal is over, a man carries around a wooden model of a corpse in a coffin, painted and carved to look as real as possible, about eighteen inches or three feet long. He shows it to each of the guests in turn and says, "Look at this, then drink and enjoy yourself, for when you are dead this is what you will be." That is what they do at their drinking parties.

79. The customs they practice are the ones they inherited from their fathers, and they do not take on any others. Among their other customs worth mentioning, they have one song, the song of Linus, the same Linus who is sung of in Phoenicia, in Cyprus and elsewhere, though he has a different name among each people. This song is exactly the same as the one the Greeks sing when they call on the name of Linus. So of the many things that amaze me about Egypt, this amazes me most of all: where did they get the song of Linus? It is clear, though, that they have been singing it since time out of mind. In the Egyptian language Linus is called Maneros. The Egyptians told me that he was the only son of the first king of Egypt, that he died young, and that the Egyptians honored him with this lament, and that this was their first and only song.

80. In another respect the Egyptians agree with some of the Greeks, namely the Spartans, though not with the rest. When younger men meet their elders, they make way for them and step aside from the path, and when their elders come near, they stand up from their seats. But in the following custom they agree with none of the Greeks at all: instead of greeting each other in the street with words, they bow, lowering a hand down to the knee.

81. They wear linen tunics with fringes around the legs, which they call calasiris, and over these they throw cloaks of white wool. But woolen clothing is never taken into the temples, and no one is buried in it, because religion forbids it. In this they agree with the rites called Orphic and Bacchic, which are really Egyptian, and also with those of the Pythagoreans: anyone who takes part in these mysteries is likewise forbidden by religious law to be buried in woolen clothing. There is a sacred story told about this.

82. Besides these things, the Egyptians have also worked out which god each month and each day belongs to, and what fortune a man born on a given day will meet with, how he will die, and what sort of man he will be. These discoveries were taken up by those Greeks who busied themselves with poetry. The Egyptians have also discovered more omens than all the rest of mankind put together. Whenever an omen occurs, they watch and write down what comes of it, and if anything like it ever happens again, they believe the outcome will be the same.

83. Their prophecy is arranged like this. The art of prophecy does not belong to any human being, but to certain of the gods. In their country there are oracles of Heracles, of Apollo, of Athena, of Artemis, of Ares and of Zeus, and also the one they honor most of all, the oracle of Leto in the city of Buto. But the method of prophecy is not yet the same everywhere among them; it differs from place to place.

84. Medicine among them is divided up like this. Each doctor is a doctor for one disease and no more, and the whole country is full of doctors. Some set up as doctors for the eyes, others for the head, others for the teeth, others for disorders of the stomach, and others for the less obvious illnesses.

85. Their customs of mourning and burial are these. Whenever a household loses a man of any standing, all the women of that house at once smear their heads, or even their faces, with mud. Then they leave the body in the house and go roaming around the city, beating their breasts, with their clothes tied up by a belt and their breasts bare, and with them go all the women who were related to the dead man. On the other side the men beat their breasts, they too with their clothes tied up by a belt. When they have done this, they take the body to be embalmed.

86. There are men who practice this as their regular trade and inherit it as a craft. Whenever a body is brought to them, they show the people who brought it wooden models of corpses, painted to look real. The finest method of embalming, they say, is that of the one whose name I think it irreverent to mention in a matter of this kind. The second method they show is not as good as the first, and cheaper; and the third is the cheapest of all. After explaining all this, they ask the family which method they want used for the body of their loved one. Then the family agree on a price and go away, and the embalmers, left behind in their workshops, embalm the body. The most perfect way is this.

First, with a hooked iron tool, they draw the brain out through the nostrils, taking out part of it this way and the rest by pouring in drugs. Next, with a sharp Ethiopian stone, they make a cut along the side and take out all the contents of the belly. They clean out the cavity and rinse it with palm wine, and then rinse it again with crushed spices. Then they fill the belly with pure crushed myrrh, cassia and other spices, all except frankincense, and sew it up again. After this they cover the body with natron, a natural salt, and keep it for embalming for seventy days; they are not allowed to embalm it for longer than that. When the seventy days are over, they wash the body and wrap the whole of it in bandages cut from fine linen, smearing their undersides with gum, which the Egyptians generally use instead of glue. Then the relatives take the body back from them and have a wooden case made in the shape of a man. When it has been made, they shut the body up inside it and store it in a burial chamber, standing it upright against the wall.

87. That is how they deal with the bodies prepared in the most expensive way. For those who want the middle method and wish to avoid great expense, they prepare the body as follows. They fill their syringes with oil made from cedarwood and pump it straight into the belly of the corpse, without cutting it open or taking out the intestines: they inject the oil through the anus and stop it from running back out. Then they keep the body the set number of days for embalming, and on the last day they let out of the belly the cedar oil they put in earlier. The oil is so powerful that it brings out with it the intestines and inner organs, dissolved; and the natron dissolves the flesh, so that nothing is left of the body but the skin and bones. When they have done this, they hand the body back just as it is, without doing any more work on it.

88. The third kind of embalming, which is used for the bodies of those with less money, is this. They clean out the belly with a purge and then keep the body for embalming for the seventy days, and right after that they give it back to the people who brought it, to take away.

89. When the wives of prominent men die, they are not handed over to be embalmed right away, nor are women who are very beautiful or more highly regarded than others. They are given to the embalmers only on the third or fourth day after death, and not before. They do this so that the embalmers will not have sex with these women. For they say that one embalmer was once caught doing this with the body of a woman who had just died, and a fellow craftsman reported him.

90. Whenever anyone, whether an Egyptian or a foreigner, is found to have been carried off by a crocodile or killed by the river itself, the people of whatever city he washes up near are obliged to embalm him, lay him out as finely as they can, and bury him in a sacred tomb. None of his relatives or friends may touch him. Instead the priests of the Nile handle the body themselves and bury it, as if it were the body of someone more than human.

91. They refuse to follow Greek customs at all, and, to put it generally, they follow the customs of no other people whatever. Most of the Egyptians keep to this rule. But there is a large city called Chemmis in the Theban district, near Neapolis, and in this city there is a square temple of Perseus, the son of Danae, with date palms growing all around it. The gateway of the temple is built of stone and is very large, and at its entrance stand two great stone statues. Inside this enclosure is a shrine, and in it stands a statue of Perseus. The people of Chemmis say that Perseus often appears in their country, and often inside the temple, and that sometimes one of his sandals is found, which he has worn, three feet long; and whenever it turns up, the whole of Egypt prospers. That is what they say. And they honor Perseus in the Greek fashion, like this: they hold athletic games that include every kind of contest, and they offer cattle, cloaks and hides as prizes. I asked them why Perseus appeared to them alone, and why they were different from all the other Egyptians in holding athletic games. They said that Perseus was by descent a man of their city. Danaus and Lynceus, they said, were men of Chemmis who had sailed to Greece, and they traced the line of descent from them down to Perseus. They told me that he came to Egypt for the reason the Greeks also give, to bring the Gorgon's head from Libya, and that on that journey he visited them too and recognized all his relatives. They said he already knew the name of Chemmis well before he came to Egypt, because he had heard it from his mother, and that they hold the athletic games for him because he ordered it himself.

92. All these are the customs of the Egyptians who live above the marshes. Those who are settled in the marshland have mostly the same customs as the other Egyptians, both in other matters and in this one: each man lives with one wife only, as the Greeks do. But to make their food go further they have come up with these additional things. When the river is full and the plains are flooded, a great many lilies grow in the water, which the Egyptians call lotus. They cut these with a sickle and dry them in the sun. Then they pound up the part in the middle of the lotus that looks like a poppy head and make loaves out of it, baked over a fire. The root of this lotus is also good to eat and tastes rather sweet; it is round and about the size of an apple. There are other lilies too, with flowers like roses, which also grow in the river. Their fruit grows in a separate pod on a stalk that springs from the root beside the plant itself, and it looks very much like a wasps' nest. Inside it grow a great many edible seeds about the size of an olive pit, and these are eaten either fresh or dried. Besides this, they pull up from the marshes the papyrus that grows there every year. They cut off the upper parts and put them to other uses, but the lower part that is left, about eighteen inches long, they eat or sell. Those who want their papyrus at its very best bake it in a red-hot oven and then eat it. Some of these people live on fish alone. They catch them, take out the guts and dry them in the sun, and then, when they are dry, they eat them.

93. Fish that swim in schools are not much bred in the rivers; they are bred in the lakes, and this is what they do. When the urge to spawn comes over them, they swim out in schools toward the sea. The males lead the way, shedding their milt as they go, and the females follow behind and swallow it up, and from it they become pregnant. When they are full of young in the sea, they swim back up again, each school to its own home waters. But now the males no longer lead the way as before: the lead passes to the females. Going ahead in schools, they do just what the males did: they shed their eggs, a few grains at a time, and the males follow behind and swallow them up. Now these grains are fish, and from the grains that survive and are not swallowed, the fish grow that are later raised. The fish caught as they swim out to sea are found to be rubbed on the left side of the head, while the ones caught as they swim back up are rubbed on the right. This happens to them because, as they swim down to the sea, they keep close to the land on the left side of the river, and as they swim back up they keep to the same bank, coming as close to it and touching it as much as they can, no doubt for fear of being swept off course by the current. When the Nile begins to rise, the hollows in the land and the low places beside the river are the first to fill, as the water seeps through from the river. As soon as they are full of water, they are all at once full of little fish. I think I can see where these most likely come from. In the year before, when the Nile goes down, the fish lay their eggs in the mud and then leave with the last of the retreating water. When the season comes around again and the water once more comes over the land, the fish I am talking about are hatched at once from these eggs.

94. So much for the fish. For anointing themselves, the Egyptians who live in the marshes use oil from the castor-oil plant, which the Egyptians call kiki. This is how they do it. They plant it along the banks of the rivers and ponds. In Greece this plant grows wild by itself, but in Egypt it is planted, and it bears a great many berries, though they smell bad. When they have gathered them, some people chop them up and press the oil out of them; others first roast them and then boil them down, and collect what runs off. The oil is thick and greasy, and no worse than olive oil for lamps, but it gives off an unpleasant smell.

95. Against the gnats, which are very plentiful, they have come up with these defenses. Those who live above the marshland are helped by towers, which they climb up to when they go to bed, because the wind keeps the gnats from flying up high. But those who live in the marshland have worked out another method instead of towers. Every man of them owns a casting net, which he uses during the day to catch fish. At night he puts it to this use: he puts the net all around the bed he sleeps in, then crawls in underneath it and goes to sleep. If he sleeps wrapped up in a cloak or a linen sheet, the gnats bite right through it, but through the net they do not even try to bite.

96. The boats they use to carry cargo are made of the thorny acacia, a tree very much like the lotus of Cyrene in shape, which gives off a gum. From this tree they cut planks about three feet long and lay them like bricks, fastening the boat together by running a great many long bolts through the three-foot planks. When they have fastened the boat together this way, they lay crossbeams over the top. They use no ribs for the sides, and on the inside they caulk the seams with papyrus. They make a single steering oar for it, which passes through the bottom of the boat. They have a mast of acacia and sails of papyrus. These boats cannot sail upstream unless a strong wind is blowing, and they are towed from the bank. Downstream, though, they travel like this. They have a raft shaped like a door, made of tamarisk wood and reed mats sewn together, and also a stone with a hole bored through it, weighing about two talents, or about 115 pounds. The boatman lets the raft float ahead of the boat, tied on with a rope, and lets the stone drag behind on another rope. As the force of the current presses on the raft, it moves along quickly and pulls the baris (that is what these boats are called), while the stone, dragging behind and sunk deep in the water, keeps the boat on a straight course. They have great numbers of these boats, and some of them carry many thousands of talents' weight.

97. When the Nile floods the land, only the cities can be seen standing above the water, looking more like the islands in the Aegean Sea than anything else. All the rest of Egypt turns into a sea, and only the cities rise above it. So whenever this happens, people travel by boat no longer along the channels of the river but straight across the middle of the plain. For example, anyone sailing up from Naucratis to Memphis then passes right by the pyramids, though that is not the usual route even here: the usual route goes by the point of the Delta and the city of Cercasorus. And if you sail across the plain from the sea and from Canopus to Naucratis, you will pass by Anthylla and the city named after Archander.

98. Of these, Anthylla is a well-known city, and it is set aside especially for the wife of whoever rules Egypt, to keep her in shoes. This has been the arrangement ever since Egypt came under the Persians. The other city, it seems to me, takes its name from Archander, the son-in-law of Danaus and the son of Phthius, the son of Achaeus; for it is called the City of Archander. There may of course have been another Archander, but in any case the name is not Egyptian.

Chapter 12: The First Kings of Egypt, Helen in Egypt, and the Thief of Rhampsinitus

99. Up to this point, what I have said has rested on my own observation, my own judgment and my own inquiry. From here on I am going to tell the history of Egypt as I heard it, though I will add to it something of what I have seen for myself.

Min was the first king of Egypt, and the priests told me that he walled off the site of Memphis from the river. The whole stream of the river used to run along the sandy range of hills on the Libyan side. But about eleven miles south of Memphis, Min built embankments that formed the river's bend there, and so he dried up the old channel and led the river to flow down the middle, between the two ranges of hills. Even now the Persians keep a very careful watch on this bend of the Nile, to make sure it stays in the channel it has been confined to, and the embankment is repaired every year. For if the river were to break through and overflow on this side, Memphis would be in danger of being swept away by the flood. When Min, the first king, had turned the land he dammed off into dry ground, he did two things. First, he founded on it the city that is now called Memphis (for Memphis, too, lies in the narrow part of Egypt). Outside the city, on the north and west, he dug a lake around it, fed from the river; on the east side the Nile itself shuts the city in. Second, he built the temple of Hephaestus in the city, a great work and very well worth mentioning.

100. After this man, the priests read out to me from a papyrus roll the names of three hundred and thirty other kings. In all these generations of men, eighteen kings were Ethiopians and one was a woman, a native Egyptian; the rest were men, and Egyptians. The woman who reigned had the same name as the Babylonian queen: Nitocris. They told me that she wanted to take revenge for her brother. He had been king of Egypt, and the Egyptians had murdered him and then given his kingdom to her. So, wanting to avenge him, she used a trick to destroy a great many of the Egyptians. She had a very large room built underground. Then, pretending she meant to hold a feast to open it, while in her mind she was planning something else, she invited the Egyptians she knew had played the biggest part in the murder, and gave a great banquet. While they were feasting, she let the river in on them through a large secret channel. That was all they told me about her, except that when she had done this, she threw herself into a room full of hot embers, to escape the revenge that would follow.

101. As for the other kings, the priests could tell me of no great works they had produced, and they said none of them was famous except the last, Moeris. He, they said, left as a memorial of himself the gateway of the temple of Hephaestus that faces the north wind. He also dug a lake (I will set out later how many miles around it is), and in it he built pyramids, whose size I will give at the same time, when I come to speak of the lake itself. These, they said, were the works Moeris produced; none of the others produced any.

102. So I will pass over these kings and turn to the king who came after them, whose name was Sesostris. The priests said that he first set out with warships from the Red Sea and conquered the peoples living along the shores of the Indian Ocean, until in his voyage he reached a sea that could not be sailed any further because of shoals. Then, the priests said, after he came back to Egypt, he took a great army and marched across the continent, conquering every nation that stood in his way. Where he found a people brave and fighting desperately for their freedom, he set up pillars in their land with inscriptions telling his own name and his country's, and how he had conquered them by his power. But where he took the cities without a fight, or easily, he inscribed the pillars with the same words as he had for the nations that had shown courage, and on top of that he carved a woman's genitals on them, wanting to show by this that the people were cowards, no better than women.

103. In this way he went right across the continent, until at last he crossed over from Asia into Europe and conquered the Scythians and the Thracians as well. These, in my opinion, were the furthest people the Egyptian army reached: the pillars can be found set up in their country, but beyond it they are found no longer. From there he turned and started for home. When he came to the river Phasis, what happened next I can't say for certain. Either King Sesostris himself split off a part of his army and left the men there to settle the land, or else some of his soldiers were worn out by his long marches and stayed behind by the river Phasis.

104. For the people of Colchis are plainly Egyptian. I noticed this for myself before I heard it from anyone else. So when it had occurred to me, I asked both peoples about it. The Colchians remembered the Egyptians better than the Egyptians remembered the Colchians, but the Egyptians said they thought the Colchians were descended from part of Sesostris' army. I guessed as much myself, partly because they are dark-skinned and have tightly curled hair (though that by itself proves nothing, since other peoples are like that too), but much more because the Colchians, the Egyptians and the Ethiopians are the only peoples in the world who have practiced circumcision from the beginning. The Phoenicians and the Syrians of Palestine admit themselves that they learned it from the Egyptians. The Syrians who live around the rivers Thermodon and Parthenius, and their neighbors the Macronians, say they learned it recently from the Colchians. These are the only peoples who practice circumcision, and they plainly do it in the same way as the Egyptians. As for the Egyptians themselves and the Ethiopians, I can't say which learned it from the other, for it is clearly a very ancient custom. But that the other nations learned it through their dealings with the Egyptians, I take this, among other things, as strong proof: those Phoenicians who have dealings with Greece stop following the Egyptians' example in this, and do not circumcise their children.

105. Now let me mention one more thing about the Colchians, to show how much they resemble the Egyptians. They and the Egyptians are the only people who work flax in the same way, and the two nations are alike in their whole way of life and in their language too. The Greeks call the linen of Colchis "Sardonic," while the linen from Egypt they call "Egyptian."

106. Most of the pillars that Sesostris of Egypt set up in the various countries can no longer be seen. But in Palestinian Syria I saw them myself, still standing, with the inscription I have mentioned and the carved emblem. In Ionia, too, there are two figures of this man carved in the rock: one on the road from the territory of Ephesus to Phocaea, and the other on the road from Sardis to Smyrna.
