In each place the figure of a man is cut in the rock, about six feet nine inches tall, holding a spear in his right hand and a bow and arrows in his left. The rest of his gear matches these, for it is both Egyptian and Ethiopian. From one shoulder to the other, across the chest, runs an inscription carved in the sacred Egyptian characters, which says: "I won this land with my own shoulders." Who he is and where he comes from he does not say in these places, though he has said it elsewhere. Some who have seen these carvings guess that the figure is Memnon, the Ethiopian king who fought at Troy, but in this they are very far from the truth.

107. As this Egyptian Sesostris was on his way back, the priests said, bringing with him many men from the nations whose lands he had conquered, he came to Daphnae in the district of Pelusium on his journey home. There his brother, to whom Sesostris had entrusted the running of Egypt, invited him and his sons to a feast. Then the brother piled brushwood all around the house and set it on fire. When Sesostris found out what was happening, he at once asked his wife for advice, since (they said) he had brought his wife along with him too. She advised him to lay two of his sons, out of the six he had, across the burning pile, making a bridge over the flames, so that the rest of them could walk over their bodies and escape. Sesostris did this, they said, and two of his sons were burned to death in this way, but the others got away safely with their father.

108. Then Sesostris came back to Egypt and took his revenge on his brother. After that he put to work the crowds of people he had brought back from the lands he had conquered, in the following way. These were the men who dragged the huge stones that were brought to the temple of Hephaestus in this king's reign. They were also forced to dig all the channels that are now in Egypt. And so, without meaning to, they made Egypt, which until then had been good country for riding horses and driving carts, no longer fit for it. For ever since that time Egypt, flat as it is, has been no good for horses or carts, and the reason is these channels, which are many and run in every direction. The king's reason for cutting up the land in this way was that those Egyptians whose cities stood not on the river but inland ran short of water whenever the river went down, and had to drink brackish water from wells.

109. That is why Egypt was cut up with channels. And they said that this king divided the land among all the Egyptians, giving each man an equal square plot, and that he got his revenue from this by making them pay a fixed rent every year. If the river carried away part of a man's plot, he would come to the king and report what had happened. The king would then send men to inspect it and measure how much smaller the plot had become, so that from then on the man would pay less, in proportion to the rent that had been set. I think this is how geometry was invented, and that it afterwards came to Greece as well. As for the sundial, the gnomon and the division of the day into twelve parts, the Greeks learned those from the Babylonians.

110. Sesostris was also the only Egyptian king who ruled over Ethiopia. As memorials of himself he left two stone statues in front of the temple of Hephaestus, each forty-five feet high, of himself and his wife, and statues of his four sons, each thirty feet high. Long afterwards, the priest of Hephaestus refused to let Darius the Persian set up a statue of himself in front of them. He said that Darius had not done deeds equal to those of Sesostris the Egyptian. For Sesostris had conquered just as many other nations as Darius had, and the Scythians besides, whereas Darius had not been able to conquer the Scythians. So it was not right, he said, for Darius to set up a statue in front of the ones Sesostris had dedicated, unless he outdid him in his deeds. And Darius, they say, took this speech in good part.

111. When Sesostris' life came to an end, they told me, his son Pheros inherited the kingdom. He made no military expeditions, and it so happened that he went blind, through the following accident. The river had come down in a flood that rose to twenty-seven feet, higher than ever before, and had spread over the fields. Then a wind struck it and the river was whipped up into waves. And this king (they say), in a fit of reckless arrogance, took a spear and hurled it into the middle of the swirling water. Right after this he got a disease of the eyes and went blind. He was blind for ten years. In the eleventh year an oracle came to him from the city of Buto, saying that his time of punishment was over and that he would see again if he washed his eyes with the urine of a woman who had slept with her own husband and no other man. He tried his own wife first, and when he was still blind after that, he went on to try all the women, one after another. When at last he got his sight back, he gathered together all the women he had tried, except the one who had given him back his sight, into one city, which is now called Erythrabolus ("Red Soil"). When he had gathered them there, he burned them all, along with the city itself. But the woman who had given him back his sight he took as his own wife. After he was cured of his eye disease, he dedicated offerings at every one of the well-known temples. In particular (to mention only the one most worth mentioning) he dedicated at the temple of the Sun works that are well worth seeing: two stone obelisks, each made of a single block, each a hundred and fifty feet long and twelve feet wide.

112. After him, they said, the throne passed to a man of Memphis whose name, in Greek, was Proteus. There is a sacred precinct for him at Memphis now, very beautiful and well kept, on the side of the temple of Hephaestus that faces the north wind. Phoenicians from Tyre live all around this precinct, and the whole district is called the Camp of the Tyrians. Inside the precinct of Proteus there is a temple called the temple of the "Foreign Aphrodite." My guess is that this is a temple of Helen, the daughter of Tyndareus. I think so partly because I have heard the story of how Helen stayed with Proteus, but above all because it is called the temple of the "Foreign Aphrodite": none of the other temples of Aphrodite anywhere has the word "foreign" added to its name.

113. When I asked them, the priests told me that what happened with Helen was this. Alexander had carried off Helen and was sailing away from Sparta to his own country. When he reached the Aegean Sea, contrary winds drove him off his course into the Egyptian Sea. From there, since the gales did not let up, he came to Egypt itself, to what is now called the Canopic mouth of the Nile, and to Taricheae. On the shore there was then, as there still is now, a temple of Heracles. If any man's slave takes refuge in it and has the sacred marks put on him, giving himself over to the god, it is forbidden to lay a hand on him. This custom has stayed the same from the beginning right down to my own time. So some of Alexander's servants, having heard about this custom of the temple, ran away from him. They sat down as suppliants of the god and, wanting to do him harm, accused Alexander, telling the whole story of Helen and of the wrong done to Menelaus. They made this accusation not only to the priests but also to the warden of that river-mouth, a man named Thonis.

114. When Thonis heard their story, he at once sent a message to Proteus at Memphis, which said: "A stranger has come here, a Teucrian (that is, a Trojan) by birth, who has done an unholy thing in Greece. He seduced the wife of his own host, and now he has come here with the woman herself and a great deal of treasure, driven to your land by the winds. Should we let him sail away unharmed, or should we first take away from him what he has brought with him?" Proteus sent back a messenger in reply, who said: "Arrest this man, whoever he is, who has committed this crime against his own host, and bring him before me, so that I can hear what he has to say for himself."

115. When he heard this, Thonis arrested Alexander and held his ships, and then brought the man himself up to Memphis, together with Helen and his treasure, and the suppliants as well. When they had all been brought up there, Proteus began asking Alexander who he was and where he was sailing from. Alexander told him his ancestry and the name of his homeland, and explained the route he had sailed. After this Proteus asked him where he had got Helen. When Alexander started to wander in his answer and did not tell the truth, the men who had become suppliants proved him a liar and told the whole story of the wrong he had done. In the end Proteus gave them his judgment: "If I did not think it a very serious thing to kill any stranger who has been driven to my land by the winds, as none ever has been until now, I would have punished you on behalf of that Greek. You are the lowest of men. He took you in as his guest, and you committed a most unholy crime against him. You seduced your own host's wife. And even that was not enough for you: you stirred up her desire and went off with her like a thief. And even that by itself was not enough for you: you have come here with loot taken from your host's house. So now, go, since I have decided that it matters a great deal not to be a killer of strangers. But I will not let you take away this woman or this treasure. I will keep them safe for the Greek who was your host, until he comes himself and wants to take them home. As for you and your shipmates, I order you to leave your anchorage within three days and go from my land to some other. If you do not, you will be treated as enemies."

116. That, the priests said, was how Helen came to Proteus. I believe Homer had heard this story too. But since it did not suit his poem as well as the other one he used, he set it aside, while still making it clear that he knew this version as well. That is plain from the way he describes Alexander's wanderings in the Iliad (and nowhere else does he take back what he said there): when Alexander was bringing Helen home, he was carried off his course and wandered to various lands, and among other places he came to Sidon in Phoenicia. The poet mentions this in the part of the Iliad called "The Valor of Diomedes," and the lines run like this:

	There were her robes of many colors, the work of the women of Sidon,
	women her own son, godlike Alexander, had carried
	away from Sidon, the time he sailed over the wide sea's paths
	bringing Helen home, the daughter of a noble father.

He mentions it in the Odyssey too, in these lines:

	Such were the drugs the daughter of Zeus possessed, drugs of exquisite cunning,
	good ones, given to her by Polydamna, the wife of Thon,
	who lived in Egypt, the land whose generous fields grow
	more drugs than any other, many good when mixed, and many deadly.

And this is what Menelaus says to Telemachus:

	The gods still kept me in Egypt, though I longed to come home,
	kept me from sailing home, since I had not made the sacrifice I owed.

In these lines Homer makes it clear that he knew of Alexander's wandering to Egypt, for Syria borders on Egypt, and the Phoenicians, whose city Sidon is, live in Syria.

117. These lines, and this passage above all, also show very clearly that the "Cyprian Epic" (the poem called the Cypria) was not written by Homer but by some other man. For the Cypria says that Alexander reached Troy with Helen on the third day after leaving Sparta, having had "a gently blowing wind and a smooth sea," whereas the Iliad says that he wandered off his course while he was bringing her.

118. So let us leave Homer and the Cyprian Epic. But I will say this. I asked the priests whether the story the Greeks tell about what happened at Troy is just an idle tale. They answered me as follows, saying that they knew it from what they had learned by questioning Menelaus himself. After Helen was carried off, they said, a large Greek army did indeed come to the land of the Teucrians to help Menelaus. When the army had come ashore from the ships and pitched its camp, they sent messengers to Troy, and Menelaus himself went with them. When they were inside the city wall, they demanded Helen back, along with the treasure Alexander had stolen from Menelaus and carried off, and they also demanded compensation for the wrongs done. The Teucrians gave the same answer then and ever afterwards, under oath and without it: that in actual fact they did not have Helen or the treasure being demanded; both were in Egypt, and it was not fair that they should be made to pay for what Proteus, the king of Egypt, was holding. The Greeks, though, thought the Trojans were mocking them, and they besieged the city until at last they took it. But when they had taken the wall and did not find Helen, and heard the same story as before, then they believed the first story and sent Menelaus himself to Proteus.

119. Menelaus came to Egypt and sailed up to Memphis. He told the truth about what had happened, and not only was he given a lavish welcome, but he also got Helen back unharmed, and all his own treasure too. And yet, after being treated like this, Menelaus repaid the Egyptians with ingratitude. When he set out to sail away, contrary winds held him back, and as this went on for a long time, he came up with an unholy plan: he took two children of local people and sacrificed them. When it became known that he had done this, he was hated for it, and when they chased him, he escaped and got away with his ships to Libya. Where he went after that, the Egyptians could not tell me. They said that they had found out part of all this by inquiry, but that what happened in their own land they reported from sure and certain knowledge.

120. That is what the Egyptian priests told me. And I myself agree with the story they told about Helen, and I add this reasoning of my own. If Helen had been in Troy, she would have been handed over to the Greeks, whether Alexander agreed or not. For surely Priam was not so mad, nor were the others of his family, as to want to risk their own lives and their children's and their city's just so that Alexander could have Helen as his wife. And even supposing they had felt that way at first, still, when many of the other Trojans were losing their lives every time they fought the Greeks, and two or three or even more of Priam's own sons were killed in every battle (if we can trust the epic poets at all), then, as things went this way, I believe that even if Priam himself had been married to Helen, he would have given her back to the Achaeans (as Homer calls the Greeks), if at least that would have freed him from the evils pressing on him. Nor was the kingdom going to pass to Alexander next, so that with Priam old the government would have been in his hands. Hector, who was both older than Alexander and more of a man, would have taken it after Priam's death. And it was not like Hector to let his brother go on with his wrongdoing, when such great evils were coming about because of him, both to Hector himself and to all the other Trojans. In truth, though, they did not have Helen to give back. And the Greeks did not believe them, even though they were telling the truth. This was because, in my opinion, the divine power was planning their total destruction, to make it plain to mankind that for great wrongs the gods send great punishments too. That is my opinion on these matters, and I have given it.

121. After Proteus, they told me, Rhampsinitus inherited the kingdom. As a memorial of himself he left the gateway of the temple of Hephaestus that faces west, and in front of the gateway he set up two statues, thirty-seven and a half feet high. The Egyptians call the one standing on the north side Summer, and the one on the south side Winter. The one they call Summer they worship and make offerings to, and to the other, called Winter, they do just the opposite. This king, they said, came to own a great fortune in silver, so great that none of the kings born after him could beat it, or even come close. Wanting to keep his treasure safe, he had a stone chamber built, with one of its walls forming part of the outside wall of his palace. But the builder had designs on it, and he worked out the following trick: he set one of the stones in such a way that two men, or even one, could easily take it out of the wall. When the chamber was finished, the king stored his money in it. Some time later the builder, coming to the end of his life, called his sons to him (he had two) and told them how he had built the king's treasury, and that he had done it all with an eye to their future, so that they would have plenty to live on. He explained to them clearly everything about taking out the stone and gave them the measurements, and told them that if they kept all this in mind, they would be the keepers of the king's treasury. Then he died. His sons lost no time getting to work. They went to the palace at night, found the stone in the wall of the chamber, removed it easily, and carried off a great deal of the treasure inside.

Then the king happened to open the chamber, and he was astonished to see that the jars were not as full as they should be. He did not know whom to blame, since the seals were unbroken and the chamber had been shut tight. But when he opened the chamber a second and a third time and each time the money was seen to have shrunk (for the thieves did not let up in their raids on it), he did this. He had traps made and set them all around the jars that held the money. When the thieves came as before and one of them went in, the moment he went near one of the jars he was caught in a trap. When he saw what a bad situation he was in, he at once called his brother, showed him what had happened, and told him to come in as quickly as he could and cut off his head, so that if he was seen and recognized he would not bring his brother to ruin as well. The other thought he was right, and was persuaded, and did it. Then he fitted the stone back in its place and went home, carrying his brother's head with him.

When day came, the king went into the chamber and was utterly amazed to see the thief's body caught in the trap without its head, and the chamber intact, with no way in or out. Not knowing what to make of it, he hung the thief's dead body on the wall and posted guards there, with orders to arrest anyone they saw weeping or mourning and bring him to the king. When the body had been hung up, the mother was deeply grieved. She spoke to the son who was still alive and ordered him to find some way, any way he could, to take down his dead brother's body and bring it home. And if he failed to do this, she threatened him in earnest, she would go to the king herself and tell him that her son had the money.

So since his mother was being so hard on him, and nothing he said to her could change her mind, the surviving son came up with the following scheme. He got some donkeys, filled some skins with wine and loaded them onto the donkeys, and then drove them off down the road. When he came to the men guarding the body that was hanging there, he pulled two or three of the skins toward him by the necks and loosened the cords that tied them shut. Then, as the wine was pouring out, he began to beat his head and shout loudly, as if he did not know which of the donkeys to deal with first. When the guards saw the wine flowing out in streams, they ran together into the road with cups in their hands and collected the spilling wine, thinking it was all profit for them. He swore at all of them furiously, pretending to be angry. But when the guards tried to calm him down, after a while he pretended to cool off and let his anger go, and finally he drove his donkeys off the road and began to put their loads right. Then they got talking some more, and one or two of the guards made jokes at his expense and got him laughing along with them, and in the end he gave them one of the skins as a present, on top of what they already had. At that they lay down right there without further ado, intending to drink, and they took him into their company and invited him to stay and drink with them. So he (as you might expect) let himself be persuaded and stayed. Then, as they toasted him in a friendly way over their drinks, he made them a present of another skin as well. And so at last, having drunk heavily, the guards got thoroughly drunk, and overcome by sleep they lay down to sleep on the very spot where they had been drinking. Then, since it was now late at night, he first took down his brother's body, and then, to mock them, shaved the right cheeks of all the guards. After that he put the dead body on the donkeys and drove them home. He had done what his mother ordered.

When the king was told that the thief's dead body had been stolen, he was furious. He was determined, whatever it took, to find out who it was who was coming up with these schemes, and so he did the following (or so they said, but I do not believe the story). He put his own daughter in a brothel and ordered her to take every man alike, but before having sex with any of them, to make him tell her the cleverest thing and the most wicked thing he had ever done in his whole life. And whoever told her the story of the thief, she was to grab him and not let him get away. So she did as her father ordered. The thief heard what all this was for, and since he wanted to outdo the king in cunning, he did this. He cut off the arm of a man who had just died, at the shoulder, and went with it hidden under his cloak. He went in to the king's daughter, and when she asked him what she asked the others, he told her that the most wicked thing he had ever done was cutting off his brother's head, when his brother was caught in a trap in the king's treasure chamber, and the cleverest was getting the guards drunk and taking down his brother's body where it hung. When she heard this, she tried to grab him. But the thief held out the dead man's arm to her in the darkness, and she seized it and held on, thinking she was holding the arm of the man himself. The thief left it in her hands and escaped out through the door.

When this too was reported to the king, he was at first astonished at the man's quick wits and daring. Then he sent messengers around to all the cities and proclaimed a free pardon for the thief, and promised him a great reward as well if he would come before him. The thief trusted the proclamation and came to the king. Rhampsinitus admired him enormously and gave him this daughter of his as his wife, reckoning him the cleverest man in the world: for the Egyptians stood out from all other people, and he stood out from the other Egyptians.

122. After these events, they said, this king went down alive to the place the Greeks call Hades, the land of the dead, and there played dice with Demeter. In some throws he beat her, and in others she beat him, and he came back up again with a gift from her, a golden handkerchief. They told me that because of Rhampsinitus' descent, the Egyptians held a festival after his return. I know for myself that they still keep it in my own time, but whether they keep the festival for this reason or for some other, I can't say. In any case, on the very day of the festival the priests weave a robe from start to finish. Then right away they tie a band over the eyes of one of the priests, lead him in the robe to the road that goes to the temple of Demeter, and go back again themselves. They say that this priest, with his eyes bound, is led by two wolves to the temple of Demeter, which is about two and a quarter miles from the city, and that afterwards the wolves lead him back again from the temple to the same spot.

123. Now, as for these stories the Egyptians tell, anyone who finds such things believable is welcome to accept them. As for me, it should be understood throughout this whole history that I write down, just as I heard it, what the people in each place report. The Egyptians say that Demeter and Dionysus rule the world below. The Egyptians are also the first to have put forward the teaching that the human soul is immortal: that when the body dies, the soul enters another creature that happens to be being born at that moment, and when it has gone the round of all the creatures of the land, the sea and the air, it enters a human body again as it is born; and that it makes this round in three thousand years. Certain Greeks have taken up this teaching, some earlier and some later, as if it were their own invention. I know their names, but I will not write them down.

Chapter 13: The Pyramid Builders, the Priests' Reckoning of Time, and the Twelve Kings

124. Down to the time when Rhampsinitus was king, they told me, there was nothing in Egypt but good order and the rule of law, and Egypt prospered greatly. But after him Cheops became king over them, and he brought them to every kind of misery. First he shut up all the temples and kept the people from sacrificing there; then he ordered all the Egyptians to work for him. Some were assigned to drag stones from the quarries in the Arabian mountains down to the Nile. Others he ordered to receive the stones after they had been ferried across the river in boats, and to drag them on to what are called the Libyan mountains. They worked in gangs of a hundred thousand men at a time, each gang for three months on end. Ten years of this oppression went by just in building the causeway along which they dragged the stones. That causeway, in my view, is a work not much smaller than the pyramid itself. It is about 3,000 feet long and sixty feet wide, and at its highest point it is forty-eight feet high, and it is built of polished stone with figures carved on it. The ten years, they said, went on this, and on the underground chambers in the hill where the pyramids stand. He had these made as burial chambers for himself, on an island, by bringing in a channel from the Nile. The building of the pyramid itself took twenty years. The pyramid is square, each side measuring eight hundred feet, and its height is the same. It is built of polished stone, fitted together perfectly, and not one of the stones is less than thirty feet long.

125. This pyramid was built in steps, which some call "rows" and others "bases." When they had first built it in this way, they lifted the remaining stones with machines made of short pieces of timber. They raised a stone from the ground to the first tier of steps, and when it got there it was set on another machine standing on the first tier, and from there it was hauled up to the second tier on yet another machine. There were as many machines as there were tiers of steps; or perhaps they moved one and the same machine, built to be easily carried, from tier to tier, so as to lift the stones. I give it both ways, since both are reported. However that may be, the top of the pyramid was finished first, then the parts just below it, and last of all the parts nearest the ground, the lowest tiers. On the pyramid there is a record in Egyptian writing of how much was spent on radishes, onions, and leeks for the workmen. If I remember rightly what the interpreter said when he read the inscription to me, the sum was 1,600 talents of silver. If that is so, how much more is likely to have been spent on the iron tools they worked with, and on bread and clothing for the workmen? After all, they spent the time I have mentioned on the building itself, and, I suppose, no small time besides on cutting the stones, hauling them, and digging out the chambers underground.

126. Cheops sank to such wickedness, they said, that when he was short of money he put his own daughter in a brothel and ordered her to earn a certain sum from her customers (how much, they did not tell me). She earned the sum her father set. But she also made a private plan to leave a monument of her own, and she asked each man who came to her to give her one stone for her building. From these stones, they told me, was built the pyramid that stands in the middle of the three in front of the great pyramid, each of its sides a hundred and fifty feet long.

127. This Cheops, the Egyptians said, reigned fifty years, and when he died his brother Chephren took over the kingdom. This king behaved in the same way as the other in everything, and in particular he too built a pyramid. It does not reach the size of his brother's (I know this because I measured it myself). Besides, there are no underground chambers beneath it, and no channel comes to it from the Nile as it does to the other. At the other one the water comes in through a conduit built for the purpose and flows around an island inside, where they say Cheops himself is buried. For the base of his pyramid Chephren built the first course of many-colored Ethiopian stone, and he made it forty feet lower than the other, building it close to the great pyramid. The two stand on the same hill, which is about a hundred feet high. And Chephren, they said, reigned fifty-six years.

128. So here they count a hundred and six years, during which, they say, the Egyptians had nothing but misery, and the temples were kept shut and never opened in all that time. The Egyptians hate these kings so much that they are not very willing to name them. In fact they even call the pyramids after Philitis the shepherd, who grazed his flocks in that area at the time.

129. After him, they said, Mycerinus became king of Egypt. He was the son of Cheops, and his father's actions did not please him. He opened the temples, and he let the people, who had been ground down to the depths of misery, go back to their own work and their sacrifices. He also judged their lawsuits more justly than any other king. For this they praise him above all the kings who had ruled Egypt before him. Not only did he give fair judgments, but when a man complained about a decision, he would compensate him out of his own property and so satisfy him. But while Mycerinus was treating his subjects kindly and behaving as I have described, disasters began to fall on him. The first was this: his daughter died, the only child he had in his house. He was grieved beyond measure at what had happened to him, and wanting to bury his daughter in a more remarkable way than anyone else, he had a cow made of wood and covered with gold, and inside it he buried this daughter who, as I said, had died.

130. This cow was not buried in the ground. It could still be seen in my own time in the city of Sais, set inside the royal palace in a richly decorated room. Every day they burn incense of every kind before it, and every night a lamp burns beside it all night long. Near this cow, in another room, stand statues of Mycerinus' concubines, as the priests at Sais told me. There are in fact huge wooden statues there, about twenty of them, carved as naked figures. But who they are I can't say, beyond what is reported.

131. Some people, however, tell the following story about this cow and the huge statues. Mycerinus, they say, fell in love with his own daughter and then raped her. After this, they say, the girl hanged herself in her grief, and he buried her in this cow. Her mother cut off the hands of the maids who had handed her daughter over to her father, and that is why the statues of them now have suffered what the maids suffered in life. In my opinion those who say this are talking nonsense, especially about the statues' hands. For we saw for ourselves that their hands had simply dropped off with age, and they were still lying at the statues' feet in my own time.

132. The cow is covered with a crimson robe, all except the head and neck, which show, overlaid very thickly with gold. Between the horns there is the disk of the sun, worked in gold. The cow is not standing up but kneeling, and it is the size of a large living cow. Every year it is carried out of its room, at the time when the Egyptians beat their breasts in mourning for that god whom I will not name in a matter like this. At that time they also carry the cow out into the light of day. For they say that when the daughter was dying she asked her father Mycerinus to let her see the sun once a year.

133. After his daughter's death, they said, a second thing happened to this king. An oracle came to him from the city of Buto, saying that he had only six more years to live and would die in the seventh. He was indignant at this, and he sent a message to the oracle reproaching the god. His father and his uncle, he complained, had shut up the temples, had forgotten the gods, and had even been destroyers of men, and yet they had lived a long time; while he, who was devout, was to die so soon. A second message came back from the oracle. It said that this was exactly why his life was being cut short: he had not done what he was supposed to do. Egypt was fated to suffer misery for a hundred and fifty years, and the two kings before him had understood this, but he had not. When Mycerinus heard this, he took it that the sentence on him could not be undone. So he had a great many lamps made, and every night when darkness fell he lit them and drank and enjoyed himself, never stopping, day or night. He roamed the marshes and the woods and wherever he heard there were the best places for pleasure. He came up with this plan because he meant to prove the oracle a liar: by turning his nights into days, he would get twelve years of life instead of six.

134. This king too left a pyramid behind him, much smaller than his father's. It is square, each side 280 feet long, and it is built of Ethiopian stone up to half its height. Some of the Greeks say this pyramid was built by Rhodopis the courtesan, but they are wrong. In fact it is clear to me that the people who say this don't even know who Rhodopis was. Otherwise they would never have credited her with building a pyramid like this one, which cost what you might call countless thousands of talents. Besides, they don't know that Rhodopis was in her prime in the reign of Amasis, not in this king's reign; Rhodopis lived a great many years after the kings who left these pyramids. She was Thracian by birth, and she was the slave of Iadmon son of Hephaestopolis, a Samian, and a fellow slave of Aesop the writer of fables. For Aesop too was once Iadmon's slave, and the best proof of it is this. When the people of Delphi, obeying an oracle, proclaimed again and again that they were looking for someone to claim the compensation owed for Aesop's death, no one came forward except, in the end, Iadmon's grandson, who was also called Iadmon, and he took it. That shows that Aesop too was Iadmon's slave.

135. As for Rhodopis, she came to Egypt brought by Xanthes the Samian. She came there to work at her trade, and she was bought out of slavery for a large sum by a man of Mytilene, Charaxus son of Scamandronymus, the brother of Sappho the poet. So Rhodopis was set free. She stayed in Egypt, and her beauty made her so popular that she earned a great deal of money for a woman like Rhodopis, though not nearly enough to pay for a pyramid like this one. In fact there is no need to credit her with great riches, since a tenth of her wealth can still be seen today by anyone who wants to look. Rhodopis wanted to leave a memorial of herself in Greece: to have something made that no one else had happened to think of and dedicate in a temple, and to dedicate it at Delphi in her own memory. So with a tenth of her wealth she had iron spits made, big enough to roast a whole ox on, as many of them as her tenth would pay for, and she sent them to Delphi. They are still lying there today, heaped together behind the altar the Chians dedicated, right opposite the temple's inner shrine. The courtesans at Naucratis, it happens, are apt to become famous. This woman first, the one the story is about, became so famous that every Greek came to know the name of Rhodopis. And after her another, named Archidice, became the subject of songs all over Greece, though she was less talked about than the first. As for Charaxus, when he went home to Mytilene after buying Rhodopis' freedom, Sappho attacked him fiercely in one of her poems. But I will say no more about Rhodopis.

136. After Mycerinus, the priests said, Asychis became king of Egypt. He built the gateway of Hephaestus' temple that faces the sunrise, by far the most beautiful and the largest of the gateways. They all have figures carved on them and countless architectural ornaments besides, but this one has far more than the rest. In this king's reign, they told me, money changed hands very slowly, so a law was made for the Egyptians that a man could borrow the money he needed by putting up his father's dead body as security. A second law was added to this one: the lender would also have a claim on the borrower's whole family tomb. And the man who gave this security faced the following penalty if he refused to repay the debt: he himself would not be allowed burial when he died, either in that family tomb or in any other, and he would not be allowed to bury any of his relatives who died. This king, wanting to outdo the kings who had ruled Egypt before him, left as his monument a pyramid made of bricks. On it there is an inscription carved in stone, which says: "Do not think less of me beside the pyramids of stone, for I surpass them as far as Zeus surpasses the other gods. They thrust a pole into the lake, and whatever mud stuck to the pole they gathered up and made into bricks, and that is how they finished me."

Those were the deeds of this king.

137. After him reigned a blind man from the city of Anysis, whose name was Anysis. In his reign the Ethiopians and Sabacus, the king of the Ethiopians, marched on Egypt with a great army. So this blind man ran away and fled into the marshes, and the Ethiopian ruled Egypt for fifty years. This is what he did in that time. Whenever an Egyptian committed a crime, he never put him to death. Instead he sentenced each man according to how serious his crime was, setting him to work heaping up an embankment in front of the city he came from. In this way the cities were raised even higher than before. They had been built up first by the men who dug the canals in the reign of Sesostris, and then a second time in the reign of the Ethiopian, and so they became very high. Other cities in Egypt also stand high, but I think the earth was piled up most of all at the town of Bubastis. In this city there is a temple well worth mentioning. There are other temples that are larger and more costly, but none is more pleasing to the eye. Bubastis, in the Greek language, is Artemis.

138. Her temple is laid out like this. Except for the entrance it is completely surrounded by water. Two channels come in from the Nile, not joining each other, but each running as far as the temple's entrance, one flowing around one side and the other around the other side. Each is a hundred feet wide and shaded with trees. The gateway is sixty feet high, and it is decorated with figures nine feet tall, very remarkable ones. The temple stands in the middle of the city, and you can look down into it from all sides as you walk around. That is because the city has been built up high, while the temple has stayed where it was first built, so it is possible to see down into it. A stone wall with figures carved on it runs around it. Inside there is a grove of very tall trees, planted around a large shrine, and in the shrine is the statue of the goddess. The temple measures six hundred feet each way. Opposite the entrance there is a road paved with stone, about a third of a mile long, which runs east through the marketplace. It is about four hundred feet wide, and trees that reach to the sky grow on both sides of it. The road leads to the temple of Hermes. That is how this temple is laid out.

139. Egypt was finally rid of the Ethiopian, they said, in this way. He fled because of a dream. In it a man seemed to come and stand over him and advise him to gather together all the priests of Egypt and cut them in half. After he had this dream, he said that it seemed to him the gods were showing him this to give him a pretext for committing a sacrilege, so that he would suffer some harm either from the gods or from men. He would not do it, he said. Besides, in truth, the time was up during which it had been foretold that he would rule Egypt before he left. For when he was in Ethiopia, the oracles the Ethiopians consult had told him that he was fated to rule Egypt for fifty years. Since that time was now running out, and the dream also troubled him, Sabacus left Egypt of his own accord.

140. When the Ethiopian had gone away out of Egypt, the blind man came back from the marshes and began to rule again. He had lived there for fifty years on an island he had made by heaping up ashes and earth. Whenever any of the Egyptians visited him with food, as each of them in turn had been assigned to do without the Ethiopian's knowledge, he told them to bring some ashes too as part of their gift. No one could find this island before Amyrtaeus; that is, for more than seven hundred years the kings before Amyrtaeus were unable to find it. The island's name is Elbo, and it is a little over a mile across each way.

141. After him the throne went to the priest of Hephaestus, whose name was Sethos. This man, they said, treated the warrior class of the Egyptians with contempt, thinking he would never need them. Among other insults, he took away the land they had been given as a special grant under the earlier kings, twelve arourae of grain land to each man (an aroura is about two-thirds of an acre). After this, Sanacharib, king of the Arabians and Assyrians, marched a great army against Egypt. Then the Egyptian warriors refused to come to the rescue. The priest, in desperate straits, went into the inner shrine of the temple and wept before the god's statue over the danger that was hanging over him. As he lamented, sleep came over him, and in his dream the god seemed to come and stand beside him and encourage him. Nothing bad would happen to him, the god said, if he went out to meet the Arabian army, because the god himself would send him helpers. Trusting in this dream, he took with him, they said, those Egyptians who were willing to follow him, and camped at Pelusium, since that was the way the invasion was coming. Not one of the warrior class went with him: his men were shopkeepers, craftsmen, and market traders. When they arrived, field mice swarmed over their enemies in the night and gnawed through their quivers and their bows, and the handles of their shields as well. So the next day the enemy fled, with no weapons to defend themselves, and a great many of them fell. And to this day this king stands in stone in the temple of Hephaestus, holding a mouse in his hand, with an inscription in which he says: "Let whoever looks at me learn to fear the gods."

142. Up to this point in the story it was the Egyptians and their priests who gave the account. They declared that from the first king down to this priest of Hephaestus, who reigned last, there had been 341 generations of men, and that in that time there had been the same number of high priests and of kings. Now 300 generations of men come to 10,000 years, since three generations make a hundred years. And the forty-one generations left over, beyond the 300, come to 1,340 years. So over a period of 11,340 years, they said, no god had appeared in human form; and they did not report anything of the kind happening either before or afterward among the remaining kings of Egypt. In this time, they said, the sun had moved from its usual place of rising four times: twice it had risen where it now sets, and twice it had set where it now rises. And all that time nothing in Egypt had changed from its normal state, not the crops that come from the earth, not what comes to them from the river, not their diseases or their deaths.

143. Some time before me, when Hecataeus the historian was in Thebes, he traced his family tree back and linked it to a god sixteen generations earlier. The priests of Zeus did for him much what they did for me (though I did not trace my ancestry). They took me into the inner hall of the temple, which is very large, and counted up the number, showing me huge wooden statues, as many as they had said. For every high priest there sets up a statue of himself during his lifetime. So the priests counted these and showed them to me, and declared that each one was a son succeeding his own father. They went through the line of statues, starting from the statue of the one who had died most recently, until they had declared this of every one of them. And when Hecataeus traced his descent and linked his family to a god in the sixteenth generation, they set a family tree of their own against his, along with their count. They would not accept from him that a man had been born from a god. They traced their own line this way: each of the statues, they said, had been a Piromis son of a Piromis, until they had declared this of all 345 statues, each one called Piromis; and they linked their line neither to a god nor to a hero. Piromis means, in Greek, "a gentleman," a good and honorable man.

144. So what they showed was that the men the statues stood for had all been like this, and very far from being gods. But before these men, they said, gods had ruled in Egypt. They did not live among men, and there was always one of them in power at a time. The last of them to be king of Egypt was Horus son of Osiris, whom the Greeks call Apollo. He was the last king of Egypt, having overthrown Typhon. Osiris, in Greek, is Dionysus.

145. Among the Greeks, Heracles, Dionysus, and Pan are thought to be the youngest of the gods. But with the Egyptians, Pan is a very ancient god, one of the gods called the Eight; Heracles belongs to the second rank, the gods called the Twelve; and Dionysus belongs to the third rank, the gods who were born from the Twelve. I have already shown how old Heracles is by the Egyptians' own reckoning, counting down to the reign of Amasis. Pan is said to have existed even longer than that, and Dionysus the shortest time of the three. Yet even for him they count 15,000 years down to the reign of Amasis. The Egyptians say they know this for certain, because they have always kept count and written down the years as they passed. But the Dionysus who is said to have been born of Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, was born about 1,600 years before my time; Heracles, the son of Alcmene, about nine hundred years; and Pan, the son of Penelope (for the Greeks say Pan was born of her and Hermes), came into being after the Trojan War, about eight hundred years before my time.

146. Of these two accounts, anyone may adopt whichever he finds more believable when he hears it. I, for my part, have already given my opinion about them. If these two, Dionysus son of Semele and Pan son of Penelope, had also appeared openly and lived out their lives to old age in Greece, as Heracles son of Amphitryon did, then one might have said that they too had been born ordinary men, and named after the gods who had come into being long before. But as it is, the Greeks say of Dionysus that as soon as he was born Zeus sewed him up in his thigh and carried him to Nysa, which is beyond Egypt in Ethiopia; and as for Pan, they cannot say where he went after he was born. So it has become clear to me that the Greeks learned the names of these gods later than those of the others, and date their birth to the time when they first learned their names.

Up to this point, then, the history is told by the Egyptians themselves.

147. But now I will tell what other peoples also tell, with the Egyptians agreeing with them, about what happened in this country. And to this I will also add something of what I have seen myself.

After the reign of the priest of Hephaestus, the Egyptians were free; but they could never live for any length of time without a king, so they set up twelve kings over themselves, dividing all of Egypt into twelve parts. These kings intermarried and ruled together. They made an agreement not to overthrow one another, and not to try to get the better of one another, but to live in perfect friendship. The reason they made these agreements, and guarded them so strictly against being broken, was this. At the very start, when they first took power, they had been given an oracle that whichever of them poured a libation from a bronze cup in the temple of Hephaestus would become king of all Egypt (for they used to meet together in all the temples).

Chapter 14: The Labyrinth, and the Reigns from Psammetichus to Amasis

148. The twelve kings also decided to join together and leave a memorial of themselves. Having decided this, they had a labyrinth built, a little above Lake Moeris and nearly opposite the place called the City of Crocodiles. I have seen it myself, and I found it greater than words can say. If you were to put together and add up all the buildings and great works the Greeks have produced, they would turn out to have cost less labor and money than this labyrinth, even though the temple at Ephesus and the one at Samos are certainly works worth noting. The pyramids, too, were greater than words can say, and each one of them is equal to many of the Greeks' works, great as those may be; but the labyrinth surpasses even the pyramids. It has twelve roofed courts, with their gates facing one another, six on the north side and six on the south, all joined to one another, and the same wall surrounds them all on the outside. There are two kinds of rooms in it, one kind below ground and the other above, built on top of them, three thousand in number, fifteen hundred of each kind. The upper rooms we saw for ourselves, walking through them, and we describe them having looked at them with our own eyes. The underground rooms we know only by report, because the Egyptians in charge of them would not on any account show them to us. They said that the tombs of the kings who first built this labyrinth were down there, and the tombs of the sacred crocodiles. So we tell about the lower rooms from what we heard, while the upper ones we saw ourselves and found to be works greater than human. The passages through the rooms, and the winding ways this way and that through the courts, which were splendidly decorated, gave us endless cause for wonder as we went from a court into the rooms beyond it, and from the rooms into colonnades, and from the colonnades into other rooms, and then from the rooms again into other courts. Over the whole of it is a roof of stone, like the walls. The walls are covered with carved figures, and each court is surrounded by a colonnade of white stone, fitted together perfectly. At the far end of the labyrinth, by its corner, there is a pyramid 240 feet high, with large figures carved on it, and an underground passage has been made leading to it.

149. That is the labyrinth. But the lake called Lake Moeris, beside which the labyrinth is built, is an even greater wonder. Its shoreline runs about 400 miles all the way around (sixty schoeni), which is the same length as the whole coast of Egypt along the sea. The lake stretches lengthwise from north to south, and where it is deepest it is 300 feet deep. It is obvious that this lake was made by hand and dug out, because near the middle of it stand two pyramids, each rising 300 feet above the water, with an equal height built below the water. On top of each one is a colossal stone statue of a man seated on a throne. So these pyramids are a hundred fathoms high, and a hundred fathoms make up a stade of six hundred feet; the fathom is six feet, or four cubits, the foot is four palms, and the cubit is six palms. The water in the lake does not come from the spot itself, since the land there is very short of water. It has been brought in from the Nile by a canal. For six months the water flows into the lake, and for six months it flows back out into the Nile. During the six months that it flows out, the fish that are caught bring a talent of silver a day into the royal treasury, and twenty minas a day while the water is flowing in.

150. The people who live there also told me that this lake has an underground outlet to the Syrtis in Libya, running west toward the interior of the continent along the mountain range above Memphis. Now, I could not see the earth from this excavation lying anywhere, and that was something that caught my attention. So I asked the people who lived nearest the lake where the earth that had been dug out had gone. They told me where it had been carried, and I easily believed them, because I had heard that something similar was once done at Nineveh, the city of the Assyrians. There, some thieves once made a plan to carry off the treasure of King Sardanapalus son of Ninus. It was a very great treasure, and it was kept in underground treasure-houses. So the thieves started from their own house and, working out their direction, dug underground toward the king's palace. Each night, when it got dark, they carried the earth from their tunnel down to the river Tigris, which flows past the city of Nineveh, until at last they got what they were after. I heard that the lake in Egypt was dug in a similar way, except that the work was done by day and not by night. As the Egyptians dug, they carried the earth they had dug out to the Nile, and the river, once it received the earth, naturally carried it off and scattered it. That, they say, is how this lake was dug.

151. The twelve kings went on ruling justly. But as time went on, this is what happened. They had offered sacrifice in the temple of Hephaestus, and on the last day of the festival they were about to pour libations. The high priest brought out the golden cups they always used for pouring them, but he miscounted and brought only eleven for the twelve kings. So the one standing last in line, Psammetichus, having no cup, took off his helmet, which was made of bronze, held it out to receive the wine, and poured his libation with it. All the other kings wore helmets too, as was their custom, and they happened to have them on then. Psammetichus held out his helmet without any treacherous intent. But the others took note of what he had done, and they remembered the oracle, which had told them that whichever of them poured a libation from a bronze cup would become the sole king of Egypt. Remembering the oracle's words, they did not think it right to kill Psammetichus, since when they questioned him they found that he had not done it on purpose. But they decided to strip him of almost all his power and drive him off into the marshes, and to forbid him from having any dealings with the rest of Egypt from there.

152. This Psammetichus had once before been an exile. He had fled from Sabacus the Ethiopian, who had killed his father Necho, and he had lived as an exile in Syria. When the Ethiopian left Egypt because of the vision he saw in his dream, the Egyptians of the district of Sais brought Psammetichus back home. Later, when he was one of the kings, it was his fate to be an exile a second time, driven out into the marshes by the eleven kings because of the helmet. Believing that they had done him a great wrong, he thought about how he could take revenge on the men who had driven him out. He sent to the oracle of Leto in the city of Buto, which is the most truthful oracle the Egyptians have, and the answer came back that his revenge would come when men of bronze appeared from the sea. He was strongly inclined not to believe that men of bronze would come to help him. But not long afterward some Ionians and Carians who had sailed out on a raid for plunder were forced to put in to the shore of Egypt. They landed, dressed in bronze armor, and one of the Egyptians, who had never before seen men in bronze armor, went to the marshes and reported to Psammetichus that men of bronze had come from the sea and were plundering the plain. Psammetichus saw that the oracle's words were coming true. He treated the Ionians and Carians in a friendly way, and with large promises he persuaded them to join his side. Once he had persuaded them, he overthrew the other kings with the help of these foreign mercenaries and of the Egyptians who supported him.

153. Now that he had power over all of Egypt, Psammetichus built for Hephaestus the gateway of the temple at Memphis that faces south. Opposite this gateway he built a court for Apis, where Apis is kept whenever he appears. It has a colonnade all around it and is covered with carved figures, and instead of columns the roof of the court is held up by colossal statues eighteen feet tall. Apis, in the Greek language, is Epaphus.

154. To the Ionians and Carians who had helped him, Psammetichus gave plots of land to live on, facing one another across the Nile, and these were called the Encampments. He gave them this land, and he also paid them everything he had promised. He also put Egyptian boys in their care to be taught the Greek language, and the present class of interpreters in Egypt is descended from these boys, who learned the language thoroughly. The Ionians and Carians lived on these lands for a long time. They lie toward the sea, a little below the city of Bubastis, on the branch of the Nile called the Pelusian mouth. Later King Amasis moved them out of there and settled them at Memphis, making them his own bodyguard against the Egyptians. Because they have lived in Egypt, we Greeks, through our dealings with them, know accurately everything that has happened in Egypt from the reign of King Psammetichus onward, for they were the first people of a foreign language to settle in Egypt. In the land they were moved from, the sheds where they hauled up their ships and the ruins of their houses were still there in my own time.

So that is how Psammetichus got Egypt.

155. I have mentioned the Egyptian oracle many times before this, and now I will give an account of it, since it deserves to be described. This oracle in Egypt is sacred to Leto, and it is in a great city near the branch of the Nile called the Sebennytic mouth, on your way upriver from the sea. The name of the city where the oracle is, as I have said before when I mentioned it, is Buto. In this Buto there is a temple of Apollo and Artemis, and the shrine of Leto, where the oracle is, is large in itself and has a gateway sixty feet high. But I will now tell what amazed me most of all the things to be seen there. In this sacred enclosure there is a shrine of Leto made from a single stone, both in height and in length, and all its walls are the same in both directions, sixty feet each. Another stone is laid on top of it to make the roof, and its cornice is six feet deep.

156. Of all the things I saw at that temple, then, this shrine is the most amazing. Next after it comes the island called Chemmis. This island lies in a deep, broad lake beside the temple at Buto, and the Egyptians say that it is a floating island. I myself never saw it floating about or moved from its place, and I am astonished to hear it said, and I wonder whether it really is a floating island. On this island there is a great shrine of Apollo, with three altars set up inside it, and many palm trees grow on the island, along with other trees, some bearing fruit and some not. When the Egyptians say that the island floats, they add this story. This island, they say, did not float before. Leto, who was one of the first eight gods to come into being, and who lived in the city of Buto, where she has this oracle, was given Apollo by Isis to look after, and she kept him safe by hiding him on this island, which is now said to float. That was at the time when Typhon came after him, searching everywhere, hoping to find the son of Osiris. They say that Apollo and Artemis are the children of Dionysus and Isis, and that Leto was their nurse and protector. In the Egyptian language, Apollo is Horus, Demeter is Isis, and Artemis is Bubastis. It was from this story, and from nowhere else, that Aeschylus son of Euphorion took the idea I am about to mention, in which he differs from all the poets before him: he made Artemis the daughter of Demeter. And this, they say, is the reason the island came to float.

That is the story they tell.

157. As for Psammetichus, he was king of Egypt for fifty-four years. For twenty-nine of those years he sat outside Azotus, a great city of Syria, besieging it, until at last he took it. Of all the cities we know of, this Azotus held out longest under a siege.

158. Psammetichus' son was Necho, and he became king of Egypt. He was the first to begin the canal leading to the Erythraean Sea, which Darius the Persian finished later. Its length is a voyage of four days, and it was dug wide enough for two triremes, the three-banked warships, to row along it side by side. Its water is brought in from the Nile. The canal leaves the Nile a little above the city of Bubastis, passes by Patumus, the Arabian city, and runs into the Erythraean Sea. It is dug first along the parts of the Egyptian plain that face Arabia. Just above them run the mountains that stretch along opposite Memphis, where the stone quarries are. The canal follows the foot of these mountains from west to east for a long way. After that it turns toward a gap in the hills and runs from these mountains southward, toward midday and the south wind, to the Arabian Gulf, the Red Sea. Now the shortest and most direct crossing from the Northern Sea to the Southern Sea (which is also called the Erythraean), that is, from the Mediterranean to the Indian Ocean, starts from Mount Casius, the boundary between Egypt and Syria; from there to the Arabian Gulf is exactly 111 miles. But the canal is much longer, since it winds a great deal. During Necho's reign, 120,000 Egyptians died digging it. Necho stopped in the middle of the digging because an oracle stood in his way: it said that he was working for the barbarian. The Egyptians call everyone who does not speak their language a barbarian.

159. After giving up work on the canal, Necho turned to making war. He had triremes built, some for the Northern Sea and others in the Arabian Gulf for the Erythraean Sea, and the sheds where they were kept can still be seen. He used these ships when he needed them. On land, too, Necho fought the Syrians at Magdolus and defeated them, and after this he took Cadytis, a great city of Syria. He dedicated the clothes he was wearing when he won these victories to Apollo, sending them to Branchidae in the territory of Miletus. After this, when he had reigned sixteen years in all, he died and handed the kingdom on to his son Psammis.

160. While this Psammis was king of Egypt, envoys came to him from the Eleans. The Eleans boasted that they ran the games at Olympia in the most just and honorable way possible, and they thought that not even the Egyptians, the wisest of men, could find anything to add to their rules. When the Eleans came to Egypt and explained what they had come for, the king called together the Egyptians who were thought to be the wisest. When these Egyptians had gathered, they heard the Eleans describe everything it was their job to do in running the games. When the Eleans had told them everything, they said they had come to learn whether the Egyptians could find anything to add that was fairer still. The Egyptians talked it over together and then asked the Eleans whether their own citizens took part in the games. The Eleans said that anyone who wanted to, whether one of their own people or any other Greek, was equally free to compete. At this the Egyptians said that in setting things up this way they had completely missed the mark of fairness. It was impossible, they said, for the Eleans not to favor a man from their own city if he was competing, and so to treat the outsider unfairly. If they really wanted to run the games fairly, as they said they did, and if this was the reason they had come to Egypt, the Egyptians advised them to set up the games so that only outsiders could compete, and no Elean would be allowed to. That was the advice the Egyptians gave the Eleans.

161. Psammis had been king of Egypt for only six years. He made an expedition into Ethiopia, and soon afterward he died. Apries, the son of Psammis, inherited the kingdom after him. Apries became the most prosperous of all the kings up to that time, except only for his great-grandfather Psammetichus. He reigned twenty-five years, and during that time he led an army against Sidon and fought a sea battle with the king of Tyre. But since it was fated that disaster should come on him, it came about through something I will tell at greater length in the Libyan part of my history, and only briefly here. Apries sent a great expedition against the people of Cyrene, and it met with a correspondingly great disaster. The Egyptians blamed him for this and rebelled against him. They believed that Apries had deliberately sent them out to certain ruin, so that (as they put it) there might be a slaughter of them, and he could rule the rest of the Egyptians more securely. Angry at this, both the men who had come back from the expedition and the friends of those who had died rose in open revolt.

162. When Apries heard this, he sent Amasis to them to talk them out of it. Amasis came and was trying to restrain the Egyptians. But while he was speaking and telling them not to do it, one of the Egyptians stood up behind him and put a helmet on his head, saying as he did it that he was putting it on him to crown him king. This was not altogether unwelcome to Amasis, as his conduct showed, for as soon as the rebel Egyptians had made him king, he got ready to march against Apries. When Apries heard this, he sent to Amasis one of the Egyptians of his own court, a man of high standing named Patarbemis, with orders to bring Amasis back to him alive. When Patarbemis arrived and summoned Amasis, Amasis, who happened to be sitting on horseback, lifted his leg and broke wind, and told him to take that back to Apries. All the same, they say, Patarbemis demanded that he go to the king, since the king had sent for him. Amasis answered that he had been getting ready to do that for some time, and that Apries would have no reason to complain of him. Patarbemis understood what he meant from what he said, and he also saw his preparations, so he left in a hurry, wanting to let the king know as quickly as possible what was going on. But when he came back to Apries without Amasis, the king would not listen to what he had to say. In a violent rage, he ordered his ears and nose to be cut off. When the rest of the Egyptians who were still on Apries' side saw the most respected man among them treated with such shameful outrage, they waited no longer. They went over to the rebels and gave themselves up to Amasis.

163. When Apries heard this too, he armed his foreign mercenaries and marched against the Egyptians. He had Carian and Ionian mercenaries with him, thirty thousand of them. His royal palace was in the city of Sais, and it was large and well worth seeing. So Apries and his army were advancing against the Egyptians, and Amasis and his men were advancing against the mercenaries. Both sides came to the city of Momemphis and were about to try their strength against each other.

164. The Egyptians are divided into seven classes. One class is called the priests, another the warriors, and the rest are the cowherds, the swineherds, the shopkeepers, the interpreters, and the boatmen. That is the number of the Egyptian classes, and they are named after the work they do. The warriors are called Calasirians and Hermotybians, and they come from the following districts, since all of Egypt is divided into districts.

165. The districts of the Hermotybians are Busiris, Sais, Chemmis, Papremis, the island called Prosopitis, and half of Natho. These are the districts the Hermotybians come from, and at their most numerous they reached 160,000. Not one of them has learned any trade; they are devoted entirely to war.

166. The districts of the Calasirians, in turn, are Thebes, Bubastis, Aphthis, Tanis, Mendes, Sebennytus, Athribis, Pharbaethus, Thmuis, Onuphis, Anytis, and Myecphoris, which last is on an island opposite the city of Bubastis. These are the districts of the Calasirians, and at their most numerous they reached 250,000 men. They, like the others, are not allowed to practice any trade. They practice only what has to do with war, and the skill is handed down from father to son.

167. Now whether the Greeks learned this too from the Egyptians I can't say for certain. I see that the Thracians, the Scythians, the Persians, the Lydians, and nearly all non-Greeks hold those of their citizens who learn trades, and their descendants, in less honor than the rest, while those who have nothing to do with working with their hands are counted noble, and above all those who are devoted to war. However that may be, all the Greeks have learned this attitude, the Spartans most of all. The Corinthians look down least on people who work at crafts.

168. This class, alone among the Egyptians apart from the priests, was given a special privilege: each man was granted twelve arourae of land, free of taxes. The aroura measures a hundred Egyptian cubits each way, about two-thirds of an acre, and the Egyptian cubit happens to be the same as the Samian. This privilege was given to all of them. They also had other benefits in turn, never the same men twice: each year a thousand Calasirians and a thousand Hermotybians served as the king's bodyguard. On top of their land, these men were given a daily ration of five pounds of bread each, two pounds of beef, and four half-pints of wine. That was the ration given to the men serving as the king's bodyguard at any one time.

169. So Apries, leading his foreign mercenaries, and Amasis, at the head of the whole body of the Egyptians, advanced on each other until they reached the city of Momemphis, and there they fought. The foreign troops fought well, but they were far fewer in number, and because of that they were beaten. Apries, they say, believed that not even a god could put an end to his rule, so firmly established did he think it was. But in that battle he was beaten. He was taken alive and brought to the city of Sais, to what had once been his own home and from then on was the palace of Amasis. He was kept in the palace there for some time, and Amasis treated him well. But in the end the Egyptians blamed Amasis, saying he was doing wrong to keep alive the man who was the worst enemy both of themselves and of him. So he handed Apries over to the Egyptians, and they strangled him and then buried him in the burial place of his ancestors. This is in the temple of Athena, close to the sanctuary, on the left as you go in. The people of Sais buried inside this temple all the kings who had come from their district. The tomb of Amasis is there too: it is farther from the sanctuary than that of Apries and his ancestors, but it is also inside the temple court. It is a great stone colonnade, with columns carved to look like date palms, and richly decorated in other ways. Inside the colonnade there are double doors, and inside the doors is the burial chamber.

170. At Sais there is also the burial place of one whose name I think it irreverent to mention in connection with such a matter. It is in the temple of Athena, behind the shrine of the goddess, and it runs along the whole length of its wall. In the sacred enclosure stand great stone obelisks, and near them is a lake, edged with stonework and neatly made in a circle. In size, it seemed to me, it is equal to the one at Delos called the Round Pool.

171. On this lake, at night, the Egyptians act out the story of his sufferings, and they call this the Mysteries. I know more fully how each of these things is done, but I will leave it unspoken. And about the secret rites of Demeter, which the Greeks call the Thesmophoria, I will also say nothing, although I know about them, except as much as religion permits me to tell. It was the daughters of Danaus who brought this rite out of Egypt and taught it to the Pelasgian women. Later, when the Dorians drove out all the inhabitants of the Peloponnese, the rite was lost, and only those Peloponnesians who were left behind and not driven out, that is, the Arcadians, kept it.

172. Now that Apries had been overthrown, Amasis became king. He came from the district of Sais, and the city he came from is called Siuph. At first the Egyptians looked down on Amasis and thought little of him, because he had been a commoner and came from no distinguished family. But later Amasis won them over by cleverness rather than by force. Among countless other treasures he owned, there was a golden footbath, in which Amasis himself and all his dinner guests always washed their feet. He had it broken up and made into the statue of a god, and he set it up in the city in the most suitable spot. The Egyptians kept coming to visit the statue and worshiped it devoutly. When Amasis learned what the people of the city were doing, he called the Egyptians together and told them the truth. The statue, he said, had been made from the footbath, which the Egyptians had once used to throw up in and urinate in and wash their feet in, and now they worshiped it devoutly. And just like the footbath, he went on, so it had gone with him: he used to be a commoner, but now he was their king. So he told them to honor him and treat him with respect.

173. That was how he won over the Egyptians, so that they agreed to serve him. And this was how he arranged his days. From early morning until the time the marketplace fills up, he worked willingly at whatever business was brought to him. After that he spent his time drinking and joking with his drinking companions, and he was frivolous and playful. His friends were troubled by this, and they warned him in words something like these:

"My king, you are not governing yourself properly when you let yourself sink into such trivial behavior. You ought to be sitting all day long in state on a stately throne and conducting your business. Then the Egyptians would be sure they were ruled by a great man, and you would have a better name. As it is, you are not acting like a king at all."

He answered them like this: "People who own bows string them when they want to use them, and when they have finished using them they unstring them again. If a bow were kept strung all the time, it would break, and then they couldn't use it when they needed it. It's the same with a man. If he wanted to be serious all the time and never let himself relax for a bit of fun at the proper time, he would either go mad or be struck senseless before he knew it. Since I know this well, I give a share of my time to each of the two ways of living."

That was his reply to his friends.

174. It is said, though, that even when he was a private citizen Amasis loved drinking and joking and was not at all a serious man. Whenever he ran out of money because of his drinking and high living, he would go around stealing. The people he stole from would accuse him of having their property, and when he denied it, they would take him for judgment to an oracle, whenever there was one in their area. Many times he was found guilty by the oracles, and many times he was acquitted. And then, when he finally became king, this is what he did. All the gods who had acquitted him and declared that he was not a thief he ignored: he gave nothing toward the upkeep of their temples, and he did not even visit them to offer sacrifice, because he considered them worthless and their oracles liars. But all the gods who had found him guilty of theft he treated with the greatest respect, because he considered them true gods with oracles that did not lie.

175. First, in Sais, he built and completed for Athena a temple gateway that is a great wonder. In it he far outdid everyone who had done such work before, both in its height and in its size, so large and so fine are its stones. Second, he dedicated great colossal statues and very large sphinxes with men's heads, and for repairs he brought in other stones of enormous size. Some of these he had brought from the stone quarries opposite Memphis, and others, of very great size, from the city of Elephantine, which is a voyage of no less than twenty days from Sais. But what amazes me most of all of them is this: a room carved from a single stone, which he brought from the city of Elephantine. It took three years to bring it, and two thousand men were assigned to haul it, all of them from the class of boatmen. On the outside this room is thirty-one and a half feet long, twenty-one feet wide, and twelve feet high. Those are the outside measurements of the one-stone room. Inside, it is twenty-eight feet three inches long, eighteen feet wide, and seven and a half feet high. It lies beside the entrance to the temple. They did not haul it inside the temple, the story goes, because while the room was being dragged along, its master builder groaned aloud, since so much time had gone into it and he was worn out by the work. Amasis took this to heart as a warning and would not let them drag it any farther. Others say, on the other hand, that one of the men moving it with levers was crushed to death under it, and that this is why it was not hauled in.

176. Amasis also dedicated, in all the other temples of any note, works that are worth seeing for their size. Among them is the colossal statue at Memphis that lies on its back in front of the temple of Hephaestus. It is seventy-five feet long, and on the same base, made of the same stone, stand two colossal statues, each twenty feet tall, one on each side of the large one. There is another stone statue of the same size at Sais, lying the same way as the one at Memphis. It was also Amasis who built and finished the temple of Isis at Memphis, which is very large and well worth seeing.

177. It is said that in the reign of Amasis Egypt was more prosperous than at any time before, both in what the river gives the land and in what the land gives its people, and that the inhabited towns in it at that time numbered twenty thousand in all. It was Amasis, too, who made the law that every year each Egyptian had to declare to the governor of his district how he made his living, and anyone who failed to do this, or who could not show that he made an honest living, was to be punished with death. Solon the Athenian took this law from Egypt and had it passed for the Athenians, and they still keep it, since it is a law no one can find fault with.

178. Amasis also became a friend of the Greeks. Among other signs of friendship that he showed to some of them, he gave the city of Naucratis to those who came to Egypt, as a place to live. To those who did not want to settle there but sailed there to trade, he gave plots of land where they could set up altars and sacred enclosures for their gods. The largest of these enclosures, and the most famous and most visited, is called the Hellenion, and it was founded jointly by the following cities: of the Ionians, Chios, Teos, Phocaea, and Clazomenae; of the Dorians, Rhodes, Cnidus, Halicarnassus, and Phaselis; and of the Aeolians, Mytilene alone. The enclosure belongs to these cities, and they are the ones that appoint the overseers of the port. Any other cities that claim a share in it are claiming something they have no right to.
