Apart from this, the Aeginetans set up a sacred enclosure of their own, dedicated to Zeus, the Samians one to Hera, and the Milesians one to Apollo.

179. In the old days Naucratis was the only trading port in Egypt; there was no other. If anyone came into any of the other mouths of the Nile, he had to swear that he had not come there of his own free will. When he had sworn this oath of innocence, he had to sail his ship around to the Canopic mouth. Or if he could not sail there because of contrary winds, he had to carry his cargo around the tip of the Delta in barges to Naucratis. That was how highly Naucratis was privileged.

180. Then there is the temple at Delphi. The temple that used to stand there had burned down by accident, and the Amphictyons, the league of neighboring states that looks after Delphi, contracted for the building of the temple that stands there now, at a price of three hundred talents. The people of Delphi were to supply a quarter of that payment, so they went around to various cities collecting contributions. When they did this, they got as much from Egypt as from anywhere. Amasis gave them a thousand talents' weight of alum, some 57,000 pounds, while the Greeks living in Egypt gave them twenty minas of silver.

181. Amasis also made a treaty of friendship and alliance with the people of Cyrene. He decided as well to marry a wife from there, either because he wanted a Greek wife, or else out of friendship for the people of Cyrene. However that may be, he married a woman who was, some say, the daughter of Battus, others say of Arcesilaus, and others of Critobulus, a respected citizen; and her name was Ladice. But whenever Amasis went to bed with her, he found he was unable to have sex with her, though with his other wives he managed as usual. This happened again and again, and Amasis said to his wife, this Ladice: "Woman, you have bewitched me with drugs, and you will die a worse death than any other woman ever has." Ladice denied it, but her denials did nothing to soften Amasis' anger against her. So she made a silent vow to Aphrodite: if Amasis had sex with her that night (since that was the only way out of her danger), she would send a statue of the goddess to be dedicated at Cyrene. And right after the vow Amasis did have sex with her, and from then on, whenever he came to her, he had sex with her, and after this he became very deeply attached to her. Ladice paid the vow she had made to the goddess: she had a statue made and sent it to Cyrene, and it was still there in my own time, standing with its face turned away from the city of Cyrene. When Cambyses conquered Egypt and learned from Ladice who she was, he sent her back to Cyrene unharmed.

182. Amasis also dedicated offerings in Greece. At Cyrene he dedicated a gilded statue of Athena and a painted portrait of himself. In the temple of Athena at Lindus he dedicated two stone statues and a remarkable linen breastplate worth seeing. And at Samos he dedicated to Hera two wooden statues of himself, which were still standing in my own time in the great temple, behind the doors. He made his offerings at Samos because of the bond of guest-friendship between himself and Polycrates son of Aeaces. At Lindus it was not because of any guest-friendship, but because the temple of Athena at Lindus is said to have been founded by the daughters of Danaus, who landed there when they were fleeing from the sons of Aegyptus. Those were the offerings Amasis dedicated. And he was the first man ever to conquer Cyprus and make it pay him tribute.

Book Three: Thalia

Chapter 15: Cambyses Conquers Egypt, and the March against the Ethiopians

1. It was against this Amasis that Cambyses son of Cyrus was now marching. He took with him the other nations he ruled, and Greeks as well, both Ionians and Aeolians. The cause of the expedition was this. Cambyses sent an envoy to Egypt and asked Amasis for his daughter. He made the request on the advice of an Egyptian, who brought this trouble on Amasis because he had a grudge against him. The grudge went back to the time when Cyrus sent to Amasis and asked him for an eye doctor, the best there was in Egypt. Amasis had picked this man out of all the doctors in Egypt, torn him away from his wife and children, and handed him over to Persia. With this grievance in mind, the Egyptian kept urging Cambyses to ask Amasis for his daughter, so that Amasis would either be hurt if he gave her up or, if he refused, would make an enemy of Cambyses. So Amasis, who was both annoyed by the power of the Persians and afraid of it, could neither bring himself to give her nor see how to refuse. He was quite certain that Cambyses meant to take her not as his wife but as a concubine. So, having thought it through, he did this. There was a daughter of Apries, the king before him, a very tall and good-looking girl and the only member of her family still alive. Her name was Nitetis. Amasis dressed this girl in fine clothes and gold and sent her off to Persia as his own daughter. But some time later, when Cambyses greeted her by her father's name, the girl said to him: "My king, you don't realize how Amasis has fooled you. He dressed me up in finery and sent me off to you as if I were his own daughter. But in truth I am the daughter of Apries, his lord and master, against whom Amasis rose up with the Egyptians and whom he murdered." It was these words, and the occasion they gave him, that led Cambyses son of Cyrus, in a towering rage, to march against Egypt.

2. That is the Persians' account. The Egyptians, though, claim Cambyses as one of their own. They say he was born to this very daughter of Apries, and that it was Cyrus, not Cambyses, who sent to Amasis for his daughter. But they are wrong to say so. And they cannot have failed to notice (for the Egyptians know the laws and customs of the Persians as well as anyone does) two things: first, that among the Persians a son born outside marriage does not become king when there is a son born of a true marriage; and second, that Cambyses was the son of Cassandane, the daughter of Pharnaspes, a man of the Achaemenid family, and not of the Egyptian woman. They twist the truth of history because they want to claim kinship with the house of Cyrus. So much for that.

3. There is also another story told, which for my part I do not believe. One of the Persian women, it goes, came to visit the wives of Cyrus. When she saw the tall, good-looking children standing beside Cassandane, she praised them loudly and could not admire them enough. Then Cassandane, the wife of Cyrus, said: "And yet, even though I am the mother of children like these, Cyrus treats me with contempt and honors the woman he has brought in from Egypt." She said this, they say, out of resentment of Nitetis. At that Cambyses, the elder of her sons, said: "Then, mother, when I am grown up, I will turn Egypt upside down: what is on top I will put at the bottom, and what is at the bottom I will put on top." He is said to have said this when he was about ten years old, perhaps, and the women were astonished. And he, they say, never forgot it, so that when at last he had grown up and become king, he made the expedition against Egypt.

4. Something else also helped bring about this expedition, and it was this. Among Amasis' foreign mercenaries there was a man from Halicarnassus named Phanes, who was both sound in judgment and brave in war. This Phanes had some quarrel with Amasis (or so we may suppose), and he fled from Egypt by ship, hoping to get a hearing with Cambyses. Since he was a man of no small standing among the mercenaries and knew every detail of Egypt's affairs, Amasis went after him and thought it a matter of real importance to catch him. He sent the most trusted of his eunuchs after him in a trireme. The eunuch caught him in Lycia, but having caught him, he did not bring him back to Egypt, because Phanes outwitted him: he got his guards drunk and escaped to Persia. Now Cambyses had made up his mind to march on Egypt, but he was at a loss about the march itself, and how he could get safely across the waterless desert. Phanes arrived just then. Besides telling him everything else about Amasis' affairs, he advised him about the march too: he should send to the king of the Arabians and ask him for safe passage through this region.

5. This is the only known way into Egypt. From Phoenicia to the borders of the city of Cadytis the land belongs to the Syrians who are called the Syrians of Palestine. Cadytis is a city not much smaller than Sardis, I would guess. From Cadytis, the trading towns along the coast as far as the city of Ienysus belong to the king of Arabia. Then from Ienysus the land belongs to the Syrians again, as far as Lake Serbonis, along whose shore Mount Casius stretches down toward the sea. From Lake Serbonis, where Typhon, the monster, is said to lie hidden, the land is Egypt. The stretch between the city of Ienysus on one side and Mount Casius and Lake Serbonis on the other is no small one: it is a full three days' journey, and it is terribly short of water.

6. And now I will tell of something that few of those who sail to Egypt have noticed. Twice every year, earthenware jars full of wine are shipped into Egypt from all over Greece and from Phoenicia as well. And yet you could almost say that you will not see a single empty wine jar anywhere in the country.

7. So what becomes of them, you will ask? I will tell you this too. The headman of each district has to collect all the earthenware jars from his own town and carry them to Memphis. The people at Memphis have to fill them with water and carry them to that same waterless region of Syria. So the jars that keep arriving in Egypt and being emptied there are carried off to Syria to join the ones that went before. It was the Persians who prepared this route into Egypt in this way, supplying it with water as I have described, from the time they first took possession of Egypt. But at the time I am speaking of, no water had yet been provided. So Cambyses, following the advice of his guest from Halicarnassus, sent envoys to the Arabian king and asked him for safe passage. He got it, after giving the king pledges of friendship and receiving pledges from him in return.

8. The Arabians respect pledges of friendship as much as any people in the world, and this is how they make them. A third man, not one of the two who want to exchange pledges, stands between them. With a sharp stone he cuts the palms of their hands along the base of the thumb. Then he takes a thread from each man's cloak and with their blood smears seven stones that lie between them, and as he does this he calls on Dionysus and Urania. When he has finished these ceremonies, the man who has given the pledge commends the stranger to his friends (or his fellow tribesman, if he is giving the pledge to a member of his own tribe), and his friends consider themselves bound to honor the pledge as well. The only gods the Arabians believe in are Dionysus and Urania. They say that they cut their hair the same way Dionysus himself had his cut: they crop it in a circle all the way around and shave the temples. They call Dionysus Orotalt, and Urania they call Alilat.

9. So when the Arabian king had given his pledge of friendship to the men who had come to him from Cambyses, he did this. He took camel skins, filled them with water, and loaded them onto every live camel he had. Then he drove them to the waterless region and waited there for Cambyses' army. That is the more believable of the two accounts. But the less believable one must be told too, since it is the one people tell. There is a great river in Arabia called the Corys, which flows out into the sea called the Erythraean, the Indian Ocean. From this river, it is said, the king of the Arabians had a pipeline made of raw oxhides and other skins sewn together, long enough to reach the waterless region. Through this, if you please, he brought the water, and he had great cisterns dug in the waterless region to take the water in and store it. Now it is a twelve days' journey from the river to this waterless region. And what is more, the story says he brought the water by three pipelines to three different parts of it.

10. Meanwhile Psammenitus son of Amasis was camped at the Pelusian mouth of the Nile, waiting for Cambyses to come. For when Cambyses marched on Egypt, he did not find Amasis still alive. Amasis had died after a reign of forty-four years in which no great misfortune had befallen him. When he died he was embalmed and buried in the tomb he had built for himself in the temple. While Psammenitus son of Amasis was king, the Egyptians witnessed the greatest omen that had ever happened to them: rain fell at Thebes in Egypt. It had never rained there before, and it has never rained there since, down to my own time, as the Thebans themselves say; for in Upper Egypt no rain falls at all. But at the time I am speaking of, rain fell at Thebes in a light drizzle.

11. The Persians crossed the whole of the waterless region and camped near the Egyptians, ready to give battle. Then the Egyptian king's foreign mercenaries, who were Greeks and Carians, turned on Phanes. They hated him for having led a foreign-speaking army against Egypt, and they came up with this plan against him. Phanes had left his children behind in Egypt. The mercenaries brought them to their camp, where their father could see them, and set up a mixing bowl between the two camps. Then they led the children up one by one and cut their throats, so that the blood ran into the bowl. When they had gone through all the children, they brought wine and water and poured them into the bowl, and only when every one of the mercenaries had drunk some of the blood did they go into battle. The battle was hard fought, and a great many fell on both sides, but in the end the Egyptians broke and ran.

12. And I saw a great wonder here, which the people of the place pointed out to me. The bones of the men who fell in this battle lie scattered about, each side's apart, for the Persian bones lie on one side, where they were separated at the start, and the Egyptian bones on the other. The skulls of the Persians are so thin that if you just hit one with a pebble you will make a hole in it, while the skulls of the Egyptians are so tough that you could hardly break one if you struck it with a big rock. The reason, they told me, and I readily believe them, is this. The Egyptians shave their heads from early childhood, and the bone thickens in the sun. This is also why they do not go bald: you see fewer bald men among the Egyptians than among any other people. That, then, is why their skulls are strong. The reason the Persians' skulls are weak is that they keep their heads soft and shaded from the start by wearing tiaras, which are felt caps. So much for that. I also saw the same sort of thing at Papremis, among those who were killed along with Achaemenes son of Darius by Inaros the Libyan.

13. After their rout in the battle, the Egyptians fled in disorder and shut themselves up in Memphis. Cambyses sent a ship from Mytilene up the river carrying a Persian herald to call on the Egyptians to come to terms. But when they saw the ship come into Memphis, they poured out of the fortress all together, wrecked the ship, tore the men on board limb from limb, and carried them back into the fortress. After this the Egyptians were besieged, and in time they surrendered. The Libyans who live on the borders of Egypt were terrified by what had happened to Egypt, and they gave themselves up without a fight. They agreed to pay tribute and sent gifts. The people of Cyrene and Barca were just as terrified as the Libyans and did the same. Cambyses accepted the Libyans' gifts graciously, but he found fault with those that came from Cyrene, because, I suppose, they were too small (the Cyreneans in fact sent five hundred pounds of silver). He grabbed the silver by handfuls and scattered it among his soldiers with his own hand.

14. Ten days after he took the surrender of the fortress at Memphis, Cambyses had Psammenitus, the king of the Egyptians, who had reigned for six months, sit in the outskirts of the city to humiliate him. He set him there along with other Egyptians, and he put his spirit to the test in this way. He dressed Psammenitus' daughter in a slave's clothes and sent her out with a pitcher to fetch water. With her he sent other girls, chosen from the daughters of the leading men, dressed the same way as the king's daughter. As the girls passed their fathers, crying and wailing, all the other men began to cry out and wail aloud at the sight of their children so mistreated. But Psammenitus, when he saw it with his own eyes and understood, bowed his head to the ground. When the water carriers had gone by, Cambyses next sent out Psammenitus' son, along with two thousand other Egyptians of the same age, with ropes tied around their necks and bits in their mouths. They were being led off to execution in revenge for the men of Mytilene who had been killed at Memphis with their ship. For the Royal Judges had ruled that for each man, ten of the noblest Egyptians should die in return. Psammenitus saw them go past him and understood that his son was leading the way to his death. But while the other Egyptians sitting around him wept and showed their grief, he did just what he had done at the sight of his daughter. When these too had gone by, it happened that one of his old table companions, a man getting on in years, came past Psammenitus son of Amasis and the Egyptians sitting in the outskirts of the city. This man had lost everything he owned and had nothing left but what a beggar has, and he was begging from the soldiers. When Psammenitus saw him, he let out a great cry of grief, called his friend by name, and beat his own head. Now there were men, it seems, posted to watch him, who reported to Cambyses everything he did each time a group went past. Cambyses was amazed at what he did, and he sent a messenger to ask him this: "Psammenitus, your master Cambyses asks why, when you saw your daughter mistreated and your son going to his death, you did not cry out or weep for them, yet you honored with these signs of grief the beggar who, he hears from others, is no relation of yours at all." That was the question, and Psammenitus answered: "Son of Cyrus, my own troubles were too great for me to weep over aloud. But my friend's trouble called for tears: he has lost great wealth and fallen into beggary on the threshold of old age." When the messenger reported this answer, they all thought it well said. And according to the Egyptians, Croesus wept (for he too, as fortune would have it, had come with Cambyses to Egypt), and the Persians who were there wept as well. Even Cambyses himself felt some pity. At once he ordered that Psammenitus' son be saved from among those who were being put to death, and that Psammenitus himself be raised from his place in the outskirts of the city and brought before him.

15. As for the son, the men sent to fetch him found that he was no longer alive: he had been the first to be cut down. But they raised Psammenitus himself from his place and brought him before Cambyses, and he lived with him from then on without suffering any violence. And if he had known how to keep out of trouble, he would have been given Egypt back to rule. For the Persians make a practice of honoring the sons of kings; even if the kings have revolted against them, they still give the power back to their sons. That this is their settled rule can be seen from many other cases, and especially from that of Thannyras son of Inaros, who got back the power his father had held, and that of Pausiris son of Amyrtaeus, who also got back his father's power. And yet it is certain that no one up to this time ever did the Persians more harm than Inaros and Amyrtaeus. As it was, though, Psammenitus plotted mischief and got what he deserved. He was caught stirring up the Egyptians to revolt. When Cambyses found out, Psammenitus drank bull's blood and died on the spot. That was how he met his end.

16. From Memphis Cambyses went to the city of Sais, meaning to do exactly what he then did. When he had entered Amasis' palace, he at once ordered Amasis' corpse to be brought out of its tomb. When this had been done, he ordered them to whip it, pull out its hair, stab it, and treat it with every other kind of indignity. They went on doing this until they were worn out, for the corpse had been embalmed and held out against their violence without falling apart anywhere. Then Cambyses ordered it to be burned. In giving this order he was commanding something forbidden by religion, for the Persians hold fire to be a god. Burning the dead is not the custom of either people at all. It is not the Persians' custom, for the reason I have given, since they say it is wrong to give a man's dead body to a god. And the Egyptians believe that fire is a living wild beast that devours everything it catches, and that when it has eaten its fill it dies along with what it is devouring. But it is certainly not their custom to give a man's corpse to wild beasts; that is why they embalm it, so that worms will not eat it as it lies in the tomb. So Cambyses was ordering them to do something the customs of neither people allow. The Egyptians, however, say that it was not Amasis who suffered this outrage, but another Egyptian of the same height and build. The Persians, they say, did their outrage to him, thinking they were doing it to Amasis. For Amasis, they say, had learned from an oracle what was going to happen to him after his death. So to ward off the threatened harm, he buried the body of this man, the one who was whipped, just inside the doors of his own burial chamber, and instructed his son to lay his own body as far back in the innermost part of the chamber as he could. In my opinion these instructions, which Amasis is supposed to have given about his burial and about this man, were never given at all. I think the Egyptians just pretend they were, out of pride, and with no good reason.

17. After this Cambyses planned three separate expeditions: one against the Carthaginians, another against the Ammonians, and a third against the "Long-lived" Ethiopians, who live in the part of Libya that lies on the Southern Sea, the Indian Ocean. As he worked out these plans, he decided to send his fleet against the Carthaginians and a picked force from his land army against the Ammonians. To the Ethiopians he decided to send spies first. They were to see whether the Table of the Sun, which is said to exist among these Ethiopians, was really there, and to spy out everything else besides, while pretending to be bringing gifts for their king.

18. The Table of the Sun is said to be like this. In the outskirts of their city there is a meadow full of the boiled meat of every kind of four-legged animal. Here, it is said, the citizens who are in office at the time take care to lay out the meat by night, and by day anyone who wants to can come and eat his fill. The natives, it is reported, say that the earth itself produces these things, over and over.

19. That is what the so-called Table of the Sun is said to be like. So when Cambyses had made up his mind to send the spies, he at once sent to the city of Elephantine for some of the Fish-Eaters (the Ichthyophagi, as the Greeks call them) who knew the Ethiopian language. While men were going to fetch them, he ordered the fleet to sail against Carthage. But the Phoenicians said they would not do it. They were bound by solemn oaths not to, they said, and it would be an impious thing to make war on their own children, since Carthage was their colony. And since the Phoenicians were unwilling, the rest of the fleet was not strong enough to make the attempt. That is how the Carthaginians escaped being enslaved by the Persians. Cambyses did not think it right to force the Phoenicians, both because they had handed themselves over to the Persians of their own accord and because the whole navy depended on them. The Cyprians too had handed themselves over to the Persians and were taking part in the expedition against Egypt.

20. As soon as the Fish-Eaters came to Cambyses from Elephantine, he sent them to the Ethiopians, telling them what to say and giving them gifts to take: a purple robe, a twisted gold necklace with bracelets, an alabaster jar of perfume, and a jar of palm wine. These Ethiopians to whom Cambyses was sending them are said to be the tallest and most handsome people in the world. Besides their other customs, which are reported to differ from those of other peoples, there is this one in particular, it is said, about their kingship: whichever man of their nation they judge to be the tallest, and to have strength to match his size, is the one they make their king.

21. So when the Fish-Eaters reached this people, they presented their gifts to the king who ruled them, and said: "Cambyses, king of the Persians, wishes to become your friend and guest-friend. He has sent us with orders to speak with you, and he gives you as gifts these things, which are the things he himself most enjoys." But the Ethiopian saw that they had come as spies, and he said to them: "The king of the Persians did not send you with gifts because he thought it very important to become my guest-friend, and you are not telling the truth (for you have come to spy on my kingdom), and he is not a just man either. If he were just, he would not have coveted any land but his own, and he would not be leading into slavery people who have done him no wrong. Now, though, give him this bow and tell him this: The king of the Ethiopians advises the king of the Persians that when the Persians can draw bows as big as this one as easily as I do, then he should march against the Long-lived Ethiopians, provided he has the larger army. But until then he should thank the gods that they do not put it into the minds of the sons of the Ethiopians to win more land in addition to their own."

22. With that he unstrung the bow and handed it over to the men who had come. Then he picked up the purple robe and asked what it was and how it was made. When the Fish-Eaters told him the truth about the purple shellfish and how the cloth is dyed, he said that the men were deceitful and so were their clothes. Next he asked about the twisted gold of the necklace and the bracelets. When the Fish-Eaters explained how they were made, the king burst out laughing; he took them for shackles, and he said that they had stronger shackles than these in his country. Third, he asked about the perfume, and when they told him how it was made and how people anoint themselves with it, he said the same thing he had said about the robe. Then he came to the wine and learned how it was made, and he was so delighted with the taste of the drink that he went on to ask what the king ate and what was the longest a Persian lived. They told him that the king ate bread, explaining first how wheat is grown, and they said that eighty years was the longest life a Persian could expect. To this the Ethiopian replied that he was not surprised that they lived so few years when they ate dung. They would not even live as long as that, he said, if they did not revive themselves with this drink, and he pointed out the wine to the Fish-Eaters. In this one thing, he said, his own people fell well short of the Persians.

23. Then the Fish-Eaters asked the king in turn how long his people lived and how they lived. He answered that most of them reached a hundred and twenty years, and some lived even longer, and that their food was boiled meat and their drink was milk. When the spies marveled at the number of years, he took them to a certain spring. When they washed in its water their skin became sleeker, as if it were a spring of oil, and it gave off a scent like violets. The water of this spring, the spies said, was so thin that nothing would float on it, neither wood nor anything lighter than wood: everything sank to the bottom. If this water of theirs is really what it is said to be, it would surely be the reason the people live so long, since they use it for everything. When they left the spring, he took them to a prison for men, and there all the prisoners were bound in chains of gold. For among these Ethiopians bronze is the rarest and most precious thing of all. When they had seen the prison, they saw the so-called Table of the Sun as well.

24. After that, last of all, they saw their coffins, which are said to be made of crystal, in this way. They dry the corpse, either the Egyptian way or some other, then coat it all over with plaster and paint it, making the figure look as much like the living man as they can. After this they put it inside a hollowed-out block of crystal, which they dig up in great quantities and which is very easy to work. The body sits in the middle of the block and can be seen through it. It gives off no unpleasant smell and nothing else offensive, and every part of it can be seen as plainly as the body itself. The dead man's closest relatives keep the block in their house for a year, giving him the first share of everything and offering sacrifices to him. After that they carry it out and set it up around the city.

25. When they had seen everything, the spies left to go back. And when they reported all this, Cambyses flew into a rage at once and marched his army against the Ethiopians. He gave no orders for any supply of food, and he never stopped to think that he was about to march an army to the farthest ends of the earth. Instead, like a madman out of his right mind, he set out the moment he heard the Fish-Eaters' report. He ordered the Greeks who were with him to stay behind in Egypt and took his whole land army with him. When in the course of the march he reached Thebes, he split off about fifty thousand men from his army and ordered them to enslave the Ammonians and burn down the oracle of Zeus, while he himself went on against the Ethiopians with the rest of the army. But before the army had covered a fifth of the way, all the food they had ran out completely, and after the food, the pack animals too were eaten until they were gone. Now if Cambyses, when he saw this, had changed his mind and led his army back, he would have been a wise man in spite of his first mistake. As it was, he paid no attention but kept on going forward. So the soldiers kept themselves alive by eating grass, as long as they could find anything growing in the ground. But when they reached the sand, some of them did a terrible thing: out of every ten men they chose one by lot and ate him. When Cambyses heard of this, he was frightened by the cannibalism. He gave up the expedition against the Ethiopians and started back, and he reached Thebes having lost a great part of his army. From Thebes he came down to Memphis and let the Greeks sail home.

Chapter 16: The Madness of Cambyses, the Ring of Polycrates, and the Son of Periander

26. That is how the expedition against the Ethiopians turned out. Meanwhile the Persians who had been sent to march against the Ammonians set out from Thebes and went on their way with guides. It is known that they reached the city of Oasis, which is inhabited by Samians said to belong to the Aeschrionian tribe, and which lies seven days' journey from Thebes across sandy desert. In Greek this place is called the "Isle of the Blessed." The army, they say, got that far. But from there on, nobody can say anything about them, except the Ammonians themselves and those who have heard the story from them; for they never reached the Ammonians, and they never came back. The Ammonians themselves add this to the story. They say that as the army was marching from this Oasis across the sandy desert to attack them, and had reached a point about halfway between them and the Oasis, a violent south wind blew down on them while they were eating their morning meal. It carried heaps of desert sand along with it and buried them, and so they vanished and were never seen again. That, according to the Ammonians, is what happened to this army.

27. When Cambyses arrived at Memphis, Apis appeared to the Egyptians; this is the god the Greeks call Epaphus. As soon as he appeared, the Egyptians began to put on their finest clothes and to hold celebrations. Cambyses saw the Egyptians doing this and was sure they were rejoicing because things had gone badly for him. So he called for the officials in charge of Memphis. When they came before him, he asked them why the Egyptians had done nothing of the kind the last time he was at Memphis, but were doing it only now, when he had come back after losing a large part of his army. They told him that a god had appeared to them, one who usually appeared only at long intervals, and that whenever he appeared, all the Egyptians rejoiced and held a festival. When Cambyses heard this, he said they were lying, and he condemned them to death as liars.

28. After putting them to death, he next called the priests before him. When the priests gave him the same answer, he said he would find out whether some tame god had come to live among the Egyptians. With that he told the priests to bring Apis to him, and they went to fetch him. Now this Apis, or Epaphus, is a calf born of a cow that is never afterward allowed to conceive another calf. The Egyptians say that a flash of light comes down from the sky upon this cow, and from it she gives birth to Apis. This calf called Apis has the following markings: he is black, with a white square on his forehead and the likeness of an eagle on his back; the hairs of his tail are double; and on his tongue there is a mark like a beetle.

29. When the priests brought Apis in, Cambyses, who was already half mad, drew his dagger. He aimed at Apis' belly but struck his thigh. Then he laughed and said to the priests: "You miserable creatures, is this what gods are like, made of flesh and blood and able to feel an iron blade? This is certainly a god worthy of the Egyptians. But you, at least, will not get away with making a fool of me." With that he ordered the men whose job it was to whip the priests without mercy, and to put to death any other Egyptian they found celebrating the festival. So the Egyptians' festival was brought to an end, the priests were punished, and Apis lay dying in the temple from the wound in his thigh.

30. When he died of the wound, the priests buried him without Cambyses' knowledge. But Cambyses, as the Egyptians say, went completely mad immediately after this crime, though he had not really been in his right mind even before. The first of his crimes was to put to death his brother Smerdis, who had the same father and the same mother as he did. He had already sent this brother away from Egypt back to Persia out of envy, because Smerdis alone of all the Persians had been able to draw the bow that the Fish-Eaters had brought from the Ethiopian king, by about two finger-widths, an inch and a half; not one of the other Persians had managed it. Then, after Smerdis had gone back to Persia, Cambyses had a dream. It seemed to him that a messenger came from Persia and reported that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne and that his head touched the sky. So he was afraid that his brother might kill him and reign in his place. He sent Prexaspes to Persia, the man he trusted most of all the Persians, with orders to kill him. Prexaspes went up to Susa and killed Smerdis. Some say he took him out hunting and killed him there; others say he took him to the Persian Gulf and drowned him.

31. This, they say, was the first of Cambyses' crimes. Next after this he put to death his sister, who had come with him to Egypt. He was also married to her, and she was his sister on both sides, by the same father and the same mother. This is how he came to marry her, for before this the Persians had never been in the habit of marrying their sisters at all. Cambyses fell in love with one of his sisters and wanted to marry her. Since what he had in mind was against custom, he called the Royal Judges and asked them whether there was any law that allowed a man who wished it to marry his sister. Now the Royal Judges are men chosen from among the Persians, and they hold office until they die or until they are found guilty of some injustice, and no longer. They give judgments for the Persians and interpret the laws handed down from their fathers, and every question is referred to them. So when Cambyses asked them, they gave him an answer that was both honest and safe. They said they could find no law that allowed a brother to marry his sister, but that they had found another law, which said that the king of the Persians could do whatever he wanted. So on the one hand they did not bend the law out of fear of Cambyses; and at the same time, so as not to be killed themselves for upholding the law, they found another law besides the one he had asked about, which suited a man who wanted to marry his sisters. So Cambyses then married the sister he was in love with, and not long afterward he married another sister as well. It was the younger of these, the one who had come with him to Egypt, whom he put to death.

32. About her death, as about the death of Smerdis, two different stories are told. The Greeks say that Cambyses had set a lion cub to fight a puppy, and this wife of his was watching too. When the puppy was losing, another puppy, its brother, broke its chain and came to help it, and once there were two of them instead of one, the puppies got the better of the cub. Cambyses was delighted to watch this, but she, sitting beside him, began to cry. Cambyses noticed and asked her why she was crying. She said she had cried when she saw the puppy come to help its brother, because she remembered Smerdis and realized that there was no one to come to his help. The Greeks say it was for saying this that Cambyses killed her. But the Egyptians say that as they were sitting at dinner, the wife took a head of lettuce and pulled off the leaves all around it. Then she asked her husband whether the lettuce looked better stripped like this or with all its leaves, and he said, "With all its leaves." Then she said: "And yet you once made something just like this lettuce, when you stripped bare the house of Cyrus." Cambyses was enraged and leaped on her. She was pregnant, and she miscarried and died.

33. These were the mad things Cambyses did to his own family, whether his madness really came about because of Apis or from some other cause, since many ills tend to fall upon men. For it is also said that Cambyses had suffered from birth from a serious illness, the one some people call the "sacred disease," epilepsy. And it was certainly nothing strange that when his body was suffering from a serious illness, his mind should not be sound either.

34. And here are the mad things he did to the other Persians. There was Prexaspes, the man he honored most, who used to carry his messages; Prexaspes' son was also Cambyses' cupbearer, and this too was no small honor. To him, it is said, Cambyses spoke as follows: "Prexaspes, what kind of man do the Persians think I am, and what do they say about me?" And Prexaspes said: "Master, in every other way they praise you highly, but they say you are too fond of wine." That is what he said about the Persians. At this Cambyses grew angry and answered: "So the Persians now say that I am given to wine, and that this has driven me out of my senses and out of my mind. Then what they said before was not sincere." For it seems that some time before this, when the Persians and Croesus were sitting with him in council, Cambyses had asked them what kind of man they thought he was compared with his father Cyrus. They answered that he was better than his father, because he not only held everything his father had held, but had also won Egypt and the sea besides. That is what the Persians said. But Croesus, who was there and was not satisfied with their judgment, said to Cambyses: "To me, son of Cyrus, you do not seem equal to your father, because you do not yet have a son like the one he left behind him in you." Cambyses was pleased to hear this and praised Croesus' judgment.

35. Remembering this, then, he said angrily to Prexaspes: "Now see for yourself whether the Persians are telling the truth, or whether when they say this it is they who are out of their senses. If I shoot at your son, standing there by the doorway, and hit him right in the middle of the heart, that will prove the Persians are talking nonsense. But if I miss, then you can say that the Persians are telling the truth and that I am not in my right mind." With that he drew his bow and hit the boy. When the boy fell, it is said that Cambyses ordered his body cut open and the wound examined. When the arrow was found lodged in the heart, he laughed with delight and said to the boy's father: "Prexaspes, you can see that it has now been proved that I am not mad and that it is the Persians who are out of their senses. Now tell me, have you ever in your life seen anyone shoot so straight?" Prexaspes saw that the man was not in his right mind, and he was afraid for himself. So he said: "Master, I don't think even a god could have hit the mark so well." That is what he did that time. On another occasion he condemned twelve Persians, men as good as the best of them, on some trivial charge, and buried them alive head downward.

36. While he was doing these things, Croesus the Lydian thought it right to warn him, in these words: "My king, do not give in to the heat of your youth and your temper in everything. Hold yourself back and keep yourself in check. It is a good thing to be prudent, and forethought is wisdom. But you are putting to death men of your own people, condemning them on trivial charges, and you are putting men's sons to death too. If you do many things like this, be careful that the Persians do not rise up against you. As for me, your father Cyrus charged me, and earnestly urged me, to warn you and to suggest to you whatever I found to be good." That was his advice, given out of goodwill. But Cambyses answered: "You dare to advise me? You, who governed your own country so very well, and gave my father such good advice when you urged him to cross the river Araxes and go against the Massagetae, when they were willing to cross over into our land! You utterly ruined yourself by misruling your own country, and you utterly ruined Cyrus, who followed your advice. But you will not escape punishment now, for I want you to know that I have long been looking for an excuse to deal with you." With that he took his bow, meaning to shoot him, but Croesus jumped up and ran out. Since Cambyses could not shoot him, he ordered his attendants to seize him and kill him. But the attendants knew his moods, so they hid Croesus. Their plan was this: if Cambyses changed his mind and wanted Croesus back, they could produce him and be rewarded for saving his life; but if he did not change his mind and did not want him back, then they would kill him. Not long afterward Cambyses did in fact want Croesus back, and the attendants, seeing this, told him that he was still alive. Cambyses said he was glad that Croesus was still alive, but that the men who had saved him would not get off: he would put them to death. And he did.

37. He did many mad things like this, both to Persians and to his allies, while he stayed at Memphis. He opened ancient tombs and examined the bodies of the dead. He also went into the temple of Hephaestus and made great fun of the god's image. For the image of Hephaestus looks very much like the Pataeci, the little figures the Phoenicians carry on the prows of their triremes; for anyone who has not seen these, I will describe it: it is the figure of a dwarf. He also went into the temple of the Cabeiri, which no one is permitted to enter except the priest alone. After mocking the images there at length, he even set them on fire. These too are like the images of Hephaestus, and they are said to be his children.

38. So it is clear to me, by every kind of proof, that Cambyses was utterly mad; otherwise he would never have set out to mock religious rites and established customs. For if you offered all the people in the world a choice, and told them to pick the best customs out of all the customs there are, every people, after looking them all over, would choose their own. That is how strongly everyone believes that their own customs are by far the best. So it is not likely that anyone but a madman would make fun of such things. There are many other proofs that all people feel this way about their customs, and this one in particular. During his reign Darius summoned the Greeks who were at his court and asked them what price would persuade them to eat their fathers' bodies when they died. They answered that no price in the world would make them do it. After this Darius summoned some of the Indians called Callatians, who eat their parents, and asked them, in front of the Greeks, who followed what was said through an interpreter, what payment would persuade them to burn their fathers' bodies when they died. They cried out loud and told him not to say such things. That is how firmly custom is fixed, and I think Pindar was right when he said that custom is king of all.

39. Now while Cambyses was marching on Egypt, the Spartans were also making an expedition against Samos and against Polycrates son of Aeaces, who had risen up and made himself ruler of Samos. At first he had divided the state into three parts and given a share to each of his brothers, Pantagnotus and Syloson. But afterward he killed one of them and drove out the younger, Syloson, and so took possession of all of Samos. Once it was his, he made a pact of guest-friendship with Amasis the king of Egypt, sending him gifts and receiving gifts from him in return. Right after this, in a short space of time, the power of Polycrates grew quickly, and he became famous not only in Ionia but across the rest of Greece too. For wherever he sent his forces, everything went his way. He had acquired a hundred fifty-oared ships and a thousand archers, and he plundered everyone, making no distinction between anyone. He used to say that he would win more gratitude from a friend by giving back what he had taken than by never taking it at all. So he had conquered many of the islands and many cities on the mainland as well. Among other things, he defeated the Lesbians in a sea battle as they were coming with all their forces to help the Milesians. He took them prisoner, and it was these men who dug the whole moat around the city wall of Samos, working in chains.

40. Now Amasis, as you might expect, did not fail to notice that Polycrates was extraordinarily lucky, and it worried him. And as more and more good fortune kept coming to Polycrates, he wrote this letter and sent it to Samos: "Amasis says this to Polycrates. It is pleasant to hear that a friend and guest-friend is doing well. But your great good fortune does not please me, because I know that heaven is jealous. For myself, and for those I care about, I think I would rather have some of our affairs go well and others fail, and so pass through life faring well and badly by turns, than be successful in everything. For I have never yet heard of anyone who was successful in everything and did not come to a thoroughly bad end at last. So take my advice and do as I say about your good fortune. Think it over, and whatever you find you value most, and would be most heartsick to lose, take that and throw it away, so that it will never again be seen by human eyes. And if from then on your good fortune still does not come mixed with disasters, use the remedy I have suggested again."

41. Polycrates read this and, thinking it over, saw that Amasis' advice was good. So he looked for which of his treasures he would be most heartsick to lose, and in looking he found the one I am about to name. He had a signet ring that he used to wear, an emerald set in gold, the work of Theodorus son of Telecles, of Samos. Since he decided this was the thing to throw away, here is what he did. He manned a fifty-oared ship with sailors, went on board himself, and told them to head out into the open sea. When he was well away from the island, he took off the signet ring and, in full view of everyone on board, threw it into the sea. After doing this he sailed home, and when he reached his house he grieved for his loss.

42. But on the fifth or sixth day after this, here is what happened to him. A fisherman caught a large and beautiful fish and thought it right to give it to Polycrates as a gift. So he carried it to the palace door and said he wanted to see Polycrates. When he was let in, he gave him the fish and said: "My king, when I caught this fish I didn't think I should take it to the market, even though I am a man who lives by the work of his hands. It seemed to me worthy of you and of your rule, so I have brought it to give to you." Polycrates was pleased with what he said and answered: "You have done very well, and you deserve double thanks, for your words and for your gift. We invite you to dinner." The fisherman went home thinking this a great honor. Then, as the servants were cutting up the fish, they found Polycrates' signet ring in its belly. As soon as they saw it and picked it up, they carried it to Polycrates, overjoyed. They gave him the ring and told him how it had been found. He realized that the hand of heaven was in this, so he wrote down everything he had done and everything that had happened to him, and when he had written it he sent the letter to Egypt.

43. When Amasis read the letter that had come from Polycrates, he understood that it is impossible for one man to rescue another from what is going to happen, and that Polycrates, who was successful in everything and even found again what he had thrown away, was not going to have a good end. So he sent a herald to him in Samos and said that he was breaking off their guest-friendship. He did this so that when some great and terrible disaster struck Polycrates, he would not himself have to grieve over him as a friend and guest.

44. It was against this Polycrates, then, successful in everything, that the Spartans were making their expedition. They had been called in to help by the Samians who later founded Cydonia in Crete. Now Polycrates, without the Samians knowing, had sent a messenger to Cambyses son of Cyrus while he was gathering an army to march against Egypt, asking him to send to Samos and request military help from him. Cambyses was very glad to hear this and sent to Samos to ask Polycrates to send a fleet with him against Egypt. So Polycrates picked out those citizens he most suspected of wanting to rise against him and sent them off in forty triremes, telling Cambyses not to send them back.

45. Now some say that these Samians sent away by Polycrates never reached Egypt. When they got as far as Carpathus on their voyage, they talked it over among themselves and decided not to sail any farther. Others say they did reach Egypt, were kept under guard there, and escaped. Then, as they were sailing back to Samos, Polycrates met them with his ships and fought them. The returning men won and landed on the island, but then they fought a battle on land there and were beaten, and so they sailed off to Sparta. Some, though, say that the men from Egypt defeated Polycrates. In my opinion that is not right. They would have had no need to call in the Spartans if they had been able to bring Polycrates to terms by themselves. Besides, it is not reasonable to think that a man with a great many foreign mercenaries and native archers was beaten by the returning Samians, who were only a few. Then Polycrates gathered up the children and wives of his citizens and shut them up in the ship-sheds. He kept them there ready, so that if his citizens went over to the returning exiles, he could burn them, sheds and all.

46. When the Samians who had been driven out by Polycrates reached Sparta, they were brought before the magistrates and made a long speech, pressing their request urgently. But at this first hearing the magistrates replied that they had forgotten what had been said at the beginning and could not understand what had been said at the end. After this they were brought in a second time. This time they brought a bag with them and said nothing but this: that the bag needed barley-meal. The Spartans replied that they had overdone it with the bag: even the word "bag" was one word too many. All the same, they decided to help them.

47. Then the Spartans got a force ready and sailed against Samos. According to the Samians, they did it to repay an old favor, because the Samians had once helped them with ships against the Messenians. But the Spartans say they made the expedition not so much because they wanted to help the Samians who asked them, as to take revenge on their own account for the theft of the mixing bowl they had been taking as a gift to Croesus, and of the linen breastplate that Amasis king of Egypt had sent them as a gift. For the Samians had carried off the breastplate too, the year before they took the bowl. It was made of linen, with many figures woven into it, and decorated with gold and with cotton. Every thread of this breastplate is a thing to marvel at: fine as each thread is, it is made of three hundred and sixty strands, every one of them visible. There is another just like it, which Amasis dedicated as an offering to Athena at Lindus.

48. The Corinthians also took part eagerly in this expedition against Samos, to make sure it happened. For the Samians had committed an outrage against them too, a generation before this expedition and at about the same time as the theft of the bowl. Periander son of Cypselus had sent three hundred sons of the leading men of Corcyra, the island now called Corfu, to Alyattes at Sardis to be castrated. The Corinthians who were taking the boys put in at Samos. When the Samians heard the story and learned why the boys were being taken to Sardis, they first told the boys to take hold of the temple of Artemis as suppliants, and then they would not let the Corinthians drag the suppliants away from the temple. And when the Corinthians cut the boys off from food, the Samians started a festival, which they still celebrate in the same way today. As long as the boys were suppliants, whenever night fell they held dances of girls and young men, and in arranging the dances they made it a rule of the festival that cakes of sesame and honey should be carried, so that the Corcyrean boys could snatch them and live on them. This went on until at last the Corinthians who were in charge of the boys gave up and left. As for the boys, the Samians took them back to Corcyra.

49. Now if the Corinthians had been on friendly terms with the Corcyreans after Periander's death, they would not have joined the expedition against Samos for the reason I have given. But as it is, the two have always been at odds with each other, ever since the Corinthians first colonized the island. This, then, was why the Corinthians bore a grudge against the Samians.

50. Periander had picked out the sons of the leading men of Corcyra and was sending them to Sardis to be castrated in order to take revenge. For the Corcyreans had started it, by doing him an outrageous wrong. After Periander had killed his wife Melissa, another misfortune happened to him on top of the one he had already suffered. This is how it went. He had two sons by Melissa, one seventeen years old and the other eighteen. Their mother's father Procles, who was tyrant of Epidaurus, sent for them and treated them kindly, as you would expect, since they were his own daughter's sons. When he was sending them home, he said to them as he said goodbye: "Do you know, boys, who killed your mother?" The elder paid no attention to this remark. But the younger, whose name was Lycophron, was so deeply hurt to hear it that when he got back to Corinth he would not speak to his father. When his father tried to talk with him, he would not talk back, and when his father asked him questions, he gave no answer, because he regarded him as his mother's murderer. In the end Periander grew furious with his son and drove him out of the house.

51. After driving him out, he asked the elder son what their grandfather had talked about with them. The elder son told him how kindly Procles had received them, but he did not remember the remark Procles had made as they left, since he had paid no attention to it. Periander said that Procles must surely have put some idea into their heads, and he kept pressing him with questions. At last the young man remembered and told him that too. Periander took note of it, and, determined to show no softness, he sent a messenger to the people his banished son was living with at the time and forbade them to take him into their houses. And whenever the boy was driven from one house and went to another, he was driven from that one too, because Periander threatened anyone who took him in and ordered them to shut him out. So, driven away again, he would go on to another house, where friends of his lived, and they took him in, perhaps because he was Periander's son, even though they were afraid.

52. At last Periander made a proclamation that anyone who took him into their house or even spoke with him would have to pay a sacred fine to Apollo, and he named the amount. Because of this proclamation, no one was willing either to speak to him or to take him into their house. And he himself did not think it right to try, since it had been forbidden. Instead he lay about in the colonnades, exposed to the weather. On the fourth day of this, Periander saw him filthy, wretched and starving, and he felt pity for him. His anger softened, and he went up to him and said: "Son, which is better: the life you are living now, or to inherit the power and wealth I have now, by doing as your father wishes? You are my son, the prince of rich Corinth, and yet you have chosen the life of a beggar by defying and raging against the one man you should least have treated that way. If any disaster has happened in the matter that makes you suspect me, it has happened to me first, and I bear more of it than anyone, since I am the one who did the deed. Now that you have learned how much better it is to be envied than to be pitied, and also what a hard thing it is to be angry with your parents and with those stronger than you, come back home." With these words Periander tried to win him back. But the son gave his father no other answer than this: that now his father owed the god a fine for having spoken with him. Then Periander saw that his son's sickness was hopeless and could not be overcome, so he sent a ship to Corcyra and sent him away out of his sight, for he was ruler of that island too. After sending him away, Periander made war on his father-in-law Procles, whom he blamed most for the state he was in. He took Epidaurus, and took Procles himself prisoner too.

53. But as time went on, Periander grew past his prime and realized that he was no longer able to oversee and manage the government of the state. So he sent to Corcyra and summoned Lycophron to come back and take power. For he did not see the ability needed in his elder son, but saw plainly that he was too slow-witted. Lycophron did not even bother to give the messenger an answer. Then Periander, who still clung to the young man out of love, sent him his own daughter, Lycophron's sister, thinking that he would listen to her more than to anyone else. She arrived and said to him: "Boy, would you rather see the tyranny fall to others, and your father's wealth carried off as plunder, than come back and have them yourself? Come home, and stop tormenting yourself. Pride is a dangerous thing to own. Do not cure one evil with another. Many people put what is fair ahead of what is strictly just, and many before now, in seeking their mother's due, have lost their father's. A tyranny is a slippery thing, and many people want it; and besides, he is an old man now and past his prime. Do not give away what is yours to others." She said the most persuasive things she could, for her father had coached her beforehand. But he answered that he would never come to Corinth as long as he heard his father was still alive. When she reported this, Periander sent a messenger for the third time. He said that he wanted to come to Corcyra himself, and he urged Lycophron at the same time to come back to Corinth and succeed him on the throne. The son agreed to return on these terms, and Periander was getting ready to sail to Corcyra and his son to Corinth. But the Corcyreans learned everything that had happened, and they killed the young man so that Periander would not come to their land. That is why Periander took his revenge on the people of Corcyra.

Chapter 17: The Siege of Samos, the False Smerdis, and the Plot of the Seven

54. So the Spartans had come with a great force and were besieging Samos. They attacked the wall and took the tower that stands by the sea in the suburb of the city, but later, when Polycrates came up to the rescue with a large body of men, they were driven out of it. Meanwhile, by the upper tower, which stands on the ridge of the mountain, the foreign mercenaries and many of the Samians themselves had come out to fight. They held their ground against the Spartans for a short while and then began to fall back, and the Spartans followed them and were cutting them down.

55. Now if all the Spartans there that day had been the equals of Archias and Lycopas, Samos would have been taken. For Archias and Lycopas alone rushed inside the wall along with the fleeing Samians, and since they were cut off from retreat, they were killed inside the city of the Samians. I myself, moreover, talked in Pitane (that was the deme he belonged to) with the third in descent from this Archias: another Archias, the son of Samius son of Archias. He honored the Samians above all other foreigners. Not only that, but he said that his own father had been named Samius because his father, Archias, had died a glorious death on Samos; and he said that he honored the Samians because the Samians had given his grandfather a public funeral.

56. When the Spartans had been besieging Samos for forty days and were getting nowhere, they set off back to the Peloponnese. But there is a less believable account that has gone around about these events: that Polycrates struck a large number of a certain local coin in lead, had them gilded over, and gave them to the Spartans, and that they took them and then left. This was the first expedition the Spartans (who are Dorians) ever made into Asia.

57. The Samians who had led the expedition against Polycrates also sailed away when the Spartans were about to abandon them, and they went to Siphnos. They needed money, and the people of Siphnos were then at the height of their prosperity and richer than all the other islanders. They had gold and silver mines on their island, so rich that there is a treasury at Delphi dedicated from a tenth of the money that came in from those mines, and furnished as splendidly as the wealthiest of the treasuries there. The people used to divide among themselves the money that came in from the mines each year. So when they were setting up the treasury, they asked the oracle whether their present prosperity could stay with them for a long time, and the Pythia gave them this reply:

	"But when the town hall in Siphnos shines out white,
	and white-browed is the marketplace, then a careful man is needed
	to beware of an army of wood and a herald in red."

Now at just that time the marketplace and town hall of the Siphnians had been decorated with Parian marble.

58. They could not understand this oracle, either then at first or when the Samians arrived. As soon as the Samians were putting in at Siphnos, they sent one of their ships to carry envoys to the city. Now in the old days all ships were painted red, and this was what the Pythia was warning the Siphnians about in advance, when she told them to guard against the "army of wood" and the "herald in red." So the messengers came and asked the Siphnians to lend them ten talents. When the Siphnians refused, the Samians began to ravage their land. As soon as the Siphnians heard of it they came out to the rescue, engaged the Samians in battle, and were defeated. Many of them were cut off from the city by the Samians and shut out of it, and after this the Samians made them pay a hundred talents.

59. Then the Samians bought the island of Hydrea, which lies near the coast of the Peloponnese, from the people of Hermione, and they handed it over to the Troezenians to look after. They themselves settled at Cydonia in Crete, though they had not sailed there for that purpose but to drive the Zacynthians out of the island. They stayed there and prospered for five years, so much so that they were the builders of the temples that stand in Cydonia today, and of the temple of Dictyna too. But in the sixth year the Aeginetans, together with the Cretans, beat them in a sea battle and made them slaves. They cut off the prows of their ships, which were shaped like boars' heads, and dedicated them in the temple of Athena on Aegina. The Aeginetans did this because they had a grudge against the Samians. The Samians had made the first attack, on Aegina, back when Amphicrates was king of Samos, and they had done the Aeginetans a great deal of harm and suffered a great deal of harm from them in return. That was the cause of it.

60. I have spoken about the Samians at greater length because they have three works that are greater than any others the Greeks have made. The first is a tunnel, started from the bottom and open at both ends, dug through a mountain that rises no less than 900 feet. The tunnel is 4,200 feet long, about four-fifths of a mile, and eight feet high and eight feet wide. All along its length a second channel has been dug, thirty feet deep and three feet wide, and through it water from a plentiful spring is carried in pipes to the city. The designer of this work was a man from Megara, Eupalinus son of Naustrophus. That is one of the three. The second is a breakwater in the sea around the harbor, built down to a depth of as much as 120 feet, and more than 1,200 feet long. The third work they have made is a temple, the largest of all the temples we know of. Its first architect was Rhoecus son of Philes, a native of Samos. That is why I have spoken at greater length about the Samians.

61. Now while Cambyses son of Cyrus was lingering in Egypt and had gone out of his mind, two brothers, both Magi, rose up against him. One of them had been left behind by Cambyses as steward of his household. This man rose against him because he saw that the death of Smerdis was being kept secret, that only a few of the Persians knew of it, and that most of them firmly believed he was still alive. So he set out to seize the kingdom, and this was his plan. He had a brother (the one who, as I said, rose up with him against Cambyses), and this brother looked very much like Smerdis son of Cyrus, whom Cambyses had killed, though Smerdis was his own brother. He looked like Smerdis, and not only that, he had the same name, Smerdis. The Magus Patizeithes persuaded this man that he would manage everything for him, and then brought him and seated him on the royal throne. After that he sent heralds around to all the provinces, and one in particular to the army in Egypt, to proclaim that from now on they must obey Smerdis son of Cyrus instead of Cambyses.

62. So the other heralds made this proclamation, and so did the one appointed to go to Egypt. He found Cambyses and his army at Ecbatana in Syria, stood up in the middle of them, and began to proclaim what the Magus had ordered him to. When Cambyses heard this from the herald, he believed the herald was telling the truth and that Prexaspes had betrayed him: that when Prexaspes had been sent to kill Smerdis, he had not done it. So Cambyses looked at Prexaspes and said: "Prexaspes, is this how you carried out the job I gave you?"

Prexaspes answered: "Master, it is not true that your brother Smerdis has risen against you, or that you will have any trouble from him, great or small. I myself did what you ordered me to do, and I buried him with my own hands. If the dead have come back to life, then you can expect Astyages the Mede to rise up against you too. But if things are as they always were, there is no fear that any trouble will spring up for you, at least not from him. So now I think we should send men after the herald and question him, and ask who sent him to proclaim to us that we are to obey Smerdis as king."

63. When Prexaspes had said this, Cambyses liked the advice, and so the herald was chased down at once and brought back. When he had come back, Prexaspes questioned him like this: "You say, man, that you have come as a messenger from Smerdis son of Cyrus. Now tell the truth and go away unharmed. I am asking you: did Smerdis himself appear before your eyes and give you this order, or was it one of his servants?"

He answered: "I have never yet seen Smerdis son of Cyrus, not since the day King Cambyses marched off to Egypt. It was the Magus whom Cambyses appointed steward of his household who gave me this order, and he said that it was Smerdis son of Cyrus who had commanded me to tell you these things."

That is what he told them, adding no lies to the truth. Then Cambyses said: "Prexaspes, you did what you were ordered like an honest man, and you are free of blame. But who among the Persians can this be who has risen up against me and taken the name of Smerdis?"

Prexaspes said: "My king, I think I understand what has happened. The Magi have risen against you: Patizeithes, whom you left as steward of your household, and his brother Smerdis."

64. When Cambyses heard the name Smerdis, he understood at once the true meaning of this news and of his dream. In his sleep he had dreamed that someone reported to him that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne and that his head touched the sky. Seeing now that he had killed his brother for no reason, he began to weep for Smerdis. When he had wept for him and grieved bitterly over the whole disaster, he leaped onto his horse, meaning to march his army to Susa as fast as he could against the Magus. But as he leaped onto his horse, the cap of his sword's scabbard fell off, and the bare blade struck him in the thigh. He was wounded in the very place where he had once struck Apis, the god of the Egyptians. Believing the blow was a fatal one, Cambyses asked what the name of that town was, and they told him "Ecbatana." Even before this, the oracle at the city of Buto had told him that he would end his life in Ecbatana. He had supposed that he would die of old age in Ecbatana in Media, the seat of all his power; but the oracle, as it turned out, meant Ecbatana in Syria. So when he asked and learned the name of the town, the shock of the disaster the Magus had caused, and of the wound at the same time, brought him back to his senses. He understood the meaning of the oracle and said: "Here is where Cambyses son of Cyrus is fated to end his life."

65. That was all he said at the time. But about twenty days later he sent for the most distinguished of the Persians who were with him and said to them: "Persians, I am now forced to reveal to you the thing I used to keep more hidden than anything else. When I was in Egypt I saw a vision in my sleep, which I wish I had never seen. I dreamed that a messenger came from home and reported to me that Smerdis was sitting on the royal throne and that his head touched the sky. I was afraid my brother would take my power from me, so I acted quickly rather than wisely. For it seems that no human being can turn aside what is fated to happen. So I, fool that I was, sent Prexaspes off to Susa to kill Smerdis. When that great wrong had been done, I lived without fear, and never thought that some other man might one day rise up against me, now that Smerdis was out of the way. I missed the mark entirely about what was going to happen. I have made myself my brother's murderer, when there was no need, and I have lost the kingdom all the same. For it was really Smerdis the Magus that heaven was warning me about in the vision, saying he would rise against me.

"So that deed has been done by me, and you must understand that Smerdis son of Cyrus is no longer alive for you. It is the Magi who are really the masters of your kingdom: the one I left as steward of my household, and his brother Smerdis. The man who above all others should have avenged the insult I have suffered from the Magi has ended his life by an unholy death, at the hands of his own nearest kin. Since he is gone, the next best thing left to me, and the most necessary, is to charge you, Persians, with what I want done for me as I die. This, then, I lay on you, calling the gods of the royal house to witness: on all of you, and most of all on those of the Achaemenids who are here. Do not let the supreme power go back to the Medes. If they have taken it by trickery, take it from them by trickery; if they have won it by force of any kind, win it back by force and a strong hand. If you do this, may the earth bear its crops for you, and may your wives and your herds be fruitful, and may you stay free forever. But if you do not win back the power, or do not even try, I pray that the opposite of these blessings will fall on you, and on top of that, that every Persian will meet an end like the one that has come on me."

As soon as he had finished saying this, Cambyses began to weep and mourn over everything that had happened to him.

66. When the Persians saw the king weeping, they all tore the clothes they were wearing and mourned without restraint. After this the bone became infected and the thigh turned gangrenous, and the wound carried off Cambyses son of Cyrus. He had reigned seven years and five months in all, and he left no children at all, neither son nor daughter. The Persians who were there meanwhile were very little inclined to believe that the power was in the hands of the Magi. On the contrary, they were quite sure that Cambyses had said what he said about the death of Smerdis to deceive them, so that all the Persians would be stirred up to make war on Smerdis. So they were quite sure that it was Smerdis son of Cyrus who had been made king. For Prexaspes too denied very firmly that he had killed Smerdis, since now that Cambyses was dead it was not safe for him to say that he had killed the son of Cyrus with his own hand.

67. So when Cambyses had ended his life, the Magus took the throne without any trouble, posing as his namesake Smerdis son of Cyrus. He reigned for the seven months that were still lacking to make up Cambyses' eight years. During that time he did great good to all his subjects, so much so that when he died, everyone in Asia except the Persians themselves mourned for him. For the Magus sent messengers out to every nation he ruled and proclaimed that they would be free from military service and from tribute for three years.

68. He made this proclamation as soon as he was established on the throne. But in the eighth month it was found out who he was, in the following way. There was a man called Otanes son of Pharnaspes, second to none of the Persians in birth and in wealth. This Otanes was the first to suspect that the Magus was not Smerdis son of Cyrus but the man he really was. He drew this conclusion from two facts: the man never went out of the citadel, and he never summoned any of the distinguished Persians into his presence. Having become suspicious, he did this. Cambyses had married Otanes' daughter, whose name was Phaedyme, and the Magus was now keeping this same daughter as his wife and living with her, as he did with all the rest of Cambyses' wives. So Otanes sent a message to his daughter and asked her who the man was she slept beside: was it Smerdis son of Cyrus, or someone else? She sent word back that she did not know, because she had never seen Smerdis son of Cyrus, and she did not know in any other way who the man living with her was. Otanes then sent a second time and said: "If you do not know Smerdis son of Cyrus yourself, then ask Atossa who this man is, the man both she and you are living with as wives. She will surely know her own brother."

69. To this his daughter sent back word: "I can't speak with Atossa or see any of the other women who live here with me. As soon as this man, whoever he is, came to the throne, he split us up and put each of us in separate rooms of our own."

When Otanes heard this, the matter became clearer and clearer to him, and he sent another message in to her, which said: "Daughter, you are nobly born, and it is right for you to take on any risk your father tells you to take. For if this really is not Smerdis son of Cyrus but the man I suspect, he must not get away unpunished, either for taking you to his bed or for ruling over the Persians; he must pay the price. So now do as I say. When he is sleeping beside you and you can tell he is sound asleep, feel his ears. If it turns out that he has ears, then believe you are living with Smerdis son of Cyrus. But if not, believe it is Smerdis the Magus."

Phaedyme sent an answer saying that if she did this she would be running a great risk. If it turned out that he had no ears and she were caught feeling for them, she was quite sure he would put her to death. Even so, she said, she would do it. So she promised her father she would do this. Now this Smerdis the Magus had had his ears cut off by Cyrus son of Cambyses, while Cyrus was king, for some serious crime. So Phaedyme, the daughter of Otanes, set about doing everything she had promised her father. When her turn came to go to the Magus (for among the Persians the wives go to their husband in turn, each one regularly), she came and lay down beside him. When the Magus was deep asleep, she felt for his ears. She found, not with difficulty but easily, that her husband had no ears, and as soon as it was day she sent and told her father what had happened.

70. Then Otanes took Aspathines and Gobryas aside, who were leading men among the Persians and his own most trusted friends, and told them the whole story. They, as it turned out, already suspected the same thing themselves, and when Otanes reported this to them, they readily accepted his proposals. They decided that each of them should bring in the one Persian he trusted most. So Otanes brought in Intaphrenes, Gobryas brought in Megabyzus, and Aspathines brought in Hydarnes. When there were six of them, Darius son of Hystaspes arrived at Susa from the land of Persia, where his father was governor. So when he came, the six Persians decided to bring Darius in with them too.

71. So these seven came together, gave each other pledges of loyalty, and talked it over. When it was Darius' turn to give his opinion, he said to them: "I thought I was the only one who knew this: that it was the Magus who was ruling as king, and that Smerdis son of Cyrus was dead. And for that very reason I have come here, in earnest, to plan the Magus' death. But since it turns out that you know too, and not just me, I think we should act at once and not put it off. Delay is not the better way."
