Otanes answered: "Son of Hystaspes, you come of a noble family, and you seem to be showing yourself in no way worse than your father. But do not rush this undertaking so hastily without thinking it through. Take it up more carefully. We must first become more in number, and then go ahead with it."

Darius said in reply: "You men here, if you follow the course Otanes suggests, you can be sure you will die miserably. For someone will carry word to the Magus, to get something for himself out of it. Your best course would have been to do this on your own risk alone. But since you decided to bring more people into it, and you told me, either we do the deed today, or you can be sure of this: if today goes by, no one will get in ahead of me as your accuser. I will tell the Magus all of it myself."

72. When Otanes saw Darius in such violent haste, he answered: "Since you are forcing us to hurry and won't let us wait, come, explain to us yourself how we are going to get into the palace and lay hands on them. There are guards posted in various places; you probably know that as well as we do, if not from seeing them then from hearing about them. How are we going to get past them?"

Darius replied: "Otanes, there are many things that cannot be explained in words, only in action. And there are other things that can be explained in words, but no famous deed comes of them. You can be sure, though, that the guards posted there are not hard to get past. In the first place, being who we are, there is no one who will not let us go by, partly, you may suppose, out of respect for us, and partly perhaps out of fear. In the second place, I have a perfectly convincing excuse to get us through. I will say that I have just come from Persia and want to give the king a message from my father. Where a lie has to be told, let it be told. We are all after the same thing, both those who lie and those who always tell the truth. The liars lie whenever they expect to gain something by getting people to believe their lies. The truth-tellers tell the truth so that they can win some gain for themselves by it, and so that people will trust them more readily. So we take different roads, but we are all after the same thing. If there were nothing to be gained by it, the truth-teller would lie and the liar would tell the truth, and neither would care. So any of the doorkeepers who lets us through willingly will be better off for it later. But any who tries to stand in our way, let him be marked as our enemy then and there. And after that, let us push our way in and get to work."

73. Then Gobryas said: "Friends, when will there ever be a better chance for us either to win back our rule, or, if we cannot get it back, to die? We are Persians, and we are being ruled by a Mede, a Magus, and a man whose ears have been cut off, at that. Besides, all of you who stood by Cambyses when he was sick surely remember what he laid on the Persians as he was dying, if they did not try to win back the power. We did not accept it then; we thought Cambyses had said it to deceive us. So now I vote that we follow Darius' advice, and that we do not leave this meeting to go anywhere except straight to attack the Magus." That is what Gobryas said, and they all approved the proposal.

74. While they were planning all this, something else was happening at the same time, by coincidence. The Magi had talked it over and decided to make Prexaspes their friend. They had three reasons. He had suffered a terrible wrong from Cambyses, who had shot his son dead with an arrow. He was the only one who knew for certain that Smerdis son of Cyrus was dead, since he had killed him with his own hands. And finally, Prexaspes was very highly respected among the Persians. For these reasons they summoned him and tried to win him over as a friend. They bound him with pledges and oaths that he would keep to himself, and reveal to no one, the trick they had played on the Persians, and they promised to give him countless things in return. When Prexaspes had promised to do this, the Magi, having persuaded him that far, proposed a second thing. They said they would call all the Persians together at the palace wall, and they told him to climb up a tower and speak to them, and tell them that they were living under the rule of Smerdis son of Cyrus and no one else. They gave him this task because they believed he was the most trusted man among the Persians, and because he had often declared that Smerdis son of Cyrus was still alive and had denied that he had killed him.

75. When Prexaspes said he was ready to do this too, the Magi called the Persians together, sent him up a tower, and told him to speak to them. But he deliberately forgot what they had asked of him. Starting from Achaemenes, he traced the ancestry of Cyrus on his father's side, and when he had come down to Cyrus himself, he went on at last to tell what great good Cyrus had done the Persians. When he had gone through all this, he went on to declare the truth. He said that he had kept it secret before, since it was not safe for him to tell what had been done, but that now he was forced to make it known. He told them how he himself had killed Smerdis son of Cyrus, because Cambyses forced him to, and that it was the Magi who were ruling now. Then he called down many curses on the Persians if they did not win back the power and take vengeance on the Magi, and with that he threw himself headfirst off the tower. So Prexaspes ended his life, a man who had been respected all his days.

76. Now the seven Persians, having decided to attack the Magi at once and not delay, prayed to the gods and set off, knowing nothing of what had happened with Prexaspes. As they were on their way, halfway there, they heard what had happened with Prexaspes. At that they stepped aside from the road and talked it over again. Otanes and his side strongly urged them to wait and not to go ahead while things were in such turmoil. Darius and his side urged them to go at once and do what they had decided, and not to delay. While they were arguing, seven pairs of hawks appeared, chasing two pairs of vultures, plucking out their feathers and tearing them. When they saw this, all seven of them approved Darius' view, and they went on to the king's palace, encouraged by the sight of the birds.

77. When they appeared at the gates, things happened very much as Darius had expected. The guards, out of respect for men who were among the first of the Persians, and not suspecting that they would do anything of the kind they intended, let them pass in, with heaven guiding them, and nobody asked them any questions. When they had passed into the courtyard, they met the eunuchs who carried messages in to the king. The eunuchs asked them what they had come for, and at the same time they threatened the gatekeepers with punishment for letting them in, and tried to stop the seven when they tried to go further. Then the seven gave each other the word, drew their daggers, and stabbed the men who were trying to stop them right there on the spot. Then they ran on toward the men's hall.

78. Now both of the Magi happened to be inside, talking over what Prexaspes had done. When they saw that the eunuchs had been attacked and heard them shouting, they both ran back, and when they saw what was happening they turned to defend themselves. One of them got down his bow and arrows before he was attacked, and the other took up his spear. Then the two sides came to grips. The one who had taken up his bow and arrows found them useless, since his enemies were close by and pressing hard on him. But the other defended himself with his spear. First he struck Aspathines in the thigh, and then Intaphrenes in the eye; Intaphrenes lost his eye from the wound, but he did not lose his life. So these two were wounded by one of the Magi. The other, when his bow and arrows turned out to be useless, ran into a bedroom that opened off the men's hall, meaning to shut the door, and two of the seven, Darius and Gobryas, rushed in with him. Gobryas was locked together with the Magus, wrestling, while Darius stood over them, not knowing what to do, because it was dark and he was afraid he would hit Gobryas. Seeing him standing there doing nothing, Gobryas asked him why he was not using his hands. Darius said: "Because I'm afraid I may stab you." And Gobryas answered: "Thrust with your sword, even if it goes through both of us." So Darius did as he said, thrust with his dagger, and happened to hit the Magus.

79. When they had killed the Magi and cut off their heads, they left their wounded behind, both because they were not able to go and so that they could hold the citadel. The other five took the heads of the Magi and ran out, shouting and clashing their weapons. They called on the other Persians to join them, told them what had been done, and showed them the heads, and at the same time they began killing every Magus who crossed their path. When the Persians heard what the seven had done and how the Magi had tricked them, they decided to do the same themselves. They drew their daggers and killed the Magi wherever they found one, so that if night had not come on and stopped them, they would not have left a single Magus alive. The Persians celebrate this day together more than any other day. They keep a great festival on it, which the Persians call the Slaughter of the Magi, and on it no Magus is allowed to appear in public; the Magi stay shut in their houses all that day.

Chapter 18: The Debate on Government, Darius Becomes King, and the Riches of India and Arabia

80. When the uproar had died down and more than five days had passed, the men who had risen against the Magi began to discuss the state of the whole country. Speeches were made then that some Greeks do not believe were really spoken, but spoken they were all the same. Otanes urged that they should hand the government over to the whole body of the Persians, and this is what he said: "I think none of us should be sole ruler from now on, because that is neither pleasant nor good. You saw how far Cambyses' arrogance went, and you have had a taste of the Magus' arrogance too. How can the rule of one man be a well-ordered thing, when a monarch can do whatever he likes without answering to anyone for what he does? Put even the best man in the world in that position and it would change him from what he used to be. The good things he has breed arrogance in him, and envy is planted in human beings from the start. With those two he has every vice, because he does many reckless and wicked things, some out of arrogance born of having too much, some out of envy. And yet a tyrant, of all people, ought to be free from envy, since he has every good thing there is. But by nature he behaves toward his subjects in just the opposite way. He resents the best men for being alive at all, he enjoys the company of the worst citizens, and he is readier than anyone to listen to slander. And he is the most inconsistent of all creatures. If you admire him in moderation, he is offended that you are not courting him hard enough; if you court him extravagantly, he is offended at you for being a flatterer. But the most important thing is what I am about to say. He overturns the customs handed down from our fathers, he forces himself on women, and he puts men to death without trial. The rule of the many, on the other hand, first of all has the finest name there is: Equality. And second, the many do none of the things a monarch does. Offices are filled by lot, officials have to answer for what they do in office, and every question is brought before the public assembly. So my opinion is that we let monarchy go and raise up the power of the people, because everything is in the many."

81. That was the opinion Otanes gave. But Megabyzus urged that they hand things over to the rule of a few, and he said: "What Otanes said against tyranny, count it as said by me too. But when he urged us to hand power to the masses, he missed the best advice. Nothing is more senseless or more arrogant than a worthless mob. For men to escape the arrogance of a tyrant only to fall into the arrogance of an unruly people is not to be endured at all. When the tyrant does something, at least he knows what he is doing; the people cannot even know. How could anyone know who has never been taught anything good by others and has never seen anything good for himself, but rushes at things headlong and without sense, like a river in flood? Let the enemies of the Persians have rule by the people. But let us choose a group of the best men and give the power to them. We ourselves will be among them, and it is likely that the best men will make the best decisions."

82. That was the opinion Megabyzus gave. Third, Darius declared his opinion, saying: "I think that what Megabyzus said about the masses was right, but what he said about the rule of a few was not. Three things are set before us, and let us suppose each is the best of its kind: the best democracy, the best oligarchy, and the best monarchy. I say the last is far better than the others. Nothing better can be found than the rule of one man, if he is the best man. Using his own best judgment, he would guard the people without fault, and the plans he made against enemies would be best kept secret that way. In an oligarchy, many men work at doing good for the state, and so strong private hatreds often spring up among them. Each one wants to be the leader himself and to have his own way in the council, so they come to hate each other bitterly. From that come factions, from factions come murders, and from murders comes the rule of one man. And that shows how much the rule of one is the best. Then again, when the people rule, corruption is bound to arise. And when corruption arises in public life, the corrupt men do not come to hate each other; they become close friends, because those who are robbing the state put their heads together to do it in secret. This goes on until someone takes the lead of the people and puts a stop to such men. Because of that, this man is admired by the people, and being admired, he suddenly turns out to be a monarch. So he too proves that the rule of one is best. Finally, to sum it all up in a word: where did our freedom come from, and who gave it to us? Was it the people, or an oligarchy, or a monarch? My opinion, then, is that since one man set us free, we should keep that form of rule. And apart from that, we should not do away with our fathers' customs when they are good ones. That is not the better way."

83. These three opinions had been put forward, and the other four of the seven sided with the last. When Otanes, who wanted to give the Persians equality, saw that his view had lost, he spoke to the gathering: "My fellow conspirators, it is clear that one of us has to become king, whether he is chosen by lot, or by leaving the decision to the whole mass of the Persians and taking whoever they choose, or in some other way. Well, I will not compete with you. I want neither to rule nor to be ruled. I withdraw my claim to rule on this condition: that I shall not be ruled by any of you, neither I nor my descendants for all time to come." When he had said this, the six agreed to his terms. He did not compete with them but withdrew from the gathering. And to this day his house is the only free one among all the Persians. It obeys only as far as it chooses, though it does not break the laws of the Persians.

84. The rest of the seven went on discussing how to set up a king in the fairest way. They decided that if the kingdom went to any of the others among the seven, Otanes and his descendants after him should receive, as special gifts, a suit of Median clothes every year and all the presents the Persians count most valuable. They decided to give him these because he was the first to propose the business and the one who brought them together. These were the special gifts for Otanes. They also decided this for all of them in common: any one of the seven who wished could walk into the royal palace without anyone going in ahead to announce him, unless the king happened to be sleeping with his wife; and the king was not allowed to marry from any family except those of the men who had risen with him. About the kingdom itself they decided this: they would ride out on their horses into the outskirts of the city, and the man whose horse neighed first after sunrise would have the kingdom.

85. Now Darius had a clever groom named Oebares. When they had left their meeting, Darius said to him: "Oebares, we have decided this about the kingdom: the man whose horse neighs first after sunrise, when we are mounted, will be king. So if you have any cleverness in you, find a way for us to win this prize, and not someone else." Oebares answered: "Master, if it really depends on this whether you become king or not, take heart and don't worry about it. Nobody else will be king before you. I have just the charm for it." Then Darius said: "If you really have a trick like that, it's time to work it out, not to put it off, because our trial is tomorrow." When Oebares heard this, here is what he did. As night was coming on, he took one of the mares, the one Darius' stallion liked best, led her into the outskirts of the city, and tied her up. Then he brought Darius' stallion to her. For some time he led him around her, close enough to brush against the mare, and at last he let the stallion mount her.

86. At dawn the six rode up on their horses, as they had agreed. As they were riding through the outskirts of the city, they came near the spot where the mare had been tied up the night before, and Darius' horse ran up to the spot and neighed. Just as the horse did this, lightning flashed and thunder sounded out of a clear sky. These signs, coming to Darius on top of the neighing, made his claim complete, because they seemed to have happened by some design. The others leapt down from their horses and bowed down before Darius.

87. Some say this was Oebares' trick, but others tell it another way (the Persians tell the story both ways). In this version, he rubbed his hand on the mare's genitals and then kept his hand hidden inside his trousers. At sunrise, when they were about to let the horses go, Oebares pulled out his hand and held it to the nostrils of Darius' horse. The horse caught the smell, snorted, and neighed.

88. So Darius son of Hystaspes was proclaimed king. In Asia everyone except the Arabians was subject to him, since Cyrus had conquered them and Cambyses after him. The Arabians, though, were never subjects of the Persians. They had become their guest-friends when they let Cambyses pass through on his way to Egypt, because the Persians could not have invaded Egypt against the Arabians' will. Darius also made the most distinguished marriages a Persian could make. He married two daughters of Cyrus, Atossa and Artystone. Atossa had been the wife first of her brother Cambyses and after that of the Magus, while Artystone was a virgin. Besides them he married the daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus, whose name was Parmys. And he also married the daughter of Otanes, the man who had found out the Magus. His power filled everything. First of all, he had a stone relief carved and set up. On it was the figure of a man on horseback, and he had it inscribed with these words: "Darius son of Hystaspes, by the excellence of his horse" (and here the horse's name was given) "and of his groom Oebares, won the kingdom of the Persians."

89. After he had done this in Persia, he set up twenty provinces, which the Persians themselves call satrapies. Once he had set up the provinces and put governors over them, he fixed the tribute each was to pay him, people by people. To each of the main peoples he joined its neighbors, or else, skipping over the nearest peoples, he assigned the more distant ones to various groups. He divided up the provinces and the yearly tribute as follows. Those who paid in silver were ordered to pay by the standard of the Babylonian talent, and those who paid in gold by the Euboean talent. The Babylonian talent is equal to seventy-eight Euboean minas, and since a mina is a sixtieth of a talent, that makes one Babylonian talent worth 1.3 Euboean talents. In the reigns of Cyrus and Cambyses nothing had been fixed about tribute; people used to bring gifts. Because Darius fixed the tribute, and did other things of the same kind, the Persians say that Darius was a shopkeeper, Cambyses a master, and Cyrus a father. Darius, because he ran all his affairs like a shopkeeper; Cambyses, because he was harsh and cared for no one; and Cyrus, because he was gentle and worked out every good thing for them.

90. From the Ionians, the Magnesians who live in Asia, the Aeolians, the Carians, the Lycians, the Milyans and the Pamphylians (he set one single sum as the tribute for all of these together) there came in four hundred talents of silver. He made this the first province. From the Mysians, the Lydians, the Lasonians, the Cabalians and the Hytennians there came in five hundred talents. This is the second province. From the Hellespontians who live on the right as you sail in, the Phrygians, the Thracians who live in Asia, the Paphlagonians, the Mariandyni and the Syrians, the tribute was three hundred and sixty talents. This is the third province. From the Cilicians there came in three hundred and sixty white horses, one for every day of the year, and five hundred talents of silver besides. Of this silver, one hundred and forty talents were spent on the cavalry that guarded the land of Cilicia, and the remaining three hundred and sixty came in to Darius year by year. This is the fourth province.

91. The province that begins at the city of Posideium, which Amphilochus son of Amphiaraus founded on the border between the Cilicians and the Syrians, runs all the way to Egypt. It does not include the territory of the Arabians, which was free from tribute. From it came three hundred and fifty talents. In this province are all of Phoenicia, the part of Syria called Palestine, and Cyprus. This is the fifth province. From Egypt and the Libyans who border on Egypt, and from Cyrene and Barca, which were assigned to the Egyptian province, there came in seven hundred talents. That is not counting the money from Lake Moeris, which came from its fish. Without counting that, I say, or the grain they also contributed by measure, there came in seven hundred talents. As for the grain, they supply 120,000 medimni of it (about 180,000 bushels) for the Persians stationed in the "White Fortress" at Memphis and for their foreign mercenaries. This is the sixth province. The Sattagydians, the Gandarians, the Dadicae and the Aparytae, grouped together, paid one hundred and seventy talents. This is the seventh province. From Susa and the rest of the land of the Cissians there came in three hundred. This is the eighth province.

92. From Babylon and the rest of Assyria there came in to him a thousand talents of silver and five hundred boys to be made eunuchs. This is the ninth province. From Ecbatana and the rest of Media, and from the Paricanians and the Orthocorybantians, came four hundred and fifty talents. This is the tenth province. The Caspians, the Pausicae, the Pantimathi and the Daritae paid together two hundred talents. This is the eleventh province. From the Bactrians as far as the Aegli the tribute was three hundred and sixty talents. This is the twelfth province.

93. From Pactyice, the Armenians, and the peoples bordering on them as far as the Black Sea came four hundred talents. This is the thirteenth province. From the Sagartians, the Sarangians, the Thamanaeans, the Utians, the Mycians, and the people who live on the islands of the Persian Gulf, where the king settles the people called the "Removed," those he has deported from their homes, from all these together came a tribute of six hundred talents. This is the fourteenth province. The Sacae and the Caspians paid two hundred and fifty talents. This is the fifteenth province. The Parthians, the Chorasmians, the Sogdians and the Areians paid three hundred talents. This is the sixteenth province.

94. The Paricanians and the Ethiopians of Asia paid four hundred talents. This is the seventeenth province. The Matienians, the Saspeirians and the Alarodians were assessed at two hundred talents. This is the eighteenth province. The Moschi, the Tibarenians, the Macrones, the Mossynoeci and the Mares were ordered to pay three hundred talents. This is the nineteenth province. The Indians are by far the most numerous people of any we know of, and they paid a tribute larger than all the rest: three hundred and sixty talents of gold dust. This is the twentieth province.

95. Now if we convert the Babylonian talents into Euboean ones, the silver comes to 9,880 talents. And if we count gold at thirteen times the value of silver, weight for weight, the gold dust comes to 4,680 Euboean talents. Add all these together, and the total collected every year in tribute for Darius comes to 14,560 Euboean talents. Sums smaller than these I leave out and do not mention.

96. This was the tribute that came in to Darius from Asia and from a small part of Libya. But as time went on, more tribute came in from the islands as well, and from the peoples of Europe as far as Thessaly. The king stores this tribute in his treasury in the following way. He melts it down and pours it into clay jars, and when the jars are full he breaks the clay away from the metal. Then, whenever he needs money, he cuts off as much as he needs at the time.

97. Those were the provinces and the tribute each was assessed. The land of Persia alone I have not listed as paying anything, because the Persians hold their land free of tribute. The following peoples had no tribute fixed for them, but brought gifts instead. First, the Ethiopians who border on Egypt, whom Cambyses conquered on his march against the Long-Lived Ethiopians, and those who live around sacred Nysa and hold festivals in honor of Dionysus. These Ethiopians and their neighbors use the same grain as the Callantian Indians, and they live in underground houses. These two peoples together brought every other year, and still bring down to my own time, two quarts of unrefined gold, two hundred logs of ebony, five Ethiopian boys, and twenty large elephant tusks. The Colchians also counted themselves among those who brought gifts, together with their neighbors as far as the Caucasus Mountains. (Persian rule reaches as far as these mountains, but the peoples who live beyond the Caucasus, toward the north wind, pay no attention to the Persians.) These peoples went on bringing the gifts they had fixed for themselves every four years, down to my own time: a hundred boys and a hundred girls. Finally, the Arabians brought a thousand talents' weight of frankincense every year (about 57,000 pounds). These were the gifts these peoples brought the king, apart from the tribute.

98. Now here is how the Indians get the great quantity of gold from which they bring the king the gold dust I mentioned. The part of India toward the sunrise is sand. Of all the peoples of Asia that we know of, or about whom anything certain is reported, the Indians live farthest to the east, toward the rising sun, since the country east of the Indians is desert because of the sand. There are many tribes of Indians, and they do not speak the same language. Some of them herd animals and some do not. Some live in the marshes of the river and eat raw fish, which they catch from boats made of cane, each boat made from a single joint of cane. These Indians wear clothes made of rushes. They gather and cut rushes from the river, weave them into a sort of mat, and wear it like a breastplate.

99. Other Indians, living to the east of these, are herders and eat raw meat. They are called the Padaei, and these are their customs. Whenever one of their tribe falls sick, woman or man, if it is a man, the men who are closest to him kill him. They say that the disease is wasting him and his flesh is being spoiled for them. All the while he flatly denies that he is sick, but they do not accept that, and after they have killed him they feast on his flesh. If it is a woman who falls sick, the women closest to her do the same to her as the men do in the other case. In fact, they even kill and feast on anyone who reaches old age. But very few of them ever get to be counted as old, because they kill everyone who falls sick before he reaches old age.

100. Other Indians, on the contrary, live like this. They kill no living thing, they sow no crops, and it is not their custom to have houses. They live on plants. They have a grain about the size of millet, in a husk, which grows wild from the ground. They gather it, boil it husk and all, and eat it. Whenever one of them falls sick, he goes off into the wilderness and lies there, and none of the others pays any attention, either to the dead or to the sick.

101. All these Indians I have spoken of have sex in the open, like cattle. They all have the same skin color, much like that of the Ethiopians. And the semen they ejaculate is not white like other peoples' but black, like their skin; the Ethiopians are the same in this respect. These tribes of Indians live beyond the reach of Persian power, toward the south wind, and they were never subjects of Darius.

102. Other Indians live on the borders of the city of Caspatyrus and the country of Pactyice, to the north of the rest of the Indians, and their way of life is much like that of the Bactrians. These are the most warlike of the Indians, and they are the ones who go on expeditions for the gold. In the parts where they live it is desert because of the sand. In this sandy desert there are ants smaller than dogs but bigger than foxes; in fact some of them, caught out there, are kept at the palace of the king of Persia. These ants make their homes underground and bring up the sand just the way the ants in Greece do, and they look very much like them too. And the sand they bring up has gold in it. To get this sand, the Indians set out into the desert, each man with three camels yoked together: a female in the middle and a male on each side, pulling like a trace horse. The man rides on the female himself, and he takes care that the one he yokes has been taken away from young she has just given birth to, the younger the better. Their female camels are as fast as horses, and they can carry much heavier loads besides.

103. I will not describe what the camel looks like, since the Greeks I am writing for already know what it looks like. But I will tell what is not commonly known about it. The camel has four thighs and four knees in its hind legs, and its genitals are between its hind legs, pointing back toward the tail.

104. So the Indians ride out for the gold in the way I have described, with their camels yoked like that. They time it so that they are carrying the gold off during the hottest part of the day, because the heat drives the ants underground. In those lands the sun is hottest in the morning, not at midday as it is elsewhere. From sunrise until the hour when the market closes, it gives off much more heat than the midday sun in Greece, so much that people there are said to soak themselves in water then. At midday the heat is about the same for the Indians as for everyone else. After midday their sun becomes like the morning sun elsewhere, and from then on, as it moves farther away, it gets cooler and cooler, until at sunset it is very cool indeed.

105. When the Indians reach the place, carrying bags, they fill them with the sand and ride back as fast as they can. The ants, the Persians say, catch the scent and at once start to chase them. This animal, they say, is faster than any other creature, so that if the Indians did not get a head start while the ants were gathering, not one of them would get away. The male camels are slower runners than the females, so if they start to drag, they are cut loose from the female's side, first one and then the other. The females, though, remembering the young they left behind, do not slacken at all. That is how the Indians get most of their gold, the Persians say. There is other gold in their country too, which they mine, but less of it.

106. It seems that the farthest parts of the inhabited world have been given the finest things, just as Greece has been given far the best-balanced climate. First, India, as I said a little earlier, is the farthest of the inhabited lands toward the east. In that land the animals, both the birds and the four-footed beasts, are much bigger than anywhere else, except for the horses, which are outdone by the Median horses called Nesaean, the famous breed of Media. There is also gold in abundance there, some of it mined, some carried down by rivers, and some stolen in the way I just explained. And there the trees that grow wild bear wool that is finer and better than sheep's wool, and the Indians wear clothes made from these trees.

107. Then again, Arabia is the farthest of the inhabited lands toward the south. It is the only land in the world where frankincense, myrrh, cassia, cinnamon and gum ladanum grow. All of these except myrrh the Arabians get only with great difficulty. They gather frankincense by burning storax, a fragrant gum, which the Phoenicians bring to Greece. They burn this to make smoke, and so they get the frankincense. The trees that bear frankincense are guarded by winged snakes, small and of many colors, great numbers of them around each tree. These are the same kind of snakes that try to invade Egypt. Nothing will drive them away from the trees except the smoke of storax.

108. The Arabians also say that the whole world would be full of these snakes by now if the same thing did not happen to them that I know happens to vipers. It seems that the forethought of the divine, wise as one would expect it to be, has made all the timid animals that are good to eat breed abundantly, so that they will not all be eaten up and die out, while it has made the fierce and harmful ones have few young. For example, because the hare is hunted by every beast and bird, and by man as well, it breeds very abundantly. It is the only animal that becomes pregnant again before its earlier young are born. It carries in its womb some young that already have fur, others still bare, and while one is just being formed in the womb, another is being conceived. That is how it is with the hare. The lioness, on the other hand, the strongest and boldest of creatures, gives birth to one cub only once in her life, because when she gives birth she casts out her womb along with her cub. The reason is this. When the cub inside its mother begins to move, its claws, which are far sharper than any other animal's, tear the womb, and the bigger it grows, the more it scratches through. At last, when the birth is near, there is nothing of the womb left whole at all.

109. In the same way, if vipers and the winged snakes of Arabia were born in the ordinary course of nature, people could not live on the earth. But as it is, when they mate and the male is in the act and releasing his seed, the female seizes him by the neck, fastens on, and does not let go until she has bitten clean through it. So the male dies in the way I said. But the female pays the price for the male in this way: while the young are still inside her, they avenge their father by eating through their mother, and once they have eaten through her belly, they make their way out. Other snakes, which do no harm to people, lay eggs and hatch a great many young from them. Now vipers are found all over the earth. But the winged snakes are found in great numbers together in Arabia and in no other land, and that is why they seem so numerous.

110. That, then, is how the Arabians get their frankincense, and here is how they get cassia, a spice bark much like cinnamon. They wrap their whole body and face, all but their eyes, in cowhide and other skins, and then they go out for the cassia. It grows in a shallow lake. Around the lake and in it there live, it seems, winged creatures very like bats, which screech horribly and fight fiercely. The men have to keep these away from their eyes while they cut the cassia.

111. Cinnamon they gather in an even more remarkable way. Where it grows and what land produces it, they cannot say, except that some say, and it is a likely story, that it grows in the regions where Dionysus was brought up. They say that large birds carry these dry sticks, the ones we have learned from the Phoenicians to call cinnamon, up to nests made of mud and stuck on the sheer faces of mountains, which no one can find any way to climb. So the Arabians have worked out this trick. They cut up the oxen and donkeys and other pack animals that die into pieces as large as they can handle, carry them to these places, and lay them down not far from the nests. Then they move off a good distance. The birds fly down and carry the pieces of the pack animals up to their nests. The nests cannot bear the weight, and they break and fall to the ground. Then the men come up and collect the cinnamon. That is how cinnamon is gathered, and from this people it reaches the other countries of the world.

112. Gum ladanum, which the Arabians call ladanon, comes about in a still stranger way. Though it is the sweetest-smelling of all things, it comes from the worst-smelling thing there is: it is found in the beards of billy goats, forming there like resin on wood. It is used in making many perfumes, and the Arabians burn it as incense more than anything else.

113. That is enough about spices. A wonderfully sweet scent of them blows from the land of Arabia. The Arabians also have two kinds of sheep worth marveling at, which are found in no other land. One kind has a long tail, no less than four and a half feet long. If the sheep were left to drag their tails behind them, they would get sores from the tails rubbing against the ground. But as it is, every shepherd there knows enough carpentry to make little carts, which they fasten under the tails, each animal's tail tied to a little cart of its own. The other kind of sheep has a broad tail, as much as a foot and a half across.

Chapter 19: The Edges of the World, the Death of Polycrates, and Democedes the Physician

114. As you go on past the south and toward the setting sun, the land of Ethiopia is the farthest of all inhabited lands in that direction. It produces gold in abundance, huge elephants, trees of every kind growing wild, and ebony; and its men are the tallest of all men, the most beautiful, and the longest-lived.

115. These, then, are the extremities of the world in Asia and in Libya. But about the extremities of Europe toward the west I cannot speak with certainty. For one thing, I do not accept the story that there is a river which the non-Greeks call the Eridanus, flowing into the sea that lies toward the north wind, and that amber comes from there. Nor do I know for a fact that there are "Tin Islands," from which our tin comes. In the first place, the name Eridanus itself shows that it is Greek, not a word from any foreign language, and that some poet made it up. In the second place, though I have taken pains to find out, I have not been able to hear from anyone who has seen it with his own eyes that there is a sea on the far side of Europe. However that may be, tin and amber certainly do come to us from the far edge of Europe.

116. Then again, in the north of Europe there is clearly far more gold than in any other land. How it is got, here again I cannot say for certain; but it is said that the Arimaspians, a race of one-eyed men, steal it from the griffins. I do not believe this story either, that nature produces one-eyed men who are in every other way like other men. Still, it does seem that the extremities, which surround the rest of the world on every side and enclose it in the middle, have the things we think the most beautiful and the most rare.

117. Now there is a plain in Asia shut in by mountains on every side, and through the mountains there are five gorges. This plain once belonged to the Chorasmians, and it lies on the borders of the Chorasmians themselves, the Hyrcanians, the Parthians, the Sarangians, and the Thamanaeans; but ever since the Persians came to power it has belonged to the king. Out of this ring of mountains flows a great river, and its name is the Aces. In the old days it watered the lands of the peoples I have named: it was divided into five streams, and each stream was led through its own gorge in the mountains to its own people. But since they came under the Persians, this is what has happened to them. The king walled up the gorges in the mountains and set gates in each one. So the water was shut off from its way out, and the plain inside the mountains has become a lake, because the river runs into it and has no way out anywhere.

So the people who used to depend on the water can no longer use it, and they are in great trouble. In winter, it is true, the sky rains on them as it does on other people, but in summer, when they sow their millet and sesame, they need the river. So when no water is given to them, they go to Persia, men and wives together, and they stand at the gates of the king's palace crying and wailing. Then the king orders that the gates leading to the land of those who need it most be opened. When their land has drunk its fill, those gates are shut, and he orders the gates opened for others, the ones of the rest who need it most. And, as I have heard, he charges them large sums of money for opening the gates, on top of their regular tribute.

118. So much for these matters. Now of the seven men who had risen against the Magus, one, Intaphrenes, was put to death soon after their uprising, for an outrage which I will now relate. He wanted to go into the palace and speak with the king. The rule was, in fact, that those who had risen against the Magus could go in to the king without being announced, unless the king happened to be in bed with a woman. So Intaphrenes did not think anyone needed to announce him; as one of the seven, he meant to walk in. But the gatekeeper and the royal messenger tried to stop him, saying that the king was in bed with a woman. Intaphrenes thought they were lying. He drew his sword and cut off their ears and noses, threaded them on his horse's bridle, tied the bridle around their necks, and let them go.

119. They then showed themselves to the king and told him why this had been done to them. Darius was afraid that the six had done it by common agreement, so he sent for each of them separately and sounded him out, to see whether he approved of what had been done. When he was fully satisfied that Intaphrenes had not acted together with them, he arrested Intaphrenes himself, with his sons and all his relatives, since he strongly suspected that Intaphrenes and his family were plotting a revolt against him. Having seized them, he put them in chains, ready for execution.

Then Intaphrenes' wife began to come to the doors of the palace, weeping and lamenting. She kept on doing this, day after day, until she made Darius pity her. So he sent a messenger to say to her: "Woman, King Darius grants you the life of one of your relatives who are in chains, whichever one of them all you choose." She thought it over and answered: "If the king really grants me the life of one, then out of them all I choose my brother." When Darius heard this he was amazed at her answer, and he sent to ask her: "Woman, the king asks you what you were thinking of, to leave your husband and your children to die and choose your brother to live, when he is surely less close to you in blood than your children, and less dear to you than your husband." She answered: "My king, if heaven willed it, I could have another husband and other children, if I lost these. But I could never have another brother, since my father and my mother are no longer alive. That is what I was thinking when I said it." Darius thought the woman had spoken well. He set free the man whose life she had asked for, and the eldest of her sons as well, because he was pleased with her; but all the others he put to death. So one of the seven had died almost at once, in the way I have told.

120. Now at about the time of Cambyses' illness, this is what happened. There was a Persian named Oroetes whom Cyrus had made governor of the province of Sardis. This man set his heart on an unholy deed. He had never suffered any harm from Polycrates of Samos, never heard an offensive word from him, and had never even seen him before; yet he wanted to seize him and put him to death. Most of those who tell the story give this reason. Oroetes and another Persian named Mitrobates, the governor of the province of Dascylium, were sitting at the king's door, and they went from talking to quarreling. As they argued over which of them was the better man, Mitrobates taunted Oroetes: "Do you call yourself a man? You never won Samos for the king, though it lies right next to your province, and it is so easy to conquer that one of the islanders rose up against the government with fifteen hoplites, heavy-armed foot soldiers, took the island, and is its tyrant now." Some say that when Oroetes heard this, the taunt stung him, and he conceived a desire, not so much to take revenge on the man who said it, as to destroy Polycrates at any cost, since Polycrates was the reason he had been insulted.

121. A smaller number of those who tell the story say this instead. Oroetes sent a herald to Samos to ask for something or other (what it was is not recorded). Polycrates happened to be lying on a couch in the men's hall of his palace, and Anacreon of Teos, the poet, was there with him. And somehow, whether on purpose, because he thought little of Oroetes' affairs, or whether it just happened by chance, the envoy from Oroetes came in and spoke to him, and Polycrates, who happened to be turned toward the wall, did not turn around or give him any answer at all.

122. Those are the two different accounts of the cause of Polycrates' death, and you may believe whichever you like. Oroetes, at any rate, who lived at the Magnesia that stands on the river Maeander, sent Myrsus son of Gyges, a Lydian, to Samos with a message, because he had seen what Polycrates was aiming at. For Polycrates was the first of the Greeks we know of who set his mind on ruling the sea, apart from Minos of Cnossus and anyone else who may have ruled the sea before him. Of what we call the human race, Polycrates was the first; and he had high hopes of becoming ruler of Ionia and the islands.

Oroetes, then, seeing that this was his plan, sent him this message: "Oroetes says this to Polycrates. I hear that you are making plans to gain great power, and that you do not have the money to match your ambitions. Now if you do as I say, you will do well for yourself, and you will save me from ruin as well. For King Cambyses is planning to have me killed; this has been reported to me so plainly that I cannot doubt it. So take me out of danger, and my money with me. Keep part of the money yourself and let me keep the rest, and then, as far as money can do it, you will be ruler of all Greece. And if you do not believe what I say about the money, send whoever you trust most, and I will show it to him."

123. When Polycrates heard this he was delighted and inclined to agree. Since he had, it seems, a great desire for money, he first sent Maeandrius son of Maeandrius, a Samian who was his secretary, to look at it. This was the same man who not long afterward dedicated to the temple of Hera all the furnishings of the men's hall in Polycrates' palace, furnishings well worth seeing. When Oroetes heard that the inspector was expected soon, this is what he did. He filled eight chests with stones, all but a shallow layer at the very top of each, and laid gold on top of the stones. Then he tied up the chests and kept them ready. So Maeandrius came and looked at them and brought back his report to Polycrates.

124. Polycrates then got ready to go there himself. His soothsayers and his friends tried hard to talk him out of it, and besides, his daughter had seen a vision in her sleep. It seemed to her that her father was lifted high up in the air, and that Zeus was washing him and the Sun was anointing him. After she saw this vision, she tried every way she could to keep Polycrates from leaving home to go to Oroetes. And as he was walking to his fifty-oared galley, she went along beside him calling out words of ill omen. He threatened her that if he came back safe she would stay unmarried for a long time. But she prayed that it would turn out so, for she said she would rather stay unmarried a long time than lose her father.

125. But Polycrates ignored every warning and sailed off to Oroetes. He took many of his friends with him, and among them Democedes son of Calliphon, of Croton, a physician who practiced his art better than any other man of his time. When he reached Magnesia, Polycrates was put to a miserable death, unworthy of himself and of his great ambitions. For apart from the men who became tyrants of Syracuse, not one of the other Greek tyrants deserves to be compared with Polycrates for magnificence. Oroetes killed him in a way not fit to be told, and then he impaled his body. Of the men who had come with him, he let go all who were Samians, telling them they should be grateful to him for their freedom; but all the others in Polycrates' company, the foreign allies and the servants, he counted as slaves and kept them. And so Polycrates, hanging there, fulfilled his daughter's vision completely: he was washed by Zeus whenever it rained, and he was anointed by the Sun as the moisture ran out of his own body.

126. That was the end of Polycrates' great good fortune, just as Amasis, king of Egypt, had foretold to him. But not long afterward vengeance for Polycrates' murder caught up with Oroetes in his turn. After Cambyses' death, during the reign of the Magi, Oroetes stayed at Sardis and did nothing to help the Persians, when the Medes had taken their empire from them. Instead, in this time of upheaval, he killed Mitrobates, the governor of Dascylium, who had thrown Polycrates in his face as a reproach, and he also killed Cranaspes son of Mitrobates, both of them men of standing among the Persians. He committed many other outrages too. Once, when a royal messenger had come to him from Darius with a message he did not like, he had men lie in wait for the messenger on his way back and kill him; and after he was dead he made away with the bodies of both the man and his horse.

127. So when Darius had become king, he wanted to punish Oroetes for all his crimes, and above all for the murder of Mitrobates and his son. But he did not think it wise to act openly and send an army against him, since his own affairs were still unsettled and he had only just come to the throne, and he heard that Oroetes was very strong. Oroetes had a bodyguard of a thousand Persian spearmen, and he held the provinces of Phrygia, Lydia and Ionia. So Darius worked out a plan. He called together the most distinguished of the Persians and said to them: "Persians, which of you will do this job for me by cleverness, not by force or by making a commotion? Where cleverness is needed, force is no use. Which of you, I say, will either bring Oroetes to me alive or kill him? He has never done the Persians any good, and he has done them great harm. First he destroyed two of us, Mitrobates and his son. Then he kills the men I send to summon him, with an arrogance no one can tolerate. So before he does the Persians any more harm, we must stop him with his death."

128. That was Darius' question, and thirty men offered to do it, each of them wanting the job for himself. Darius stopped their arguing and told them to draw lots. When they drew, Bagaeus son of Artontes won the lot out of them all. Having won it, this is what Bagaeus did. He wrote many letters on all sorts of business, sealed them with Darius' seal, and took them with him to Sardis. When he got there and came before Oroetes, he took the covers off the letters one by one and handed them to the royal secretary to read aloud (every provincial governor has a royal secretary). Bagaeus handed over the letters to test the spearmen of the guard, to see whether they would accept a call to turn against Oroetes. He saw that they showed great respect for the letters, and even more for what was read out of them. So he handed over another letter, which said: "Persians, King Darius forbids you to serve as Oroetes' bodyguard." When they heard this they lowered their spears to him. Seeing that they obeyed the letter this far, Bagaeus took courage and gave the last of the letters to the secretary, and in it was written: "King Darius commands the Persians at Sardis to kill Oroetes." When the spearmen of the guard heard this, they drew their swords and killed him on the spot. So vengeance for the murder of Polycrates of Samos caught up with Oroetes.

129. When Oroetes' wealth had arrived, or been carried, up to Susa, it happened not long afterward that King Darius, out hunting wild animals, twisted his foot as he jumped down from his horse. It was twisted, it seems, quite badly, for the ball of his ankle joint was dislocated. Now he had long kept around him the Egyptians who were considered the best in the art of medicine, and he used their help now. But they twisted and forced the foot and only made the injury worse and worse. For seven days and seven nights Darius could not sleep for the pain. At last, on the eighth day, when he was in a bad way, someone who had heard talk at Sardis of the skill of Democedes of Croton told Darius about him, and Darius ordered them to bring him in at once. They found him somewhere among Oroetes' slaves, overlooked, and they brought him out before everyone, dragging his chains and dressed in rags.

130. When he was standing in front of them all, Darius asked him whether he knew the art of medicine. But he would not admit it, because he was afraid that if he showed what he really was, he would lose all hope of ever returning to Greece. Darius could see clearly that he did know the art and was trying to trick him, and he ordered the men who had brought him to fetch whips and goads. At that he spoke up, saying that he did not know it well, but that he had spent time with a physician and had some poor knowledge of the art. After this, when Darius had put himself in his hands, Democedes used Greek remedies and applied gentle treatment after the earlier rough methods. He got the king to sleep, and in a short time he made him completely well, though Darius had never expected to have a sound foot again.

After this Darius gave him a present of two pairs of golden chains. Democedes asked him whether he was deliberately doubling his misery as a reward for making him well. Darius was pleased with this remark and sent him to visit his wives. The eunuchs who took him in told the women that this was the man who had given the king back his life. Then each of them dipped a bowl into a chest of gold and gave it to Democedes, a gift so lavish that his servant, whose name was Sciton, followed along picking up the coins that fell from the bowls, and collected a very large sum of gold for himself.

131. This Democedes came from Croton, and this is how he had come to be with Polycrates. At Croton he was always quarreling with his father, who had a harsh temper, and when he could not stand him any longer, he left and went to Aegina. He settled there, and in his first year he outdid all the other physicians, though he had no equipment and none of the instruments used in the art. In his second year the city of Aegina hired him for a fee of one talent; in the third the Athenians hired him for a hundred pounds of silver; and in the fourth Polycrates hired him for two talents. That is how he came to Samos. And it was because of this man, more than anything else, that the physicians of Croton became famous. For this was the time when the physicians of Croton began to be spoken of as the best in Greece, with those of Cyrene in second place. At about this same time the Argives too had the reputation of being the best musicians in Greece.

132. So now, having cured King Darius, Democedes had a very large house in Susa and had been made one of the king's table companions. He had everything except the one thing he wanted: to go home to Greece. To begin with, when the Egyptian physicians who had tried to cure the king before him were about to be impaled for being outdone by a Greek physician, he asked the king to spare their lives and saved them from death. Second, he rescued a soothsayer from Elis who had come with Polycrates and had been overlooked among the slaves. In short, Democedes stood very high in the king's favor.

133. Not long after this, something else happened. Atossa, the daughter of Cyrus and wife of Darius, had a growth on her breast, which later broke open and kept spreading. As long as it was small, she hid it and told no one, because she was ashamed. But later, when it had become serious, she sent for Democedes and showed it to him. He said that he would cure her, and he made her swear that in return she would do for him whatever he asked her; and he said he would ask nothing shameful.

134. So after he had treated her and made her well, Atossa, coached by Democedes, said something like this to Darius in their bedroom: "My king, you have such great power, and yet you sit still and win no new nation or power for the Persians. But it is only right for a man who is young and master of great wealth to be seen doing some great deed, so that the Persians may know for sure that it is a real man who rules them. Doing this will help you in two ways: the Persians will know that their ruler is a man, and they will be worn down by war and have no time to plot against you. Now is the time when you could do some great deed, while you are still young. For as the body grows older the spirit grows old along with it, and goes dull for any kind of action."

That was what she said, as she had been told, and he answered her: "Woman, you have said all the things I already have in mind to do. I have decided to build a bridge joining this continent to the other and to march against the Scythians, and these plans will be carried out before long." Then Atossa said: "Listen, don't go against the Scythians first. They will be yours whenever you want them. Instead, please, march against Greece. I have heard about the women there, and I want Spartan women for my maids, and Argive, Athenian and Corinthian ones. And you have the man best fitted of all men to show you everything about Greece and be your guide: the man who cured your foot." Darius answered: "Woman, since you think we should try Greece first, I think it is better to send some Persians there first, together with the man you speak of, to scout it out. When they have learned and seen everything, they can report it all to us in detail, and then I will go and attack them knowing everything."

135. So he said, and he made his words into deeds at once. As soon as day dawned, he summoned fifteen Persians of high standing and ordered them to travel along the coasts of Greece with Democedes, and to make sure that Democedes did not escape from them, but to bring him back at all costs. Having given them these orders, he next summoned Democedes himself and asked him to guide the Persians through all of Greece and show it to them, and then come back. He told him to take all his household goods and carry them as presents to his father and brothers, and said he would give him many times as much in their place. On top of that, he said, he would add to the presents a merchant ship loaded with all kinds of goods, which would sail with him. In my opinion Darius made him these promises with no trick in mind. But Democedes was afraid that Darius was testing him, and he was in no hurry to accept everything offered. He said he would leave his own things where they were, so that he would have them when he came back; but he did accept the merchant ship Darius promised him for the presents to his brothers. Having given these orders to him as well, Darius sent them off to the coast.

136. So they went down to Phoenicia, to the city of Sidon, and at once manned two triremes and also loaded a large cargo ship with all kinds of goods. When they had everything ready they sailed for Greece. They put in at various places along its coasts, looked them over, and wrote down descriptions, until, when they had seen most of the famous places, they came to Taras in Italy. There Aristophilides, the king of Taras, as a favor to Democedes, unfastened and removed the steering oars of the Persian ships, and also locked the Persians up in prison, on the grounds, he said, that they had come as spies. While this was being done to them, Democedes got away and reached Croton. And when he had reached his own home city, Aristophilides set the Persians free and gave them back the parts of their ships he had taken.

137. Then the Persians sailed from there in pursuit of Democedes and reached Croton. They found him in the marketplace and seized him. Some of the men of Croton, afraid of Persian power, were ready to hand him over; but others grabbed hold of him and beat the Persians with their staffs. The Persians pleaded with them like this: "Men of Croton, be careful what you are doing. You are rescuing a runaway slave of King Darius. How do you think King Darius will take an insult like this? And how will it turn out well for you if you take him away from us? What city do you think we will march against before this one, and what city will we try to enslave first?" But for all they said, they did not persuade the men of Croton. Democedes was taken away from them, and so was the cargo ship they had brought with them, and they set sail back to Asia. Without their guide, they made no further attempt to visit or learn about any more of Greece. But as they were putting out to sea, Democedes gave them this message, telling them to say to Darius that Democedes was engaged to the daughter of Milo. For the wrestler Milo had a great name at the king's court. And I suppose that Democedes pushed hard for this marriage, spending a great deal of money on it, so that Darius would see that he was a man of honor in his own country too.

138. After the Persians put out from Croton, they were shipwrecked in Iapygia, the heel of Italy. While they were held there as slaves, Gillus, an exile from Taras, rescued them and brought them back to King Darius. In return Darius offered to give him whatever he wanted. Gillus chose to be allowed to return to Taras, and first he told the story of his misfortune. But so as not to throw all of Greece into turmoil, as would happen if a great armada sailed to invade Italy on his account, he said it would be enough for him if the men of Cnidus alone brought him back, and no one else. He thought that since they were friends of the people of Taras, they could most easily arrange his return from exile. Darius promised and kept his promise: he sent a message to Cnidus ordering them to bring Gillus back to Taras. The men of Cnidus obeyed Darius, but they could not persuade the people of Taras, and they were not strong enough to use force. That is how these things turned out. These were the first Persians who came from Asia to Greece, and they were sent as spies for the reason I have told.

Chapter 20: The Cloak of Syloson, and Zopyrus Takes Babylon

139. After this, King Darius took Samos, the first of all the cities he captured, Greek or non-Greek, and this is how it came about. When Cambyses son of Cyrus was marching on Egypt, a great many Greeks came to Egypt. Some, as you would expect, joined the campaign to make a profit, and some came just to see the country. Among them was Syloson son of Aeaces, the brother of Polycrates, who was then in exile from Samos. A stroke of good luck came Syloson's way, and it was this. He had put on a flame-red cloak and was walking around the marketplace in Memphis. Darius, who was then one of Cambyses' spearmen and not yet a man of any great importance, saw him and wanted the cloak. He went up to him and offered to buy it. Syloson saw how badly Darius wanted the cloak, and by some divine prompting he said: "I won't sell this for any price. But I'll give it to you for nothing, if it seems it simply has to be yours." Darius accepted and took the cloak from him.

140. Syloson assumed without a doubt that he had simply lost it through his own good nature. But in time Cambyses died, the seven Persians rose up against the Magus, and out of the seven it was Darius who won the throne. Then Syloson heard that the kingdom had gone to the very man who had once asked him for his cloak in Egypt, and to whom he had given it. So he went up to Susa, sat down at the entrance to the king's palace, and announced that he was a benefactor of Darius. The doorkeeper heard this and reported it to the king. Darius was amazed and said to him: "What Greek is my benefactor, that I should owe him gratitude? I have held the throne only a short time, and hardly a single Greek has come up to our court yet. I can almost say I owe nothing to any Greek. Still, bring him in, so that I can find out what he means by this." So the doorkeeper brought Syloson in. When he stood before the king, the interpreters asked him who he was and what he had done to call himself the king's benefactor. Syloson told the whole story of the cloak and how he was the man who had given it. Darius answered: "Most generous of men, you are the one who gave me a gift when I had no power at all. It may have been a small gift, but the kindness counts with me as much as if someone gave me something great today. So in return I will give you gold and silver in abundance, so that you will never be sorry you did a service for Darius son of Hystaspes." Syloson replied: "My king, don't give me gold or silver. Win back my homeland, Samos, and give it to me. Now that my brother Polycrates has been killed by Oroetes, it is in the hands of our slave. Give it to me without bloodshed and without selling anyone into slavery."

141. When Darius heard this, he made ready to send an expedition under the command of Otanes, who had been one of the seven, with orders to carry out everything Syloson had asked. So Otanes went down to the coast and began preparing the expedition.

142. Now Samos was being ruled by Maeandrius son of Maeandrius, who had been left in charge of the government by Polycrates. He wanted to be the most just of men, but he did not manage it. When the news of Polycrates' death reached him, this is what he did. First he set up an altar to Zeus the Liberator and marked out a sacred precinct around it, the one that is still there today in the suburb outside the city. After he had done this, he called an assembly of all the citizens and said: "As you know as well as I do, the scepter of Polycrates and all his power have been entrusted to me, and right now I could be your ruler. But what I blame in my neighbor I will not do myself, as far as I can help it. I never approved of Polycrates being master over men who were just as good as he was, and I don't approve of anyone else who does that sort of thing. Well, Polycrates has met his destiny. I now hand the power over to the people, and I proclaim equality for you all. I do think it right, though, that I should be granted a few privileges: six talents should be taken out of Polycrates' wealth and given to me as a special gift, and on top of that I choose for myself, and for my descendants after me, the priesthood of Zeus the Liberator, since I founded his temple myself, and I am giving you your freedom." Those were the offers he made to the Samians. But one of them stood up and said: "No, you're not fit to rule us anyway. You're low-born, and a nasty piece of work besides. You'd do better to think about how you're going to account for the money you've been handling."

143. The man who said this was a citizen of good standing named Telesarchus. Maeandrius realized that if he gave up the power, someone else would set himself up as tyrant in his place, so he dropped all thought of giving it up. He withdrew into the citadel and sent for the leading men one at a time, pretending he was going to give an account of the money. Instead he seized them and put them in chains. So these men were in chains. But after this Maeandrius fell sick, and his brother, whose name was Lycaretus, expected him to die. To make it easier to take power over Samos himself, he put all the prisoners to death. And all this happened, it seems, because the Samians did not choose to be free.

144. So when the Persians arrived at Samos bringing Syloson home from exile, no one lifted a hand against them. In fact Maeandrius and his party said they were ready to leave the island under a truce. Otanes agreed to these terms and made a treaty, and the highest-ranking Persians had chairs set out for them in front of the citadel and were sitting there.

145. Now the tyrant Maeandrius had a brother who was somewhat out of his mind, named Charilaus. For some offense he had committed, he had been shut up in an underground dungeon. At the time I am describing, he heard what was going on, and when he put his head out of the dungeon and saw the Persians sitting there in peace, he began to shout that he wanted to speak with Maeandrius. Maeandrius heard his voice and ordered him to be released and brought before him. As soon as Charilaus was brought in, he began to abuse and insult his brother, trying to talk him into attacking the Persians. This is what he said: "You lowest of men! You put me in chains and thought me fit for an underground dungeon, me, your own brother, who had done nothing to deserve chains. And now you see the Persians throwing you out of your country and making you homeless, and you don't dare take any revenge, even though they are so easy to beat? Well, if you really are afraid of them, give me your mercenaries, and I'll make them pay for coming here. As for you, I'm willing to let you leave the island."

146. That is what Charilaus said, and Maeandrius took him up on it. In my opinion this was not because he had sunk so far into folly as to think his own forces could beat the king's. It was rather that he begrudged Syloson getting the city from him without any trouble and with no damage done to it. So he wanted to provoke the Persians to anger and leave Samos as weak as possible before he handed it over. He was well aware that once the Persians had suffered harm, they would probably be just as bitter against the Samians as against the men who had done the harm. And he knew he had a safe way off the island whenever he wanted it, because he had had a secret tunnel dug from the citadel down to the sea. So Maeandrius himself sailed away from Samos. Charilaus armed all the mercenaries, threw open the gates, and sent them out against the Persians. The Persians were expecting nothing of the kind; they thought everything had been settled. The mercenaries fell on them and began killing the Persians of the highest rank, the ones who had been carried there in their chairs. While they were busy with this, the rest of the Persian force came to the rescue, and the mercenaries were driven back and forced to retreat into the citadel.

147. Then Otanes, the Persian commander, seeing that the Persians had suffered heavy losses, deliberately forgot the orders Darius had given him when he sent him out: not to kill a single Samian or sell any into slavery, but to hand the island over to Syloson without any harm done to it. He deliberately forgot those orders and told his army to kill everyone they caught, man or boy, without distinction. So while part of the army besieged the citadel, the rest killed everyone who crossed their path, in a sanctuary or out of one, it made no difference.

148. Meanwhile Maeandrius had escaped from Samos and was sailing to Sparta. When he got there, he had the things he had brought away with him carried up to the city, and this is what he did. He would set out his silver and gold cups, and while the servants were polishing them, he would be talking with Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, who was then king of Sparta, and walk him along to his house. When Cleomenes saw the cups he was struck with wonder at them, and Maeandrius would tell him to take away as many as he liked. Maeandrius said this two or three times. But here Cleomenes proved himself the most honest of men. Not only did he refuse to take what was offered, but he saw that Maeandrius would give presents to other citizens and so win support for himself. So he went to the ephors and told them it would be better for Sparta if this foreigner from Samos left the Peloponnese, in case he persuaded Cleomenes himself or some other Spartan to do something base. The ephors took his advice and banished Maeandrius by public proclamation.

149. As for Samos, the Persians swept it clean of its people and handed it over to Syloson empty of men. Later, though, the commander Otanes even helped to settle people there again. He was moved to do it by a vision he had in a dream and by a disease that struck him, a disease of the genitals.

150. While the fleet had gone against Samos in this way, the Babylonians revolted, and they were extremely well prepared for it. All through the reign of the Magus and the uprising of the seven, through all that time and the confusion that came with it, they had been getting ready to stand a siege, and somehow nobody noticed what they were doing. When they revolted openly, this is what they did. First they set aside their mothers. Then each man also set aside for himself one woman of his own household, whichever one he chose. All the rest of the women they gathered together and strangled. Each man kept the one woman I mentioned to bake his bread, and they strangled the rest so that they would not eat up the food supplies.

151. When Darius heard this, he gathered all his forces and marched against them. He brought his army up to Babylon and began to besiege the city. But the Babylonians did not care in the least about the siege. They would climb up onto the battlements of the wall and jeer at Darius and his army with gestures and with words, and one of them said this: "Why are you sitting here, Persians, instead of going away? You'll take us only when mules have foals." The Babylonian who said this did not imagine that a mule would ever have a foal.

152. So when a year and seven months had gone by, Darius and his whole army with him began to grow frustrated, because they could not conquer the Babylonians. Darius had tried every trick and every possible means against them, and even so he could not take the city. Among his other schemes he had tried the very one by which Cyrus had taken it, but the Babylonians were terribly watchful, and he could not conquer them.

153. Then in the twentieth month a portent came to Zopyrus, the son of the Megabyzus who had been one of the seven men who killed the Magus. To this Zopyrus son of Megabyzus, I say, a portent happened: one of the mules that carried his supplies had a foal. When this was reported to him, he did not believe it, and he went and saw the foal for himself. Then he ordered the men who had seen it not to tell anyone what had happened, and he thought over what to do. He kept in mind the words of the Babylonian who had said at the start that the wall would be taken when mules had foals. With this omen in mind, it seemed to Zopyrus that Babylon could now be taken. For he believed that it was by the will of heaven both that the man had said those words and that his own mule had foaled.

154. Since it seemed to him that Babylon was now fated to fall, he went to Darius and asked him whether he thought conquering Babylon was a matter of very great importance. When Darius answered that he thought it of great importance indeed, Zopyrus considered again how he could be the one to take it, and how the achievement could be his own; for among the Persians good service to the king is honored very highly. He decided that the only way he could bring the city down was to mutilate himself and desert to the Babylonians. So, holding himself cheap, he mutilated his own body past all cure. He cut off his nose and his ears, shaved his hair in a disgraceful way, whipped himself, and in that state went before Darius.

155. Darius was deeply distressed to see the most distinguished man in his service mutilated like this. He leaped up from his seat, cried out, and asked who had done this to him, and for what. Zopyrus answered: "There is no man except you who has power enough to put me in this state. No stranger did this, my king. I did it to myself, because I could not bear that the Assyrians should laugh at the Persians." Darius replied: "You most reckless of men, you have put the fairest name on the foulest deed when you say you have maimed yourself beyond cure because of the people we are besieging. How, you fool, will the enemy surrender to us any faster because you have mutilated yourself? You must have gone out of your mind to ruin yourself like this." Zopyrus said: "If I had told you what I was about to do, you would not have let me do it. So I did it on my own. Now, unless you fail to do your part, we will take Babylon. I'm going straight to the wall as a deserter. I'll tell them that you did this to me. And I think that once I have convinced them, I will be given command of part of their forces. On the tenth day after I get inside the wall, take a thousand men from the troops whose loss you won't mind, and station them by the gate called the gate of Semiramis. After that, on the seventh day after the tenth, station two thousand more, please, by the gate called the gate of the Ninevites. After that seventh day, let twenty days go by, and then bring four thousand others and station them by the gate called the gate of the Chaldeans. Neither the first groups nor this one should have any weapons to defend themselves except daggers; let them have those. Then, right after the twentieth day, order the rest of the army to attack the wall all the way around, and post the Persians, please, by the gates called the gate of Belus and the gate of Cissia. For I think that once I have done great deeds for them, the Babylonians will trust me with everything else, including the keys that draw the bolts of the gates. After that, it will be up to me and the Persians to do what has to be done."

156. With these instructions given, he set off for the gate of the city, turning to look behind him as he went, as if he really were a deserter. The men posted on that part of the wall saw him from the towers and ran down. They opened one leaf of the gate a crack and asked him who he was and what he had come for. He told them he was Zopyrus and that he had come over to them as a deserter. When the gatekeepers heard this, they took him to the Babylonian assembly. Brought before it, he began to lament his misfortunes. He said that the injuries he had in fact done to himself had been done to him by Darius, and that it was because he had advised the king to withdraw his army, since there really seemed to be no way of taking the city.
