"And now," he went on, "I have come to you, Babylonians, for your very great good, and for the very great harm of Darius and his army and the Persians. He will certainly not get away with treating me like this. And I know every one of his plans."

157. That is what he said. The Babylonians saw the most distinguished man among the Persians with his nose and ears cut off and covered with blood from the whipping, and they were quite sure he was telling the truth and had come to help them. So they were ready to give him whatever he asked for, and what he asked for was the command of a body of troops. When he had got this from them, he did what he had agreed with Darius to do. On the tenth day he led out the Babylonian troops, surrounded the thousand men he had told Darius to station there first, and killed them. The Babylonians saw that his deeds matched his words, and they were overjoyed and ready to obey him in everything. Then, when the agreed number of days had passed, he again picked out a force of Babylonians, led them out, and killed the two thousand of Darius' troops. When they saw this deed too, all the Babylonians had the name of Zopyrus on their lips and were loud in his praise. Then again, when the agreed days had passed, he led them out to the appointed place, surrounded the four thousand, and killed them. After this too, Zopyrus was everything to the Babylonians, and they made him both commander of their army and guardian of their walls.

158. But when Darius attacked the wall all the way around, as they had agreed, Zopyrus revealed his whole trick. While the Babylonians were up on the wall defending it against the attack of Darius' army, Zopyrus opened the gates called the Cissian gate and the gate of Belus and let the Persians inside the wall. Those Babylonians who saw what had happened fled to the temple of Zeus Belus. Those who did not see it stayed each at his own post, until in the end they too found out that they had been betrayed.

159. So Babylon was taken for the second time. When Darius had conquered the Babylonians, he first tore down the wall around their city and pulled down all the gates. When Cyrus took Babylon before him, he had done neither of these things. Next, Darius impaled the leading men, about three thousand of them. But he gave the city back to the rest of the Babylonians to live in. And to make sure the Babylonians would have wives, so that their people would go on having children, Darius did the following. (As I said at the beginning of this account, the Babylonians had strangled their own wives to make their food supplies last.) He ordered the peoples who lived around Babylon to send women there, setting a fixed number for each people, so that in all 50,000 women were brought together. It is from these women that the Babylonians of today are descended.

160. As for Zopyrus, in Darius' judgment no Persian ever surpassed him in good service, either among those who came after or among those who had gone before, except Cyrus alone; for no Persian has ever yet dared to compare himself with Cyrus. And Darius is said to have declared many times that he would rather have Zopyrus unharmed than gain twenty more Babylons on top of the one he had. He also gave him great honors. Every year he gave him the gifts the Persians count most honorable, and he granted him Babylon to rule free of tribute for as long as he lived, and he added many other gifts besides. This Zopyrus had a son, Megabyzus, who was made commander in Egypt against the Athenians and their allies; and this Megabyzus had a son, Zopyrus, who deserted from the Persians and went over to Athens.

Book Four: Melpomene

Chapter 21: The Origins of the Scythians, and the Peoples of the Far North

1. After Babylon was taken, Darius himself marched against the Scythians. Asia was now flourishing, full of people, and large sums were coming in as revenue, so Darius conceived a desire to take revenge on the Scythians. They had been the first to invade the land of the Medes and had beaten in battle those who stood against them; so they had started the wrong. In fact, as I said before, the Scythians had ruled Upper Asia for twenty-eight years. They had invaded Asia in pursuit of the Cimmerians, and they had ended the rule of the Medes, who had ruled Asia before the Scythians came. But when the Scythians had been away from their own land for twenty-eight years and were coming home after all that time, they met a struggle no less hard than their war with the Medes. They found a sizable army drawn up against them. The reason was that the Scythians' wives, since their husbands had been away from them for so long, had been sleeping with the slaves.

2. Now, the Scythians blind all their slaves, because of the milk they drink. This is how they do it. They take blowpipes made of bone, just like flutes, insert them into the mare's vagina, and blow with their mouths, while others milk as they blow. They say they do this because blowing fills the mare's veins with air and makes the udder let down its milk. When they have drawn the milk, they pour it into hollowed-out wooden vessels, set the blind slaves around the vessels, and have them churn the milk. They skim off what rises to the top, which they think the more valuable part; what settles to the bottom they consider less good. That is why the Scythians blind everyone they capture: they are not farmers but nomads.

3. So it was from these slaves and the Scythians' wives that a generation of young men had been born and raised. When these young men learned how they had been born, they set out to resist the Scythians on their way home from Media. First they cut off their land by digging a wide trench from the Tauric mountains, the mountains of the Crimea, to Lake Maeotis, at the point where the lake is widest. Then, when the Scythians tried to invade, they took up a position against them and fought. They fought many times, and the Scythians could gain no advantage in the fighting. At last one of the Scythians said: "Scythians, what are we doing? We are fighting our own slaves. Every time we fight, more of us are killed, so there are fewer of us; and we are killing them too, so we will have fewer to rule in the future. So here is what I think we should do. Let's put down our spears and bows, and let each man take his horsewhip and go right up to them. As long as they saw us with weapons in our hands, they thought they were our equals and as well born as we are. But when they see us carrying whips instead of weapons, they will understand that they are our slaves, and once they admit that, they will not stand their ground."

4. When the Scythians heard this, they did what he said. The others were so terrified by what they saw that they forgot about fighting and ran. That is how the Scythians had ruled Asia, and how, after the Medes drove them out again, they had come back to their own land. And this is what Darius wanted to take revenge for, and why he was gathering an army to march against them.

5. The Scythians say that their nation is the youngest of all nations, and that this is how it began. The first man ever to live in their country, which was empty at that time, was a man named Targitaus. They say his parents were Zeus and the daughter of the river Borysthenes, the Dnieper. I do not believe this myself, but that is what they say. That, they say, was where Targitaus came from, and he had three sons: Lipoxais, Arpoxais, and the youngest, Colaxais. While these three were ruling, certain objects made of gold fell from the sky into the land of Scythia: a plow, a yoke, a battle-axe, and a cup. The eldest saw them first and went up to them, wanting to take them, but as he came near, the gold blazed up in fire. When he had gone away, the second brother went up to it, and the gold did the same thing again. So the gold drove these two away by blazing with fire. But when the third and youngest came up to it, the flames went out, and he carried the objects home. The two older brothers understood what this meant, and they handed over the whole of the kingship to the youngest.

6. From Lipoxais, they say, are descended the Scythians called the Auchatae clan; from the middle brother, Arpoxais, those called the Catiari and the Traspians; and from the youngest, the royal clan, called the Paralatae. All of them together, they say, are called Scoloti, after the name of their king; it was the Greeks who named them Scythians.

7. That is how the Scythians say they came into being. From their beginning, that is, from their first king, Targitaus, to Darius' crossing into their land, they say there were a thousand years and no more. The kings guard this sacred gold with the greatest care and visit it every year with solemn sacrifices to win the gods' favor. If anyone who is guarding the gold out in the open during the festival falls asleep, the Scythians say he will not live out the year; and he is given as much land as he can ride around on his horse in one day. Since the country was large, they say, Colaxais set up three kingdoms for his sons, and he made one of them larger than the others, and that is where the gold is kept. As for the regions farther north, beyond the people who live above their land, they say you cannot see any farther or travel any farther because of the feathers that pour down. The earth and the air are full of feathers, and that is what blocks the view.

8. That is what the Scythians say about themselves and about the country beyond them. But the Greeks who live around the Black Sea tell it this way. Heracles, driving the cattle of Geryon, came to this land, which was empty then and is now inhabited by the Scythians. Geryon, the story goes, lived far from the Black Sea, on the island the Greeks call Erythea, near Gadeira, which is Cádiz, outside the Pillars of Heracles, on the Ocean. (As for the Ocean, they say it flows around the whole earth, starting from where the sun rises, but they do not prove it with facts.) From there Heracles came to the land now called Scythia. A storm came over him, along with bitter cold, so he pulled his lion's skin over himself and went to sleep. While he slept, the mares that were harnessed to his chariot were grazing, and by some miraculous chance they disappeared.

9. When Heracles woke up, he went looking for them. He searched the whole country and at last came to the region called Hylaea, the Woodland. There, in a cave, he found a creature of double form, half girl and half serpent: from the buttocks up she was a woman, but below she was a snake. He looked at her in amazement and then asked whether she had seen any mares wandering anywhere. She said she had them herself and would not give them back until he had sex with her, and Heracles slept with her on condition that he would get them back. Then she kept putting off returning the mares, because she wanted to keep Heracles with her as long as she could, while he wanted to get the mares and leave. At last she gave them back and said: "When these mares wandered here, I kept them safe for you, and you have paid me for keeping them, because I am carrying three sons of yours. So tell me, what should I do with them when they grow up? Should I settle them here, since I alone rule this land, or send them away to you?" That was her question, and he answered, they say: "When you see that the boys have grown to be men, do this and you will not go wrong. Whichever of them you see can draw this bow the way I do now, and can put on this belt, make him the one who settles this land. Whichever of them fails at the tasks I am setting, send him out of the country. If you do this, you will be happy yourself, and you will have done what you were told."

10. With that he drew one of his bows (up to that time, they say, Heracles used to carry two) and showed her the belt. Then he gave her both the bow and the belt, which had a golden cup hanging from the end of its clasp, and once he had given them to her, he left. When her sons were born and had grown to be men, she first gave them names: she called one Agathyrsus, the next Gelonus, and the youngest Scythes. Then, remembering his instructions, she did what she had been told. Two of her sons, Agathyrsus and Gelonus, could not manage the task set for them, and they left the country, driven out by their own mother. But Scythes, the youngest, did the task and stayed in the land. From Scythes son of Heracles, they say, all the later kings of the Scythians are descended. And they say that it is because of that cup that the Scythians still wear cups hanging from their belts to this day. That one thing his mother arranged for Scythes' sake. That is the story told by the Greeks who live around the Black Sea.

11. But there is another story too, and this is the one I lean toward myself. It goes like this. The nomad Scythians who lived in Asia were hard pressed in war by the Massagetae, so they left their home, crossed the river Araxes, and moved toward the land of the Cimmerians. (The land the Scythians now occupy is said to have belonged to the Cimmerians in the old days.) When the Scythians were coming against them, the Cimmerians held a council, since they could see a great host coming to attack them. It turned out that they were split between two opinions, each held fiercely, though the better one was the kings'. The common people thought they ought to leave and not risk a fight against so many. The kings thought they ought to fight the invaders for their land. The people would not agree to the kings' plan, and the kings would not agree to the people's. So the people planned to leave without a fight and hand the country over to the invaders, while the kings decided to die and be buried in their own land rather than flee with the crowd. They thought of all the good fortune they had enjoyed there, and of all the misery that would likely come on them if they fled their native country. Once they had decided this, they split into two groups of equal size and fought each other. When they had all died at one another's hands, the Cimmerian people buried them beside the river Tyras, the Dniester, where their grave can still be seen. After they had buried them, they left the country, and when the Scythians arrived they found the land empty.

12. Even now there are Cimmerian walls in Scythia, and a Cimmerian ferry. There is also a region called Cimmeria, and the strait called the Cimmerian Bosporus, between the Crimea and the land to its east. It is also known that the Cimmerians, fleeing into Asia from the Scythians, settled on the peninsula where the Greek city of Sinope now stands. And it is known that the Scythians, chasing them, lost their way and invaded the land of Media. The Cimmerians kept to the coast all along as they fled, while the Scythians pursued them with the Caucasus on their right until finally they turned inland and burst into Media. So that is the other story, and Greeks and non-Greeks both tell it.

13. But Aristeas son of Caystrobius, a man of Proconnesus, said in the poem he wrote that he was seized by Phoebus Apollo and traveled to the land of the Issedonians. Beyond the Issedonians, he said, live the Arimaspians, a one-eyed people; beyond them, the griffins that guard the gold; and beyond them, the Hyperboreans, whose land stretches all the way to the sea. All of these except the Hyperboreans, starting with the Arimaspians, were always making war on their neighbors. The Issedonians were gradually pushed out of their country by the Arimaspians, the Scythians by the Issedonians, and so the Cimmerians, who lived on the southern sea, were pressed by the Scythians and left their land. So he does not agree with the Scythians' account of this country either.

14. I have already said where this Aristeas, the author of that poem, came from. Now I will also tell the story I heard about him in Proconnesus and Cyzicus. They say that Aristeas, who was as well born as any citizen there, went into a fuller's shop in Proconnesus, a cloth-cleaner's, and died there. The fuller shut up his workshop and went off to tell the dead man's relatives. The news that Aristeas was dead had spread around the city when a man of Cyzicus, who had come from the town of Artace, began to argue with the people who were saying so. He said he had met Aristeas on the road to Cyzicus and talked with him. While he was arguing hotly, the dead man's relatives came to the fuller's shop with everything they needed to take up the body for burial. But when the shop was opened, Aristeas was not there, dead or alive. In the seventh year after this he appeared in Proconnesus and composed the poem that the Greeks now call the Arimaspea, and after he had composed it he disappeared a second time.

15. That is what those cities tell. But I know that the following happened to the people of Metapontum in Italy two hundred and forty years after Aristeas disappeared the second time, as I worked out by putting together what I learned at Proconnesus and at Metapontum. The people of Metapontum say that Aristeas himself appeared in their country and told them to set up an altar to Apollo, and beside it a statue bearing the name of Aristeas of Proconnesus. He told them that theirs was the only land of all the Greeks in Italy that Apollo had come to, and that he, who was now Aristeas, had come with him; at the time when he went with the god, he had been a raven. After saying this he disappeared. The Metapontines say they sent to Delphi to ask the god what the apparition of the man meant. The Pythia told them to obey the apparition, and said that if they obeyed, it would go better for them. So they accepted this answer and did what they had been told. And there stands a statue bearing the name of Aristeas right beside the altar dedicated to Apollo, with laurel trees standing around it; the altar is set up in the marketplace. So much for Aristeas.

16. As for the land that this part of my account has begun to describe, nobody knows for certain what lies beyond it. I have not been able to hear of anyone who claims to know it as an eyewitness. Even Aristeas, the man I was just talking about, did not claim, even in his poem, that he went farther than the Issedonians. What lies beyond them he described from hearsay, and he said it was the Issedonians who told him these things. But as far as we have been able to reach certain knowledge by hearsay, pushing our inquiries as far as they would go, all of it will be told.

17. Start from the trading post of the Borysthenites, since of all the coast of Scythia this is the midpoint. Starting from there, the first land is held by the Callipidae, who are Greek Scythians. Beyond them is another people, called the Alazones. The Alazones and the Callipidae live like the Scythians in every other way, but they both sow grain and eat it, and also onions, leeks, lentils, and millet. Beyond the Alazones live Scythians who farm, and these sow their grain not to eat but to sell.

18. Beyond them live the Neuri, and beyond the Neuri, toward the north wind, the land is uninhabited, as far as we know. These peoples live along the river Hypanis, the Bug, west of the Dnieper. But once you cross the Dnieper, the first land from the coast is Hylaea. Beyond that, as you go up the river, live farming Scythians. The Greeks who live on the Bug call them Borysthenites, though they call themselves citizens of Olbia. These farming Scythians hold the land that stretches east for three days' journey, as far as a river called the Panticapes, and north for eleven days' sailing up the Dnieper. Right beyond them begins the desert, which runs a long way. On the far side of the desert live the Androphagi, the Man-eaters, a people all their own, with no connection to the Scythians. Beyond them begins land that is truly empty, with no people living in it, as far as we know.

19. East of these farming Scythians, once you cross the river Panticapes, live nomad Scythians, who neither sow anything nor plow the ground. This whole region is bare of trees except for Hylaea. These nomads hold a country that stretches east for fourteen days' journey, as far as the river Gerrhus.

20. On the other side of the Gerrhus are the lands called royal, and the Scythians who are the bravest and most numerous and who regard all the other Scythians as their slaves. These reach south as far as the Tauric land, the Crimea, and east as far as the trench dug by the sons of the blind slaves, and as far as the trading post called Cremni on Lake Maeotis. Some parts of their country reach the river Tanais, the Don. North of the Royal Scythians, toward the north wind, live the Melanchlaeni, the Black Cloaks, a different people and not Scythian. Beyond the Melanchlaeni the land is marshy and empty of people, as far as we know.

21. Once you cross the Don, you are no longer in Scythia. The first of the regions there belongs to the Sauromatae. Starting from the corner of Lake Maeotis, they hold land that stretches north toward the north wind for fifteen days' journey, completely bare of trees, both cultivated and wild. Above them, in the next region, live the Budini, whose land is entirely covered in forest of every kind of tree.

22. North of the Budini there is first desert, seven days' journey across. After the desert, turning somewhat more toward the east, you come to the land of the Thyssagetae, a large people and a separate race from the others. They live by hunting. Next to them, in the same regions, live a people called the Irycae, who also live by hunting, and this is how they do it. The hunter climbs a tree and lies in wait there for his game (there are plenty of trees all through this country). Each man keeps a horse ready, trained to lie down flat on its belly to keep low, and a dog as well. When he spots a wild animal from the tree, he first shoots his arrow, then mounts his horse and chases it, and the dog seizes it. Beyond these, toward the east, live other Scythians, who rebelled against the Royal Scythians and so came to this region.

23. As far as the country of these Scythians, all the land I have described is level plain with deep soil, but from there on it is stony and rough. After you have crossed a long stretch of this rough country, there are people living at the foot of high mountains who are said to be bald from birth, men and women alike. They have flat noses and large chins and speak a language of their own. They dress like Scythians and live on the fruit of trees. The tree whose fruit they live on is called the Pontic tree, and it is about the size of a fig tree. Its fruit is the size of a bean and has a stone in it. When the fruit is ripe, they strain it through cloths, and a thick black juice runs out of it, which is called aschy. They lick this up or drink it mixed with milk, and from the dregs, the solid part, they make cakes and eat them; they do not have many cattle, because the pasture there is not good at all. Each man lives under a tree. In winter he covers the tree all around with thick white felt, and in summer he leaves it uncovered. No one harms these people, because they are said to be sacred, and they own no weapons of war. They are also the ones who settle the quarrels that arise among their neighbors, and besides, any fugitive who takes refuge with them is harmed by no one. They are called the Argippaei.

24. As far as these bald men, there is plenty of clear information about the land and the nations on this side of them. Some Scythians travel to them, and it is not hard to get information from them, and so do some of the Greeks from the trading post on the Dnieper and the other trading posts on the Black Sea coast. The Scythians who go to them do their business through seven interpreters, in seven different languages.

25. As far as these people, then, the land is known. But nobody can say for certain what lies north of the bald men, because high mountains that no one can cross cut it off, and no one goes over them. The bald men do say (though I do not believe it) that the mountains are inhabited by men with goats' feet, and that beyond them are other people who sleep for six months of the year. This I do not accept at all. But the country east of the bald men is known for certain: the Issedonians live there. What lies north of both the bald men and the Issedonians, toward the north wind, is unknown, except for what we know from the reports of these peoples I have just mentioned.

26. The Issedonians are said to have these customs. When a man's father dies, all his relatives bring cattle to the house. They kill the animals and cut up the meat, and they also cut up the dead body of their host's father, mix all the meat together, and serve it as a feast. The skull, however, they strip of flesh, clean out, and cover with gold, and from then on they treat it as a sacred object and offer great sacrifices for the dead man every year. Each son does this for his father, just as the Greeks keep a memorial day for their dead. In other respects this people too is said to live justly, and their women have equal rights with the men.

27. So these people too are known. But as for the region beyond them, it is the Issedonians who report that one-eyed men live there, and griffins that guard the gold. The Scythians repeat this, having heard it from the Issedonians, and we, the rest of mankind, have taken our belief from the Scythians. We call these people by a Scythian name, Arimaspians, because the Scythians call the number one arima, and the eye spu.

28. The whole country I have described has a climate so harsh that for eight months of the year the frost is unbearably hard. During that time, if you pour out water, you will not make mud; you can make mud only by lighting a fire. The sea freezes, and so does the whole Cimmerian Bosporus, so that the Scythians who live inside the trench make expeditions across the ice and drive their wagons over into the country of the Sindians. So it is winter for eight months on end, and even in the other four it is cold there. This winter is different in character from the winters anywhere else in the world. In the season when rain usually falls, it hardly rains at all, while in summer it rains all the time. Thunder does not come when it comes in other countries; it is very frequent in summer, and if there is thunder in winter, people wonder at it as a portent. In the same way, if there is an earthquake in Scythia, in summer or in winter, it is taken as a portent. Horses can endure this winter, but mules and donkeys cannot endure it at all; whereas in other countries horses that stand in the frost get frostbite and lose their limbs to it, while donkeys and mules endure it.

29. I think it is also for this reason that the hornless breed of cattle there grow no horns. There is a line of Homer in the Odyssey that supports my view. It goes:

	"And Libya, where the lambs grow horns so quickly,"

and it is rightly said that in hot places horns grow quickly, while in extreme cold animals grow no horns at all, or hardly any.

30. In Scythia, then, this happens because of the cold. But (since my account has gone looking for side-stories from the start) I am puzzled that in the whole land of Elis no mules can be bred, though the region is not cold and there is no other obvious cause. The Eleans themselves say that mules are not conceived in their country because of a curse. So when the time comes for the mares to conceive, they drive them out into the neighboring lands, and there, in their neighbors' country, they put the male donkeys to them until the mares are pregnant, and then they drive them home again.

31. As for the feathers that the Scythians say fill the air, so that they cannot see or travel through the farther parts of the continent, here is my opinion. In the lands beyond Scythia it snows all the time, though less in summer than in winter, as you would expect. Anyone who has seen thick snow falling close up knows what I mean without further explanation, because snow is like feathers. And because the winter there is as harsh as I have described, the northern parts of this continent are uninhabitable. So I think that when the Scythians and their neighbors talk about feathers, they are speaking figuratively and mean snow. That, then, is as far as the reports go.

32. About a Hyperborean people the Scythians report nothing, and neither do any of the other peoples who live in that region, except perhaps the Issedonians. But in my opinion the Issedonians do not report anything either, because if they did, the Scythians would report it too, as they do about the one-eyed people. Hesiod, however, has spoken of the Hyperboreans, and so has Homer in the poem the Epigoni, at least if Homer really was the author of that epic.

33. But much the most is said about them by the people of Delos. They say that sacred offerings wrapped in wheat straw are carried from the land of the Hyperboreans and come to the Scythians. From the Scythians, each neighboring nation in turn receives them and carries them westward, and they end up as far west as the Adriatic. From there they are sent on south, and the people of Dodona are the first of the Greeks to receive them. From Dodona they come down to the Malian Gulf and are carried across to Euboea, where city passes them on to city as far as Carystus. After that Andros is skipped, because the Carystians carry them to Tenos, and the Tenians carry them to Delos. That, they say, is how these sacred offerings come to Delos. But in the beginning, they say, the Hyperboreans sent two girls to carry the offerings, whose names, according to the Delians, were Hyperoche and Laodice. With them, to protect them, the Hyperboreans sent five men of their own people as an escort, the ones now called the Perpherees, the Bearers, who are greatly honored on Delos. But since the people they had sent out never came back, the Hyperboreans were troubled at the thought that it would always be their lot to send people out and never get them back. So they carried the offerings, wrapped in wheat straw, to the border of their country and charged their neighbors to send them on from there to the next nation. That, they say, is how these things are passed along until they reach Delos. And I know for myself that something similar to these offerings is done: the women of Thrace and Paeonia, when they sacrifice to Artemis the Queen, never make their offerings without wheat straw.

34. These women, I know, do as I have said. And for the Hyperborean girls who died on Delos, the girls and boys of Delos cut their hair. The girls, before their marriage, cut off a lock, wind it around a spindle, and lay it on the tomb (the tomb is on the left as you go into the temple of Artemis, and an olive tree grows over it). All the Delian boys wind some of their hair around a green shoot of some plant and lay it on the tomb as well.

35. That is the honor the people of Delos pay these girls. The same people say that Arge and Opis also came to Delos from the Hyperboreans, passing through the same nations I have named, and that they came even before Hyperoche and Laodice. Hyperoche and Laodice, they say, came bringing Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth, the tribute their people had pledged in return for a quick and easy birth. But Arge and Opis came along with the gods themselves, and the people of Delos have given them honors of a different kind. The women, they say, take up a collection for them and call on them by name in the hymn that Olen, a man from Lycia, composed in their honor. The people of the other islands and the Ionians have learned from the Delians to sing hymns calling on Opis and Arge by name and to take up collections. (This Olen came from Lycia and also composed the other ancient hymns that are sung on Delos.) They say, too, that when the thighbones of the sacrificed animals have been burned on the altar, their ashes are thrown on the grave of Opis and Arge. Their grave is behind the temple of Artemis, facing east, close to the banquet hall of the Ceans.

36. That is enough about the Hyperboreans. I will not tell the story of Abaris, who is said to have been a Hyperborean, and how he carried the arrow all over the earth without eating anything. But if there are Hyperboreans, people beyond the north wind, then there must also be Hypernotians, people beyond the south wind. And I laugh when I see how many people before now have drawn maps of the earth, and not one of them has explained it sensibly. They draw Ocean flowing all around the earth, and the earth perfectly round, as if drawn with a compass, and they make Asia the same size as Europe. In a few words I will show how big each of these divisions is and what shape each one has.

Chapter 22: The Shape of the World, the Rivers of Scythia, and the Customs of the Scythians

37. The Persians live in Asia, and their land reaches down to the Southern Sea, the one called the Erythraean, which is the Indian Ocean. Above them, toward the north wind, live the Medes. Above the Medes live the Saspeirians, and above the Saspeirians the Colchians, whose land reaches to the Northern Sea, the Black Sea, where the river Phasis flows out. These four nations fill the land from sea to sea.

38. From there two peninsulas stretch westward out of Asia into the sea, and I will describe them both. The first peninsula has a northern side and a southern side. On the north it begins at the Phasis and runs along the coast of the Black Sea and the Hellespont, as far as Sigeum in the land of Troy. On the south the same peninsula runs from the Myriandric Gulf, which lies near Phoenicia, toward the sea as far as the headland of Triopium. Thirty different peoples live in this peninsula.

39. That is one of the peninsulas. The other begins from the land of the Persians and stretches along the Erythraean Sea. It takes in Persia, then Assyria next to Persia, and Arabia after Assyria. It ends (or rather, it is commonly supposed to end) at the Red Sea, into which Darius dug a channel from the Nile. Now, along the stretch from the land of the Persians as far as Phoenicia, the land is broad and there is plenty of room. But past Phoenicia this peninsula runs along the shore of our own sea, the Mediterranean, by Palestine, Syria and Egypt, where it ends. Only three nations live in it.

40. Those are the parts of Asia that lie west of the Persian land. As for what lies beyond the Persians, the Medes, the Saspeirians and the Colchians, toward the east and the sunrise, on one side the Erythraean Sea runs along it, and on the north both the Caspian Sea and the river Araxes, which flows toward the rising sun. Asia is inhabited as far as India. But from there on to the east it is desert, and no one can say what sort of land it is.

41. That is the shape and size of Asia. Libya is part of the second peninsula, since Libya begins right where Egypt ends. Around Egypt this peninsula is narrow: from our sea to the Erythraean Sea the distance there is 600,000 feet, which comes to about 115 miles. But past this narrow neck, the part of the peninsula called Libya happens to be extremely broad.

42. So I am surprised at the people who have marked out the world and divided it into Libya, Asia and Europe, because the difference between them is not small. In length Europe stretches along beside both of the others, and in breadth it seems to me far larger than either, beyond all comparison. Libya, for its part, gives proof that it is surrounded by sea, except for the part that borders on Asia. The first person we know of to show this was Necho, king of the Egyptians. When he had stopped digging the canal that runs from the Nile to the Red Sea, he sent out some Phoenicians in ships. He ordered them to sail around and come back through the Pillars of Heracles into the Northern Sea, the Mediterranean, and so home to Egypt. So the Phoenicians set out from the Red Sea and sailed into the Southern Sea. Whenever autumn came, they would put in to shore wherever in Libya they happened to be on their voyage, sow the land, and wait for the harvest. Once they had reaped the grain they sailed on. In this way, after two years had gone by, in the third year they rounded the Pillars of Heracles and came back to Egypt. And they reported something I cannot believe, though someone else may: that as they sailed around Libya they had the sun on their right hand.

43. That is how this country was first found to be what it is. After this it is the Carthaginians who report on it. For Sataspes son of Teaspis, the Achaemenid, did not sail around Libya, though he was sent to do exactly that. The length of the voyage and the emptiness of the land frightened him, so he turned back and never finished the task his mother had set him. Here is how that came about. This man had raped a young unmarried daughter of Zopyrus son of Megabyzus. King Xerxes was about to have him impaled for this crime, when Sataspes' mother, who was a sister of Darius, begged for his life. She said that she herself would lay a heavier penalty on him than Xerxes would: he would be forced, she said, to sail around Libya, until in sailing around it he came to the Red Sea. Xerxes agreed to these terms. So Sataspes went to Egypt, got a ship and sailors from the Egyptians, and sailed to the Pillars of Heracles. He sailed through them, rounded the point of Libya called Cape Soloeis, and sailed on toward the south. He crossed a great deal of sea over many months, but there was always more and more still to sail, so he turned around and sailed back to Egypt. From there he went to King Xerxes and made his report. At the farthest point he reached, he said, he was sailing past a people of very small stature who wore clothes made from the palm tree. Whenever he and his crew came to land with their ship, these people would leave their towns and run away to the mountains. His men, he said, did them no harm when they went into the towns; they only took food. And the reason he had not sailed all the way around Libya, he said, was that the ship could go no farther but was stuck fast. Xerxes did not believe he was telling the truth. Since Sataspes had not done the task he was given, the king had him impaled, carrying out the penalty pronounced before. Sataspes had a eunuch who, as soon as he heard that his master was dead, ran away to Samos with a great deal of money. A man of Samos took that money for himself. I know his name, but I am leaving it out on purpose.

44. Most of Asia was explored by Darius. He wanted to know where the river Indus flows out into the sea. (The Indus is the second of all the rivers in the world that produce crocodiles.) So he sent ships, with men he trusted to tell the truth, and among them was Scylax, a man of Caryanda. They started from the city of Caspatyrus and the land of Pactyice and sailed down the river toward the east and the sunrise until they reached the sea. Then they sailed west across the sea, and in the thirtieth month they came to the very place from which the king of the Egyptians had sent out the Phoenicians I spoke of before, to sail around Libya. After these men had made their voyage along the coast, Darius conquered the Indians and made use of this sea. In this way it has been found that Asia too, except for the parts toward the rising sun, is like Libya, surrounded by water.

45. But as for Europe, no one clearly knows whether it is surrounded by sea, either on the side toward the rising sun or on the north. What is known is that in length it stretches along beside both of the other two. And I cannot understand why the earth, which is one, should have three different names, all of them women's names, or why the boundaries set to divide it should be the Nile, the river of Egypt, and the Phasis in Colchis (or, as some say, the Don, the river of Maeotis, and the Cimmerian Strait). Nor can I find out who the people were who drew these boundaries, or why they gave the names. Most Greeks say that Libya is named after Libya, a woman of that country, and Asia after the wife of Prometheus. But the Lydians claim this last name for themselves. They say Asia was named after Asies son of Cotys son of Manes, and not after Asia the wife of Prometheus, and they say the Asian tribe in Sardis takes its name from him too. As for Europe, no one knows whether it is surrounded by sea, and it is not clear where it got this name or who gave it, unless we say that the land took its name from Europa of Tyre. If so, it would seem that before this it had no name, like the others. But this Europa was plainly from Asia, and she never came to the land the Greeks now call Europe. She went only from Phoenicia to Crete, and from Crete to Lycia. Enough said about these matters; we will go by the accounts that are generally accepted.

46. Now the region of the Black Sea, which Darius was preparing to invade, holds the most ignorant nations of any land, apart from the Scythians. We cannot point to a single nation living around the Black Sea that stands out for its intelligence, nor do we know of any man of learning who has come from there, except the Scythian nation and Anacharsis. The Scythians have worked out the most important thing in all human affairs more cleverly than any other people we know of. In other respects I do not admire them much. But this most important thing they have discovered is this: no one who comes to attack them can escape, and no one can catch them if they do not want to be found. A people that has no towns and no walls, that carries its houses along with it, that fights as mounted archers, that lives not by the plow but by its herds, and whose homes are on wagons: how could such people be anything but unbeatable and impossible to come to grips with?

47. They have found this out because their land is suited to it and their rivers fight on their side. First of all, the land is flat, grassy and well watered. Then there are rivers running through it, not many fewer in number than the canals of Egypt. I will name the ones that are worth mentioning and can be sailed up from the sea. There is the Danube, with five mouths, and after it the Dniester, the Bug, the Dnieper, the Panticapes, the Hypacyris, the Gerrhus and the Don. Here is how they flow.

48. The Danube, the greatest of all the rivers we know, always flows with the same volume, summer and winter alike. It is the first of the Scythian rivers from the west, and it has become the greatest of all rivers because other rivers flow into it. These are the ones that make it great. Five of them flow through the land of Scythia: the one the Scythians call the Porata and the Greeks the Pyretus, and besides that the Tiarantus, the Ararus, the Naparis and the Ordessus. The first of these is a large river lying to the east, and there it joins its waters with the Danube. The second, the Tiarantus, is farther west and smaller. The Ararus, the Naparis and the Ordessus run between these two and flow into the Danube.

49. Those are the native Scythian rivers that swell its stream. From the land of the Agathyrsians the Maris flows in and joins the Danube. From the peaks of Haemus three other large rivers, the Atlas, the Auras and the Tibisis, flow north and fall into it. Through Thrace and the land of the Thracian Crobyzians flow the rivers Athrys, Noes and Artanes, which empty into the Danube. From the Paeonians and Mount Rhodope the river Cius cuts through the middle of Haemus and runs into it as well. From the Illyrians the river Angrus flows north into the Triballian plain and into the river Brongus, and the Brongus flows into the Danube; so the Danube takes in both of them, and they are large rivers. From the region above the Ombricans, the river Carpis and another river, the Alpis, also flow north and run into it. For the Danube in fact flows through the whole of Europe. It begins in the land of the Celts, who, after the Cynesians, live farthest west of all the peoples of Europe. So it flows through all of Europe and empties into the sea along the side of Scythia.

50. So it is because all these rivers I have named, and many others, add their water to it that the Danube becomes the greatest of rivers. If we compare single streams, river against river, the Nile carries more water, since no river or spring flows into the Nile to add to its volume. And the reason the Danube always runs at the same level, summer and winter, is something like this, I think. In winter it is its natural size, or only a little larger than its nature, because that country gets very little rain in winter but has snow all the time. In summer, though, the snow that fell in great quantities during the winter melts and runs into the Danube from every side. This snow runs into the river and helps swell it, and so do many violent rainstorms, since it rains there in summer. So the water that pours into the Danube is greater in summer than in winter by about as much as the water the sun draws up to itself in summer is greater than what it draws up in winter. When these things are set against each other, they balance out, and so the river is always seen at the same volume.

51. So the Danube is one of the Scythians' rivers. After it comes the Dniester, which starts in the north and begins its course from a large lake that forms the boundary between the land of the Scythians and the land of the Neuri. At its mouth live Greeks who are called Tyritae.

52. The third river is the Bug. It starts in Scythia and flows out of a great lake around which white wild horses graze, and this lake is rightly called the Mother of the Bug. This is where the Bug rises, and for five days' sail it runs shallow and still sweet. But from there to the sea, for four days' sail, it is very bitter. That is because the water of a bitter spring flows into it, a spring so extremely bitter that, small as it is, it changes the water of the Bug when it mixes with it, though the Bug is a river few can equal in size. This spring lies on the border between the land of the farming Scythians and that of the Alazones. The spring, and the place it flows from, are called Exampaeus in Scythian, which is in Greek Hierai Hodoi, the Sacred Ways. Now the Dniester and the Bug come close to each other in their windings in the land of the Alazones, but after that each turns away, and they flow on with a widening space between them.

53. The fourth is the Dnieper. It is the largest of these rivers after the Danube, and in my opinion it is the most useful, not only of the Scythian rivers but of all the rivers in the world besides, except the Nile of Egypt, since no other river can be compared with the Nile. Of the rest, though, the Dnieper is the most useful. It provides the finest and richest pastures for cattle, and fish that are far better and more plentiful than in any other river. Its water is the sweetest to drink and runs clear, while the rivers beside it are muddy. Along its banks crops grow better than anywhere else, and where the land is not sown the grass grows deepest. At its mouth, salt forms by itself in great quantities. It also produces huge fish with no spine, which they call antacaei and use for salting, and many other things worth wondering at. As far as the region of the Gerrhi, which is forty days' voyage upstream, the Dnieper is known to flow from the north. Above that no one can say what nations it flows through. It is certain, though, that it runs through empty country down to the land of the farming Scythians, since these Scythians live along its banks for ten days' sail. This river and the Nile are the only two whose sources I cannot tell, and I think no other Greek can either. When the Dnieper comes near the sea, the Bug joins it, running out into the same marsh. The land between these two rivers, which juts out like a ship's beak, is called the Point of Hippoles. A temple of the Mother stands on it, and opposite the temple, on the Bug, live the Borysthenites.

54. So much for these rivers. After them there is a fifth river as well, called the Panticapes. This one too flows from the north and from a lake. The farming Scythians live in the land between this river and the Dnieper. It runs out into the region of Hylaea, and after passing through it, it joins the Dnieper.

55. Sixth comes the river Hypacyris. It starts from a lake, flows through the middle of the nomad Scythians, and runs out into the sea by the city of Carcinitis, skirting on its right bank the region of Hylaea and the place called the Racecourse of Achilles.

56. Seventh is the Gerrhus. It branches off from the Dnieper at about the point in that country where the Dnieper stops being known. It branches off, as I say, in this region, and it has the same name as the region itself, Gerrhus. As it flows to the sea it forms the border between the land of the nomad Scythians and that of the Royal Scythians, and it runs out into the Hypacyris.

57. The eighth is the Don. It starts at first from a large lake and runs out into a still larger lake called Maeotis, which is the boundary between the Royal Scythians and the Sauromatae. Another river, called the Hyrgis, flows into this Don.

58. These are the notable rivers the Scythians are supplied with. As for their cattle, the grass that grows in Scythia produces more bile in them than any other grass we know of, and you can see for yourself that this is so when you cut the cattle open.

59. So they have plenty of the things that matter most. As for the rest, their customs are these. The only gods they worship are these: first and foremost Hestia, then Zeus and Earth (they believe Earth is the wife of Zeus), and after these Apollo, Heavenly Aphrodite, Heracles and Ares. All the Scythians have established worship for these gods, and the ones called the Royal Scythians sacrifice to Poseidon as well. In Scythian, Hestia is called Tabiti; Zeus is called Papaeus, which means Father, and in my opinion that is exactly the right name for him; Earth is Api; Apollo is Oetosyrus; Heavenly Aphrodite is called Argimpasa; and Poseidon is Thagimasadas. It is not their custom to make images, altars or temples for any god except Ares; for him it is their custom to make them.

60. They have one and the same way of sacrificing established for all their rites alike, and it is done like this. The animal stands with its forefeet tied together. The priest who is making the sacrifice stands behind it, pulls the end of the cord, and throws the beast down. As it falls he calls on the god he is sacrificing to. Then at once he throws a noose around its neck, puts a small stick through the noose, and twists it until the animal is strangled. He lights no fire, makes no first offering from the victim, and pours no wine over it. When he has strangled it and skinned it, he sets about boiling it.

61. Since the land of Scythia has very little wood, they have invented this way of boiling the meat. When they have skinned the victims, they strip the flesh off the bones and put it into cauldrons, if they happen to have any. These are made in their own country and look very much like the mixing bowls of Lesbos, except that they are much larger. They put the meat into these and boil it by lighting the victim's bones underneath. If they have no cauldron at hand, they put all the meat into the animals' stomachs, add water, and light the bones underneath. The bones burn beautifully, and the stomachs easily hold the meat once it has been stripped off the bones. So an ox is made to boil itself, and each of the other victims boils itself too. When the meat is cooked, the man making the sacrifice takes a first offering of the meat and of the vital organs and throws it on the ground in front of him. They sacrifice various kinds of livestock, but horses most of all.

62. That is how they sacrifice to the rest of the gods, and those are the animals they use. But to Ares they sacrifice as follows. In each district of each of their provinces they have a temple of Ares, built like this. Bundles of brushwood are heaped up to make a pile about 1,800 feet long and as many wide, but not as high. On top of it a flat square is made. Three of its sides are sheer, but on the fourth side the pile can be climbed. Every year they heap on a hundred and fifty wagonloads of brushwood, because the pile is always settling under the weather. On top of this pile each people has an ancient iron sword set up, and this is the sacred image of Ares. Every year they bring offerings of cattle and horses to this sword, and on top of what they offer the other gods, they make it one more sacrifice besides: of all the enemies they take prisoner in war, they sacrifice one man in every hundred. They do not do it the way they sacrifice cattle, but in a different way. First they pour wine over the men's heads. Then they cut their throats over a bowl, so that the blood runs into it. Then they carry the bowl up to the top of the brushwood pile and pour the blood over the sword. That is what they carry up. Meanwhile, down below beside the temple, they do this: they cut off the right arms of all the slaughtered men, hands and all, and throw them up into the air. Then, when they have finished offering the other victims, they go away. Each arm lies wherever it happened to fall, and the body lies apart from it.

63. Those are the sacrifices established among them. They make no use of pigs, and in fact they will not keep them in their country at all.

64. War is arranged among them like this. When a Scythian kills his first man, he drinks some of his blood. He takes the heads of all the men he kills in battle to the king, because if he brings a head he gets a share of the plunder they have taken, and if not, he gets none. He takes the skin off the head by cutting all the way around it at the ears, then taking hold of the scalp and shaking it loose. After that he scrapes off the flesh with an ox's rib and works the skin with his hands. When he has softened it this way, he keeps it as a napkin to wipe his hands on. He hangs it from the bridle of the horse he rides himself, and he is proud of it, because the man who has the most of these skins to wipe his hands on is judged the bravest. Many of them also make cloaks to wear out of the skins they have taken off, stitching them together like shepherds' leather coats. Many also take the skin, fingernails and all, off the right hands of their dead enemies and make it into covers for their quivers. Human skin, it seems, is thick and glossy, a brighter white than any other skin. And many take the skin off whole bodies, stretch it on wooden frames, and carry it around on their horses.

65. Those are their established customs in these matters. With the skulls themselves (not everyone's, but those of their worst enemies) they do this. The man saws off everything below the eyebrows and cleans out the inside. If he is poor, he just stretches oxhide around the outside and uses it as it is. If he is rich, he stretches oxhide around it and also gilds the inside, and uses it as a drinking cup. They do this with their own relatives as well, if one of them has quarreled with a man and the man has beaten him in a trial before the king. When guests he thinks highly of come to visit, he brings out these skulls and tells them how these men, though they were his own family, made war on him, and how he beat them. They count this as proof of a man's courage.

66. Once a year each governor of a district mixes a bowl of wine in his own district, and the Scythians who have killed enemies drink from it. Those who have not done this do not taste the wine, but sit apart in disgrace, and this is the greatest shame there is among them. But those who have killed a great many men drink from two cups together at the same time.

67. There are many soothsayers among the Scythians, and they tell the future with a lot of willow rods, in this way. They bring large bundles of rods, lay them on the ground and untie them. Then they set out each rod separately and make their prophecies. While they are speaking, they gather the rods together again, and then lay them out one by one a second time. This way of divining has come down to them from their fathers. But the Enarees, the "man-women," say that Aphrodite gave them the gift of prophecy, and they divine with the bark of the linden tree. The man splits the linden bark into three strips, braids them together in his fingers and unbraids them again, and as he does this he speaks the oracle.

68. When the king of the Scythians falls ill, he sends for the three soothsayers with the best reputation, who divine in the way I have described. What they usually say is something like this: that so-and-so has sworn falsely by the king's hearth. And they name one of the citizens, whoever it happens to be. (It is the Scythians' general custom to swear by the king's hearth when they want to take their most solemn oath.) The man they say has sworn falsely is seized at once and brought in, held on both sides. When he arrives, the soothsayers accuse him: their divination shows, they say, that he has sworn falsely by the king's hearth, and that this is why the king is in pain. He denies it, insists he did not swear falsely, and protests in outrage. When he denies it, the king sends for twice as many other soothsayers. If these too look into their divination and find him guilty of false swearing, they cut off his head at once, and the first soothsayers divide his property among themselves by lot. But if the soothsayers who came in second acquit him, more soothsayers come in, and then more after them. If most of them acquit the man, the sentence is that the first soothsayers must be put to death themselves.

69. They put them to death in this way. First they fill a wagon with brushwood and yoke oxen to it. Then they tie the soothsayers' feet, bind their hands behind them, gag their mouths, and fasten them down in the middle of the brushwood. Then they set it on fire, frighten the oxen, and let them go. Often the oxen are burned to death along with the soothsayers. Often, too, they get away singed, once the pole they are yoked to has burned through. They burn soothsayers in this way for other reasons as well, calling them false prophets. And when the king puts anyone to death, he does not leave their sons alive either. He kills all the males, but does no harm to the females.

70. When the Scythians swear an oath to anyone, they do it like this. They pour wine into a large earthenware cup and mix into it blood from the men who are swearing to each other, taking it either by pricking themselves with an awl or by making a small cut in their bodies with a dagger. Then they dip a sword, arrows, a battle-axe and a javelin into the cup. When they have done this, they call down many curses on whoever breaks the oath, and then they drink it, both the men making the oath and the most respected of their followers.

71. The kings are buried in the land of the Gerrhi, at the point up to which the Dnieper can be navigated. There, when their king dies, they dig a large square pit in the ground. When they have it ready, they take up the body. It has been coated all over with wax, and its belly has been slit open, cleaned out, filled with chopped galingale, spices, parsley seed and anise, and sewn up again. They carry it on a wagon to another nation. The people who receive the body when it is brought to them do the same as the Royal Scythians: they cut off part of an ear, shave their heads all around, cut their arms all over, gash their foreheads and noses, and drive arrows through their left hands. From there they carry the king's body on the wagon to another of the nations they rule, and the people they visited before go along with them. When they have carried the body around to all of them, they are in the land of the Gerrhi, who live farthest away of all the nations they rule, and they have reached the place of burial. Then they lay the body in the tomb on a bed of leaves, plant spears on either side of it, lay pieces of wood across them, and roof the place over with matting. In the rest of the space in the tomb they strangle and bury one of the king's concubines, his cupbearer, his cook, his groom, his personal servant and his messenger, and also horses, and first portions of everything else, and gold cups; they use no silver at all, and no bronze either. When they have done this, they all work together to heap up a great mound, competing with one another and striving hard to make it as large as possible.

72. Then, when the year comes around again, they do this. They take the most capable of the king's remaining servants. These are native Scythians, since the king is served by whomever he himself orders to serve him; his servants are not bought with money. Of these attendants they strangle fifty, and also fifty of the finest horses. They take out their guts, clean out the belly, fill it with chaff and sew it up again. Then they fix half of a wheel, hollow side up, on two stakes, and the other half of the wheel on two other stakes, and they set up a number of these in this way. After that they run thick poles through the horses lengthwise, up to the neck, and mount them on the half-wheels. The front half-wheels hold up the horses' shoulders, and the back ones support their bellies near the thighs, and both the front and back legs hang in the air. They put bridles and bits on the horses, pull the reins tight in front of them, and tie them to pegs. Then they take each of the fifty strangled young men and mount him on his horse. To do this they first run a straight stake through each body along the spine up to the neck. Part of this stake sticks out at the bottom, and they fix it into a socket in the other pole, the one that runs through the horse. When they have set horsemen like these in a circle around the tomb, they ride away.

73. That is how they bury their kings. As for the other Scythians, when they die their nearest relatives lay them in wagons and carry them around to their friends one after another. Each friend, when he receives the body, gives a feast for the people who come with it, and serves the dead man about the same amount of every dish as he serves the others. Ordinary people are carried around like this for forty days, and then they are buried. After the burial the Scythians purify themselves in this way. They soap their heads and wash them well. Then, for their bodies, they set up three poles leaning toward one another and stretch woolen felt blankets around them. When they have closed these up as tightly as they can, they throw red-hot stones into a basin set in the middle, among the poles and the felt blankets.

74. Now, hemp grows in their country. It is very much like flax, except in thickness and height, and in these the hemp is far greater. It grows both wild and under cultivation. The Thracians even make clothes out of it, very much like linen ones, so that anyone who did not know it well could not tell whether the clothes were made of flax or of hemp. And someone who had never seen hemp cloth before would think the garment was made of flax.

75. The Scythians take the seed of this hemp, creep in under the felt blankets, and throw the seed onto the red-hot stones. It smolders like incense and gives off so thick a vapor that no steam bath in Greece could beat it. The Scythians are delighted with this steam bath and howl like wolves. It takes the place of washing for them, since in fact they never wash their bodies in water at all. Their women, though, grind cypress, cedar and frankincense wood on a rough stone, adding water as they grind, and they plaster this thick paste all over their bodies and faces. This not only makes them smell sweet, but when they take the plaster off the next day, their skin is clean and shining.

Chapter 23: Anacharsis and Scyles, Darius Marches on Scythia, and the Amazons

76. This nation, too, is strongly against adopting foreign customs. They reject even those of other tribes among themselves, but above all those of the Greeks, as the story of Anacharsis, and later of Scyles, proved. First, Anacharsis. He had traveled to many lands and shown great wisdom in them, and he was on his way back to the Scythians' country. As he sailed through the Hellespont he put in at Cyzicus, and there he found the people of Cyzicus celebrating a festival in honor of the Mother of the gods with great splendor. So Anacharsis made a vow to the Mother: if he got home to his own land safe and sound, he would sacrifice to her with the same rites he saw the people of Cyzicus using, and he would also hold an all-night festival for her. When he reached Scythia, he went down into the region called Hylaea. (It lies alongside the Racecourse of Achilles, and it happens to be full of trees of every kind.) Into this woodland Anacharsis went down, and there he performed the whole ceremony of the goddess' festival, with a drum, and with little images hung all over himself. But one of the Scythians saw him doing it and reported it to Saulius the king. The king came himself, and when he saw Anacharsis doing this, he shot him with an arrow and killed him. And so today, if you ask about Anacharsis, the Scythians say they do not know him, and the reason is that he went abroad to Greece and took up foreign customs. As I heard from Tymnes, the steward of Ariapeithes, Anacharsis was the uncle, on the father's side, of Idanthyrsus king of the Scythians, and he was the son of Gnurus, the son of Lycus, the son of Spargapeithes. If Anacharsis really was of this family, then let it be known that he died at the hand of his own brother. For Idanthyrsus was the son of Saulius, and Saulius was the man who killed Anacharsis.

77. I have heard another story too, told by the Peloponnesians. They say that Anacharsis was sent out by the king of the Scythians and became a student of Greece. When he came back, they say, he told the king who had sent him that all the Greeks were busy with every kind of cleverness except the Spartans, but that the Spartans alone knew how to talk sensibly with one another. But this story is a groundless invention of the Greeks themselves. Whatever the truth of it, the man was killed in the way I described above.

78. That is how badly Anacharsis fared because of foreign customs and his dealings with Greeks. And many years later Scyles the son of Ariapeithes met almost the same fate. Ariapeithes king of the Scythians had other sons, and Scyles was one of them. He was born of a woman from Istria, a Greek city on the coast, and certainly not a native of Scythia, and his mother taught him the Greek language and Greek letters. Some time later Ariapeithes was killed by treachery at the hands of Spargapeithes, king of the Agathyrsi, and Scyles succeeded to the throne. He took over not only the kingdom but also his father's wife, whose name was Opoea. This Opoea was a native Scythian, and she had borne Ariapeithes a son named Oricus. Now when Scyles was king of the Scythians, he was not at all satisfied with the Scythian way of life. Because of the way he had been brought up, he leaned much more toward Greek ways, and this is what he used to do. Whenever he came with his Scythian troops to the city of the Borysthenites (these Borysthenites say they are colonists from Miletus), he would leave his band in the outskirts, go inside the walls himself, and have the gates shut. Then he would take off his Scythian gear and put on Greek clothes. Dressed like that, he would walk about the marketplace with no bodyguard and nobody else with him. Meanwhile people kept watch on the gates, so that no Scythian would see him in this dress. He lived like a Greek in other ways too, and he worshiped the gods according to Greek custom. After staying a month or more, he would put on his Scythian clothes again and leave. He did this many times. He even built himself a house in Borysthenes and took a local woman there as his wife.

79. But since it was fated that things would go badly for him, it came about in this way. He conceived a desire to be initiated into the rites of Dionysus as Bacchus, and just as he was about to be initiated, a very great portent happened. He had a house in the city of the Borysthenites, the one I mentioned a little earlier, very large and built at great expense, with sphinxes and griffins of white stone set all around it. Zeus struck this house with a thunderbolt, and it burned to the ground. All the same, Scyles went through with his initiation. Now the Scythians hold these Bacchic rites against the Greeks. They say it is not right to make up a god like this, who drives people mad. So when Scyles had been initiated into the rites of Bacchus, one of the Borysthenites went off to the Scythians and said: "You laugh at us, Scythians, because we perform the Bacchic rites and the god takes hold of us. Well, now this god has taken hold of your own king too. He is joining in the Bacchic rites, and the god is driving him mad. If you don't believe me, follow me and I will show you." The leading men of the Scythians followed him, and the Borysthenite brought them secretly into the town and placed them on a tower. So when Scyles went by with his band of revelers and the Scythians saw him taking part in the Bacchic rites, they were deeply upset. They went out and told the whole army what they had seen.

80. After this, when Scyles rode back home, the Scythians rose up against him and set up his brother Octamasades as their leader. Octamasades was the son of the daughter of Teres. When Scyles saw what was being done against him, and why, he fled to Thrace for refuge. Octamasades heard of it and marched against Thrace. When he reached the Danube, the Thracians met him. They were about to join battle when Sitalces sent a messenger to Octamasades with this message: "Why should we test each other in a fight? You are my sister's son, and you have my brother in your hands. Give him back to me, and I will hand over your brother Scyles to you. Let neither of us put our armies at risk, neither you nor I." That was the offer Sitalces sent him by a herald, because a brother of Sitalces was with Octamasades, having fled into exile out of fear of him. Octamasades agreed. He handed over his own uncle, his mother's brother, to Sitalces, and received his brother Scyles in exchange. Sitalces took his brother and led him away a prisoner, but Octamasades cut off Scyles' head right there on the spot. That is how carefully the Scythians guard their own customs, and those are the penalties they inflict on anyone who takes up foreign ones besides their own.

81. How many Scythians there are I could not find out exactly. I heard different reports of their number: some say they are very many, others that they are few, at least as far as the true Scythians go. But this much they showed me with my own eyes. Between the rivers Dnieper and Bug there is a place called Exampaeus, which I mentioned a little earlier when I said there was a spring of bitter water in it, whose water flows out and makes the Bug undrinkable. In this place stands a bronze bowl at least six times the size of the mixing bowl at the mouth of the Black Sea, the one dedicated by Pausanias the son of Cleombrotus. For anyone who has never seen that one, I will make it clear this way: the bowl in Scythia easily holds six hundred amphoras, about 6,000 gallons, and this Scythian bowl is six finger-widths thick, about four and a half inches. The people of the place told me it had been made from arrowheads. Their king, they said, whose name was Ariantas, wanted to know how many Scythians there were. So he ordered every Scythian to bring him one arrowhead, each from his own arrow, and he threatened death to anyone who did not bring one. A huge pile of arrowheads was brought in, and he decided to make a memorial out of them and leave it behind him. So, they said, he made this bronze bowl out of them and dedicated it here at Exampaeus.

82. That is what I heard about the number of the Scythians. This land has no marvels, except that its rivers are by far the largest and the most numerous of any land. But there is one thing worth mentioning that it has to show, which is worth wondering at besides the rivers and the vastness of the plain. They point out a footprint of Heracles in the rock by the bank of the river Dniester. It is shaped like the print of a man's foot, but it is three feet long. So much for that. Now I will go back to the story I set out to tell at the beginning.

83. Darius was preparing to march against the Scythians. He was sending messengers out with orders: some peoples were to supply a land army, others ships, and others were to bridge the Thracian Bosporus. Meanwhile Artabanus son of Hystaspes, Darius' brother, begged him not to make the expedition against the Scythians at all, telling him how hard the Scythians were to deal with. But though his advice was good, he did not persuade him, and he stopped urging it. When all his preparations were made, Darius began to march his army out of Susa.

84. Then one of the Persians, Oeobazus, who had three sons all serving in the expedition, asked Darius to leave one of them behind for him. Darius answered that since he was a friend and his request was a reasonable one, he would leave all of them behind. Oeobazus was overjoyed, thinking his sons had been released from service. But Darius ordered the officers in charge of such things to put all the sons of Oeobazus to death.

85. So they were left behind, killed on the spot where they stood. Meanwhile Darius set out from Susa and reached the place on the Bosporus, in the territory of Chalcedon, where the bridge of boats had been built. There he went aboard a ship and sailed to the so-called Cyanean Rocks, which the Greeks say once moved back and forth. He sat down at the temple there and gazed out at the Black Sea, which is well worth seeing. Of all seas it is the most marvelous by nature. It is about 1,230 miles long, and about 370 miles wide at its widest point. The mouth of this great sea is only about half a mile across. The length of the mouth, that is, of the neck of water called the Bosporus, where, as I said, the bridge of boats had been built, is no less than about thirteen miles. The Bosporus runs into the Propontis, the Sea of Marmara. The Propontis is about fifty-five miles wide and about 155 miles long, and it empties into the Hellespont, which is less than a mile wide at its narrowest point, though it is about forty-four miles long. The Hellespont runs out into the open stretch of sea called the Aegean.

86. I worked out these measurements as follows. On average a ship covers about 78 miles in a long day and about 67 miles in a night. Now we know that from the mouth of the sea to the river Phasis (which is where the Black Sea is longest) is a voyage of nine days and eight nights. That comes to about 1,230 miles. Then from the land of the Sindians to Themiscyra on the river Thermodon (which is where the Black Sea is widest) is a voyage of three days and two nights, which comes to about 370 miles. That is how I have measured this sea, the Bosporus and the Hellespont, and they are as I have described them. The Black Sea also has a lake that empties into it, not much smaller than the sea itself. It is called Maeotis, and also the "Mother of the Black Sea."

87. After gazing at the Black Sea, Darius sailed back to the bridge, whose chief builder was Mandrocles of Samos. He gazed at the Bosporus too, and then he set up two pillars of white stone beside it, carved with writing, one in Assyrian letters and the other in Greek. They listed all the nations he was leading with him, and he was leading every nation he ruled. Not counting the fleet, the whole army was reckoned at 700,000 men, cavalry included, and six hundred ships had been gathered. Some time after the events I am describing, the people of Byzantium carried these pillars off to their city and used them for the altar of Artemis Orthosia, except for one stone covered with Assyrian writing, which was left standing beside the temple of Dionysus in Byzantium. The place on the Bosporus where Darius built his bridge is, by my reckoning, halfway between Byzantium and the temple at the mouth of the Black Sea.

88. After this Darius, pleased with his floating bridge, rewarded its chief builder, Mandrocles of Samos, with gifts tenfold. From these gifts Mandrocles paid for a painting as an offering, showing the whole scene: the bridge over the Bosporus, King Darius sitting in a seat of honor, and his army crossing. He had this painted and dedicated it in the temple of Hera, with this inscription:

	He bridged the Bosporus and its waters thick with fish, and to Hera
	Mandrocles gives this as a record of his work.
	He set a crown on his own head and won the Samians glory,
	and he did everything for Darius just as he wished.

89. That was the memorial left by the man who built the bridge. And Darius, after rewarding Mandrocles with gifts, crossed over into Europe. Before crossing, he ordered the Ionians to sail into the Black Sea as far as the Danube, and when they reached the Danube to wait for him there, building a bridge over the river in the meantime. For the leading part of his fleet was made up of Ionians, Aeolians and men of the Hellespont. So the fleet sailed through between the Cyanean Rocks and headed straight for the Danube. They sailed up the river two days' voyage from the sea and began to build a bridge across its neck, so to speak, where the mouths of the Danube branch off. Darius, meanwhile, crossed the Bosporus on the floating bridge and marched through Thrace. When he came to the sources of the river Tearus, he camped there for three days.

90. The people who live near the Tearus say it is the best of all rivers for healing in general, and especially for curing skin diseases in both men and horses. It has thirty-eight springs, all flowing from the same rock, some of them cold and some warm. The way to them is the same length from the city of Heraeum near Perinthus and from Apollonia on the Black Sea: two days' journey by either road. This Tearus runs into the river Contadesdus, the Contadesdus into the Agrianes, and the Agrianes into the Hebrus, which flows into the sea by the city of Aenus.

91. So Darius came to this river and camped there. He was so pleased with it that he set up a pillar there too, with this inscription: "The headwaters of the river Tearus give the best and finest water of all rivers. To them came, leading an army against the Scythians, the best and finest of all men, Darius son of Hystaspes, king of the Persians and of the whole continent." Those were the words written there.

92. Darius set out from there and came to another river, called the Artescus, which flows through the land of the Odrysians. When he reached this river he did this: he marked out a spot for his army and ordered every man to put one stone on that spot as he went past it. When the army had done this, he marched it on, leaving great piles of stones behind.

93. But before he reached the Danube, the first people he conquered were the Getae, who believe they are immortal. The Thracians who hold Salmydessus and live inland from the cities of Apollonia and Mesambria, the ones called the Cyrmianae and the Nipsaei, surrendered to Darius without a fight. But the Getae, who are the bravest and most law-abiding of all the Thracians, stubbornly resisted, and they were conquered at once.

94. This is their belief about immortality. They hold that they do not die, but that anyone who dies goes to Salmoxis, a divine being, whom some of them call Gebeleizis.
