Every four years they choose one of their own by lot and send him as a messenger to Salmoxis, with instructions about whatever they want to ask for at the time. This is how they send him. Some of them, appointed for the job, stand holding three javelins. Others take the man who is being sent to Salmoxis by his hands and feet, swing him up, and throw him into the air so that he falls on the spear points. If he is pierced through and dies, they think the god is favorable to them. If he does not die, they blame the messenger himself, saying he is a worthless man, and after blaming him they send another. They give him his instructions beforehand, while he is still alive. These same Thracians also shoot arrows up at the sky when there is thunder and lightning, threatening the god, since they do not believe there is any god but their own.

95. I hear from the Greeks who live around the Hellespont and the Black Sea that this Salmoxis was a man, and that he was a slave on Samos; in fact he was the slave of Pythagoras the son of Mnesarchus. Then, they say, he was freed and made a great deal of money, and afterward he went back to his own country. The Thracians lived a hard life and were rather simple-minded. But this Salmoxis knew the Ionian way of life and manners more refined than the Thracians were used to, since he had spent time among Greeks, and not just any Greek but Pythagoras, by no means the least of the Greek philosophers. So he built a banquet hall, where he entertained and feasted the leading men of his people, and taught them as he did so that neither he nor his guests nor their descendants after them would ever die. Instead, he said, they would go to a place where they would live forever and have every good thing. While he was doing what I have described and saying these things, he was also building himself a chamber underground. When the chamber was finished, he vanished from among the Thracians, went down into it, and lived there for three years. The Thracians missed him and mourned for him as if he were dead. Then in the fourth year he appeared to them again, and that is how they came to believe what Salmoxis had told them.

96. That is what they say he did. As for this business of the underground chamber, I neither disbelieve it nor believe it very strongly. But I think this Salmoxis lived many years before Pythagoras. In any case, whether there was ever a man called Salmoxis or whether he is simply a native god of the Getae, let us say goodbye to him now.

97. These Getae, with the customs I have described, were conquered by the Persians and marched on with the rest of the army. When Darius and his land army reached the Danube and everyone had crossed, Darius ordered the Ionians to break up the floating bridge and to follow him overland, together with the rest of the troops from the ships. The Ionians were about to break it up and do as he ordered when Coes son of Erxander, the commander of the men of Mytilene, spoke to Darius, after first asking whether he would be willing to hear an opinion from someone who wanted to give one. "My king," he said, "you are about to march into a land where you will see no farmland and no inhabited town. So let this bridge stand where it is, and leave the men who built it to guard it. Then if we find the Scythians and things go the way we want, we have a way back. And even if we cannot find them, at least our way back is safe. I have never yet been afraid that the Scythians would beat us in battle. What I fear is that we may not be able to find them, and may come to some disaster wandering around. Perhaps someone will say I am saying this for my own good, so that I can stay behind. But in truth, my king, I am offering you the opinion I think best for you, and I myself will go with you and will not be left behind." Darius was very pleased with this advice and answered him: "My friend from Lesbos, when I have come home safely to my palace, be sure to come and see me, so that I can repay your good advice with good deeds."

98. When he had said this, he tied sixty knots in a leather strap, called the Ionian tyrants to a meeting and said: "Men of Ionia, I have given up the opinion I gave you earlier about the bridge. Take this strap and do as I tell you. From the moment you see me set out against the Scythians, begin untying one knot each day. If I am not back within that time, and you find that the days counted by the knots have run out, sail home to your own lands. Until then, since we have changed our plan, guard the floating bridge, and do everything you can to keep it safe and protect it. If you do this, you will be doing me a very great service." That is what Darius said, and he hurried on his march.

99. Now Thrace lies out in front of Scythia toward the sea. Where a bay is formed in this land, Scythia begins, and the Danube flows out into the sea there, its mouth facing southeast. Starting from the Danube, I will now describe the coastline of Scythia proper and give its measurements. Right at the Danube begins the old land of Scythia, which faces south toward midday and the south wind and stretches as far as the city called Carcinitis. Beyond this, the land along the coast of the same sea, a mountainous country that juts out into the Black Sea, is held by the Tauric people as far as the peninsula called the Rugged Chersonese, and this reaches to the sea that lies to the east. For two sides of Scythia's borders run along the sea, one along the sea to the south and the other along the sea to the east, just as with Attica. In fact the Tauri hold a part of Scythia much like a part of Attica. It is as if, in Attica, some other people and not the Athenians held the hill country of Sunium, if you imagine that it juts farther out into the sea at the point: the region, that is, cut off by a line from Thoricus to Anaphlystus. That, if I may compare small things with great, is the shape of the Tauric land. But for anyone who has not sailed along that part of the coast of Attica, I will make it clear with another comparison. It is as if, in Iapygia, some other people and not the Iapygians had cut off and held the tip of the land bounded by a line from the harbor of Brentesium, Brindisi, to Taras. In naming these two similar cases, I am suggesting many others that the Tauric land resembles too.

100. Right after the Tauric land come Scythians again. They hold the country above the Tauri and the coast of the eastern sea, that is, the land west of the Cimmerian Bosporus and of Lake Maeotis, as far as the river Don, which runs into the corner of this lake. On its inland side, as we know, Scythia is bounded first by the Agathyrsi, starting from the Danube, then by the Neuri, then by the Androphagi, and last by the Melanchlaeni.

101. So Scythia can be thought of as a square, with two of its sides along the sea, and its boundaries are the same length in each direction, the one running inland and the one running along the sea. From the Danube to the Dnieper is ten days' journey, and from the Dnieper to Lake Maeotis is ten days more. And the distance inland to the Melanchlaeni, who live beyond the Scythians, is a journey of twenty days. I have reckoned a day's journey at about twenty-two miles. By this reckoning the sides of Scythia that run across would be about 440 miles long, and the sides that run inland would be the same. That is the size of this land.

102. The Scythians, meanwhile, reasoned that they could not drive off Darius' army on their own in a pitched battle, so they sent messengers to their neighbors. The kings of these nations had already met and were holding a council together, since so great an army was marching against them. The kings who had come together were those of the Tauri, the Agathyrsi, the Neuri, the Androphagi, the Melanchlaeni, the Gelonians, the Budini and the Sauromatae.

103. Of these, the Tauri have the following customs. They sacrifice to the Maiden both shipwrecked sailors and any Greeks they can capture by putting out to sea against them. This is how they sacrifice them. After the opening rites over the victim, they strike him on the head with a club. Some say they then push the body off the top of the cliff (for the temple stands on a cliff) and set the head up on a stake. Others agree about the heads but say that the body is not pushed off the cliff but buried in the ground. The Tauri themselves say that this goddess they sacrifice to is Iphigenia the daughter of Agamemnon. With enemies they have defeated, they do this: each man cuts off a head and carries it home, then sticks it on a long pole and sets it up high above his house, usually above the chimney. These heads hung up there, they say, are guards that protect the whole household. This people lives by plunder and war.

104. The Agathyrsi live in great luxury and wear gold ornaments most of the time. They also have their women in common, so that they may all be brothers, and since they are all close kin, they feel no envy or ill will toward one another. In their other customs they have come to resemble the Thracians.

105. The Neuri follow Scythian customs. One generation before Darius' expedition, it happened that they were forced to leave their land entirely because of snakes. Their own land produced huge numbers of snakes, and even more came down on them from the desert country beyond their borders, until at last, hard pressed, they left their land and settled among the Budini. These people may be sorcerers. For the Scythians, and the Greeks who live in Scythia, say that once every year each of the Neuri turns into a wolf for a few days and then turns back into his own shape. For my part, I do not believe them when they say this, but they say it all the same, and they swear to it too.

106. The Androphagi have the most savage ways of any people on earth. They recognize no justice and keep no law. They are nomads and dress like the Scythians, but they have a language of their own, and alone of all these nations they eat human flesh.

107. The Melanchlaeni all wear black clothes, which is where their name, the Black Cloaks, comes from. They follow Scythian customs.

108. The Budini are a great and numerous people, and they all have very blue eyes and fair skin. In their land there is a city built of wood, called Gelonus. Each side of its wall is about three and a third miles long, and the wall is high and all of wood. Their houses are wooden too, and so are their temples. For there are temples of Greek gods there, furnished in the Greek way with sacred images, altars and shrines, all of wood. Every other year they hold a festival for Dionysus and celebrate his Bacchic rites. That is because the Gelonians were originally Greeks. They moved away from the trading posts on the coast and settled among the Budini, and their language is partly Scythian and partly Greek. But the Budini do not speak the same language as the Gelonians, and their way of life is different.

109. The Budini are native to the land and nomads, and alone of the peoples in this region they eat pine cones. The Gelonians farm the land, eat grain and have gardens, and are nothing like the Budini in looks or in coloring. The Greeks, however, call the Budini Gelonians too, which is not right. Their whole land is thickly covered with forests of every kind of tree. In the thickest forest there is a large, deep lake, surrounded by marshland and reeds. Otters are caught in it, and beavers, and other wild animals with square faces. Their fur is sewn as a trim around the edges of the people's leather coats, and their testicles are used as a remedy for diseases of the womb.

110. About the Sauromatae, this story is told. When the Greeks fought against the Amazons, the warrior women of legend (the Scythians call the Amazons Oeorpata, which in Greek means "man-killers," for "oior" is their word for "man" and "pata" means "to kill"), then, as the story goes, the Greeks won the battle at the river Thermodon and sailed away, carrying off in three ships as many Amazons as they had been able to take prisoner. Out at sea the Amazons attacked the men and threw them overboard. But they knew nothing about ships, or how to use a rudder or sails or oars. So after throwing the men overboard they were driven along by wind and wave, and they came to the place on Lake Maeotis where Cremni stands. Cremni is in the land of the free Scythians. There the Amazons got off their ships and made their way inland. The first thing they came across was a herd of horses grazing. They seized them, and mounted on these horses they raided the Scythians' property.

111. The Scythians could not make sense of it. They did not know the raiders' language or their dress or what people they belonged to, and they wondered where they had come from. They took them for men, all of about the same young age they appeared to be, and in the end they fought a battle with them. After the battle the Scythians took possession of the bodies of the dead, and that is how they found out they were women. So they held a council and decided not to go on trying to kill them at all, but to send out their youngest men against them, guessing at their number so as to send just as many men as there were women. These young men were told to camp near the women and to do whatever they did. If the women came after them, they were not to fight but to fall back, and when the women stopped, they were to come close and camp near them again. The Scythians adopted this plan because they wanted to have children by them.

112. So the young men were sent out and did as they had been told. When the Amazons saw that they had not come to do them any harm, they left them alone. Every day the two camps moved closer together. The young men, like the Amazons, had nothing but their weapons and their horses, and they made their living, just as the Amazons did, by hunting and raiding.

113. At midday the Amazons used to scatter, one at a time or two together, going off some distance from each other to relieve themselves. The Scythians noticed this and did the same. One of the Scythians came up to one of these Amazons who was off on her own, and she did not push him away but let him have sex with her. She could not speak to him, since they did not understand each other's language. But she made signs with her hand for him to come the next day to the same place and bring another man with him, signaling that there should be two of them and that she would bring another woman with her. When the young man got back, he told the others. The next day he came to the place himself and brought another man with him, and he found the Amazon waiting with another woman. When the rest of the young men heard about this, they won over the rest of the Amazons for themselves in the same way.

114. After this they joined their camps and lived together, each man keeping as his wife the woman he had first been with. The men could not learn the women's language, but the women picked up the men's. When they understood each other, the men said this to the Amazons: "We have parents and we have property. So let us not live this kind of life any longer. Let us go back to the main body of our people and live with them. We will have you as our wives, and no others." But the women answered: "We could not live with your women, because our customs and theirs are not the same. We shoot with bows, throw javelins and ride horses, but we never learned women's work. Your women do none of the things we have mentioned. They stay in the wagons and do women's work, and never go out hunting or anywhere else. So we could not get along with them. But if you want to keep us as your wives and be thought honorable men, go to your parents and get your share of their property, and then let us go off and live by ourselves."

115. The young men agreed and did this. When they had got the share of property that was theirs and come back to the Amazons, the women said to them: "We are full of fear and dread at the thought of living in this place. We have separated you from your fathers, and we have done great damage to your land. Since you think it right to have us as your wives, do this with us: come, let us leave this land, cross the river Don and live there."

116. The young men agreed to this too. They crossed the Don and traveled east, toward the rising sun, for three days' journey from the Don, and north, toward the north wind, for three days' journey from Lake Maeotis. When they reached the place where they live now, they settled there. And ever since, the women of the Sauromatae have kept their old way of life. They go out hunting on horseback, both with the men and without them; they go to war; and they wear the same clothes as the men.

117. The Sauromatae speak the Scythian language, but they have spoken it badly from the start, because the Amazons never learned it properly. Their rule about marriage is this: no girl may marry until she has killed a man of the enemy. Some of them grow old and die unmarried, because they cannot fulfill the law.

Chapter 24: The War in the Empty Land, the Scythian Riddle, and the Bridge on the Danube

118. These, then, are the nations I have listed in order, and it was to their kings that the Scythians' messengers came. They found them gathered together in one place, and told them what was happening. The Persian king, they said, had already brought everything in the other continent under his power. He had laid a bridge across the narrow neck of the Bosporus and crossed over to this continent, and once across he had conquered the Thracians. Now he was building a bridge over the Danube, because he wanted to bring all these lands under his power as well. "So whatever you do," they said, "don't stand aside and let us be destroyed. Let's all be of one mind and stand together against the man who is coming at us. If you won't do this, we will be forced by necessity either to leave our land, or to stay in it and come to terms with the invader. What else can we do, if you refuse to help us? And after that, things will be no easier for you. The Persian has come against you just as much as against us, and once he has conquered us he won't be content to leave you alone. We can give you strong proof that what we say is true. If the Persian were making this expedition against us alone, because he wanted revenge for the time when his people were our subjects, he would have left everyone else alone and come straight to invade our land. That way he would have made it clear to all that he was marching against the Scythians and not against anyone else. But in fact, ever since he crossed over to this continent, he has forced everyone in his path to submit to him. He already holds the rest of the Thracians, and the Getae too, who are our nearest neighbors."

119. When the Scythians made this proposal, the kings who had come from the various nations talked it over, and their opinions were divided. The kings of the Gelonians, the Budini and the Sauromatae agreed with one another and accepted the proposal: they would help the Scythians. But the kings of the Agathyrsians, the Neuri, the Androphagi, the Melanchlaeni and the Tauri gave the Scythians this answer: "If you had not been the first to wrong the Persians and to start the war, then we would certainly think you were in the right to ask for what you are asking now. We would have agreed to your request and shared your fortunes. As it is, though, you invaded their land without us, and you ruled over the Persians for as long as heaven allowed you to. Now they, stirred up by the same heaven, are paying you back in kind. As for us, we did these men no wrong back then, and we will not start wronging them now, unprovoked. If the Persians come against our land too, and wrong us first, then we too will refuse to submit. But until we see that happen, we will stay where we are. In our opinion the Persians have not come against us at all, but against the people who started the wrong."

120. When this answer was reported to the Scythians, they decided not to fight an open, pitched battle, since these nations would not join them as allies. Instead they would fall back before the Persians and drive their cattle away ahead of them. As they went, they would choke up the wells and springs they passed with earth and destroy the grass on the ground. For this they split themselves into two bodies. They decided that the Sauromatae should be added to one of their divisions, the one Scopasis was king of. If the Persians turned in their direction, this force was to move straight toward the river Don, retreating before the enemy along the shore of Lake Maeotis; and when the Persian marched back again, they were to follow and harry him. That was one division of their kingdom, assigned to the route I have described. The other two kingdoms, the large one ruled by Idanthyrsus and the third, ruled by Taxacis, were to join together into one force, with the Gelonians and the Budini added to them. They too were to fall back before the Persians, staying one day's march ahead of them, getting out of their way and carrying out the plan. First they were to head straight for the lands of the nations that had refused to be their allies, so as to drag them into the war as well. These peoples had not taken up the war with the Persians willingly, but they would be dragged into it all the same, against their will. After that the Scythians would turn back to their own land and attack the enemy, if they decided in council that this was the thing to do.

121. With this plan made, the Scythians went out to meet Darius' army, sending their best horsemen ahead as scouts. But all the wagons that their children and women lived in they sent on ahead, along with all their cattle, except for as much as they needed for food, and ordered them to keep moving steadily toward the north. So the wagons were carried on ahead.

122. When the scouts riding in front of the Scythians found the Persians, about three days' march from the Danube, the Scythians, having found them, kept pitching their camp one day's march ahead of them, utterly destroying everything that grew from the ground. When the Persians saw that the Scythian horsemen had appeared, they came after them, following in their tracks, while the Scythians kept moving on. After this, since the Persians had set off after the first of the divisions, they kept on pursuing eastward, toward the river Don. When the Scythians crossed the Don, the Persians crossed after them and kept up the pursuit, until they had gone right through the land of the Sauromatae and come to that of the Budini.

123. Now as long as the Persians were marching through Scythia and the land of the Sauromatae, they had nothing to destroy, since the land was bare. But when they invaded the land of the Budini, they came upon the wooden-walled city there. The Budini had abandoned it and left it completely empty, and the Persians burned it down. After that they kept following the enemy's tracks onward, until they had passed through the whole of that land and reached the desert. This desert has no people living in it at all. It lies beyond the land of the Budini and stretches for seven days' journey. Beyond the desert live the Thyssagetae, and four large rivers flow down from their country through the land of the Maeotians and empty into what is called Lake Maeotis. Their names are the Lycus, the Oarus, the Don and the Syrgis.

124. So when Darius came to the desert, he stopped his advance and halted his army on the river Oarus. Then he began to build eight large forts, at equal distances from one another, about seven miles apart; their ruins were still standing in my own time. While he was busy with this, the Scythians he was chasing circled around through the country to the north and went back into Scythia. Since they had vanished completely and the Persians could no longer see them anywhere, Darius left the forts half finished, turned back, and began to march west. He supposed that these were the whole body of the Scythians, and that they were fleeing toward the west.

125. He marched his army as fast as he could, and when he reached Scythia he ran into the two combined divisions of the Scythians. When he came upon them he kept up the pursuit, while they kept withdrawing out of his way, always a day's march ahead. Since Darius would not stop coming after them, the Scythians, following the plan they had made, kept retreating before him toward the lands of the nations that had refused to be their allies, and first toward that of the Melanchlaeni. When the Scythians and the Persians together had invaded the Melanchlaeni and thrown them into turmoil, the Scythians led the way into the country of the Androphagi. When these had been thrown into turmoil too, they went on into the land of the Neuri; and while these too were in turmoil, the Scythians kept retreating before the enemy toward the Agathyrsians. But the Agathyrsians saw their neighbors fleeing from the Scythians in turmoil, and before the Scythians could invade their land they sent a herald. He warned the Scythians not to set foot across their borders: if they tried to invade the country, they would first have to fight the Agathyrsians. After giving this warning, the Agathyrsians marched out in arms to their borders, meaning to drive back anyone who came at them. But the Melanchlaeni, the Androphagi and the Neuri, when the Persians and Scythians invaded them together, did not put up a brave defense. They forgot their earlier threats and fled in confusion, farther and farther north, into the desert. As for the Scythians, once the Agathyrsians had warned them off, they made no further attempt to go there. Instead they led the Persians out of the country of the Neuri and back into their own land.

126. This went on for a long time and showed no sign of ending, so Darius sent a horseman to Idanthyrsus, the king of the Scythians, with this message: "You strange, extraordinary man, why do you keep running away, when you could do one of two things? If you think you are strong enough to stand up to my power, then stop wandering about, stand still, and fight. But if you admit you are too weak, then in that case too stop running, and come and talk with your master, bringing him the gifts of earth and water that show you submit."

127. Idanthyrsus, the king of the Scythians, answered him this way: "This is how things stand with me, Persian. I have never yet run away out of fear, not from any other man before now, and not from you now. What I am doing now is no different from what I do in peacetime too. And I will tell you why I don't fight you right away. We have no cities and no farmland that we need to worry might be captured or laid waste, which would make us join battle with you sooner. But if you absolutely must come to a fight soon, then know this: we have tombs where our fathers are buried. So come on, find them, and try to destroy them, and then you will see whether we fight you for the tombs or not. Until then, unless we feel like it, we will not join battle with you. That is enough said about fighting. As for masters, I recognize none but Zeus, my forefather, and Hestia, the queen of the Scythians. Instead of gifts of earth and water, I will send you the kind of gifts that you deserve to get. And in return for your calling yourself my master, I say: be damned to you." This is what is proverbially called "the Scythian saying."

128. So the herald had gone off to report this to Darius. The kings of the Scythians, hearing talk of being subject to a master, were filled with fury. They sent off the division that had been assigned to join the Sauromatae, the one commanded by Scopasis, with orders to go and talk with the Ionians, the ones guarding the bridge over the Danube. Meanwhile those who stayed behind decided to stop leading the Persians around in circles, and to attack them constantly whenever they were out gathering food. So they watched Darius' soldiers as they foraged and carried out what they had decided. The Scythian cavalry always routed the Persian cavalry. But the Persian horsemen, as they fled, would fall back on their foot soldiers, and the infantry would come up to help them; and at that point the Scythians, having driven in the cavalry, would turn back, because they were afraid of the men on foot. The Scythians made attacks like these by night as well.

129. Now I will tell you the thing that, strange to say, most helped the Persians and most hindered the Scythians when they attacked Darius' camp: it was the braying of the donkeys and the look of the mules. For Scythia produces neither donkeys nor mules, as I have explained before, and because of the cold there is not a single donkey or mule anywhere in the Scythian country. So the donkeys, braying wildly, would throw the Scythian cavalry into confusion. Often, just as the Scythians were in the middle of a charge against the Persians, their horses would hear the donkeys' voices and turn back in confusion, amazed, pricking up their ears. They had never heard a sound like that before, or seen a creature of that shape.

130. So for a small part of the war the Persians had the upper hand in this. But whenever the Scythians saw that the Persians were growing uneasy, they did something to keep them in Scythia longer, so that by staying they would suffer from running short of everything. They would leave some of their own cattle behind with the herdsmen and ride off somewhere else, and the Persians would come upon the cattle and take them, and having taken them they were pleased with themselves.

131. This happened again and again, until at last Darius began to be in difficulties. When the kings of the Scythians saw this, they sent a herald bringing Darius gifts: a bird, a mouse, a frog and five arrows. The Persians asked the man who brought them what the gifts meant. But he said that his only orders were to hand them over and get away as fast as possible. If the Persians were clever, he said, they could work out for themselves what the gifts were meant to say.

132. When they heard this, the Persians discussed it among themselves. Darius' opinion was that the Scythians were surrendering to him, giving him both themselves and their earth and water. He reasoned it out this way: a mouse is born in the earth and eats the same food from the earth as a man does; a frog lives in the water; a bird is very like a horse; and in giving the arrows they were handing over their own fighting strength. That was the opinion Darius put forward. But Gobryas, one of the seven men who killed the Magus, disagreed. He guessed that the gifts were saying this: "Unless you turn into birds, Persians, and fly up into the sky, or turn into mice and sink down under the earth, or turn into frogs and leap into the lakes, you will never get back home. You will be shot down by these arrows."

133. So the Persians were trying to guess the meaning of the gifts. Meanwhile the single division of the Scythians, the one that had first been assigned to keep guard along Lake Maeotis and then to go to the Danube and talk with the Ionians, reached the bridge and said this: "Ionians, we have come to bring you freedom, if only you are willing to listen to us. We are told that Darius ordered you to guard the bridge for sixty days only, and if he had not arrived within that time, to go home to your own land. So now, if you do what we say, neither he nor we will have anything to blame you for. Stay the number of days you were given, and after that, go." When the Ionians promised to do this, the Scythians hurried back again by the fastest route.

134. Meanwhile, after the gifts had come to Darius, the Scythians who had stayed behind drew themselves up against the Persians, foot and horse together, meaning to give battle. But when the Scythians were in battle order, a hare darted out through their ranks into the space between the two armies. Every company of them that saw the hare started to chase it. The Scythians fell into disorder and raised a great shouting, and Darius asked what all the noise from the enemy was about. When he heard that they were chasing the hare, he said to the men he usually talked things over with: "These men think very little of us. I see now that Gobryas was right about the Scythian gifts. Since I now think so myself, we need good advice on how to make our way home safely." Gobryas answered him: "My king, even from what people said, I was nearly sure how hard these men would be to deal with. Since I came here I have learned it even better, because I could see they were making fun of us. So here is my advice. As soon as night falls, let us light the campfires as we always do, and deceive with some false story the men least able to bear hardship. Let us tie up all the donkeys and get away, before the Scythians make for the Danube to destroy the bridge, or the Ionians decide on something that could be the end of us."

135. That was Gobryas' advice, and when night came Darius acted on it. He left behind in the camp the men who were worn out with fatigue and whose loss mattered least, and he left the donkeys there too, tied up. His reasons for leaving the donkeys and the weaker part of his army were these: the donkeys, so that their noise would be heard; the men, in reality because of their weakness, but on the pretext, which he announced openly, that he was going to attack the Scythians with the fit part of the army, and that they were to guard the camp in the meantime. Once he had given these instructions to the men he was leaving, and had the campfires lit, Darius hurried away by the fastest route toward the Danube. The donkeys, no longer having the usual crowd around them, brayed all the more loudly because of it. So the Scythians, hearing the donkeys, were quite sure the Persians were still where they had been.

136. But when day came, the men who had been left behind realized that Darius had betrayed them. They held out their hands to the Scythians in surrender and told them how things stood. When the Scythians heard this, they gathered as fast as they could, the two combined divisions of the Scythians and the single division together, with the Sauromatae, the Budini and the Gelonians too, and set off after the Persians, heading straight for the Danube. But most of the Persian army was on foot, and it did not know the roads, since the roads there are not marked out with tracks; while the Scythian army was all on horseback and knew the shortcuts. So the two armies missed each other, and the Scythians reached the bridge long before the Persians. Finding out that the Persians had not yet arrived, they said to the Ionians, who were in their ships: "Ionians, the number of your days is up, and you are not doing right by staying here still. Before, it was fear that kept you here. Now break up the crossing as fast as you can and go away free and unharmed, and thank the gods and the Scythians for it. As for the man who used to be your master, we will deal with him so thoroughly that he will never again march with an army against anyone."

137. At this the Ionians held a council. Miltiades the Athenian, who was the commander and tyrant of the people of the Chersonese on the Hellespont, the Gallipoli peninsula, was for taking the Scythians' advice and setting Ionia free. But Histiaeus of Miletus held the opposite opinion. At present, he said, each one of them ruled his city as tyrant thanks to Darius. If Darius' power were destroyed, neither he himself would be able to go on ruling the Milesians, nor would any of the others be able to go on ruling any other city, because every one of the cities would choose to be governed by its people rather than by a tyrant. When Histiaeus put forward this view, they all went over to it at once, though at first they had been siding with Miltiades.

138. The men who cast their votes between the two views, and who counted for something in the king's eyes, were these. First, the tyrants of the Hellespont: Daphnis of Abydos, Hippoclus of Lampsacus, Herophantus of Parium, Metrodorus of Proconnesus, Aristagoras of Cyzicus and Ariston of Byzantium; these were the ones from the Hellespont. From Ionia there were Strattis of Chios, Aeaces of Samos, Laodamas of Phocaea, and Histiaeus of Miletus, whose view was the one set against Miltiades'. Of the Aeolians the only man of importance there was Aristagoras of Cyme.

139. Once these men had adopted Histiaeus' view, they decided to add to it the following words and deeds. They would break up the part of the bridge on the Scythian side, as far out as an arrow can fly. That way they would seem to be doing something, when in fact they were doing nothing, and it would also stop the Scythians from trying to force their way across the Danube by the bridge. And while they were breaking up the part of the bridge toward Scythia, they would say that they would do everything the Scythians wanted. They added this to the view they had adopted, and then Histiaeus stepped forward from among them and answered the Scythians this way: "Scythians, you have brought good news, and you have hurried to bring it just in time. You are giving us good guidance, and we are doing you good service in return. As you can see, we are breaking up the crossing, and we will show every eagerness in our wish to be free. While we break up the bridge, you should be out searching for those men you talk about, and when you find them, take revenge on them, for us as well as for yourselves, the way they deserve."

140. So the Scythians, believing a second time that the Ionians were telling the truth, turned back to search for the Persians, but they missed their line of march through the country altogether. The Scythians themselves were to blame for this, since they had destroyed the horse pastures in that region and choked up the springs with earth. If they had not done that, they could easily have found the Persians if they had wanted to. As it was, the very measures they thought they had planned best were what made them fail. The Scythians went through the parts of their own land where there was grass for horses and springs of water and searched for the enemy there, thinking that the Persians too would be retreating through country like that. But in fact the Persians marched carefully along the track they had made before, and so they found the crossing of the river, though only with difficulty. They arrived by night, and when they found the bridge broken up they were terrified that the Ionians had deserted them.

141. Now Darius had with him an Egyptian with the loudest voice of any man on earth. Darius ordered this man to stand on the bank of the Danube and call for Histiaeus of Miletus. He did so, and Histiaeus heard the very first shout. He brought up all the ships to ferry the army across, and put the bridge back together as well.

142. That is how the Persians escaped, and the Scythians, searching for them, missed them a second time. And this is the Scythians' verdict on the Ionians: if you look at them as free men, they are the most worthless and cowardly of all men; but if you look at them as slaves, they are the most devoted to their master and the least likely to run away of all slaves. That is the insult the Scythians throw at the Ionians.

143. Darius marched through Thrace and came to Sestos in the Chersonese. From there he crossed over with his ships to Asia himself, but he left Megabazus, a Persian, in command of his army in Europe. This was the man Darius once honored, in Persia, with the following remark. Darius was starting to eat some pomegranates, and as soon as he opened the first one, his brother Artabanus asked him what he would like to have as many of as there were seeds in the pomegranate. Darius said he would rather have that many men like Megabazus than have Greece under his rule. That was how he honored him in Persia, with those words; and now he left him in command, with 80,000 men of his army.

144. This Megabazus made one remark that left an undying memory of him among the peoples of the Hellespont. Once, when he was at Byzantium, he heard that the people of Chalcedon, across the strait, had settled there seventeen years before the Byzantines. When he heard it, he said that the people of Chalcedon must have been blind at the time. Surely they would never have chosen the worse site, when they could have settled on the better one, if they had not been blind. It was this Megabazus who was now left in command in the land of the Hellespont, and he set about conquering everyone who was not on the Persian side.

Chapter 25: Thera, Cyrene, and the Kings of the House of Battus

145. That, then, was what Megabazus was doing. At this very same time another great expedition was being made, this one against Libya. I will tell what brought it about, but first I must tell the story that follows. The grandchildren of the men who sailed in the Argo had been driven out of Lemnos by the Pelasgians, the same Pelasgians who carried off the Athenian women from Brauron. Driven out of Lemnos by them, they left and sailed to Sparta, and there they sat down on Mount Taygetus and lit a fire. When the Spartans saw this, they sent a messenger to ask who they were and where they came from. They answered the messenger's question by saying that they were Minyans, children of the heroes who sailed in the Argo; for these heroes, they said, had put in at Lemnos and fathered the people they were descended from. The Spartans heard this story of the Minyans' descent and sent a second time to ask what they had come into the country for, and why they were making a fire blaze. They said that they had been thrown out by the Pelasgians and had now come to the land of their fathers, for that was the most just thing to do. And they said that what they asked was to be allowed to live among the Spartans, with a share of the rights of citizens and a portion of the land allotted to them. The Spartans were willing to take in the Minyans on the very terms the Minyans themselves wanted. What moved them to this most of all was that the sons of Tyndareus had been among the crew of the Argo. So they took the Minyans in, gave them a share of land, and distributed them among the tribes. The Minyans at once married Spartan wives, and gave the women they had brought with them from Lemnos in marriage to other men.

146. But before very long the Minyans grew arrogant. They demanded a share of the royal power and did other unholy things as well. So the Spartans resolved to put them to death; they seized them and threw them into prison. Now the Spartans carry out every execution they carry out at night, never by day. So when they were about to kill them, the wives of the Minyans, who were Spartan-born and daughters of the leading men of Sparta, begged to be allowed into the prison so that each of them could speak with her own husband. The Spartans let them in, never suspecting any trick from them. But once they were inside, the women handed over to their husbands all the clothes they were wearing and put on their husbands' clothes themselves. So the Minyans dressed in the women's clothes and walked out of the prison as women. Having escaped this way, they went back to Taygetus and sat down there again.

147. Now at this very same time Theras son of Autesion, son of Tisamenus, son of Thersander, son of Polynices, was getting ready to set out from Sparta to found a colony. This Theras was of the line of Cadmus, and he was the uncle, on their mother's side, of the sons of Aristodemus, Eurysthenes and Procles. While these sons were still children, Theras held the royal power in Sparta as their guardian. But when his nephews grew up and took power into their own hands, Theras could not bear to be ruled by others after he had had a taste of ruling himself. He said he would not stay in Sparta but would sail away to his kinsmen. Now on the island that is now called Thera, but was formerly called Callista, there lived descendants of Membliarus son of Poeciles, a Phoenician. For Cadmus son of Agenor, while he was searching for Europa, put in at the island now called Thera. Whether it was that the country pleased him when he landed, or whether he chose to do it for some other reason, he left on this island a number of Phoenicians, among them one of his own kinsmen, Membliarus. These people had lived on the island called Callista for eight generations before Theras came from Sparta.

148. It was to these people that Theras was getting ready to set out, taking with him men from the tribes. He meant to settle there alongside them, not to drive them out; on the contrary, he very strongly claimed them as his kin. And when the Minyans, after escaping from the prison, went and sat down on Taygetus, and the Spartans were planning to put them to death, Theras begged the Spartans to let there be no killing, and promised that he himself would take them out of the country. The Spartans agreed to this, and he sailed away with three thirty-oared ships to the descendants of Membliarus. He did not take all the Minyans with him by any means, only a few. Most of them turned instead toward the land of the Paroreatae and the Caucones. They drove these peoples out of their country, divided themselves into six groups, and founded the following towns in their territory: Lepreum, Macistus, Phrixae, Pyrgus, Epium, and Nudium. The Eleans sacked most of these within my own lifetime. The island, meanwhile, took its name of Thera from Theras, who led the colony.

149. Theras' son said he would not sail with him. So Theras said that he would leave him behind like a sheep among wolves. Because of that saying, the young man got the name Oeolycus, "Sheep-Wolf," and as it happened this name won out over the one he had before. Oeolycus fathered Aegeus, after whom the Aegids are named, a powerful clan in Sparta. The men of this clan found that their children were not living to grow up, so on the advice of an oracle they founded a temple to the Furies of Laius and Oedipus, the avenging spirits of that house. After this, the descendants of these men kept up the same custom in Thera.

150. Up to this point in the story the Spartans and the people of Thera tell it the same way. But what comes next, only the people of Thera say happened as follows. Grinnus son of Aesanius, a descendant of the Theras I have mentioned, and king of the island of Thera, came to Delphi bringing a hecatomb, a sacrifice of a hundred beasts, from his city. Among the citizens who came with him was Battus son of Polymnestus, who by descent belonged to the family of Euphemus, of the line of the Minyans. While Grinnus, the king of the Therans, was consulting the oracle about other matters, the Pythia answered by telling him to found a city in Libya. He replied: "Lord, I am already rather old and slow to get moving. Tell one of these younger men to do it." As he said this, he pointed at Battus. That was all for the time being. But afterward, when they had come home, they were at a loss what to do about the oracle's words. They knew nothing about Libya, not even what part of the world it was in, and they did not dare to send a colony off into the unknown.

151. After this, for seven years no rain fell on Thera, and in those years every tree on the island withered up except one. When the Therans consulted the oracle, the Pythia declared that the cause was this business of colonizing Libya. So, since they had no other remedy for their trouble, they sent messengers to Crete to find out whether any of the Cretans, or any foreigners living in Crete, had ever been to Libya. As these messengers wandered around the island, they came to the city of Itanus. There they met a fisherman who caught the shellfish for purple dye, a man named Corobius. He told them that he had been carried off course by the winds to Libya, and in Libya to the island of Platea. They paid this man to come with them and took him to Thera. From Thera a party set sail to explore, only a few men at first. Corobius guided them to this same island of Platea, and they left him there with enough food for a certain number of months. Then they sailed back as fast as they could to report about the island to the people of Thera.

152. But they stayed away longer than the time they had agreed on, and Corobius ran out of everything. Then a Samian ship, whose captain was Colaeus, was blown off course on its way to Egypt and came to this island of Platea. The Samians heard the whole story from Corobius and left him food for a year. Then they put out to sea from the island and sailed on, trying to reach Egypt, but they were driven steadily westward by the east wind. Since the wind never let up, they passed through the Pillars of Heracles and came to Tartessus, guided there by the hand of heaven. Now at that time no one had ever traded at this market, so when the Samians came home again they made a bigger profit from their cargo than any other Greeks we have certain knowledge of, except at least for Sostratus son of Laodamas, of Aegina; no other man can compete with him. The Samians set aside six talents, a tenth of their profits, and had a bronze vessel made in the shape of an Argive mixing bowl, with the heads of griffins projecting in a row all around its rim. They dedicated this as an offering in the temple of Hera, and set it on three colossal bronze statues, each about ten and a half feet tall, kneeling on their knees. It was this deed above all that first made the people of Cyrene and Thera close friends of the Samians.

153. Meanwhile the Therans who had left Corobius on the island arrived back at Thera and reported that they had settled an island off the coast of Libya. The people of Thera resolved to send one of every two brothers, chosen by lot, along with men from all the districts of the island, of which there are seven. They resolved, too, that Battus should be both their leader and their king. So they sent off two fifty-oared ships to Platea.

154. That is the Therans' account. From this point on, for the rest of the story, the Therans agree with the people of Cyrene, but only from this point on, because about Battus the Cyreneans tell a very different tale. Their account goes like this. There is a city in Crete called Oaxus, where a man named Etearchus became king. He had a daughter named Phronime, whose mother had died, and in spite of her he took another wife. This woman came into the house and decided to be a stepmother to Phronime in deed as well as in name. She treated her badly and schemed in every way she could to hurt her, and in the end she accused her of sleeping around and persuaded her husband that it was true. He was convinced by his wife and plotted an unholy deed against his daughter. There was in Oaxus a merchant from Thera named Themison. Etearchus made him his guest-friend and had him swear to do him whatever service he asked. When he had made him swear this, he brought out his daughter, handed her over, and told him to take her away and throw her into the sea. Themison was furious at being tricked into the oath. He broke off his friendship with Etearchus, and this is what he did. He took the girl and sailed away, and when he was out on the open sea, to clear himself of the oath Etearchus had made him swear, he tied ropes around her, lowered her into the sea, pulled her up again, and went on to Thera.

155. After that, Polymnestus, a man of standing among the Therans, took Phronime from Themison and kept her as his concubine. In time she bore him a son who had a speech impediment and a lisp. Both the Therans and the Cyreneans say he was given the name Battus. But I think he was given some other name at first, and only took the name Battus after he came to Libya, adopting it as a title because of the oracle that was given him at Delphi and the rank he had won. For the Libyans' word for king is "battus," and that, I think, is why the Pythia called him that in her prophecy: she used the Libyan word because she knew he would be a king in Libya. For when he had grown up, he went to Delphi to ask about his voice, and when he asked, the priestess answered him:

	Battus, you came for a voice; but Phoebus Apollo, your lord,
	sends you to settle in Libya, the land so rich in sheep.

It was just as if she had said in Greek, "King, you came for a voice." He answered: "Lord, I came to you to ask about my voice, and you answer me with other things, impossible things, telling me to go and found a colony in Libya. With what power, with what army of men, am I supposed to go?" Saying this did nothing to persuade her to give him any other answer, and as she began prophesying the same things to him again, Battus walked out while she was still speaking and went home to Thera.

156. After this, things went badly both for Battus himself and for the rest of the people of Thera. The Therans did not understand what was happening to them, and they sent to Delphi to ask about the troubles they were suffering. The Pythia answered that if they joined Battus in founding Cyrene in Libya, they would do better. So after this the Therans sent Battus out with two fifty-oared ships. These sailed to Libya, but then came back again to Thera, because they did not know what else to do. The Therans pelted them with missiles when they tried to land, would not let them come ashore, and told them to sail back. So, having no choice, they sailed back and founded a settlement on an island off the coast of Libya, which, as I said before, is called Platea. This island is said to be the same size as the city of Cyrene as it is today.

157. They stayed on this island for two years. But since things did not go well for them, they left one of their number behind, and all the rest sailed away to Delphi. When they came to the oracle, they consulted it, saying that they were living in Libya, and that for all their living there they were no better off. The Pythia answered them like this:

	If you know Libya, the land so rich in sheep, better than I do,
	you who have not been there, than I who have, I marvel at your wisdom.

When Battus and his companions heard this, they sailed back again; for the god plainly would not let them off the duty of founding a colony until they had come to Libya itself. They came to the island, picked up the man they had left there, and founded a settlement on the mainland of Libya itself, at a place opposite the island called Aziris. It is shut in on both sides by very beautiful woods, and a river runs past it on one side.

158. They lived in this place for six years. In the seventh year the Libyans persuaded them to leave, asking them to go and saying that they would lead them to a better region. So the Libyans led them away from that place, getting them to set out toward evening. They had worked out the hours of daylight so that they could lead them past the finest place of all by night, and the Greeks would not see it as they went through. This region is called Irasa. Then they brought them to what is called the Spring of Apollo and said: "Greeks, here is a good place for you to live, for here the sky is full of holes." They meant that it rained there.

159. Now in the lifetime of the first settler, Battus, who reigned forty years, and of his son Arcesilaus, who reigned sixteen years, the Cyreneans lived there in the same numbers as when they first set out to found the colony. But in the time of the third king, called Battus the Prosperous, the Pythia gave an oracle urging Greeks everywhere to sail out and join the Cyreneans in settling Libya. For the Cyreneans were inviting them, promising them a share of the land. The oracle she gave was this:

	Whoever comes to lovely Libya too late,
	after the land is shared out, I say he will one day regret it.

Then great numbers of people gathered at Cyrene. The Libyans who lived around them had large pieces of their land cut away, and so they and their king, whose name was Adicran, since they were being robbed of their country and also treated with great arrogance by the Cyreneans, sent to Egypt and put themselves in the hands of Apries, the king of Egypt. He gathered a great army of Egyptians and sent it against Cyrene. The men of Cyrene marched out to the region of Irasa and the spring of Theste, and there they fought the Egyptians and defeated them. The Egyptians had never before tested themselves against Greeks in battle and so looked down on them, and they were slaughtered so badly that only a few of them got back to Egypt. Because of this, and because they blamed Apries for it, the Egyptians revolted against him.

160. This Battus had a son named Arcesilaus. As soon as he became king, he quarreled with his own brothers, until finally they left and went to another part of Libya. There they struck out on their own and founded the city that was called Barca then and is still called Barca now. At the same time as they were founding it, they persuaded the Libyans to revolt from the Cyreneans. After this, Arcesilaus marched against the Libyans who had taken his brothers in and had also revolted from Cyrene. The Libyans were afraid of him and fled toward the Libyan tribes in the east. Arcesilaus followed them as they fled, chasing them all the way to Leucon in Libya, and there the Libyans decided to attack him. They fought a battle and beat the Cyreneans so completely that seven thousand Cyrenean hoplites fell there. After this disaster Arcesilaus fell sick and had taken some medicine when his brother Haliarchus strangled him. Then Haliarchus was murdered by a trick by Arcesilaus' wife, whose name was Eryxo.

161. Then Battus son of Arcesilaus inherited the kingdom. He was lame and could not walk properly. In view of the disaster that had struck them, the Cyreneans sent men to Delphi to ask what kind of government they should set up so as to live as well as possible. The Pythia told them to bring in a reformer from Mantinea in Arcadia to set their state in order. So the people of Cyrene asked for one, and the Mantineans gave them the most respected of their citizens, a man named Demonax. This man came to Cyrene and looked thoroughly into everything. First, he gave them three tribes, divided like this: one tribe he made of the Therans and the people living around them, another of the Peloponnesians and Cretans, and a third of all the islanders. Second, he set aside royal estates and priesthoods for King Battus, but all the other powers the kings had held before, he handed over to the people as public property.

162. In the reign of this Battus things stayed that way. But in the reign of his son Arcesilaus there was great unrest over the offices of state. For Arcesilaus, the son of Battus the Lame and of Pheretime, said he would not put up with the arrangements Demonax of Mantinea had made, and demanded back the royal rights of his ancestors. After this he stirred up civil strife, lost, and went into exile in Samos, while his mother went to Salamis in Cyprus. At that time the ruler of Salamis was Euelthon, the man who dedicated the incense burner at Delphi, a piece well worth seeing, which stands in the treasury of the Corinthians. Pheretime came to him and asked him for an army to restore herself and her son to Cyrene. But Euelthon was ready to give her anything rather than that. Whenever she accepted what he gave her, she would say that this too was a fine gift, but a finer one would be the gift she was asking for, an army. Since she said this about every gift, in the end Euelthon sent her a present of a golden spindle and distaff, with wool on it too. When Pheretime said the same thing again about this present, Euelthon said that these were the sort of gifts given to women, not armies.

163. Meanwhile Arcesilaus, in Samos, was gathering everyone he could by promising a redistribution of land. While a great host was being collected, Arcesilaus set out for Delphi to ask the oracle about his return from exile. The Pythia gave him this answer: "For four named Battus and four named Arcesilaus, eight generations of men, Loxias grants you to be kings of Cyrene; beyond that he advises you not even to try. As for you, keep quiet when you have come back to your country. If you find the kiln full of jars, do not fire the jars hard, but send them off with a fair wind. But if you do fire the kiln hard, do not go into the place that has water all around it; for if you do, you will die, both you and the bull that is the finest of the herd."

164. That was the Pythia's answer to Arcesilaus. He took the men from Samos with him and made his return to Cyrene. But once he had got control of the government, he forgot what the oracle had said and set about punishing the men of the opposing party for driving him out. Some of them escaped from the country altogether, but some Arcesilaus got into his hands, and he sent them off to Cyprus to be put to death. These men were driven off course to Cnidus, and the people of Cnidus rescued them and sent them away to Thera. Some other Cyreneans took refuge in a great tower that belonged to a private citizen named Aglomachus, and Arcesilaus piled brushwood around it and burned them alive. After he had done this, he realized that this was what the oracle meant when the Pythia forbade him, if he found the jars in the kiln, to fire them hard. So he deliberately kept away from the city of Cyrene, afraid of the death the oracle had foretold, and supposing that Cyrene was the place with water all around it. Now he was married to a kinswoman of his, the daughter of the king of Barca, whose name was Alazeir. He went to Alazeir, and some men of Barca, together with some of the exiles from Cyrene, caught sight of him walking in the marketplace and killed him, and his father-in-law Alazeir along with him. So Arcesilaus, whether he missed the meaning of the oracle on purpose or not, fulfilled his own destiny.

165. Meanwhile his mother Pheretime, all the time that Arcesilaus was living at Barca after bringing ruin on himself, held her son's royal power at Cyrene herself. She exercised all his other rights and also sat in the council. But when she heard that her son had been killed in Barca, she left and fled to Egypt. For she had in her favor the services Arcesilaus had done for Cambyses son of Cyrus: this was the Arcesilaus who had handed Cyrene over to Cambyses and had agreed to pay him tribute. So Pheretime came to Egypt and sat down as a suppliant before Aryandes, asking him to help her. Her reason, she said, was that her son had been killed because he took the side of the Persians.

166. Now this Aryandes had been made governor of Egypt by Cambyses. Some time after these events he lost his life for trying to make himself Darius' equal. He had heard, and seen for himself, that Darius wanted to leave behind a monument to himself that no other king had ever made, and he copied him, until in the end he got what he deserved. For Darius refined gold to the greatest possible purity and had coins struck from it; and Aryandes, as governor of Egypt, did the same thing with silver. Even now the purest silver is the kind called Aryandic. When Darius learned that he was doing this, he put him to death, though on a different charge: that he was plotting a revolt.

167. But at the time I am speaking of, this Aryandes took pity on Pheretime and gave her all the forces in Egypt, both the army and the navy. He appointed Amasis, a Persian of the Maraphian tribe, to command the army, and Badres, of the Pasargadae, to command the fleet. But before he sent the force off, Aryandes sent a herald to Barca to ask who it was that had killed Arcesilaus. The people of Barca all took the responsibility on themselves, for they said they had suffered many great wrongs at his hands in the past. When he heard this, Aryandes at last sent off the army, and Pheretime with it. That was the pretext given; but in fact, I believe, the army was being sent to conquer Libya. For the Libyans are many peoples of every kind, and only a few of them were subjects of the king, while most of them paid no attention to Darius at all.

Chapter 26: The Peoples of Libya, and the Vengeance of Pheretime

168. Now this is how the Libyans are settled. Starting from Egypt, the first of the Libyans are the Adyrmachidae. For the most part they follow the same customs as the Egyptians, but they dress like the other Libyans. Their women wear a bronze ring on each leg and let the hair on their heads grow long. When one of them catches her lice, she bites each one back in revenge and then throws it away. They are the only Libyans who do this. They are also the only ones who show their girls to the king when they are about to be married, and whichever of them pleases the king is deflowered by him. These Adyrmachidae stretch along the coast from Egypt as far as the harbor called Plynus.

169. Next after them come the Giligamae, who hold the country toward the west as far as the island of Aphrodisias. Within this stretch, off the coast, lies the island of Platea, where the Cyreneans made their first settlement; and on the mainland coast there is Port Menelaus, and Aziris, where the Cyreneans used to live. From here the silphium begins, and it grows along the coast from the island of Platea as far as the mouth of the Syrtis. This people has customs much like those of the rest.

170. West of the Giligamae are the Asbystae. They live inland above Cyrene and do not reach down to the sea, because the land along the sea is held by the Cyreneans. More than any other Libyans they drive four-horse chariots, and in most of their customs they try to copy the Cyreneans.

171. Next after the Asbystae, to the west, come the Auschisae. They live inland above Barca and reach down to the sea at Euesperides. In the middle of the Auschisae's country live the Bacales, a small tribe, who reach down to the sea at the town of Taucheira in the territory of Barca. They follow the same customs as the people above Cyrene.

172. West of the Auschisae come the Nasamonians, a large people. In summer they leave their flocks behind by the sea and go up to the region of Augila to harvest the dates from the palm trees there, which grow thick and very tall and all of them bear fruit. They hunt the wingless locusts, dry them in the sun, pound them up, and then sprinkle them on milk and drink them. Their custom is for each man to have many wives, and they have sex with them in common, in much the same way as the Massagetae: a man sets up his staff in front of the door and then has sex with the woman inside. When a Nasamonian man marries for the first time, it is the custom for the bride, on the first night, to go around all the guests in turn and have sex with each of them; and each man, after he has slept with her, gives her a gift, whatever he has brought with him from home. Their oaths and their ways of telling the future are these. They swear by the men among them who are said to have been the most just and the bravest, laying their hands on those men's tombs as they swear. And to learn the future they go to the burial mounds of their ancestors, pray, and lie down to sleep on them; whatever the man sees in his dream, he takes as his answer. They pledge their word to each other like this: each one gives the other a drink from his own hand and drinks from the other's hand in turn. If they have nothing to drink, they pick up some dust from the ground and lick it.

173. Next to the Nasamonians is the country of the Psylli. They have been wiped out completely, in this way. The south wind blew on them and dried up all their water tanks, and their land, which lies entirely inside the Syrtis, was left without water. So they held a council, agreed on a plan together, and marched out in arms against the south wind. (I am only reporting what the Libyans report.) When they reached the sandy country, the south wind blew and buried them in the sand. So they were wiped out completely, and from that time on the Nasamonians have held their land.

174. Above these, to the south, in the country of the wild beasts, live the Garamantians. They run from every man and avoid the company of everyone; they own no weapon of war and do not know how to defend themselves against an enemy.

175. These live inland above the Nasamonians. Next to the Nasamonians along the coast, toward the west, come the Macae. They shave their heads so as to leave tufts: they let the hair in the middle grow long and shave it close to the skin all around. For fighting they carry shields made of ostrich skin. Through their land the river Cinyps runs out into the sea. It flows from a hill called the Hill of the Charites. This hill is thickly covered with forest, while the rest of Libya I have described so far is bare of trees. From the sea to this hill is about twenty-two miles.

176. Next to these Macae are the Gindanes. Each of their women wears a number of anklets made of animal skin, and the reason, so they say, is this: for every man who has slept with her, a woman ties on an anklet; and the woman with the most anklets is thought the finest, since she has been loved by the greatest number of men.

177. On a headland that juts out into the sea from the land of these Gindanes live the Lotophagi, the Lotus-Eaters, who live on nothing but the fruit of the lotus. The lotus fruit is about the size of the berry of the mastic tree, and it tastes like a date. The Lotus-Eaters even make wine out of it.

178. After the Lotus-Eaters along the coast come the Machlyans. They also use the lotus, but less than the people I just mentioned. Their land reaches to a great river called the Triton, which runs out into a great lake called Tritonis, and in this lake there is an island named Phla. They say that an oracle once told the Spartans to found a settlement on this island.

179. This story is told as well. When Jason had finished building the Argo at the foot of Mount Pelion, he put on board a hecatomb and a bronze tripod besides, and sailed around the Peloponnese, meaning to go to Delphi. But as he was sailing near Cape Malea, a north wind caught his ship and carried it off to Libya, and before he caught sight of land he found himself in the shallows of Lake Tritonis. He did not know how to get his ship out. Then, the story goes, Triton appeared to him and told Jason to give him the tripod, saying that in return he would show them the channel and send them on their way unharmed. Jason agreed. So Triton showed them the way out between the shallows and set the tripod in his own temple. But first he spoke a prophecy over the tripod and told Jason and his crew the whole matter: whenever one of the descendants of the men who sailed with him on the Argo carried off this tripod, it was fated that a hundred Greek cities would be founded around Lake Tritonis. When the native Libyans heard this, they hid the tripod.

180. Next to these Machlyans are the Auseans. They and the Machlyans live around Lake Tritonis, and the river Triton is the border between them. The Machlyans let their hair grow long at the back of the head, and the Auseans let it grow long in front. At a yearly festival of Athena their girls form two sides and fight each other with stones and sticks. In doing this, they say, they are performing the rites their fathers handed down for the goddess who was born in their land, the one we call Athena. Any girls who die of their wounds they call "false maidens." But before they let the fight begin, they do this: all of them together dress up the girl judged the most beautiful that year in a Corinthian helmet and a full set of Greek armor, put her up in a chariot, and drive her all around the lake. What they dressed the girls in long ago, before the Greeks settled near them, I cannot say. But I suppose they used to dress them in Egyptian armor, since it was from Egypt, I maintain, that both the shield and the helmet came to the Greeks. They also say that Athena is the daughter of Poseidon and of Lake Tritonis, and that she had some quarrel with her father, so she gave herself to Zeus, and Zeus made her his own daughter. That is the story they tell. These people have sex with women in common: they do not marry, but couple like cattle. When a woman's child is well grown, the men hold a meeting within three months, and the child is brought before it; whichever man the child looks like is counted as its father.

181. Those, then, are the nomadic Libyans who live along the coast. Above them, inland, is the part of Libya where the wild beasts live. Above the wild-beast country stretches a ridge of sand that runs from Thebes in Egypt to the Pillars of Heracles. Along this ridge, about every ten days' journey, there are great lumps of salt piled up into hills. At the top of each hill, from the middle of the salt, a spring of cold, sweet water shoots up. People live around these springs, at the farthest edge toward the desert, beyond the wild-beast country. The first, ten days' journey from Thebes, are the Ammonians. Their temple is copied from the temple of Theban Zeus; for at Thebes too, as I have said before, the image of Zeus has a ram's head. The Ammonians, as it happens, also have another spring of water. In the early morning it is warm. At the hour when the market fills up it is cooler, and by noon it is quite cold; that is when they water their gardens. As the day wears on, it loses its chill, until at sunset the water is warm. It keeps getting hotter until midnight, when it boils and bubbles up. After midnight it cools down little by little until dawn. This spring is called the Fountain of the Sun.

182. After the Ammonians, as you go on along the ridge of sand, there is, again ten days' journey on, a hill of salt like the Ammonians' and a spring of water, with people living around it. This place is called Augila. It is here that the Nasamonians come every year to harvest the dates.

183. From Augila, again ten days' journey on, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, and a great many date palms bearing fruit, as there are in the other places too. The people who live here are called the Garamantians, a very large people. They carry earth and spread it over the salt, and then they sow their crops in it. From here is the shortest way to the Lotus-Eaters: it is thirty days' journey from them to the country of the Garamantians. Among the Garamantians, too, are found the cattle that graze walking backward. They graze backward for this reason: their horns curve down and forward, and so they walk backward as they graze; they cannot go forward, because their horns would stick into the ground in front of them. In no other way are they different from other cattle, except in this and in the thickness and toughness of their hide. These Garamantians I am speaking of hunt the Cave-Dwelling Ethiopians from their four-horse chariots. For the Cave-Dwelling Ethiopians are the fastest runners of all the peoples we hear reports about. The Cave-Dwellers live on snakes and lizards and other such creeping things, and they speak a language like no other: they squeak in it exactly like bats.

184. From the Garamantians, again ten days' journey on, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, and the people who live around it are called the Atarantians. They are the only people we know of who have no names. All of them together are called Atarantians, but no one of them has a name of his own. They curse the sun when it is high overhead and heap every kind of foul abuse on it, because its burning heat wears them down, both them and their land. After this, ten days' journey on, there is another hill of salt and spring of water, with people living around it. Near this salt hill is a mountain called Atlas. It is narrow and round on every side, and it is said to be so tall that no one can see its peaks, because the clouds never leave them, summer or winter. The natives say it is the pillar of the sky. These people took their name from this mountain, for they are called Atlantians. They are said to eat nothing that has life in it and never to have dreams.

185. As far as these Atlantians I can give in order the names of the peoples who live along the ridge of sand, but beyond them I can no longer do so. The ridge, however, stretches as far as the Pillars of Heracles and beyond them too. On it, ten days' journey from the Atlantians, there is a salt mine with people living by it. All of these people build their houses of blocks of salt, since these parts of Libya we have now reached get no rain; if it rained, walls made of salt could not last. The salt dug there is both white and purple. Beyond the ridge, to the south and into the interior of Libya, the land is empty of people, without water, without wild beasts, without rain and without trees, and there is not a trace of moisture in it.

186. So from Egypt as far as Lake Tritonis, as I have said, the Libyans are nomads who eat meat and drink milk. They will not taste the meat of cows, for the same reason the Egyptians avoid it, and they do not keep pigs. The women of Cyrene, too, think it wrong to eat beef, because of the Egyptian goddess Isis, and they even keep fasts and hold festivals in her honor. The women of Barca will not taste pork either, as well as beef.

187. So much for that. But west of Lake Tritonis the Libyans are no longer nomads. They do not follow the same customs, and they do nothing like what the nomads do to their children. For the nomadic Libyans (whether all of them, I can't say for certain, but many of them) do this: when their children are four years old, they burn the veins on the crown of their heads with a greasy tuft of sheep's wool, and some of them burn the veins at the temples. This is so that for the rest of their lives the cold phlegm will not run down from their heads and harm them. And this, they say, is why they are so healthy. In fact the Libyans are the healthiest of all the peoples we know of. Whether this is the reason I can't say for certain, but the healthiest they certainly are. If a child has a convulsion while they are burning him, they have found a cure for that too: they sprinkle him with a he-goat's urine and so save him. I am reporting what the Libyans themselves report.

188. The nomads sacrifice like this. They cut off a piece of the animal's ear as a first offering and throw it over the house, and when they have done this they wring the animal's neck. They sacrifice only to the Sun and the Moon. All the Libyans sacrifice to these two, but those who live around Lake Tritonis sacrifice most of all to Athena, and after her to Triton and Poseidon.

189. It seems, too, that the Greeks copied the dress and the aegis of Athena's statues from the Libyan women. Except that the Libyan women's dress is of leather, and the tassels hanging from their aegis are not snakes but leather thongs, in every other way Athena is dressed just like them. The name itself shows that the dress of the statues of Pallas came from Libya. For over their other clothes the Libyan women wear goatskins, aigeas, with the hair taken off, fringed with tassels and dyed red with madder; and from the name of these goatskins the Greeks made the word aegis. I think too that the loud, wailing cry raised during sacred rites first began here, since the Libyan women do it very well. And it was from the Libyans that the Greeks learned to yoke four horses together.

190. The nomads bury their dead exactly the way the Greeks do, except for the Nasamonians. They bury their dead sitting up. When a man is dying they take care to sit him up, and they do not let him die lying on his back.
