Their houses are made of asphodel stalks woven together with rushes, and they are built so that they can be carried about. Those are the customs of these tribes.

191. West of the river Triton, next after the Auseans, come Libyans who farm the land and are used to living in fixed homes. They are called the Maxyans. They let their hair grow long on the right side of their heads and cut it short on the left, and they paint their bodies with red ochre. They say they are descended from the men who came from Troy.

This country, and the rest of Libya to the west, has far more wild beasts and far more forest than the nomads' country. For the eastern part of Libya, where the nomads live, is low and sandy as far as the river Triton; but the part that comes after it to the west, where the farmers live, is very mountainous, thickly wooded, and full of wild beasts. In their land are found the giant snakes and the lions, the elephants, bears, poisonous snakes and horned asses, and also the dog-headed men and the headless men with their eyes in their chests (at least, so the Libyans say), and the wild men and wild women, and a great many other animals that are not made up like these.

192. In the nomads' country, though, there are none of these, but other animals instead: white-rumped antelopes, gazelles, buffaloes, and asses, not the horned kind but another kind that goes without water (in fact they never drink at all); oryxes, whose horns are used for the arms of the Phoenician lyre (this animal is about the size of an ox); small foxes, hyenas, porcupines, wild rams, wolves, jackals, panthers, boryes, land crocodiles about four and a half feet long that look very much like lizards, ostriches, and small snakes, each with one horn. All these wild animals are found in this country, as well as those found elsewhere, except for the deer and the wild boar; Libya has no deer and no wild boars at all. There are also three kinds of mice in this country: one is called the "two-legged" mouse, another the zegeris (a Libyan name, which means "hill" in Greek), and the third the "prickly" mouse. There are also weasels that live in the silphium, very much like the ones at Tartessus. Those are the wild animals of the Libyans' land, as far as we could find out by inquiring as widely as we could.

193. Next to the Maxyan Libyans are the Zaueces, whose women drive their chariots for them in war.

194. Next to them are the Gyzantes. In their country bees make a great deal of honey, but men, they say, make a great deal more, working at it as a trade. However that may be, all these people paint themselves with red ochre and eat monkeys, which are very plentiful in their mountains.

195. Off their coast, the Carthaginians say, lies an island called Cyrauis. It is about twenty-two miles long but narrow, and you can walk across to it from the mainland. It is full of olive trees and vines. On the island, they say, there is a pool, and the local girls bring up gold dust out of its mud with birds' feathers smeared with pitch. Whether this is true I do not know; I am writing down what is reported. But anything is possible, for on Zacynthus I have seen with my own eyes pitch being drawn up out of a pool of water. There are several pools there, and the largest of them is seventy feet across each way and twelve feet deep. They plunge into it a pole with a myrtle branch tied to the end, and with the myrtle branch they bring up pitch. It smells of asphalt, but in every other way it is better than the pitch of Pieria. They pour it into a pit dug next to the pool, and when they have collected a good deal, they pour it from the pit into jars. Anything that falls into the pool goes underground and comes up again in the sea, which is less than half a mile from the pool. So the report about the island off the coast of Libya may well be true too.

196. The Carthaginians tell this story as well. There is a place in Libya, they say, with people living there, beyond the Pillars of Heracles. When the Carthaginians come there, they unload their goods from their ships and lay them out in a row along the beach. Then they go back on board and send up a smoke signal. When the natives see the smoke, they come down to the sea, put down gold in exchange for the goods, and then move back a good distance from the goods. The Carthaginians then come ashore and look at it. If they think the gold is a fair price for their goods, they take it and go on their way. If not, they go back on board their ships and sit there, and the natives come up and add more gold to what they put down before, until the Carthaginians are satisfied. And they say that neither side cheats the other: the Carthaginians do not touch the gold until it matches the value of their goods, and the natives do not touch the goods until the Carthaginians have taken the gold.

197. These are the Libyan tribes we are able to name. Most of them pay no attention to the king of the Medes now, and they paid none then either. I have this much more to say about this land: as far as we know, four peoples live in it and no more. Two of these peoples are native to the land and two are not. The Libyans and the Ethiopians are native, the one living in the northern parts of Libya and the other in the southern; the Phoenicians and the Greeks are newcomers.

198. Besides that, I think that in the quality of its soil Libya is not especially good compared with Asia or Europe, except for the region of Cinyps, which has the same name as its river. This region is as good as the best land anywhere for growing grain, Demeter's gift, and it is not like the rest of Libya at all. It has black soil and is watered by springs; it has nothing to fear from drought, and it is not harmed by drinking in too much rain (for in this part of Libya it does rain). Its crops yield as much as the land of Babylon does. The land of the Euesperites is good too: in its best years it yields a hundredfold, but the land around Cinyps sometimes yields as much as three hundredfold.

199. The land of Cyrene, too, which is the highest part of the Libya held by the nomads, has three harvest seasons within its borders, which is something to marvel at. First the crops along the coast are ripe for reaping and the grapes for picking. When these have been gathered in, the land above the coast, the middle belt they call the Hills, is ripe for harvest. And as soon as this middle crop has been gathered in, the crop in the highest part of the country ripens and is ready. So by the time the first crop has been eaten and drunk, the last one is just coming in. In this way the Cyreneans' harvest lasts eight months. Let what I have said about these things be enough.

200. Now when Pheretime's Persian allies, sent from Egypt by Aryandes, arrived at Barca, they laid siege to the city. They demanded that the people of Barca hand over the men guilty of the murder of Arcesilaus. But since the whole people had shared in the guilt, they refused. So the Persians besieged Barca for nine months, digging tunnels toward the wall and making fierce attacks on it. The tunnels were discovered by a bronzesmith, using a shield plated with bronze. This was his idea. He carried the shield all around the inside of the wall, laying it on the ground of the city. In most places where he laid it, it made no sound, but wherever there was digging going on, the bronze of the shield rang. So the men of Barca would dig a countertunnel there and kill the Persians who were digging. That is how the tunnels were discovered, as I have said, and the attacks were beaten back by the men of Barca.

201. A long time passed in this hardship, and many were falling on both sides, especially on the Persian side. Then Amasis, the commander of the land army, came up with a plan. Seeing that the people of Barca could not be beaten by force but might be beaten by a trick, he did this. At night he dug a wide trench and laid weak planks across it, and on top of the planks he spread earth, so that it was level with the rest of the ground. At daybreak he invited the men of Barca to a parley. They were glad to come, and in the end they agreed to make a treaty. They swore the treaty with each other standing over the hidden trench. The terms were these: as long as this ground stayed as it was, the oath would stand firm; the people of Barca promised to pay the king a fair tribute, and the Persians would do the people of Barca no further harm. After the oath, the people of Barca trusted the agreement. They came out of the city themselves, opened all the gates, and let any of the enemy who wished come inside the walls. But the Persians broke down the hidden bridge and then rushed into the city. The reason they broke down the bridge they had made was so that they would be keeping their oath. They had sworn to the men of Barca that the oath would stand firm for as long as the ground stayed as it then was; once they had broken the bridge down, the oath no longer stood.

202. When the Persians handed the most guilty of the people of Barca over to Pheretime, she impaled them in a ring all around the city wall. She cut off their wives' breasts and set those, too, in a row around the wall. The rest of the people of Barca she told the Persians to take away as plunder, except for those who belonged to the house of Battus and had no share in the murder. To these Pheretime handed over the city.

203. So the Persians enslaved the rest of the people of Barca and set out for home. When they appeared at the gates of Cyrene, the Cyreneans let them pass through their city, so as not to neglect some oracle. While the army was going through, Badres, the commander of the fleet, urged that they capture the city. But Amasis, the commander of the land army, would not agree, saying that they had been sent against no Greek city but Barca. When they had passed through, however, and were camped on the hill of Zeus Lycaeus, they were sorry they had not taken Cyrene, and they tried to get into it again. But the Cyreneans would not let them in. Then, though no one was fighting them, a sudden panic fell on the Persians, and they ran about seven miles before they made camp. After they had pitched camp there, a messenger came from Aryandes calling them back. So the Persians asked the Cyreneans for food for their march, and they got it. With the food they set off for Egypt. From then on the Libyans picked them off: any who lagged or straggled behind at any point, they killed for their clothes and gear, until at last the Persians reached Egypt.

204. This Persian army got as far as Euesperides, and that was the farthest they went into Libya. The people of Barca whom they had enslaved were taken on from Egypt to the king, and King Darius gave them a village in the land of Bactria to settle in. They named the village Barca, and it was still inhabited by them in my own time, in the land of Bactria.

205. But Pheretime did not end her life happily either, any more than they did. As soon as she had come back from Libya to Egypt, after taking her revenge on the people of Barca, she died a horrible death: while she was still alive she suddenly swarmed with worms. For, as it seems, punishments that are too harsh, when men inflict them, are hateful to the gods. Such, and so great, was the vengeance that Pheretime, the wife of Battus, took on the people of Barca.

Book Five: Terpsichore

Chapter 27: Thrace, the Persian Envoys in Macedonia, and Histiaeus Called to Susa

1. Meanwhile the Persians whom Darius had left behind in Europe, under the command of Megabazus, had conquered the people of Perinthus. They were the first of the peoples on the Hellespont to be subdued, because they refused to become Darius' subjects. The Perinthians had been roughly handled once before, in earlier times, by the Paeonians. The Paeonians from the river Strymon had been commanded by an oracle of their god to march against the Perinthians. If the Perinthians, when they were camped facing them, shouted aloud and called them by their name, the Paeonians were to attack; but if they did not shout to them, they were not to attack. And that is what the Paeonians did. The Perinthians camped facing them in the outskirts of their city, and a challenge was made to single combat in three different forms: they matched man against man, horse against horse, and dog against dog. The Perinthians were winning two of the three contests, and in their delight they raised the victory shout "Paean!" The Paeonians guessed that this was the very thing the oracle had spoken of, and no doubt they said to one another, "Now surely the oracle is coming true for us. Now it is time to act." So the Paeonians attacked the Perinthians after they had raised the shout of "Paean!", and they had much the better of the fight and left only a few of them alive.

2. That is what had happened to the Perinthians at the hands of the Paeonians in earlier times. This time, although the Perinthians proved themselves brave men in defense of their freedom, the Persians under Megabazus got the better of them by sheer numbers. After Perinthus had been conquered, Megabazus marched his army through the length of Thrace, forcing every city and every people living there to submit to the king. Those were Darius' orders to him: to subdue Thrace.

3. The Thracians are the most numerous people in the world, after the Indians. If they were ruled by one man, or could agree among themselves, they would be unbeatable in war and by far the strongest of all nations, in my opinion. But this is impossible for them, and there is no way it will ever happen; and that is why they are in fact weak. They have many names, one for each of their tribes in its own region, but they all follow customs that are nearly the same in every respect, except for the Getae, the Trausians, and the people who live north of the Crestonians.

4. Of these, I have already described the practices of the Getae, who believe they are immortal. The Trausians do everything else the same way as the other Thracians, but at a birth and a death they do as follows. When a child is born, its nearest relatives sit around it and mourn over all the troubles it will have to live through, now that it is born, listing every one of the sorrows of human life. But when a man dies, they bury him in the earth with laughter and rejoicing, telling one another how many great troubles he has escaped and how he is now completely happy.

5. The people who live north of the Crestonians do this. Each man has many wives, and when a man dies, there is a great contest among his wives, with their friends working hard on their behalf, over which of them their husband loved best. The one who is judged the winner, and so honored, is first praised by both the men and the women; then her nearest relative cuts her throat over the grave, and she is buried with her husband. The other wives are bitterly upset, because for them this is the greatest disgrace.

6. Among the other Thracians, the custom is to sell their children to be taken abroad. They do not watch over their unmarried girls, but let them have sex with any men they please; their wives, though, they watch very closely. They buy their wives from the women's parents for large sums of money. To be tattooed is considered a mark of noble birth, and to have no tattoos is a sign of low birth. Not working is thought the most honorable thing of all, and working the land the most dishonorable. Living by war and plunder is the most honorable life there is.

7. Those are their most remarkable customs. Of the gods, they worship only Ares, Dionysus, and Artemis. Their kings, however, unlike the rest of the people, worship Hermes above all the gods and swear by him alone, and they say they are descended from Hermes.

8. This is how the rich among them are buried. For three days they lay out the corpse for people to see, and they sacrifice every kind of animal and feast, after first mourning. Then they bury the body, either burning it or putting it in the ground unburned. When they have heaped up a mound over it, they hold games with every kind of contest, and the biggest prizes, as is only reasonable, go to single combat. That is how the Thracians bury their dead.

9. As for the region farther north of this country, no one can say for certain who lives there. But the land just beyond the Danube is known to be empty and enormous. The only people I can hear of who live beyond the Danube are said to be called the Sigynnae, and they dress in the Median fashion. Their horses, it is said, are covered all over with shaggy hair as much as five fingers (nearly four inches) long. The horses are small and snub-nosed and too weak to carry men, but yoked to chariots they are very spirited, so the people of the country drive chariots. This people's territory reaches, it is said, as far as the land of the Eneti, who live on the Adriatic. They say the Sigynnae are colonists from the Medes. How they could have come to be colonists from the Medes I cannot work out for myself, but anything can happen in the long course of time. However that may be, the Ligurians who live inland above Massalia (the Greek city that is now Marseille) call traders "sigynnae," and the people of Cyprus use the same word for spears.

10. The Thracians say that the land on the other side of the Danube is full of bees, and that because of them it is impossible to get through and go any farther. But to me, when they say this, they seem to be saying something unlikely. Bees are known to hate the cold, and it seems to me that it is the cold climate that makes the lands toward the north uninhabitable. These, then, are the stories told about this country. However that may be, Megabazus was now bringing its coastal regions under Persian rule.

11. Meanwhile Darius, as soon as he had crossed the Hellespont and reached Sardis, remembered the service Histiaeus of Miletus had done him and the advice of Coes of Mytilene. He sent for them to come to Sardis and offered them a choice of rewards. Histiaeus, since he was already tyrant of Miletus, did not ask to rule anywhere else in addition. Instead he asked for Myrcinus, a district in the land of the Edonians, because he wanted to found a city there. That was Histiaeus' choice. Coes, who was not a tyrant but an ordinary citizen, asked to be made tyrant of Mytilene.

12. Both men got what they wanted, and each went off to what he had chosen. At this same time it happened that Darius saw something that made him want to order Megabazus to conquer the Paeonians and move them by force out of Europe into Asia. This is what it was. There were two Paeonians named Pigres and Mantyas. After Darius had crossed back into Asia, they came to Sardis, because they wanted to become rulers of the Paeonians themselves, and they brought their sister with them, a tall, good-looking woman. They waited for a time when Darius was sitting in public in the outskirts of the Lydian city. Then they dressed up their sister as well as they could and sent her out to fetch water. She carried a water jar on her head, led a horse behind her by a bridle looped over her arm, and was spinning flax as she went. As the woman passed by him on her way out of the city, Darius took notice, because what she was doing was not the Persian way, nor the Lydian way, nor the custom of any people in Asia. So he sent some of his spearmen and told them to watch what the woman would do with the horse. They followed her. When she reached the river, she watered the horse. After she had watered it and filled her jar, she came back the same way, carrying the water on her head, leading the horse behind her by the bridle looped over her arm, and turning her spindle as she went.

13. Darius was amazed both at what he heard from the men he had sent to watch and at what he saw for himself, and he ordered them to bring her before him. When she was brought, her brothers came too; they had been watching all this from not far off. Darius asked what country she came from, and the young men said that they were Paeonians and that she was their sister. He replied, "Who are these Paeonians, and where on earth do they live?" He also asked them what they wanted, that they had come to Sardis. They told him that they had come to put themselves in his hands; that Paeonia was a country on the river Strymon; that the Strymon was not far from the Hellespont; and finally that they were colonists from the Teucrians of Troy. They told him all of this, point by point. Then he asked whether all the women of their country were as hardworking as their sister. They were very quick to say that yes, they were, because that was the very point of what they had been doing.

14. Then Darius wrote a letter to Megabazus, whom he had left in command of his army in Thrace, ordering him to uproot the Paeonians from their homes and bring them to the king, the men themselves together with their children and their wives. At once a horseman set off at full speed to carry the message to the Hellespont. He crossed over to the other side and gave the letter to Megabazus. Megabazus read it, got guides from Thrace, and set out to march on Paeonia.

15. When the Paeonians learned that the Persians were coming against them, they gathered all their forces and marched out toward the sea, thinking that the Persians would make their attack from that side when they invaded. So the Paeonians were ready, as I said, to drive back Megabazus' army when it came. But the Persians heard that the Paeonians had gathered their forces and were guarding the approach from the sea. With their guides, they took the upper road instead, slipped past the Paeonians without being seen, and fell on their cities, which had been left empty of men. Finding them undefended, they took them easily. When the Paeonians heard that their cities were in enemy hands, they scattered at once, each tribe to its own home, and began to surrender to the Persians. And so it was that these tribes of the Paeonians, namely the Siropaeonians, the Paeoplians, and all the tribes as far as Lake Prasias, were uprooted from their homes and taken to Asia.

16. But the peoples around Mount Pangaeum, around the Doberians, the Agrianians, and the Odomantians, and around Lake Prasias itself, were not conquered by Megabazus at all. He did try to remove even the people who live on the lake itself. Their homes are built like this. A platform, fastened together and set on tall piles, stands out in the middle of the lake, and a single narrow bridge leads to it from the shore. The piles that hold up the platform were no doubt set up in the first place by all the members of the community working together. But since then they have gone on setting them by this rule: every man who marries brings three piles from the mountain called Orbelus for each wife and sets them up as supports, and each man takes many wives. This is how they live. Each man has a hut of his own on the platform, where he lives, and a trapdoor leading down through the platform to the lake. They tie their small children by the foot with a rope, for fear they will roll into the water. They feed their horses and pack animals on fish. There are so many fish that if a man opens his trapdoor and lets an empty basket down into the lake on a cord, he waits only a very short time and then pulls it up full of fish. There are two kinds of fish, which they call paprax and tilon.

17. So the Paeonians who had been conquered were being taken off to Asia. Meanwhile Megabazus, after conquering the Paeonians, sent seven Persians as envoys to Macedonia; after himself, they were the most distinguished men in the army. They were sent to Amyntas to demand earth and water for King Darius. From Lake Prasias it is a very short way into Macedonia. First, right next to the lake, there is the mine that later brought Alexander a talent of silver every single day. Past the mine, once you have crossed the mountain called Dysorum, you are in Macedonia.

18. When the Persians sent to Amyntas arrived, they came before him and demanded earth and water for King Darius. He was willing to give it, and he also invited them to be his guests. He prepared a magnificent dinner and received the Persians with every kindness. When dinner was over and they were drinking toasts to one another, the Persians said, "Our Macedonian host, it is the custom among us Persians, when we give a great dinner, to bring in our concubines and our lawful wives as well, to sit beside us. You have welcomed us readily, you are entertaining us magnificently as your guests, and you are willing to give King Darius earth and water. So agree to follow our custom." Amyntas answered, "Persians, that is not our custom here. With us men and women are kept apart. But since you are our masters and you ask this as well, you shall have this too." With that Amyntas sent for the women. When they had been summoned and came, they sat down in a row facing the Persians. Then the Persians, seeing that the women were beautiful, spoke to Amyntas and told him that what he had done was not at all well thought out. It would have been better for the women not to come at all than to come and not sit beside them, but sit across from them and be a torment to their eyes. So Amyntas, under pressure, told the women to sit beside the Persians. As soon as the women did so, the Persians, who were very drunk, began to fondle their breasts, and some, no doubt, also tried to kiss them.

19. Amyntas saw this and kept quiet, angry as he was, because he was terribly afraid of the Persians. But his son Alexander, who was there and saw it, was young and had never known disaster, and he could not stand it any longer. Unable to bear it, he said to Amyntas, "Father, give in to your age: go and rest, and don't stay on drinking any longer. I will stay here and see that our guests have everything they need." Amyntas understood that Alexander meant to do something violent, and he said, "Son, you are burning with anger, and I think I understand what you are saying: you want to send me away and then do something violent. So I am asking you not to do anything violent to these men, or it will be the ruin of us. Put up with what is happening and watch it. As for my leaving, though, I will do as you say."

20. When Amyntas had made this request and gone, Alexander said to the Persians, "Guests, you are completely free to do as you like with these women: sleep with all of them, if you wish, or with as many of them as you want. You shall have the say in this. But now, since it is almost time for you to go to bed and I can see you have had a good deal to drink, let these women go and bathe, if that suits you, and when they have bathed, take them back into your company." With that, since the Persians readily agreed, he sent the women out, and when they had gone he sent them to the women's quarters. Then Alexander took young men with no beards yet, as many as there were women, dressed them in the women's clothes, gave them daggers, and led them into the banquet hall. As he led them in, he said to the Persians, "Persians, I think you have been treated to a feast that lacked nothing. Everything we had, and everything besides that we could find and provide, has all been set before you. And on top of that there is this, the greatest gift of all: we freely give you our own mothers and sisters as well, so that you may see that we honor you as fully as you deserve, and so that you may report to the king who sent you that a Greek, his governor of the Macedonians, entertained you well at table and in bed." With that, Alexander seated a Macedonian man dressed as a woman beside each Persian, and when the Persians tried to lay hands on them, the Macedonians killed them.

21. So the envoys died this way, they and their servants with them. For they had brought carriages and servants and all the usual baggage of a great embassy, and all of it disappeared along with them. Not long afterward the Persians made a great search for these men. But Alexander was clever enough to stop it. He gave a large sum of money, and his own sister, whose name was Gygaea, to Bubares, a Persian who commanded the men searching for the missing envoys. By giving these things to Bubares, Alexander stopped the search.

22. And so the death of these Persians was hushed up. Now, that these descendants of Perdiccas are Greeks, as they themselves say, I happen to know for myself, and what is more, I will prove it later in my history. The Hellanodicae, the judges who run the games at Olympia, have also ruled that they are Greeks. When Alexander wanted to compete in the games and had come down into the arena for this purpose, the Greeks who were to run against him tried to keep him out, saying that the contest was for Greeks, not for barbarians. But Alexander proved that he was of Argive descent, and he was judged to be a Greek. He entered the footrace, and his lot was drawn to run in the first heat.

23. That is how these things turned out. At the same time Megabazus arrived at the Hellespont with the Paeonians, crossed the strait from there, and came to Sardis. Histiaeus of Miletus was already building a wall around the place he had asked for and been given by Darius as a reward for keeping the bridge of boats safe. This place was the one called Myrcinus, on the bank of the river Strymon. Megabazus had seen what Histiaeus was doing, and as soon as he reached Sardis with the Paeonians he said to Darius, "My king, what is this you have done? You have let a clever, cunning Greek found a city in Thrace, in a place where there is plenty of timber for shipbuilding, a great deal of wood for oars, and silver mines, and where huge numbers of Greeks and non-Greeks live all around. Once they have a leader, they will do whatever he tells them, day and night. So stop this man from doing it, so that you won't find yourself in a war at home. Stop him by sending for him politely. But once you have him in your hands, make sure he never goes back to Greek lands again."

24. With these words Megabazus easily persuaded Darius, who thought he had seen clearly what was likely to happen. So Darius sent a messenger to Myrcinus with this message: "Histiaeus, King Darius says this. Thinking it over, I find there is no one more truly loyal than you to me and to my power, and I know this from deeds, not words. Now, since I have great plans in mind, you must come to me, so that I can share them with you." Histiaeus believed these words, and he also thought it a great thing to become one of the king's advisers, so he came to Sardis. When he arrived, Darius said to him, "Histiaeus, this is why I sent for you. When I came back from Scythia and you were gone out of my sight, I never wanted anything so soon as I wanted then to see you and to talk with you. For I have come to see that the most valuable thing a man can have is a friend who is both wise and truly loyal, and I know you have both these qualities. I can bear witness to them from my own affairs. So now, since you have done well to come, this is what I offer you. Leave Miletus and your new city in Thrace, come with me to Susa, and share everything I have. Eat at my table and be my adviser."

25. So said Darius. He appointed Artaphernes, his brother by the same father, governor of Sardis, and marched off to Susa, taking Histiaeus with him, after first naming Otanes commander of the people along the coast. This Otanes' father, Sisamnes, had been one of the Royal Judges. King Cambyses had put him to death because he had taken money to give an unjust verdict, and had flayed off all his skin. Once the skin was torn off, Cambyses had it cut into strips of leather and stretched them across the chair where Sisamnes used to sit to give judgment. When he had stretched them across the seat, Cambyses appointed the son of the Sisamnes he had killed and flayed to be judge in his father's place, and told him to remember what seat he was sitting in when he gave judgment.

26. This Otanes, then, who was made to sit in that chair, now succeeded Megabazus in the command. He conquered the Byzantines and the Chalcedonians, and he conquered Antandrus in the Troad, and Lamponium. Then, with ships he got from the Lesbians, he conquered Lemnos and Imbros, both of which were still inhabited at that time by Pelasgians.

27. Of these, the Lemnians fought well and held out for a long time, but in the end they were ruined. Over those who survived, the Persians set up as governor Lycaretus, the brother of the Maeandrius who had been king of Samos. This Lycaretus ruled Lemnos until he died. And the reason was this: he went on enslaving and subduing everyone, accusing some of deserting to the Scythians and others of attacking Darius' army as it came back from Scythia.

Chapter 28: The Ionian Revolt Begins, and Aristagoras at Sparta

28. That much, then, Otanes achieved after he was made commander. After this there was a short break from troubles. Then troubles began to fall on the Ionians a second time, and they came from Naxos and Miletus. Naxos was richer than any of the other islands, and Miletus, at that very same time, had just reached the height of its prosperity and was the jewel of Ionia. But before this, for two generations, Miletus had suffered terribly from civil strife, until the Parians set it in order. The Milesians had chosen the Parians, out of all the Greeks, to reform their state.

29. This is how the Parians healed their divisions. Their best men came to Miletus, and seeing that the Milesians were in a badly ruined state, they said they wanted to go over the land. They did this, passing through the whole territory of Miletus, and wherever they saw a well-farmed field in the middle of that ruined countryside, they wrote down the name of the field's owner. When they had gone through the whole country and had found only a few such men, they went straight back to the city, called a general assembly, and put these men, the ones whose fields they had found well farmed, in charge of the state. They said they thought these men would take care of public affairs the way they had taken care of their own. And they ordered the rest of the Milesians, who had been split into factions before, to obey these men.

30. So that is how the Parians reformed the Milesians. But at the time I am speaking of, troubles began to come to Ionia from these two states in the following way. Certain men of the wealthier class were driven out of Naxos by the common people, and once in exile they came to Miletus. Now the man in charge of Miletus at that time happened to be Aristagoras son of Molpagoras. He was both the son-in-law and the cousin of Histiaeus son of Lysagoras, whom Darius was keeping at Susa. For Histiaeus was the tyrant of Miletus, and he happened to be at Susa at the time when the Naxians came; and these Naxians had been guest-friends of Histiaeus in earlier days. So when the Naxians arrived, they asked Aristagoras whether he might give them a force, so that they could return from exile to their own land. Aristagoras thought that if they went home with his help, he would become ruler of Naxos. But he used his guest-friendship with Histiaeus as a pretext, and he made them this proposal: "I can't promise to give you a force big enough to bring you back from exile against the will of the Naxians who control the state. I hear that the Naxians have an army 8,000 shields strong and many warships. But I will do everything I can to find a way, and this is my plan. It happens that Artaphernes is my friend. Artaphernes, you should know, is a son of Hystaspes and the brother of King Darius. He governs all the peoples of the coast of Asia, and he has a great army and many ships. I think this man will do whatever we ask of him." When the Naxians heard this, they handed the matter over to Aristagoras to manage as best he could. They told him to promise gifts and the costs of the expedition, which they said they would pay themselves. For they fully expected that when they appeared at Naxos, the Naxians would do whatever they told them, and so would the other islanders too. For of these islands, the Cyclades, not one was yet under Darius.

31. So Aristagoras went to Sardis and told Artaphernes that Naxos was an island not large in size, but beautiful all the same, with rich soil, close to Ionia, and full of wealth and slaves. "So send an expedition against this land," he said, "and bring back the men who are now exiled from it. If you do this, first, I have large sums of money ready for you, apart from the costs of the expedition, which it is only fair that we who lead it should pay. Second, you will win for the king not only Naxos itself but also the islands that depend on it, Paros and Andros and the others called the Cyclades. And starting out from these you will easily attack Euboea, a large and wealthy island, as big as Cyprus, and very easy to conquer. A hundred ships are enough to subdue them all." Artaphernes answered him in these words: "You are bringing good news to the king's house, and all your advice is good, except for the number of ships. Instead of one hundred, two hundred will be ready for you by the beginning of spring. But the king himself must approve this too."

32. When Aristagoras heard this, he went back to Miletus delighted. Meanwhile Artaphernes sent to Susa and reported what Aristagoras had said, and when Darius himself had approved it too, he got ready two hundred triremes and a very large force of Persians and their allies. He appointed as their commander Megabates, a Persian of the Achaemenid clan, a cousin both of himself and of Darius. (It was to this man's daughter, at least if the story is true, that Pausanias the Spartan, son of Cleombrotus, later got himself engaged, because he had conceived a desire to become tyrant of Greece.) Having made Megabates commander, Artaphernes sent the force off to Aristagoras.

33. Megabates took the force on board, together with the Naxians, and sailed, pretending to be heading for the Hellespont. But when he reached Chios, he steered his ships to Caucasa, so that he could cross from there to Naxos with a north wind. Then, since it was not fated that the Naxians should be destroyed by this expedition, something happened that I will now tell. As Megabates was making his rounds of the guards posted on the ships, it happened that on a ship from Myndus there was no one on watch. He was furious, and he ordered his spearmen to find the ship's captain, a man named Scylax, and tie him through one of his ship's oar-holes, with his head outside the ship and his body inside. When Scylax had been tied up this way, someone reported to Aristagoras that Megabates had tied up his guest-friend from Myndus and was treating him shamefully. So Aristagoras came and asked the Persian to release him. When he got nothing of what he asked for, he went himself and set Scylax loose. When Megabates was told of this, he was extremely angry and burst out in rage at Aristagoras. But Aristagoras answered him: "What business is this of yours? Didn't Artaphernes send you to obey me, and to sail wherever I order? Why are you meddling in things that are none of your concern?" That is what Aristagoras said. Megabates was enraged by this, and when night came he sent men in a ship to Naxos to tell the Naxians about all the danger that threatened them.

34. For the Naxians had not been expecting this expedition to be aimed at them at all. But when they were told, they at once brought everything they had in the fields inside the wall, stocked up food and drink as if for a siege, and strengthened their wall. So they were getting ready for the war that was coming at them. The others, meanwhile, crossed with their ships from Chios to Naxos, and when they attacked, they found the place well defended. They besieged it for four months. Then, when the money the Persians had brought with them had all been spent, and Aristagoras himself had spent a great deal on top of that, and the siege kept demanding more and more, they built a fortress for the Naxian exiles and went back to the mainland, having failed.

35. So Aristagoras was not able to keep his promise to Artaphernes. At the same time he was hard pressed by the demand to pay the costs of the expedition, and he was afraid, both because the force had failed and because he had made an enemy of Megabates. He supposed he would be stripped of his rule over Miletus. With all these fears together, he began to plan a revolt. For it also happened that just at this time the man with the marked head had come from Histiaeus at Susa, telling Aristagoras to revolt from the king. Histiaeus wanted to tell Aristagoras to revolt, but he had no other safe way to do it, since the roads were guarded. So he shaved the head of the most trusted of his slaves, marked it by pricking letters into the skin, and waited until the hair had grown back. As soon as it had grown, he sent him off to Miletus with no other instructions than this: when he got to Miletus, he was to tell Aristagoras to shave his hair off and look at his head. And the marks, as I said before, meant revolt. Histiaeus was doing this because he was deeply frustrated at being held at Susa. He had high hopes that if a revolt broke out, he would be sent down to the coast; but if nothing changed at Miletus, he expected never to go back there again.

36. So Histiaeus sent the messenger with this aim, and it happened that all these things came upon Aristagoras at the same moment. So he held a council with his supporters, and he told them both his own view and the message from Histiaeus. All the rest gave the same opinion, urging him to revolt, except Hecataeus the historian. First Hecataeus advised them not to go to war with the king of the Persians, listing all the nations Darius ruled and the extent of his power. When he could not persuade them of that, he advised next that they should make themselves masters of the sea. This could not happen in any other way, as far as he could see, he went on, because he knew the Milesians' forces were weak. But if they seized the treasures in the temple at Branchidae, the offerings that Croesus the Lydian had dedicated, he had high hopes that they could become masters of the sea. That way they would have the wealth to use themselves, and the enemy would not be able to carry it off as plunder. These treasures were of great value, as I showed in the first part of my history. This advice did not win the day. But they did decide to revolt, and to send one of their number by sea to Myus, to the force that had come back from Naxos and was there at the time, to try to seize the commanders who had sailed with the ships.

37. Iatragoras was sent to do this, and by a trick he seized Oliatus son of Ibanollis of Mylasa, Histiaeus son of Tymnes of Termera, Coes son of Erxander, to whom Darius had given Mytilene as a gift, Aristagoras son of Heraclides of Cyme, and many others. Then Aristagoras revolted openly and planned every harm he could against Darius. First, so that the Milesians would be willing to join his revolt, he pretended to give up his sole power and gave Miletus equality under the law. After that he did the same thing in the rest of Ionia too. Some of the tyrants he drove out; but the ones he had taken from the ships that had sailed with him to Naxos he handed over, because he wanted to please their cities, giving each man up to the city he came from.

38. Now the people of Mytilene, as soon as they had Coes in their hands, took him outside the city and stoned him to death. But the people of Cyme let their tyrant go, and most of the others let theirs go as well. So the tyrants were deposed in the different cities. And after deposing the tyrants, Aristagoras the Milesian told each people to appoint generals in their own cities, and then he himself set out as an envoy to Sparta; for he really did need to find some powerful ally.

39. Now at Sparta, Anaxandrides son of Leon was no longer alive and king, but had come to the end of his life, and Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides held the kingship. He had not gained it by merit, but by right of birth. For Anaxandrides had married his own sister's daughter, and he loved her very much, but no children were born to him by her. That being so, the ephors called him before them and said: "If you will not look out for your own interests in time, we still cannot allow the line of Eurysthenes to die out. So send away the wife you have now, since, as you know, she bears you no children, and marry another. If you do that, you will please the Spartans." He answered that he would do neither of these two things. They were not giving him honorable advice, he said, when they told him to send away the wife he had, though she had done him no wrong, and to bring another into his house. In short, he would not follow their advice.

40. At this the ephors and the Council of Elders consulted together and put this proposal to Anaxandrides: "Since we see that you are firmly attached to the wife you have now, agree to do this, and don't oppose it, or the Spartans may make some decision about you that nobody would want. We are not asking you to send away the wife you have. Go on giving her everything you give her now, but also take another wife into your house besides her, to bear you children." When they spoke to him this way, Anaxandrides agreed. So he had two wives, which was not at all the Spartan way.

41. Not long after this, the second wife gave birth to this Cleomenes we have been speaking of. And just as she was bringing an heir to the Spartan throne into the world, the first wife, who had been childless all that time before, somehow became pregnant, as it happened just at that very time. And though she really was with child, the relatives of the second wife, when they heard of it, made an uproar against her. They said she was making an empty boast and meant to pass off someone else's child as her own. Since they made such a show of outrage, when her time was close the ephors, who did not believe her either, sat around her and watched while she gave birth. She bore Dorieus, then right away conceived Leonidas, and right after him Cleombrotus. Some even say that Cleombrotus and Leonidas were twins. But the wife who had borne Cleomenes, the one who had come in after the first wife, the daughter of Primetades son of Demarmenus, never had another child.

42. Now Cleomenes, it is said, was not quite in his right mind but on the edge of madness, while Dorieus was the first of all the young men of his age, and he was confident that he would become king on merit. So he held that opinion. But when Anaxandrides died, the Spartans followed their usual custom and made the eldest, Cleomenes, king. Dorieus resented this and did not think it right to be ruled by Cleomenes. So he asked the Spartans for a body of men and led them off to found a colony. He did not ask the oracle at Delphi what land he should go to and settle, and he did none of the things that are usually done. Instead, in his anger he sailed off with his ships to Libya, with men from Thera as his guides. When he reached the Cinyps, he founded a settlement in the finest spot in all Libya, along the banks of the river. But in the third year he was driven out of there by the Macae, the Libyans and the Carthaginians, and he went back to the Peloponnese.

43. Then Antichares, a man of Eleon, advised him, on the strength of the oracles of Laius, to found a settlement at Heraclea in Sicily. The whole land of Eryx, he said, belonged to the Heraclids, since Heracles himself had won it. When Dorieus heard this, he went straight to Delphi to ask the oracle whether he would be able to conquer the land he was setting out for. The Pythia answered that he would conquer it. So Dorieus took with him the force he had led to Libya before and sailed along the coast of Italy.

44. Now at this time, the people of Sybaris say, they and their king Telys were about to march against Croton. The people of Croton were terrified and asked Dorieus to help them, and he agreed. So Dorieus joined them in their campaign against Sybaris and helped them take it. That is what the Sybarites say about what Dorieus and his men did. But the people of Croton say that no foreigner helped them in the war against the Sybarites except Callias of Elis, a seer and one of the descendants of Iamus. And he helped them this way, they say: he ran away from Telys, the tyrant of the Sybarites, when the sacrifices he was making for the expedition against Croton did not turn out favorable, and so he came over to them.

45. Those are the stories the two sides tell, and each of them offers the following evidence for its own. The Sybarites point to a sacred precinct and a temple beside the dried-up bed of the Crathis, which they say Dorieus set up to Athena "of the Crathis" after he had helped to take the city. Besides this, they consider Dorieus' own death the strongest evidence of all. He died, they think, because he went against the oracle he had been given. If he had not done anything on the side, but had stuck to what he had been sent to do, he would have conquered the land of Eryx and held it once he had conquered it, and he and his army would not have been destroyed. The people of Croton, on the other hand, point out that many special grants of land in the territory of Croton were given to Callias of Elis, which Callias' descendants still held in my own time, while nothing was given to Dorieus or to Dorieus' descendants. Yet if Dorieus had really helped them in the war with Sybaris, they say, he would have been given many times as much as Callias. That is the evidence the two sides produce, and we may each agree with whichever of them we find more believable.

46. Other Spartans also sailed with Dorieus as co-founders of the colony: Thessalus, Paraebates, Celeas and Euryleon. When they had reached Sicily with their whole force, they were defeated in battle by the Phoenicians and the people of Egesta and were killed. Of the co-founders, only Euryleon survived this disaster. He gathered together the survivors of the expedition and took over Minoa, the colony of Selinus, and helped the people of Selinus to free themselves from their tyrant Peithagoras. But afterward, when he had deposed Peithagoras, he seized the tyranny of Selinus himself and ruled there alone, though only for a short time. For the people of Selinus rose against him and killed him, even though he had fled for refuge to the altar of Zeus of the Marketplace.

47. Another man who went with Dorieus and died with him was Philip son of Butacides, a man of Croton. He had become engaged to the daughter of Telys the Sybarite, and for that he was exiled from Croton. Then, when the marriage fell through, he sailed away to Cyrene, and from there he set out and joined Dorieus with a trireme of his own, paying the costs of the crew himself. This man had won at the Olympic Games, and he was the most handsome Greek of his day. Because of his good looks he received from the people of Egesta something no one else ever received from them: they built a hero's shrine over his grave, and they still offer sacrifices to win his favor.

48. That is how Dorieus ended his life. But if he had put up with being ruled by Cleomenes and had stayed in Sparta, he would have been king of Sparta himself. For Cleomenes did not reign very long, and he died leaving no son to succeed him, only a daughter, whose name was Gorgo.

49. Anyway, Aristagoras, the tyrant of Miletus, arrived at Sparta while Cleomenes was king, and it was with him that he came to talk. He brought with him, as the Spartans say, a bronze tablet with a map of the whole earth engraved on it, with all the sea and all the rivers. When he came to talk with Cleomenes, he said this to him: "Don't be surprised, Cleomenes, at how eager I was to come here, for this is how things stand. That the sons of the Ionians should be slaves instead of free men is a disgrace and a grief, most of all to us ourselves, but of everyone else, most of all to you, since you are the leaders of Greece. So now I beg you, by the gods of Greece, to rescue the Ionians, your own kin, from slavery. And you can do it easily. For the foreigners are not brave fighters, while you have reached the very peak of courage in war. This is how they fight: with bows and arrows and a short spear, and they go into battle wearing trousers and with caps on their heads. So they are easy to beat. Besides, the people who live on that continent have more good things than all the other nations of the world put together: first gold, then silver and bronze, embroidered clothing, pack animals and slaves. All of it could be yours, if you wanted it. And these nations live next to each other in the order I will now show you. Here are the Ionians. Next to them are the Lydians, who not only live in a fertile land but are extremely rich in gold and silver." And as he said this he pointed to the map of the earth, which he had brought with him engraved on the tablet. "And here, next to the Lydians," Aristagoras went on, "are the Eastern Phrygians, who have more sheep and cattle than any people I know, and the richest crops as well. Next to the Phrygians are the Cappadocians, whom we call Syrians. Bordering on them are the Cilicians, whose land comes down to this sea here, where the island of Cyprus lies. They pay the king five hundred talents a year in tribute. Next to these Cilicians are the Armenians, here, as you can see, and they too have great numbers of sheep and cattle. Next to the Armenians are the Matienians, who hold this country here. And next to them is the land of Cissia, here, and in that land, on the banks of this river, the Choaspes, stands the city of Susa, where the great king lives and where his money is stored in treasuries. Once you have taken that city, you can boldly challenge Zeus himself in wealth. Tell me, can it really be that you feel you must risk battles against the Messenians and the Arcadians and the Argives, who are an even match for you, for land that is not large or very fertile, and for borders that are small, when these peoples have no gold or silver at all, the things that make a man want to fight and die? Can that be, I ask you, and will you choose that way now, when you could easily rule all of Asia?" That is what Aristagoras said, and Cleomenes answered: "My friend from Miletus, I will put off my answer until the day after tomorrow."

50. That is as far as they got that time. When the day set for the answer came and they met at the agreed place, Cleomenes asked Aristagoras how many days' journey it was from the Ionian sea to where the king lived. Now Aristagoras, who had been clever in everything else and had been handling Cleomenes well, made a mistake here. He should not have told him the truth, at least if he wanted to bring the Spartans out to Asia. But in fact he told him it was a journey of three months inland from the sea. Cleomenes cut short the rest of the description of the road that Aristagoras had started to give, and said: "My friend from Miletus, get out of Sparta before sunset. What you are saying does not sound good to Spartan ears, wanting to take them a three months' journey away from the sea."

51. After saying this, Cleomenes went home. But Aristagoras took up an olive branch, the sign of a suppliant, and went to Cleomenes' house. He went in as a suppliant and asked Cleomenes to send the child away and listen to him. For Cleomenes' daughter, whose name was Gorgo, was standing beside him; she happened to be his only child, and she was eight or nine years old. But Cleomenes told him to say what he wanted to say and not to hold back because of the child. Then Aristagoras began to promise him money if he would do what he was asking, starting with ten talents. When Cleomenes refused, Aristagoras kept raising the sum he offered, until at last he had promised fifty talents. At that the child cried out: "Father, the stranger will do you harm, unless you leave him and go." Cleomenes was pleased with the child's advice and went off into another room, and Aristagoras left Sparta altogether. He never got the chance to explain any further about the road inland from the sea to the king's residence.

52. As for this road, the truth is as follows. All along it there are royal stations with excellent inns, and the whole road runs through country that is inhabited and safe. Through Lydia and Phrygia there are twenty stations, covering ninety-four and a half parasangs, about 315 miles. After Phrygia comes the river Halys, where there is a gate you must pass through to cross the river, and a strong guard-post stands there. Then, after crossing into Cappadocia, it is twenty-eight stations, or 104 parasangs, about 347 miles, along this road to the borders of Cilicia. On the Cilician border you pass through two separate gates and go by two separate guard-posts. After passing these, it is three stations, fifteen and a half parasangs, about fifty-two miles, to travel through Cilicia. The boundary between Cilicia and Armenia is a river you can sail on, called the Euphrates. In Armenia there are fifteen stations with inns, covering fifty-six and a half parasangs, about 188 miles, and there is a guard-post on the way. Then, when you leave Armenia and enter the land of Matiene, there are thirty-four stations, covering 137 parasangs, about 457 miles. Four navigable rivers flow through this land, and they can only be crossed by ferry. First is the Tigris. The second and third are both called by the same name, though they are not the same river and do not flow from the same region: the first of these two flows from Armenia and the other from the land of the Matienians. The fourth river is called the Gyndes, the one Cyrus once split into three hundred and sixty channels. Going on from there into the land of Cissia, there are eleven stations, forty-two and a half parasangs, about 142 miles, to the river Choaspes, which is also navigable; and on it the city of Susa is built. These stations come to one hundred and eleven in all.

53. That is the number of stations with inns as you go up from Sardis to Susa. Now if the royal road has been measured correctly in parasangs, and if a parasang equals thirty stades, as it certainly does, then the distance from Sardis to what is called the palace of Memnon is 13,500 stades, which is 450 parasangs, about 1,500 miles. So if you travel 150 stades, about seventeen miles, a day, the journey takes exactly ninety days.

54. So Aristagoras of Miletus spoke correctly when he told Cleomenes the Spartan that the journey up from the sea to the king's residence took three months. But if anyone wants an even more exact figure than this, I will give him that too. We should also add the length of the road from Ephesus to Sardis. So I say that the whole distance from the Greek sea to Susa (for that is the name of the city of Memnon) is 14,040 stades, about 1,560 miles, since from Ephesus to Sardis is 540 stades, about sixty miles. And so the three months' journey is lengthened by three days.

Chapter 29: Athens Frees Itself: the End of the Tyrants and the Reforms of Cleisthenes

55. So Aristagoras, driven out of Sparta, went on to Athens. Athens had been set free from its tyrants, and I will tell how. Hipparchus, the son of Pisistratus and brother of the tyrant Hippias, had seen a vision in a dream that plainly foretold his fate, and after it he was killed by Aristogeiton and Harmodius, who were Gephyraeans by descent. But for four years after this the Athenians went on living under tyranny just as before, and in fact under a harsher one.

56. This was the dream Hipparchus had. On the night before the Panathenaea, the great festival of Athena, he dreamed that a tall, handsome man came and stood over him and spoke these riddling verses:

	"Endure, lion, with an enduring heart, what cannot be endured:
	no man who does wrong will escape the punishment appointed for him."

As soon as it was day he told these verses openly to the interpreters of dreams. But afterward he put the vision out of his mind and took his part in the procession, and it was during that procession that he was killed.

57. The Gephyraeans, the family the murderers of Hipparchus belonged to, say that they came originally from Eretria. But as I find when I trace the matter back, they were Phoenicians, part of the company who came with Cadmus to the land now called Boeotia, and they lived in the district of Tanagra, which had been allotted to them there. The Cadmeans were driven out first, by the Argives; then these Gephyraeans in their turn were driven out by the Boeotians, and they turned toward Athens. The Athenians took them in as citizens on certain fixed terms, laying down rules that shut them out of a number of things not worth mentioning here.

58. These Phoenicians who came with Cadmus, the Gephyraeans among them, settled in this land of Boeotia and brought many skills to the Greeks. Above all they brought writing, which, as it seems to me, the Greeks did not have before this. At first they used the same letters all Phoenicians use, but as time went on they changed the shape of the letters along with their language. In most of the places around them at that time the Greeks who lived nearest were Ionians. The Ionians learned the letters from the Phoenicians, changed their shape a little, and used them, and when they did they called them "phoenicians," which was only fair, since the Phoenicians had brought them into Greece. The Ionians have also called papyrus "skins" from ancient times, because once, when papyrus was scarce, they wrote on the skins of goats and sheep. Even in my own time many non-Greeks still write on such skins.

59. I have seen Cadmean letters myself, in the temple of Ismenian Apollo at Thebes in Boeotia, carved on some tripods, and for the most part they look like the Ionian letters. One of these tripods carries the inscription:

	"Amphitryon dedicated me, home from the land of the Teleboans."

This inscription would date from about the time of Laius son of Labdacus, son of Polydorus, son of Cadmus.

60. A second tripod says, in hexameter verse:

	"Scaeus dedicated me to you, Apollo who shoots from afar,
	when he won the boxing match, a beautiful gift in your honor."

This Scaeus would be the son of Hippocoon, if it really was he who dedicated it and not another man with the same name as the son of Hippocoon, and he would have lived about the time of Oedipus son of Laius.

61. The third tripod, also in hexameter verse, says:

	"Laodamas, while he was king, dedicated me to you, Apollo of the true aim,
	from his own wealth, a beautiful gift in your honor."

It was in the reign of this very Laodamas son of Eteocles that the Cadmeans were driven out by the Argives and went off to the Enchelians. The Gephyraeans were left behind then, and later the Boeotians forced them to withdraw to Athens. They have temples of their own established in Athens, in which the other Athenians have no share. These are different from the rest, and the chief of them is a temple of Demeter Achaea, with her secret rites, the Mysteries.

62. I have now told about the dream Hipparchus saw, and where the Gephyraeans came from, the family his murderers belonged to. Now I must go back and continue the story I set out to tell at the start: how the Athenians were freed from their tyrants.

Hippias was tyrant, and he was treating the Athenians harshly because of Hipparchus' death. The Alcmaeonids, an Athenian family who had been exiled by the sons of Pisistratus, had joined the other Athenian exiles in an attempt to come home by force and set Athens free. They fortified Leipsydrium, above Paeonia, but the attempt failed and they suffered a heavy defeat. After that the Alcmaeonids, still trying every means against the sons of Pisistratus, took the contract to build the temple at Delphi, the one that stands there now, which did not yet exist then. They were wealthy and had been men of standing from ancient times, and they built the temple more beautifully than the plan required. In particular, though the contract was for a temple of ordinary limestone, they built its front of Parian marble.

63. Then, as the Athenians say, these men stayed at Delphi and bribed the Pythia to tell any Spartans who came to consult the oracle, whether on private business or public, that they should set Athens free. Since the Spartans got the same answer every time, they sent Anchimolius son of Aster, a man of standing among their citizens, with an army to drive the sons of Pisistratus out of Athens. They did this even though the sons of Pisistratus were bound to them by close ties of guest-friendship, because they held that the god's business must come before men's. They sent this force by sea, in ships.

Anchimolius put in at Phalerum, the harbor of Athens, and landed his army. But the sons of Pisistratus had learned of it in advance and called for help from Thessaly, since they had an alliance with the Thessalians. At their request the Thessalians, by public decree, sent a thousand cavalry and their king Cineas, a man of Conium. With these allies in hand, the sons of Pisistratus made a plan. They cut down the trees on the plain of Phalerum to make the ground fit for horses, and then they sent the cavalry against the enemy's camp. The cavalry fell on it and killed many of the Spartans, Anchimolius himself among them, and they shut the survivors up in their ships. That was how the first expedition from Sparta ended. Anchimolius' tomb is at Alopece in Attica, near the temple of Heracles at Cynosarges.

64. After this the Spartans fitted out a larger expedition and sent it against Athens. They made their king Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides its commander, and this time they sent it by land instead of by sea. When they invaded Attica, the Thessalian cavalry met them first, and before long the Thessalians were routed and lost more than forty men. The survivors went straight home to Thessaly without more ado. Then Cleomenes, along with those Athenians who wanted to be free, came to the city and began to besiege the tyrants, who had shut themselves up behind the Pelasgian Wall.

65. The Spartans would never have captured the sons of Pisistratus at all. They had no plans for a long blockade, and the defenders were well supplied with food and drink, so after a siege of a few days the Spartans would have gone back home to Sparta. But as it happened, something occurred just then that was bad luck for one side and help for the other: the children of the sons of Pisistratus were captured as they were being smuggled out of the country. When that happened, all their plans were thrown into confusion. To get their children back they surrendered on the Athenians' terms, which were that they should leave Attica within five days. So they left the country and went to Sigeum on the Scamander, after their family had ruled the Athenians for thirty-six years. They too were originally Pylians, descendants of Neleus, from the same ancestors as the family of Codrus and Melanthus, who had come from abroad earlier and become kings of Athens. That was why Hippocrates had named his son Pisistratus, as a reminder, after Pisistratus the son of Nestor.

So the Athenians were freed from their tyrants. Before I go any further, I will first set out the things worth telling that they did or suffered after they were freed, up to the time when Ionia revolted from Darius and Aristagoras of Miletus came to Athens and asked them for help.

66. Athens had been great even before, but now, rid of its tyrants, it grew greater still. Two men held power there. One was Cleisthenes, a descendant of Alcmaeon, the man who is said to have bribed the Pythia. The other was Isagoras son of Tisander, of a highly respected family; I can't say what his family's origins were, but his relatives sacrifice to Carian Zeus. These two men fought each other for power, and when Cleisthenes was getting the worst of it, he made the common people his partners. After this he divided the Athenians into ten tribes instead of the old four. He did away with the old tribal names, which came from the sons of Ion (Geleon, Aegicores, Argades and Hoples), and found new names for them after other heroes, all of them native Athenians except Ajax. Ajax he added, although he was no Athenian, as a neighbor and an ally.

67. In this, it seems to me, this Cleisthenes was imitating his mother's father, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon. When that Cleisthenes went to war with Argos, the first thing he did was stop the contests of the rhapsodes, the reciters of Homer, in Sicyon, because Homer's poems are full of praise for the Argives and Argos almost from end to end. The second thing was this. In the marketplace of Sicyon there was (and there still is) a shrine to the hero Adrastus son of Talaus, and Cleisthenes wanted to throw him out of the country, because he was an Argive.

So he went to Delphi and asked the oracle whether he should throw Adrastus out. The Pythia answered that Adrastus was king of the Sicyonians, and Cleisthenes was only fit to stone them. Since the god would not let him do it, he went home and thought about how to make Adrastus leave of his own accord. When he thought he had found a way, he sent to Thebes in Boeotia and said he wanted to bring Melanippus son of Astacus into his city, and the Thebans let him. So Cleisthenes brought Melanippus in, gave him a sacred precinct in the town hall itself, and set him up there in the strongest spot. Cleisthenes brought in Melanippus (I must tell this too) because he had been Adrastus' worst enemy: he had killed both Adrastus' brother Mecisteus and his son-in-law Tydeus. Once he had given Melanippus his precinct, he took the sacrifices and festivals away from Adrastus and gave them to Melanippus.

The Sicyonians had been in the habit of honoring Adrastus very greatly. This land had once belonged to Polybus, and Adrastus was Polybus' grandson, his daughter's son; and when Polybus died without sons, he left his kingdom to Adrastus. So the Sicyonians gave Adrastus other honors, and in particular they honored him for his sufferings with tragic choruses, paying that honor not to Dionysus but to Adrastus. Cleisthenes, however, gave the choruses back to Dionysus, and the rest of the rites he gave to Melanippus.

68. That is what he did to Adrastus. He also changed the names of the Dorian tribes, so that the Sicyonians would not have the same tribes as the Argives. In this he made a great mockery of the Sicyonians, because he took the new names from the words for "pig" and "donkey," changing only the endings, except for his own tribe, which he named after his own rule. So the men of his tribe were called Archelai, the "Rulers of the People," while of the rest, one tribe was called the Hyatae, the "Hog-men," another the Oneatae, the "Donkey-men," and the last the Choereatae, the "Swine-men." The men of Sicyon used these tribal names not only while Cleisthenes ruled but for sixty years after his death. Then, however, they talked it over and changed them to Hylleis, Pamphyli and Dymanatae, and added a fourth tribe, which they called the Aegialeis after Aegialeus son of Adrastus.

69. That is what Cleisthenes of Sicyon had done. And the Athenian Cleisthenes, his daughter's son, who was named after him, despised the Ionians, I suppose, as his grandfather despised the Dorians, and so he imitated his namesake to keep the Athenians from having the same tribes as the Ionians. At the time I am speaking of, he had won over to his side the whole body of the Athenian common people, whom he had looked down on before. So he changed the names of the tribes and made more of them than there had been: he made ten tribal chiefs instead of four, and he divided the demes among the tribes, ten to each. With the common people on his side, he was far stronger than his rivals.

70. Then Isagoras, losing in his turn, came up with a countermove. He called in Cleomenes of Sparta to help him. Cleomenes had been his guest-friend ever since the siege of the sons of Pisistratus, and Cleomenes was also accused of having an affair with Isagoras' wife. First Cleomenes sent a herald to Athens demanding that Cleisthenes be banished, and many other Athenians with him, calling them "the accursed." He sent this message on Isagoras' instructions, because the Alcmaeonids and their party were blamed for the killing this name referred to, while Isagoras and his friends had no part in it.

71. This is how the Athenians "under the curse" got their name. There was a man in Athens named Cylon, a victor at the Olympic games. He grew arrogant and wanted to make himself tyrant. He formed a band of young men his own age and tried to seize the Acropolis, but when he could not take it, he sat down as a suppliant at the statue of the goddess. The presidents of the naucraries, the officials who ran Athens at that time, persuaded them to leave sanctuary on a promise that they would face any punishment short of death. But they were killed, and the Alcmaeonids are blamed for killing them. All this happened before the time of Pisistratus.

72. When Cleomenes sent his demand that Cleisthenes and the accursed be banished, Cleisthenes himself slipped away. But even so, Cleomenes came to Athens afterward with a fairly small force. When he arrived, he banished seven hundred Athenian families as accursed, families whose names Isagoras had given him. Having done this, he next tried to dissolve the Council, and he put the offices of state in the hands of three hundred of Isagoras' supporters. But the Council resisted and refused to obey, and so Cleomenes, Isagoras and his supporters seized the Acropolis. Then the rest of the Athenians, all of one mind, joined together and besieged them for two days. On the third day all of them who were Spartans left the country under a truce.

So the ominous words that had been spoken to Cleomenes came true. When he went up to the Acropolis intending to take it over, he was going into the shrine of the goddess to pray to her. But the priestess rose from her seat before he had got through the door and said: "Spartan stranger, go back. Do not enter the temple. It is not lawful for Dorians to come in here." He said: "Woman, I am not a Dorian. I am an Achaean." So, paying no attention to the omen, he made his attempt, and then he was thrown out again along with the Spartans. The rest of the men the Athenians put in chains, to be executed. Among them was Timesitheus of Delphi, about whom I could tell of very great deeds of strength and courage.

73. So these men were put in chains and executed. After this the Athenians called back Cleisthenes and the seven hundred families Cleomenes had banished. Then they sent envoys to Sardis, wanting to make an alliance with the Persians, because they were sure that Cleomenes and the Spartans were now their deadly enemies. When the envoys arrived at Sardis and were delivering the message they had been given, Artaphernes son of Hystaspes, the governor of Sardis, asked who these people were who wanted to be allies of the Persians, and where on earth they lived. When the envoys had told him, he gave them his answer in short: if the Athenians would give earth and water to Darius, he would make an alliance with them; if not, they could leave. The envoys, acting on their own authority, said they would do it, because they wanted the alliance.

74. When they got home, they were sharply condemned for it. Meanwhile Cleomenes, who felt that the Athenians had insulted him outrageously in word and deed, was raising an army from the whole of the Peloponnese. He did not say what he was raising it for, but he wanted revenge on the Athenian people, and he meant to make Isagoras tyrant, since Isagoras too had come out of the Acropolis with him. So Cleomenes marched into Eleusis with a large army. At the same time the Boeotians, by agreement with him, took Oenoe and Hysiae, the demes on the very edge of Attica, and on the other side the Chalcidians invaded and began plundering various parts of Attica. The Athenians were attacked on more than one side, but they decided they would remember the Boeotians and the Chalcidians later, and they drew up their army to face the Peloponnesians at Eleusis.

75. Then, just as the armies were about to engage, the Corinthians were the first to change their minds. They decided among themselves that they were not doing right, and they left. After them Demaratus son of Ariston did the same. He was the other king of Sparta besides Cleomenes, and he had led the army out from Sparta together with him, and until then he had never been at odds with Cleomenes. Because of this split, a law was made at Sparta that when an army went out, both kings might not go with it, as they had both done up to then. And since one of the kings was now released from service, one of the sons of Tyndareus was to be left at home as well; before this both of them had been called on for help and had gone out with the armies.

76. So at Eleusis the rest of the allies, seeing that the kings of Sparta disagreed and that the Corinthians had left their place in the line, also left and hurried away. This was the fourth time the Dorians had come into Attica: twice they had invaded it to make war, and twice they had come to help the Athenian common people. The first was when they also founded Megara (this expedition may rightly be dated to the time when Codrus was king of Athens); the second and third were when they marched from Sparta to drive out the sons of Pisistratus; and the fourth was this one, when Cleomenes led the Peloponnesians into Eleusis. So this was the fourth time the Dorians invaded Athens.

77. Once this army had broken up so ingloriously, the Athenians wanted revenge, and they marched first against the Chalcidians. The Boeotians came to the Euripus, the strait between the mainland and Euboea, to help the Chalcidians. When the Athenians saw the Boeotian relief force, they decided to attack the Boeotians before the Chalcidians. So they fought the Boeotians and beat them soundly. They killed a great many and took seven hundred prisoners. On that very same day the Athenians crossed over to Euboea and fought the Chalcidians as well. They beat them too, and they left 4,000 settlers, each given an allotment of land, on the land of the "Horse-breeders," as the wealthier Chalcidians were called.

All the Chalcidians they captured they kept in prison along with the Boeotian prisoners, bound in fetters. Later they let them go, setting their ransom at two minas a head. But they hung up the fetters they had been bound with on the Acropolis, and these were still there in my own time, hanging on walls scorched by the Persians' fire, facing the shrine that looks toward the west. They also dedicated a tenth of the ransom as an offering and made a bronze four-horse chariot out of it. It stands on the left as you enter the Propylaea, the great gateway of the Acropolis, and on it is this inscription:

	"When the tribes of Boeotia and Chalcis met them in the work of war,
	the sons of Athens won, and broke them in battle.
	In dark chains of iron they quenched their arrogance,
	and from the ransom they give these horses to Athena, a tenth."

78. So the Athenians grew in power. And it is clear, not from one example only but in every way, that equality is an excellent thing.
