While the Athenians were ruled by tyrants they were no better at war than any of their neighbors, but once they were rid of the tyrants they became by far the best. This proves that while they were held down they held back on purpose, because they were working for a master, but once they were free, each man was eager to achieve something for himself.

79. That was how the Athenians were doing. After this the Thebans sent to the god at Delphi, wanting to be avenged on the Athenians. The Pythia said that they could not get revenge by their own strength alone. She told them to lay the matter before "the many-voiced" and to ask help from "those nearest" to them. So when the men sent to the oracle returned, the Thebans held a general assembly and the envoys reported the answer. When the Thebans heard that they were to ask help from those nearest to them, they said: "Surely the people who live nearest to us are the men of Tanagra and Coronea and Thespiae. They always fight hard on our side and see the war through with us to the end. Why should we need to ask them? Perhaps that isn't what the oracle means."

80. While they were discussing it this way, at last someone saw the point and said: "I think I understand what the oracle means to tell us. Asopus, they say, had two daughters, Thebe and Aegina. Since these two are sisters, I think the god's answer means that we should ask the men of Aegina to be our helpers." No one could offer a better opinion than this, so they sent at once to the Aeginetans and asked them for help, calling on them in the name of the oracle. When the Thebans made their request, the Aeginetans said they would send the sons of Aeacus, their heroes, to help them.

81. The Thebans tried their luck with the sons of Aeacus as allies and were roughly handled by the Athenians. So they sent again, gave the Aeginetans back the sons of Aeacus, and asked them for men instead. The Aeginetans, riding high on great prosperity and remembering an old grudge against the Athenians, answered the Thebans' request by starting a war on the Athenians without a declaration. While the Athenians were busy with the Boeotians, they sailed against Attica in warships and ravaged Phalerum and many demes along the rest of the coast, and by doing this they made the Athenians very angry indeed.

Chapter 30: The Old Feud with Aegina, and Socles on the Tyrants of Corinth

82. Now the grudge the Aeginetans already owed the Athenians had its beginning in this way. The land of the Epidaurians produced no crops for the people who lived there. So, because of this disaster, the Epidaurians went to Delphi to ask the oracle about it. The Pythia told them to set up statues of Damia and Auxesia, and said that once they had set these up, their luck would improve. The Epidaurians then asked a further question: should they make the statues of bronze or of stone? The Pythia told them to use neither, but to make them from the wood of a cultivated olive tree. So the Epidaurians asked the Athenians to let them cut down an olive tree, since they believed the Athenian olives were the most sacred. Some people even say that at that time there were no olive trees anywhere on earth except at Athens. The Athenians said they would allow it on one condition: that every year the Epidaurians would bring the proper offerings to Athena Polias, the guardian of the city, and to Erechtheus, the hero-king of early Athens. The Epidaurians agreed to these terms and got what they asked for. They made statues out of the olive wood and set them up, and their land bore crops again, and they went on doing for the Athenians what they had agreed to do.

83. Now during this time, and before it too, the Aeginetans were subject to the Epidaurians. Among other things, they used to cross over to Epidaurus to have their lawsuits against one another settled there. But after this time they built ships for themselves and, out of sheer stubbornness, revolted from the Epidaurians. Since they were now at odds with them, they kept doing them damage, for in fact they controlled the sea. Above all, they stole these very statues of Damia and Auxesia from them. They carried them off and set them up in the interior of their own island, at a place called Oea, about two and a quarter miles from their city. Once they had set them up in this spot, they worshipped them with sacrifices and with choruses of women who sang mocking, insulting songs. Ten men were appointed for each of the two goddesses to provide the choruses. The choruses insulted no man, only the women of the place. The Epidaurians had these same rites too; and they also have rites that may not be revealed.

84. Once these statues had been stolen, the Epidaurians stopped doing for the Athenians what they had agreed to do. So the Athenians sent to the Epidaurians and complained. The Epidaurians, though, argued that they were doing nothing wrong. As long as they had the statues in their country, they said, they had kept their agreement; but since they had been robbed of them, it was not fair that they should go on making the offerings. They told the Athenians to demand the offerings from the men of Aegina, who had the statues now. So the Athenians sent to Aegina and demanded the statues back. But the Aeginetans said they had no business with the Athenians at all.

85. The Athenians say that after this demand, the citizens sent out by the state went in a single trireme. When they reached Aegina, they tried to pull the statues off their bases, claiming that they were made of wood that belonged to Athens, so that they could carry them home. But they could not get hold of them that way (so the Athenians say), so they threw ropes around them and began to haul on them. Suddenly, as they hauled, there came thunder, and with the thunder an earthquake. The crew of the trireme who were hauling were driven out of their minds by these things. In that state they killed one another as if they were enemies, until in the end only one man out of all of them was left, and he went back alone to Phalerum.

86. That is how the Athenians say it happened. But the Aeginetans say that the Athenians did not come with just one ship. One ship, they say, or even a few more than one, they could easily have driven off, even if they had happened to have no ships of their own. Instead, they say, the Athenians sailed against their country with a large fleet, and they themselves gave way before them and did not fight a sea battle. But they cannot say for certain whether they gave way because they admitted they were not strong enough to fight at sea, or because they meant to do something like what they actually did. The Athenians, they say, since no one came out to fight them, landed from their ships and went for the statues. They could not pull them off their bases, so at last they threw ropes around them and began to haul, until the statues, as they were being hauled, both did the same thing. (And here they tell something I cannot believe, though someone else may.) They say that the statues fell on their knees in front of the Athenians, and have stayed in that position ever since. That, they say, is what the Athenians were doing. Meanwhile they themselves (so the Aeginetans say) had learned that the Athenians were about to attack them, and had got the Argives ready to help. Just as the Athenians had landed on Aeginetan soil, the Argives arrived to rescue them. They had crossed over unnoticed from Epidaurus to the island, and they fell on the Athenians before the Athenians had heard anything about it, cutting them off from the way back to their ships. And it was at this very moment that the thunder and the earthquake came upon them.

87. This is the account the Argives and the Aeginetans both give, and the Athenians too agree that only one of their men survived and came back to Attica. Only, the Argives say this one man was left alive when they destroyed the Athenian army, while the Athenians say the destroyer was the divine. But even this one man did not stay alive. He died, they say, in the following way. When he came back to Athens, he reported the disaster. The wives of the men who had gone on the expedition to Aegina heard it, and they were furious that he alone out of all of them had survived. So they gathered around this man and stabbed him with the brooch pins of their cloaks, each of them asking him where her husband was. That is how he was killed. And to the Athenians the women's deed seemed even more terrible than the disaster itself. Not knowing, it is said, how else to punish the women, they changed their style of dress to the Ionian. Before this, the Athenian women had worn Dorian dress, very like the Corinthian; now the Athenians changed it to the linen tunic, so that the women would have no use for brooches.

88. The truth is, though, that this style of dress is not Ionian in origin but Carian. The old Greek dress for women everywhere was the same as the one we now call Dorian. It is said, too, that because of these events the Argives and Aeginetans each made it a custom in their own country to have brooch pins made half as long again as the size then in use. Their women were to offer brooches above all in the temple of these two goddesses. And no Athenian pottery, or anything else made in Athens, was to be brought into the temple; instead, the custom from then on was to drink there only from pitchers made in their own lands.

89. From this time on, the women of the Argives and Aeginetans, because of the quarrel with the Athenians, went on wearing larger brooches than before, and they still do even in my time. And that is how the Athenians' hostility toward the Aeginetans began. So at this time, when the Thebans made war on the Athenians, the Aeginetans readily came to the help of the Boeotians, remembering what had happened over the statues. The Aeginetans, then, were raiding the coast of Attica, as I have said. The Athenians were determined to make war on the Aeginetans, but an oracle came to them from Delphi. It told them to wait for thirty years, counted from the time of the Aeginetans' wrong, and in the thirty-first year to mark out a sacred precinct for Aeacus, the hero who was Aegina's legendary ancestor, and then begin the war against the Aeginetans; then they would succeed as they wished. But if they attacked at once, it said, they would suffer a great deal of harm in the meantime and also do a great deal, but in the end they would conquer them. When the Athenians heard this report, they marked out a sacred precinct for Aeacus, the one that now stands next to the marketplace. But they could not bear to hear that they must wait thirty years, when they had suffered wrongs from the Aeginetans.

90. But while they were getting ready to take revenge, trouble arose from the Spartans and got in their way. The Spartans had learned what the Alcmaeonids had arranged with the Pythia, and what the Pythia had arranged against them and against the sons of Pisistratus. They were doubly upset: first, because they had driven into exile men who were their guest-friends, and second, because after they had done it the Athenians had shown them no gratitude at all. On top of this, they were spurred on by the oracles which said that they would suffer many wrongs at the hands of the Athenians. They had known nothing of these oracles before, but they knew of them now, because Cleomenes had brought them to Sparta. In fact, Cleomenes had taken them from the Acropolis of Athens. The sons of Pisistratus had owned them before and had left them in the temple when they were driven out, and Cleomenes picked them up after they had been left behind.

91. So at this time the Spartans had got hold of the oracles, and they saw that the Athenians were growing in power and were not at all willing to obey them. They realized that the Athenian people, now that it was free, was becoming a match for their own, whereas under tyrants it had been weak and ready to take orders. Seeing all this, they sent for Hippias son of Pisistratus to come from Sigeum on the Hellespont, where the family of Pisistratus goes for refuge. When Hippias came at their summons, the Spartans also sent for envoys from their other allies, and spoke to them as follows:

"Allies, we know in our own hearts that we have not acted rightly. Stirred up by false oracles, we drove into exile men who were very close friends of ours, bound to us as guest-friends, and who promised to keep Athens obedient to us. Then, having done that, we handed the city over to an ungrateful mob. As soon as it had raised its head, freed by our efforts, it threw out us and our king with insult and violence. And now, swollen with pride, it is growing in power, so that its neighbors first of all, the Boeotians and the Chalcidians, have already learned that they made a mistake, and perhaps others will learn it later on. But since we went wrong in doing what we have described, we will now try to take revenge on them, going there together with you. That is exactly why we sent for Hippias, whom you see here, and for you too, to come from your cities: so that with shared counsel and a shared army we might bring him back to Athens and give back to him what we once took away."

92. That is what they said; but most of the allies did not approve of their words. The rest kept silent, but Socles of Corinth spoke as follows:

"Surely now the sky will be below the earth, and the earth will be lifted up above the sky, and men will live in the sea, and fish will live where men lived before, now that you, Spartans, are doing away with free governments and preparing to bring tyranny back into our cities. There is nothing among men more unjust than tyranny, and nothing more murderous. If you really think it a good thing for cities to be ruled by tyrants, then set up a tyrant in your own state first, and after that try to set them up for others. As things are, you are treating your allies unfairly: you have never had any experience of tyrants yourselves, and at Sparta you take the greatest care that it never happens. If you had had experience of it, as we have, you would be able to offer better judgement about it than you do now.

"This is how the Corinthian state was arranged. The government was an oligarchy, and the oligarchs, who were called the Bacchiads, ran the state and married only among themselves. Now one of these men, named Amphion, had a daughter who was lame, and her name was Labda. Since none of the Bacchiads wanted to marry her, she was taken as wife by Aetion son of Echecrates, who came from the village of Petra but was by descent a Lapith, one of the race of Caeneus. Neither by this wife nor by any other did he have children, so he set off to Delphi to ask about having a family. As soon as he came in, the Pythia greeted him with these lines:

	'You deserve great honor, yet no one gives you honor.
	Labda is with child, and she will bear a rolling boulder that will crash
	down on the heads of the kings, and bring punishment on Corinth.'

"Somehow this answer given to Aetion was reported to the Bacchiads. An earlier oracle had come to Corinth that they had not been able to understand, an oracle that pointed to the same thing as Aetion's and said this:

	'An eagle is with child among the rocks, and will bear a lion,
	strong and savage, who will loosen the knees of many.
	Think this over well, Corinthians, you who live
	around the fair spring of Peirene and in steep Corinth.'

"This oracle, which had come to the Bacchiads earlier, had been a riddle to them. But afterward, when they heard the one that had come to Aetion, they understood the first one at once: it agreed with Aetion's. And understanding this one too, they kept quiet, intending to kill the child that would be born to Aetion. So as soon as his wife gave birth, they sent ten of their own number to the village where Aetion lived, to kill the child. When these men had come to Petra and gone into the courtyard of Aetion's house, they asked for the child. Labda had no idea why they had come. She supposed they were asking for the baby out of friendship for its father, so she brought it out and put it in the hands of one of them. Now they had decided on the way, it seems, that whichever of them first took the child would dash it to the ground. But when Labda brought it and handed it over, it so happened, by the hand of heaven, that the baby smiled at the man who had taken it. He saw this, and pity kept him from killing it. Moved by pity, he handed it to the next man, and he to the third. So it passed through the hands of all ten, handed from one to the next, since not one of them could bring himself to kill it. So they gave the child back to its mother and went outside. And then, standing by the door, they argued and blamed one another, especially the man who had taken the child first, because he had not done what they had agreed. At last, after some time, they decided to go in again and all share in the murder.

"But it was fated that evils would grow for Corinth from Aetion's offspring. For Labda was listening to all this as she stood right by the door. Afraid that they would change their minds, take the child a second time and kill it, she carried it off and hid it in the place she thought least likely to be found: a grain chest. She was sure that if they came back to search, they would look everywhere. And that is exactly what happened. When they came and searched and could not find it, they decided to go back and tell those who had sent them that they had done everything they had been ordered to do.

"So they went away and said this. After that, Aetion's son grew up, and because he had escaped this danger, he was given the name Cypselus, after the grain chest (in Greek, kypsele). When Cypselus had grown to manhood and was consulting the oracle, he was given an answer at Delphi that could be read two ways. Trusting in it, he made his attempt on Corinth and took control of it. The answer was this:

	'Happy indeed is the man who now comes into my house:
	son of Aetion, who will be king of famous Corinth,
	Cypselus, he and his sons, but his sons' sons no longer.'

"That was the oracle. And once Cypselus became tyrant, this is the kind of man he was: many of the Corinthians he drove into exile, many he robbed of their wealth, and far more of their lives.

"He ruled for thirty years and ended his life in prosperity, and his son Periander succeeded him as tyrant. At first Periander was gentler than his father. But after he had been in touch through messengers with Thrasybulus, the tyrant of Miletus, he became far more murderous even than Cypselus. He sent a messenger to Thrasybulus to ask what arrangement of affairs would be safest for him to make, so that he could govern his city best. Thrasybulus led the man who had come from Periander out of the city and went into a field of growing grain. As he walked through the crop, he kept questioning the messenger, over and over, about why he had come from Corinth; and all the while, whenever he saw an ear of grain standing taller than the rest, he cut its head off. As he cut the heads off, he threw them away, until in this way he had destroyed the finest and richest part of the crop. Then, having gone through the field, he sent the messenger away without offering a single word of advice. When the messenger got back to Corinth, Periander was eager to hear the advice he had been given. But the man said that Thrasybulus had given him none. He added that he was amazed Periander had sent him to such a man, for the man was out of his mind and was destroying his own property; and he told what he had seen Thrasybulus do.

"Periander understood what had been done. He saw that Thrasybulus was advising him to put to death the most outstanding of his citizens, and from then on he showed every kind of cruelty to the people of his city. Whatever killing and exiling Cypselus had left undone, Periander finished. And in a single day he stripped all the women of Corinth of their clothes, because of his own wife Melissa. He had sent messengers to the Thesprotians, on the river Acheron, to ask the oracle of the dead about some money a guest-friend had left with him for safekeeping. Melissa appeared, and said she would not tell where the money had been put, because she was cold and naked: the clothes he had buried with her were of no use to her, since they had not been burned. And as proof that she was telling the truth, she said, Periander had put his loaves into a cold oven. When this was reported back to Periander, the token convinced him, for he had had sex with Melissa after she was dead. Right after he got the message, he had it proclaimed that all the women of Corinth were to come out to the temple of Hera. So they came as if to a festival, in their finest clothes. He had hidden the spearmen of his bodyguard in ambush, and he stripped them all alike, the free women and their maidservants too. He gathered all their clothes into a pit and burned them, praying to Melissa as he did it. After he had done this and sent to her a second time, the ghost of Melissa told him where he had put the money his guest-friend had left with him.

"There, Spartans, you have it: that is what tyranny is, and those are its deeds. We Corinthians were amazed at first when we saw you sending for Hippias, and now we are even more amazed to hear you say these things. We call on the gods of Greece and beg you not to set up tyrannies in the cities. But if you will not give up your plan, and try to bring Hippias back against all justice, then know this: the Corinthians, for their part, do not consent to what you are doing."

93. That was the speech of Socles, the envoy of Corinth. Hippias answered him, calling on the same gods as he had, and said that the Corinthians, more than anyone, would surely long for the sons of Pisistratus when the appointed days came for them to be harassed by the Athenians. That was Hippias' answer, for he knew the oracles more exactly than any other man. But the rest of the allies, who had held themselves back for a while and kept silent, now heard Socles speak his mind, and every one of them spoke out and said what he felt. They sided with the Corinthian envoy and begged the Spartans not to do any violence to a Greek city.

94. So that plan came to nothing. When Hippias was sent away from there, Amyntas king of the Macedonians offered him Anthemus, and the Thessalians offered him Iolcus. But he accepted neither, and went back again to Sigeum. Pisistratus had taken this city by force of arms from the Mytilenians. Once he had it, he made his own illegitimate son Hegesistratus, born to him by a woman of Argos, tyrant of the place. But Hegesistratus did not keep what he received from Pisistratus without a fight. For the Mytilenians and the Athenians fought a long war, with their strongholds at Achilleum and at Sigeum respectively. The Mytilenians demanded the place back. The Athenians, for their part, refused, and argued that the Aeolians had no better claim to the land of Troy than they themselves and all the other Greeks who had helped Menelaus take revenge for the carrying off of Helen.

95. While they were fighting this war, among the many and various things that happened in the battles, there was this. Once, in a fight the Athenians were winning, Alcaeus the poet ran away. He himself escaped, but the Athenians kept his armor and hung it up on the walls of the temple of Athena at Sigeum. Alcaeus wrote a song about this and sent it to Mytilene, telling his own misfortune to a man named Melanippus, a friend of his. In the end, Periander son of Cypselus made peace between the Athenians and the Mytilenians, for they referred the matter to him to decide. He made peace between them on condition that each side should keep the land it then held.

96. That is how Sigeum came under Athenian rule. Meanwhile, when Hippias had come back to Asia from Sparta, he left no stone unturned. He stirred up hostility between the Athenians and Artaphernes, and he did everything he could to bring Athens under the rule of himself and Darius. That, then, was what Hippias was doing. When the Athenians heard of it, they sent envoys to Sardis and tried to keep the Persians from listening to the exiled Athenians. But Artaphernes ordered them, if they wanted to be saved, to take Hippias back. When this answer was reported, the Athenians were not at all inclined to accept it. And since they did not accept it, it became the settled view among them at once that they were enemies of the Persians.

Chapter 31: Athens Joins the Revolt, the Burning of Sardis, and the Death of Aristagoras

97. The Athenians were thinking this way, and had already been set at odds with the Persians, when at this very moment Aristagoras of Miletus arrived in Athens, after Cleomenes the Spartan had ordered him out of Sparta. He came to Athens because it was the most powerful of all the other cities, after Sparta. Aristagoras came before the assembly of the people and said the same things he had said at Sparta: how much wealth there was in Asia, and how the Persians made war, using neither shield nor spear, so that they were easy to beat. That is what he said, and he added this too: the Milesians were colonists from Athens, and it was only reasonable that the Athenians, with all their power, should rescue them. There was nothing he did not promise, so hard did he press his request, until at last he won them over. It seems it is easier to deceive many people than one: he could not deceive Cleomenes the Spartan on his own, but he managed it with thirty thousand Athenians. So the Athenians, persuaded, voted to send twenty ships to help the Ionians, and they appointed as commander Melanthius, one of their citizens, a man highly respected in every way. These ships were the beginning of troubles for Greeks and non-Greeks alike.

98. Aristagoras, however, sailed on ahead and came to Miletus. There he worked out a plan that was not likely to do the Ionians any good. In fact that was not why he was doing it; he did it to annoy King Darius. He sent a man to Phrygia, to the Paeonians whom Megabazus had carried off as captives from the river Strymon, and who were living by themselves in a district and village of Phrygia. When the messenger reached the Paeonians, he said: "Paeonians, Aristagoras the tyrant of Miletus has sent me to offer you a way to save yourselves, if you are willing to do as he says. All Ionia has now revolted from the king, and you have a chance to get home safe to your own land. Getting to the sea is your business; after that, it will be ours." The Paeonians welcomed this as the best news they could have heard. They took their children and their women and fled for the sea, though some of them were afraid and stayed where they were. When the Paeonians reached the coast they crossed over to Chios. They were already on Chios when a large force of Persian cavalry arrived on their trail, chasing them. Since the horsemen had not caught them, they sent over to Chios to order the Paeonians to come back. The Paeonians refused. Instead the people of Chios carried them from Chios to Lesbos, the Lesbians brought them to Doriscus, and from there they went on by land and reached Paeonia.

99. Meanwhile the Athenians arrived with their twenty ships, bringing with them five triremes from Eretria as well. The Eretrians had not joined the expedition for the Athenians' sake but for the Milesians', to repay a debt they owed them. In earlier times the Milesians had stood with the Eretrians through the whole of their war with the Chalcidians, at the time when the Samians were helping the Chalcidians against the Eretrians and Milesians. So when these ships had arrived and the other allies were on the spot, Aristagoras launched a march on Sardis. He did not go on this march himself. He stayed in Miletus and put others in command of the Milesians: his brother Charopinus, and one of the other citizens, Hermophantus.

100. With this force the Ionians came to Ephesus. They left their ships at Coresus in Ephesian territory and went inland themselves in a large body, with Ephesians to guide them on the march. They marched along the river Cayster, crossed the range of Tmolus, and when they arrived they took Sardis without a fight, all except the citadel. The citadel Artaphernes saved from capture himself, since he had a sizable force of men with him.

101. They took the city, but they were kept from plundering it, and this is why. Most of the houses in Sardis were built of reeds, and even the ones built of brick had roofs thatched with reeds. One of these houses was set on fire by a soldier, and at once the fire spread from house to house over the whole town. As the town burned, the Lydians and all the Persians who were in the city were cut off: the fire had hold of the outskirts all around them, and they had no way out of the town. So they streamed together into the marketplace and to the river Pactolus. The Pactolus carries down gold dust for them from Tmolus. It flows right through the middle of their marketplace and then runs out into the river Hermus, and the Hermus into the sea. At the Pactolus and in the marketplace, then, the Lydians and Persians gathered and were forced to defend themselves. When the Ionians saw some of the enemy standing their ground and others coming on to attack in great numbers, they lost their nerve and pulled back to the mountain called Tmolus. Then, at nightfall, they set off for their ships.

102. So Sardis was burned, and with it the temple of Cybebe, the goddess of that country. Later the Persians used this as their reason for burning the temples in Greece in return. At the time I am speaking of, though, the Persians who held provinces on this side of the river Halys had learned of the attack beforehand and were gathering to come to the Lydians' help. As it happened, when they got there they found the Ionians already gone from Sardis. But they followed hard on their trail and caught up with them at Ephesus. The Ionians lined up against them, but when the battle was joined they were badly beaten. The Persians cut down many men of note, and among those who fell was Eualcides, the Eretrian commander, a man who had won garlands at the games and whom Simonides of Ceos praised again and again in his poems. The Ionians who survived the battle scattered to their various cities.

103. That was how they fought that time. After the battle the Athenians abandoned the Ionians altogether. Aristagoras sent messenger after messenger begging for their help, but they said they would not help them. Even without their Athenian allies, though, the Ionians went on preparing for war with the king, since they had already done Darius so much harm. They also sailed to the Hellespont and brought Byzantium and all the other cities in that region under their control. Then they sailed out of the Hellespont and won most of Caria over to their alliance as well. Even Caunus, which had refused to become their ally before, joined them too after they had burned Sardis.

104. The Cyprians also joined their alliance of their own accord, all except the people of Amathus. They too had revolted from the Persians, and this is how. There was a man named Onesilus, the younger brother of Gorgus king of Salamis in Cyprus. He was the son of Chersis, son of Siromus, son of Euelthon. Even in earlier times this man had often urged Gorgus to revolt from the king, and now, when he heard that the Ionians had revolted, he pressed him very hard and tried to drive him to it. But since he could not persuade Gorgus, Onesilus waited for a time when Gorgus had gone out of the city of Salamis, and then, with the men of his own faction, he shut him out of the gates. Robbed of his city, Gorgus fled to the Persians for refuge. Onesilus became ruler of Salamis and tried to persuade all the Cyprians to revolt with him. He persuaded the rest. But the people of Amathus refused to do what he wanted, so he camped before their city and laid siege to it.

105. So Onesilus was besieging Amathus. Meanwhile King Darius was told that Sardis had been taken and burned by the Athenians and the Ionians together, and that the leader of the alliance that had brought all this about was Aristagoras of Miletus. It is said that when he first heard the news, he paid no attention to the Ionians, because he knew that they at any rate would not get away with their revolt unpunished. But he asked who the Athenians were. When he had been told, he asked for his bow. He took it, fitted an arrow to the string, and shot it upward toward the sky, and as he shot it into the air he said: "Zeus, grant that I may take revenge on the Athenians!" After saying this he ordered one of his servants to say to him three times, every time his dinner was served: "Master, remember the Athenians."

106. After giving this order, he called in Histiaeus of Miletus, whom he had now kept with him for a long time, and said: "I am told, Histiaeus, that your deputy, the man you left in charge of Miletus, has rebelled against me. He brought men over against me from the other continent, and he persuaded the Ionians too (who will pay me the penalty for what they have done) to join them, and so he robbed me of Sardis. Now, how do you think this looks? And how could anything like this have been done without your advice? Be careful you don't find yourself to blame for this later." Histiaeus answered: "My king, what are you saying? That I advised something that was likely to cause you trouble, great or small? What more could I want than what I have, that I would do such things? What do I lack? I have everything you have, and you think me worthy to hear all your plans. No: if my deputy really is doing anything like what you say, you can be sure he has done it entirely on his own. For my part I don't even accept the report as true, that the Milesians and my deputy are doing anything rebellious against your rule. But if it turns out that they really are doing something of the kind, and what you have heard, my king, is the truth, then see what you did when you took me away from the coast. It seems that once I was out of the Ionians' sight, they did what they had long wanted to do. If I had been in Ionia, not one city would have stirred. So let me set out for Ionia as quickly as possible, so that I can put everything back as it was for you and hand over to you this deputy of Miletus who has plotted all this. And when I have done this to your satisfaction, I swear by the gods of the royal house that I will not take off the tunic I am wearing when I go down to Ionia until I have made Sardinia, the largest island in the world, pay you tribute."

107. That was what Histiaeus said, trying to deceive the king. Darius was persuaded and let him go, ordering him to come back to him at Susa when he had done what he had promised.

108. Meanwhile, while the news about Sardis was going up to the king, and while Darius, after what he did with the bow, was talking with Histiaeus, and while Histiaeus, released by Darius, was making his way down to the coast, all through that time the following events were taking place. As Onesilus of Salamis was besieging the people of Amathus, he received word that a Persian named Artybius was expected to arrive in Cyprus shortly, bringing a large Persian army with him by ship. When he heard this, Onesilus sent heralds to various places in Ionia to call the Ionians to his help. They talked it over among themselves and came at once with a large force. The Ionians arrived in Cyprus just when the Persians had crossed over by ship from Cilicia and were marching overland to attack Salamis, while the Phoenicians with the fleet were sailing around the headland called the "Keys of Cyprus."

109. Things being so, the tyrants of Cyprus called the Ionian commanders together and said: "Ionians, we Cyprians give you the choice of which enemy you would rather fight, the Persians or the Phoenicians. If you would rather line up on land and try your strength against the Persians, then it is time for you to get off your ships and form up on land, and for us to board your ships and fight the Phoenicians. But if you would rather take on the Phoenicians, then whichever of the two you choose, you must do your best, as far as it lies with you, to see that both Ionia and Cyprus are free." The Ionians answered: "We were sent out by the common council of the Ionians to guard the sea, not to hand our ships over to the Cyprians and fight the Persians on land ourselves. So we will try to serve well at the post we were given. And you must remember all you suffered when you were slaves of the Persians, and prove yourselves brave men."

110. That was the Ionians' answer. Afterward, when the Persians had come into the plain of Salamis, the Cyprian kings drew up their battle line. They chose the best of the troops from Salamis and from Soli to face the Persians, and set the other Cyprians against the rest of the enemy's troops. And Onesilus, by his own choice, took his place in the line facing Artybius, the Persian commander.

111. Now Artybius rode a horse that had been trained to rear up against a hoplite. Onesilus heard about this. He had a shield-bearer, a Carian by birth, who had a fine reputation as a soldier and was full of courage besides, and he said to him: "I am told that Artybius' horse rears straight up and attacks with both its hooves and its teeth anyone it is driven against. So think it over, and tell me right away which of the two you would rather watch for and strike, the horse or Artybius himself." His attendant answered: "My king, I am ready to do both, or either one, and in every case to do whatever you order. But I will tell you the way I think best suits your position. I say it is right for a king and commander to fight a king and commander. If you kill the enemy commander, it brings you great glory; and on the other hand, if he kills you, which heaven forbid, even death at the hands of a worthy enemy is only half a misfortune. For us who serve under you, it is right to fight the others who serve under him, and his horse. And don't be afraid of the horse's tricks at all. I promise you that after this, at least, it will never stand up against any man again." That is what he said, and soon afterward the two sides joined battle, on land and with their ships.

112. On that day the Ionians fought outstandingly and beat the Phoenicians, and of the Ionians the Samians fought best. Meanwhile on land the armies met, came to close quarters, and fought. As for the two commanders, this is what happened. When Artybius rode at Onesilus on his horse, Onesilus, as he had arranged with his shield-bearer, struck at Artybius himself as he came at him. And when the horse planted its hooves on Onesilus' shield, the Carian struck with a curved sword and cut off the horse's feet.

113. So Artybius, the Persian commander, fell there on the spot, together with his horse. While the rest were still fighting, Stesenor, the tyrant of Curium, deserted them with a large body of men (these men of Curium are said to be settlers from Argos), and as soon as the men of Curium deserted, the war chariots of the men of Salamis did the same as they had. When this happened, the Persians got the upper hand over the Cyprians. Their army was routed, and many fell. Among them were Onesilus son of Chersis, the man who had brought about the Cyprians' revolt, and also the king of Soli, Aristocyprus son of Philocyprus: that same Philocyprus whom Solon the Athenian, when he came to Cyprus, praised in verse above all other tyrants.

114. The people of Amathus cut off Onesilus' head, because he had besieged them. They took it to Amathus and hung it over the city gate. As the head hung there, once it had become hollow, a swarm of bees got into it and filled it with honeycomb. When this happened, the people of Amathus consulted an oracle about the head. The answer told them to take it down and bury it, and to sacrifice to Onesilus every year as a hero; if they did this, things would go better for them.

115. The people of Amathus went on doing this down to my own time. As for the Ionians who had fought the sea battle off Cyprus, they saw that Onesilus' cause was lost and that the Cyprian cities were under siege, all except Salamis, and that the Salaminians had handed Salamis over to Gorgus, their former king. As soon as they saw this, the Ionians sailed back to Ionia. Of the cities in Cyprus, Soli held out against the siege the longest. The Persians took it in the fifth month by digging a tunnel under the wall all around.

116. So the Cyprians, after being free for one year, had been made slaves once again. Meanwhile Daurises, who was married to a daughter of Darius, and Hymaees and Otanes, who were also Persian commanders and also married to daughters of Darius, had chased the Ionians who had marched on Sardis, beaten them in battle and driven them back to their ships by force. After this they divided the cities among themselves and set about sacking them.

117. Daurises headed for the cities on the Hellespont. He took Dardanus, Abydos, Percote, Lampsacus and Paesus, one each day. As he was marching from Paesus against the city of Parium, word came that the Carians had made common cause with the Ionians and revolted from the Persians. So he turned back from the Hellespont and marched his army against Caria.

118. As it happened, news of this reached the Carians before Daurises arrived. When they heard it, the Carians gathered at the place called the "White Pillars," on the river Marsyas, which flows from the region of Idrias and empties into the Maeander. When the Carians had gathered there, many plans were put forward. The best of them, I think, was that of Pixodarus son of Mausolus, a man from Cindya, who was married to the daughter of Syennesis, king of the Cilicians. His advice was that the Carians should cross the Maeander and fight the Persians with the river at their backs. That way the Carians, unable to run away and forced to stand where they were, would prove even braver fighters than they naturally were. This advice did not carry the day. Instead they decided that the Persians, and not they themselves, should have the Maeander at their backs. Their idea, clearly, was that if the Persians were routed and beaten in the battle, they would never get home but would end up in the river.

119. After this the Persians arrived and crossed the Maeander, and the Carians met them on the river Marsyas. They fought a hard battle that went on a long time, but in the end the Carians were beaten by sheer numbers. As many as two thousand Persians fell, but ten thousand Carians. Those of them who escaped were penned in at Labraunda, in the sanctuary of Zeus Stratius, Zeus of Armies, which is a large sacred grove of plane trees. The Carians are the only people we know of who sacrifice to Zeus Stratius. Penned in there, they were discussing how to save themselves: whether they would do better to surrender to the Persians or to leave Asia altogether.

120. While they were discussing this, the Milesians and their allies came to their aid. Then the Carians dropped the plans they had been considering and got ready to start the war all over again. When the Persians came to attack them, they met them and fought a battle, and were beaten even worse than before. Many fell on every side, but the Milesians suffered most.

121. Later on, though, the Carians made up for this loss and recovered from their defeat. They learned that the Persians had set out to march against their cities, and they laid an ambush on the road near Pedasus. The Persians fell into it by night and were wiped out, they and their commanders, Daurises, Amorges and Sisimaces; and Myrsus son of Gyges died with them too. The leader of this ambush was Heraclides son of Ibanollis, a man from Mylasa.

122. That was how these Persians were destroyed. Meanwhile Hymaees, another of those who had pursued the Ionians who marched on Sardis, headed for the Propontis and took Cius in Mysia. After conquering this city, when he heard that Daurises had left the Hellespont and was marching toward Caria, he left the Propontis and led his army to the Hellespont. There he conquered all the Aeolians who live in the region of Troy, and also the Gergithes, who are what is left of the ancient Teucrians. While he was conquering these peoples, Hymaees himself died of an illness in the Troad.

123. So he came to his end. Then Artaphernes, the governor of the province of Sardis, was appointed, together with Otanes, the third of the commanders, to march against Ionia and the part of Aeolis next to it. In Ionia they took the city of Clazomenae, and in Aeolis, Cyme.

124. While the cities were being taken, Aristagoras of Miletus showed, in this case, that he was not a man of any great courage. He had stirred up Ionia and set great things going, and when he saw how matters stood, he thought of running away. Besides, it had become clear to him that there was no way to beat King Darius. With all this in mind, he called the men of his own party together and talked it over with them. He told them it would be better to have a refuge ready for themselves, in case they were driven out of Miletus after all. And he put the question to them whether he should lead them from there to Sardinia to found a colony, or to Myrcinus in the land of the Edonians, which Histiaeus had been fortifying after receiving it as a gift from Darius. That was the question Aristagoras put to them.

125. Now the advice of Hecataeus son of Hegesander, the historian, was that he should not lead a colony to either of these places. Instead, if he were forced out of Miletus, he should build himself a fortress on the island of Leros and lie low. Later, using this as his base, he would be able to return to Miletus.

126. That was Hecataeus' advice. But Aristagoras leaned most toward going to Myrcinus. So he handed the government of Miletus over to Pythagoras, a respected man among the citizens, and he himself sailed off to Thrace, taking with him everyone who wanted to go, and took possession of the region he had set out for. But setting out from there to make war, he was killed by the Thracians, both Aristagoras himself and his army, while he was camped around a certain city whose Thracian defenders wanted to leave it under a truce.

Book Six: Erato

Chapter 32: The Battle of Lade, the Fall of Miletus, and the End of Histiaeus

1. So Aristagoras, after causing Ionia to revolt, came to his end in this way. Meanwhile Histiaeus, the tyrant of Miletus, had been let go by Darius and had arrived at Sardis. When he came from Susa, Artaphernes, the governor of Sardis, asked him why he supposed the Ionians had revolted. Histiaeus said that he could not tell. What is more, he expressed surprise at what had happened, pretending that he knew nothing about the state of affairs. But Artaphernes saw that he was being dishonest, and since he knew the truth about the revolt, he said: "This is how it is with you and these matters, Histiaeus. You stitched this shoe, and Aristagoras put it on."

2. That is what Artaphernes said about the revolt. Histiaeus was afraid of Artaphernes, because Artaphernes understood the business, so as soon as night fell the next evening he ran away to the coast. He had deceived King Darius: he had promised to bring Sardinia, the largest of the islands, under the king's control, and instead he was trying to take over the leadership of the Ionians in their war against Darius. He crossed over to Chios, and there the Chians put him in chains, accusing him of working on Darius' orders to overthrow their government. But when the Chians learned the whole story and heard that he was an enemy of the king, they set him free.

3. Then the Ionians asked Histiaeus why he had pressed Aristagoras so urgently to revolt from the king and had brought so great a disaster on the Ionians. He did not by any means tell them the real reason. Instead he told them that King Darius had decided to move the Phoenicians out of their country and settle them in Ionia, and to settle the Ionians in Phoenicia; and that, he said, was why he had sent the message. In this way he tried to frighten the Ionians, though the king had never decided anything of the kind.

4. After this Histiaeus used a messenger, a man of Atarneus named Hermippus, to send letters to some Persians at Sardis, written as though he had already talked over a revolt with them. But Hermippus did not deliver the letters to the men he was sent to. He took them instead and handed them to Artaphernes. Artaphernes, seeing everything that was going on, told Hermippus to carry Histiaeus' letters on and deliver them to the men they were meant for, and then to hand over to him the replies the Persians sent back to Histiaeus. Once all this had been found out, Artaphernes put many of the Persians to death.

5. So the plan at Sardis came to nothing. When Histiaeus had been let down in this hope, the Chians tried to bring him back to Miletus, at his own request. But the Milesians had been glad before to be rid of Aristagoras, and they were by no means eager to take another tyrant into their country, now that they had had a taste of freedom. In fact, when Histiaeus tried to get back into Miletus by force, under cover of night, one of the Milesians wounded him in the thigh. Driven away from his own city, he went back to Chios. From there, since he could not persuade the Chians to give him ships, he crossed over to Mytilene and tried to persuade the people of Lesbos to give him some. They manned eight triremes and sailed with Histiaeus to Byzantium. They stationed themselves there and seized the ships sailing out of the Black Sea, except those whose crews said they were ready to do whatever Histiaeus told them.

6. While Histiaeus and the men of Mytilene were doing this, a great army, both a fleet and a land force, was getting ready to attack Miletus itself. The Persian commanders had joined their forces into one single army and were marching on Miletus, counting the other towns of less importance. Of the fleet, the most eager were the Phoenicians, and with them served the Cyprians, who had just been conquered, and the Cilicians and the Egyptians.

7. So these forces were advancing on Miletus and the rest of Ionia. Meanwhile the Ionians, when they heard of it, sent delegates chosen from among themselves to the Panionium. When the delegates arrived there and talked it over, they decided not to gather a land army to face the Persians. The Milesians would defend their walls by themselves, and the Ionians would man their fleet, leaving out not a single ship, and then gather as soon as possible at Lade to fight a sea battle in defense of Miletus. Lade is a small island lying opposite the city of Miletus.

8. Then the Ionians manned their ships and came to Lade, and with them came the Aeolians who live on Lesbos. They were drawn up in this order. The eastern end of the line was held by the Milesians themselves, who supplied eighty ships. Next to them were the men of Priene with twelve ships and the men of Myus with three. Next to the men of Myus were the men of Teos with seventeen ships, and after the men of Teos, the Chians with a hundred. After them were stationed the men of Erythrae and of Phocaea, the first with eight ships and the second with three. Next to the Phocaeans were the Lesbians with seventy ships. Last of all, holding the western end of the line, were the Samians with sixty ships. All together these came to 353 triremes.

9. Those were the Ionian ships, and the ships on the non-Greek side numbered six hundred. When these too had arrived off the coast of Miletus, and the whole land army was there as well, the Persian commanders learned how many ships the Ionians had. They were afraid that they might not be able to beat them. In that case they would not be able to take Miletus, since they would not control the sea, and at the same time they would be in danger of being punished by Darius. With this in mind they gathered the tyrants of the Ionians. These men had been driven out of their cities by Aristagoras of Miletus and had fled to the Persians, and they happened to be taking part in the expedition against Miletus. The commanders called together those of them who were there and spoke to them like this: "Men of Ionia, now let each of you show that he is a benefactor of the king's house. That is, let each of you try to separate his own people from the rest of the alliance. Make them an offer, and promise them at the same time that they will suffer nothing unpleasant because of the revolt: neither their temples nor their homes will be burned, and they will be treated no worse than they were before. But if they will not do this, and are determined to fight it out with us, then threaten them, and tell them what will truly happen to them. If they are beaten in the battle, they will be made slaves. We will make their sons eunuchs, we will carry their young girls off to Bactria, and we will hand their land over to others."

10. That is what they said, and the tyrants of Ionia each sent a message by night to his own people, telling them this. But the Ionians who received these messages stood firm and would not consider betraying their cause. Each people thought the Persians were sending this message to them alone.

11. This happened as soon as the Persians arrived at Miletus. After this the Ionians who had gathered at Lade held meetings. Others no doubt made speeches to them too, but above all the Phocaean commander Dionysius, who said this: "Men of Ionia, our fortunes stand on a razor's edge: whether we will be free or slaves, and slaves who are treated as runaways at that. So if you are willing to take on hardships now, you will have hard work for the time being, but you will be able to beat the enemy and be free. But if you go on being soft and undisciplined, I have no hope that you will escape paying the king the penalty for your revolt. So do as I say, and put yourselves in my hands. If the gods give us a fair fight, I promise you that either the enemy will not fight us at all, or, if he does, he will be badly beaten."

12. When they heard this, the Ionians put themselves in Dionysius' hands. Every day he would take the ships out in single file, so that he could train the rowers by having the ships break through each other's line, and so that the marines on board would be armed and ready. Then for the rest of the day he would keep the ships at anchor. So he kept the Ionians working the whole day long. For seven days they put up with it and did what he ordered. But on the day after that, the Ionians, who were not used to such hard work and were worn out by the labor and the hot sun, said to one another: "Which of the gods have we offended, to fill up our share of misery like this? We have surely handed ourselves over to a Phocaean, a fraud, who brings only three ships. He has got us in his hands and is treating us so badly that we will never recover. Many of us have already fallen sick, and many more are likely to suffer the same thing soon. It would be better for us to put up with anything else in the world than these miseries, and better to face the slavery that is coming, whatever it turns out to be, than to be crushed by the one we have now. Come on, let's not obey him any more." That is what they said, and at once every one of them refused to obey him. They pitched their tents on the island like an army camp and stayed in the shade, and they would not go on board their ships or do any training.

13. When the Samian commanders saw what the Ionians were doing, they at last accepted the offer that Aeaces son of Syloson had sent them earlier at the Persians' bidding, asking them to leave the Ionian alliance. The Samians accepted this offer because they saw how completely undisciplined the Ionians were. At the same time it was clear to them that it was impossible to beat the king's power, and they knew well that even if they beat the fleet Darius had there now, another five times as large would come against them. So they seized on this excuse, and as soon as they saw that the Ionians refused to do their duty, they thought it would be a gain for themselves to save their temples and their own property. This Aeaces, whose offer the Samians accepted, was the son of Syloson son of Aeaces. He had been tyrant of Samos, and like the other tyrants of Ionia he had been deprived of his power by Aristagoras of Miletus.

14. So when the Phoenicians sailed out to attack, the Ionians also put out their ships against them, sailing in single file. When they came close and the battle began, I cannot say for certain from that point on which of the Ionians proved themselves cowards and which proved themselves brave in this sea battle, because they all blame each other. But it is said that the Samians, as they had agreed with Aeaces, then raised their sails, left their place in the line, and sailed off home to Samos, all except eleven ships. The captains of these stayed in their places and fought in the battle, refusing to obey the commanders of their squadron. Because of this the Samian state granted them the honor of having their names, and their fathers' names too, inscribed on a pillar as men who had proved themselves brave, and this pillar still stands in their marketplace. Then the Lesbians, when they saw the ships next to them in the line running away, did the same as the Samians had done, and so did most of the Ionians.

15. Of those who stayed and fought, the Chians were hit hardest, because they did brilliant deeds and refused to play the coward. As I said before, they had supplied a hundred ships, and on each of them forty picked men from among their citizens served as marines. When they saw most of their allies deserting them, they did not think it right to behave like the cowards among them. Left with only a few of their allies, they kept on fighting and kept breaking through the enemy's line, until at last, after they had captured many enemy ships, they lost most of their own.

16. The Chians then fled home to their own island with the rest of their ships. But the Chians whose ships had been disabled by damage were chased, and they fled for refuge to Mycale. There they ran their ships aground and left them, and went on overland on foot. On the way the Chians entered the territory of Ephesus. They came into it at night, at a time when the women of the place were celebrating the Thesmophoria. The Ephesians had not heard beforehand what had happened to the Chians, and when they saw an armed band entering their land, they were quite sure these men were robbers who had come after the women. So they turned out in full force to the rescue and killed the Chians.

17. That was the fate of these men. But Dionysius the Phocaean, when he saw that the Ionian cause was lost, captured three enemy ships and sailed away. He did not go back to Phocaea, because he knew very well that it would be made slaves along with the rest of Ionia. Instead he sailed at once straight for Phoenicia. There he sank some merchant ships and took a great deal of plunder, and then he sailed on to Sicily. With Sicily as his base he became a pirate, though he never plundered any Greeks, only Carthaginians and Etruscans.

18. So the Persians, having beaten the Ionians in the sea battle, besieged Miletus by land and by sea. They dug mines under the walls and brought every kind of siege engine against it. In the sixth year after the revolt of Aristagoras they took the city completely and made the people slaves, so that the disaster agreed with the oracle that had been given about Miletus.

19. For when the Argives were consulting the oracle at Delphi about the safety of their city, they were given an oracle with two parts. One part was about the Argives themselves, while the part added on at the end was about the Milesians. The part about the Argives I will record when I reach that point in my history. But what the oracle said about the Milesians, who were not there, is this:

	"And at that time, Miletus, you plotter of evil deeds,
	you will be made a feast and a glorious prize for many.
	Your wives will wash the feet of the long-haired men,
	and others will tend my temple at Didyma."

These things came upon the Milesians at the time I am speaking of. Most of their men were killed by the Persians, who wear their hair long, and their women and children were treated as slaves. The temple at Didyma, with its shrine and the seat of the oracle, was plundered and then burned. I have often mentioned the treasures in this temple in other parts of my history.

20. After this the Milesians who had been taken prisoner were brought to Susa. King Darius did them no further harm. He settled them on the sea called the Erythraean, the Persian Gulf, in the city of Ampe, where the river Tigris flows past on its way out to the sea. Of the land of Miletus, the Persians kept for themselves the country around the city and the plain, and they gave the hill country to the Carians of Pedasa to own.

21. When the Milesians suffered this at the hands of the Persians, the people of Sybaris, who had lost their own city and were living in Laus and Scidrus, did not repay them in kind. When Sybaris was taken by the men of Croton, all the Milesians, from the young men up, had shaved their heads and gone into deep mourning; for these two cities were bound by closer ties of friendship than any others we know of. The Athenians were not like the Sybarites. They made it plain that they were grieved at the capture of Miletus, in many other ways and especially in this one. When Phrynichus wrote a play called "The Capture of Miletus" and put it on the stage, the whole audience burst into tears. The Athenians fined the poet a thousand drachmas for reminding them of their own misfortunes, and they ordered that no one should ever put on that play again.

22. So Miletus was stripped of its old inhabitants. But among the Samians, the men of property were not at all happy with the deal their fleet's commanders had made with the Persians. They held a meeting right after the sea battle, and they decided to sail away and found a colony before their tyrant Aeaces arrived in the country, rather than stay behind and be slaves to the Persians and to Aeaces. For just at this time the people of Zancle in Sicily were sending messengers to Ionia, inviting the Ionians to come to the "Fair Shore," because they wanted to found a city of Ionians there. This place called the Fair Shore is in the land of the Sicels, the native people of Sicily, on the side of the island that faces Tyrrhenia. So when the Zanclaeans made this invitation, the Samians alone of all the Ionians set out, taking with them those Milesians who had escaped. And in the course of this business, here is what happened.

23. On their way to Sicily the Samians reached Locri Epizephyrii, the Locri of the West. At that same time the people of Zancle, along with their king, whose name was Scythes, were camped around a town of the Sicels, trying to capture it. When Anaxilaus, the tyrant of Rhegium, saw this, since he was on bad terms with the Zanclaeans, he got in touch with the Samians and persuaded them to leave the Fair Shore alone, where they were sailing, and seize Zancle instead, since it was now left without men to defend it. The Samians did as he said and took Zancle. When the Zanclaeans learned that their city was in enemy hands, they set out to rescue it, and they called in Hippocrates, the tyrant of Gela, who was their ally, to help them. But when Hippocrates had come up with his army to rescue them, first he put Scythes, the ruler of the Zanclaeans, in chains, on the grounds that he was to blame for the loss of the city, and with him his brother Pythogenes, and he sent them off to the town of Inycus. Then he betrayed the rest of the Zanclaeans by coming to terms with the Samians and exchanging oaths with them. In return for this the Samians had promised that Hippocrates would receive as his share half of all the movable goods and the slaves in the city, and everything out in the countryside. So he put most of the Zanclaeans in chains and kept them as his own slaves. But the leading men among them, three hundred in number, he handed over to the Samians to be put to death. The Samians, however, did not do it.

24. Scythes, the ruler of the Zanclaeans, escaped from Inycus to Himera, and from there he went to Asia and up to the court of Darius. Darius considered him the most honest of all the men who had come up to him from Greece. For he got the king's permission to go away to Sicily, and then came back again from Sicily to the king; and at last he died among the Persians, an old man and very rich. So the Samians, having escaped the rule of the Persians, had won themselves the fine city of Zancle without any effort.

25. After the sea battle that was fought for Miletus, the Phoenicians, on the Persians' orders, brought Aeaces son of Syloson back to Samos, because he had been of great service to them and had done great things for them. Of all who had revolted from Darius, the Samians alone did not have their city or their temples burned, because of the ships that deserted in the sea battle. Then, after the capture of Miletus, the Persians at once took possession of Caria. Some of the cities submitted to them of their own free will, and others they brought over by force.

26. That is how these things turned out. Meanwhile Histiaeus of Miletus was at Byzantium, seizing the Ionians' merchant ships as they sailed out of the Black Sea, when the news reached him of what had happened at Miletus. He handed over his business in the Hellespont to Bisaltes son of Apollophanes, a man of Abydos, while he himself sailed with the Lesbians to Chios. When a garrison of the Chians would not let him land, he fought them at the place in Chian territory called the "Hollows." Histiaeus killed many of them. Then, using Polichne in Chios as his base, he and the Lesbians conquered the rest of the Chians too, since they had suffered heavy losses in the sea battle.

27. Heaven usually, I suppose, gives some sign beforehand when great disasters are about to fall on a city or a people. And the Chians too had had remarkable signs before these events. First, when they had sent a chorus of a hundred young men to Delphi, only two came home again; the other ninety-eight were struck down by a plague and died. Second, in their city at about the same time, a little before the sea battle, the roof fell in on some children while they were being taught their letters in school, so that of 120 children only one escaped. These were the signs heaven showed them beforehand. After that the sea battle came upon them and brought their state to its knees, and since the Chians had suffered such heavy losses, Histiaeus conquered them without difficulty.

28. From there Histiaeus led an expedition against Thasos, with a large force of Ionians and Aeolians. While he was camped around the town of Thasos, news came to him that the Phoenicians were sailing up from Miletus to conquer the rest of Ionia. When he heard this, he left Thasos unconquered and hurried to Lesbos himself, taking his whole army with him. Then, since his army was short of food, he crossed over from Lesbos to harvest the grain in Atarneus, and also the grain in the plain of the Caicus, which belonged to the Mysians. In those parts there happened to be a Persian named Harpagus in command of a sizable army. He fought Histiaeus after he had landed, took Histiaeus himself prisoner, and destroyed most of his army.

29. This is how Histiaeus was taken prisoner. The Greeks were fighting the Persians at Malene in the district of Atarneus. When they had been fighting hand to hand for a long time, the cavalry at last charged and fell on the Greeks; in fact it was the cavalry that decided the battle. So when the Greeks had been put to flight, Histiaeus, trusting that the king would not put him to death for the wrong he had just done, was seized with a love of life. When he was being caught in his flight by a Persian, and was just about to be run through at the moment of his capture, he spoke in Persian and told the man who he was: Histiaeus of Miletus.

30. Now if he had been taken prisoner and brought to King Darius, he would not, I think, have suffered any harm; Darius would have forgiven him the crime he was charged with. But as it was, for this very reason, and so that he would not escape punishment and become powerful with the king again, Artaphernes, the governor of Sardis, and Harpagus, the man who had captured him, put him to death on the spot when he reached Sardis on his way to the king. They impaled his body, but they embalmed his head and sent it up to Darius at Susa. When Darius learned of this, he blamed the men who had done it, because they had not brought Histiaeus up to him alive. He ordered that Histiaeus' head be washed and properly cared for, and then buried as the head of a man who had been a great benefactor both of the king himself and of the Persians.

31. That is what happened to Histiaeus. Meanwhile the Persian fleet wintered near Miletus, and when it put to sea again the next year, it easily conquered the islands lying off the mainland, Chios, Lesbos and Tenedos. Whenever they took one of the islands, the Persians, as each was conquered, swept it clear of its people with a dragnet. This is how they do it. The men link hands, each holding the hand of the next, and stretch in a line from the sea on the north to the sea on the south, and then they march across the whole island, hunting the people out of it. They also took the Ionian cities on the mainland in the same way, except that they did not sweep off the inhabitants like this, because it was not possible.

32. Then the Persian commanders proved that their threats against the Ionians, made when the two sides were camped facing each other, had not been empty. When they conquered the cities, they picked out the best-looking boys and castrated them, making them eunuchs, and they carried off the most beautiful girls by force to the king. And not only this: they also burned the cities, temples and all. So the Ionians had been made slaves for the third time, first by the Lydians and then twice in a row by the Persians.

33. Leaving Ionia, the fleet went on to conquer all the places on the left-hand side of the Hellespont as you sail in; those on the right had already been conquered by the Persians themselves, coming at them by land. The cities on the European side of the Hellespont are these. First comes the Chersonese, which has many cities in it; then Perinthus, the forts along the Thracian border, Selymbria, and Byzantium. The people of Byzantium, and the people of Chalcedon across the strait from them, did not even wait for the Phoenician ships to come. They had left their own land first and gone away into the Black Sea, and there they settled in the city of Mesambria. So the Phoenicians burned the places I have named and then headed for Proconnesus and Artace. When they had set fire to these too, they sailed back to the Chersonese to destroy the remaining cities, the ones they had not sacked when they put in there before. But they did not sail against Cyzicus at all, because the people of Cyzicus had already submitted to the king of their own accord, even before the Phoenicians sailed in. They had made terms with Oebares son of Megabazus, the Persian governor at Dascylium.

34. In the Chersonese, then, the Phoenicians took all the cities except Cardia. Up to that time the tyrant of these cities had been Miltiades son of Cimon son of Stesagoras. An earlier Miltiades, the son of Cypselus, had won this rule in the way I will now describe. The people who lived in this Chersonese were Thracians called the Dolonci. These Dolonci were being hard pressed in a war with the Apsinthians, so they sent their kings to Delphi to consult the oracle about the war. The Pythia answered that they must bring into their country, as the founder of a settlement, the first man who offered them hospitality on their way back from the temple. So the Dolonci went along the Sacred Way through the lands of the Phocians and the Boeotians, and since no one invited them in, they turned aside and came to Athens.

35. At that time Pisistratus held power in Athens, but Miltiades son of Cypselus was also a man of some influence. He came from a family rich enough to keep four-horse chariot teams. The family was descended in the beginning from Aeacus and the nymph Aegina, though in more recent times it had been Athenian; the first of the house to become an Athenian was Philaeus son of Ajax. This Miltiades was sitting in the porch of his house when he saw the Dolonci going by, wearing clothes that were not Athenian in style and carrying spears. He called out to them, and when they came over, he offered them a place to stay and his hospitality. They accepted, and after he had entertained them they told him everything the oracle had said. When they had told it, they asked him to do as the god had said. As soon as Miltiades heard it, he was inclined to agree, because he was tired of Pisistratus' rule and wanted to be out of the way. So he set out at once for Delphi to ask the oracle whether he should do what the Dolonci were asking of him.

36. The Pythia told him to do it too. So Miltiades son of Cypselus, who had already won the four-horse chariot race at Olympia, took with him every Athenian who wanted to join the expedition, sailed with the Dolonci, and took possession of the land; and the people who had invited him made him their tyrant. The first thing he did was build a wall across the isthmus of the Chersonese, from the city of Cardia to Pactye, so that the Apsinthians could not invade the land and do them harm. At this point the isthmus is about four miles across, and from this isthmus the Chersonese inside it is about forty-seven miles long in all.

37. When Miltiades had walled off the neck of the Chersonese and had kept the Apsinthians out in this way, the first people he made war on were the people of Lampsacus. The Lampsacenes laid an ambush and took him prisoner. Now Miltiades had become a friend of Croesus the Lydian. So when Croesus heard what had happened, he sent word to the Lampsacenes, ordering them to let Miltiades go; if not, he threatened to wipe them out like a pine tree. The Lampsacenes went round in circles arguing over what Croesus could mean by this threat, that he would wipe them out like a pine tree. At last one of the older men worked out the truth, with difficulty. He said that the pine is the only tree that, once it has been cut down, never puts out any new shoots, but dies and is gone for good. So the Lampsacenes, out of fear of Croesus, set Miltiades free and let him go.

38. So Miltiades escaped, thanks to Croesus. But later he died without leaving a son, and he passed his power and his property to Stesagoras, the son of Cimon, his half-brother on his mother's side. The people of the Chersonese still offer sacrifices to Miltiades since his death, as the custom is for a city's founder, and they hold a contest of horse races and athletics in his honor, in which no one from Lampsacus is allowed to compete. After this there was war with the Lampsacenes, and Stesagoras too died without a son. He was struck on the head with an axe in the town hall by a man who pretended to be a deserter, but who turned out in fact to be an enemy, and a rather hot-tempered one at that.

39. After Stesagoras had died in this way, Miltiades son of Cimon, the brother of the dead Stesagoras, was sent out in a trireme to the Chersonese to take over the government. The sons of Pisistratus sent him. They had treated him well at Athens too, pretending that they had had no part in the death of his father Cimon; how that death came about I will explain in another part of my history. When Miltiades arrived in the Chersonese, he stayed shut up in his house, apparently paying honor to the memory of his brother Stesagoras. When the leading men of the Chersonese in every town heard of this, they gathered from all the cities and came in a body to offer their sympathy, and when they arrived he had them thrown in chains. So Miltiades held the Chersonese, keeping a force of five hundred mercenaries. He married Hegesipyle, the daughter of Olorus, king of the Thracians.

40. Now this Miltiades son of Cimon had only recently come back to the Chersonese at the time I am speaking of. After he came back, worse misfortunes fell on him than the ones that had already happened. Two years before this he had been driven out of the country by the Scythians. The nomad Scythians, provoked by King Darius, had joined forces in a body and marched as far as this Chersonese. Miltiades had not waited for them to attack, but had fled from the Chersonese, until at last the Scythians went away and the Dolonci brought him back again. All this happened two years before the troubles that now pressed on him.

41. But now, when he learned that the Phoenicians were at Tenedos, he loaded five triremes with the property he had at hand and sailed off for Athens. He set out from the city of Cardia and was sailing across the Gulf of Melas. As he was passing along the coast of the Chersonese, the Phoenicians came upon his ships. Miltiades himself escaped to Imbros with four of his ships, but the fifth was caught by the Phoenicians as they chased him. It happened that the captain of this ship was Metiochus, the eldest of Miltiades' sons, whose mother was not the daughter of Olorus the Thracian but another woman. The Phoenicians captured him along with his ship. When they found out that he was Miltiades' son, they took him up to the king, thinking that they would earn a great deal of gratitude for it. For it was Miltiades who had given his opinion to the Ionians that they should do as the Scythians said, back when the Scythians asked them to break up the bridge of boats and sail home. But when the Phoenicians brought Metiochus son of Miltiades up to Darius, Darius did him no harm at all. On the contrary, he did him a great deal of good. He gave him a house and property and a Persian wife, and the children she bore him have been counted as Persians. Meanwhile Miltiades made his way from Imbros to Athens.

42. During this year the Persians did nothing more against the Ionians that led to conflict, but in this same year they did the following things, which were very much to the Ionians' advantage. Artaphernes, the governor of Sardis, sent for envoys from all the cities and made the Ionians agree among themselves to settle their disputes by law and not to raid one another's land. He forced them to do this. He also measured their territories in parasangs, which is what the Persians call a distance of thirty stades, about three and a third miles. Using this measure, he fixed an amount of tribute for each people. That tribute has stayed unchanged from that time down to my own day, just as Artaphernes fixed it; and he fixed it at nearly the same amount for each people as it had been before.

Chapter 33: Mardonius in Thrace, Earth and Water, and Cleomenes against Demaratus

43. These measures made for peace among the Ionians. But at the beginning of spring, after the king had removed all the other commanders, Mardonius son of Gobryas came down to the coast.
