He brought with him a very large army and a very large fleet. He was a young man, and he had recently married Artozostra, the daughter of King Darius. When Mardonius reached Cilicia at the head of this army, he went on board a ship himself and sailed on with the rest of the fleet, while other commanders led the land army to the Hellespont. Mardonius sailed along the coast of Asia and came to Ionia. And here I will report something that will amaze those Greeks who refuse to believe that Otanes, speaking to the seven Persians, gave it as his opinion that the Persians ought to be governed by the people. For Mardonius removed all the Ionian tyrants and set up democracies in the cities. After doing this he hurried on to the Hellespont. When a huge number of ships and a large land army had been gathered there, they crossed the Hellespont in the ships and began to march through Europe. Their goal was Eretria and Athens.

44. Those two cities, that is, were their excuse for the expedition. But what they had in mind was to conquer as many of the Greek cities as they could. First, with the fleet, they conquered the Thasians, who did not even lift a hand to defend themselves. Then with the land army they made the Macedonians their subjects, adding them to the peoples they already ruled; for all the nations east of the Macedonians had already come under their power before this. So they crossed from Thasos to the mainland opposite and went along close to the shore as far as Acanthus. Then, setting out from Acanthus, they tried to round Mount Athos. But as they were sailing around it, a violent north wind fell on them. They could do nothing against it, and it handled them very roughly, wrecking a great many of their ships on Athos. In fact, it is said that three hundred ships were destroyed and more than twenty thousand men. For the sea around Athos is full of sea monsters, and some of the men were seized by these and died that way; others were dashed against the rocks; some did not know how to swim and drowned for that reason; and others died of the cold.

45. That is what happened to the fleet. Meanwhile, while Mardonius and the land army were camped in Macedonia, the Brygian Thracians attacked them by night. The Brygians killed many of them and wounded Mardonius himself. Even so, not even the Brygians escaped being enslaved by the Persians, for Mardonius did not leave that region until he had made them his subjects. But once he had conquered them, he led his army back home, since he had suffered heavy losses, with his land army in the fighting against the Brygians and with his fleet in the voyage around Athos. So this expedition went back to Asia having won no glory in its struggles.

46. In the year after this, Darius first sent a messenger to the Thasians, whose neighbors had accused them of planning a revolt. He ordered them to pull down the wall around their town and bring their ships to Abdera. The fact was that the Thasians, having been besieged by Histiaeus of Miletus, and having large revenues coming in at the same time, were spending their money on building warships and on surrounding their city with a stronger wall. Their revenues came from the mainland and from the mines. From the gold mines at Scapte Hyle there generally came in eighty talents a year, and from the mines on Thasos itself somewhat less than that. Altogether the Thasians, who paid no taxes on what their land produced, generally had a revenue from the mainland and the mines of two hundred talents a year, and in the best years three hundred.

47. I saw these mines myself. By far the most remarkable of them were the ones discovered by the Phoenicians who first settled this island together with Thasos; the island got the name it has now from this Thasos, the Phoenician. These Phoenician mines are in the part of Thasos between the places called Aenyra and Coenyra, opposite Samothrace, where there is a great mountain that has been turned completely upside down in the search for metal. So much for that. At the king's command the Thasians tore down their walls and brought all their ships to Abdera.

48. After this Darius began to test the Greeks, to find out what they meant to do: whether they would make war on him or surrender themselves. So he sent heralds out, assigning them to different places all over Greece, and ordered them to demand earth and water for the king. He sent these to Greece. At the same time he was sending other heralds to the tribute-paying cities of his own along the coast, ordering them to build warships and also transport ships for horses.

49. So they were busy preparing these. Meanwhile, when the heralds arrived in Greece, many of the peoples on the mainland gave what the Persian demanded, and so did all the islanders the heralds came to with their demand. The islanders gave earth and water to Darius, and among them were the Aeginetans. As soon as they had done so, the Athenians went after them hard. They believed the Aeginetans had given it out of hostility to themselves, meaning to join the Persians in an attack on Athens; and they were also glad to get hold of an excuse against them. So they went back and forth to Sparta, accusing the Aeginetans of what they had done and charging them with having betrayed Greece.

50. Because of this accusation, Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, king of the Spartans, crossed over to Aegina, meaning to arrest the Aeginetans who were most to blame. But when he tried to seize them, some of the Aeginetans resisted him, above all Crius son of Polycritus. Crius said that Cleomenes would not get away with carrying off a single Aeginetan. He was doing this, Crius said, without the authority of the Spartan state, because the Athenians had bribed him to do it; otherwise he would have come with the other king to arrest them. He said this because of a message he had received from Demaratus. As Cleomenes was leaving Aegina, he asked Crius what his name was, and Crius told him the truth. Cleomenes, playing on the name, which means "Ram" in Greek, said to him: "Well then, Ram, you had better plate your horns with bronze now, because you are about to run into big trouble."

51. Meanwhile Demaratus son of Ariston had stayed behind in Sparta and was making accusations against Cleomenes. Demaratus too was king of the Spartans, but of the junior house. This house is junior in no other way, since both houses descend from the same ancestor; but the house of Eurysthenes has always been honored more, apparently because he was the elder brother.

52. For the Spartans, who on this point disagree with all the poets, say that it was Aristodemus son of Aristomachus son of Cleodaeus son of Hyllus, while he was their king, who led them himself into the land they now hold, and not the sons of Aristodemus. Not long afterward, they say, Aristodemus' wife, whose name was Argeia, gave birth to twins. She was the daughter, they say, of Autesion son of Tisamenes son of Thersander son of Polynices. Aristodemus lived just long enough to see his children, and then he fell sick and died. The Spartans of that time decided, following their established custom, to make the elder of the children their king. But they did not know which one to choose, because the two were alike and the same size. When they could not tell them apart (or even before this), they asked the mother. She said that even she could not tell one from the other. She said this although in fact she knew perfectly well, because she wanted both of them to become kings somehow. So the Spartans were at a loss, and being at a loss, they sent to Delphi to ask what they should do. The Pythia told them to treat both children as their kings, but to give more honor to the elder. That, they say, was the answer the priestess gave them. But the Spartans were still at a loss how to find out which was the elder, until a Messenian named Panites gave them a suggestion. Panites suggested that the Spartans watch the mother and see which of the children she washed and fed first. If she was seen to do it always in the same order, then they would have everything they were looking for and wanted to find out. But if she too was uncertain and did it in a different order at different times, it would be clear to them that she knew no more than anyone else, and they would have to try some other way. So the Spartans, following the Messenian's advice, watched the mother of Aristodemus' sons, and they found that she always gave first place to the firstborn, both in feeding and in washing; for she did not know why she was being watched. So they took the child its mother favored and brought it up at public expense as the firstborn, and it was named Eurysthenes, while the other was called Procles. When the two grew up, they say, though they were brothers, they quarreled with each other their whole lives long, and their descendants have gone on the same way.

53. That is the account the Spartans give, and they alone of all the Greeks. But what follows I write according to what the Greeks in general say. I mean that these kings of the Dorians are correctly listed by the Greeks back as far as Perseus the son of Danae (leaving out the god, Zeus, who was Perseus' father), and are shown to be Greek by descent; for even at that time they were already counted as Greeks. I said "as far as Perseus" and did not take the line back any higher, because no mortal father is named for Perseus, the way Amphitryon is named as the mortal father of Heracles. So I had good reason, as you can see, to say "correctly as far as Perseus." But if you trace their ancestors back generation by generation from Danae the daughter of Acrisius, the leaders of the Dorians will turn out to be Egyptians by direct descent.

54. That is how I have traced the line according to the Greeks' account. But according to the story the Persians tell, Perseus himself was an Assyrian who became a Greek, and Perseus' ancestors were not Greeks. As for the ancestors of Acrisius, who according to this account were not related to Perseus at all, the Persians say that they were Egyptians, just as the Greeks say.

55. Let that be enough said about these matters. How and by what deeds these men, who were Egyptians, came to hold the royal scepter over the Dorians, I will leave out, since others have told it. But I will speak of the things other writers have not dealt with.

56. These are the royal privileges the Spartans have given their kings. First, two priesthoods: of Zeus Lacedaemon and of Zeus Uranius, "Zeus of the Sky." Next, the right to make war on any land they please; no Spartan may stand in the way of this right, and anyone who does falls under a curse. When they go out on campaign, the kings go out first and come back last. A hundred picked men guard them on campaign. On their expeditions they may use as many cattle for sacrifice as they wish, and they take the hides and the chines of all the animals that are sacrificed.

57. Those are their privileges in war. In peace, the following has been granted to them. Whenever a sacrifice is made at public expense, the kings have the right to sit down to the feast before everyone else. The servers begin with them, and serve each of them a double portion of everything the other guests get. They have the first pouring of the libations, and the hides of the animals sacrificed. On the first day of every month, and on the seventh, each of them is given at public expense a full-grown animal for sacrifice in the temple of Apollo, along with a bushel and a half of barley meal and a Laconian "quarter" of wine. At all the games they have seats of honor set apart for them. It is also their privilege to appoint whichever citizens they like as protectors of foreigners, the official hosts of visiting strangers, and each king chooses two "Pythians." The Pythians are men sent to consult the god at Delphi, and they eat with the kings at public expense. If the kings do not come to the public dinner, the rule is that two quarts of barley meal apiece and half a pint of wine are sent out to them at their houses. If they are present, they are given a double share of everything; and they are honored in this same way when private citizens invite them to dinner. The kings also have charge of the oracles that are given, though the Pythians know them as well. The rule is that the kings alone decide the following cases, and only these: who should marry a girl who has inherited her father's property, if her father has not engaged her to anyone; and cases about the public roads. And if a man wants to adopt a son, he must do it in the presence of the kings. They also sit in council with the Elders, who number twenty-eight. If the kings do not come, the Elders most closely related to them hold the kings' privileges and cast two votes for them besides their own, which makes three in all.

58. These are the rights the Spartan state has granted its kings while they are alive. After they die they receive the following. Horsemen ride all through Laconia announcing what has happened, and in the city women go around beating on bronze kettles. Whenever this happens, two free people from every household, a man and a woman, must go into mourning, and heavy penalties are laid down for those who fail to do it. Now the Spartans' custom at the deaths of their kings is the same as that of the non-Greek peoples of Asia; for most non-Greeks follow the same customs at the deaths of their kings. Whenever a king of the Spartans dies, a fixed number of the "dwellers around" (the free men of the Laconian towns, who are not Spartan citizens) must come from all over Lacedaemon, not counting the Spartans themselves, to the funeral.

59. When many thousands of these men, and of the helots (the serfs of the Spartans), and of the Spartans themselves, have gathered in one place, with their women mixed among them, they beat their foreheads with a will and wail without end, saying that this king, the one who has died most recently, was the best of them all. Whenever one of their kings is killed in war, they make an image of him and carry it out for burial on a couch spread with fine coverings. After they have buried him, no assembly meets for ten days and there is no meeting to elect officials; instead they mourn through those days. In another way, too, the Spartans are like the Persians. When a king dies and another takes the throne, the new king, on coming to power, frees any Spartan who owed a debt to the king or to the state. Among the Persians, likewise, the king who comes to the throne cancels the tribute that all the cities owe him in arrears.

60. In this point the Spartans are also like the Egyptians: their heralds, flute-players and cooks inherit their fathers' trades. A flute-player is the son of a flute-player, a cook of a cook, and a herald of a herald. Other men do not push into the job because they have loud, clear voices and so shut these out of it; they carry on the trade they inherited from their fathers.

61. That is how these things are done. At the time I am speaking of, while Cleomenes was on Aegina working for the common good of Greece, Demaratus was bringing charges against him, not so much because he cared about the Aeginetans as because he was envious and jealous of him. So Cleomenes, after he came back from Aegina, made plans to remove Demaratus from the kingship, and he attacked him through the following matter. When Ariston was king in Sparta, he had married two wives, but no children were born to him. Since he would not admit that he himself was the cause of this, he married a third wife. This is how he married her. He had a friend, a Spartan, to whom he was closer than to any other citizen. It happened that this man's wife was by far the most beautiful woman in Sparta, and what is more, she had become the most beautiful after being the ugliest. As a baby she had been plain to look at. Her nurse saw that she was the daughter of rich people and yet was ugly, and she saw too that the parents were unhappy about it. Taking all this in, the nurse came up with a plan. Every day she carried the child to the temple of Helen, which is in the place called Therapne, above the temple of Phoebus Apollo. Each time she carried her there, she stood her in front of the statue and prayed the goddess to free the child from her ugliness. Once, the story goes, as the nurse was leaving the temple, a woman appeared to her and asked what she was carrying in her arms. The nurse told her she was carrying a child. The woman asked her to show it to her, but the nurse refused, because the parents had forbidden her to show the child to anyone. But the woman kept urging her in every way to show it. So the nurse, seeing how badly the woman wanted to see the child, showed it to her. Then the woman stroked the child's head and said that she would be the most beautiful of all the women in Sparta. And from that day on her looks changed. Later, when she was old enough to marry, she married Agetus son of Alcides, the friend of Ariston I spoke of.

62. Now Ariston, it seems, was always burning with desire for this woman, so he came up with a plan. He made an agreement with his friend, whose wife she was: he would give his friend any one thing from his own possessions that the friend chose, and he asked his friend to make him the same offer in return. The friend had no fears for his wife, since he saw that Ariston had a wife too, so he agreed; and on these terms they swore oaths to each other. Then Ariston, for his part, gave Agetus whatever it was that Agetus had chosen from his treasures. And when he came to claim the same from him in return, he tried to take his friend's wife away from him. Agetus said that he agreed to give anything but this one thing. But at last, forced by his oath and by the trick that had been played on him, he let her be taken from him.

63. So Ariston sent away his second wife and brought the third into his house. And this wife, in less than the full ten months, gave birth to the Demaratus we have been speaking of. One of his servants brought him the news that a son had been born to him while he was sitting in council with the ephors. Ariston knew when he had taken the woman as his wife, and he counted up the months on his fingers and swore an oath, saying, "He can't be mine." The ephors heard this, but at the time they thought nothing of it. The child grew up, and Ariston was sorry for what he had said, since he believed that Demaratus was certainly his own son. He named him Demaratus, which means "Prayed for by the People," for this reason: before all this happened, the Spartan people had all prayed together that a son might be born to Ariston, who was the most famous of all the kings Sparta had ever had.

64. That is why he was named Demaratus. As time went on Ariston died, and Demaratus became king. But it was fated, it seems, that these things should come out and cost Demaratus his throne. And so Demaratus had fallen out badly with Cleomenes, once before, when he led his army away from Eleusis, and now above all, when Cleomenes had crossed over to arrest the Aeginetans who had gone over to the Persians.

65. So Cleomenes, eager for revenge, made an arrangement with Leotychides son of Menares son of Agis, who was of the same royal house as Demaratus. The deal was that if Cleomenes made him king in place of Demaratus, Leotychides would go with him against the Aeginetans. Now Leotychides had become a bitter enemy of Demaratus for the following reason. Leotychides had been engaged to Percalus, the daughter of Chilon son of Demarmenus, but Demaratus plotted against him and robbed him of his marriage, carrying Percalus off first and making her his own wife. That was how Leotychides' hatred of Demaratus began. And now, urged on by Cleomenes, Leotychides swore a formal charge against Demaratus, saying that he was not the lawful king of the Spartans because he was not Ariston's son. After making this charge he brought a lawsuit against him. He dragged up the old words Ariston had spoken when his servant brought him the news that a son was born to him, when Ariston counted up the months and swore that the child was not his. Basing his case on these words, Leotychides set out to prove that Demaratus was not Ariston's son and was not the lawful king of Sparta. As witnesses he brought forward the ephors who happened to have been sitting in council with Ariston at the time and had heard him say it.

66. In the end, since there was a dispute about these matters, the Spartans decided to ask the oracle at Delphi whether Demaratus was Ariston's son. Cleomenes arranged for the question to be put to the Pythia, and then he won over Cobon son of Aristophantus, the most powerful man in Delphi. Cobon persuaded Perialla, the prophetess of the oracle, to say what Cleomenes wanted said. So when the envoys sent to consult the god asked their question, the Pythia ruled that Demaratus was not Ariston's son. Later, however, all this came out. Cobon was banished from Delphi, and Perialla the prophetess was removed from her office.

67. That is how Demaratus came to be deposed. But he became an exile and went to the Persians because of an insult, which I will now tell. After he was deposed, Demaratus held a public office he had been elected to. It was the time of the Gymnopaedia, the festival of the Naked Youths, and Demaratus was there watching. Leotychides, who was now king himself in place of Demaratus, sent his servant to ask Demaratus, to mock and insult him, what it was like to be an official after having been king. Demaratus, stung by the question, answered that he himself had now tried both, but Leotychides had not; this question, though, he said, would be the beginning for the Spartans either of countless troubles or of countless blessings. After saying this he covered his head and left the theater for his own house. He made preparations at once and sacrificed an ox to Zeus, and after the sacrifice he called for his mother.

68. When his mother came, he put some of the animal's innards into her hands and pleaded with her, saying: "Mother, I beg you, in the name of all the other gods and above all of Zeus here, the guardian of our house, tell me the truth: who is really my father? Leotychides said in our quarrel that you were already pregnant by your former husband when you came to Ariston. And others tell an even sillier story: that you slept with one of the servants, the man who looked after the donkeys, and that I am his son. So I beg you by the gods to tell me the truth. If you have done any of the things people say, you're not the only one; many other women have done the same. And there's a common rumor in Sparta that Ariston was not able to father children, since otherwise his earlier wives would have had children too."

69. That is what he said, and she answered him: "My son, since you plead with me so earnestly to tell you the truth, I will tell you the whole truth. When Ariston had brought me into his house, on the third night a phantom came to me that looked like Ariston. It slept with me, and then it put on me the garlands it was wearing. The phantom left at once, and after that Ariston came. When he saw me wearing garlands, he asked who had given them to me. I said that he had, but he would not admit it. So I began to swear to it, and I said he was wrong to deny it, since he had come in, I said, only a little while before, slept with me, and given me the garlands. When Ariston saw that I was swearing to it, he realized that this was the work of the gods. For one thing, the garlands turned out to come from the hero's shrine that stands by the courtyard gate of the house, the one they call the shrine of Astrabacus. For another, the seers answered that it was this same hero who had come to me. So there you have it, my son, everything you want to know. Either you were fathered by this hero, and the hero Astrabacus is your father, or Ariston is your father; for I conceived you that night. As for the point your enemies hold on to hardest, saying that Ariston himself, when your birth was announced, declared in front of many people that you were not his son because the full time, the ten months, had not yet passed: he blurted that out because he did not know about such things. For women give birth at nine months and even at seven, and not all of them after a full ten months. And I gave birth to you, my son, at seven months. Not long afterward Ariston himself realized that he had spoken foolishly. So do not believe any other stories about your birth, for you have heard the whole truth. And as for Leotychides and the people who tell these stories, may their own wives bear them children by donkey-keepers!"

70. That is what she said. Demaratus, having learned what he wanted to know, packed supplies for a journey and set out for Elis, pretending that he was going to Delphi to consult the oracle. But the Spartans suspected that he was trying to escape, and they went after him. As it happened, Demaratus had already crossed over from Elis to Zacynthus before they got there. The Spartans crossed after him, laid hands on him, and took his servants away from him. But since the people of Zacynthus refused to hand him over, he crossed from there to Asia, to King Darius. Darius received him as a guest with great honor and also gave him land and cities. That is how Demaratus came to Asia, and such was the fortune he had met with. He had won distinction among the Spartans in many ways, both by his deeds and by his advice, and above all he had won them a victory at Olympia in the four-horse chariot race. He was the only one of all the kings Sparta ever had who did this.

71. After Demaratus was deposed, Leotychides son of Menares succeeded to the kingship. He had a son, Zeuxidemus, whom some of the Spartans called Cyniscus. This Zeuxidemus never became king of Sparta, because he died before Leotychides, leaving a son, Archidemus. After losing Zeuxidemus, Leotychides married a second wife, Eurydame, the sister of Menius and daughter of Diactorides. By her he had no son, only a daughter, Lampito, whom Leotychides gave in marriage to Archidemus son of Zeuxidemus.

72. But Leotychides himself did not grow old in Sparta. He paid for what he had done to Demaratus, in this way. He led a Spartan army in an invasion of Thessaly, and when he could have brought the whole country under control, he took bribes amounting to a large sum. He was caught in the act, there in the camp, sitting on a glove full of money. So he was put on trial and banished from Sparta, and his house was torn down. He went into exile at Tegea and died there.

Chapter 34: The Death of Cleomenes, the Story of Glaucus, and the War with Aegina

73. Those things happened later. But at this time, as soon as Cleomenes had carried his business with Demaratus through to success, he took Leotychides with him and went straight against the Aeginetans, because he was furious with them for the insults they had given him. Now that both kings had come against them, the Aeginetans for their part decided to resist no longer. The Spartans picked out the ten Aeginetans who stood highest in wealth and birth and took them away as prisoners. Among them were Crius son of Polycritus and Casambus son of Aristocrates, who had the most power in Aegina. They carried these men off to Attica and left them in the keeping of the Athenians, who were the Aeginetans' bitterest enemies.

74. After this it became known that Cleomenes had plotted against Demaratus, and he grew afraid of the Spartans and slipped away to Thessaly. From there he went to Arcadia and began to stir up trouble, trying to unite the Arcadians against Sparta. He made them swear various oaths that they would certainly follow him wherever he led them, and besides these he was very eager to bring the chief men of Arcadia to the city of Nonacris and make them swear by the water of the Styx, the river of the underworld by which even the gods swear. For the Arcadians say that the water of the Styx is near this city, and there is in fact something of the kind there: a little stream of water can be seen trickling down from a rock into a hollow ravine, and a wall of rough stones runs around the ravine. Nonacris, where this spring happens to be, is a city of Arcadia near Pheneus.

75. When the Spartans heard what Cleomenes was doing, they were afraid, and they brought him back to Sparta to rule on the same terms as before. But as soon as he came back he was struck by madness (he had been a little out of his mind even before this). Whenever he met any Spartan, he would jab his staff into the man's face. Since he kept doing this and had gone completely out of his senses, his relatives bound him in the stocks. While he was bound like this, he saw that his guard had been left alone by the others, and he asked him for a knife. At first the guard refused, but Cleomenes threatened him with what he would do to him later if he did not, until at last the guard, who was one of the helots, was frightened by the threats and gave him a knife. Once Cleomenes had the blade, he began to mutilate himself, starting from his legs. He went on slicing his flesh lengthwise from his shins to his thighs, and from his thighs to his hips and sides, until he came at last to his belly. He cut this into strips, and that is how he died. Most of the Greeks say this happened to him because he persuaded the Pythia to say what she said about Demaratus. The Athenians alone say it was because when he invaded Eleusis he ravaged the sacred precinct of the goddesses, Demeter and her daughter. And the Argives say it was because he called out of their sanctuary of Argos the Argives who had taken refuge there after the battle and cut them down, and then set fire to the sacred grove itself, with no respect for it at all.

76. This is what happened. When Cleomenes consulted the oracle at Delphi, he was told that he would conquer Argos. So he led out the Spartans and came to the river Erasinus, which is said to flow out of the Stymphalian lake. This lake, they say, drains away into a hidden chasm and comes up again above ground in the land of Argos, and from that point on the Argives call its water the Erasinus. When he reached this river, Cleomenes made sacrifices to it. The omens were not at all favorable for crossing, so he said he admired the Erasinus for not betraying its own countrymen, but that even so the Argives would not get away. After this he drew back from there and led his army down to Thyrea. There he sacrificed a bull to the Sea, and then he carried his men in ships to the land of Tiryns and Nauplia.

77. When the Argives learned of this, they marched down to the sea to defend their country. When they had come near Tiryns, to the place called Hesipeia, they camped facing the Spartans, leaving no very wide space between the two armies. There the Argives were not afraid of fighting in the open. What they feared was being beaten by a trick, because they thought this was what the oracle meant that the Pythia had given to them and to the Milesians together. It went like this:

	But when the female at last conquers the male in battle,
	drives him out, and wins glory among the Argives,
	then many Argive wives will tear both their cheeks in mourning,
	so that someday a man of a later age will say,
	"The terrible three-coiled serpent perished, beaten down by the spear."

All these things coming together made the Argives afraid, and to deal with it they decided to make use of the enemy's herald. Having decided this, here is what they did: whenever the Spartan herald gave an order to the Spartans, the Argives did the same thing too.

78. Cleomenes noticed that the Argives were doing whatever the Spartan herald announced. So he passed the word to the Spartans that when the herald announced that they were to get their breakfast, they should instead pick up their arms and go and attack the Argives. The Spartans did exactly that. While the Argives were getting their breakfast as the herald had ordered, the Spartans attacked them. They killed many of them, but many more fled for safety into the sacred grove of Argos, and the Spartans sat down around the place and kept watch on them. Then Cleomenes did the following.

79. He had deserters with him, and by questioning them he found out the names of the Argives who were shut up in the sanctuary. Then he sent a herald to call them out one by one by name, saying that he had received their ransom. Among the Peloponnesians the ransom is fixed at two minas of silver for each prisoner. So Cleomenes called out about fifty of the Argives one at a time and killed them. As it happened, the rest of the men inside the grove did not notice this was going on. The grove was thick, and those inside could not see what was happening to those outside, at least until one of them climbed a tree and saw from above what was being done. After that they no longer came out when they were called.

80. So then Cleomenes ordered all the helots to pile brushwood around the sacred grove, and when they had done it he set the grove on fire. When it was already burning, he asked one of the deserters which god the grove belonged to. The man answered that it belonged to Argos, the hero the city was named after. When Cleomenes heard that, he groaned aloud and said, "Apollo, god of oracles, you have badly deceived me when you said that I would conquer Argos. I take it the oracle has already been fulfilled for me."

81. After this Cleomenes sent most of his army back to Sparta, but he himself took a thousand of his best men and went to the temple of Hera to sacrifice. When he wanted to sacrifice at the altar, the priest forbade him, saying that religious law did not allow a foreigner to sacrifice there. But Cleomenes told the helots to take the priest away from the altar and whip him, and he made the sacrifice himself. When he had done this, he went back to Sparta.

82. After his return his enemies brought him before the ephors. They accused him of taking bribes, and said that was why he had not conquered Argos when he could easily have taken it. He gave them an answer. Whether he was lying or telling the truth, I can't say for certain; at any rate, this is what he said. When he had captured the sanctuary of Argos, he thought the god's oracle had been fulfilled for him. So he did not think it right to make an attempt on the city, at least not before he had sacrificed and learned whether the goddess would allow it or was standing against him. And while he was sacrificing for omens in the temple of Hera, a flame blazed out from the breasts of the statue. From this he knew the truth of the matter: he would not conquer Argos. If the fire had blazed out from the statue's head, he would have conquered the city from top to bottom. But since it blazed from the breasts, everything the god meant to happen had already been done for him. When he said this, the Spartans thought his account was believable and reasonable, and he got away from his accusers easily.

83. Argos, however, was so emptied of men that the slaves took over the whole state, ruling it and running its affairs until the sons of the men who had been killed grew up. Then these young men, trying to win Argos back for themselves, drove the slaves out, and the slaves, once driven out, took Tiryns by force. For a time the two sides were on friendly terms. But later a prophet named Cleander came to the slaves, a Phigalian from Arcadia by birth. This man persuaded the slaves to attack their masters, and as a result there was war between them for a long time, until at last, with difficulty, the Argives got the better of them.

84. The Argives say, then, that this is why Cleomenes went mad and came to a bad end. But the Spartans themselves say that Cleomenes was not driven mad by any divine power. They say he had picked up the habit of drinking his wine unmixed from spending time with Scythians, and that this was what made him go mad. The nomad Scythians, they say, after Darius had invaded their land, were eager to pay him back. So they sent to Sparta and tried to make an alliance. Their plan was that the Scythians themselves would try to invade Media by way of the river Phasis, while the Spartans would set out from Ephesus and march inland, and then the two armies would meet in one place. And they say that when the Scythians came to Sparta for this purpose, Cleomenes spent a great deal of time with them, and from spending more time with them than was good for him, he learned to drink his wine unmixed with water. That, the Spartans think, is why he went mad. And from that time on, as they say themselves, whenever they want a stronger drink they say, "Pour it Scythian-style." That is what the Spartans say about Cleomenes. But to me it seems that this was the price Cleomenes paid for what he did to Demaratus.

85. When the Aeginetans heard that Cleomenes was dead, they sent messengers to Sparta to accuse Leotychides over the hostages who were being held at Athens. The Spartans convened a court and ruled that Leotychides had treated the Aeginetans outrageously. They sentenced him to be taken to Aegina and handed over in exchange for the men who were being held at Athens. Then, as the Aeginetans were about to take Leotychides away, Theasides son of Leoprepes, a man of high standing in Sparta, said to them: "What are you planning to do, men of Aegina? Do you mean to carry off the king of the Spartans, now that his own fellow citizens have handed him over to you? The Spartans have decided this now because they are angry. But be careful: if you do this, they may someday bring ruin on your land that will destroy it." When they heard this, the Aeginetans held back from taking him. Instead they agreed that Leotychides should go with them to Athens and get the men back for the Aeginetans.

86. But when Leotychides came to Athens and asked for the hostages he had left there, the Athenians did not want to give them up, and they made excuses for refusing. They claimed that two kings had left the men with them, and they did not think it right to give them back to one without the other. So when the Athenians said they would not give them back, Leotychides spoke to them like this:

"Athenians, do whichever you want. You know that if you give them up, you are doing what religion requires, and if you refuse, you are doing the opposite. But I want to tell you what happened once in Sparta over something left in someone's keeping. We Spartans tell how, about two generations before my time, there lived in Sparta a man named Glaucus son of Epicydes. We say this man was first-rate in every way, and above all everyone living in Sparta at that time spoke well of him for his honesty. And we tell how in due course this happened to him. A man from Miletus came to Sparta and asked to speak with him, and he gave these reasons: 'I am a Milesian,' he said, 'and I have come here because I want to profit from your honesty, Glaucus. All over the rest of Greece, and in Ionia too, there is a great deal of talk about your honesty. So I thought it over. Ionia is always in danger, while the Peloponnese is safe and settled, and we never see wealth stay with the same people for long. Thinking about all this and talking it over with myself, I decided to turn half of everything I own into money and leave it with you, since I am sure that if it is with you, it will be safe. So please take the money, and take and keep these tallies too. Whoever comes and asks for the money back with the tokens that match these, give it back to him.'

"That was what the stranger from Miletus said, and Glaucus accepted the money on the terms offered. Then, after a long time had passed, the sons of the man who had left the money with Glaucus came to Sparta. They went to talk with Glaucus, showed him the tokens, and asked for the money back. But he turned them away with this answer: 'I don't remember the matter, and nothing you say brings it back to my mind. But I do want to remember and to do everything that is right. If I took the money, I want to return it honestly. And if I never took it at all, I will deal with you according to the customs of the Greeks. So I am putting off settling the matter with you for three months from today.'

"So the Milesians went away unhappy, because they thought they had been robbed of their money. But Glaucus set off for Delphi to consult the oracle. When he asked the oracle whether he should rob them of the money by swearing an oath, the Pythia rebuked him with these lines:

	Glaucus, son of Epicydes, for the moment it pays you better
	to win the case by an oath and rob them of the money.
	Swear, then: death waits for the man who keeps his oath as well.
	But know that Oath has a son, who has no name, no hands,
	no feet; yet without feet he pursues, without hands he seizes, until
	he has destroyed the whole race and house of the man who breaks his oath.
	But the race of the man who keeps his oath fares better in time to come.

"When Glaucus heard this, he begged the god to forgive him for what he had said. But the priestess told him that to put the god to the test and to do the deed came to the same thing.

"So Glaucus sent for the Milesians and gave them back their money. But now, Athenians, I will tell you why I set out to tell you this story. Today there is no descendant of Glaucus left, and no household that is counted as Glaucus' own. He has been wiped out root and branch from Sparta. So it is a good thing, when people have left something in your keeping, not even to think about it except to give it back when they ask for it."

87. That is what Leotychides said, but even so the Athenians would not listen to him, and he went home. Now the Aeginetans had not yet paid the penalty for the wrongs they had done the Athenians earlier, when they attacked them to please the Thebans. But before they paid it, they did this. They complained about the way the Athenians had treated them and thought they had been wronged, so they got ready to take revenge on the Athenians. The Athenians were holding their festival at Sunium, which comes every four years, so the Aeginetans lay in wait for the sacred ship that was sent to it and captured it. The ship was full of leading Athenians, and once they had taken it, they put the men in chains.

88. After the Aeginetans had done them this wrong, the Athenians no longer held back from plotting every possible harm against them. Now there was a man of some standing in Aegina, Nicodromus son of Cnithus. He had a grievance against the Aeginetans because they had earlier driven him out of the island. When he heard that the Athenians had made up their minds to do the Aeginetans harm, he made an agreement with the Athenians to betray Aegina to them. He told them on what day he would make his attempt, and by what day they would need to come and help him.

89. After this Nicodromus seized what is called the Old City, as he had agreed with the Athenians. But the Athenians did not arrive in time to support him. As it happened, they did not have enough ships to fight the Aeginetans. So while they were asking the Corinthians to lend them ships, their cause fell apart. The Corinthians, who were very friendly with them at this time, gave the Athenians twenty ships when they asked. They handed them over by selling them at five drachmas each, since their law did not allow them to give ships away as a free gift. The Athenians took these ships and their own, manned seventy ships in all, and sailed to Aegina. They arrived one day later than the day agreed.

90. Meanwhile, since the Athenians had not come to support him in time, Nicodromus boarded a ship and escaped from Aegina, and some other Aeginetans went with him. The Athenians gave them Sunium to live in, and from there these men kept raiding the Aeginetans on the island.

91. That happened later. But at the time I am talking about, the wealthy Aeginetans got the upper hand over the common people, who had risen up against them together with Nicodromus. Once they had them in their power, they began leading their prisoners out to be executed. Because of this a curse fell on them, and they could not wash it away with sacrifices, though they tried every means they could think of. They were driven out of the island before the goddess was appeased. Here is what happened. They had taken seven hundred of the common people prisoner and were leading them out to execution, when one of them broke free of his chains and fled for sanctuary to the doorway of the temple of Demeter the Lawgiver. He took hold of the door handle and clung to it. When they found they could not drag him away from it by pulling, they cut off his hands and carried him off that way, and his hands were left clinging to the door handle.

92. That is what the Aeginetans did to one another. When the Athenians arrived, the Aeginetans fought them with seventy ships. They were beaten in the sea battle, and so they called for help from the same people they had called on before, the Argives. But this time the Argives would not come to help them. They held a grudge because Aeginetan ships, pressed into service by Cleomenes, had put in on the coast of Argos, and their crews had gone ashore with the Spartans. Men from ships of Sicyon had also landed with them in that same invasion. As a penalty for this the Argives had laid a fine of a thousand talents on them, five hundred for each state. The Sicyonians admitted they had done wrong and made an agreement to pay a hundred talents and be let off the rest. But the Aeginetans would not admit their wrong and were more stubborn. For this reason, when they asked for help this time, no Argives came at the state's expense. But volunteers came, about a thousand of them, and their leader was a commander named Eurybates, a man who had trained in the pentathlon, the five-event contest. Most of these men never came home but were killed by the Athenians on Aegina. Their commander Eurybates himself fought in single combat, killed three men that way, and was killed by the fourth, Sophanes of Decelea.

93. The Aeginetans, however, attacked the Athenian fleet while it was in disorder and beat it, and they captured four of their ships along with the crews.

Chapter 35: Eretria, and the Battle of Marathon

94. So the Athenians were at war with the Aeginetans. Meanwhile the Persian king was pushing ahead with his plan. His servant kept reminding him, as he had ordered, to remember the Athenians; the sons of Pisistratus were close at hand and kept bringing charges against the Athenians; and at the same time Darius himself wanted to seize on this pretext to conquer those peoples of Greece that had not given him earth and water. Since Mardonius had fared so badly on his expedition, Darius removed him from his command. He appointed other generals and sent them out against Eretria and Athens. They were Datis, a Mede by birth, and Artaphernes son of Artaphernes, the king's own nephew. Darius sent them off with orders to enslave Athens and Eretria and to bring the slaves back into his presence.

95. These newly appointed commanders marched from the king's court to the Aleian plain in Cilicia, bringing with them a large and well-equipped land army. While they were camped there, the whole fleet came up to join them, the ships that the various subject peoples had been ordered to supply. With it came the horse transports, which Darius had ordered his tributaries to get ready the year before. They put their horses on board these, embarked the land army on the ships, and sailed for Ionia with six hundred triremes. From there they did not keep their ships along the mainland coast toward the Hellespont and Thrace. Instead they set out from Samos and made their way across the Icarian Sea and through the islands. The reason, I think, is that they feared the voyage around Athos more than anything else, since the year before they had met with a great disaster when they went that way. Naxos also drew them this way, since it had not been conquered the time before.

96. They came at Naxos from the Icarian Sea, for Naxos was the first place the Persians meant to attack, because they remembered what had happened there before. But the Naxians did not wait for them. They fled at once to the mountains. The Persians enslaved all of them they could catch and set fire to both the temples and the town. After this they put out to sea to attack the other islands.

97. While they were doing this, the Delians too had left Delos and fled to Tenos. As the fleet sailed toward Delos, Datis went ahead and would not let the ships anchor at the island of Delos. He had them anchor instead at Rhenaea, across the channel. He found out by asking where the Delians had gone, and he sent a herald to them with this message: "Holy men, why have you run away, thinking so badly of me? I have sense enough of my own, and besides, the king has ordered me not to do any harm to the land where the two gods were born, neither to the land itself nor to the people who live there. So now go back to your homes and live on your island." That was the message he sent the Delians by his herald. After this he heaped up three hundred talents' weight of frankincense on the altar, about 17,000 pounds, and burned it.

98. When he had done this, Datis sailed away with his army to attack Eretria first, taking Ionians and Aeolians along with him. After he had put out to sea from there, Delos was shaken by an earthquake. The Delians told me that the island had never been shaken before that time, or since, down to my own day. And surely this was a sign from heaven, showing men the troubles that were coming. For in the time of Darius son of Hystaspes, of Xerxes son of Darius, and of Artaxerxes son of Xerxes, three generations one after another, more troubles came upon Greece than in all the twenty generations before Darius. Some of these troubles came from the Persians, and others from the leading Greek states themselves, fighting one another for supremacy. So it was not unreasonable that Delos should be shaken, though it had never been shaken before. And there was an oracle written about it, which said:

	"I will shake even Delos, though it has never been shaken."

In Greek, these names mean the following: Darius means "Doer," Xerxes "Warrior," and Artaxerxes "Great Warrior." That is what the Greeks would rightly call these kings in their own language.

99. After they left Delos, the Persians put in at the islands as they went. From each they picked up more troops and took the sons of the islanders as hostages. Sailing around among the islands, they put in at Carystus too. But the Carystians would neither give them hostages nor agree to join an expedition against their neighbors, by which they meant Eretria and Athens. So the Persians laid siege to them and ravaged their land, until in the end the Carystians also came around to doing what the Persians wanted.

100. Meanwhile the Eretrians learned that the Persian fleet was sailing to attack them, and they asked the Athenians for help. The Athenians did not refuse. As helpers they gave them the four thousand settlers who had been given the land of the wealthy Chalcidians. But it turned out that the Eretrians had no sound plan. They had sent for the Athenians, but they were of two minds. Some of them proposed to leave the city and take to the heights of Euboea, while others, expecting to profit personally from the Persians, were getting ready to betray the place. Aeschines son of Nothon, one of the leading men of Eretria, found out about both these plans. He told the Athenians who had come the whole state of affairs and begged them to leave and go home, so that they would not be destroyed along with everyone else. The Athenians took Aeschines' advice.

101. So they crossed over to Oropus and saved themselves. The Persians, meanwhile, sailed on and brought their ships to land at Temenus, Choereae and Aegilea, in the territory of Eretria. When they had taken these places, they began at once to unload their horses and to prepare to advance against the enemy. The Eretrians did not mean to come out and fight. Their aim was to hold out behind their walls if they could, since the proposal to abandon the city had been voted down. Then the Persians made a violent assault on the wall, and for six days many men fell on both sides. But on the seventh day two respected citizens, Euphorbus son of Alcimachus and Philagrus son of Cyneus, betrayed the city to the Persians. The Persians entered the city, plundered the temples and set them on fire, in revenge for the temples that had been burned at Sardis. They also enslaved the people, as Darius had commanded.

102. Once they had Eretria in their power, they stayed a few days and then sailed for Attica. They pressed on hard, expecting that the Athenians would do just what the Eretrians had done. Marathon was the best place in Attica for cavalry to operate, and it was also very close to Eretria, so it was to Marathon that Hippias son of Pisistratus guided them.

103. When the Athenians learned of this, they too marched out to Marathon to defend their land. They were led by ten generals. The tenth was Miltiades, whose father Cimon son of Stesagoras had been forced into exile from Athens by Pisistratus son of Hippocrates. While he was in exile, Cimon happened to win a victory at the Olympic games with a four-horse chariot. In winning it he did the same thing his half-brother Miltiades had done, who had the same mother as he did. Then at the next Olympic games he won again with the same mares, and let Pisistratus be proclaimed the winner. Having handed the victory over to him, he came back to his own country under a peace agreement. Then, after he had won with the same mares at yet another Olympic festival, it was his fate to be killed by the sons of Pisistratus, Pisistratus himself being no longer alive. They killed him near the town hall, after setting men to lie in wait for him at night. Cimon is buried outside the city, beyond the road called Through Coele (the Hollow), and directly opposite him are buried the mares that won at three Olympic games. The mares of Evagoras the Laconian did the same thing, but no others ever have. Cimon's elder son, Stesagoras, was at that time being raised in the Chersonese by his father's brother Miltiades. The younger son was being raised in Athens with Cimon himself, and he had been named Miltiades after Miltiades who founded the settlement in the Chersonese.

104. This Miltiades, then, had come from the Chersonese and was now a general of the Athenians, after escaping death twice over. First, the Phoenicians had chased him as far as Imbros, very eager to catch him and bring him up to the king. Then, after he had escaped them and reached his own country and seemed to be safe from then on, his enemies were lying in wait for him there. They brought him to court and prosecuted him for his rule as tyrant in the Chersonese. He escaped them too, and had then been made a general of the Athenians, elected by the people.

105. First of all, while they were still in the city, the generals sent a herald off to Sparta. This was Pheidippides, an Athenian, who was also a long-distance runner who did this for a living. As Pheidippides himself said, and as he reported to the Athenians, Pan met him on Mount Parthenium, above Tegea. Pan called out Pheidippides' name and told him to take a message to the Athenians: why did they pay no attention to him, when he was friendly to the Athenians, had been useful to them many times before, and would be again? The Athenians believed this story was true. So when their affairs had come out well, they built a shrine of Pan below the Acropolis, and because of this message they have honored him ever since with yearly sacrifices and a torch race.

106. But at that time, the time when he said Pan appeared to him, this Pheidippides, sent by the generals, was in Sparta on the day after he left Athens. He came before the magistrates and said: "Men of Sparta, the Athenians ask you to come to their help, and not to let the most ancient city in Greece fall into slavery at the hands of foreigners. Eretria has already been enslaved, and Greece is the weaker by one famous city." He delivered the message he had been given, and the Spartans resolved to help the Athenians. But they could not do it at once, because they did not want to break their law. It was the ninth day of the month, and they said they would not march out on the ninth, or until the moon was full.

107. So the Spartans waited for the full moon. Meanwhile Hippias son of Pisistratus was guiding the Persians in to Marathon. The night before, he had seen a vision in his sleep: it seemed to Hippias that he slept with his own mother. From this dream he concluded that he would return to Athens, get back his power, and end his life as an old man in his own country. That is what he concluded from the dream. Then, as he guided the Persians in, he first landed the slaves from Eretria on an island that belongs to the Styrians, called Aegleia. Next, as the ships came to shore at Marathon, he anchored them there, and when the troops had come ashore from the ships, he set about posting them in their places. While he was arranging all this, he happened to sneeze and cough more violently than usual. He was an old man, and most of his teeth were loose, so the cough shook them, and one of them flew out with the force of it. The tooth fell into the sand, and he tried hard to find it. But when it could not be found, he groaned aloud and said to the men around him: "This land is not ours, and we will not be able to conquer it. Whatever share of it was mine, the tooth has."

108. Hippias decided that this was how his vision had come true. Meanwhile, when the Athenians had taken up their position in the sacred precinct of Heracles, the Plataeans came to help them with their whole force. The Plataeans had given themselves into the Athenians' keeping, and the Athenians had already gone through a great deal of trouble on their behalf. This is how the Plataeans had given themselves to them. When the Thebans were pressing them hard, the Plataeans first tried to give themselves to Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides and the Spartans, who happened to be in the area. But the Spartans would not accept them. They said: "We live too far away, and help like ours would be cold comfort to you. You could be enslaved many times over before any of us even heard about it. We advise you to give yourselves to the Athenians instead. They are your neighbors, and they are not bad at helping." The Spartans gave this advice not so much out of goodwill toward the Plataeans as because they wanted the Athenians to have trouble on their hands, tangled in a conflict with the Boeotians. That was the Spartans' advice to the men of Plataea, and the Plataeans took it. When the Athenians were sacrificing to the Twelve Gods, the Plataeans sat down at the altar as suppliants, and in that way gave themselves to Athens. When the Thebans heard of this, they marched against the Plataeans, and the Athenians came to their aid. They were about to join battle when the Corinthians, who happened to be there, stopped them and settled the quarrel. Both sides left the matter to them, and the Corinthians fixed boundaries for the land, on condition that the Thebans should leave alone any Boeotians who did not want to be counted as Boeotians. After giving this decision the Corinthians left. But as the Athenians were going home, the Boeotians attacked them, and were beaten in the fight. At that the Athenians went beyond the boundaries the Corinthians had set for the Plataeans, and made the river Asopus itself the boundary between Thebes and the lands of Plataea and Hysiae. That, then, is how the Plataeans had given themselves to the Athenians, and now they came to Marathon to help them.

109. The Athenian generals were divided in their opinions. One side urged them not to fight, because they were too few to take on the Persian army. The others, Miltiades among them, urged them to fight. They were split, and the worse opinion was about to win. But there was an eleventh vote, belonging to the man chosen by lot to be polemarch of the Athenians, the war-archon (in the old days the Athenians gave the polemarch an equal vote with the generals). At that time the polemarch was Callimachus of the deme of Aphidnae. Miltiades went to him and said: "Callimachus, it is up to you now. You can bring Athens into slavery, or you can make her free and leave behind you, for as long as men live, a memorial greater than even Harmodius and Aristogeiton left. The Athenians have now come to the greatest danger they have faced since they first became a people. If they give in to the Persians, it is already settled what they will suffer, once they are handed over to Hippias. But if this city wins, it may become the first of the cities of Greece. How this can happen, and how the decision comes to rest with you of all people, I will now explain. We generals, ten of us, are divided: some say we should fight, and some say we should not. Now, if we do not fight, I expect some great spirit of discord will fall on the Athenians and shake their resolve until they go over to the Persians. But if we fight before any rot sets in among any part of the Athenian people, then, if the gods give us a fair chance, we can win the battle. All of this now belongs to you and depends on you. If you side with my view, you will have a country that is free and a city that will be the first in Greece. But if you choose the view of those who are dead set against fighting, you will have the opposite of all the good things I have just described."

110. With these words Miltiades won Callimachus over. With the polemarch's vote added, it was decided to fight. After this, the generals who had voted to fight each handed over his command to Miltiades when his day to command came around. Miltiades accepted, but he still would not start the battle until his own day to command had come.

111. When his day came round, the Athenians were drawn up for battle in this order. The polemarch Callimachus led the right wing, since it was the Athenian custom at that time for the polemarch to hold the right wing. After him, with him in the lead, came the tribes in the order of their numbers, one after another, and last of all the Plataeans were drawn up on the left wing. Ever since this battle, when the Athenians offer sacrifices at the great festivals held every four years, the Athenian herald prays "that blessings may come to the Athenians and the Plataeans both." At this time, though, as the Athenians were being drawn up at Marathon, something like this happened. Their line was made as long as the Persian line, and so the center was only a few ranks deep, and there the army was weakest, while each wing was strong in numbers.

112. When they had taken their places and the sacrifices came out favorable, the Athenians were let loose, and they charged the enemy at a run. The distance between the two armies was at least 4,800 feet, nearly a mile. When the Persians saw them coming at a run, they got ready to meet them, and they thought the Athenians had gone mad, a madness that would destroy them, since there were so few of them and yet they were rushing forward at a run, with no cavalry and no archers. That is what the Persians thought. But once the Athenians closed with them all together, they fought in a way that deserves to be remembered. They were the first Greeks we know of who charged the enemy at a run, and the first who stood their ground at the sight of Median dress and the men who wore it. Until then, the Greeks had been terrified just to hear the name of the Medes.

113. The fighting at Marathon went on for a long time. In the center of the line, where the Persians themselves and the Sacae were posted, the Persians were winning. There they broke through and chased the Athenians inland. But on both wings the Athenians and the Plataeans each won. Having won, they let the beaten part of the enemy run away unchallenged, brought their two wings together, and fought the troops who had broken through their center. And the Athenians won. Then they followed the fleeing Persians, cutting them down, until they reached the sea. There they called for fire and began to lay hold of the ships.

114. In this part of the fighting the polemarch Callimachus was killed, after proving himself a brave man. One of the generals, Stesilaus son of Thrasylaus, was also killed. Besides these, Cynegirus son of Euphorion took hold of the ornament on the stern of a ship, had his hand cut off with an axe, and fell. And many other well-known Athenians were killed as well.

115. In this way the Athenians captured seven of the ships. With the rest, the Persians pushed off from shore. They picked up the Eretrian captives from the island where they had left them and sailed around Sunium, meaning to reach the city before the Athenians. A charge went around among the Athenians that the Alcmaeonids had put them up to this plan. The Alcmaeonids, it was said, had an understanding with the Persians and held up a shield as a signal to them when they were already back on their ships.

116. So the Persians were sailing around Sunium. Meanwhile the Athenians hurried back as fast as they could to defend the city, and they got there before the Persians arrived. They had come from the precinct of Heracles at Marathon, and now they camped at another precinct of Heracles, the one at Cynosarges. The Persians came and lay at anchor off Phalerum, which was the harbor of Athens at that time. They anchored their ships off this place for a while, and then sailed back to Asia.

117. In this battle at Marathon about 6,400 of the Persians were killed, and 192 of the Athenians. That was the number who fell on each side. A strange thing also happened there. An Athenian, Epizelus son of Cuphagoras, was fighting in the thick of it and proving himself a brave man when he lost the sight of his eyes, though he had not been struck anywhere on his body or hit by anything thrown. He stayed blind for the rest of his life. I was told that he used to tell this story about what happened to him: it seemed to him that a tall man in full armor stood against him, whose beard overshadowed his whole shield; this figure passed him by and killed the man standing next to him. That, as I was told, is the story Epizelus told.

118. Datis, though, on his way back to Asia with his army, saw a vision in his sleep when he reached Myconos. What the vision was is not reported. But as soon as day dawned he had the ships searched, and in a Phoenician ship he found a gilded statue of Apollo. He asked where it had been taken from, and when he learned which temple it came from, he sailed in his own ship to Delos. The Delians had returned to their island by then. Datis set the statue in the temple and told the Delians to take it back to Delium in Theban territory, which lies on the coast directly opposite Chalcis. After giving this order, Datis sailed away. The Delians, however, never took the statue back. Twenty years later the Thebans themselves brought it to Delium, because of an oracle.

119. As for the Eretrians who had been enslaved, Datis and Artaphernes took them up to Susa when they reached Asia. King Darius had been very angry with the Eretrians before they were captured, because they had wronged him first, without provocation. But when he saw them brought before him and in his power, he did them no further harm. Instead he settled them in the land of Cissia, on one of his own estates, called Ardericca. This is about twenty-three miles from Susa, and about four and a half miles from the well that yields three different things: they draw asphalt, salt and oil from it. This is how it is done. The liquid is drawn up with a swing-pole, which has half a skin tied to it instead of a bucket. A man dips this down into the well, draws it up, and pours it into a cistern. From there it runs into another vessel and separates three ways. The asphalt and the salt harden at once. The oil, which the Persians call rhadinace, is black and has an unpleasant smell. That is where King Darius settled the Eretrians, and they were still living in that land in my time, keeping their old language. So much for what happened to the Eretrians.

120. Two thousand Spartans came to Athens after the full moon. They were in such a hurry to be in time that they reached Attica on the third day after leaving Sparta. Although they had come too late for the battle, they still wanted to see the Persians. So they went out to Marathon and looked at the bodies of the dead. Then they went home, praising the Athenians and what they had done.

Chapter 36: The Alcmaeonids, the Wooing of Agariste, and the Fall of Miltiades

121. Now it amazes me, and I do not accept the report, that the Alcmaeonids could ever have held up a shield as a signal to the Persians by a prior arrangement, wanting the Athenians to be under the non-Greeks and under Hippias. For they plainly hated tyrants as much as, or more than, Callias did, the son of Phaenippus and father of Hipponicus. Callias, for his part, was the only man in all Athens who dared to buy the property of Pisistratus when it was put up for sale by the state after Pisistratus was driven out of Athens, and in other ways too he plotted every kind of hostility against him.

122. This Callias deserves to be remembered by everyone, for many reasons. First, for what I have just said: he was a man of real distinction in freeing his country. Then also for what he did at the Olympic games, where he won the horse race and came second in the chariot race; and before that he had won at the Pythian games, so that he was famous among all the Greeks for the money he spent. And finally, because he showed himself so generous toward his daughters, who were three in number. When they were old enough to marry, he gave them the most magnificent dowry and also let them have their own way: whichever man in all Athens each of them wanted to choose as her husband, to that man he gave her.

123. And just like him, the Alcmaeonids hated tyrants as much as he did, or more. So this amazes me, and I do not accept the charge that they were the ones who held up the shield. They were in exile, away from the tyrants, the whole time the tyrants ruled, and it was by their scheming that the sons of Pisistratus gave up their power. It follows that they were the ones who set Athens free, much more than Harmodius and Aristogeiton were, in my judgment. Those two, by killing Hipparchus, only enraged the rest of Pisistratus' family; they did nothing at all to end the others' tyranny. But the Alcmaeonids plainly did set Athens free, at least if they really were the men who persuaded the Pythia to tell the Spartans to set Athens free, as I have explained before.

124. It might be said, however, that they had some grievance against the Athenian people, and so tried to betray their own city. But on the contrary, no men had a higher reputation than they did, at least among the Athenians, and none had been more highly honored. So it is not reasonable to suppose that they would have held up a shield for any such purpose. A shield was held up, though; that cannot be denied, because it happened. But as to who it was who held it up, I cannot say any more than this.

125. Now the family of the Alcmaeonids was distinguished in Athens even in the earliest times, and from the time of Alcmaeon, and of Megacles after him, they became very distinguished indeed. First, Alcmaeon son of Megacles made himself a helper to the Lydians who came from Croesus at Sardis to the oracle at Delphi, and he assisted them eagerly. When Croesus heard from the Lydians who had gone to the oracle that this man had done him good service, he sent for him to come to Sardis. When he came, Croesus offered him a gift of as much gold as he could carry away on his own body at one time. With that gift in mind, and since it was a gift of that kind, Alcmaeon got himself ready and made his preparations like this. He put on a large tunic, leaving a deep fold in it hanging down in front, and he pulled onto his feet the widest boots he could find, and in these he went into the treasury they led him to. There he fell on a heap of gold dust. First he packed as much gold down beside his legs as his boots would hold. Then he filled the whole fold of his tunic with gold, sprinkled some of the gold dust in his hair, and took some into his mouth. After that he came out of the treasury, barely able to drag his boots along and looking like anything in the world rather than a man, since his mouth was stuffed full and every part of him was swollen out. Croesus burst out laughing when he saw him, and not only gave him all of that but gave him as much again on top of it. That is how this house became enormously rich, and that is how this Alcmaeon came to keep chariot horses and won a victory at Olympia.

126. Then, in the next generation, Cleisthenes the tyrant of Sicyon raised the family up, so that it became far better known among the Greeks than it had been before. Cleisthenes son of Arisonymus, son of Myron, son of Andreas, had a daughter named Agariste, and he wanted to find the best man in all Greece and give her to him in marriage. So when the Olympic games were being held and Cleisthenes won at them with a four-horse chariot, he had a proclamation made: any Greek who thought himself worthy to be Cleisthenes' son-in-law should come to Sicyon by the sixtieth day, or earlier if he liked, because Cleisthenes meant to settle the marriage within a year, counting from the sixtieth day. Then all the Greeks who were proud either of themselves or of their families came as suitors, and Cleisthenes had a running track and a wrestling ground built for them and kept them for their use alone.

127. From Italy came Smindyrides son of Hippocrates, of Sybaris, the man who went further in luxury than anyone else on earth (Sybaris was then at the height of its prosperity), and Damasus of Siris, the son of the Amyris who was called the Wise. Those came from Italy. From the Ionian Gulf came Amphimnestus son of Epistrophus, of Epidamnus; he came from the Ionian Gulf. From Aetolia came Males, the brother of the Titormus who was stronger than any other Greek and who fled from human company to the farthest corners of the Aetolian land. From the Peloponnese came Leocedes son of Pheidon, the tyrant of Argos. This was the Pheidon who set up the measures the Peloponnesians use, and who outdid all other Greeks in arrogance, since he threw out the officials the Eleans had appointed to run the games and ran the games at Olympia himself. His son came, and so did Amiantus son of Lycurgus, an Arcadian from Trapezus; and Laphanes, an Azanian from the city of Paeus, son of the Euphorion who (so the story goes in Arcadia) received the Dioscuri as guests in his house, and from then on made a practice of entertaining everyone who came; and Onomastus son of Agaeus, of Elis. Those came from the Peloponnese itself. From Athens came Megacles, the son of the Alcmaeon who went to Croesus, and besides him Hippocleides son of Tisander, who outdid the other Athenians in wealth and good looks. From Eretria, which was flourishing at that time, came Lysanias, the only one from Euboea. From Thessaly came Diactorides of Crannon, one of the Scopad family. And from the Molossians came Alcon.

128. That is how many suitors there were. When they had arrived by the appointed day, Cleisthenes first asked each of them about his country and his family. Then he kept them for a year, testing them continually for their courage, their temper, their upbringing and their manners. He spent time with each of them alone and with all of them together. He tested them by taking the younger ones out to athletic exercises, and above all at the shared table: for the whole time he kept them he did everything that could be done, and at the same time he entertained them magnificently. As it happened, the suitors who pleased him most were the ones from Athens, and of these he rather preferred Hippocleides son of Tisander, both for his manly qualities and because he was related by descent to the Cypselids at Corinth.

129. Then the appointed day came for the wedding feast and for Cleisthenes himself to announce which of them all he had chosen. Cleisthenes sacrificed a hundred oxen and feasted both the suitors themselves and all the people of Sicyon. When dinner was over, the suitors began to compete with each other in music and in speeches before the whole company. As the drinking went on, Hippocleides, who was very much holding everyone's attention, told the flute player to play him a dance tune. When the flute player did, he danced. And it so happened that he was very pleased with his own dancing, but Cleisthenes watched the whole performance with suspicion. After a while Hippocleides told someone to bring in a table. When the table came in, he first danced Laconian figures on it, then Attic ones as well, and third, he planted his head on the table and waved his legs in the air. While he was dancing the first and second rounds, Cleisthenes was already disgusted at the thought that Hippocleides might still become his son-in-law, because of his dancing and his shamelessness, but he held himself back, not wanting to explode at him. But when he saw him waving his legs in the air, he could not hold back any longer, and said:

"You have danced away your marriage, son of Tisander!"

And Hippocleides answered:

"Hippocleides doesn't care!"

130. And that is where the saying comes from. Then Cleisthenes called for silence and spoke to the company: "Suitors of my daughter, I think well of you all, and if it were possible I would satisfy you all, not picking one of you out above the others or rejecting the rest. But since I am deciding about only one girl, it is not possible to please everyone. So to those of you who are turned down for this marriage I give a talent of silver each, for the honor you did me in wanting to marry into my house, and for your time away from home. And to Megacles son of Alcmaeon I engage my daughter Agariste, according to the laws of the Athenians." Megacles said that he accepted the engagement, and so Cleisthenes settled the marriage.

131. That is how the judging of the suitors turned out, and that is how the Alcmaeonids became famous all over Greece. From this marriage was born the Cleisthenes who set up the tribes and the democracy for the Athenians. He was named after his mother's father, Cleisthenes of Sicyon. He was one son born to Megacles; Hippocrates was another. Hippocrates had a son, another Megacles, and a daughter, another Agariste, named after Agariste the daughter of Cleisthenes. This Agariste married Xanthippus son of Ariphron, and when she was pregnant she had a dream in which she seemed to give birth to a lion. A few days later she bore Xanthippus a son, Pericles.

132. After the defeat of the Persians at Marathon, Miltiades, who had already been well thought of in Athens, rose much higher still in the Athenians' esteem. He asked them for seventy ships, an army and money. He did not tell them which country he meant to attack, but said he would make them rich if they followed him, because he would lead them to a land where they could easily get gold in abundance. That was what he said as he asked for the ships, and the Athenians, carried away by his words, handed them over.
