133. Once he had the army, Miltiades sailed for Paros. His excuse was that the Parians had started it, by sending triremes with the Persians to Marathon. That was the pretext he gave, but he also had a grudge against the Parians because of Lysagoras son of Tisias, a Parian by birth, who had slandered him to Hydarnes the Persian. When Miltiades arrived where he was sailing, he shut the Parians up inside their wall and laid siege to them with his army. He sent a herald in to demand a hundred talents, saying that if they refused, his army would not go home until it had captured them. But the Parians had no intention of giving Miltiades any money. All their thought was on how to defend their city. They came up with various plans, and this one besides: wherever the wall was open to attack at any point, they built it up at night to twice its former height.

134. Up to this point the story is told by all the Greeks, but what happened next only the Parians tell, and they say it went like this. When Miltiades was at a loss, the story goes, a woman came to talk with him. She was a prisoner of war, a Parian by birth named Timo, an under-priestess of the Earth goddesses. She came before Miltiades, they say, and advised him that if he thought it very important to take Paros, he should do what she would suggest; and then she told him what she meant. So he went to the hill in front of the city and, since he could not open the gate, jumped over the fence of the temple of Demeter the Lawgiver. Once over, he went on toward the shrine to do something inside, whether to lay hands on some of the things that must not be touched or whatever else he meant to do. But when he reached the door, a shuddering terror came over him at once, and he started back the way he had come. As he jumped down from the rough stone wall, he dislocated his thigh, or, as others say, he hit his knee against the wall.

135. So Miltiades, in a bad way, sailed for home. He brought the Athenians no wealth and had not won Paros for them; he had besieged the city for twenty-six days and laid waste the island. When the Parians learned that Timo, the under-priestess of the goddesses, had guided Miltiades, they wanted to punish her for it. As soon as they had a breathing space after the siege, they sent messengers to Delphi to consult the god. The messengers were to ask whether they should put to death the under-priestess of the goddesses, who had guided their enemies to the capture of her own city and had revealed to Miltiades the mysteries that no man may be told. But the Pythia forbade it. Timo, she said, was not the real cause of these things; since it was fated that Miltiades would come to a bad end, she had appeared to him to lead him on to his ruin.

136. That was the Pythia's answer to the Parians. Meanwhile, when Miltiades got back from Paros, the Athenians had a great deal to say about him, and Xanthippus son of Ariphron more than anyone. He brought Miltiades to trial before the people on a capital charge and prosecuted him for deceiving the Athenians. Miltiades did not speak in his own defense, though he was there; he could not, because his thigh was rotting. Instead he lay on a couch in full view, while his friends spoke for him. They talked a great deal about the battle at Marathon and about the taking of Lemnos: how he had conquered Lemnos, punished the Pelasgians, and handed the island over to the Athenians. The people came over to his side so far as to acquit him of the death penalty, but they fined him fifty talents for his wrongdoing. After this Miltiades died, when his thigh turned gangrenous and rotted, and his son Cimon paid the fifty talents.

137. Now this is how Miltiades son of Cimon had taken Lemnos. The Pelasgians had been driven out of Attica by the Athenians, whether justly or unjustly. On that point I can only tell what is reported, which is this. Hecataeus son of Hegesander said in his history that it was done unjustly. According to him, the Athenians had given the Pelasgians the land below Mount Hymettus to live on, as payment for the wall they had once built around the Acropolis. When the Athenians saw that this land, which had been poor and worthless before, was now well farmed, they were seized with envy and a longing to have it, and so they drove the Pelasgians out, without giving any other excuse. But according to the Athenians' own account, they drove them out justly. For the Pelasgians, settled below Hymettus, used it as a base to wrong them, like this. The Athenians' daughters and sons used to go regularly for water to the spring called Enneacrunus, the Nine Fountains, because at that time neither the Athenians nor any other Greeks had household slaves yet. And whenever the girls came, the Pelasgians, out of arrogance and contempt for the Athenians, would assault them. Not content with that, they were finally caught in the act of plotting to attack the city. And the tellers say that in this the Athenians proved themselves better men than the Pelasgians: they could have killed the Pelasgians, who had been caught plotting against them, but they chose not to, and only ordered them to leave the country. Having left the country in this way, the Pelasgians took over various places, and Lemnos in particular. The first story is the one Hecataeus told; the second is the one the Athenians tell.

138. These Pelasgians, then, living on Lemnos after this, wanted revenge on the Athenians. Since they knew the Athenian festivals well, they got some fifty-oared galleys and lay in wait for the Athenian women when they were celebrating the festival of Artemis at Brauron. They carried off a number of them from there, sailed away home, took the women to Lemnos, and kept them as concubines. As these women had more and more children, they made a point of teaching their sons the Attic language and the Athenian ways. These boys would not mix with the sons of the Pelasgian women, and if any one of them was hit by one of those boys, they all came running in a body to help each other. On top of that, the boys claimed the right to rule over the other boys, and easily got the better of them. When the Pelasgians saw this, they talked it over among themselves. As they discussed it, fear came over them. If these boys were already determined to stand by each other against the sons of the lawful wives, and were already trying from the start to rule over them, what would they do once they were grown men? So they decided to kill the sons of the Athenian women, and they actually did it; and along with the sons they killed their mothers too. Because of this deed, and the one done before it, when the women of Lemnos killed Thoas and the rest of their own husbands, it has become the custom all over Greece to call any deed of great cruelty a "Lemnian deed."

139. After the Pelasgians had killed their own sons and wives, the earth bore them no crops, and their women and their flocks and herds did not bear young as they had before. Hard pressed by famine and childlessness, they sent to Delphi to ask how they might be released from the evils that were on them. The Pythia told them to pay the Athenians whatever penalty the Athenians themselves should name. So the Pelasgians went to Athens and announced that they were willing to pay the penalty for all the wrong they had done. The Athenians spread a couch in the town hall as beautifully as they could, set beside it a table loaded with every good thing, and told the Pelasgians to hand over their land to them in that same condition. The Pelasgians answered: "When a ship sails from your land to ours with a north wind in a single day, then we will hand it over." They said this because they were sure it could never happen, since Attica lies far to the south of Lemnos.

140. That was how things stood at that time. Very many years later, after the Chersonese on the Hellespont had come under Athenian control, Miltiades son of Cimon, while the Etesian winds were blowing steadily, made the voyage in a single ship from Elaeus in the Chersonese to Lemnos. He told the Pelasgians to leave the island, reminding them of the oracle, which the Pelasgians had never expected to see fulfilled. The people of Hephaestia obeyed. But the people of Myrina refused to admit that the Chersonese was Attica, and were besieged until at last they too gave in. That is how the Athenians and Miltiades took Lemnos.

Book Seven: Polymnia

Chapter 37: Xerxes Decides on War, and the Dream

1. When the news of the battle fought at Marathon reached Darius son of Hystaspes, the king was angrier than ever. He had been furious with the Athenians even before this, because of their attack on Sardis, but now his indignation was far greater, and he was far more eager to march against Greece. So he sent messengers at once to the various cities and ordered them to get an army ready. He assigned each people a much larger share than they had supplied before, and not only warships but also horses, provisions and transport ships. When these orders went round, all Asia was in turmoil for three years, because the best men everywhere were being enlisted for the expedition against Greece and were getting ready for it. In the fourth year, however, the Egyptians, whom Cambyses had conquered, revolted from the Persians. Then Darius was even more eager to march, and against both nations.

2. While Darius was preparing to set out against Egypt and against Athens, a great quarrel broke out among his sons over who should hold the supreme power. According to Persian custom, they said, he must not set out on his campaigns until he had named one of them king. Darius had three sons born to him before he became king, by his first wife, the daughter of Gobryas, and four more after he became king, by Atossa the daughter of Cyrus. The eldest of the first group was Artobazanes, and the eldest of the later group was Xerxes. Since they did not have the same mother, the two of them were rivals. Artobazanes argued that he was the eldest of all the sons, and that it was a custom held by all mankind that the eldest should rule. Xerxes argued that he was the son of Atossa, the daughter of Cyrus, and that it was Cyrus who had won the Persians their freedom.

3. Darius had not yet announced his decision when it happened that Demaratus son of Ariston arrived in Susa at this very time. He had been stripped of his kingship in Sparta and had sent himself into exile from Laconia. When this man heard of the dispute between Darius' sons, he came to Xerxes (so the story goes) and advised him to add something to the arguments he was already making. Xerxes should say, Demaratus suggested, that he had been born to Darius when Darius was already king and held supreme power over the Persians, while Artobazanes had been born when Darius was still a private citizen. It was therefore neither fitting nor just that anyone else should have the honor ahead of him. Even in Sparta, Demaratus pointed out, this was the custom: if some sons were born before their father became king, and another was born later, while he was reigning, the succession to the kingdom belonged to the one born later. So Xerxes used Demaratus' suggestion, and Darius, seeing that what he said was just, named him king. My own opinion, however, is that Xerxes would have become king even without this advice, because Atossa held all the power.

4. Having named Xerxes to the Persians as their king, Darius was ready to set out on his campaigns. But in the year after this, and after the revolt of Egypt, Darius himself died, after reigning thirty-six years in all. So he never got his revenge, either on the Egyptians who had revolted or on the Athenians.

5. When Darius was dead, the kingdom passed to his son Xerxes. At first Xerxes was not at all eager to march against Greece, though he went on gathering an army against Egypt. But Mardonius son of Gobryas, who was Xerxes' cousin (his mother was Darius' sister), was always at his side, and he had more influence with him than any other Persian. He kept saying things like this: "Master, it is not right that the Athenians should do the Persians such great harm and not pay the penalty for what they have done. For now, why not finish the work you have in hand? Then, when you have tamed Egypt, which has risen against us so insolently, march an army against Athens. That way men will speak well of you, and in future everyone will think twice before attacking your land." That much of his argument was about revenge. To it he would add that Europe was a very beautiful country, that it grew every kind of cultivated fruit tree, that it was wonderfully fertile, and that the king alone of all mortals deserved to own it.

6. He kept saying these things because he had an appetite for risky ventures and wanted to be governor of Greece under the king himself. In time he won Xerxes over and persuaded him to do it, because other things also worked on his side and helped him persuade Xerxes. First, messengers had come from Thessaly, sent by the Aleuadae, inviting the king to invade Greece and showing great zeal for his cause. (These Aleuadae were the kings of Thessaly.) Second, the sons of Pisistratus who had come up to Susa were inviting him too. They used the same arguments as the Aleuadae, and they offered him something more besides. There was an Athenian named Onomacritus, who delivered oracles and had also collected and arranged the oracles of Musaeus, the legendary poet and seer. The Pisistratids had brought this man up with them to Susa, after first making up their old quarrel with him. For Onomacritus had been banished from Athens by Hipparchus son of Pisistratus. Lasus of Hermione had caught him slipping into the works of Musaeus an oracle of his own, which said that the islands lying off Lemnos would disappear under the sea. That was why Hipparchus banished him, though before that he had consulted him a great deal. Now, however, Onomacritus had come up to Susa with them. Whenever he came into the king's presence, the sons of Pisistratus praised him in grand terms, and he recited some of the oracles. If any of them foretold disaster for the Persians, he said nothing about it. Instead he picked out the most favorable ones, and told how it was fated that a Persian would yoke the Hellespont with a bridge, and he described how the march would go. So he kept pressing Xerxes with oracles, while the sons of Pisistratus and the Aleuadae pressed him with their advice.

7. Once Xerxes had been persuaded to make war on Greece, he marched first against the rebels, in the year after Darius' death. He crushed them and reduced all Egypt to a far harsher slavery than it had known under Darius, and he handed over the government of the country to his own brother Achaemenes, a son of Darius. Later, while he was governor of Egypt, this Achaemenes was killed by Inaros son of Psammetichus, a Libyan.

8. After conquering Egypt, Xerxes was about to take the expedition against Athens in hand. So he called together an assembly of the leading Persians, both to hear their opinions and to tell them all, face to face, what he meant to do. When they had gathered, Xerxes spoke to them as follows:

"Persians, I am not going to be the first to bring in a new custom among you. I received this one from others, and I will follow it. As I am told by those older than I am, we have never yet sat still since we took over this supremacy from the Medes, when Cyrus overthrew Astyages. It is a god who leads us this way, and when we busy ourselves with many things, it turns out well for us. About the nations that Cyrus and Cambyses and my father Darius conquered and added to our empire, there is no need for me to speak: you know them well. As for me, from the day I inherited this throne I sit on, I have always thought hard about how I might not fall short of those who held this high place before me, nor add less power to the empire of the Persians. And thinking hard about it, I find a way by which we can win glory, and a land no smaller and no worse than the one we have now (and in fact richer in what it produces), and at the same time get our vengeance and our revenge. That is why I have called you together now, to tell you what I have in mind to do.

"I intend to yoke the Hellespont with a bridge and march an army through Europe against Greece, so that I can punish the Athenians for everything they have done to the Persians and to my father. You saw how my father Darius was also planning to march against these men. But he has died, and he never got his revenge on them. I, though, on his behalf and on behalf of the rest of the Persians, will not stop until I have taken Athens and burned it, since they wronged me and my father without any provocation. First they came to Sardis with Aristagoras of Miletus, our slave, and set fire to the sacred groves and the temples. And second, you all know well, I think, what they did to us when we landed in their country, at the time when Datis and Artaphernes were in command of our army.

"For these reasons I have decided to march against them, and when I count up what we stand to gain, I find these good things, as you will hear. If we conquer these people and their neighbors, who live in the land of Pelops the Phrygian, we will make the Persian land border on nothing but the sky of Zeus. The sun will look down on no land that borders ours. With your help I will make all lands into one land, once I have passed through the whole of Europe. For I am told the situation is this: once the people I have just mentioned are out of the way, there is no city of men left, and no race of human beings, that will be able to stand up to us in battle. So those who have wronged us will bear the yoke of slavery, and so will those who have done us no wrong.

"Here is how you will please me best. Whenever I signal to you the time you should come, every one of you must report, and report eagerly. And whoever comes with the best-equipped force, to him I will give the gifts our country counts most honorable. That is how this must be done. But so that I may not seem to you to be following my own advice alone, I put the matter before you for discussion, and I invite any of you who wishes to give his opinion."

9. With that he stopped, and after him Mardonius spoke: "Master, you are the best not only of all the Persians who have lived before you, but of all who will come after. In everything else you have said, your words have hit on what is best and truest, and on top of that you will not allow the Ionians who live in Europe to make fools of us, when they have no right to. It would be a strange thing indeed if we have conquered Sacae, Indians, Ethiopians, Assyrians and many other great nations, who never did the Persians any wrong, and keep them as our subjects, simply because we wanted to enlarge our empire, and yet we do not take revenge on the Greeks, who wronged us without provocation.

"What should we be afraid of? Their numbers? The size of their wealth? We know how they fight, and we know their resources are weak. Besides, we have already conquered their sons, I mean the ones settled in our land who are called Ionians, Aeolians and Dorians. I myself have tried marching against these men before, under orders from your father. I marched as far as Macedonia, and came close to reaching Athens itself, and no one came out to fight me.

"It is true that the Greeks do make war, but from what I hear they go about it very foolishly, out of stubbornness and lack of skill. When they have declared war on one another, they look for the finest, flattest stretch of ground they can find, and they go down there and fight. The result is that even the winners come away with heavy losses, and as for the losers, I won't even mention them, because they are wiped out completely. Since they all speak the same language, they ought to use heralds and messengers to settle their differences, any way at all rather than by battle. And if they absolutely must fight each other, each side ought to find the place where it is hardest to beat, and make its stand there. So the Greeks, since their way of war is no good, did not even make up their minds to fight me when I had marched as far as Macedonia.

"Who, then, is likely to stand against you, my king, and offer you war, when you are leading the whole multitude of Asia and the whole of your fleet? For my part, I don't think the Greek states have grown as bold as that. But if after all I turn out to be wrong, and they are carried away by reckless folly and come out to fight us, they will learn that we are the best soldiers in the world. Whatever happens, let us leave nothing untried. Nothing comes about by itself; everything men achieve comes from trying."

10. With these words Mardonius had smoothed the way for Xerxes' proposal, and he stopped. The other Persians kept silent and did not dare to offer an opinion against what had been proposed. Then Artabanus son of Hystaspes, who was Xerxes' uncle, his father's brother, and who relied on that relationship, spoke as follows:

"My king, if opposing opinions are not spoken, it is impossible to choose the better one; you have to accept whatever has been said. But if opposing opinions are spoken, then you can choose. It is like pure gold: we cannot tell it is pure when it lies by itself, but when we rub it on the touchstone beside other gold, then we can tell which is better. I advised your father Darius, my own brother, not to march against the Scythians, a people who have no settled city anywhere on earth. But he expected to conquer those nomad Scythians, and he did not listen to me. He marched, and he came back having lost many good men from his army. You, my king, are planning to march against men far better than the Scythians, men said to be excellent fighters both at sea and on land. What there is to fear in this, it is only right that I should tell you.

"You say you will yoke the Hellespont with a bridge and march an army through Europe to Greece. Now suppose we happen to be beaten, either on land or at sea, or even both, for these men are said to be brave fighters. (And we can judge for ourselves that it is true, since the Athenians on their own destroyed that great army that came to Attica with Datis and Artaphernes.) Or suppose they do not win on both. Still, if they attack with their ships and win a sea battle, and then sail to the Hellespont and break up the bridge, that alone, my king, will put us in great danger.

"I am not guessing at this out of any wisdom of my own. I am only guessing at the kind of disaster that very nearly fell on us the last time, when your father had yoked the Thracian Bosporus and bridged the Danube, and had crossed over to attack the Scythians. At that time the Scythians tried every kind of plea to persuade the Ionians, who had been given the job of guarding the bridges over the Danube, to break up the crossing. And at that time, if Histiaeus the tyrant of Miletus had gone along with the opinion of the other tyrants and had not opposed them, the power of the Persians would have come to an end. Yet it is a frightening thing even to hear it said that the whole power of the king once hung on a single human being.

"So do not plan to run into any such danger when there is no need. Do as I say instead. Dismiss this assembly for now. Then later, whenever you see fit, once you have thought it over carefully by yourself, announce whatever seems best to you. For I hold that good planning is the greatest gain there is. Even if something goes against us, the plan was no less good; it was simply defeated by bad luck. But a man who planned badly, if luck goes with him, has stumbled on a prize by chance, and his plan was bad all the same.

"You see how the god strikes with his thunderbolts the creatures that stand out above the rest, and does not let them show off, while the small ones do not provoke his jealousy at all. You see also how he always hurls his bolts at the tallest buildings and the tallest trees. For the god likes to cut down everything that stands out above the rest. In the same way a huge army is destroyed by a small one, in a way like this: when the god grows jealous of them and sends panic among them, or thunder from the sky, they are destroyed utterly, in a way they did not deserve. For the god does not allow anyone but himself to think big thoughts.

"Besides, hurrying any business breeds failures, and great losses usually come from them. But in waiting there are many good things, and even if they do not look good at first, in time you will find that they are.

"That is my advice to you, my king. But you, son of Gobryas, Mardonius, stop talking nonsense about the Greeks. They do not deserve to be belittled. By slandering the Greeks you are urging the king himself to march against them, and that, I think, is exactly what you are straining every nerve to bring about. Don't let it happen. Slander is a terrible thing: in slander there are two wrongdoers and one victim. The slanderer does wrong because he speaks against someone who is not there. The listener does wrong because he believes the story before he finds out the truth of it. And the man who is not present when the words are spoken is wronged by both: slandered by the one, and taken for a bad man by the other.

"But if we really must march against these men, then come: let the king himself stay at home in the land of the Persians, and let the two of us stake our sons on it. Then you lead the army by yourself, choosing whatever men you like and taking as large an army as you think fit. If things turn out for the king the way you say, let my sons be put to death, and let me be put to death with them. But if they turn out the way I predict, let your sons suffer that, and you with them, if you ever come home. And if you are not willing to submit to this test, but are set on leading an army against Greece no matter what, then I say this: those left behind here will one day hear that Mardonius has done the Persians great harm and lies torn apart by dogs and birds somewhere in the land of the Athenians, or else perhaps in the land of the Spartans, unless it has happened even before that, along the way. And they will hear that you have learned at last what kind of men you are persuading the king to march against."

11. That was what Artabanus said. Xerxes was furious, and answered him: "Artabanus, you are my father's brother, and that will save you from getting the reward your foolish words deserve. But I lay this disgrace on you, since you are a coward with no spirit in you: you will not march with me against Greece, but stay here with the women. And I will accomplish everything I said even without your help. May I not be descended from Darius son of Hystaspes, son of Arsames, son of Ariaramnes, son of Teispes, or from Cyrus son of Cambyses, son of Teispes, son of Achaemenes, if I do not take revenge on the Athenians! For I know well that if we keep quiet, they will not. They will march against our land again, if we can judge by what they have already done, since they burned Sardis and marched into Asia. So it is impossible for either side to back away from this quarrel. The question before us is whether we act or are acted on: whether all these lands of ours fall under the Greeks, or all of theirs under the Persians. In our hostility there is no middle way. So it is right for us, since we were wronged first, to take our revenge. That way I will also find out what this terrible thing is that I am going to suffer if I lead an army against these men, men whom Pelops the Phrygian, a slave of my forefathers, conquered so thoroughly that to this day both the people themselves and their land are named after the man who conquered them."

12. That was how far the talk went. But later, when night came on, Artabanus' opinion kept tormenting Xerxes. He made the night his counselor, and he decided that it was not at all in his interest to march against Greece. Having made this new decision, he fell asleep, and in the night, as the Persians tell it, he saw a vision like this. Xerxes dreamed that a tall, handsome man came and stood over him and said: "So you are changing your mind, Persian, about leading an army against Greece, now that you have proclaimed that the Persians are to gather their forces? You do wrong to change your mind, and the one who stands here before you will not forgive you for it. Go the way you decided to go in the daytime."

13. When he had said this, Xerxes dreamed that the man flew away. When day came, Xerxes paid no attention to this dream. He called together the same Persians he had assembled before and said to them: "Persians, forgive me for changing my plans so quickly. My judgment has not yet come to its full strength, and those who urge me to do what I said never leave me alone for long. When I first heard Artabanus' opinion, my youthful temper boiled over, so that I threw out words I should not have said to a man older than I am. But now I admit he is right, and I will follow his advice. So consider that I have changed my mind about marching against Greece, and stay quietly at home."

14. When the Persians heard this they were delighted, and they bowed down before him. But when night came on, the same dream came again and stood over Xerxes as he slept and said: "Son of Darius, so it is plain that you have given up this expedition in front of the Persian assembly, and that you have paid no attention to my words, as if you had heard them from nobody at all. So be quite sure of this: if you do not set out on your march at once, this is what will come of it for you. Just as you became great and mighty in a short time, so you will quickly be brought low again."

15. Xerxes was badly shaken by fear of the vision. He leapt up from his bed and sent a messenger to summon Artabanus. When he came, Xerxes said to him: "Artabanus, at first I lost my head, when I spoke foolish words to you in return for your good advice. But not long after I changed my mind and saw that I ought to do what you had suggested. But I cannot do it, though I want to. Ever since I turned around and changed my mind, a dream keeps visiting me, and it will not allow me to do it at all. Just now it has left me with a threat. Now, if it is a god who sends it to me, and it is his absolute will that an army should go against Greece, this same dream will fly to you as well, and give you the same orders it has given me. And it occurs to me that this might happen if you take all my clothes and put them on, and then sit on my throne, and after that lie down to sleep in my bed."

16. That was what Xerxes said to him. At first Artabanus was unwilling to obey, because he did not think himself worthy to sit on the royal throne. But at last, when he was pressed further, he did as he was told, though first he said this:

"In my judgment, my king, it is equally good for a man to be wise himself or to be willing to follow good advice from someone else. You have both of these good things, but the company of bad men leads you astray. It is like what they say of the sea, the most useful of all things to mankind: the blasts of wind that fall on it keep it from behaving according to its own nature. As for me, when you insulted me, I was not hurt so much by that. What hurt me was this. Two opinions were put before the Persians. One tended to increase arrogance. The other tended to check it, and said what a bad thing it is to teach the soul always to want more than it has. And when these two opinions were put before us, you chose the one that was more dangerous both for yourself and for the Persians.

"Now that you have turned to the better plan, you say that when you were ready to give up the expedition against the Greeks, a dream sent by some god kept haunting you and forbidding you to abandon the enterprise. But here too you are mistaken, my son. This has nothing divine about it. I am many years older than you, and I will tell you what kind of thing these dreams are that come drifting to men in their sleep. The visions in our dreams mostly take the shape of whatever we were thinking about during the day. And in these past days we have been very much taken up with this campaign.

"But if after all this is not what I take it to be, and there is something divine in it, then you have said everything there is to say: let it appear to me too, as it did to you, and give me orders. But if it wants to appear to me at all, it is not any more bound to appear to me if I am wearing your clothes than if I am wearing my own, or any more if I am resting in your bed than in mine. Surely this thing, whatever it is, that appears to you in your sleep is not so foolish that it will see me and think I am you, just because I am wearing your clothes. What we have to find out now is this: whether it will take no notice of me and not see fit to appear to me, whether I have my own clothes on or yours, but go on haunting you. If it really does keep haunting you, I will be inclined to say myself that it is divine. But if you have made up your mind that it shall be done this way, and there is no turning you from it, and I must go to sleep in your bed, very well: let it appear to me too, when I have done these things. But until then I will hold to the opinion I have now."

17. Having said this, Artabanus did what he was told, expecting to prove that Xerxes was talking nonsense. He put on Xerxes' clothes, sat on the royal throne, and after that went to bed. And when he had fallen asleep, the same dream that had been coming to Xerxes came to him. It stood over Artabanus and said: "So you are the one who is trying to talk Xerxes out of marching against Greece, pretending that you are looking out for him? But you will not get away unpunished, either in the future or now, for trying to turn aside what is fated to happen. As for Xerxes, what he must suffer if he disobeys has already been shown to the man himself."

18. That was how the dream seemed to Artabanus to threaten him, and at the same moment it seemed about to burn out his eyes with red-hot irons. He leapt up from his bed with a loud cry, and sitting down beside Xerxes, he told him the whole vision of the dream from start to finish. Then he said to him: "My king, I have seen many great things brought down by lesser ones, and so I urged you not to give in to every impulse of your youth, since I knew how bad it is to want too many things. I remembered how Cyrus' march against the Massagetae turned out, and also Cambyses' march against the Ethiopians, and I myself took part with Darius in the campaign against the Scythians. Knowing these things, I believed that as long as you stayed quiet, all men would count you fortunate. But since there is a push from heaven, and, it seems, a destruction sent by the gods is taking hold of the Greeks, I am changing my mind myself, and I reverse my opinion. Tell the Persians the message heaven has sent you, and order them to carry out the preparations you first commanded. And see to it that nothing is lacking on your side, since the god is putting this into your hands." After this was said, both of them were encouraged by the vision. As soon as it was day, Xerxes told the Persians about it, and Artabanus, who before had been the only one to come forward and argue against the plan, now came forward to urge it on.

19. Xerxes was now eager to make the expedition, and after this a third vision came to him in his sleep. When the Magi heard it, they explained that it referred to dominion over the whole earth, and meant that all mankind would be his subjects. The vision was this. Xerxes dreamed that he had been crowned with a wreath of olive, and that shoots growing from the olive tree spread over the whole earth, and that after that the wreath, set on his head as it was, vanished. When the Magi had interpreted the vision this way, every one of the Persians who had been assembled went straight home to his own province and set about carrying out the orders with every kind of zeal, each man wanting to win for himself the gifts that had been offered. And so Xerxes went on gathering his army, searching every region of the continent.

Chapter 38: The Canal at Athos, Pythius the Lydian, and the Bridges on the Hellespont

20. For four full years after the conquest of Egypt, Xerxes was getting the army ready, along with everything the army would need. Then, in the course of the fifth year, he set out on campaign with an enormous host. Of all the armies we know of, this one was by far the greatest. Next to it, the army Darius led against the Scythians looks like nothing at all. So does the Scythian host, back when the Scythians chased the Cimmerians, invaded the land of the Medes, and conquered and occupied nearly all of upper Asia, the invasion Darius later tried to punish them for. So does the army the sons of Atreus, Agamemnon and Menelaus, led to Troy, to judge by what is reported of that expedition. And so does the army of the Mysians and Teucrians before the Trojan War, who crossed over into Europe by the Bosporus, conquered all the Thracians, and came down as far as the Ionian Sea and as far south as the river Peneus.

21. All these expeditions put together, with any others there may have been added to them, do not equal this one alone. For what nation of Asia did Xerxes not lead out against Greece? And what water was not drunk dry by his host, except for the great rivers? Some peoples supplied ships, and others were assigned to serve in the land army. Some were ordered to provide cavalry, and others ships to carry horses, while also serving in the expedition themselves. Others were told to provide warships for the bridges, and others again ships loaded with provisions.

22. First of all, since the earlier fleet had come to disaster sailing around Athos, preparations had been going on at Athos for about three years. Triremes lay at anchor at Elaeus in the Chersonese, and with this as their base, men of every nation in the army were made to dig, driven to it with whips. They went to the work in regular shifts, one group after another. The people who lived around Athos dug too. Two Persians were put in charge of the work: Bubares son of Megabazus and Artachaees son of Artaeus.

Athos is a great and famous mountain that runs down into the sea, and people live on it. Where the mountain ends on the landward side, the place is like a peninsula, with an isthmus about a mile and a third across. This isthmus is flat ground or low hills, running from the sea off Acanthus to the sea off Torone. On this isthmus, where Athos ends, stands a Greek city called Sane. Beyond Sane, out on the peninsula of Athos itself, are other cities, and at this time the Persian king had decided to make them island cities instead of mainland ones. They are Dion, Olophyxus, Acrothoum, Thyssus and Cleonae.

23. Those are the cities on Athos. And this is how they dug. The ground was divided among the various peoples of the army for the work. At the city of Sane they drew a straight line across the isthmus. When the channel got deep, the men standing at the bottom dug, and handed the earth as it came out to other men standing above them, as if on steps. These passed it up to others in turn, until it reached the men at the very top, who carried it away and dumped it. All of them except the Phoenicians had twice the work, because the steep sides of their trench kept caving in. They were trying to make the opening at the top the same width as the bottom, so something like that was bound to happen as they worked. But the Phoenicians, who show their skill in everything they build, showed it in this work too. When they had been given their share by lot, they started digging with the opening at the top twice as wide as the channel itself was meant to be. As the work went down, they kept narrowing it, so that by the time they reached the bottom their section was the same width as everyone else's. There is a meadow there, where a market was set up for them, a place for buying and selling, and large amounts of grain came for them regularly from Asia, already ground into flour.

24. Making my own guess about this work, it seems to me that Xerxes ordered the canal dug out of a love of grandeur. He wanted to show off his power and leave a monument behind him. For they could have dragged the ships across the isthmus without much trouble, but he ordered them to dig a channel for the sea wide enough for two triremes to be rowed through it side by side. The same men who were assigned the digging were also assigned to bridge the river Strymon, joining its two banks.

25. So that was how Xerxes was going about these things. Meanwhile he also had cables prepared for the bridges, made of papyrus and of white flax, and gave this job to the Phoenicians and the Egyptians. He was also arranging to store up provisions along the route, so that neither the army nor the pack animals would go short as they marched against Greece. He found out by inquiry which places were best, and ordered depots set up in the most convenient spots, with supplies shipped in to different points by merchant ships and ferryboats from every country in Asia. Most of the grain was carried to a place in Thrace called Leuce Acte, "White Cape." Others carried supplies to Tyrodiza in the territory of Perinthus, others to Doriscus, others to Eion on the Strymon, and others to Macedonia, the work being divided among them.

26. While these people were working at the jobs they had been given, the whole land army had been gathered and was marching with Xerxes to Sardis, setting out from Critalla in Cappadocia. That was where the whole army that was to go with Xerxes himself by land had been ordered to assemble. Which of the provincial governors brought the best-equipped force and won the prizes the king had offered, I can't say, because I do not know that it ever even came to a judging. After they crossed the river Halys and entered Phrygia, they marched through that country and came to Celaenae. There the springs of the river Maeander rise, and also those of another river no smaller than the Maeander, called the Catarractes. This one rises right in the marketplace of Celaenae and runs into the Maeander. Also in this city hangs the skin of Marsyas the Silenus, the satyr who challenged Apollo to a music contest; the Phrygians say Apollo flayed it off him and hung it up there.

27. In this city a Lydian, Pythius son of Atys, was waiting for the king. He entertained Xerxes himself and his whole army with the most lavish hospitality, and declared he was ready to supply money for the war as well. When Pythius offered money, Xerxes asked the Persians who were with him who this Pythius was and how much money he had, to make an offer like that. They said: "My king, this is the man who gave your father Darius the golden plane tree and the golden vine. And even now he is the richest man we know of, after you alone."

28. Xerxes was amazed at the last part of this, and next he asked Pythius himself how much money he had. Pythius said: "My king, I will not hide the truth from you, or pretend I don't know what I own. I will count it out for you exactly, since I know the truth of it. As soon as I heard that you were coming down to the Greek sea, I wanted to give you money for the war, so I found out the facts. When I added it up, I found I had 2,000 talents of silver, and of gold, 4,000,000 daric staters, the Persian gold coin, less 7,000. All of this I give to you. For myself, my slaves and my estates give me enough to live on."

29. That is what he said. Xerxes was pleased with his words and replied: "My Lydian host, since I left the land of Persia I have met no one else up to now who wanted to entertain my army, or who came before me and offered of his own free will to contribute money to me for the war, no one except you. You have not only entertained my army magnificently, you are now offering me huge sums of money as well. So in return I give you these rewards. I make you my guest-friend. And I will make up your 4,000,000 staters by giving you the 7,000 myself, so that your 4,000,000 will not fall 7,000 short, and you will have a round sum, made complete by me. Keep what you have earned for yourself, and be sure always to act like this. If you do, you will never be sorry for it, either now or later."

30. Having said this and kept his promise, he marched on. He passed a Phrygian city called Anaua and a lake where salt is harvested, and came to Colossae, a great city of Phrygia. There the river Lycus drops into an opening in the earth and disappears from sight. Then, after about half a mile, it comes up into view again, and this river too flows into the Maeander. Setting out from Colossae toward the border of Phrygia and Lydia, the army reached the city of Cydrara. A pillar stands there, set up by Croesus, with an inscription declaring that the border is at that spot.

31. From Phrygia, then, he entered Lydia. Here the road splits in two. The left-hand road leads toward Caria, and the right-hand one to Sardis. Taking the right-hand road, you have to cross the river Maeander and pass the city of Callatebus, where the men make honey for a living, out of the tamarisk tree and wheat flour. Xerxes took this road, and on it he found a plane tree so beautiful that he adorned it with gold and appointed a man to guard it forever, one keeper after another. On the next day he came to the Lydians' capital.

32. When he reached Sardis, the first thing he did was send heralds to Greece to demand earth and water, and also to give notice in advance that dinners should be prepared for the king. He sent to every state except Athens and Sparta; to those two he did not send to ask for earth. The reason he sent a second time to ask for earth and water was this: he thought that all those who had not given it when Darius sent before would certainly give it now, out of fear. He wanted to know this for certain, and so he sent.

33. After this he got ready to march to Abydos. Meanwhile his men were bridging the Hellespont from Asia to Europe. In the Chersonese on the Hellespont, between the city of Sestos and Madytus, there is a broad headland running down into the sea directly opposite Abydos. This is the place where, not long afterward, the Athenians under Xanthippus son of Ariphron captured Artayctes, a Persian who was governor of Sestos, and nailed him alive to a plank with his hands and feet stretched out. (He was the man who used to bring women into the temple of Protesilaus at Elaeus and do things there that are forbidden.)

34. It was to this headland that the men given the job built their bridges, starting from Abydos. The Phoenicians built one with cables of white flax, and the Egyptians the other, made with papyrus cables. From Abydos to the opposite shore is a distance of about 4,200 feet, a little under a mile. But when the strait had been bridged, a great storm blew up, smashed all the work to pieces and broke it apart.

When Xerxes heard this he was furious. He ordered the Hellespont to be given three hundred lashes with the whip and a pair of shackles to be dropped into the sea. I have even heard that he sent branders along with them to brand the Hellespont. In any case, he ordered them, as they whipped it, to say these barbarous and arrogant words: "You bitter water, your master lays this punishment on you, because you wronged him when he had done you no wrong. And King Xerxes will cross you whether you like it or not. It is right, it seems, that no man offers you sacrifice, since you are a treacherous and salty river." That was how he ordered them to punish the sea. And he ordered that the men in charge of bridging the Hellespont should have their heads cut off.

36. So the men who had been given this ugly duty carried it out, and meanwhile other master builders set to work on the bridges. This is how they built them. They lashed together fifty-oared galleys and triremes, 360 to go under the bridge on the Black Sea side and 314 under the other. The ships lay along the line of the Hellespont's current (though crosswise to the Black Sea), to take the strain of the cables. They set them side by side like this and let down very large anchors: on the one side, toward the Black Sea, because of the winds that blow out from it, and on the other side, toward the west and the Aegean, because of the southeast and south winds. They also left a gap to pass through, so that anyone who wanted could sail into the Black Sea in small boats, and out of it again.

When this was done, they stretched the cables tight from the shore, hauling them taut with wooden windlasses. This time they did not use the two kinds of cable separately. Instead they gave each bridge two cables of white flax and four of papyrus. The thickness and the quality of the work were the same for both, but the flax cables were heavier in proportion: every foot and a half of this cable weighed a talent, about fifty-seven pounds. When the strait was bridged, they sawed up logs, cut them to the width of the bridge, and laid them across the taut cables. Once they had set them in a row, they fastened them down on top. When this was done, they brought on brushwood, and when the brushwood was in place, they brought earth on top of that. When they had stamped the earth down hard, they built a fence along each side, so that the pack animals and horses would not be frightened by looking out over the sea.

37. When the bridges had been finished, and word came that the works at Athos were fully complete, both the canal itself and the breakwaters at its two mouths (these were built to keep the surf from filling up the mouths), the army, which had spent the winter at Sardis, set out from there at the beginning of spring, fully equipped, to march to Abydos. Just as it was setting out, the sun left its place in the sky and vanished, though there were no clouds and the sky was perfectly clear, and day turned into night. When Xerxes saw and understood this, it worried him, and he asked the Magi what the sign meant. They declared that the god was showing the Greeks in advance that their cities would be abandoned. The sun, they said, foretold the future for the Greeks, but the moon for the Persians. When he heard this, Xerxes went on with the march overjoyed.

38. As he was leading his army out, Pythius the Lydian, alarmed by the sign in the sky and made bold by the gifts he had received, came to Xerxes and said: "Master, I would like to ask you for something. It happens to be an easy thing for you to grant, but a great thing for me, if I get it." Xerxes, who thought the request would be anything but what it turned out to be, said he would grant it, and told him to say what he wanted. When Pythius heard this, he took courage and said: "Master, it happens that I have five sons, and it is their lot to be marching with you, all of them together, against Greece. So, my king, take pity on me, now that I have come to such an old age, and release one of my sons from serving in the expedition, the eldest, so that he can take care of me and of my property. Take the other four with you, and when you have done what you have in mind, may you come home safe."

39. Xerxes was furiously angry and answered him: "You miserable man! I am marching against Greece myself, taking my sons and my brothers and my relatives and friends, and you dare to mention a son of yours? You, who are my slave, and who ought to be following me yourself with your whole household, your wife included? Now understand this: a man's spirit lives in his ears. When it hears good things it fills the body with delight, but when it hears the opposite it swells up with rage. When you did us good service before and offered to do more of the same, you could not boast of having outdone the king in generosity. And now that you have turned shameless, you will not get what you deserve, but less than you deserve. Your hospitality will save you and four of your sons from death. But you will pay the penalty with the life of the one you cling to most." After giving this answer, he immediately ordered the men whose job it was to find Pythius' eldest son and cut him in half through the middle. When they had cut him in two, they were to set the halves on either side of the road, one on the right and one on the left, and the army was to march out between them.

40. When they had done this, the army marched out between the halves. First came the baggage carriers with their pack animals, and after them the host of every kind of nation, all mixed together without distinction. When more than half of these had gone by, a space was left, to keep them apart from the king. In front of the king came first a thousand horsemen, picked from all the Persians. After them came a thousand spearmen, also picked from all the Persians, carrying their spears with the points turned down toward the ground. Then came ten sacred horses called "Nesaean," in the finest possible harness. The horses are called Nesaean for this reason: there is a wide plain in Media called the Nesaean plain, and it breeds the big horses I am talking about. Behind these ten horses came the sacred chariot of Zeus, drawn by eight white horses. Behind the horses followed the charioteer on foot, holding the reins, since no human being ever climbs up onto the seat of that chariot. Behind this came Xerxes himself, in a chariot drawn by Nesaean horses, and beside him rode a charioteer whose name was Patiramphes, son of Otanes, a Persian.

41. That was how Xerxes marched out of Sardis, and whenever he felt like it he would change from the chariot to a covered carriage. Behind him came a thousand spearmen, the best and noblest of the Persians, holding their spear points up in the usual way. After them came another thousand horsemen picked from the Persians, and after the horsemen ten thousand men picked from the rest of the Persians. These went on foot. A thousand of them had golden pomegranates on their spears instead of the spikes on the butt end, and these thousand surrounded the others on the outside, while the other nine thousand marched inside them and had silver pomegranates. The men with their spear points turned toward the ground also had golden pomegranates, and those who followed right behind Xerxes had golden apples. Behind the ten thousand came a body of ten thousand Persian cavalry. After the cavalry a gap of as much as 1,200 feet was left, and then the rest of the host came marching along without distinction.

42. So the army made its way from Lydia to the river Caicus and the land of Mysia. Setting out from the Caicus, and keeping Mount Cane on its left, it marched through the region of Atarneus to the city of Carene. From there it went through the plain of Thebe, passing the city of Adramyttium and Antandrus of the Pelasgians. Then, keeping Mount Ida on its left, it came into the land of Troy. The first thing that happened there was that when it stopped for the night right under Mount Ida, thunder and lightning bolts fell on it and killed a great many men on that very spot.

43. Then the army came to the river Scamander. Of all the rivers they had reached since setting out from Sardis on their march, this was the first whose stream gave out and was not enough for the army and its animals to drink. When Xerxes had come to this river, he went up to the citadel of Priam, because he wanted to see it. When he had seen it and asked about everything there, one thing after another, he sacrificed a thousand heifers to Athena of Troy, and the Magi poured offerings to the heroes. After they had done this, a panic fell on the army in the night. At daybreak he marched on from there, keeping on his left the cities of Rhoeteum, Ophryneum and Dardanus, which borders on Abydos, and on his right the Gergithian Teucrians, a people descended from the old Trojans.

44. When Xerxes had reached the middle of Abydos, he wanted to see his whole army. A raised throne of white stone had already been built for him on purpose on a hill there; the people of Abydos had made it on the king's orders, given in advance. There he sat, looking down at the shore, and gazed at both the land army and the ships. As he looked at them he wanted to see the ships race. The race was held, and the Phoenicians of Sidon won it, and he was delighted both with the race and with his whole force.

45. And when he saw the whole Hellespont covered with ships, and all the shores and plains of Abydos full of men, Xerxes called himself a happy man, and after that he began to weep.

46. His uncle Artabanus noticed. This was the same man who had at first spoken his mind so boldly, advising Xerxes not to march against Greece. Seeing that Xerxes was weeping, he asked: "My king, how different from each other are what you did just now and what you did a moment ago! You called yourself a happy man, and now you are in tears." Xerxes said: "Yes, because as I was counting them up, it came into my mind to feel pity at how short the whole of a man's life is, since out of all these thousands, not one will be alive a hundred years from now." Artabanus answered: "There is something else we suffer in the course of our lives that is more pitiful than that. Short as life is, no man, whether among these here or anywhere else, is born so happy that the wish to be dead rather than alive will not come to him many times, and not just once. Misfortunes fall on us, and diseases trouble us, and they make life seem long, short as it really is. So, since life is full of trouble, death has become the most welcome refuge for a man. And heaven, which has given us a taste of how sweet life is, turns out in this to be full of jealousy."

47. Xerxes answered: "Artabanus, human life is what you say it is, but let us stop talking about it, and let's not remember bad things when we have good things in hand. Tell me this instead. If the vision in the dream had not appeared so clearly, would you still hold your earlier opinion and be trying to stop me from marching against Greece, or would you have changed your mind? Come, tell me exactly." Artabanus answered: "My king, may the vision in the dream come true the way we both want it to! But even now I am full of fear and can hardly contain myself. I am taking many things into account, and above all I see that the two greatest things of all are your bitter enemies."

48. Xerxes answered: "You strangest of men, what are these two things you say are my bitter enemies? Is there something wrong with the size of the land army? Do you think the Greek army will turn out to be many times bigger than ours? Or that our fleet will fall short of theirs? Or both together? If you think our power falls short in these ways, another force could be gathered at once."

49. Artabanus answered: "My king, no one with any sense would find fault with this army, or with the number of the ships. In fact, if you gather more, the two things I mean will become even more your enemies. These two things are the land and the sea. On the sea, as I imagine, there is no harbor anywhere big enough to take in this fleet of yours if a storm blows up, and to keep the ships safe until it is over. And there ought to be not just one such harbor, but harbors like it all along the coast of the mainland you are sailing past. Since there are no harbors to take in your ships, understand that men do not rule chance; chance rules men. Now that I have told you one of the two things, I will tell you the other. The land is your enemy in this way. If nothing comes to oppose you, the land grows more hostile to you the farther you advance, always drawn on a little farther, for men are never satisfied with good fortune. What I am saying is this: with no one standing against you, the land you cover will keep growing as time goes on, and it will bring you famine. A man is at his best when he is afraid while he is making his plans, counting on suffering everything that could possibly happen, but bold when he is carrying them out."

50. Xerxes answered: "Artabanus, what you say about these things is reasonable. But don't fear everything, or weigh every danger equally. If you were to weigh every danger equally in every matter that came up, you would never do anything at all. It is better to have courage about everything and suffer half the evils that threaten than to be afraid of everything in advance and suffer nothing at all. And if you argue against everything that is proposed, but never point out the safe course, then you are just as open to the charge of failure as the man who argues the opposite. So the two are evenly matched. But how can a mere man know the safe course? I don't think he can. As a rule, the people who are willing to act are the ones who gain, while those who weigh everything and hold back don't gain much. You see the power of the Persians, how great it has grown. If the kings before me had held opinions like yours, or, without holding them, had had advisers like you, you would never have seen it come this far. As it is, they brought it this far by taking risks, because great power is generally won by taking great risks. So we are following their example. We are marching at the finest season of the year, and when we have conquered all Europe we will come home again without having met famine anywhere or suffered anything else unpleasant. For one thing, we are marching with great stores of food of our own. For another, we will have the grain crops of every people whose land we come to. And we are marching against men who farm the soil, not against nomads."

51. Then Artabanus said: "My king, since you will not let us fear anything, at least take one piece of advice from me. When there is a lot to discuss, it takes a lot of talk. Cyrus son of Cambyses conquered all of Ionia except Athens, and made it pay tribute to the Persians. My advice is that you should on no account lead these Ionians against the people they came from. We are strong enough to beat our enemies even without them. Suppose they come with us. Then they must either prove themselves great wrongdoers, by helping to enslave their mother city, or great doers of right, by helping to set her free. If they turn out great wrongdoers, they don't add very much to our gains. But if they turn out great doers of right, they are in a position to do your army a great deal of damage. So take to heart this old saying too, how true it is: at the beginning of a thing, its end is never fully in view."

52. Xerxes answered: "Artabanus, of all the opinions you have given, this one is the most mistaken. You are afraid the Ionians will change sides. But about them we have the surest proof there is. You are a witness to it yourself, and so are all the others who went with Darius on his march against the Scythians. At that time the safety of the whole Persian army depended on these men, whether they chose to destroy it or to save it. And they showed honesty and loyalty, and nothing hostile at all. Besides, since they have left their children and wives and property in our land, we must not even imagine that they will rebel. So don't be afraid of this either. Keep up your courage, and keep my house and my rule safe. For to you, out of all men, I am handing over my scepter."

53. After saying this, Xerxes sent Artabanus back to Susa. Next he summoned the most distinguished of the Persians, and when they had come before him he said to them: "Persians, I have brought you together because I want this from you: that you show yourselves brave men and do not disgrace the deeds the Persians have done before, which are great and glorious. Let each one of us on his own, and all of us together, put our hearts into this enterprise, because what we are working for is the common good of all. And I urge you to keep at this war without letting up, because, as I am told, we are marching against brave men. If we beat them, there is no other army in the world that will ever stand against us. So let us begin the crossing, after we have prayed to the gods who have Persia in their keeping."

54. All that day they were getting ready to cross. On the next day they waited for the sun, wanting to see it rise, and meanwhile they burned all kinds of incense on the bridges and strewed the road with myrtle branches. Then, as the sun was rising, Xerxes poured an offering into the sea from a golden cup and prayed to the sun that no accident would happen to him that would stop him from conquering Europe until he had reached its farthest borders. After this prayer he threw the cup into the Hellespont, and with it a golden mixing bowl and a Persian sword of the kind they call an akinakes. But whether he threw them into the sea as an offering to the sun, or whether he regretted whipping the Hellespont and wanted to give the sea a gift to make up for it, I can't say for certain.

55. When Xerxes had done this, they began to cross. The whole fighting army, foot and horse, went over by one bridge, the one on the Black Sea side, while the pack animals and the camp followers went over by the other, toward the Aegean. First came the ten thousand Persians, all wearing wreaths, and after them the mixed host of every kind of nation. These crossed on the first day. On the next day the first to cross were the horsemen and the men who carried their spear points turned down, these also wearing wreaths. After them came the sacred horses and the sacred chariot, then Xerxes himself with the spearmen and the thousand horsemen, and after them the rest of the army. Meanwhile the ships too put out from shore and crossed to the other side. But I have also heard another account, which says that the king crossed over last of all.

56. When Xerxes had crossed into Europe, he watched his army crossing under the whip. His army took seven days and seven nights to cross, going on without a break. And then, it is said, when Xerxes had crossed the Hellespont, a man who lived there on the shore cried out: "Zeus, why have you taken the shape of a Persian man and the name of Xerxes instead of Zeus, and why are you bringing all the nations of the world with you to lay Greece waste? You could have done it without any of them."

Chapter 39: The Great Review at Doriscus, and Xerxes Questions Demaratus

57. When they had all crossed over and set out on their way, a great portent appeared to them. Xerxes took no notice of it, although its meaning was easy to guess: a mare gave birth to a hare. The meaning was easy to guess in this way: Xerxes was about to march an army against Greece in great pride and splendor, but he would come back again to the place he started from, running for his life. There had also been a portent of another kind while he was still at Sardis. A mule gave birth, and the foal was a mule with sex organs of both kinds, male and female, with the male organs above. But Xerxes took no notice of either portent. He went on his way, and the land army with him.

58. Meanwhile the fleet was sailing out of the Hellespont and along the coast, heading in the opposite direction from the land army. The fleet was sailing west, making for the headland of Sarpedon, where it had been ordered in advance to go and wait for the army. The land army, meanwhile, was marching east, toward the sunrise, through the Chersonese. It kept the tomb of Helle the daughter of Athamas on its right and the city of Cardia on its left, and it marched straight through the middle of a town called Agora. From there it curved around the gulf called Melas and crossed the river Melas, which gives the gulf its name. That river's water was not enough for the army this time, and it ran dry. After crossing it, the army went on westward, past Aenus, a city of the Aeolians, and past the lake of Stentoris, until at last it came to Doriscus.

59. Doriscus is a beach and a very large plain in Thrace, and the great river Hebrus flows through it. A royal fortress had been built there, the one that is now called Doriscus, and Darius had kept a garrison of Persians in it ever since the time he marched against the Scythians. So it seemed to Xerxes that this was a convenient place to put his army in order and count it, and that is what he did. When the commanders of the fleet arrived at Doriscus, on Xerxes' orders they brought all their ships to the beach next to Doriscus. On that stretch of coast stand Sale, a city of the Samothracians, and Zone, and at its far end is the well-known headland of Serrheum; in ancient times the region belonged to the Ciconians. They brought their ships in to this beach, hauled them up on land, and let them dry out. During this time Xerxes was counting the army at Doriscus.

60. Now I cannot give exact figures for the number each separate nation supplied, because no one reports it. But the whole land army taken together came to 1,700,000 men. This is how they counted them. They gathered 10,000 men together in one place, packed them in as tightly as they could, and drew a circle around them on the outside. Once they had drawn the circle, they let the 10,000 men go, and built a wall of rough stones around the line of the circle, up to the height of a man's navel. When this was done, they made other men go into the walled space, and then others, until in this way they had counted them all. After they had counted them, they arranged them by nations.

61. Those who served were as follows.

The Persians, with this equipment. On their heads they wore soft felt caps called tiaras. On their bodies they wore colorful tunics with sleeves, covered with iron scales that looked like the scales of a fish, and on their legs they wore trousers. Instead of ordinary shields they carried shields of wickerwork, with their quivers hanging underneath. They had short spears, large bows, arrows of reed, and daggers hanging from their belts beside the right thigh. Their commander was Otanes, the father of Xerxes' wife Amestris. In ancient times the Greeks called these Persians Cephenes, but they called themselves Artaeans, and so did their neighbors. Then Perseus, the son of Danae and Zeus, came to Cepheus the son of Belus and married his daughter Andromeda. A son was born to them, and Perseus named him Perses. He left this son behind there, since Cepheus happened to have no male children, and the people took their name from him.

62. The Medes served in the army with exactly the same equipment, for this equipment is in fact Median, not Persian. Their commander was Tigranes, an Achaemenid. In ancient times everyone called them Arians, but when Medea the Colchian came from Athens to these Arians, they changed their name too. That is what the Medes themselves say about themselves. The Cissians served with equipment like the Persians' in other respects, but instead of felt caps they wore headbands. The commander of the Cissians was Anaphes the son of Otanes. The Hyrcanians were armed like the Persians. Their leader was Megapanus, the same man who later became governor of Babylon.

63. The Assyrians served wearing helmets of bronze on their heads, or else helmets woven in a foreign style that is hard to describe. They had shields and spears, daggers like the Egyptian knives, wooden clubs studded with iron, and linen breastplates. The Greeks call these people Syrians, but the non-Greeks have always called them Assyrians. Among them were the Chaldeans. Their commander was Otaspes the son of Artachaees.

64. The Bactrians served wearing on their heads almost the same headgear as the Medes, with native bows of reed and short spears. The Sacan Scythians wore tall caps on their heads, stiff and upright and coming to a point. They wore trousers and carried native bows and daggers, and also battle-axes of the kind called sagaris. These were called Amyrgian Sacae, though in fact they were Scythians, for the Persians call all Scythians Sacae. The commander of the Bactrians and Sacae was Hystaspes, the son of Darius and of Cyrus' daughter Atossa.

65. The Indians wore clothes made of tree-wool, that is, cotton. They had bows of reed and arrows of reed tipped with iron. That was how the Indians were equipped. They served under Pharnazathres the son of Artabates.

66. The Arians were equipped with Median bows, and otherwise like the Bactrians. The commander of the Arians was Sisamnes the son of Hydarnes. The Parthians, the Chorasmians, the Sogdians, the Gandarians and the Dadicans served with the same equipment as the Bactrians. Their commanders were Artabazus the son of Pharnaces, over the Parthians and Chorasmians; Azanes the son of Artaeus, over the Sogdians; and Artyphius the son of Artabanus, over the Gandarians and Dadicans.

67. The Caspians served wearing coats of skin, with native bows of reed and short swords. That was how they were equipped, and their leader was Ariomardus, the brother of Artyphius. The Sarangians stood out from the rest because they wore dyed clothes. They had boots that came up to the knee, and Median bows and spears. Their commander was Pherendates the son of Megabazus. The Pactyans wore coats of skin and had native bows and daggers. Their commander was Artayntes the son of Ithamitres.

68. The Utians, the Mycians and the Paricanians were equipped like the Pactyans. Their commanders were Arsamenes the son of Darius, over the Utians and Mycians, and Siromitres the son of Oeobazus, over the Paricanians.

69. The Arabians wore loose cloaks belted up, and carried long bows at their right side that bent backward. The Ethiopians wore the skins of leopards and lions tied on them. Their bows were made from a strip of palm wood and were very long, at least six feet. With these they used small arrows of reed tipped not with iron but with a sharpened stone, the same kind of stone they use to carve seals. They also had spears, and on them, for a spearhead, the sharpened horn of a gazelle. They also had studded clubs. When they went into battle they painted half of their bodies with white and the other half with red. The commander of the Arabians and of the Ethiopians who live beyond Egypt was Arsames, the son of Darius and of Artystone the daughter of Cyrus. Artystone was the wife Darius loved most of all his wives, and he had a statue of her made of beaten gold.

70. So Arsames commanded the Ethiopians from beyond Egypt and the Arabians. But the Ethiopians from the east (for there were two bodies of Ethiopians) had been assigned to serve with the Indians. They were no different from the other Ethiopians except in their language and their hair. The eastern Ethiopians have straight hair, while the Ethiopians of Libya have the thickest, most tightly curled hair of any people on earth. These Ethiopians from Asia were armed mostly like the Indians, but on their heads they wore the skin of a horse's forehead, stripped off with the ears and the mane still on it. The mane served as a crest, and they kept the horse's ears standing up straight and stiff. Instead of shields they held up in front of them guards made of the skins of cranes.

71. The Libyans came in leather gear and used javelins hardened in the fire at the point. Their commander was Massages the son of Oarizus.

72. The Paphlagonians served with woven helmets on their heads, small shields, spears of no great size, javelins and daggers. On their feet they wore native boots reaching halfway up the shin. The Ligyans, the Matienians, the Mariandynians and the Syrians served with the same equipment as the Paphlagonians. (These Syrians are the people the Persians call Cappadocians.) The commander of the Paphlagonians and Matienians was Dotus the son of Megasidrus. The commander of the Mariandynians, the Ligyans and the Syrians was Gobryas, the son of Darius and Artystone.

73. The Phrygians had equipment very much like the Paphlagonians', with only small differences. According to the Macedonians, the Phrygians were called Brigians for as long as they lived in Europe as neighbors of the Macedonians. But when they moved to Asia they changed their name along with their country and were called Phrygians. The Armenians were armed exactly like the Phrygians, since they are colonists of the Phrygians. The commander of these two peoples together was Artochmes, who was married to a daughter of Darius.

74. The Lydians had weapons very close to those of the Greeks. In old times the Lydians were called Meonians, and they changed their earlier name and took a new one from Lydus the son of Atys. The Mysians wore native helmets on their heads, carried small shields, and used javelins hardened in the fire at the point. They are colonists of the Lydians, and they are called Olympieni after Mount Olympus. The commander of the Lydians and Mysians was Artaphernes the son of Artaphernes, the man who invaded at Marathon together with Datis.

75. The Thracians served wearing fox skins on their heads and tunics on their bodies, with colorful loose cloaks wrapped over them. On their feet and lower legs they wore boots of deerskin. They also had javelins, small round shields and little daggers. When they crossed over into Asia they came to be called Bithynians, but before that, as they themselves say, they were called Strymonians, because they lived on the river Strymon. They say they were driven out of their homes by the Teucrians and the Mysians. The commander of the Thracians who lived in Asia was Bassaces the son of Artabanus.

76. The next people's name has dropped out of the text as it has come down to us. They had small shields of raw oxhide, and each man carried two hunting spears of Lycian make. On their heads they wore bronze helmets, and on the helmets were the ears and horns of an ox, made of bronze, and crests on top of those. Their lower legs were wrapped in strips of red cloth. These people have an oracle of Ares.

77. The Meonian Cabelians, who are called Lasonians, had the same equipment as the Cilicians, and I will explain what that was when I come to the Cilician contingent in the course of my list. The Milyans had short spears and wore their clothes fastened with brooches. Some of them had Lycian bows, and on their heads they wore leather caps. The commander of all these was Badres the son of Hystanes.

78. The Moschians wore wooden helmets on their heads and carried shields and small spears with long points set on them. The Tibarenians, the Macronians and the Mossynoecians served with equipment like the Moschians'. These were grouped together under the following commanders. The Moschians and Tibarenians were under Ariomardus, the son of Darius and of Parmys, who was the daughter of Smerdis son of Cyrus. The Macronians and Mossynoecians were under Artayctes the son of Cherasmis, who was governor of Sestos on the Hellespont.

79. The Mares wore native woven helmets on their heads and carried small shields of hide and javelins. The Colchians wore wooden helmets on their heads and carried small shields of raw oxhide, short spears and also knives. The commander of the Mares and Colchians was Pharandates the son of Teaspis. The Alarodians and the Saspeirians served armed like the Colchians, and their commander was Masistius the son of Siromitres.

80. The island peoples who came with the army from the Persian Gulf, from the islands where the king settles the people called "the Removed," had clothing and weapons very much like the Medes'. The commander of these islanders was Mardontes the son of Bagaeus, who was one of the generals at Mycale the year after these events and was killed in the battle.
