81. These were the nations that served on land in this campaign and had been assigned to the infantry. The men I have named were the commanders of this army. They were the ones who arranged it in divisions and counted it, and who appointed the commanders of thousands and the commanders of ten thousands. The commanders of hundreds and of tens were appointed by the commanders of ten thousands. There were also others who were leaders of companies and nations.

82. The men I have named were the commanders of the army. Over them, and over the whole infantry together, the generals were Mardonius the son of Gobryas; Tritantaechmes the son of that Artabanus who had advised against the march on Greece; Smerdomenes the son of Otanes (these two were sons of Darius' brothers, and so cousins of Xerxes); Masistes the son of Darius and Atossa; Gergis the son of Ariazus; and Megabyzus the son of Zopyrus.

83. These were the generals of the whole infantry together, except for the 10,000. The general of those 10,000 picked Persians was Hydarnes the son of Hydarnes. These Persians were called the "Immortals," because whenever any one of them dropped out of the number, carried off by death or by sickness, another man was chosen in his place. So they were never more and never fewer than 10,000. Of all the nations, the Persians made the most splendid show, and they were also the best fighters. They had the equipment I have described, and besides that they stood out from the rest because they wore gold in great quantities, lavishly. They brought carriages with them, and in them their concubines and a crowd of well-equipped servants. Camels and pack animals carried their food, separate from the rest of the soldiers'.

84. The nations that serve as cavalry are these, though not all of them supplied cavalry, only the ones listed here. The Persians were equipped the same way as their infantry, except that some of them wore headpieces of hammered bronze or iron.

85. There are also certain nomads called Sagartians, Persian by race and language, whose dress is halfway between that of the Persians and that of the Pactyans. These supplied 8,000 horsemen. It is not their custom to carry any weapons of bronze or iron except daggers. Instead they use ropes plaited out of strips of leather, and rely on these when they go to war. This is how these men fight. When they meet the enemy, they throw the ropes, which have nooses at the end. Whatever a man catches with his throw, horse or man, he drags toward himself, and the victims, tangled up in the coils, are killed.

86. That is how these men fight, and they were posted next to the Persians. The Medes had the same equipment as their infantry, and so did the Cissians. The Indians were armed the same way as their infantry, and they both rode horses and drove chariots pulled by horses or wild donkeys. The Bactrians were equipped like their infantry, and so were the Caspians. The Libyans were equipped like their infantry too, and they all drove chariots as well. In the same way, the Caspians and Paricanians were equipped like their infantry, and they all rode camels, which were every bit as fast as horses.

87. These nations alone served as cavalry, and the number of the cavalry came to 80,000, not counting the camels and the chariots. The rest of the cavalry was drawn up in squadrons, but the Arabians were posted behind them, last of all. The horses could not stand the camels, and so the Arabians were placed last to keep the horses from being frightened.

88. The commanders of the cavalry were Harmamithres and Tithaeus, the sons of Datis. The third commander of cavalry with them, Pharnuches, had been left behind sick at Sardis. Just as they were setting out from Sardis, he met with an unlucky accident. As he was riding, a dog ran under his horse's feet. The horse, which had not seen it coming, took fright, reared up and threw Pharnuches off its back. He vomited blood from the fall, and his illness turned into a wasting disease. As for the horse, his servants did at once what he ordered: they led it away to the place where it had thrown its master and cut off its legs at the knees. That is how Pharnuches lost his command.

89. The number of the triremes came to 1,207, and these are the peoples who supplied them. The Phoenicians, together with the Syrians who live in Palestine, supplied 300. They were equipped like this: on their heads they wore leather helmets made very much in the Greek style, and they wore linen breastplates and carried shields without rims, and javelins. These Phoenicians, as they themselves say, lived in ancient times on the Persian Gulf. From there they crossed over and settled on the coast of Syria, and this part of Syria, and all the land as far as Egypt, is called Palestine. The Egyptians supplied 200 ships. They wore woven helmets on their heads and carried hollow shields with broad rims, spears made for fighting at sea, and large axes. Most of them wore breastplates and carried large knives.

90. That was how these men were equipped. The Cyprians supplied 150 ships, and were equipped as follows. Their kings wore headbands wound around their heads, and the rest wore tunics, but in other respects they were like the Greeks. They are made up of various peoples: some come from Salamis and Athens, some from Arcadia, some from Cythnus, some from Phoenicia and some from Ethiopia, as the Cyprians themselves say.

91. The Cilicians supplied 100 ships. They too wore native helmets on their heads, and for shields they carried small round targets of raw oxhide. They wore woolen tunics, and each man had two javelins and a sword made very much like the Egyptian knives. In old times they were called Hypachaeans, and they took their later name from Cilix the son of Agenor, a Phoenician. The Pamphylians supplied 30 ships and were armed in the Greek style. These Pamphylians are descended from the people who were scattered from Troy with Amphilochus and Calchas.

92. The Lycians supplied 50 ships. They wore breastplates and greaves, and carried bows of cornel wood, arrows of reed without feathers, and javelins. They wore goatskins hanging over their shoulders, and on their heads felt caps with a ring of feathers around them. They also had daggers and curved swords. The Lycians were once called Termilae and came originally from Crete. They took their later name from Lycus the son of Pandion, an Athenian.

93. The Dorians of Asia supplied 30 ships. They had Greek weapons and came originally from the Peloponnese. The Carians supplied 70 ships. They were equipped like Greeks in other respects, but they also had curved swords and daggers. What their earlier name was I have already told in the first part of my history.

94. The Ionians supplied 100 ships and were equipped like Greeks. As long as the Ionians lived in the Peloponnese, in the land now called Achaea, before Danaus and Xuthus came to the Peloponnese, they were called, as the Greeks say, the Pelasgians of the Coast. Later they were called Ionians after Ion the son of Xuthus.

95. The islanders supplied 17 ships and were armed like Greeks. They too are a Pelasgian people, but later they came to be called Ionian by the same rule as the Ionians of the twelve cities, who came from Athens. The Aeolians supplied 60 ships. They were equipped like Greeks, and in old times they were called Pelasgians, as the Greeks say. The Hellespontians supplied 100 ships, except for the people of Abydos, whom the king had ordered to stay at home and guard the bridges. The rest of those who joined the expedition from the Black Sea region supplied these 100 ships, and they were equipped like Greeks. They are colonists of the Ionians and the Dorians.

96. On all the ships the fighting men were Persians, Medes or Sacae. Of the ships, the best sailers were supplied by the Phoenicians, and among the Phoenicians, by the men of Sidon. Over all these men, and over the ones of them assigned to the land army too, each people had its own native chiefs. I do not mention them, since the course of my inquiry does not oblige me to. For one thing, the chiefs of each separate nation were not worth mentioning; for another, in each nation there were as many chiefs as there were cities. These men came on the expedition not as commanders but as slaves, like the rest of the soldiers. The generals who held full power and commanded the different nations, the ones who were Persians, I have already named.

97. The commanders of the navy were Ariabignes the son of Darius, Prexaspes the son of Aspathines, Megabazus the son of Megabates, and Achaemenes the son of Darius. Ariabignes, the son of Darius and of Gobryas' daughter, commanded the Ionian and Carian fleet. Achaemenes, Xerxes' full brother on both his father's and his mother's side, commanded the Egyptians. The other two commanded the rest of the fleet. In addition, ships of thirty oars and of fifty oars, light boats, and long transports for carrying horses had been brought together, and their number came to 3,000.

98. Of the men who sailed in the fleet, after the commanders, these were the most notable: from Sidon, Tetramnestus son of Anysus; from Tyre, Matten son of Siromus; from Aradus, Merbalus son of Agbalus; from Cilicia, Syennesis son of Oromedon; from Lycia, Cyberniscus son of Sicas; from Cyprus, Gorgus son of Chersis and Timonax son of Timagoras; and from Caria, Histiaeus son of Tymnes, Pigres son of Hysseldomus, and Damasithymus son of Candaules.

99. I make no mention of the rest of the officers, since I am not obliged to, except for Artemisia. She amazes me more than anyone, a woman who joined the expedition against Greece. Her husband had died, and she held power herself. She had a son who was a young man, so no necessity was laid on her, but she went on the expedition out of her own high spirit and a man's courage. Her name, as I said, was Artemisia. She was the daughter of Lygdamis, and by descent she came from Halicarnassus on her father's side and from Crete on her mother's. She ruled the people of Halicarnassus, Cos, Nisyros and Calydna, and supplied five ships. The ships she supplied had the best reputation in the whole fleet after the Sidonians', and of all the king's allies she gave him the best advice. The states I said she led are, I declare, all Dorian by race: the people of Halicarnassus are Troezenians, and the rest are Epidaurians. So much for the navy.

100. When Xerxes had counted the army and it had been drawn up in divisions, he wanted to drive through it himself and inspect it, and afterward he did. He drove through in a chariot past each nation, asking questions about them, while his scribes wrote down the names, until he had gone from one end to the other of both the cavalry and the infantry. When he had done this, the ships were launched into the sea. Xerxes stepped from his chariot onto a ship of Sidon, sat down under a golden canopy and sailed along past the prows of the ships, asking about all of them just as he had about the land army, and having the answers written down. The captains had taken their ships out about four hundred feet from the beach and anchored them there, all with their prows turned toward the shore in an even line and all their fighting men armed as if for battle. He inspected them by sailing along the inside, between the prows of the ships and the beach.

101. When he had sailed past them all and had come ashore from his ship, he sent for Demaratus the son of Ariston, who was marching with him against Greece. When he had called him, he asked him this:

"Demaratus, it is my pleasure now to ask you something I want to know. You are a Greek, and not only that: as I hear both from you and from the other Greeks who come and talk with me, you are from a city that is neither the smallest nor the weakest in Greece. So tell me this: will the Greeks dare to raise their hands against me? As I see it, even if all the Greeks and all the remaining peoples who live in the west were gathered together, they would not be strong enough in battle to stand up to my attack, if they were my enemies. But I want to hear your opinion as well, and what you have to say about these matters."

That was his question, and Demaratus answered: "My king, shall I tell you the truth, or what will please you?"

Xerxes told him to tell the truth, and said that he would suffer nothing unpleasant for it, any more than he had before.

102. When Demaratus heard this, he said: "My king, since you order me by all means to tell the truth, and to speak as a man who will never later be caught by you in a lie, I say this. In Greece, poverty has always been native to the soil, while courage is something brought in, won by good sense and the strength of law. By means of courage Greece keeps off both poverty and slavery to a master. Now I have praise for all the Greeks who live in those Dorian lands, but what I am about to say does not concern them all, only the Spartans. About the Spartans I say, first, that there is no way they will ever accept your terms, which mean slavery for Greece. And second, I say that they will meet you in battle even if all the other Greeks take your side. And as for their numbers, do not ask how many of them there are, that they can do this. If a thousand of them happen to march out into the field, those thousand will fight you, and so will any number, whether fewer than that or more."

103. When Xerxes heard this he laughed and said: "Demaratus, what a thing to say, that a thousand men will fight this enormous army! Come, tell me this. You say you were once king of these men. Would you be willing, then, to fight ten men on your own, here and now? And yet if your whole state is the way you describe it, you, as their king, ought by your laws to take on twice as many as anyone else. If each of them is a match for ten men of my army, then I expect you to be a match for twenty. That would prove what you say. But if you, who boast so loudly, are men like the Greeks who usually come and talk with me, and no bigger than you yourself are, then watch out that what you have said does not turn out to be empty bragging. Come, let me look at it from every side, and see what is likely. How could a thousand, or ten thousand, or even fifty thousand men stand against so great an army, if they were all equally free and not ruled by one man? Suppose there are five thousand of them: we would still be more than a thousand against each one. If they were ruled by one man, the way we are, they might perhaps, out of fear of him, become braver than their nature, or they might be driven by the whip to fight against greater numbers though they were fewer. But left free, they would do neither. For my part I believe that even if the numbers were equal, the Greeks would hardly dare to fight the Persians alone. No, what you are talking about exists among us, but only in a few men, and rarely. Among my spearmen there are Persians who would gladly fight three Greeks at once. But you have no experience of such things, and so you are talking a great deal of nonsense."

104. To this Demaratus replied: "My king, I was sure from the start that if I told the truth I would not say what pleased you. But since you forced me to speak the plain truth, I told you how things stand with the Spartans. And yet how fond I am of them at present, you know better than anyone. First they took away the rank and the privileges that came to me from my fathers, and then they made me a man without a country, an exile. But your father took me in and gave me a living and a house to live in. Surely no sensible man is likely to push away kindness when it is offered to him; he will accept it and be grateful. Now I do not claim that I can fight ten men, or two. If I had my way, I would not even fight one. But if I had to, or if there were some great cause driving me into the fight, I would most gladly fight one of these men of yours who say they are a match for three Greeks. In the same way, the Spartans are as good as any men in the world when they fight one by one, and when they fight together they are the best of all men. For though they are free, they are not free in everything. They have a master over them, the Law, and they fear it far more than your people fear you. At any rate they do whatever it commands, and it always commands the same thing: never to run from battle, however many men they face, but to stay in their place and either win or die. But if you think I am talking nonsense when I say these things, then from now on I would rather keep silent about the rest. I spoke now only because you made me. Still, my king, may it all turn out as you wish."

Chapter 40: The March through Thrace and Macedonia, and the Heralds Sent to Greece

105. That was Demaratus' answer. Xerxes turned the whole thing into a joke, showed no anger at all, and sent him away kindly. After this conversation, Xerxes appointed Mascames son of Megadostes to be governor there at Doriscus, removing the governor Darius had appointed. Then he marched his army on through Thrace to invade Greece.

106. Mascames, the man he left behind there, proved to be of such quality that Xerxes used to send gifts to him alone, because he considered him the best of all the governors that either he or Darius had ever appointed. He sent him these gifts every year, and Artaxerxes son of Xerxes did the same for Mascames' descendants. For even before this march, governors had been appointed in Thrace and all around the Hellespont. After the expedition, all of them, both those in Thrace and those on the Hellespont, were conquered by the Greeks, all except the one at Doriscus. Mascames at Doriscus no one was ever able to conquer, though many tried. That is why the gifts keep coming for him from whoever is king of Persia.

107. Of the governors the Greeks did conquer, Xerxes did not think any was a good man except Boges, who was at Eion. Him he never stopped praising, and he gave the highest honors to the children of Boges who survived him in Persia. And truly Boges proved himself worthy of great praise. When he was besieged by the Athenians under Cimon son of Miltiades, he could have marched out under a truce and gone home to Asia. He chose not to, for fear the king would think he had saved his life through cowardice, and he held out to the very end. Then, when there was no food left inside the walls, he built a great pyre. He cut the throats of his children, his wife, his concubines and his servants, and threw them into the fire. After this he scattered all the gold and silver in the city from the wall into the river Strymon, and when he had done that, he threw himself into the fire. So the Persians rightly praise him to this day.

108. From Doriscus Xerxes went on toward Greece, and as he went he forced every people he came to, one after another, to join his march. For, as I have explained before, the whole country as far as Thessaly had been made subject and was paying tribute to the king, conquered first by Megabazus and later by Mardonius. On his way from Doriscus he passed first the strongholds of the Samothracians, of which the farthest to the west is a city called Mesambria. Next to this comes Stryme, a city belonging to the Thasians, and between the two flows the river Lisus. At this time its water was not enough to supply Xerxes' army, and the stream ran dry. This country used to be called Gallaica but is now called Briantica; strictly speaking, though, it too belongs to the Cicones.

109. After crossing the dried-up bed of the river Lisus, he passed by these Greek cities: Maronea, Dicaea and Abdera. He passed them by, and also the well-known lakes that lie near them: the Ismarian lake, between Maronea and Stryme, and the Bistonian lake near Dicaea, into which two rivers pour their water, the Travus and the Compsantus. At Abdera Xerxes passed no lake worth mentioning, but he did pass the river Nestus, which flows into the sea there. After these places he went by the mainland cities. Near one of them there happens to be a lake about three and a third miles around, full of fish and very salty. The baggage animals alone drank it dry. The name of this city is Pistyrus.

110. These coastal cities, which belonged to Greeks, he passed by, keeping them on his left. The Thracian tribes through whose country he marched were these: the Paetians, the Cicones, the Bistones, the Sapaeans, the Dersaeans, the Edonians and the Satrians. Of these, the ones settled along the coast went with him in their ships, and the ones who lived inland, whom I have just listed, were forced to go with him by land, all except the Satrians.

111. The Satrians have never yet obeyed any man, as far as we know. Down to my own time they remain free, the only Thracians who are. They live in high mountains covered with every kind of forest and with snow, and they are also very skilled at war. These are the people who own the oracle of Dionysus, which is on their highest mountains. Among the Satrians the ones who serve as prophets of the temple are the Bessians. It is a priestess who speaks the oracles, as at Delphi, and beyond this there is nothing remarkable about it.

112. After crossing the land I have described, Xerxes next passed the strongholds of the Pierians, one called Phagres and the other Pergamus. He marched this way, close under their walls, keeping on his right Mount Pangaeum. It is a great, high mountain, and in it there are gold and silver mines owned by the Pierians and the Odomantians, and above all by the Satrians.

113. So, passing the Paeonians, the Doberes and the Paeoplae, who live north of Pangaeum, he went on westward until at last he came to the river Strymon and the city of Eion. Boges, the man I was speaking of a little while ago, was commander there as long as he lived. The country around Mount Pangaeum is called Phyllis. It stretches west to the river Angites, which flows into the Strymon, and south to the Strymon itself. At this river the Magi made a sacrifice for good omens, killing white horses.

114. They did this, and many other things besides, as charms to win over the river. Then, at the Nine Ways in the land of the Edonians, they went on by the bridges, for they found the Strymon already spanned by bridges. When they learned that the place was called the Nine Ways, they buried alive there that many boys and girls, children of the local people. Burying people alive is a Persian custom. I am told that Amestris, Xerxes' wife, when she had grown old, also buried fourteen children of distinguished Persians, as a thank-offering for her own life to the god who is said to live beneath the earth.

115. As the army marched on from the Strymon, it came to a stretch of beach running toward the sunset and passed the Greek city of Argilus, which stands there. This region, and the land above it, is called Bisaltia. From there, keeping on its left the gulf that lies off Posideium, it went through what is called the plain of Syleus, passing Stagirus, a Greek city, and so came to Acanthus. As it went it took along every one of these tribes, and also the peoples who live around Mount Pangaeum, just as it had the ones I listed before: the men who lived on the coast served in the ships, and those who lived inland went along on foot. The road along which King Xerxes marched his army the Thracians do not disturb and do not plant crops on; they treat it with the greatest reverence down to my own time.

116. When Xerxes reached Acanthus, he declared the people of Acanthus his guest-friends, presented them with Median dress, and praised them, because he saw how eager they were to help him in the war and because he had heard about the digging of the canal.

117. While Xerxes was at Acanthus, it happened that the man who had been put in charge of making the canal, Artachaees by name, died of an illness. He was a man Xerxes valued highly, and he belonged to the Achaemenid family. He was also the tallest man in Persia, just four finger-widths short of five royal cubits, a little over eight feet, and he had the loudest voice of any man alive. So Xerxes was deeply grieved at his loss. He gave him a magnificent funeral and burial, and the whole army helped to raise a mound over him. The people of Acanthus, at the bidding of an oracle, sacrifice to this Artachaees as a hero, calling on him by name in their worship.

118. So King Xerxes was deeply grieved at the loss of Artachaees. Meanwhile the Greeks who were hosting his army and giving Xerxes dinner had been brought to utter ruin, to the point of being driven from house and home. Take the Thasians, for example. They hosted Xerxes' army and gave him dinner on behalf of their towns on the mainland, and Antipater son of Orgeus, a citizen as respected as any, who had been appointed to handle it, reported that four hundred talents of silver had been spent on that dinner.

119. In the other cities, too, the men in charge reported the bill to be about the same, or nearly so. For the dinner was ordered a long time in advance, and the cities treated it as a matter of great importance. It was done like this. First of all, as soon as they heard the news from the heralds who went around announcing it, the citizens of each city divided grain among their households, and everyone spent many months grinding wheat and barley flour. Then they fattened cattle, searching out the finest animals and paying high prices for them. They kept birds, both land birds and water birds, in cages and ponds, all to entertain the army. Then they had cups and mixing bowls made of gold and silver, along with everything else that goes on a table. These were made for the king himself and for those who ate with him; for the rest of the army only food was provided. Whenever the army arrived somewhere, a tent stood ready and pitched, and Xerxes himself stayed in it, while the rest of the army camped in the open. When dinnertime came, the hosts had all the work. But the guests, once they had eaten their fill and spent the night there, tore down the tent the next day, took all the furnishings with them, and marched on, leaving nothing behind and carrying everything away.

120. It was then that Megacreon, a man of Abdera, made a well-turned remark. He advised the people of Abdera to go all together, men and women alike, to their temples and sit there as suppliants of the gods, begging them to keep off half of the troubles still to come in the future as well. And he told them to be very thankful to the gods for what had already happened, because King Xerxes had not seen fit to eat twice a day. If they had been ordered to prepare breakfast in the same way as dinner, the people of Abdera would have had two choices: either not wait for Xerxes to come at all, or stay and be ruined worse than anyone else on earth.

121. So, hard pressed as they were, the cities carried out what they had been ordered to do. From Acanthus Xerxes sent the fleet off on its own course, after ordering the commanders to wait for him at Therma. This is the Therma that lies on the Thermaic Gulf, which takes its name from it. He did this because he was told that this was the shortest way. From Doriscus as far as Acanthus the army had marched in this order. Xerxes had divided the whole land army into three divisions. One he had sent along the coast to keep pace with the fleet; its commanders were Mardonius and Masistes. Another third of the army had been assigned the inland route, and its generals were Tritantaechmes and Gergis. Meanwhile the third division, with which Xerxes himself traveled, marched in the middle between the other two, and its commanders were Smerdomenes and Megabyzus.

122. When Xerxes let the fleet go, it sailed straight through the canal that had been cut through Athos. The canal ran across to the gulf on which stand the cities of Assa, Pilorus, Singus and Sarte. After picking up a contingent from these cities as well, the fleet sailed on unhindered for the Thermaic Gulf. Rounding Ampelus, the headland of Torone, it passed by these Greek cities, taking ships and men from them: Torone, Galepsus, Sermyle, Mecyberna and Olynthus. This region is called Sithonia.

123. Then Xerxes' fleet cut straight across from the headland of Ampelus to the headland of Canastraeum, which runs farthest out to sea of all Pallene. There it picked up ships and men from Potidaea, Aphytis, Neapolis, Aege, Therambo, Scione, Mende and Sane, since these are the cities of the region now called Pallene, which used to be called Phlegra. Sailing along this coast too, the fleet held its course for the place I mentioned before, picking up contingents also from the cities that come after Pallene and border on the Thermaic Gulf. Their names are Lipaxus, Combrea, Lisae, Gigonus, Campsa, Smila and Aenea, and the region these cities are in is called Crossaea to this day. Sailing on from Aenea, the name I ended my list of cities with, the fleet went straight into the Thermaic Gulf and to the region of Mygdonia, and so it reached Therma, which I mentioned, and the cities of Sindus and Chalestra on the river Axius. This river is the border between Mygdonia and Bottiaea, a district whose narrow strip of coast is held by the cities of Ichnae and Pella.

124. While the fleet was camped near the river Axius, the city of Therma and the cities in between, waiting for the king to arrive, Xerxes and the land army were on their way from Acanthus, cutting straight across the middle by the shortest route to reach Therma. He went through Paeonia and Crestonia to the river Cheidorus. This river rises in the land of the Crestonians, runs through the region of Mygdonia, and comes out beside the marsh at the river Axius.

125. As he was marching this way, lions attacked the camels carrying his supplies. The lions used to come down regularly every night, leaving their own haunts, but they touched nothing else, neither pack animal nor man. They killed only the camels. I wonder what the cause was, and what it was that drove the lions to leave everything else alone and attack only the camels, animals they had never seen before and knew nothing about.

126. In these parts there are many lions, and also wild oxen, the ones with the enormous horns that are often brought into Greece. The lions are found only within certain limits: the river Nestus, which flows through Abdera, on one side, and on the other the Achelous, which flows through Acarnania. East of the Nestus you would not see a lion anywhere in the whole of Europe in front of it, and none in the rest of the continent west of the Achelous; they live only in the land between these two rivers.

127. When Xerxes reached Therma, he settled his army there. His camp took up no less than this stretch of the coast: beginning at the city of Therma and at Mygdonia, it reached as far as the river Lydias and the Haliacmon, which form the border between Bottiaea and Macedonia, joining their waters in one and the same stream. So the king's army was camped in these parts. Of the rivers I have listed, only the Cheidorus, which flows from the land of the Crestonians, was not enough for the army to drink, and its stream ran dry.

128. From Therma Xerxes could see the mountains of Thessaly, Olympus and Ossa, and how very high they were. He learned that between them there was a narrow gorge through which the Peneus flows, and he heard that this way there was a good road into Thessaly. So he wanted to sail there and look at the mouth of the Peneus. He was planning to march by the upper road, through the land of the Macedonians who live inland, until he reached the Perrhaebians, passing by the city of Gonnus, because he had been told that this was the safest way to go. And as he wished, so he did. He went aboard a Sidonian ship, the one he always used whenever he wanted to do anything of this kind, and he signaled for the others to put out to sea as well, leaving the land army where it was. When Xerxes saw the mouth of the Peneus, he was filled with great wonder. He called his guides and asked them whether it would be possible to turn the river aside and lead it out to the sea some other way.

129. Thessaly, they say, was a lake in ancient times, since it is shut in on every side by very high mountains. On the east it is closed off by the ranges of Pelion and Ossa, whose foothills join one another; on the north by Olympus; on the west by Pindus; and on the south by Othrys. The region in the middle, between these mountains, is Thessaly, a kind of bowl. Many rivers flow into it, five of them especially well known: the Peneus, the Apidanus, the Onochonus, the Enipeus and the Pamisus. These gather their waters from the mountains that ring Thessaly and flow down into this plain, each under its own name. But they flow out to the sea by one channel, and a narrow one, after first all joining together in one and the same stream. As soon as they have joined, from that point on the Peneus' name wins out over the rest and the others lose their own names. In ancient times, they say, before there was this channel and outlet between the mountains, these rivers, and besides them Lake Boebeis, did not have names as they do now, but their waters made all of Thessaly one sea. The Thessalians themselves say that Poseidon made the gorge the Peneus flows through, and that is a reasonable thing for them to say. Anyone who believes that Poseidon is the one who shakes the earth, and that cracks made by earthquakes are this god's work, would say on seeing this gorge that Poseidon had made it. For the splitting of the mountains is the work of an earthquake, as is clear to me.

130. So when Xerxes asked whether the Peneus had any other possible outlet to the sea, the guides, who knew the facts exactly, said: "My king, this river has no other way out to the sea but this one, because all of Thessaly is ringed with mountains like a crown." To this Xerxes is said to have replied: "So the Thessalians are sensible men. This, it seems, is what they were guarding against in good time when they changed their minds. They thought about this above everything else: that they had a country that is easy to conquer and can be taken quickly. All anyone would have to do is let the river flood their land, by building a dam to keep it out of the gorge and so turning it from the channel it flows through now, and all of Thessaly except the mountains would be under water." He said this with the sons of Aleuas in mind, since they were Thessalians and the first of the Greeks to give themselves up to the king; Xerxes thought they were offering him friendship on behalf of their whole nation. After saying this and looking over the place, he sailed back to Therma.

131. He stayed in the region of Pieria for many days, because a third of his army was meanwhile cutting the road over the Macedonian mountains, so that the whole host could cross by that way into the land of the Perrhaebians. And now the heralds who had been sent to Greece to demand earth came back, some empty-handed and some bringing earth and water.

132. Among those who gave what was demanded were these: the Thessalians, the Dolopians, the Enianians, the Perrhaebians, the Locrians, the Magnesians, the Malians, the Achaeans of Phthiotis, and the Thebans, together with the rest of the Boeotians except the Thespians and the Plataeans. Against these the Greeks who took up the war against the invader swore an oath. The oath was this: any Greeks who had surrendered to the Persians without being forced to, they would, once their own affairs turned out well, dedicate as an offering to the god at Delphi.

133. That was the oath the Greeks swore. But Xerxes had not sent heralds to Athens or to Sparta to demand earth, and this was the reason. Once before, when Darius had sent heralds for this very purpose, the Athenians had thrown the men who made the demand into the pit where they cast condemned criminals, and the Spartans had thrown theirs into a well, and told them to get earth and water from there and take it to the king. That is why Xerxes did not send anyone to make this demand. What disaster came on the Athenians for doing this to the heralds, I cannot say, except that their land and their city were laid waste; but I do not think it happened for that reason.

134. On the Spartans, though, fell the wrath of Talthybius, Agamemnon's herald in the war against Troy. There is a temple of Talthybius in Sparta, and there are also descendants of Talthybius called the Talthybiads, who have been given the right to carry out every herald's mission that goes out from Sparta. After this event, whenever the Spartans sacrificed, they could not get favorable omens. This went on with them for a long time. The Spartans were distressed and saw it as a great disaster. They held assembly after assembly and made a proclamation asking whether any Spartan was willing to die for Sparta. At last Sperthias son of Aneristus and Bulis son of Nicolaus, Spartans of noble birth and among the very wealthiest, volunteered to pay the penalty to Xerxes for Darius' heralds who had been killed at Sparta. So the Spartans sent these two to the Persians to be put to death.

135. The courage these men showed then deserves admiration, and so do the things they said as well. On their way to Susa they came to Hydarnes, a Persian by birth and commander of the peoples on the coast of Asia, who offered them hospitality and entertained them. While they were his guests he asked them: "Spartans, why do you run away from becoming the king's friends? You can see that the king knows how to honor good men, when you look at me and my position. So you too, if you gave yourselves to the king, since he already thinks of you as good men, could each of you rule over Greek land as a gift from the king." They answered: "Hydarnes, the advice you give us is lopsided. You advise us having tried one thing but with no experience of the other. You know very well what it is to be a slave, but you have never tried freedom, to find out whether it tastes sweet or not. If you ever did try it, you would advise us to fight for it not just with spears, but with axes too."

136. That was their answer to Hydarnes. Then they went up to Susa and came before the king. First the spearmen of the guard ordered them to bow down to the ground before the king, and tried to force them to do it. They said they would never do such a thing, not even if the guards shoved them down headfirst, because it was not their custom to bow down to a man, and that was not what they had come for. When they had fought this off, they next said these words, or words to this effect: "King of the Medes, the Spartans have sent us in place of the heralds who were killed in Sparta, to pay the penalty for their lives." When they said this, Xerxes, moved by a generous spirit, replied that he would not act like the Spartans. They had broken the law that all men keep by killing heralds, but he would not do himself the very thing he blamed them for, nor would he free the Spartans from their guilt by killing these men in return.

137. So the wrath of Talthybius stopped for the time being, even though the Spartans had done no more than this, and even though Sperthias and Bulis came home to Sparta. But a long time afterward it was stirred up again, during the war between the Peloponnesians and the Athenians, as the Spartans tell it. This, I think, was most plainly the work of heaven. That the wrath of Talthybius fell on messengers and did not stop until it had been fully satisfied was only justice. But that it happened to fall on the sons of the very men who had gone up to the king because of it, on Nicolaus son of Bulis and Aneristus son of Sperthias (the Aneristus who defeated the men of Halieis, settlers from Tiryns, by sailing into its harbor in a merchant ship full of soldiers), makes it clear to me that this came about through the work of heaven, because of that wrath. These two men had been sent by the Spartans as envoys to Asia. They were betrayed by Sitalces son of Teres, king of the Thracians, and by Nymphodorus son of Pythes, a man of Abdera, and were captured at Bisanthe on the Hellespont. They were taken off to Attica and put to death by the Athenians, and with them Aristeas son of Adeimantus, the Corinthian. These things happened many years after the king's expedition. Now I return to my earlier story.

Chapter 41: Athens and the Wooden Wall, and the Greeks Appeal to Argos and to Gelon

138. In name, the king's expedition was marching against Athens, but in fact it was aimed at the whole of Greece. The Greeks had known this for a long time, but they did not all take it the same way. Those who had given earth and water to the Persian felt confident, supposing that the invader would do them no harm. Those who had not given it were terrified. There were not enough ships in Greece to meet the invader in battle, and most of the cities were unwilling to take up the war and were eager to go over to the Persians.

139. Here I am forced to state an opinion that most people will resent. Even so, I will not hold back from saying what I clearly see to be the truth. If the Athenians had been gripped by fear of the danger coming at them and had abandoned their land, or if they had stayed without leaving it and surrendered to Xerxes, then no one would have tried to oppose the king at sea. And if no one had opposed Xerxes at sea, this is roughly what would have happened on land. The Peloponnesians might have thrown wall after wall across the Isthmus, layer on layer like so many tunics, but the Spartans would still have been deserted by their allies. The allies would not have left them willingly but because they had no choice, since the Persian fleet would have conquered them city by city. So the Spartans would have been left alone, and after doing great deeds of courage, they would have died nobly. Either they would have suffered that fate, or else, seeing the rest of the Greeks also going over to the Persians, they would have come to terms with Xerxes before it came to that. Either way, Greece would have fallen under Persian rule. For I cannot discover what good the walls across the Isthmus would have done, once the king was master of the sea.

As it is, anyone who says that the Athenians were the saviors of Greece would hit the truth exactly. Whichever side they took, the scales were likely to tip that way. They chose that Greece should go on living in freedom, and it was they who roused the whole of Greece that was left, all of it, that is, that had not gone over to the Persians. And it was they who, after the gods at least, drove back the king. Not even the terrifying oracles that came from Delphi and filled them with dread could persuade them to abandon Greece. They stayed where they were and stood their ground to meet the invader of their land.

140. For the Athenians had sent messengers to Delphi and were ready to consult the oracle. When these men had performed the usual rites in the sacred precinct and had gone into the inner shrine and sat down, the Pythia, whose name was Aristonice, gave them this oracle:

	Wretched ones, why do you sit here? Run to the ends of the earth,
	leave your homes and the heights of your city, round as a wheel!
	For neither the head nor the body is safe any longer,
	nor the feet below, nor the hands, nor the middle is left you:
	all is destroyed together. Fire and the fierce god of war,
	driving his Syrian chariot hard, will hurl them to ruin.
	Not yours alone: he will bring down many more strongholds,
	and hand many temples of the gods to the ravening fire,
	temples that stand even now with the sweat of terror streaming down them,
	shaking with dread; and look, from the top of the roof to the floor
	dark blood is trickling, foretelling the evil no one can escape.
	Out, get out of the shrine, and steep your souls in sorrow!

141. When the men the Athenians had sent to consult the oracle heard this, they were deeply distressed. As they sat there in despair at the disaster that had been foretold for them, Timon son of Androbulus, a man of Delphi as highly respected as anyone there, advised them to take a suppliant's branch and go in a second time to consult the oracle as suppliants. The Athenians did as he advised and said: "Lord Apollo, give us some better oracle about our homeland, out of respect for these suppliant branches we have brought you. Otherwise we will not leave the shrine. We will stay right here, where we are now, until we die." When they said this, the priestess gave them a second oracle, as follows:

	Pallas cannot win over great Zeus of Olympus,
	though she pleads with him in many words and closely woven cunning.
	But I will tell you this as well, and make it fast as adamant.
	All else will be taken that the borders of Cecrops
	hold within them, and the dark glens of holy Cithaeron.
	At the last Zeus grants to Athena, the Trito-born, a wooden wall
	alone to stand unsacked, and it will help you and your children.
	Do not wait there for the horsemen and the foot soldiers without number;
	do not sit still as the army comes from the mainland, but pull back
	and turn your back to the enemy: one day you will face him yet.
	Divine Salamis, you will bring death to the sons of women,
	whether the grain is being sown or gathered in.

142. This seemed to them to be a milder answer than the first, as in truth it was. So they had it written down and went back to Athens with it. When the messengers had returned and reported it to the people, many different opinions were offered by those trying to work out what the oracle meant. Two of them stood most directly opposed to each other. Some of the older men said they thought the god had prophesied that the Acropolis would survive. In the old days the Acropolis of Athens had been fenced with a hedge of thorns, and so they guessed that the "wooden wall" meant that fence. Others said, on the contrary, that the god meant their ships, and they urged the Athenians to let everything else go and get the ships ready. But those who said the ships were the wooden wall were thrown off by the last two lines the priestess had spoken:

	Divine Salamis, you will bring death to the sons of women,
	whether the grain is being sown or gathered in.

These lines upset the view of those who said the ships were the wooden wall. For the interpreters of oracles took them to mean that if the Athenians prepared for a sea battle, they were fated to be defeated off Salamis.

143. Now there was a man among the Athenians who had lately been making his way into the front rank, whose name was Themistocles; he was called the son of Neocles. This man said that the interpreters of oracles had not worked out the whole of it correctly. If the words really referred to the Athenians, he argued, he did not think the oracle would have put it so gently. It would have said "Cruel Salamis" instead of "Divine Salamis," at least if the people living there were fated to die around it. The truth was that the god had spoken the oracle about the enemy, if one understood it rightly, and not about the Athenians. So he advised them to get ready to fight at sea, since the ships were their wooden wall. When Themistocles had declared his view this way, the Athenians judged that it was better to follow him than the interpreters of oracles. The interpreters told them not to prepare for a sea battle, and in short not to lift a hand against the enemy at all, but to leave the land of Attica and settle somewhere else.

144. Before this, another proposal of Themistocles' had also turned out to be the best one at the critical moment. The Athenians had a great sum of money in the public treasury, which had come in from the mines at Laurium, and they were about to share it out among themselves, ten drachmas to each man. Themistocles persuaded them to give up this plan of dividing it, and to use the money instead to build two hundred ships for the war, meaning the war with the Aeginetans. That war, by breaking out when it did, turned out to be the saving of Greece at that time, because it forced the Athenians to become a sea power. The ships were never used for the purpose they were built for, and so they were there for Greece when she needed them. So the Athenians had these ships already, built beforehand, and they needed to build more besides. After the oracle was given, they took counsel and resolved to obey the god: they would meet the invader of Greece at sea with their whole force, together with any of the other Greeks who were willing to join them.

145. Those were the oracles that had been given to the Athenians. Now the Greeks who had the better attitude toward Greece came together in one place, talked over their situation, and exchanged pledges with one another. In their deliberations they decided that the first thing to do, before anything else, was to put an end to their quarrels and the wars they were fighting among themselves. There were wars going on between various cities, but the biggest was the one between the Athenians and the Aeginetans. Next, when they learned that Xerxes was at Sardis with his army, they decided to send spies to Asia to look over the king's forces. They also resolved to send envoys to Argos to make an alliance against the Persian, to send others to Sicily to Gelon son of Deinomenes and to Corcyra to urge them to come to the help of Greece, and others again to Crete. Their aim was that, if possible, the whole Greek people might be united and might all act together toward the same goal, since the danger threatened all the Greeks alike. And Gelon's power was said to be great, far greater than that of any other Greek.

146. After they had made these decisions, they settled their quarrels and then, first of all, sent three men to Asia as spies. These men reached Sardis and gathered information about the king's army, but they were caught. The generals of the land army questioned them and they were being led away to be executed. Their death had been decided. But when Xerxes heard of it, he found fault with the generals' decision and sent some of his bodyguard of spearmen, with orders to bring the spies before him if they found them still alive. They found them still living and brought them before the king. Then Xerxes, once he had learned what they had come for, ordered the spearmen to take them around and show them the whole army, infantry and cavalry both. When they had looked their fill, the guards were to let them go unharmed to whatever country they wished.

147. That was his order, and he gave his reason for it at the same time. If the spies had been put to death, he said, the Greeks would not have learned in advance how far beyond all description his power was, while killing three men would not do the enemy much harm. But when these men went back to Greece, he thought it likely that the Greeks would hear about his power and hand over their freedom to him of their own accord, before the expedition now being set in motion ever took place, and then there would be no need for the trouble of marching an army against them at all.

This opinion of his is like his way of thinking on other occasions too. When Xerxes was at Abydos, he saw ships carrying grain from the Black Sea sailing out through the Hellespont on their way to Aegina and the Peloponnese. The men sitting beside him, when they learned that the ships belonged to the enemy, were ready to capture them, and kept looking at the king to see when he would give the word. But Xerxes asked where the men were sailing. They answered: "To your enemies, master, carrying grain to them." And he replied: "Aren't we sailing to the same place ourselves, supplied with grain as well as everything else we need? So how are they wronging us, if they're carrying provisions there for our use?"

148. So the spies, after looking at everything in this way and then being sent off, returned to Europe. Meanwhile, after sending out the spies, the Greeks who had sworn alliance against the Persian next sent envoys to Argos.

Now the Argives say that their part in this happened as follows. They learned, they say, at the very beginning about the movement the Persians were setting on foot against Greece. Once they knew of it, and saw that the Greeks would try to win them as allies against the Persians, they sent messengers to Delphi to ask the god what they should do to come off best. For not long before, six thousand of them had been killed by the Spartans and by Cleomenes son of Anaxandrides, and that in fact was why they sent to ask. When they asked, the Pythia answered them this way:

	Hated by your neighbors, beloved by the immortal gods,
	keep your spear drawn in, and sit well guarded behind it.
	Guard the head, and the head will keep the limbs and the body safe.

This, they say, was the answer the Pythia had given them before. Afterward, when the envoys of the Greeks came to Argos, as I said, they went into the Council chamber and delivered the message they had been given. To this the Council replied that the Argives were ready to do what was asked, on two conditions: that they could make a thirty years' peace with the Spartans, and that they could have half the leadership of the whole alliance. And yet by strict right, they said, the whole leadership belonged to them; even so, half was enough for them.

149. That, they say, is the answer the Council gave, even though the oracle had forbidden them to make the alliance with the Greeks. They were eager to have the thirty-year truce, they say, even though they were afraid of the oracle, so that, as they claim, their sons might grow to manhood in those years. Without a truce, they were afraid that if a second disaster struck them in fighting the Persian, on top of the one that had already befallen them, they might be subject to the Spartans for all time to come.

Those of the envoys who came from Sparta answered what the Council had said. As for the truce, they would refer it to their public assembly. But as for the leadership, they had been given authority to answer themselves, and so they said this: the Spartans had two kings and the Argives had one, and it was not possible to remove either of Sparta's two from the leadership, but nothing prevented the Argive king from having an equal vote with each of their two. At that, the Argives say, they could not stand the greed of the Spartans. They chose to be ruled by the non-Greeks rather than give way at all to the Spartans, and they told the envoys to leave Argive territory before sunset, or else they would be treated as enemies.

150. That is how much the Argives themselves report about these matters. But there is another story told in Greece. According to it, Xerxes sent a herald to Argos before he set out on his expedition against Greece, and when this herald arrived, they say, he spoke as follows: "Men of Argos, King Xerxes says this to you. We believe that Perses, our ancestor, was the son of Perseus son of Danae, and that his mother was Andromeda, daughter of Cepheus. If that is so, it seems we are descended from you. So it would not be right for us to march against our own forefathers, or for you to oppose us by helping others. It would be right for you to keep quiet and stay out of it. For if things go the way I intend, I will hold no people in higher honor than you." The Argives, it is said, thought a great deal of this offer. So at first they offered no help and asked for no share in anything. But later, when the Greeks tried to bring them in, they knew perfectly well that the Spartans would not give them a share of the command, and so they demanded it only to have an excuse for keeping out of the war.

151. Some of the Greeks also report that something happened many years later which agrees with this account. Envoys of the Athenians, they say, happened to be at Susa, the city of Memnon, on some other business: Callias son of Hipponicus and those who had gone up with him. At that same time the Argives had also sent envoys to Susa. These envoys asked Artaxerxes son of Xerxes whether the friendship they had formed with Xerxes still held good, as they wished it to, or whether he now regarded them as enemies. And King Artaxerxes said that it most certainly still held, and that there was no city he considered a better friend than Argos.

152. Now whether Xerxes really did send a herald to Argos with the message that has been reported, and whether envoys of the Argives went up to Susa and asked Artaxerxes about their friendship, I can't say for certain, and I offer no opinion on these matters beyond what the Argives themselves say. But I do know this much. If all the peoples of the world were to bring their own troubles together into one place, wanting to trade them with their neighbors, each of them, after taking a close look at the troubles of the others, would gladly carry back home the ones they had brought. So the Argives are not the ones who acted most shamefully of all. I am obliged to report what is said, but I am not obliged to believe all of it, and let that hold for this whole history. For I must add that this too is said: that it was actually the Argives who invited the Persian to invade Greece, because their war with the Spartans had gone badly for them, and they were willing to suffer anything at all rather than the misery they were in at the time.

153. So much for the Argives. Meanwhile envoys from the allies had come to Sicily to confer with Gelon, and among them, from Sparta, was Syagrus. Now Gelon's ancestor, the first of his family to settle at Gela, came from the island of Telos, which lies off Triopium. When Gela was founded by the Lindians from Rhodes together with Antiphemus, he went along too. In the course of time his descendants became priests of the mysteries of the Earth goddesses, and they kept that office. It had been won by Telines, one of their ancestors, in the following way. Certain men of Gela had been beaten in a struggle between factions and had fled to Mactorium, the town that stands above Gela. Telines brought these men back to Gela from exile, with no force of men at all, only the sacred objects of these goddesses. Where he got them from, or whether he came by them on his own, I cannot say. In any case, trusting in them, he brought the men back from exile on condition that his descendants would be priests of the goddesses' mysteries.

It has also surprised me, given what I am told, that Telines was able to do such a great deed. Deeds like that, I think, do not come from just anyone, but from a man with a brave spirit and manly strength, whereas the people of Sicily say that Telines was just the opposite: a soft, effeminate man with rather a poor spirit.

154. So that was how he won this privilege. Cleander son of Pantares had been tyrant of Gela for seven years when he came to his end, killed by Sabyllus, a man of Gela. Then Hippocrates, Cleander's brother, took over the sole rule. While Hippocrates was tyrant, Gelon, a descendant of Telines the priest of the mysteries, was one of Hippocrates' bodyguard of spearmen, along with many others, among them Aenesidemus son of Pataecus. Not long after, he was made commander of the whole cavalry because of his courage. For when Hippocrates besieged Callipolis, Naxos, Zancle and Leontini one after another, and Syracuse too, and many towns of the non-Greeks, Gelon proved himself a brilliant fighter in those wars. Of the cities I just named, not one except Syracuse escaped being conquered by Hippocrates. The Syracusans were beaten in battle at the river Elorus, but they were rescued by the Corinthians and the Corcyreans. These rescued them and settled the quarrel on the condition that the Syracusans hand over Camarina to Hippocrates. In ancient times Camarina had belonged to Syracuse.

155. Then it was Hippocrates' turn to die, after being tyrant for the same number of years as his brother Cleander. He was killed at the city of Hybla, where he had gone on campaign against the Sicels. When the citizens of Gela refused to obey any longer, Gelon made a show of standing up for Hippocrates' sons, Eucleides and Cleander. But in fact, once he had beaten the men of Gela in battle, he robbed Hippocrates' sons of the power and ruled himself. After this stroke of luck, Gelon brought back the Syracusans called the "landholders," who had been driven into exile by the common people and by their own slaves, the ones called Cyllyrians. He brought them back from the town of Casmene to Syracuse, and so he got hold of that city too. For when Gelon marched against them, the common people of Syracuse handed over their city and themselves to him.

156. Once he had Syracuse in his power, he cared less about Gela, which he also ruled, and he put it in the charge of his brother Hieron while he built up Syracuse. Right away the city shot up and flourished. First he brought all the people of Camarina to Syracuse and made them citizens, and razed the town of Camarina to the ground. Second, he did the same to more than half the citizens of Gela as he had done to the people of Camarina. Then there were the Megarians of Sicily. When they were besieged and surrendered on terms, Gelon brought their wealthy men to Syracuse and made them citizens, even though they had started the war against him and expected to be put to death for it. But the common people of Megara had no part in causing this war and expected no harm. Gelon brought them to Syracuse too, and sold them as slaves to be carried out of Sicily. He did the same to the Euboeans in Sicily, making the same distinction between them. He treated these two cities this way because he thought the common people were the most unpleasant people to have in a state.

157. That is how Gelon had become a powerful tyrant. At this time the envoys of the Greeks arrived at Syracuse, and when they were given a hearing they said: "The Spartans and their allies have sent us to win you to our side against the Persian. You must know, surely, about the man who is about to invade Greece. A Persian means to bridge the Hellespont and lead all the armies of the East out of Asia against Greece. He pretends he is marching on Athens, but in fact he means to bring all Greece under his rule. You have risen to great power, and as ruler of Sicily you hold no small share of Greece. So come and help those who are working to free Greece, and join in making her free. For if all Greece is gathered together as one, it makes a great force, and we are a match in battle for those coming against us. But if some of us go over to the enemy and others refuse to help, and the healthy part of Greece is small, then right away there is a danger that all Greece will fall. Do not hope that if the Persian beats us in battle he will not come on to you. Guard yourself against that in advance. By helping us you are helping yourself. And a plan that is wisely made usually turns out well in the end."

158. That is what the envoys said. Gelon came down on them hard, answering like this: "Men of Greece, this is a selfish speech you have dared to come here with, inviting me to be your ally against the foreigner. Not long ago I asked you to join me in fighting an army of foreigners, when I had a quarrel with the Carthaginians. I urged you to take vengeance on the people of Egesta for the death of Dorieus son of Anaxandrides, and I offered at the same time to help free the trading ports that have brought you such great profit and gain. And you did not come to help me, either for my own sake or to avenge the death of Dorieus. As far as you are concerned, all that country would still be under the rule of foreigners now. But things turned out well for us, and better than that. And now that the war has come around and reached you, you have finally remembered Gelon.

"But though you treated me with contempt, I will not behave the way you did. I am ready to come to your help, with two hundred triremes and 20,000 hoplites, along with 2,000 horsemen, 2,000 archers, 2,000 slingers, and 2,000 light-armed men to run beside the horsemen. What is more, I promise to supply grain for the whole Greek army until we have finished the war. I promise all this on one condition: that I am the commander and leader of the Greeks against the foreigner. On any other condition I will neither come myself nor send anyone else."

159. When Syagrus heard this, he could not contain himself, and he said: "Agamemnon son of Pelops would groan aloud indeed, if he heard that the Spartans had been robbed of the leadership by Gelon and the Syracusans! No, don't mention this condition again, that we should hand the leadership over to you. If you want to come to the help of Greece, understand that you will be under the command of the Spartans. And if you really refuse to take orders, then don't come to help us at all."

160. Gelon saw how hostile Syagrus' speech was, and so he laid out his final offer to them: "My Spartan friend, insults that sink into a man's heart usually stir him to anger in return. But though you have insulted me in what you said, you will not provoke me into answering you in an unseemly way. Since you lay claim to the leadership so hard, it would be fair for me to claim it even more than you, since I lead an army many times larger and far more ships. But since this condition is so distasteful to you, we will give up something of our first proposal. Suppose you lead the land army and I lead the fleet. Or if you would rather lead at sea, I am willing to lead on land. Either you must be content with these terms, or go home without the alliance I have to give."

161. Those were the offers Gelon made, and the Athenian envoy, speaking before the Spartan could, answered him this way: "King of the Syracusans, Greece did not send us to you because she needs a leader, but because she needs an army. But you hold out no hope that you will send an army unless you lead Greece, and what you are really after is becoming commander of the Greek armies. As long as you were demanding to lead the whole Greek army, it was enough for us Athenians to keep quiet, knowing that the Spartan could speak up for both of us. But now, since you have been turned down for the whole and are asking to command the fleet, here is how things stand. Even if the Spartan lets you command it, we will not. The fleet at least is ours, if the Spartans do not want it themselves. If they wish to lead it, we do not oppose them, but we will allow no one else to command the ships. Otherwise it would be pointless for us to own the largest navy of all the Greeks, if we, Athenians, handed the leadership over to Syracusans. We can boast that ours is the most ancient people of all, the only Greeks who have never moved from one land to another. One of our own was the man whom Homer, the epic poet, called the best of all who came to Troy at drawing up an army and setting it in battle order. So no one can fairly blame us for saying these things."

162. Gelon answered: "My Athenian friend, it seems you have plenty of commanders, but you will not have anyone to command. Since you will not give way at all and want to have everything, you had better go home as fast as you can and tell the Greeks that the spring has been taken out of their year." This is what the saying means. The spring is plainly the finest part of the year, and he meant that his army was the finest part of the Greek army. So Greece, deprived of his alliance, was, he said, like a year with the spring taken out of it.

Chapter 42: Corcyra, Crete and Thessaly, the Storm off Sepias, and the Fleets at Artemisium

163. After this conference with Gelon, the Greek envoys sailed away. Gelon was afraid for the Greeks, that they would not be able to defeat the invader. On the other hand, he thought it outrageous and not to be endured that he, the tyrant of Sicily, should go to the Peloponnese and take orders from the Spartans. So he gave up on that road and took another. As soon as he heard that the Persian king had crossed the Hellespont, he sent Cadmus son of Scythes, a man of Cos, to Delphi with three fifty-oared galleys, carrying a great deal of money and a friendly message. Cadmus was to wait there and watch how the battle would turn out. If the Persian won, he was to give him the money and offer him earth and water on behalf of the lands Gelon ruled. If the Greeks won, he was to bring the money back.

164. Before all this, Cadmus had inherited from his father the rule of Cos, in a flourishing state. Then, of his own free will, with no danger threatening him, moved only by his own sense of right, he had handed the government over to the people of Cos and gone off to Sicily. There, with the Samians, he took and resettled the city of Zancle, which had changed its name to Messene. This was the Cadmus, who had come to Sicily in the way I have described, that Gelon was now sending, having picked him for the honesty he had seen in him in other dealings. And on top of the other honest things this man had done, he left behind him this one too to be remembered, and it was not the least of them. He had in his hands that great sum of money Gelon had trusted him with, and he could have kept it for himself, but he chose not to. When the Greeks had won the sea battle and Xerxes had marched away and gone, Cadmus too came back to Sicily, bringing the whole sum with him.

165. The people who live in Sicily also tell another story: that Gelon would have come to help the Greeks even though he would have been under Spartan command, except for what happened at that very moment. Terillus son of Crinippus, tyrant of Himera, had been driven out of Himera by Theron son of Aenesidemus, the ruler of Acragas. And just at this time Terillus was bringing in an army of 300,000 Phoenicians, Libyans, Iberians, Ligurians, Elisyci, Sardinians and Corsicans, under the command of Hamilcar son of Hanno, the king of the Carthaginians. Terillus had won Hamilcar over partly through their bond as guest-friends, but above all through the eager help of Anaxilaus son of Cretines, the tyrant of Rhegium. Anaxilaus was married to Terillus' daughter, whose name was Cydippe, and to help his father-in-law he worked to bring Hamilcar into Sicily, and gave him his own sons as hostages. That, they say, is why Gelon could not come to help the Greeks, and why he sent the money to Delphi instead.

166. They also say that, as it happened, Gelon and Theron defeated Hamilcar the Carthaginian on the very same day that the Greeks defeated the Persian at Salamis. This Hamilcar was a Carthaginian on his father's side and a Syracusan on his mother's, and he had become king of the Carthaginians because of his own merit. When the battle was joined and he was losing, he vanished, so I am told. He was never seen again anywhere on earth, alive or dead, though Gelon searched for him with every effort.

167. The Carthaginians themselves tell a story about this too, and what they say is believable enough. The non-Greeks and the Greeks fought in Sicily from early morning until late in the afternoon (that is how long the battle is said to have dragged on). All that time Hamilcar stayed in the camp, offering sacrifices to get good omens, burning the bodies of the victims whole on a great pyre. And when he saw his own army being routed, he happened to be in the act of pouring a libation over the victims, and he threw himself into the fire. So he was burned up and vanished. Whether Hamilcar vanished in this way, as the Phoenicians tell it, or in some other way, the Carthaginians offer sacrifices to him now, and at the time they set up memorials to him in all their colonies, with the greatest one in Carthage itself.

168. So much for the affairs of Sicily. As for the Corcyreans, here is the answer they gave the envoys, and here is what they did afterward, as I will tell. The same men who had gone to Sicily also tried to win their help, saying the same things they had said to Gelon. At the time the Corcyreans promised to send a force and help defend Greece. They declared that they must not let Greece be destroyed without lifting a hand, because if it fell, they themselves would be enslaved from the very first day; no, they must give all the help they could. That was the fine-sounding answer they gave. But when the time came to send help, they had other plans in mind. They manned sixty ships, and after a great deal of delay they put out to sea and reached the Peloponnese. Then they kept their ships at anchor off Pylos and Taenarum in Spartan territory, waiting, as Gelon did, to see how the war would turn out. They did not expect the Greeks to win; they thought the Persian would beat them easily and become master of all Greece. So they were acting on purpose, so that they could say something like this to the Persian: "My king, when the Greeks tried to get our help for this war, we would not oppose you or do anything you would not like, even though our power is not the smallest, and we could have supplied ships, not the fewest in number either, but the most after the Athenians." By saying this they hoped to come off better than the rest, and in my opinion that is just what would have happened. Meanwhile they had an excuse ready for the Greeks, and it is the one they actually used. When the Greeks blamed them for not coming to help, they said they had manned sixty triremes but had not been able to get around Cape Malea because of the Etesian winds. That, they said, was why they had not reached Salamis; it was not from any lack of courage that they had missed the sea battle.

169. That is how the Corcyreans got out of what the Greeks asked of them. The Cretans did this. When the Greeks who had been appointed to deal with them tried to win their help, the Cretans joined together and sent men to ask the god at Delphi whether it would be better for them to help Greece. The Pythia answered: "Fools, do you think the sorrows were too few that Minos sent you in his anger for the help you gave Menelaus? The others did not join you in avenging his death at Camicus, but you joined them in avenging the woman a foreigner carried off from Sparta." When the Cretans heard this answer, they held back from giving any help.

170. The story goes that Minos went to Sicania, which is now called Sicily, in search of Daedalus, the craftsman who had fled from him, and there he died a violent death. Some time later, the Cretans, urged on by a god, all of them except the men of Polichne and Praesus, came to Sicania with a great expedition and besieged the city of Camicus for seven years. In my time Camicus was occupied by the people of Acragas. In the end they could neither take it nor stay on outside it, because they were hard pressed by famine, so they gave up and left. But as they sailed past the coast of Iapygia, a great storm caught them and drove them ashore. Their ships were smashed to pieces, and since they could see no way of getting back to Crete, they founded the city of Hyria there. They stayed there, and they were changed: instead of Cretans they became Messapians of Iapygia, and instead of islanders they became people of the mainland. From Hyria they founded the other settlements that the people of Taras, long afterward, tried to destroy, and suffered a great disaster in the attempt. In fact this turned out to be the greatest slaughter of Greeks that we know of, both of the people of Taras themselves and of the citizens of Rhegium. Micythus son of Choerus had forced these men of Rhegium to go and help the people of Taras, and three thousand of them were killed this way. Of the people of Taras who were killed there, no count was ever made. This Micythus was a servant of Anaxilaus, and Anaxilaus had left him in charge of Rhegium. He is the man who, after he was driven out of Rhegium, settled at Tegea in Arcadia and dedicated all those statues at Olympia.

171. This story of the men of Rhegium and the people of Taras has been a side-story in my account. But in Crete, as the men of Praesus tell it, once the island had been emptied of its people in this way, various other peoples settled there, especially Greeks. In the third generation after the death of Minos came the Trojan War, in which the Cretans proved to be far from the worst of those who came to help Menelaus. Then after this, when they came home from Troy, famine and plague fell on both men and cattle, until Crete was emptied of people a second time. Now a third population of Cretans lives there, together with those who were left of the earlier ones. By reminding them of all this, the Pythia stopped the Cretans from helping the Greeks, though they wanted to.

172. As for the Thessalians, they had at first sided with the Persians against their will, and they showed that they did not like what the Aleuadae were planning. As soon as they heard that the Persian was about to cross into Europe, they sent envoys to the Isthmus. Gathered at the Isthmus were delegates of Greece, chosen by the cities that had the better attitude toward Greece. The Thessalian envoys came before them and said: "Greeks, you must guard the pass by Mount Olympus, so that Thessaly and the whole of Greece may be sheltered from the war. We are ready to guard it with you, but you must send a large force too. If you do not send one, you can be sure we will come to terms with the Persian. It is not right that we, posted so far out in front of the rest of Greece, should die alone in your defense. If you are not willing to come and help us, you have no way to force anything on us, since no force can make the powerless do what they cannot. We will try to find some way of saving ourselves."

173. That is what the Thessalians said. So the Greeks decided to send an army of foot soldiers by sea to Thessaly to guard the pass. When the army had gathered, it sailed through the Euripus and came to Alus in Achaea. There the men landed, left the ships behind at Alus, and marched into Thessaly. They arrived at Tempe, the pass that leads from lower Macedonia into Thessaly along the river Peneus, between Mount Olympus and Mount Ossa. There the Greeks camped, about ten thousand hoplites in all, and the Thessalian cavalry joined them. The commander of the Spartans was Euaenetus son of Carenus, who had been chosen from among the polemarchs, Sparta's senior army officers, and was not of the royal family. The commander of the Athenians was Themistocles son of Neocles. But they stayed there only a few days. Messengers came from Alexander son of Amyntas, the Macedonian, advising them to leave and not stay in the pass to be trampled underfoot by the invading army, and telling them how huge the army was and how many ships there were. When these men gave them this advice, the Greeks took it, because they thought it was good advice and the Macedonian was plainly well disposed toward them. But in my opinion it was fear that persuaded them, once they learned that there was another pass into Thessaly besides this one, through upper Macedonia, through the land of the Perrhaebians and past the town of Gonnus. That is in fact the way Xerxes' army came in. So the Greeks went back down to their ships and made their way back to the Isthmus.

174. That was the expedition to Thessaly, and it took place when the king was about to cross from Asia into Europe and was already at Abydos. So the Thessalians, left without allies, now went over to the Persians wholeheartedly and no longer with any hesitation, so that as events went on they proved very useful to the king.
