175. When the Greeks had come back to the Isthmus, they discussed, with what Alexander had told them in mind, where they should make their stand and in what regions they should fight. The view that won was to guard the pass at Thermopylae. They could see it was narrower than the pass into Thessaly, and it was a single pass, and nearer to their own land besides. As for the path by which the Greeks who fell at Thermopylae were caught, they did not even know it existed until they reached Thermopylae and the people of Trachis told them. So they decided to guard this pass and keep the invader from getting through into Greece, and they decided that the fleet should sail to Artemisium in the territory of Histiaea. These places are near each other, so that each part of their forces could find out what was happening to the other. And here is how the places lie.

176. Take Artemisium first. Coming out of the Thracian Sea, the wide water narrows down to the slim channel between the island of Sciathus and the mainland of Magnesia. Right after the strait, on Euboea, comes the beach called Artemisium, where there is a temple of Artemis. Second, the way into Greece through Trachis is, at its narrowest, only fifty feet wide. But that is not where the narrowest part of the whole region lies. It is in front of Thermopylae and also behind it. At Alpeni, which lies behind Thermopylae, there is room for only a single cart track, and again at the river Phoenix, near the town of Anthela, there is room for only a single cart track. To the west of Thermopylae rises a mountain that cannot be climbed, sheer and very high, stretching away toward the range of Oeta. To the east of the road lie the sea and marshes, right up against it. In this pass there are hot springs, which the local people call the "Pots," and an altar of Heracles stands near them. A wall had once been built across this pass, and in the old days there was a gate in it. The Phocians built it, out of fear, when the Thessalians came from the land of the Thesprotians to settle in the Aeolian land, the country they hold now. Since the Thessalians, as the Phocians supposed, were trying to conquer them, the Phocians protected themselves in advance. They let the water of the hot springs run over the pass, to turn the place into a gully, and they tried every means to keep the Thessalians from invading their land. This old wall had been built long before, and by then most of it had fallen into ruin with age. The Greeks decided to build it up again and to hold the invader back from Greece at this spot. Very near the road there is a village called Alpeni, and the Greeks counted on getting their supplies from it.

177. So the Greeks judged that these places suited their purpose. They had thought everything through in advance and worked out that the invaders would not be able to make use of either their greater numbers or their cavalry there, and so they decided to meet the invader of Greece at this place. When they learned that the Persian was in Pieria, they broke camp at the Isthmus and set out on the campaign, some by land to Thermopylae, others by sea to Artemisium.

178. So the Greeks were hurrying to the rescue, each to his assigned post. Meanwhile the people of Delphi, terrified, consulted the oracle of the god on behalf of themselves and of Greece. They were told to pray to the Winds, because the Winds would be powerful allies of Greece in the fighting. When the Delphians received the oracle, they first passed it on to those Greeks who wanted to be free, and by telling them at a time when they were deeply afraid of the invader, they earned their undying gratitude. After this the people of Delphi set up an altar to the Winds at Thyia, where the sacred precinct of Thyia daughter of Cephisus is, the woman this place is named after, and they began offering the Winds sacrifices.

179. To this day the Delphians, following the oracle, offer sacrifices to win the Winds' favor. Meanwhile, Xerxes' fleet had set out from the city of Therma, and ten of its ships, the fastest sailers, crossed straight over toward Sciathus. There three Greek ships, one from Troezen, one from Aegina and one from Athens, were keeping watch as an advance guard. When the crews of these ships caught sight of the enemy ships, they ran for it.

180. The ship from Troezen, commanded by Prexinus, was chased and taken at once by the enemy. The Persians then took the best-looking of the marines on board and cut his throat on the ship's prow, making the first and handsomest Greek they had captured into a good omen for themselves. The name of this man who was sacrificed was Leon, which means "lion," and perhaps his name had something to do with what happened to him.

181. The Aeginetan ship, whose captain was Asonides, gave them some trouble to take, because Pytheas son of Ischenous was serving on board as a marine, and he proved himself a very brave man that day. When the ship was being taken, he kept fighting until he was cut all to pieces. He fell, but he did not die; there was still breath in him. So the Persians serving as marines on the ships did everything they could to save his life, because of his courage. They treated his wounds with ointments of myrrh and bound him up in strips of the finest linen. When they got back to their own main force, they showed him off to the whole army, making a marvel of him and treating him well. But the rest of the men they had taken on this ship they treated as slaves.

182. So two of the three ships were captured in this way. The third, whose captain was Phormus of Athens, ran aground at the mouth of the river Peneus as it fled. The enemy got the ship but not the crew. As soon as the Athenians ran the ship aground they leaped out of her, made their way through Thessaly, and got back to Athens.

183. The Greeks stationed at Artemisium learned of all this from fire signals sent from Sciathus. When they heard, they were frightened, and they moved their anchorage from Artemisium to Chalcis, meaning to guard the Euripus, but they left lookouts on the heights of Euboea by day. Of the ten enemy ships, three sailed up to the reef called Myrmex, which lies between Sciathus and Magnesia, and set up a stone pillar on it, which they had brought along for the purpose. Once the hazards of the passage had been cleared up in this way, the main fleet set out from Therma and sailed there with all its ships, eleven days after the king had set out on his march from Therma. It was Pammon of Scyros who had told them about this reef lying right in the middle of the channel. Sailing all day, the enemy fleet reached Sepias in Magnesia and the beach between the city of Casthanaea and the headland of Sepias.

184. As far as this place, and as far as Thermopylae, the army had suffered no disaster. By my own calculation its numbers at that point were still as follows. There were 1,207 ships from Asia. If you count two hundred men to a ship, I find that the original crews provided by the various nations came to 241,400 men. On board each of these ships, besides the marines from its own nation, there served thirty marines who were Persians, Medes or Sacae, and they come to another 36,210 men. To this and to the first figure I will also add the crews of the fifty-oared galleys, assuming there were about eighty men in each, more or less. There were 3,000 of these vessels gathered together, as I said before, so there would have been 240,000 men in them. That was the naval force that came from Asia, 517,610 men in all. The infantry had been counted at 1,700,000, and the cavalry at 80,000. To these I will add the Arabian camel-drivers and the Libyan chariot-drivers, and I put them at 20,000 men. So the ships' crews and the land army together come to 2,317,610. That is the figure for the army brought out of Asia itself, not counting the servants who came with it, or the grain transports and the men who sailed in them.

185. On top of everything added up so far, there is still the force that was being brought along from Europe to be counted, and of this we must give a likely estimate. The Greeks of Thrace and of the islands off the coast of Thrace supplied one hundred and twenty ships, which makes 24,000 men. As for the land force supplied by the Thracians, Paeonians, Eordians, Bottiaeans, the people who live in Chalcidice, the Brygians, Pierians, Macedonians, Perrhaebians, Enianians, Dolopians, Magnesians, Achaeans, and all who live along the coast of Thrace, I estimate that these various nations came to 300,000 men. Adding these to the men from Asia makes a total of 2,641,610 fighting men.

186. That was the number of fighting men. As for the servants who came with them, and the men in the small grain boats and in the other vessels that sailed along with the army, I suppose that they were not fewer than the fighting men but more. But I will assume that they were exactly equal in number, neither more nor fewer. If they were equal to the fighting force, they make up the same number again. So the number of men Xerxes son of Darius led as far as Sepias and Thermopylae was 5,283,220.

187. That is the number of Xerxes' whole army. But as for the women who baked bread for it, and the concubines and the eunuchs, no one could give an exact number, nor could anyone give the number of the draft animals and other pack animals, or of the Indian hounds that came along, there were so many of them. So it does not surprise me that the water of some rivers ran out. What surprises me more is how there was enough food for so many hundreds of thousands. I find by calculation that if each man got a quart of wheat a day and nothing more, then 110,340 medimni, about 165,000 bushels, were used up every day. And here I am not counting anything for the women, the eunuchs, the pack animals or the dogs. Of all these men, so many hundreds of thousands of them, not one was more worthy than Xerxes himself to hold this power, for his good looks and his height.

188. So the fleet set out and sailed. When it put in on the coast of Magnesia, at the beach between the city of Casthanaea and the headland of Sepias, the first ships to arrive lay moored to the shore and the rest rode at anchor behind them. Since the beach was not long, they lay at anchor eight ships deep, with their prows pointing out to sea. They lay like this that night. But at dawn, after clear skies and a dead calm, the sea began to boil, and a great storm fell on them with a strong east wind, the wind the people who live around there call the Hellespontias. Those who noticed the wind rising, and who were moored in a way that let them do it, hauled their ships up on land before the storm hit, and so they and their ships survived. But of the ships the storm caught out at sea, it threw some onto the place called Ipni on Mount Pelion, and others onto the beach. Some were wrecked on the headland of Sepias itself, others at the city of Meliboea, and others were cast up on shore at Casthanaea. The storm was too violent to withstand.

189. There is a story that the Athenians had called on Boreas, the North Wind, to help them, because of an oracle. Another answer had come to them from the god, telling them to call on their brother-in-law for help. Now according to the Greek story, Boreas has a wife from Attica, Orithyia daughter of Erechtheus. Because of this marriage tie, so the story that has gone around says, the Athenians guessed that their "brother-in-law" was Boreas. So when they saw the wind rising, as they lay with their ships at Chalcis in Euboea, or even before that, they offered sacrifices and called on Boreas and Orithyia to help them and to destroy the invaders' ships, as they had done before around Mount Athos. Whether this was the reason the North Wind fell on the invaders as they lay at anchor, I can't say. But however that may be, the Athenians say that Boreas had helped them before, and that this time too he did what I have described for them. When they got home they built a temple to Boreas by the river Ilissus.

190. In this disaster, according to those who give the lowest figure, no fewer than four hundred ships were lost, with men beyond counting and an enormous amount of treasure. So much so that this shipwreck made a fortune for Ameinocles son of Cretines, a Magnesian who owned land around Sepias. He picked up many gold cups that washed up on the shore afterward, and many silver ones too. He found strongboxes that had belonged to the Persians, and he came by other gold things beyond description. But though he became very rich from what he found, in other ways this man was not lucky. He too had his share of misfortune: he was grieved by the killing of a child.

191. Of the grain transports and other vessels that were lost, no count was made. The loss was so great that the commanders of the fleet were afraid the Thessalians might attack them now that they were in such bad shape, and they threw a high stockade around their camp, built from the wreckage. The storm lasted three days. In the end the Magi, sacrificing victims and chanting spells to calm the wind, and also making offerings to Thetis and the Nereids made it stop on the fourth day; or else it died down on its own for some other reason. They sacrificed to Thetis because the Ionians had told them the story that Peleus carried her off from this place, and that the whole headland of Sepias belonged to her and the other Nereids.

192. So the storm had stopped on the fourth day. Meanwhile, on the day after the storm began, the lookouts had run down from the heights of Euboea and told the Greeks everything about the shipwreck. When the Greeks heard it, they first prayed to Poseidon the Savior and poured libations, and then they hurried back to Artemisium, expecting to find only a very few enemy ships left to face them.

193. So they came back a second time and lay with their ships off Artemisium, and from that day to this they have kept calling Poseidon by the name "Savior." Meanwhile, once the wind had dropped and the swell had calmed, the invaders hauled their ships back into the sea and sailed along the coast of the mainland. They rounded the tip of Magnesia and sailed straight into the gulf that leads to Pagasae. In this Magnesian gulf there is a place where Heracles, they say, was left behind by Jason and his companions. They had sent him from the Argo to fetch water, when they were sailing to Aea in Colchis for the Golden Fleece. They meant to cast off from there into the open sea once they had taken on water, and from this the place has come to be called Aphetae, "the Casting-off." This is where Xerxes' fleet now anchored.

194. It happened that fifteen of these ships put out to sea a good deal later than the rest, and they caught sight of the Greek ships at Artemisium. The crews took them for their own ships, so they sailed toward them and fell right among the enemy. Their commander was Sandoces son of Thamasius, the governor of Cyme in Aeolis. Some time before this, King Darius had arrested this Sandoces, who was one of the Royal Judges, and crucified him, because he had taken money to give an unjust verdict. But after Sandoces had been hung up, Darius worked it out and found that the good services he had done the royal house outweighed his offenses. Having found this, and realizing that he himself had acted more hastily than wisely, Darius let him go. So Sandoces escaped King Darius with his life; he did not die but survived. But this time, when he sailed in toward the Greeks, he was not going to escape a second time. When the Greeks saw these ships sailing toward them, they realized the mistake that was being made, put out against them, and captured them easily.

195. On one of these ships they captured Aridolis, tyrant of Alabanda in Caria. On another they took the commander from Paphos, Penthylus son of Demonous. He had brought twelve ships from Paphos, lost eleven of them in the storm off Sepias, and was now captured sailing in toward Artemisium with the one that had survived. After questioning these men about what they wanted to know of Xerxes' forces, the Greeks sent them off in chains to the Isthmus of Corinth.

196. So the invaders' fleet had arrived at Aphetae, all except the fifteen ships that, as I said, Sandoces commanded. Meanwhile Xerxes and the land army had marched through Thessaly and Achaea, and two days earlier had already entered the land of the Malians. In Thessaly he had held a race for his own horses, also testing the Thessalian cavalry, because he had been told it was the best among the Greeks; and in this contest the Greek horses were left far behind. Of the rivers in Thessaly, only the Onochonus did not have enough water for the army to drink. But of the rivers that flow in Achaea, even the largest of them, the Epidanus, held out only barely.

197. When Xerxes reached Alus in Achaea, his guides, who were showing him the way and wanted to tell him everything, told him a local legend about the temple of Zeus Laphystius. They told how Athamas son of Aeolus plotted the death of Phrixus together with Ino, and how after that, by command of an oracle, the Achaeans impose these trials on his descendants. On whoever is the eldest of this family they lay a ban: he is forbidden to enter the town hall, and they themselves keep watch. The Achaeans call the town hall the "Hall of the People." If he does enter it, he may never come out again except to be sacrificed. They also told him that many of those who were going to be sacrificed had before now run away in fear to another country, and that if later on they came back to their own land and were caught, they were put into the town hall. And they described how the man is sacrificed all covered over with wreaths, and in what kind of procession he is led out to the sacrifice. This is done to the descendants of Cytissorus son of Phrixus. When the Achaeans, on the command of an oracle, were making Athamas son of Aeolus a sacrifice to cleanse the land of its guilt, and were just about to sacrifice him, this Cytissorus came from Aea in Colchis and rescued him, and by doing so he brought the anger of the gods down on his own descendants. When Xerxes heard all this and came to the sacred grove, he kept out of it himself and ordered his whole army to do the same. And he showed reverence both to the house of the descendants of Athamas and to their sacred precinct.

198. That is what happened in Thessaly and in Achaea. From there Xerxes went on into the Malian country, along a gulf of the sea where the tide comes in and goes out every day. Around this gulf there is a stretch of flat ground, broad in some places and very narrow in others. High mountains that cannot be crossed surround this flat ground and shut in the whole Malian land; they are called the Rocks of Trachis. The first city on this gulf as you come from Achaea is Anticyra, where the river Spercheus, flowing from the land of the Enianians, runs out into the sea. About two and a quarter miles from this river there is another, called the Dyras, which is said to have sprung up to help Heracles when he was burning. Then about two and a quarter miles from this there is another river, called the Melas.

199. The city of Trachis is just over half a mile from the river Melas. Here, where Trachis lies, is the widest part of this whole district, from the mountains to the sea, for the plain covers about five thousand acres. In the range of mountains that shuts in the land of Trachis there is a gorge to the south of Trachis itself, and through this gorge the river Asopus flows, running along the foot of the mountain.

200. There is another river, the Phoenix, to the south of the Asopus. It is not a large one; it flows down from these mountains into the Asopus. At the river Phoenix is the narrowest place, for the road built there has room for only a single cart track. From the river Phoenix it is about a mile and two-thirds to Thermopylae. Between the river Phoenix and Thermopylae there is a village called Anthela, past which the Asopus flows on into the sea. Around this village there is a wide open space, where a temple of Demeter of the Amphictyons stands, and there are seats for the members of the Amphictyonic Council and a temple of Amphictyon himself.

Chapter 43: Thermopylae

201. So King Xerxes was camped in the district of Trachis, in the land of the Malians, and the Greeks were camped inside the pass. Greeks in general call this place Thermopylae, the "Hot Gates," but the people who live there and in the country around it call it simply Pylae, "the Gates." Both sides, then, were camped in this area. The one side held everything beyond Trachis toward the north wind, and the other held everything on this side of the mainland, toward the south wind and the midday sun.

202. These were the Greeks who waited in this place for the Persian attack. From Sparta came three hundred hoplites. From Tegea and Mantinea came a thousand, half from each city; from Orchomenus in Arcadia, a hundred and twenty; and from the rest of Arcadia, a thousand. That was the Arcadian total. From Corinth came four hundred, from Phlius two hundred, and from Mycenae eighty. Those were the men who came from the Peloponnese. From the Boeotians came seven hundred Thespians and four hundred Thebans.

203. Besides these, the Locrians of Opus had been called up to come with their whole force, and the Phocians with a thousand men. The Greeks themselves had sent for them. Their messengers said that they had come ahead as an advance guard for the rest, that the other allies were expected any day, and that the sea was safely guarded, watched over by the Athenians, the Aeginetans and the others assigned to the fleet. There was nothing to fear, they said, because the one coming to attack Greece was not a god but a man. There was no mortal, and never would be one, whose fortune had not had some evil mixed into it from the moment he was born, and the greatest evils fell to the greatest men. So the man marching against them, being mortal, was bound to fall short of what he expected. When the Locrians and Phocians heard this, they came to Trachis to help the others.

204. These troops had other commanders as well, each from his own city, but the man everyone looked up to most, who led the whole army, was the Spartan Leonidas. He was the son of Anaxandrides, son of Leon, son of Eurycratides, son of Anaxander, son of Eurycrates, son of Polydorus, son of Alcamenes, son of Teleclus, son of Archelaus, son of Hegesilaus, son of Doryssus, son of Leobotes, son of Echestratus, son of Agis, son of Eurysthenes, son of Aristodemus, son of Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus, son of Heracles. He had become king of Sparta when no one expected it.

205. He had two brothers older than himself, Cleomenes and Dorieus, so he had been far from any thought of becoming king. But Cleomenes died without a son, and Dorieus was no longer alive either: he too had come to his end, in Sicily. So the kingship came to Leonidas, both because he was older than Cleombrotus (Cleombrotus was the youngest of Anaxandrides' sons) and because he was married to Cleomenes' daughter. At this time, then, he went to Thermopylae with the three hundred men the law assigned to a king, and he chose men who happened to have sons living. On the way there he also picked up the Thebans I counted when I listed the numbers of the troops; their commander was Leontiades son of Eurymachus. Leonidas was eager to bring these men, out of all the Greeks, for one reason: they had been strongly accused of siding with the Persians. So he called them out to the war because he wanted to find out whether they would send troops with him or openly renounce their alliance with the Greeks. They sent men, but all the while they had something else in mind.

206. The Spartans sent Leonidas and his men out first so that the other allies would see them and join the campaign, and so that the allies would not go over to the Persians themselves on hearing that Sparta was holding back. Later, once they had kept their festival (the Carneia, the Spartans' festival of Apollo, stood in their way), they meant to leave a garrison in Sparta and come quickly to help with their whole force. The rest of the allies had planned to do the same, because the Olympic festival happened to fall at the same time as these events. They did not think the fighting at Thermopylae would be decided so soon, so they sent only their advance guards.

207. That was what they intended. Meanwhile the Greeks at Thermopylae, when the Persians came near the pass, were frightened and discussed retreating from their position. The rest of the Peloponnesians thought it best to go back to the Peloponnese and guard the Isthmus. But the Phocians and Locrians were furious at this idea, and Leonidas voted to stay where they were and at the same time to send messengers to the various cities, telling them to come up and help, since they were too few to drive back the army of the Medes.

208. While they were deliberating, Xerxes sent a mounted scout to see how many they were and what they were doing. He had heard while he was still in Thessaly that a small force had gathered at this place, and that its leaders were Spartans, among them Leonidas, a descendant of Heracles. When the horseman rode up toward their camp, he looked them over, though he could not see their whole army. The men posted inside the wall, which they had rebuilt and were guarding, could not be seen. But he did see the ones outside, whose post was in front of the wall, and as it happened, the Spartans were the ones posted outside at that time. He saw some of the men exercising and others combing their long hair. He was amazed at the sight, and at the same time he took note of their numbers. When he had noted everything exactly, he rode back undisturbed. Nobody tried to chase him; they paid him almost no attention at all. When he got back, he told Xerxes everything he had seen.

209. When Xerxes heard this, he could not grasp the truth, which was that the men were getting ready to die and to kill as many of the enemy as they could. It seemed to him that they were behaving in a way that was simply ridiculous. So he sent for Demaratus son of Ariston, who was in his camp. When Demaratus came, Xerxes asked him about each of these things, wanting to understand what the Spartans were doing. Demaratus said, "You heard me speak about these men once before, when we were setting out against Greece. When you heard me, you laughed at me, because I told you how I saw things would turn out. For me, the greatest goal of all is always to tell you the truth, my king. So hear me now as well. These men have come to fight us for the pass, and that is what they are getting ready to do. They have a custom: whenever they are about to risk their lives, they arrange their hair. But you can be sure of this: if you defeat these men and the rest of them who stayed behind in Sparta, there is no other people on earth that will stand and face you, my king, or raise a hand against you. You are now about to fight the finest kingdom and city among the Greeks, and the best men."

What Demaratus said seemed completely unbelievable to Xerxes, and he asked a second time how, being so few, they would fight against his army. Demaratus answered, "My king, treat me as a liar if things do not turn out the way I say."

210. Saying this did not convince Xerxes. He let four days go by, expecting all the time that they would run away. But on the fifth day, when they had not left but were still there, out of sheer impudence and folly, as he thought, he grew angry and sent the Medes and the Cissians against them, with orders to take them alive and bring them before him. The Medes charged and attacked the Greeks, and many of them fell. Others kept coming up in their place, and they were not driven off, though they lost heavily. They made it clear to everyone, and not least to the king himself, that he had many human beings but few men. This fighting went on all day.

211. When the Medes had been badly mauled, they pulled out of the battle. Then the Persians the king called the "Immortals," whose commander was Hydarnes, took their place and came on to the attack, thinking that they at least would beat the enemy easily. But when these too came to grips with the Greeks, they did no better than the Median troops. They did exactly as badly, because they were fighting in a narrow space, with shorter spears than the Greeks, and could not make use of their numbers. The Spartans, meanwhile, fought in a way worth remembering. Among the other skills they showed, as men who knew everything about fighting facing men who knew nothing, they would turn their backs on the enemy and pretend to run away. The enemy, seeing them run, would chase after them with shouting and clashing of weapons. Then, just as they were being caught, the Spartans would turn and face their pursuers, and in turning they killed countless numbers of Persians. A few of the Spartans themselves fell in these clashes too. So, since the Persians could make no headway in trying for the entrance, though they attacked it by divisions and in every way they could think of, they withdrew.

212. During these attacks, it is said, the king, who was watching, leaped up from his seat three times in fear for his army. That was how they fought that day. On the next day the enemy did no better. They went into battle expecting that, since their opponents were so few, they would be crippled by their wounds and unable to lift a hand against them any longer. But the Greeks were drawn up by companies and by nations, and each fought in its turn, except for the Phocians, who had been posted on the mountain to guard the path. So when the Persians found nothing different from what they had seen the day before, they withdrew from the fight.

213. The king was at a loss about what to do next, and then Ephialtes son of Eurydemus, a Malian, came to talk with him, thinking he would get a very large reward from the king. He told him of the path that leads over the mountain to Thermopylae, and so he brought about the destruction of the Greeks who stayed there. Later, out of fear of the Spartans, he fled to Thessaly. While he was in exile, the Amphictyons' delegates, at a meeting of the Amphictyonic assembly at Pylae, put a price on his head. Some time after that he came back to Anticyra and was killed by Athenades, a man of Trachis. This Athenades killed Ephialtes for a different reason, which I will explain later in my history, but the Spartans honored him for it all the same.

214. That is how Ephialtes was killed afterward. But there is another story told: that it was Onetes son of Phanagoras, a man of Carystus, and Corydallus of Anticyra who showed the Persians the way around the mountain. I don't accept this at all. In the first place, we have to judge by this fact: the delegates of the Greeks did not put a price on the heads of Onetes and Corydallus, but on that of Ephialtes of Trachis, and they surely had the most exact information on the matter. In the second place, we know that Ephialtes went into exile to escape this charge. It is true that Onetes could have known about the path, even though he was not a Malian, if he had spent a lot of time in that country. But it was Ephialtes who led them around the mountain by the path, and so it is Ephialtes I write down as the guilty man.

215. Xerxes was delighted with what Ephialtes promised to do, and at once, full of joy, he sent off Hydarnes and the men under Hydarnes' command. They left the camp at about lamp-lighting time. This path had been discovered by the Malians who live in that country, and after discovering it they had used it to lead the Thessalians against the Phocians, back when the Phocians had walled off the pass and were sheltering behind the wall from their attacks. That is how long ago the Malians had shown that the pass was worth nothing.

216. The path runs like this. It begins at the river Asopus, which flows through the gorge. The mountain and the path have the same name, Anopaea. This Anopaea runs along the ridge of the mountain and ends near the town of Alpeni, the first town of the Locrians on the side toward Malis, and near the rock called Black Buttocks and the Seats of the Cercopes. That is where the path is at its very narrowest.

217. Along this path, then, the Persians crossed the Asopus and marched all night, with the mountains of the Oetaeans on their right and those of the Trachinians on their left. At dawn they reached the top of the mountain. On this part of the mountain, as I explained before, a thousand Phocian hoplites were standing guard, to protect their own country and to hold the path. While the pass below was held by the men I have named, the path over the mountain was guarded by the Phocians, who had volunteered to Leonidas for the job.

218. While the Persians were climbing, the Phocians could not see them, because the whole mountain was covered in oak trees. This is how the Phocians found out that they had made the climb. The day was still, and the Persians made a good deal of noise, as you would expect with leaves lying spread over the ground under their feet. At this the Phocians jumped up and began putting on their armor, and by then the enemy was right on top of them. When the Persians saw men arming themselves, they were astonished. They had expected no one to appear against them, and instead they had run into an armed force. Then Hydarnes, afraid that the Phocians might be Spartans, asked Ephialtes what people these troops belonged to. When he had been told exactly, he drew up the Persians for battle. But the Phocians, struck by thick volleys of arrows, fled at once to the highest peak of the mountain, convinced that the enemy had come to attack them in particular, and there they were ready to die. That was what the Phocians had in mind. But the Persians with Ephialtes and Hydarnes paid no attention to the Phocians and went down the mountain as fast as they could.

219. The Greeks at Thermopylae had their first warning from the seer Megistias. He looked into the sacrificed victims and announced the death that would come to them at dawn. After that, deserters brought the news that the Persians were going around. They reported it while it was still night. Third came the lookouts, who ran down from the heights just as day was breaking. Then the Greeks held a council, and their opinions were divided: some urged that they must not abandon their post, while others argued against it. After this they broke up, and some left and scattered, each to his own city, while others were ready to stay there with Leonidas.

220. It is also said, though, that Leonidas himself sent them away, out of concern that they should not be killed, but that he thought it would not be right for himself and the Spartans with him to leave the post they had come to guard in the first place. I lean more toward this second view. I think that Leonidas saw that the allies had lost heart and did not want to face the danger with him to the end, so he ordered them to leave, but he believed it would be dishonorable for him to go. If he stayed, he would leave a great name behind him, and Sparta's prosperity would not be wiped out. For the Pythia had given the Spartans an oracle, when they consulted her about this war just as it was first starting, saying that either Sparta must be destroyed by the invaders or their king must lose his life. She gave them this answer in hexameter verse, and it went like this:

	As for you who live in the wide spaces of Sparta:
	either your glorious city is sacked by the sons of Perses,
	or, if not, then all within the borders of broad Lacedaemon
	will mourn for a dead king of the line of Heracles.
	Neither the strength of bulls nor the fury of lions will stop him,
	for he has the strength of Zeus; I tell you, he will not be held back
	until he has torn one or the other of these to pieces.

I believe Leonidas had this in mind, and wanted to win glory for himself above all the other Spartans, and so he sent the allies away. I don't think the ones who left went off in such disorder simply because they disagreed.

221. To my mind, one of the strongest pieces of evidence for this is the following. It is well known that Leonidas tried to send away the seer as well, the one who was with this army, Megistias the Acarnanian, who was said to be descended from Melampus. He did not want him to die with them after he had read in the victims what was going to happen to them. But when Megistias was told to go, he would not leave himself. Instead he sent away his son, who was serving with him in the army and was his only child.

222. So the allies who were dismissed did as Leonidas said and left, and only the Thespians and the Thebans stayed behind with the Spartans. Of these, the Thebans stayed against their will, not because they wanted to: Leonidas kept them, treating them as hostages. But the Thespians stayed very willingly. They said they would not go away and abandon Leonidas and the men with him. So they stayed behind and died with them. Their commander was Demophilus son of Diadromes.

223. Meanwhile Xerxes poured libations at sunrise and then waited for a while, until about the hour when the marketplace fills up, in mid-morning, and then he advanced on them. Ephialtes had told him to do this, since the way down the mountain is shorter, and the distance much less, than the way around and up. So the invaders with Xerxes moved forward to the attack. And the Greeks with Leonidas, knowing they were marching out to their deaths, now went much farther out than at first, into the wider part of the pass. On the earlier days, while the wall was being guarded, they had fought by falling back into the narrow part of the pass. But now they met the enemy outside the narrows, and a great many of the invaders fell. Behind the enemy ranks, the officers of the divisions stood with whips in their hands, lashing every man and driving them on and on toward the front. Many of them were pushed into the sea and drowned, and even more were trampled alive by their own side, and no one counted how many died. For the Greeks knew that death was coming for them from the men who were going around the mountain, and so they threw all the strength they had against the enemy, as hard as they could, with no thought for danger, as if possessed by a reckless frenzy.

224. By now most of them had broken their spears in this fighting, as it happened, and they were killing Persians with their swords. In this fighting Leonidas fell, having proved himself a very brave man, and with him other Spartans of note. I learned their names, as men who had shown themselves worthy, and in fact I learned the names of all three hundred. Many notable Persians fell here too, among them two sons of Darius, Abrocomes and Hyperanthes, whose mother was Phratagune, daughter of Artanes. Artanes was King Darius' brother and the son of Hystaspes son of Arsames. When he gave his daughter to Darius in marriage, he gave her his whole estate along with her, because she was his only child.

225. So two of Xerxes' brothers fell fighting here. Meanwhile a great struggle broke out between the Persians and the Spartans over the body of Leonidas, until the Greeks, by sheer courage, dragged it away from the enemy, after driving them back four times. This struggle went on until the men with Ephialtes arrived. When the Greeks learned that they had come, from that moment the fight changed character. They fell back to the narrow part of the road, went past the wall, and took up a position on the little hill there, all together in a body, except for the Thebans. This hill is at the entrance to the pass, where the stone lion in honor of Leonidas now stands. On this spot they defended themselves with daggers, those who still had them, and with their hands and teeth, until the enemy buried them under a hail of missiles. Some of the enemy had followed straight after them and torn down the wall, and others had come around and surrounded them on every side.

226. That is how the Spartans and Thespians proved their courage. But the Spartan Dieneces, they say, proved himself the bravest man of all. He is the one who, they report, made this remark before they joined battle with the Medes. A man of Trachis told him that when the enemy fired their arrows, they blotted out the sun with the sheer number of arrows, so huge was their army. Dieneces was not shaken by this at all. Thinking nothing of the numbers of the Medes, he said that their friend from Trachis had brought them very good news: if the Medes hid the sun, they would be fighting in the shade instead of in the sun.

227. They say that Dieneces the Spartan left behind this saying and others like it to be remembered by. After him, they say, the bravest of the Spartans were two brothers, Alpheus and Maron, the sons of Orsiphantus. Of the Thespians, the man who won the most honor was named Dithyrambus son of Harmatides.

228. The men were buried where they fell. For them, and for those who had died before Leonidas sent the allies away, there is an inscription that reads:

	Here once four thousand men from the Peloponnese
	stood and fought against three million.

That inscription is for them all. For the Spartans alone there is this one:

	Stranger, go tell the Spartans that we lie
	here in this place, obedient to their laws.

That one is for the Spartans. And for the seer, this:

	This is the tomb of the famous Megistias, whom the Medes
	killed where the Spercheus flows, as they crossed the stream.
	He was a seer, and he knew clearly the fate that was coming,
	yet he could not bring himself to leave the leaders of Sparta.

It was the Amphictyons who honored the dead with these inscriptions and memorial pillars, except for the seer's inscription. That one, for the seer Megistias, was inscribed by Simonides son of Leoprepes, because the two were guest-friends.

229. Two of the three hundred, it is said, Eurytus and Aristodemus, could have done either of two things if they had agreed with each other. Leonidas had sent them away from the camp, and they were lying at Alpeni, suffering badly from an eye disease. So they could have come home safe to Sparta together, or, if they did not want to go home, they could have died with the rest. They could have done either one, but they would not agree, and they split. When Eurytus, they say, learned that the Persians had gone around, he asked for his armor, put it on, and ordered his helot to lead him to where the fighting was. When the helot had led him there, he ran away and left, and Eurytus plunged into the thick of the fighting and was killed. But Aristodemus lost his nerve and stayed behind. Now if Aristodemus had been the only one who was ill, and had come home to Sparta, or if both of them had come back together, I don't believe the Spartans would have shown any anger toward them. But as it was, one of them had died, and the other, holding on to the same excuse that the first could also have used, had refused to die. So the Spartans were bound to be furious with Aristodemus.

230. Some say Aristodemus came home safe to Sparta in this way and with the excuse I have described. Others say he had been sent from the camp as a messenger, and though he could have gotten back in time to find the battle still going, he chose not to. He lingered on the road and so saved his life, while the man sent with him as a fellow messenger reached the battle and was killed.

231. When Aristodemus came home to Sparta, he met with disgrace and dishonor. This is the dishonor he suffered: no Spartan would give him a light for his fire or speak to him, and he was disgraced with the name "Aristodemus the Coward."

232. But in the battle at Plataea he made up for all the blame laid on him. It is also reported that another of the three hundred survived, a man named Pantites, who had been sent to Thessaly as a messenger. When he came back to Sparta and found himself in disgrace, they say, he hanged himself.

233. The Thebans, whose commander was Leontiades, stayed with the Greeks and fought against the king's army for a while, because they had no choice. But when they saw the Persian side winning, then, and not before, while the Greeks with Leonidas were hurrying to the little hill, they broke away from them. They held out their hands and went up to the enemy, saying something that was perfectly true: that they were on the Persians' side, that they had been among the first to give earth and water to the king, that they had come to Thermopylae because they had been forced to, and that they were not to blame for the losses the king had suffered. By saying this they saved their lives, since they also had the Thessalians to vouch for what they said. Still, their luck was not good all the way through. Some were killed as they came forward, and when they had come over and the enemy had them in their power, most of them were branded with the royal marks on Xerxes' orders, starting with their commander Leontiades. This was the Leontiades whose son Eurymachus was later killed by the Plataeans, when he led four hundred Thebans and seized the city of Plataea.

234. That is how the Greeks fought at Thermopylae. Then Xerxes sent for Demaratus and questioned him, beginning like this: "Demaratus, you are a good man. I judge that by the truth of what you told me, because everything you said turned out just as you said it would. Now tell me: how many Lacedaemonians are left, and how many of them are like these men in war? Or are they all like this?"

Demaratus said, "My king, there are a great many Lacedaemonians and many cities of them, but you will learn what you want to know. In Lacedaemon there is the city of Sparta, with about eight thousand men. These are all the equals of the men who fought here. The other Lacedaemonians (the free men of the Laconian towns, who are not citizens of Sparta) are not equal to these, but they are good men too."

To this Xerxes said, "Demaratus, how can we beat these men with the least trouble? Come, explain it to us. You know the ways they think and plan, since you were once their king."

235. Demaratus answered, "My king, if you are seriously asking my advice, it is right that I tell you the best course. What if you sent three hundred ships from your fleet to attack the coast of Laconia? There is an island lying near it called Cythera. Chilon, who was a very wise man among us, said that it would be better for the Spartans if that island sank beneath the sea than if it stayed above it. He always expected that something would come from it of exactly the kind I am now describing to you. Not that he knew about your expedition in advance; he feared every expedition of men alike. So let your forces set out from this island and keep the Spartans in fear. While they have a war of their own right on their doorstep, you will have nothing to fear from them; they will not come to the rescue while the rest of Greece is being conquered by your land army. Then once the rest of Greece is subdued, from that moment the Spartan power will be left alone, and so it will be weak. But if you don't do this, I will tell you what you can expect. There is a narrow isthmus leading into the Peloponnese, and in that place you can expect other battles, harder than the ones that have been fought already, because all the Peloponnesians have sworn an alliance against you. But if you do the other thing I spoke of, this isthmus and the cities inside it will come over to you without a battle."

236. After him spoke Achaemenes, Xerxes' brother and the commander of the fleet. He happened to be present for this conversation, and he was afraid Xerxes would be persuaded to do it. "My king," he said, "I see you are listening to the words of a man who envies your good fortune, or is even a traitor to your cause. This is just the sort of temper the Greeks delight in: they envy a man his good luck, and they hate whatever is stronger than they are. Four hundred of our ships have been wrecked, on top of our other misfortunes. If you send away another three hundred from the fleet's station to sail around the Peloponnese, your opponents will be a match for you in a fight. But while the fleet is all together, it is hard for them to deal with, and they will not be a match for you at all. Besides, the whole navy will support the army and be supported by it if they move forward together. But if you split them up, you will be no use to them, and they will be no use to you. My view is rather that you should put your own affairs in good order and not worry about the enemy's: where they will make their stand, what they will do, or how many of them there are. It is enough for them to look out for themselves, and for us to do the same for ourselves. And if the Spartans come out to face the Persians in battle, they certainly will not heal the wound they are suffering from now."

237. Xerxes answered him like this: "Achaemenes, I think you are right, and I will do as you say. But Demaratus says what he believes is best for me, even if his advice loses out to yours. I certainly will not accept what you said, that he is not loyal to my cause. I judge that both by what he said to me before this and by the plain truth. It is true that one citizen envies another for his good fortune and shows his hostility by keeping silent. A citizen whom a fellow citizen consults will not suggest what he really thinks is best, unless he has reached a great height of virtue, and such men are surely few. But a guest-friend is more loyal than anything on earth to a guest-friend who is doing well, and if his friend asks his advice, he will give him the best counsel he can. So, as for this slander against Demaratus, who is my guest-friend, I order everyone to stop it from now on."

238. After saying this, Xerxes went out among the bodies of the dead. When he heard that Leonidas had been the Spartans' king and commander, he ordered his men to cut off his head and crucify him. It has become clear to me from many other pieces of evidence, but from none more strongly than this, that King Xerxes was more furious with Leonidas while he lived than with any other man on earth. Otherwise he would never have committed this outrage against his corpse, because of all the people I know, the Persians are the ones most accustomed to honor men who are brave in war. So the men who were given these orders carried them out.

239. Now I will go back to the point in my story where I left it unfinished. The Spartans had been the first of all to learn that the king was preparing an expedition against Greece. That was how they came to send to the oracle at Delphi, where they were given the answer I reported a little earlier. They learned the news in a strange way. Demaratus son of Ariston, after he had fled to the Persians, was not friendly toward the Spartans, in my opinion, and likelihood supports my opinion. But anyone may guess for himself whether he did what follows out of goodwill or to gloat over them. When Xerxes had decided to march against Greece, Demaratus, who was at Susa and had learned of it, wanted to send word to the Spartans. There was no other way he could get the message to them, since he was in danger of being caught, so he came up with this trick. He took a folding writing tablet and scraped off the wax that covered it. Then he wrote the king's plan on the wood of the tablet, and after that he melted the wax and poured it back over the writing, so that the tablet, carried blank, would not get its bearer into trouble with the guards on the roads. When it reached Sparta, the Spartans could not make anything of it, until finally, as I am told, Gorgo, the daughter of Cleomenes and wife of Leonidas, worked it out herself and suggested a plan: she told them to scrape off the wax, and they would find writing on the wood. They did as she said, found the writing and read it, and then sent word to the rest of the Greeks. This, they say, is how it happened.

Book Eight: Urania

Chapter 44: The Sea Fights off Artemisium, and the Attack on Delphi

1. These were the Greeks who had been assigned to serve in the fleet. The Athenians supplied 127 ships. The Plataeans, moved by courage and eagerness for the cause, joined the Athenians in manning those ships, even though they had no experience of the sea at all. The Corinthians supplied 40 ships and the Megarians 20. The Chalcidians manned 20 ships, which the Athenians provided for them. The Aeginetans supplied 18 ships, the Sicyonians 12, the Spartans 10, the Epidaurians 8, the Eretrians 7, the Troezenians 5, and the Styrians 2. The Ceans supplied 2 ships and 2 fifty-oared galleys. And the Locrians of Opus also came to help the rest with 7 fifty-oared galleys.

2. These were the peoples who joined the expedition to Artemisium, and I have listed them by the number of ships each supplied. So the number of ships gathered at Artemisium, not counting the fifty-oared galleys, was 271. The commander with supreme authority was supplied by the Spartans: Eurybiades son of Eurycleides. This was because the allies said they would not follow the Athenians' lead, and that unless a Spartan was in command they would break up the expedition that was being planned.

3. The reason was that, from the very beginning, even before they sent to Sicily to look for allies, there had been talk that the fleet ought to be put under the Athenians' command. But since the allies opposed this, the Athenians gave way. They cared deeply that Greece should be saved, and they saw that if they quarreled with one another over who should lead, Greece would be lost. And in this they judged rightly: civil strife among people of the same race is worse than a war fought with one mind, by as much as war is worse than peace. Since they understood this, they did not press their claim but gave way, for as long as they badly needed the allies. Their later conduct proved it. For once they had driven the Persians out of their own country and were fighting for the Persians' land rather than their own, they used Pausanias' arrogance as an excuse and took the leadership away from the Spartans. But that happened later.

4. At this point, though, the Greeks who had come to Artemisium saw that a great many ships had put in at Aphetae and that the whole place was full of the enemy's forces. They were struck with fear, because things had turned out for the Persians very differently from what they had expected, and they began to discuss retreating from Artemisium into the interior of Greece. When the Euboeans saw them discussing this, they asked Eurybiades to stay with them for a short while, until they could get their children and their households out of the country. They could not persuade him, so they went elsewhere and persuaded Themistocles, the Athenian commander, with a payment of thirty talents, on condition that the fleet would stay and fight the sea battle in front of Euboea.

5. This is how Themistocles got the Greeks to stay. He gave Eurybiades five talents of the money, pretending that it came from his own pocket. Once Eurybiades had been talked round, Adeimantus son of Ocytus, the Corinthian commander, was the only one of all the rest who still held out. He said he would sail away from Artemisium and would not stay with the others. So Themistocles said to him, with an oath: "You at least will not abandon us. I will give you bigger presents than the king of the Persians would send you for deserting your allies." As he said this, he sent three talents of silver over to Adeimantus' ship. So all of them were won over by gifts and changed their minds; at the same time the Euboeans got what they had asked for, and Themistocles himself made a profit. No one knew that he had kept the rest of the money, and those who got a share of it were fully convinced that it had come from the Athenian state for this purpose.

6. So they stayed at Euboea and fought a sea battle, and this is how it happened. The Persians arrived at Aphetae early in the afternoon. They had already been told before they came that a few Greek ships were stationed around Artemisium, and now they could see them for themselves, so they were eager to attack and see if they could capture them. But they did not think it wise to sail straight at them yet, for fear that the Greeks would see them coming and take to flight, and that darkness would come down on them as they fled. That way, the Persians thought, they would probably get away; whereas by the Persians' reckoning not even the fire-bearer should escape with his life. (The fire-bearer carried the sacred fire for an army's sacrifices and was spared by custom, so "not even the fire-bearer" meant not a single man.)

7. With this in mind they worked out the following plan. From their whole fleet they detached two hundred ships and sent them around Euboea, past Caphereus and around Geraestus to the Euripus. These ships went outside Sciathus so that the enemy would not see them sailing around Euboea. The idea was that this squadron would come up that way and block the Greeks' retreat, while the main fleet advanced on them from the front, and so they would surround them on every side. Having made this plan, they sent off the ships assigned to it. They themselves had no intention of attacking the Greeks that day, or until the ships sailing around showed them the agreed signal that they had arrived. So they were sending these ships around, and meanwhile they were counting the rest of the fleet at Aphetae.

8. While they were counting their ships, this happened. There was in that camp a man from Scione named Scyllias, the best diver of anyone in his time. In the shipwreck off Pelion he had saved a great deal of property for the Persians, and he had also taken a great deal for himself. This Scyllias, it seems, had intended for some time to desert to the Greeks, but until then he had had no chance to do it. How he actually reached the Greeks after this, I can't say for certain, but I am amazed if the story people tell is true. For it is said that he dived into the sea at Aphetae and did not come up until he reached Artemisium, covering a distance of about nine miles underwater. There are several other stories told about this man that look like lies, but some that are true. On this matter, though, let me give it as my opinion that he came to Artemisium in a boat. As soon as he arrived, he told the commanders about the shipwreck and how it had happened, and about the ships that had been sent around Euboea.

9. When the Greeks heard this, they talked it over among themselves. After a good deal of argument, the view that won was that they should stay where they were that day and camp on shore, and then, after midnight had passed, put to sea and go to meet the ships sailing around Euboea. But after this, since no one sailed out to attack them, they waited until late in the afternoon and then sailed out themselves to attack the Persians. They wanted to test the enemy's way of fighting and their maneuver of breaking through the line.

10. When the men in Xerxes' army, and their commanders too, saw the Greeks sailing against them like this with so few ships, they thought they must be out of their minds. They put out to sea themselves, expecting to capture them easily. And it was a reasonable expectation, since they could see that the Greek ships were few, while their own were many times as numerous and sailed better. With this confidence they came around and closed the Greeks in, in the middle. Now some of the Ionians were friendly to the Greeks and were serving in the expedition against their will. When they saw the Greeks being surrounded, they were deeply grieved, convinced that not one of them would get home again, so weak did they think the Greek force was. But those Ionians who were pleased by what was happening competed with one another, each trying to be the first to take an Athenian ship and win gifts from the king. For in the Persian camps there was more talk of the Athenians than of anyone else.

11. When the first signal was given, the Greeks drew up with their prows facing the enemy and their sterns pulled close together in the middle. When the second signal was given, they set to work hard, even though they were penned into a small space and fighting prow to prow. They captured thirty enemy ships, and also Philaon son of Chersis, the brother of Gorgus, king of Salamis in Cyprus, a man of great reputation in the army. The first Greek to capture an enemy ship was an Athenian, Lycomedes son of Aeschraeus, and he received the prize for valor. So they fought this sea battle with neither side winning, until nightfall parted them. The Greeks sailed back to Artemisium and the Persians to Aphetae, after a contest very different from what they had expected. In this sea fight Antidorus of Lemnos was the only one of the Greeks serving with the king who deserted to the Greek side, and for this the Athenians gave him a piece of land on Salamis.

12. When darkness had fallen, even though it was the middle of summer, there came a tremendous downpour of rain that lasted all night, with crashing thunder from Mount Pelion. The bodies of the dead and pieces of wreckage were washed up at Aphetae, where they got tangled around the prows of the ships and knocked against the blades of the oars. The men of the fleet there heard these things and grew afraid. They expected that they were certainly going to die, so many troubles had come upon them. For before they had even had a chance to catch their breath after the shipwreck and the storm off Mount Pelion, they had been hit by a hard sea battle, and after the sea battle by a violent rainstorm, with torrents rushing down to the sea and crashing thunder.

13. That was the kind of night these men had. Meanwhile the ships that had been assigned to sail around Euboea went through that very same night, but it raged much more fiercely against them, because it caught them out on the open sea. And it ended badly for them. The storm and the rain came on them as they sailed, when they were off the "Hollows" of Euboea. They were driven by the wind without knowing where they were being carried, and they were wrecked on the rocks. All this was being done by heaven, so that the Persian force would be brought nearer to the size of the Greek one and would not be so very much larger.

14. So these men were dying around the Hollows of Euboea. Meanwhile, at Aphetae, the Persians were glad to see the day dawn. They kept their ships quiet, content in their sorry state to stay still for the time being. But fifty-three Athenian ships came to reinforce the Greeks. Their arrival put new heart into the Greeks, and at the same time they were encouraged by news that the Persian ships sailing around Euboea had all been destroyed by the storm. So they waited until the same time of day as before, then sailed out and fell on some Cilician ships. After destroying these, they sailed away when darkness came on and went back to Artemisium.

15. On the third day the Persian commanders were furious that such a small number of ships should do them so much damage, and they were afraid of what Xerxes might do. So this time they did not wait for the Greeks to start the battle. They passed the word to one another and put out to sea around midday. Now it so happened that these battles at sea and the battles on land at Thermopylae were fought on the same days. For the men fighting at sea, the whole aim of the struggle was the channel of the Euripus, just as the aim of Leonidas and his men was to guard the pass. So the Greeks urged one another not to let the invaders through into Greece, while the Persians cheered one another on to destroy the Greek fleet and take control of the straits.

16. While Xerxes' fleet was sailing toward them in formation, the Greeks stayed quietly at Artemisium. The Persians arranged their ships in a crescent so as to close them in, and were trying to surround them. Then the Greeks put out to sea and engaged them. In this battle the two sides were about evenly matched. Xerxes' fleet did itself damage because of its sheer size and numbers, since its ships were thrown into confusion and kept running into one another. Even so it held its ground and did not give way, because they were too proud to be put to flight by so few ships. So many Greek ships were destroyed and many men were killed, but many more ships and men on the Persian side. After fighting in this way, they broke off and each went back to its own station.

17. In this sea battle the Egyptians did best of all those fighting for Xerxes. Besides other great feats they performed, they captured five Greek ships together with their crews. On the Greek side, those who did best that day were the Athenians, and of the Athenians Cleinias son of Alcibiades. He was serving with two hundred men and a ship of his own, paying the whole cost out of his own pocket.

18. After they broke off, both sides were glad to hurry back to their anchorages. Once they had separated and come out of the sea battle, the Greeks were in possession of the bodies of the dead and the wrecks of the ships. But they had been badly mauled, and especially the Athenians, half of whose ships were damaged. So they began to discuss retreating into the interior of Greece.

19. Themistocles, however, had come to the conclusion that if the Ionian and Carian peoples could be pried away from the Persian force, the Greeks would be able to beat the rest. The Euboeans were driving their flocks down to the shore at that point, and Themistocles called the generals together. He told them he thought he had a scheme by which he hoped to make the best of the king's allies abandon him. He revealed this much and no more. As for their present situation, he said, this is what they must do. Every one of them should slaughter as many of the Euboeans' sheep and goats as he wanted, since it was better for their own army to have them than the enemy. He also advised each of them to order his men to light a fire. As for the time of their departure, he would see to it that they got back to Greece safely. They were happy to do this, and as soon as they had lit their fires they turned their attention to the flocks.

20. For in fact the Euboeans had ignored the oracle of Bacis as if it meant nothing at all. They had not moved anything out of their country, nor had they laid in any store of food, as people do when they expect a war to come upon them; and so by their own behavior they had brought trouble on themselves. This is how the oracle Bacis gave about these things runs:

	"Watch: when a man of foreign speech yokes the sea with papyrus,
	then make your plans to move the loud-bleating goats out of Euboea."

In the troubles that were on them at this time, or soon to be expected, they had good reason to be sorry that they had paid no attention to these lines.

21. While they were busy with this, the lookout arrived from Trachis. There was a lookout at Artemisium named Polyas, a native of Anticyra, whose job was to report to the men at Thermopylae if the fleet was defeated, and he had a boat fitted out and ready for the purpose. In the same way there was an Athenian with Leonidas, Abronichus son of Lysicles, ready to carry the news to the men at Artemisium in a thirty-oared galley if anything went wrong for the land army. It was this Abronichus who now arrived, and he told them what had happened to Leonidas and his army. When they heard it, they put off their retreat no longer. They set out in the order in which each had been posted, the Corinthians first and the Athenians last.

22. Themistocles, however, picked out the fastest Athenian ships and went around to the places where there was drinking water, cutting messages into the stones there. The Ionians read them when they came to Artemisium the next day. This is what the messages said: "Men of Ionia, you are doing wrong in making war on your forefathers and trying to enslave Greece. The best thing would be for you to come over to our side. But if you cannot do that, then even now stand aside from the fight against us, and ask the Carians to do the same as you. If neither of these is possible, and you are held down by a compulsion too strong to let you revolt, then when we meet in battle hold back on purpose. Remember that you are descended from us, and that our quarrel with the foreigner began in the first place because of you." Themistocles wrote this, I suppose, with two things in mind at once. Either the messages would escape the king's notice and make the Ionians change sides and come over to the Greeks, or, if they were reported to Xerxes and the Ionians accused, they would make him distrust the Ionians, and so he would keep them out of the sea battles.

23. So Themistocles set up these inscriptions. Immediately after this, a man from Histiaea came to the Persians in a boat with the news that the Greeks had pulled out of Artemisium. The Persians did not believe it. They kept the messenger under guard and sent fast ships ahead to look. When these reported that it was true, the whole fleet sailed together to Artemisium, just as daylight was spreading across the sky. They stayed there until midday, and then sailed on to Histiaea. When they arrived, they took the city of Histiaea and overran all the villages along the coast in the district of Ellopia, which is Histiaean territory.

24. While they were there, Xerxes sent a herald to the fleet, after first making arrangements about the bodies of the dead. The arrangements he made beforehand were these. Of all the men of his army who lay dead at Thermopylae, and there were as many as twenty thousand in all, he left about a thousand where they were. The rest he buried in trenches he had dug, covering them with leaves and heaping earth over them, so that the men of the fleet would not see them. When the herald had crossed over to Histiaea, he called an assembly of the whole force and said: "Allies, King Xerxes gives permission to any of you who wish to leave his post and come and see how he fights against those utterly senseless men who expected to defeat the power of the king."

25. When the herald had made this announcement, boats became the scarcest thing of all, so many men wanted to see the sight. They crossed over and walked among the dead bodies, looking at them. Everyone supposed that the men lying there were all Spartans or Thespians, though there were helots too among the bodies they saw. But the men who had crossed over could not fail to see what Xerxes had done, as I mentioned, with the bodies of his own dead. In fact it was enough to make a person laugh: on one side a thousand bodies could be seen lying, while the others lay all gathered together in one place, four thousand of them. They spent that day looking, and the next day they sailed back to the ships at Histiaea, while Xerxes and his army set out on their march.

26. A few deserters from Arcadia had also come over to them, men with no means of living who wanted to be taken into service. The Persians brought these men before the king and asked them about the Greeks and what they were doing; one man asked the questions on behalf of all the rest. The Arcadians told them that the Greeks were holding the Olympic festival and watching contests of athletics and horse racing. The Persian then asked what prize was offered, for which they competed, and they told him about the wreath of olive that is given. At this Tigranes son of Artabanus spoke out a very noble thought, though it got him called a coward by the king. When he heard that the prize was a wreath and not money, he could not keep quiet, but said in front of everyone: "Mardonius, what kind of men are these you have brought us to fight, who compete not for money but for honor!" That is what this man said.

27. Meanwhile, as soon as the disaster at Thermopylae had happened, the Thessalians at once sent a herald to the Phocians. They had always had a grudge against the Phocians, and especially because of the latest defeat they had suffered at their hands. Not many years before the king's expedition, the Thessalians and their allies had invaded Phocis in full force, and the Phocians had beaten them and handled them roughly. The Phocians had been shut up on Mount Parnassus, and with them was a seer, Tellias of Elis. This Tellias came up with a trick for them. He took six hundred men, the best of the Phocians, and whitened them all over with chalk, both the men and their armor. Then he attacked the Thessalians by night, telling the Phocians beforehand to kill every man they saw who was not painted white. The Thessalian sentries saw them first and were terrified, thinking it was some supernatural thing and not what it really was; and after the sentries, the main body of the army panicked too. As a result the Phocians were left in possession of four thousand dead men and their shields. They dedicated half of the shields at Abae and half at Delphi. And from a tenth of the plunder taken in that battle were made the large statues that stand in front of the temple at Delphi, showing the struggle for the tripod; others like them are dedicated as an offering at Abae.

28. That is what the Phocians had done to the Thessalian infantry when it was besieging them. And they had done damage to their cavalry too, past all repair, when it invaded their land. In the pass near Hyampolis they dug a great trench and laid empty wine jars in it. Then they carried earth, spread it on top, and made the place look like the rest of the ground, and waited for the Thessalians to invade. The Thessalians, thinking they would make short work of the Phocians, came charging at full speed and rode straight onto the wine jars, and there their horses' legs were smashed.

29. Since they held a grudge for both of these things, the Thessalians sent a herald with this message: "Phocians, we advise you to start thinking better of it now and to admit that you are not our equals. In the past, among the Greeks, for as long as we chose to be on that side, we were always ranked above you. And now we have so much influence with the Persian that it is in our power to have you stripped of your land and sold into slavery as well. But although we hold all the power, we bear no malice. Pay us fifty talents of silver for it, and we promise to turn aside the dangers that threaten your land."

30. That was the Thessalians' proposal. For the Phocians were the only people in that whole region who were not siding with the Persians, and, as I judge, for no other reason than their feud with the Thessalians. If the Thessalians had supported the Greek cause, it is my opinion that the Phocians would have been on the Persian side. When the Thessalians made this proposal, the Phocians said they would not give the money. They said it was open to them to go over to the Persians just as much as it was to the Thessalians, if they wanted to for other reasons; but they would never of their own free will be traitors to Greece.

31. When this answer was reported, the Thessalians were angry with the Phocians and became guides to the Persian army, showing it the way. From the territory of Trachis they entered Doris. A narrow strip of Dorian land stretches in that direction, a little over three miles wide, lying between Malis and Phocis; in ancient times it was called Dryopis, and this land is the mother country of the Dorians of the Peloponnese. The Persians did not ravage this land of Doris when they entered it, because its people were siding with the Persians, and also because the Thessalians did not want it ravaged.

32. When they passed from Doris into Phocis, though, they did not catch the Phocians themselves. Some of the Phocians had gone up onto the heights of Parnassus. There is a peak of Parnassus, called Tithorea, which stands on its own near the town of Neon and has plenty of room for a great many people, and some of them had carried their goods up there and gone up themselves. But most of them had moved their goods out to the Ozolian Locrians, to the town of Amphissa, which lies above the Crissaean plain. The Persians, however, overran the whole of Phocis, since that is where the Thessalians led the army. Everything they came to on their march they burned or cut down, and they set fire to towns and temples alike.

33. They laid everything waste, advancing this way along the river Cephisus. They burned the town of Drymus, and also these: Charadra, Erochus, Tethronium, Amphicaea, Neon, Pedieis, Triteis, Elatea, Hyampolis, Parapotamii and Abae. At Abae there was a rich temple of Apollo, well stocked with treasuries and offerings, and there was an oracle there then, as there still is now. They plundered this temple and burned it. They also chased down some of the Phocians in the mountains and caught them, and some women died from being raped by many men, one after another.

34. Passing Parapotamii, the Persians came to Panopeus, and from there their army split and went different ways. The largest and strongest part of the army went with Xerxes himself against Athens and entered Boeotia, coming into the territory of Orchomenus. Now the Boeotians as a whole were siding with the Persians, and their towns were being held by Macedonians sent by Alexander, one group assigned to each town. They were holding them with this purpose: to make it plain to Xerxes that the Boeotians were on the Persian side.

35. That was the direction these Persians took. But others, with guides, had set out for the temple at Delphi, keeping Parnassus on their right. All the parts of Phocis they marched through they ravaged; they set fire to the towns of Panopeus, Daulis and Aeolis. The reason they marched that way, split off from the rest of the army, was to plunder the temple at Delphi and hand its treasures over to King Xerxes. Xerxes knew everything of any value that was in it better, I am told, than he knew the things he had left in his own palace at home, since many people kept talking about them, and especially about the offerings of Croesus son of Alyattes.

36. Meanwhile the Delphians had heard of this and were thrown into the utmost fear. In their terror they consulted the oracle about the sacred treasures, whether they should bury them in the ground or carry them away to another country. But the god told them not to touch them, saying that he was able to look after his own property himself. When they heard this, they began to think about themselves. They sent their children and women across the gulf to Achaea, while most of the men climbed up toward the peaks of Parnassus and carried their belongings into the Corycian cave, and others went off for refuge to Amphissa in Locris. In short, all the Delphians had left the town except sixty men and the prophet of the oracle.

37. When the Persians had come close and could see the temple, the prophet, whose name was Aceratus, saw weapons lying in front of the inner shrine. They had been carried out from the sanctuary, and they were sacred arms that no human being was allowed to touch. So he went to announce this omen to the Delphians who were still there. But when the Persians, pressing forward, came level with the temple of Athena Pronaea, still greater omens happened to them than the one before.
