That one was certainly a marvel, that weapons of war should appear of their own accord, laid out in front of the shrine; but what happened right after it deserves to be marveled at above all other wonders. Just as the Persians came level with the temple of Athena Pronaea, thunderbolts fell on them from the sky, and two crags broke off from Parnassus and came crashing down on them with a tremendous roar, falling on many of them. And from the temple of Pronaea came a shout, and a war cry was raised.

38. All these things together threw the Persians into terror. The Delphians, seeing them in flight, came down after them and killed a great many of them, and the survivors fled straight to Boeotia. Those of the Persians who got back reported, so I am told, that besides what I have described they saw other miraculous things too. Two armed men, they said, taller than any human being, followed them, killing and chasing them.

39. The Delphians say these two were the local heroes Phylacus and Autonous, whose sacred precincts are near the temple: Phylacus' right beside the road above the temple of Pronaea, and Autonous' near the Castalian spring, under the peak called Hyampea. What is more, the rocks that fell from Parnassus were still there in my own time, lying in the precinct of Athena Pronaea, where they came to rest after crashing through the Persian ranks. That is how these men left the temple.

Chapter 45: Athens Abandoned, the Acropolis Taken, and the Council at Salamis

40. Meanwhile the Greek fleet, after leaving Artemisium, put in at Salamis at the request of the Athenians. The Athenians asked them to put in at Salamis for this reason: they wanted to move their children and their wives out of Attica to a place of safety, and also to discuss what they ought to do. In their present situation they meant to make new plans, because their expectations had let them down. They had expected to find the Peloponnesians waiting in full force for the invaders in Boeotia. They found nothing of the kind. Instead they were told that the Peloponnesians were building a wall across the Isthmus of Corinth, because they valued the safety of the Peloponnese above everything else and were keeping guard over that, and that they were ready to let everything else go. When they learned this, the Athenians asked the fleet to put in at Salamis.

41. So the others brought their ships to land at Salamis, but the Athenians crossed over to their own country. When they arrived, they made a proclamation that every Athenian should save his children and his household as best he could. Most of them sent their families to Troezen, but some sent them to Aegina and some to Salamis. They were eager to get them out of danger, partly because they wanted to obey the oracle, and especially for another reason, which was this. The Athenians say that a great serpent lives in the temple and guards the Acropolis. They not only say this; they even set out monthly offerings for it, as if it really were there, and the offering is a honey-cake. This honey-cake had always been eaten up before, but at this time it was left untouched. When the priestess announced this, the Athenians left the city much more readily and eagerly than before, since even the goddess, as they believed, had abandoned the Acropolis. Then, when everything they owned had been moved out of danger, they sailed to join the fleet in its camp.

42. When the ships that came from Artemisium had put in at Salamis, the rest of the Greek navy heard of it and came over from Troezen in groups to join them, for they had been ordered beforehand to gather at Pogon, the harbor of the Troezenians. So many more ships were gathered now than had fought at Artemisium, and from more cities. The admiral in command of the whole was the same man as at Artemisium, Eurybiades son of Eurycleides, a Spartan but not of the royal house. But the Athenians supplied by far the largest number of ships, and the ones that sailed best.

43. These were the peoples who joined the muster. From the Peloponnese: the Spartans, with sixteen ships; the Corinthians, with the same number as at Artemisium; the Sicyonians, with fifteen ships; the Epidaurians, with ten; the Troezenians, with five; and the men of Hermione, with three. All of these except the Hermionians are of Dorian and Macednian stock, and they made their last migration from Erineus and Pindus and the land of Dryopis. But the people of Hermione are Dryopians, who were driven out by Heracles and the Malians from the land now called Doris.

44. Those were the Peloponnesians in the fleet. From the mainland outside the Peloponnese came the following. The Athenians supplied more ships than all the rest, one hundred and eighty, and they served alone. The Plataeans did not fight beside the Athenians in the sea battle at Salamis, because when the Greeks were leaving Artemisium and had come near Chalcis, the Plataeans landed on the opposite shore of Boeotia and set about moving their households to safety. So, being busy rescuing their families, they had been left behind. As for the Athenians: in the days when the Pelasgians held what is now called Greece, the Athenians were Pelasgians and were named Cranai. In the time of King Cecrops they came to be called Cecropidae. Then, when Erechtheus took over the power, their name was changed to Athenians; and after Ion son of Xuthus became the Athenians' commander, they were called Ionians after him.

45. The Megarians supplied the same number of ships as at Artemisium. The Ambraciots came to help the rest with seven ships, and the Leucadians with three; these two peoples are Dorians by descent, from Corinth.

46. Of the islanders, the Aeginetans supplied thirty ships. They had other ships manned as well, but they were using those to guard their own land, and they fought in the sea battle at Salamis with the thirty that sailed best. The Aeginetans are Dorians from Epidaurus, and their island used to be called Oenone. After the Aeginetans came the Chalcidians, with the twenty ships they had had at Artemisium, and the Eretrians with their seven; these are Ionians. Next came the Ceans, with the same number as before; they are Ionians by descent, from Athens. The Naxians supplied four ships. Their fellow citizens had sent them out to join the Persians, as the other islanders had done; but they ignored these orders and came over to the Greeks, urged on by Democritus, a man of good standing among the citizens and at that time the captain of a trireme. The Naxians are Ionians, originally from Athens. The Styrians supplied the same ships as at Artemisium, and the men of Cythnus one ship and one fifty-oared galley; both of these peoples are Dryopians. The Seriphians, the Siphnians and the Melians also served with the rest, for they were the only islanders who had not given earth and water to the Persian king.

47. All the peoples named so far lived on the near side of the land of the Thesprotians and the river Acheron. The Thesprotians border on the land of the Ambraciots and the Leucadians, and those two were the ones who came from farthest away to serve. Of all the people who live beyond these limits, the men of Croton were the only ones who came to help Greece in her danger. They sent one ship, and its captain was Phayllus, a man who had won three victories at the Pythian games. The men of Croton are Achaeans by descent.

48. All the others in the fleet supplied triremes, but the Melians, Siphnians and Seriphians supplied fifty-oared galleys. The Melians, who are descended from the Spartans, supplied two; the Siphnians and Seriphians, who are Ionians from Athens, one each. The total number of ships, not counting the fifty-oared galleys, was 378.

49. When the commanders from the cities I have named had gathered at Salamis, they began their discussion. Eurybiades proposed that anyone who wished should give his opinion on where, in the territory the Greeks still controlled, he thought it best to fight a sea battle. Attica had already been given up, and so it was the remaining territory that he was asking about. Most of the speakers agreed on one view: that they should sail to the Isthmus and fight a sea battle there in defense of the Peloponnese. Their reasoning was that if they were beaten in a sea battle at Salamis, they would be trapped and besieged on an island where no help could reach them, but at the Isthmus they could get ashore among their own people.

50. While the commanders from the Peloponnese were arguing this way, an Athenian arrived with news that the invaders had reached Attica and that the whole country was being laid waste with fire. The army that had marched with Xerxes through Boeotia had burned the city of the Thespians, whose people had left it and gone to the Peloponnese, and the city of the Plataeans as well. Now it had come to Athens and was laying waste everything in that region. Xerxes had burned Thespiae and Plataea because the Thebans told him that these cities were not on the Persian side.

51. So the invaders reached Attica three months after crossing the Hellespont, where their march began, counting the one month they spent there while they crossed over into Europe. It was the year when Calliades was archon at Athens, the magistrate who gave the year its name. They took the lower city, which was deserted. Then they found that there were still a few Athenians left in the temple on the Acropolis, either temple stewards or poor men. These men had barricaded the entrance to the Acropolis with doors and a fence of timber and were trying to defend themselves against the enemy's attacks. They had not gone over to Salamis, partly because of their poverty, and also because they thought that they alone had worked out the meaning of the oracle the Pythia had given the Athenians: that the "wooden bulwark" would never be taken. This, they believed, was the safe refuge the oracle meant, and not the ships.

52. So the Persians took up a position on the hill facing the Acropolis, which the Athenians call the Hill of Ares, and besieged them in this way: they wrapped tow, a coarse flax fiber, around their arrows, set it alight, and shot them at the fence. Even so, the Athenians under siege kept on defending themselves, although they had reached the last extremity of distress and their fence had failed them. They would not listen to terms of surrender when the sons of Pisistratus brought them forward. Instead they went on defending themselves and came up with all sorts of devices against the enemy. Among other things, they rolled down great boulders whenever the invaders came near the gates. So for a long time Xerxes was at a loss, unable to take them.

53. In the end, however, a way in appeared for the invaders out of their difficulties, since according to the oracle the whole mainland of Attica was fated to come under the Persians. This is how it happened. On the front side of the Acropolis, but behind the gates and the road leading up to the entrance, there was a spot where no one was on guard, and where no one would have thought any man could climb up. Here, by the shrine of Aglaurus the daughter of Cecrops, some men climbed up, even though the place is a sheer cliff. When the Athenians saw that they had climbed up onto the Acropolis, some of them threw themselves down from the wall and died, while others took refuge in the inner chamber of the temple. The Persians who had climbed up went first to the gates and opened them, and then they killed the suppliants. When they had killed them all, they plundered the temple and set fire to the whole Acropolis.

54. Then Xerxes, now in complete possession of Athens, sent a messenger on horseback to Susa to report his success to Artabanus. On the day after he sent the herald, he called together the Athenian exiles who were traveling with him and told them to go up to the Acropolis and offer sacrifices in their own way. Perhaps he had seen some vision in a dream that made him give this order, or perhaps he had misgivings because he had set fire to the temple. The Athenian exiles did as they were told.

55. Now I will explain why I have mentioned this. On this Acropolis there is a temple of Erechtheus, who is said to have been born from the Earth, and in it there is an olive tree and a pool of salt water. According to the story the Athenians tell, Poseidon and Athena set these there as tokens of their claims when they were competing for the land. It so happened that this olive tree was burned by the invaders along with the rest of the temple. But on the day after the fire, when the Athenians whom the king had ordered to sacrifice went up to the temple, they saw that a shoot about a foot and a half long had sprung up from the stump. They reported this.

56. Meanwhile the Greeks at Salamis, when they heard what had happened to the Acropolis of the Athenians, were so badly shaken that some of the commanders did not even wait for a vote on the question that had been put. They rushed to their ships and began hoisting their sails, meaning to get away fast. Those who stayed behind finally decided to fight at sea in defense of the Isthmus. Night came on, and they broke up from the council and went to their ships.

57. When Themistocles reached his ship, an Athenian named Mnesiphilus asked him what they had decided. When Themistocles told him that they had resolved to take the ships to the Isthmus and fight a sea battle in defense of the Peloponnese, Mnesiphilus said: "Then if they sail away from Salamis with the ships, you won't fight any more sea battles for your country at all. They will all head off to their own cities, and neither Eurybiades nor anyone else will be able to hold them back or stop the fleet from breaking up. Greece will be ruined by bad decisions. If there is any way at all, go and try to undo what has been decided. Perhaps you can persuade Eurybiades to change his plans and stay here."

58. Themistocles liked this advice very much. Without a word in reply, he went to Eurybiades' ship. When he got there, he said that he wanted to discuss a matter of common concern with him, and Eurybiades told him to come aboard and say whatever he wished. Then Themistocles sat down beside him and repeated everything he had heard Mnesiphilus say, passing it off as his own thinking and adding a good deal more. At last, by pressing hard, he persuaded Eurybiades to come off his ship and call the commanders together in council.

59. When they had gathered, before Eurybiades could even put forward the business he had called the commanders together for, Themistocles began to speak at length and with great force, since he was very eager to get his way. While he was speaking, the Corinthian commander, Adeimantus son of Ocytus, said: "Themistocles, at the games, those who start before the signal are beaten with rods." Themistocles defended himself: "Yes, but those who are left behind at the start never win the crown."

60. This time he answered the Corinthian mildly. And to Eurybiades he did not now say any of what he had said before, that if they sailed from Salamis they would scatter in all directions, because it would not be proper for him to accuse the allies to their faces. Instead he took a different line of argument. "It is in your power now to save Greece," he said, "if you will take my advice and stay here and fight a sea battle here, and not take the advice of those among these men who tell you to move the ships to the Isthmus. Listen to both plans and compare them. If you fight at the Isthmus, you will be fighting in the open sea, and that is the last place it suits us to fight, since our ships are heavier and fewer than the enemy's. Second, you will lose Salamis and Megara and Aegina, even if we succeed in everything else. For their army will come along with their fleet, and so you will lead them to the Peloponnese yourself and put all of Greece at risk.

"But if you do what I say, you will find these advantages in it. First, if we fight in narrow waters with few ships against many, and the battle goes the way we can reasonably expect, we will have much the better of it. Fighting at sea in a narrow space works in our favor; fighting in a wide-open space works in theirs. Then again, Salamis will be saved, where our children and wives have been taken for safety. And there is this to be gained as well, which is what you all care about most: by staying here you will be fighting for the Peloponnese just as much as if the battle were at the Isthmus, and, if you are wise, you will not lead the enemy to the Peloponnese. And if what I expect comes true and we win with our ships, the invaders will not come to you at the Isthmus or advance any farther than Attica. They will retreat in disorder, and we will gain by saving Megara and Aegina and Salamis, where an oracle actually tells us we will defeat our enemies. When men make reasonable plans, reasonable results generally follow. But when they do not, heaven does not usually choose to go along with human plans."

61. When Themistocles said this, Adeimantus the Corinthian attacked him a second time. He told him to be quiet, since he had no country, and urged Eurybiades not to put to the vote the proposal of a man who was a citizen of no city. Themistocles, he said, could offer opinions to the council if he could show that he had a city, but not otherwise. He made this objection because Athens had been taken and was held by the enemy. At that Themistocles said many harsh things about him and about the Corinthians as well. He declared that he and his people really did have a city and a country greater than the Corinthians', as long as they had two hundred ships fully manned, for none of the Greeks could beat off the Athenians if they came to attack them.

62. Having made this point, he turned to Eurybiades and spoke still more urgently: "If you stay here, and by staying here prove yourself a brave man, all is well. If not, you will bring about the ruin of Greece, for all our strength in this war depends on the ships. No, do as I advise. But if you will not, we will pick up our households at once and sail to Siris in Italy, which has been ours since ancient times, and the oracles say we are destined to settle it. And you, when you are left alone, robbed of allies like us, will remember what I said."

63. When Themistocles said this, Eurybiades was persuaded to change his mind. In my opinion, he changed it mainly because he was afraid the Athenians would leave them if he took the ships to the Isthmus; for if the Athenians abandoned them and left, the rest would no longer be strong enough to fight the enemy. So he chose this plan: to stay where they were and decide the matter there with a sea battle.

64. So the men at Salamis, after their skirmish of words, began preparing for a sea battle there, since Eurybiades had decided on it. As day came on, just as the sun rose, an earthquake was felt both on land and at sea. They resolved to pray to the gods and to call on the sons of Aeacus to come and help them. And as they had resolved, so they did. They prayed to all the gods, and then they called Ajax and Telamon to their aid from Salamis itself, where the fleet was, and they sent a ship to Aegina to bring Aeacus himself and the other sons of Aeacus.

65. Dicaeus son of Theocydes, an Athenian who was an exile and had won a high reputation among the Persians at this time, told the following story. At the time when the land of Attica, deserted by the Athenians, was being ravaged by Xerxes' army, he happened to be with Demaratus the Spartan in the Thriasian plain. He saw a cloud of dust rising from Eleusis, as if raised by a crowd of about 30,000 men, and the two of them wondered what men could be raising it. Then all at once they heard the sound of voices, and Dicaeus recognized the sound as the mystic cry "Iacchus!" But Demaratus, who knew nothing of the sacred rites held at Eleusis, asked him what it was that was making the sound. Dicaeus said: "Demaratus, some great disaster is surely about to strike the king's army. It is perfectly plain, since Attica is deserted, that whatever is making this sound comes from the gods, and that it is going from Eleusis to help the Athenians and their allies. If it comes down on the Peloponnese, then the king himself and his army on the mainland are in danger. But if it turns toward the ships at Salamis, the king is in danger of losing his fleet. The Athenians celebrate this festival every year for the Mother and the Daughter, and any of them who wishes, and any of the other Greeks too, is initiated into the mysteries. The sound of voices you hear is the cry 'Iacchus!' that they raise at this festival." To this Demaratus said: "Keep quiet, and don't tell this story to anyone else. If these words of yours are reported to the king, you will lose your head, and neither I nor any other man on earth will be able to save you. So keep quiet, and the gods will take care of this expedition." That was Demaratus' advice. After the cloud of dust and the sound of voices, a mist rose into the air and was carried toward Salamis, to the camp of the Greeks. And so, Dicaeus said, they understood that Xerxes' fleet was doomed to be destroyed. That was the account Dicaeus son of Theocydes gave, calling on Demaratus and others as witnesses.

66. Meanwhile the men assigned to Xerxes' fleet, after viewing the disaster of the Spartans at Trachis, crossed over from there to Histiaea. They waited three days, then sailed through the Euripus, and in another three days they had reached Phalerum. In my judgment they were no fewer in number, by land and by sea, when they attacked Athens than when they had arrived at Sepias and Thermopylae. For against those of them who died in the storm, and those killed at Thermopylae and in the sea battles at Artemisium, I set those who had not yet joined the king at that time: the Malians, Dorians, Locrians and Boeotians (who joined him in full force, except the Thespians and Plataeans), and also the people of Carystus, Andros and Tenos, along with all the other islanders except the five cities whose names I mentioned before. For the farther the Persian king advanced into the heart of Greece, the more peoples went along with him.

67. So all these came to Athens except the Parians, who had stayed behind at Cythnus to wait and see how the war would turn out. When all the rest had come to Phalerum, Xerxes himself came down to the ships, wanting to visit them and to hear the views of the men who sailed in them. When he had arrived and taken his seat in a prominent place, the tyrants of the various nations and the commanders of the squadrons were summoned from their ships and came before him. They took their seats in the order of rank the king had given each of them: first the king of Sidon, then the king of Tyre, and after them the rest. When they were seated in order, Xerxes sent Mardonius to test each one by asking whether he should fight a sea battle.

68. So Mardonius went around asking them, beginning with the king of Sidon. All the others gave the same opinion, advising him to fight at sea. But Artemisia said this: "Mardonius, please tell the king this from me, from one who has proved herself not the worst in the sea battles fought off Euboea and has done deeds as good as anyone's. Master, it is right for me to tell you the opinion I really hold, and to say what I happen to think is best for your cause. And this is what I say: spare your ships and do not fight a sea battle. Their men are as much stronger than your men at sea as men are stronger than women. Why must you take the risk of a sea battle at all? Don't you hold Athens, the city you set out on this campaign to take? And don't you hold the rest of Greece? No one stands in your way. Those who did stand against you got what they deserved.

"Now I will tell you how I think things will turn out for your enemies. If you do not rush into a sea battle, but keep your ships here close to land, and either stay here yourself or even advance into the Peloponnese, then what you came to do, Master, will easily be done. The Greeks cannot hold out against you for long. You will soon scatter them, and they will run off to their own cities. For they have no food with them on this island, as I hear, and if you march your army against the Peloponnese, it is not likely that the men who came from there will stay put. They will have no wish to fight a battle in defense of Athens.

"But if you rush to fight at once, I am afraid that damage to the fleet may bring ruin on the army as well. And consider this too, my king: good men tend to have bad servants, and bad men good ones. You are the best of all men, and you have bad servants, the ones who are counted as your allies: the Egyptians, the Cyprians, the Cilicians and the Pamphylians, who are no use at all."

69. When she said this to Mardonius, those who were friendly to Artemisia were upset at her words, thinking she would be punished by the king for urging him not to fight at sea. But those who envied and resented her, because she had been honored above all the allies, were delighted by her opposition, thinking that now she was finished. But when the opinions were reported to Xerxes, he was very pleased with Artemisia's. He had thought highly of her even before, and now he praised her still more. Even so, he gave orders to follow the advice of the majority. He thought that off Euboea his men had held back deliberately because he was not there himself, whereas now he had arranged to watch them as they fought the sea battle.

70. So when the order was passed to put out to sea, they took their ships out toward Salamis and quietly drew them up in their stations along the shore. There was not enough daylight left for them to fight, since night had come on, but they made their preparations to fight the next day. The Greeks, meanwhile, were gripped by fear and dismay, especially the ones from the Peloponnese. They were dismayed because they were staying at Salamis to fight for the land of the Athenians, and if they were beaten they would be cut off and trapped on an island, leaving their own land unguarded. And in fact the invaders' army was marching toward the Peloponnese that very night.

71. Yet every possible step had been taken to keep the invaders from getting into the Peloponnese by land. As soon as the Peloponnesians heard that Leonidas and his men had died at Thermopylae, they hurried together from their cities and took up a position at the Isthmus. Their commander was Cleombrotus son of Anaxandrides, the brother of Leonidas. Once in position at the Isthmus, they destroyed the Scironian Road, and after that, having agreed on it among themselves, they began to build a wall across the Isthmus. There were tens of thousands of them, and every man joined in the work, so it went forward fast. Stones and bricks and timbers and baskets full of sand were carried to it without a break, and the men who had come to help never stopped working, night or day.

72. These were the Greeks who came in full force to the Isthmus to defend their country: the Spartans, the Arcadians of every district, the Eleans, the Corinthians, Sicyonians, Epidaurians, Phliasians, Troezenians and Hermionians. These were the ones who came to help Greece in her danger and who were anxious for her. The rest of the Peloponnesians did not care. And by this time the Olympic and Carnean festivals were already over.

73. Seven peoples live in the Peloponnese. Two of them are native to the soil and are settled now where they lived in ancient times: the Arcadians and the Cynurians. One people, the Achaeans, never left the Peloponnese, but long ago they did leave their own land, and they now live in land that was not theirs. The remaining four peoples came in from outside: the Dorians, the Aetolians, the Dryopians and the Lemnians. The Dorians have many famous cities; the Aetolians have Elis alone; the Dryopians have Hermione and Asine, which is opposite Cardamyle in Laconia; and the Lemnians have all the Paroreatae. The Cynurians, who are native to the soil, seem to be the only Ionians among them, but they have become Dorians completely, through being ruled by the Argives and through the passing of time. They are the people of Orneae and the countryside around it. Of these seven peoples, all the cities except the ones I listed just now stood aside and did nothing. And if I may speak freely, by standing aside they were in fact taking the Persians' side.

74. So the men at the Isthmus were throwing themselves into the work I have described, since they were now running a race with their very survival at stake, and they did not expect the fleet to win any brilliant success. The men at Salamis, though they heard about this work, were dismayed all the same, fearing not so much for themselves as for the Peloponnese. For a while they talked about it privately, one man muttering to the next, and they wondered at Eurybiades' folly. But in the end it broke out into the open. So a meeting was held, and much was said on the same points as before. Some said they ought to sail away to the Peloponnese and risk everything in its defense, rather than stay and fight for a land the enemy had already captured. But the Athenians, Aeginetans and Megarians urged that they should stay where they were and defend themselves.

75. Then, when Themistocles saw that the Peloponnesians were about to outvote him, he slipped out of the meeting unnoticed. Once outside, he sent a man in a boat to the Persian camp, with instructions on what to say. This man's name was Sicinnus. He was a servant of Themistocles and tutor to his children. After these events Themistocles had him enrolled as a citizen of Thespiae, when the Thespians were admitting new citizens, and made him a rich man. At this time Sicinnus came in the boat and said this to the commanders of the invaders: "The commander of the Athenians has sent me secretly, without the knowledge of the other Greeks. As it happens, he favors the king's cause and would rather see your side win than the Greeks. He sent me to tell you that the Greeks are panic-stricken and are planning to run away. Now you have the chance to do a splendid deed, if you do not let them escape. They are not of one mind with one another, and they will not stand up to you. Instead you will see them fighting a sea battle against each other, those on your side against those who are not."

76. Having delivered this message, Sicinnus went away. The commanders believed the message, and first they landed a large force of Persians on the little island of Psyttalea, which lies between Salamis and the mainland. Then, at midnight, they moved the western wing of their fleet out to sea and around toward Salamis, and the ships stationed around Ceos and Cynosura also put out, and they filled the whole strait with their ships as far as Munychia. They put their ships out for this reason: so that the Greeks could not even escape, but would be trapped at Salamis and pay the price for the battles at Artemisium. And they landed Persians on the little island called Psyttalea for this reason: when the battle came, they could save the men of one side and kill those of the other, since that was where the men and the wrecks were most likely to be washed ashore, for the island lay right in the path of the coming battle. They did all this in silence, so that the enemy would not find out.

77. So they made these preparations in the night, without getting any sleep at all. As for oracles, I cannot argue that they are not true. I have no wish to try to discredit them when they speak clearly, when I look at things like the one that follows:

	"But when they bridge with their ships the sacred shore of the goddess,
	Artemis of the golden sword, and you, sea-washed Cynosura,
	driven by a frenzied hope, after plundering shining Athens,
	then divine Justice will quench Excess, the firstborn of Insolence,
	raging to overturn all things and panting fiercely for bloodshed.
	Bronze will clash with bronze, and Ares will redden the sea,
	staining its waves with blood. Then a day of freedom for Greece
	comes from far-seeing Zeus and from Victory, lady and mother."

When I look at things like this, and when Bacis speaks so clearly, I do not dare to raise objections about oracles myself, and I will not accept them from others.

78. Meanwhile there was fierce argument among the commanders at Salamis. They did not yet know that the invaders were surrounding them with their ships, but thought they were still in the positions they had seen them in by day.

79. While the commanders were quarreling, Aristides son of Lysimachus crossed over from Aegina. He was an Athenian who had been ostracized by the people, that is, banished by their vote. From what I hear of his character, I believe he was the best and most honorable man in Athens. This man came to the council and called Themistocles out. Themistocles was not his friend; he was his bitterest enemy. But because of the size of the present danger, Aristides put all that out of his mind and called him out, because he wanted to talk with him. He had already heard that the Peloponnesians were pressing to take the ships away to the Isthmus. So when Themistocles came out to him, Aristides said this: "At any other time when the chance arises, and especially at this moment, we ought to compete with each other over which of us can do more for our country. I tell you that it makes no difference now whether the Peloponnesians say much or little about sailing away from here. I have seen it with my own eyes, and I tell you that now, even if the Corinthians and Eurybiades himself want to sail out, they won't be able to. We are surrounded by the enemy. So go in and tell them this."

80. Themistocles answered: "That is very good advice, and the news you bring is good too, since you have come and seen with your own eyes what I wanted to happen. You should know that what the Persians are doing was done at my suggestion. When the Greeks would not come to a battle of their own free will, they had to be brought to it against their will. But since you have come with good news, report it to them yourself. If I tell them, they will think I have made it up, and I won't convince them; they will think the enemy is doing no such thing. So come forward and speak yourself, and tell them how things stand. When you have told them, if they believe you, that will be best. But if they don't believe it, it will make no difference to us, since they won't be able to run away any longer if we are surrounded on all sides, as you say."

81. So Aristides came forward and told them. He said that he had come from Aegina and had barely slipped past the blockading ships without being seen, since the whole Greek camp was surrounded by Xerxes' ships, and he advised them to get ready to defend themselves. After saying this he withdrew. And again an argument broke out among them, because most of the commanders did not believe the report.

82. While they were still doubting, a trireme manned by men of Tenos arrived, deserting from the enemy. Its captain was Panaetius son of Sosimenes, and it brought them the whole truth. For this deed the Tenians were inscribed at Delphi on the tripod, among those who had defeated the invaders. With this ship that deserted at Salamis, and the Lemnian ship that had deserted earlier and come over at Artemisium, the Greek fleet was brought up to a full 380 ships. Before this it had been two ships short of that number.

Chapter 46: The Battle of Salamis, and Xerxes Turns for Home

83. So the Greeks, believing what the Tenians had told them, got ready for a sea battle. As dawn broke they called an assembly of the men who fought on board the ships, and speeches were made. Themistocles' speech was the finest of all. The heart of it was a setting-out of everything that is better against everything that is worse, among all the things that arise in human nature and the human condition. He urged them to choose the better, and with that he wound up his speech and ordered them to board their ships. So they began to board. Meanwhile the trireme arrived from Aegina, the one that had gone off to bring the sons of Aeacus.

84. Then the Greeks put out with all their ships, and while they were still putting out from shore the enemy attacked them at once. Most of the Greeks began backing water and were about to run their ships aground. But Ameinias of Pallene, an Athenian, put out with his ship and rammed one of the enemy's. His ship got locked together with it and the men could not break free, so the others joined the fight to help Ameinias. That is how the Athenians say the battle began. But the Aeginetans say that the ship that had gone to Aegina to bring the sons of Aeacus was the one that started the fight. There is also a story that a phantom woman appeared to them and urged them to fight, so loudly that the whole Greek force heard her. But first she scolded them: "Madmen, how much farther are you going to back water?"

85. Facing the Athenians were the Phoenicians, who held the wing toward Eleusis and the west. Facing the Spartans were the Ionians, who held the wing that stretched east toward Piraeus. A few of the Ionians fought badly on purpose, as Themistocles had urged them to, but most did not. I could give the names of many ship captains who destroyed Greek ships, but I will use none of them except Theomestor son of Androdamas and Phylacus son of Histiaeus, both of them Samians. I mention these two and not the rest for this reason: because of this deed the Persians made Theomestor tyrant of Samos, and Phylacus was entered on the list of the king's benefactors and given a great deal of land as a reward. In the Persian language the king's benefactors are called orosangae.

86. So it went with these two. But most of the king's ships at Salamis were disabled, destroyed some by the Athenians and some by the Aeginetans. For the Greeks fought in good order, each ship in its place, while the enemy had lost all order and did nothing with any plan, so it was likely that things would turn out much as in fact they did. And yet on this day the king's men were far braver than they had been in the fighting off Euboea. Every one of them fought hard out of fear of Xerxes, each man thinking that the king was watching him in particular.

87. As for the rest, I cannot speak of each one separately or say exactly how each man fought, whether foreigner or Greek. But in Artemisia's case, this is what happened, and it raised her even higher in the king's esteem than before. When the king's side had fallen into great confusion, at that moment Artemisia's ship was being chased by an Athenian ship. She could not escape, because ahead of her were other ships of her own side, and her ship, as it happened, was the one nearest the enemy. So she decided what to do, and it turned out very much to her advantage that she did it. With the Athenian ship hard after her, she charged at full speed into a ship of her own side, crewed by Calyndians and carrying Damasithymus, the king of the Calyndians himself. Now it may be true that she had quarreled with him earlier, while they were still at the Hellespont. Even so, I cannot say whether she did this on purpose, or whether the Calyndian ship just happened to fall in her path. But she rammed it and sank it, and her luck brought her a double gain. First, the captain of the Athenian ship, seeing her ram a ship of the king's fleet, turned away and went after others. He supposed that Artemisia's ship was either Greek or had deserted from the enemy and was fighting for the Greeks.

88. That, then, was her first piece of luck: she escaped and was not destroyed. The second was that, though she had done harm to her own side, the very same act won her a great reputation with Xerxes. For it is said that the king, watching the battle, noticed her ship ramming the other one, and one of the men beside him said: "Master, do you see how well Artemisia is fighting? She has just sunk an enemy ship!" He asked whether it was really Artemisia who had done it, and they said it was, since they knew her ship's ensign very well. And they were sure that the ship she had destroyed was one of the enemy's. Among the other things that went her way, as I have said, there was this too: not one man of the Calyndian ship's crew survived to accuse her. And Xerxes, they say, answered what had been said to him with these words: "My men have become women, and my women men." That, they say, is what Xerxes said.

89. Meanwhile, in this struggle, the commander Ariabignes was killed, the son of Darius and brother of Xerxes, and many other notable men of the Persians and Medes and of the allies were killed too. Of the Greeks only a few died. Since the Greeks knew how to swim, those whose ships were destroyed and who were not killed in hand-to-hand fighting swam across to Salamis. But most of the king's men could not swim, and they died in the sea. The greatest number died when the front ships turned to run. The ships stationed behind were trying to push through to the front so that they too could do some brave deed for the king to see, and they ran into their own side's ships as those fled.

90. It also happened, in all this confusion, that some of the Phoenicians whose ships had been destroyed came to the king and accused the Ionians. They said their ships had been lost because of the Ionians, who had betrayed the cause. But as it turned out, not only did the Ionian commanders not lose their lives, but the Phoenicians who accused them got the reward I will now tell. While they were still speaking, a Samothracian ship rammed an Athenian ship. As the Athenian ship was sinking, an Aeginetan ship came at the Samothracian and ran it down. Then the Samothracians, who were skilled javelin-throwers, hurled their javelins and cleared the fighting men off the ship that had wrecked theirs, then boarded it and took it over. This saved the Ionians from punishment. For when Xerxes saw them do so great a deed, he turned on the Phoenicians, since he was bitterly upset and ready to find fault with everyone, and ordered their heads cut off, so that men who had been cowards themselves would not accuse their betters. Xerxes was sitting at the foot of the mountain opposite Salamis called Aegaleos, and whenever he saw any man of his own side do a brave deed in the battle, he asked who had done it, and his scribes wrote down the captain's name, with his father's name and his city. Besides this, Ariaramnes, a Persian who was there and a friend of the Phoenicians, shared their fate. So they went off to deal with the Phoenicians.

91. Meanwhile, as the king's ships turned to run and were sailing out toward Phalerum, the Aeginetans lay in wait for them in the strait and did deeds worth remembering. While the Athenians, in the confusion and uproar, were disabling both the ships that fought back and the ones that fled, the Aeginetans were destroying the ones trying to sail away. Whenever any ship escaped the Athenians, it ran at full speed straight into the Aeginetans.

92. Then two ships met: Themistocles' ship, which was chasing an enemy ship, and that of Polycritus son of Crius, the Aeginetan. Polycritus had just rammed a ship of Sidon. It was the same ship that had captured the Aeginetan guard ship stationed ahead at Sciathus, the one that carried Pytheas son of Ischenous. The Persians had kept Pytheas on board their ship, all cut to pieces as he was, because they marveled at his courage. So now the Sidonian ship was captured with Pytheas on it, along with the Persians I mentioned, and that is how Pytheas came home safe to Aegina. When Polycritus looked at the Athenian ship, he recognized the ensign of the admiral's ship. He shouted across at Themistocles, mocking him about the charge that the Aeginetans had gone over to the Persians, and taunting him with it. Polycritus flung this taunt at Themistocles right after he had rammed the Sidonian ship. Meanwhile the enemy ships that had escaped destruction fled to Phalerum, to be under the protection of the land army.

93. In this sea battle, of all the Greeks the Aeginetans won the highest praise, and after them the Athenians. Of the individual men, the most praised were the Aeginetan Polycritus and two Athenians, Eumenes of Anagyrus and Ameinias of Pallene, the one who had chased Artemisia. If Ameinias had known that Artemisia was sailing in that ship, he would not have stopped until he had either taken her or been taken himself. For the Athenian captains had been given orders about her, and a prize of 10,000 drachmas was offered besides to whoever took her alive, since they thought it an outrage that a woman should make war on Athens. But she, as I said before, had escaped. And the others whose ships had escaped destruction were at Phalerum too.

94. As for Adeimantus, the Corinthian commander, the Athenians say that right at the start, when the ships were closing for battle, he was seized with panic and terror, hoisted his sails and ran away. When the Corinthians saw their admiral's ship running away, they left too. After this, as the story goes, when they had fled as far as the temple of Athena Sciras on Salamis, a light boat met them, sent by the hand of heaven. No one was ever found who had sent it, and it came up to the Corinthians at a time when they knew nothing of how things stood with the fleet. This is why people guess the hand of heaven was in it. For when the boat came near the ships, the men in it said: "Adeimantus, you have turned your ships around and taken to flight, deserting the Greeks. But they are winning, and getting the better of their enemies just as they hoped." When they said this, Adeimantus did not believe it, so they spoke a second time and said that he could take them as hostages and kill them if the Greeks turned out not to be winning. So he turned his ship back, he and the others with him, and they reached the fleet when the work was already done. That is the story the Athenians spread about them. The Corinthians, however, do not accept it. They hold that they were among the first in the fighting, and the rest of Greece backs them up.

95. Aristides son of Lysimachus, the Athenian, whom I mentioned a little earlier as a very good man, did this in the uproar around Salamis. He took a number of the Athenian-born hoplites who had been posted along the shore of Salamis, landed with them on the island of Psyttalea, and they killed all the Persians on that islet.

96. When the sea battle was over, the Greeks towed back to Salamis all the wrecks that happened to be still in the area, and held themselves ready for another sea battle, since they expected the king to use the ships he had left that were undamaged. But the west wind caught many of the wrecks and carried them to the beach in Attica called Colias. So it fulfilled not only all the rest of the oracle spoken about this sea battle by Bacis and Musaeus, but also, and especially as to the wrecks washed up there, a line spoken many years before in an oracle by Lysistratus, an Athenian prophet, which none of the Greeks had understood:

	The women of Colias will roast their barley over fires of oars.

This was to come true after the king had marched away.

97. When Xerxes understood the disaster that had happened to him, he was afraid that one of the Ionians might suggest to the Greeks, or that they might think of it themselves, to sail to the Hellespont and break up the bridges. Then he would be cut off in Europe and in danger of being destroyed completely. So he began to think about running away. But he did not want his plan to be noticed by the Greeks or by his own side. So he tried to build a causeway across to Salamis, and he lashed together Phoenician merchant ships to serve him as both a bridge and a wall, and he made preparations for war as if he meant to fight another battle at sea. Everyone else who saw him doing this was sure he was in earnest and meant to stay and fight. But Mardonius was not fooled: he saw what all this really meant, since long experience had taught him exactly how the king thought.

98. While Xerxes was doing this, he sent a messenger to Persia to announce the disaster that had come on them. Nothing mortal travels faster than these messengers, so cleverly have the Persians devised the system. For they say that however many days the whole journey takes, that many horses and men are posted at intervals along the road, one man and one horse for each day's journey. Neither snow nor rain nor heat nor the dark of night keeps them from finishing their appointed stage at top speed. The first rider delivers the message he carries to the second, and the second to the third, and from there it passes from hand to hand down the line, like the torch race the Greeks run in honor of Hephaestus. The Persians call this relay of horses angareion.

99. The first message that reached Susa, announcing that Xerxes had taken Athens, delighted the Persians who had been left at home so much that they strewed all the roads with myrtle branches, kept burning incense without end, and gave themselves up to sacrifices and feasting. But the second message, which came after it, upset them so badly that they all tore their clothes and gave themselves up to endless weeping and wailing, laying the blame on Mardonius. And the Persians did this not so much out of grief for the ships as out of fear for Xerxes himself.

100. This went on among the Persians the whole time until Xerxes himself came home and put a stop to it. Meanwhile Mardonius saw that Xerxes was badly shaken by the sea battle, and he suspected that the king meant to run away from Athens. He thought about his own position. He would be punished for having persuaded the king to march against Greece, and it was better for him to take the risk of either conquering Greece or dying with honor, staking his life on a great goal. Even so, he leaned toward thinking that he would conquer Greece. He weighed all this, and then he made the king this speech: "Master, don't grieve and don't be so troubled over what has happened. Our whole fate does not hang on a contest of planks and timbers, but on men and horses. None of these Greeks who now think they have finished the job will get off their ships and try to stand against you, and neither will anyone here on the mainland. The ones who did stand against us have paid for it. So if you think it best, let us attack the Peloponnese at once; or if you think it best to wait, we can do that. But don't lose heart. There is no way for the Greeks to escape being your slaves, once they have first paid the price for what they have done to you, now and in the past. That would be the best course. But if you have really decided to go back yourself and take your army with you, I have other advice for that case too. My king, do not let the Persians become a laughingstock to the Greeks. None of your affairs has suffered because of the Persians, and you cannot name a single place where we acted like cowards. If Phoenicians or Egyptians or Cyprians or Cilicians acted like cowards, the disaster that followed has nothing to do with the Persians. So now, since it is not the Persians who have wronged you, take my advice. If you have decided not to stay here, then go back to your own home and take the main body of the army with you. And it will be my job to hand Greece over to you, conquered, if I can choose 300,000 men from the army to do it."

101. When Xerxes heard this he was glad and pleased, as far as he could be after his misfortunes, and he told Mardonius that he would think it over and then answer him and say which of the two courses he would take. So when he was consulting with the Persians who had been called to advise him, he decided to send for Artemisia to advise him as well, because before the battle she alone had shown that she saw what ought to be done. When Artemisia came, Xerxes sent everyone else away, both his Persian counselors and his spearmen of the guard, and said to her: "Mardonius urges me to stay here and attack the Peloponnese. He says the Persians and the land army have had no share in my disaster, and that they would gladly prove it to me. So he urges me either to do this, or else he wants to choose 300,000 men from the army himself and hand Greece over to me, conquered, while I go back home with the rest of the army. Now, you gave me good advice about the sea battle that has been fought, when you urged me not to fight it. So advise me now too, which of these things I should do, so that I may decide well."

102. That was his question, and she answered: "My king, it is hard to hit on the best answer when someone asks for advice. But in the present situation I think you should go back home and leave Mardonius here, if he wants to and promises to do this, with the men he wants to have. For on the one hand, if he conquers the people he says he wants to conquer, and the plans he has in mind when he talks this way succeed, then the deed is yours after all, Master, since it was your slaves who did it. On the other hand, if things turn out the opposite of what Mardonius intends, it will be no great misfortune, since you yourself will be safe, and so will the power of your house in that part of the world. For as long as you and your house are safe, the Greeks will have to fight many battles, many times over, for their own survival. As for Mardonius, if anything bad happens to him, no one will care much. And if the Greeks win, it is a victory that is no victory, since they will only have destroyed one of your slaves. And you will go home having done what you made your march to do: you will have burned Athens to the ground."

103. Xerxes was delighted with this advice, since she had managed to say exactly what he himself meant to do. In my opinion, not even if every man and every woman in the world had been advising him to stay would he have stayed, he was so terrified. So he praised Artemisia and sent her off to take his sons to Ephesus, for some of his illegitimate sons had come along with him.

104. To look after these sons he sent with them Hermotimus, a native of Pedasa, who in the king's eyes was second to none of his eunuchs. The Pedasians live inland from Halicarnassus, and at Pedasa something like this happens. Whenever some trouble is about to come, within a certain time, on all the people who live around this city, the priestess of Athena there grows a long beard. This has already happened to them twice.

105. Hermotimus was one of these Pedasians. And of all the men we know of up to now, he took the greatest revenge for a wrong done to him. He had been captured by enemies and was being sold as a slave, and he was bought by Panionius, a man of Chios, who had set himself to make his living by the most unholy trade there is. Whenever he got hold of boys who had any good looks, he castrated them and took them to Sardis or Ephesus and sold them for large sums of money. For among non-Greeks, eunuchs are thought more valuable than men who are not eunuchs for every kind of position of trust. Panionius castrated many boys, since that was how he made his living, and among them was this man I am speaking of. But Hermotimus was not unlucky in everything. He was sent from Sardis to the king along with other gifts, and as time went on he came to be honored by Xerxes above all his other eunuchs.

106. When the king was at Sardis, setting the Persian army in motion to march against Athens, Hermotimus went down on some business to the part of Mysia called Atarneus, which the Chians occupy, and there he found Panionius. He recognized him and spoke to him in a very friendly way. First he went over all the good things he had because of him, and then he promised to do him many good things in return, if Panionius would bring his household and come to live there. So Panionius gladly accepted the offer and brought his children and his wife. Then, when Hermotimus had caught him with his whole household, he said: "You have made your living by the most unholy deeds of any man who ever lived. What harm did I, or any of my ancestors, ever do to you or to anyone of yours, that you made me nothing instead of a man? Did you think the gods would never notice the things you did then? But the gods, following the law of justice, have delivered you into my hands for your unholy deeds, so you will have no cause to complain about the punishment I am going to give you." When he had finished reproaching him, he had Panionius' sons brought in, four of them, and Panionius was forced to castrate his own sons. He was forced, and he did it. And when he had done it, the sons were forced to do the same to him. So vengeance, by the hand of Hermotimus, caught up with Panionius.

107. When Xerxes had entrusted his sons to Artemisia to take back to Ephesus, he called Mardonius and told him to choose whatever men he wanted from the army, and to make his deeds match his words, if he could. That is as far as things went that day. Then in the night, on the king's orders, the commanders of the fleet began withdrawing their ships from Phalerum toward the Hellespont, each one as fast as he could, to guard the bridges for the king to cross. When the king's ships were near Zoster on their voyage, they saw the little points of rock that jut out into the sea from that part of the mainland, took them for ships, and fled a good distance. In time, though, they realized these were not ships but rocks, gathered together again, and went on with their voyage.

108. When day came, the Greeks saw that the land army was still in its place, and they supposed that the ships were still around Phalerum too. They expected another sea battle and got ready to fight it off. But when they learned that the ships had gone, they decided at once to chase them. So they chased them as far as Andros, but never caught sight of Xerxes' fleet. When they reached Andros, they held a council about what to do. Themistocles' view was that they should make their way through the islands chasing the ships, and then sail straight to the Hellespont and break up the bridges. But Eurybiades argued the opposite. He said that if they broke up the floating bridges, they would be doing Greece the greatest harm possible. For if the Persian king were cut off and forced to stay in Europe, he would try not to sit still. If he sat still, none of his affairs could move forward, no way home would open up for him, and his army would starve to death. But if he took action and kept at it, all Europe might come over to him, city by city and nation by nation, either conquered or surrendering on terms before they could be conquered. And they would have the Greeks' harvest, year after year, to live on. But Eurybiades thought that, beaten at sea as he was, the Persian would not stay in Europe. So they should let him run away until his flight brought him home to his own country. After that, he said, they could start fighting for the Persian king's land. The commanders of the other Peloponnesians also held to this view.

109. When Themistocles saw that he could not persuade them, or at least most of them, to sail to the Hellespont, he changed his tune and turned to the Athenians. They were the angriest at the enemy's escape, and were eager to sail to the Hellespont even on their own if the others would not. To them he said: "I have been there myself many times before now, and I have heard of many more cases, when something like this has happened: men driven into a tight corner have fought again after a defeat and made good their earlier disaster. As for us, we have had the luck to save ourselves and Greece by driving off so huge a cloud of men. So let us not chase enemies who are running from us. For we are not the ones who did this, but the gods and heroes. They grudged that one man should be king of both Asia and Europe, and a man at that who was wicked and arrogant, who made no difference between things sacred and things profane, who burned and threw down the statues of the gods, and who even had the sea whipped and lowered chains into it. But as things stand now, it is best for us to stay in Greece and take care of ourselves and our families. Let each man rebuild his house and see to the sowing of his fields, now that he has driven the invader out completely. Then at the start of spring let us sail for the Hellespont and Ionia." He said this to build up a store of gratitude with the Persian king, so that if any trouble ever came to him at the hands of the Athenians, he would have somewhere to take refuge. And that is in fact what happened.

110. So Themistocles said this to deceive them, and the Athenians did as he said. He had long had a reputation as a clever man, and now he had shown that he really was both clever and wise, so they were ready to follow his advice in everything. Once they were persuaded, Themistocles at once sent off some men in a boat, men he could trust to keep silent no matter what test they were put to, with a message he ordered them to give the king. One of them, again, was his servant Sicinnus. When they reached Attica, the others stayed behind in the boat while Sicinnus went up to Xerxes and said: "Themistocles son of Neocles, the commander of the Athenians and the best and ablest man of all the allies, has sent me to tell you this. Themistocles the Athenian, wanting to do you a service, has held back the Greeks when they were eager to chase your ships and break up the bridges on the Hellespont. So now you can go home in peace." When they had delivered this message, they sailed back.

111. The Greeks, meanwhile, having decided not to chase the king's ships any farther or sail to the Hellespont to break up the crossing, were besieging Andros, meaning to take it. For the Andrians were the first of the islanders to refuse when Themistocles asked them for money. Themistocles put it to them that the Athenians had come with two great gods on their side, Persuasion and Compulsion, so the Andrians absolutely had to give them money. The Andrians answered that it was no wonder, then, that Athens was great and prosperous, since the Athenians were so well supplied with useful gods. But the Andrians, they said, were poor, as poor as anyone could be, and they had two useless gods who never left their island but always stayed fondly there, namely Poverty and Helplessness. Since the Andrians had these gods, they would not give money; for the power of the Athenians could never be stronger than their inability.

112. So, having given this answer and refused the money, the Andrians were under siege. And Themistocles, who never stopped wanting money, sent threatening messages to the other islands asking them for money, using the same messengers he had sent to the king. He said that if they did not give what was asked of them, he would bring the Greek fleet against them and besiege them and take them. By saying this he collected great sums of money from the Carystians and the Parians. They heard that Andros was under siege because it had gone over to the Persians, and that Themistocles was more highly regarded than any of the other commanders, and out of fear of this they sent money. Whether any other islanders also gave money I can't say for certain, but I think some others did, and not these alone. Even so, the Carystians at least got no relief from trouble because of it; but the Parians escaped attack, because they won Themistocles over with money. So Themistocles, with Andros as his base, was collecting money for himself from the islanders without the other commanders knowing.

Chapter 47: The Retreat of the King, and Alexander of Macedon at Athens

113. Xerxes and his army, meanwhile, stayed on for a few days after the sea battle, and then they all began to march away toward Boeotia, by the same road they had come. Mardonius thought it was a good idea to escort the king on his way, and he also thought it was now too late in the year to carry on the war. It would be better, he thought, to spend the winter in Thessaly and then, at the start of spring, to make his attempt on the Peloponnese. When they reached Thessaly, Mardonius chose his men. First he took all the Persians called the "Immortals," except only their commander Hydarnes, because Hydarnes said he would not be left behind by the king. After them he took, from the other Persians, those who wore breastplates, and the corps of a thousand cavalry; also the Medes, the Sacae, the Bactrians and the Indians, both infantry and cavalry. These peoples he took whole. From the other allies he picked out a few men at a time, choosing those who looked fine and those he knew had done good service. He chose more Persians than men of any other single nation, and these wore collars of twisted metal and bracelets. After them came the Medes, who in fact were not fewer in number than the Persians, only weaker in body. The result was that there were 300,000 men in all, counting the cavalry.

114. During this time, while Mardonius was choosing his army and Xerxes was in Thessaly, an oracle had come from Delphi to the Spartans. It told them to demand satisfaction from Xerxes for the killing of Leonidas, and to accept whatever he gave them. So the Spartans sent a herald as fast as they could. He found the whole army still in Thessaly, came before Xerxes, and spoke these words: "King of the Medes, the Spartans and the sons of Heracles of Sparta demand satisfaction from you for a killing, because you killed their king while he was fighting to defend Greece." Xerxes laughed and then said nothing for some time. After that he pointed to Mardonius, who happened to be standing beside him, and said: "Then Mardonius here will give them satisfaction, the kind they deserve to have."

115. The herald accepted this answer and left. Xerxes left Mardonius in Thessaly and went on himself in a hurry to the Hellespont. He reached the place where the crossing was in thirty-five days, bringing back next to nothing of his army, you might say. Wherever they came on the march, whatever people they came to, they seized that people's crops and ate them. If they found no crops, they ate the grass growing out of the ground, and they stripped the bark off the trees and pulled down the leaves and devoured them, from cultivated trees and wild ones alike. They left nothing behind them; that is what hunger drove them to. Then plague broke out in the army too, and dysentery, which killed men along the way. Some of the sick the king left behind, ordering the cities he happened to be passing through at the time to take care of them and feed them. He left some in Thessaly, some at Siris in Paeonia, and some in Macedonia. In these parts he had also left behind the sacred chariot of Zeus when he was marching against Greece, but on his way back he did not get it back. The Paeonians had given it to the Thracians, and when Xerxes asked for it again, they said the mares had been carried off while they were out at pasture by the Thracians of the upper country, who live around the source of the Strymon.

116. It was here, too, that a Thracian, the king of the Bisaltians and of the Crestonian country, did a deed of extraordinary horror. He had said that he would never of his own free will be a subject of Xerxes, and he had gone off up into Mount Rhodope; and he had also forbidden his sons to march against Greece. But they, either because they did not care about his orders or because they had a sudden longing to see the war, marched with the Persian. When they came home, all six of them unhurt, their father gouged out their eyes for it.

117. That was the reward they got. As for the Persians, when they had passed on out of Thrace and come to the crossing, they hurried over the Hellespont to Abydos in the ships, because they found the floating bridges no longer stretched across: a storm had broken them up. While they stayed there for a time, they were given more food than they had had on the way. From eating without restraint to satisfy their hunger, and from the change of water as well, many of the men in the army who had survived until then died. The rest reached Sardis with Xerxes.

118. There is also another story told, which goes like this. When Xerxes, marching away from Athens, came to Eion on the Strymon, he went no farther by road from there. He handed his army over to Hydarnes to lead back to the Hellespont, while he himself boarded a Phoenician ship and set out for Asia. As he sailed, a wind from the Strymon caught him, violent and raising great waves. The storm tossed him more and more, and the ship was heavily loaded, because there were a great many Persians on deck, the ones traveling with Xerxes. At that the king grew frightened. He shouted to the pilot and asked whether there was any way for them to be saved. The pilot said: "Master, there is none, unless we find some way to get rid of all these extra passengers." Then, they say, when Xerxes heard this, he said: "Persians, now let each of you show how much he cares for the king. My safety, it seems, depends on you." That, they say, is what he said, and the Persians bowed down before him and leaped into the sea. So the ship was lightened and came safely to Asia. As soon as they had landed, they say, Xerxes did two things. First he gave the pilot a gold wreath, for saving the king's life; then he cut off his head, for causing the deaths of so many Persians.

119. That is the other story told about Xerxes' return, but I for my part cannot believe it at all, either in other respects or in this matter of what happened to the Persians. If the pilot had really said this to Xerxes, I don't believe one person in ten thousand would disagree with me about what the king would have done. He would have sent the men on deck down below into the hold, since they were Persians, and Persians of the highest rank. Then, from the rowers, who were Phoenicians, he would have thrown into the sea the same number of men. In fact, as I said before, he made his way back to Asia by road, together with the rest of the army.

120. Here is strong evidence that this is so. Xerxes is known to have come to Abdera on his way back, and to have made a pact of guest-friendship with its people and presented them with a Persian sword of gold and a tiara spangled with gold. And as the people of Abdera themselves say (though I for my part cannot believe it at all), it was there that he loosened his belt for the first time on his flight back from Athens, because he thought himself safe. Now, Abdera lies farther toward the Hellespont than the river Strymon and Eion, where the story says he boarded the ship.

121. The Greeks, meanwhile, when it turned out that they could not take Andros, turned toward Carystus. They laid waste the land of the Carystians and then left and went to Salamis. First of all they set apart the first fruits of the spoils for the gods. Among these were three Persian triremes. One was to be dedicated at the Isthmus, and it was still there in my time; another at Sunium; and the third to Ajax, there at Salamis where they were. After this they divided the spoils among themselves and sent the first fruits to Delphi. From these a statue was made, eighteen feet tall, holding the beak of a ship in its hand. This statue stands in the same place as the golden statue of Alexander the Macedonian.

122. When the Greeks had sent the first fruits to Delphi, they asked the god, on behalf of all of them, whether the first fruits he had received were full and acceptable to him. He said that from the Greeks in general he had received enough, but not from the Aeginetans, and he demanded from them the prize for bravery they had won in the sea battle at Salamis. When the Aeginetans heard this, they dedicated three golden stars set on a bronze ship's mast, which stand in the corner close to Croesus' mixing bowl.

123. After the spoils were divided, the Greeks sailed to the Isthmus to give the prize for bravery to the Greek who had proved himself most deserving of it in this war. When they got there, the commanders cast their votes at the altar of Poseidon, choosing out of them all who was first in merit and who was second. Every one of them voted for himself for first place, each man thinking that he himself had been the best. But for second place most of the votes agreed, and they gave it to Themistocles. So for first place each of them had only his own vote, while for second place Themistocles was far ahead of the rest.

124. The Greeks would not make a decision on this out of envy, and they sailed away each to his own city without deciding. Even so, Themistocles was talked about and admired all over Greece as by far the cleverest man of all the Greeks. And since the men who had fought at Salamis had not honored him for his victory, even though he had come first in the voting, he went straight to Sparta after this, wanting to be honored there. The Spartans gave him a fine welcome and great honors. They gave Eurybiades a wreath of olive as the prize for bravery, and to Themistocles too they gave a wreath of olive, for his wisdom and skill. They also presented him with the finest chariot in Sparta. After praising him highly, they escorted him on his way home with three hundred picked Spartans, the ones called the "Horsemen," as far as the border of Tegea. He is the only man we know of to whom the Spartans ever gave an escort on his way.

125. But when he came back to Athens from Sparta, Timodemus of Aphidnae attacked him. This Timodemus was one of Themistocles' enemies, though not otherwise a man of any importance, and he was mad with envy. He threw Themistocles' trip to Sparta in his face, saying that it was because of Athens that he had received those honors from the Spartans, not because of himself. Timodemus kept on saying this over and over, until Themistocles said: "Here is how it is. If I had been a native of Belbina, that little island, I would never have been honored like this by the Spartans. But neither would you, my friend, even though you are an Athenian." So much for those matters.

126. Artabazus son of Pharnaces, meanwhile, a man already well thought of among the Persians and even more so after the events at Plataea, was escorting the king as far as the crossing with 60,000 men of the army Mardonius had chosen for himself. When the king was in Asia and Artabazus, on his march back, came near Pallene, he found that Mardonius was wintering in Thessaly and Macedonia and was in no hurry for him to come and join the rest of the army. So he thought it would not be right to pass by without enslaving the people of Potidaea, whom he found in revolt. For when the king had marched past them and the Persian fleet had fled from Salamis, the people of Potidaea had openly revolted from the Persians, and so had the others who live in Pallene.

127. So Artabazus began to besiege Potidaea. He also suspected that the people of Olynthus were planning to revolt from the king, so he began to besiege that city too. It was held by Bottiaeans who had been driven out of the area around the Thermaic Gulf by the Macedonians. When he had taken the city by siege, he led these men out to a lake and slaughtered them there. He handed the city over to Critobulus of Torone to govern, and to the people of Chalcidice; and that is how the Chalcidians came to possess Olynthus.

128. After taking this city, Artabazus attacked Potidaea in earnest. While he was hard at work at this, Timoxenus, the commander of the troops from Scione, came to an agreement with him to betray the town. How he managed it at first I cannot say, because that is not reported. In the end, though, it went like this. Whenever Timoxenus wrote a note he wanted to send to Artabazus, or Artabazus one he wanted to send to Timoxenus, they wound it around the notched end of an arrow, put the feathers over the paper, and shot it to a place they had agreed on. But it came out that Timoxenus was trying to betray Potidaea. Artabazus shot an arrow at the agreed spot, missed it, and hit a man of Potidaea in the shoulder. When he was hit, a crowd gathered around him, as usually happens in wartime. They took the arrow at once, found the paper, and carried it to the commanders. Troops from the rest of Pallene were there as allies too. When the commanders had read the paper and discovered who the traitor was, they decided not to convict Timoxenus of treason in public, for the sake of the city of Scione, so that the people of Scione would not be thought traitors for all time to come.

129. That is how Timoxenus was found out. When Artabazus had been besieging the town for three months, the sea drew back in a great ebb that lasted a long time. The Persians, seeing that the water had become shallow, tried to get through into the Pallene peninsula. But when they had gone two-fifths of the way, with three-fifths still to go before they would be in Pallene, a great flood tide came in on them, higher than ever before, so the local people say, though high tides there are frequent. Those of them who could not swim drowned, and those who could were killed by the men of Potidaea, who came out at them in boats. The cause of the high tide and the flood, and of what happened to the Persians, was this, according to the Potidaeans: these same Persians who were destroyed by the sea had committed sacrilege against the temple of Poseidon and his statue in the suburb of their town. And in saying that this was the cause, I think they are right. Artabazus led the survivors of his army away to Thessaly to join Mardonius. That is how things went for the men who escorted the king on his way.

130. What was left of Xerxes' fleet, after it reached Asia in its flight from Salamis and had ferried the king and his army across from the Chersonese to Abydos, spent the winter at Cyme. When spring came, it gathered early at Samos, where some of the ships had even spent the winter. Most of the fighting men on board were still Persians and Medes. Mardontes son of Bagaeus and Artayntes son of Artachaees came to command them, and sharing the command with them was Ithamitres, Artayntes' nephew, whom Artayntes himself had chosen. Since they had taken a heavy blow, they did not go any farther west, and no one forced them to. They stayed at Samos and kept watch over Ionia so that it would not revolt, with three hundred ships, counting the Ionians'. They did not expect the Greeks to come to Ionia; they thought the Greeks would be content to guard their own land, judging from the fact that they had not chased them as they fled from Salamis but had been happy then to go home. So at sea the Persians had lost heart, but on land they thought Mardonius would have much the better of it. They stayed at Samos, then, making plans to do their enemies some harm if they could, and at the same time listening for news of how things would turn out for Mardonius.

131. The Greeks were stirred into action both by the coming of spring and by Mardonius' presence in Thessaly. Their land army had not yet begun to gather when the fleet arrived at Aegina, one hundred and ten ships. Its commander and admiral was Leotychides son of Menares, son of Hegesilaus, son of Hippocratides, son of Leotychides, son of Anaxilaus, son of Archidemus, son of Anaxandrides, son of Theopompus, son of Nicander, son of Charilaus, son of Eunomus, son of Polydectes, son of Prytanis, son of Euryphon, son of Procles, son of Aristodemus, son of Aristomachus, son of Cleodaeus, son of Hyllus, son of Heracles.
