He was of the other of Sparta's two royal houses. All of these men had been kings of Sparta except the two named first after Leotychides. The commander of the Athenians was Xanthippus son of Ariphron.

132. When all the ships had arrived at Aegina, envoys from Ionia came to the Greek camp. A little before this they had also gone to Sparta and asked the Spartans to set Ionia free. One of them was Herodotus son of Basilides. These men had banded together and plotted to kill Strattis, the tyrant of Chios. There had been seven of them at first, but when one of the plotters informed on them and their plot against him was discovered, the other six escaped from Chios. They went to Sparta, and now to Aegina, asking the Greeks to sail across to Ionia. But it was all they could do to bring the Greeks as far as Delos. Everything beyond that frightened the Greeks. They had no experience of those parts, everything there seemed to them to be full of soldiers, and they were convinced that it was as far to Samos as to the Pillars of Heracles. So it happened that at the same time the Persians, struck with fear, did not dare sail any farther west than Samos, and the Greeks, though the Chians begged them, did not dare go any farther east than Delos. So fear kept guard over the space between them.

133. The Greeks, then, sailed to Delos. Mardonius, meanwhile, had been wintering in Thessaly. From there he sent a man named Mys, a native of Europus, around to the various oracles, with orders to go and consult every one of them that he could be allowed to try. What he wanted to find out from the oracles when he gave these orders I cannot say, because that is not reported. My own guess is that he sent to ask about his present situation and nothing else.

134. This Mys is known to have gone to Lebadea and to have paid one of the local men to go down into the cave of Trophonius. He also went to the oracle of the Phocians at Abae. And when he first came to Thebes, he not only consulted Ismenian Apollo (there you can consult the god through sacrificed victims, just as at Olympia) but also paid a foreigner, a man who was not a Theban, to lie down and sleep in the temple of Amphiaraus. No Theban is allowed to seek a prophecy in that temple, and here is why. Amphiaraus, through his oracles, told the Thebans to choose which of two things they wanted: to have him as their prophet or as their ally in war, and to do without the other. They chose to have him as their ally in war. That is why no Theban is allowed to sleep in that temple.

135. After this, the Thebans say, something happened that seems to me a very great marvel. It seems that this Mys of Europus, on his round of all the oracles, came also to the sacred precinct of Ptoan Apollo. This temple is called the Ptoum. It belongs to the Thebans and lies above Lake Copais, at the foot of the mountains, very near the town of Acraephia. When the man called Mys came to this temple, three men went with him, chosen from the citizens and sent by the state to write down whatever the god would say in his prophecy. At once, it is said, the god's prophet began to prophesy in a foreign language. The Thebans who had come with Mys were amazed to hear a foreign language instead of Greek, and they did not know what to make of it. Then, it is said, Mys, the man from Europus, snatched the tablet they had brought from them and wrote on it what the prophet was saying; and he said that the prophet was answering in the Carian language. When he had written it down, he left and went back to Thessaly.

136. Mardonius read what the oracles had said, whatever that was. After this he sent Alexander son of Amyntas, the Macedonian, to Athens as his envoy. He sent him partly because the Persians were related to Alexander by marriage. Alexander's sister Gygaea, the daughter of Amyntas, had married a Persian, Bubares, and had borne him that Amyntas who lived in Asia, named after his mother's father, to whom the king gave Alabanda, a great city of Phrygia, to hold. Mardonius was also sending him because he had learned that Alexander was the official guest-friend and a benefactor of the Athenians. That way, he thought, he would have the best chance of winning the Athenians over to his side. He had heard that they were a numerous people and brave in war, and he knew besides that they more than anyone else had brought about the disasters the Persians had suffered at sea. If they joined him, he thought, he would easily be master of the sea (and that would in fact have been the case), while on land he believed he was already much stronger. So he reckoned that his power would be far greater than that of the Greeks. Perhaps, too, the oracles had told him this in advance, advising him to make the Athenians his allies, and he was sending in obedience to their advice.

137. Now, this Alexander's ancestor seven generations back was that Perdiccas who first became tyrant of the Macedonians, and he won the throne in the following way. Three brothers, descendants of Temenus, fled from Argos to the Illyrians: Gauanes, Aeropus and Perdiccas. From the Illyrians they crossed over into upper Macedonia and came to the town of Lebaea. There they worked for wages as farm hands in the king's household. One looked after the horses, the second the cattle, and the youngest, Perdiccas, the sheep and goats. In the old days even the people who ruled over men were poor in money, not just the common people, and the king's wife cooked their food for them herself. Whenever she baked bread, the loaf of the boy, their servant Perdiccas, rose to twice its natural size. When this kept happening, again and again, she told her husband. As soon as he heard it, he concluded that it was an omen and pointed to something great. So he called in the farm hands and told them to leave his land. They said that it was only right that they should be paid the wages they were owed before they went. Now, it happened that the sun was shining down into the house through the smoke hole in the roof. When the king heard them talk about wages, heaven had taken away his wits, and he said: "This is the pay I give you, and it is what you deserve," and he pointed to the sunlight. Gauanes and Aeropus, the older brothers, stood there stunned when they heard this. But the boy happened to have a knife in his hand, and he said: "We accept what you give, my king." He traced a line with his knife around the patch of sunlight on the floor of the house. When he had traced the line around it, he three times scooped up the sunlight into the fold of his robe. Then he left, and his brothers with him.

138. So they went away. Then one of the men sitting near the king told him what the boy had done, and how the youngest of them had accepted what was given with some purpose in mind. When the king heard this he was angry, and he sent horsemen after them to kill them. Now, there is a river in this country to which the descendants of these men from Argos sacrifice as their savior. As soon as the sons of Temenus had crossed it, this river rose in such a flood that the horsemen could not get across. So the brothers came to another part of Macedonia and settled near the place called the gardens of Midas son of Gordias, where roses grow wild, each with sixty petals and a scent sweeter than any others. It was in these gardens, too, that Silenus was caught, as the Macedonians tell it. Above the gardens rises a mountain called Bermius, which no one can climb because of the cold. When they had taken possession of that region, they used it as their base and went on to conquer the rest of Macedonia as well.

139. Alexander was descended from this Perdiccas as follows. Alexander was the son of Amyntas, Amyntas was the son of Alcetes, Alcetes' father was Aeropus, Aeropus' father was Philip, Philip's father was Argaeus, and Argaeus' father was Perdiccas, the one who first won the kingdom.

140. That, then, was Alexander son of Amyntas' descent. When he came to Athens on Mardonius' errand, he said this: "Athenians, Mardonius has this to say. 'A message has come to me from the king, and this is what it says: "I forgive the Athenians all the wrongs they have done me. Now, Mardonius, do this. First, give them back their land. Then let them choose another land besides, whichever they want, and live under their own laws. And rebuild all their temples, which I burned, if they are willing to make a treaty with me." Since this message has come to me, I must do it, unless you stop me. And so I say this to you now. Why are you so mad as to wage war against the king? You will never defeat him, and you cannot hold out against him forever. You have seen the great size of Xerxes' army and what it did, and you have heard about the force I have with me now. So even if you get the better of us and win (and if you have any sense you can have no hope of that), another army many times as large will come. So do not try to match yourselves against the king, only to lose your land and be forever running for your lives. Make peace with him instead. You have the most honorable chance to make peace you could have, since the king himself has taken this road. Make an alliance with us, then, honestly and without deceit, and stay free.'

"That is what Mardonius told me to say to you, Athenians. As for me, I will say nothing about my own goodwill toward you, since this would not be the first time you have learned of it. But I ask you to do as Mardonius says, because I can see that you will not be able to fight Xerxes forever. If I saw that you had the strength for it, I would never have come to you with this message. The king's power is more than human, and his arm is very long. So if you do not come to terms at once, when they are offering you such great terms for a treaty, I am afraid for you. Of all your allies, you live the most squarely on the road the armies travel, and you are always the ones destroyed, alone, because the land you hold lies out by itself, between the armies that are fighting each other. No, be persuaded. It is a great thing for you that, of all the Greeks, you are the only ones whose wrongs the Great King forgives and whose friend he wants to be."

141. That is what Alexander said. The Spartans had heard that Alexander had come to Athens to bring the Athenians to make a treaty with the Persians. They remembered the oracles which said that they and the other Dorians were destined to be driven out of the Peloponnese by the Medes and the Athenians together, and they had been very much afraid that the Athenians would make a treaty with the Persians. So they had at once decided to send envoys. It happened that the Spartan envoys were brought in to speak at the same time as Alexander, because the Athenians had waited for them, dragging out the time. They were quite sure that the Spartans would hear that an envoy had come from the Persians to make a treaty, and that when they heard it, they would send envoys of their own as fast as they could. So the Athenians did it on purpose, to let the Spartans see where they stood.

142. So when Alexander had finished speaking, the envoys from Sparta spoke right after him and said: "The Spartans have sent us to ask you not to do anything new that would harm Greece, and not to accept the foreigner's proposals. That would not be just in any way, or honorable, for any of the Greeks to do, and least of all for you, for many reasons. It was you who stirred up this war, when we wanted nothing of the kind. The fight began over your territory, but now it involves all of Greece. Besides, it is not to be endured that you Athenians, who started all of this, should turn out to be the cause of slavery for the Greeks, when you have always, from ancient times, been known as the liberators of many. We do feel for you in your sufferings, because you have lost two harvests and your property has been in ruins for a long time now. To make up for this, the Spartans and their allies offer to feed your wives and all the members of your households who cannot fight, for as long as this war lasts. But do not let Alexander the Macedonian win you over by making Mardonius' words sound smooth. It suits him to do it, since he is a tyrant himself and is working with a tyrant. But it does not suit you, if you have any sense, because you know that there is no faith or truth in barbarians."

That was what the envoys said.

143. The Athenians answered Alexander like this: "We know well enough ourselves that the Persians' forces are many times greater than ours, so there is no need for you to throw that in our faces. All the same, because we long for freedom, we will defend ourselves as best we can. Do not try to persuade us to make a treaty with the foreigner, because we will not be persuaded. Now take this message back to Mardonius from the Athenians: As long as the sun keeps the course it keeps now, we will never come to terms with Xerxes. We will go out to defend ourselves against him, trusting in the gods and the heroes as our allies, the ones he had no respect for when he burned their houses and their sacred images. And from now on, do not come before the Athenians with any proposals like these, and do not think you are doing them a service by urging them to do what is wrong. We do not want anything unpleasant to happen to you at the hands of the Athenians, since you are their official guest-friend and their friend."

144. That was their answer to Alexander. To the envoys from Sparta they said this: "It was natural enough, no doubt, for the Spartans to be afraid that we would make a treaty with the foreigner. But it seems an unworthy fear for men who know the spirit of the Athenians so well. There is not so much gold anywhere on earth, nor any land so far beyond all others in beauty and richness, that we would take it as our price for going over to the Persians and enslaving Greece. There are many great reasons that would stop us from doing this, even if we wanted to. First and greatest, the statues and houses of the gods that have been burned or thrown down in ruins. We are bound to avenge them to the utmost, rather than come to terms with the man who did these things. Second, there is our Greekness: we are of one blood and one language, we share the temples of the gods and the sacrifices, and our ways of life are the same. It would not be right for the Athenians to betray all this. And know this, if you did not know it before: as long as a single Athenian is left alive, we will never come to terms with Xerxes. Still, we admire the care you have shown for us, in thinking of us now that our property has been destroyed and in being willing to feed our households. As far as you are concerned, the kindness has been done in full. But we will go on holding out as best we can and will not be a burden to you in any way. Now, things being as they are, send out an army as quickly as you can. As we judge it, the foreigner will be here invading our land before long, as soon as he hears our answer, that we will do none of the things he asked of us. So before he gets here into Attica, the right thing is for you to come to our help quickly in Boeotia." That was the Athenians' answer, and with it the envoys went away back to Sparta.

Book Nine: Calliope

Chapter 48: Mardonius Takes Athens Again, and the Armies Gather at Plataea

1. After Alexander came back and reported to Mardonius what the Athenians had said, Mardonius set out from Thessaly and led his army toward Athens with all speed, and in every country he came to he took the people of that land along with him. The leaders of Thessaly, meanwhile, felt no regret at all for what they had already done. On the contrary, they urged the Persian on even more. Thorax of Larissa, who had helped escort Xerxes on his flight, now openly offered Mardonius a way through to invade Greece.

2. When the army on its march reached Boeotia, the Thebans tried to keep Mardonius there. They advised him that there was no better place for him to make his camp than this one. They urged him not to go any farther, but to settle there and try to bring the whole of Greece under his power without a fight. To beat the Greeks by open force while they were united, as they had been of one mind before, would be hard, they said, even for the whole world put together. "But," they went on, "if you do what we advise, you will have all their plans for resistance in your hands with very little trouble. Send money to the men who hold power in their cities. By sending it you will split Greece into two parties, and after that, with the help of your own party, you will easily bring down those who are not on your side."

3. That was their advice, but he did not take it. A great desire had taken hold of him to capture Athens a second time, partly out of stubbornness, and partly because he meant to signal to the king in Sardis, by beacon fires across the islands, that he held Athens. Yet even this time, when he came to Attica, he did not find the Athenians there. He learned that most of them were either on Salamis or on the ships, and he took the city empty. The king's capture of the city had taken place ten months before this later expedition of Mardonius against it.

4. When Mardonius reached Athens, he sent Morychides, a man from the Hellespont, over to Salamis with the same proposals that Alexander the Macedonian had carried to the Athenians. He sent them this second time knowing already that the Athenians were not friendly to him. But he hoped they would give way and drop their stubbornness, now that the land of Attica had been captured and was in his hands.

5. That is why he sent Morychides to Salamis. Morychides came before the Council and reported Mardonius' message. Then one of the councillors, Lycidas, gave his opinion that it would be better to accept the proposal Morychides had brought and to put it before the assembly of the people. He gave this opinion either because he had taken money from Mardonius or because it was what he really thought. But the Athenians, both the members of the Council and those outside it, were furious the moment they heard it. They surrounded Lycidas and stoned him to death, though they sent Morychides the Hellespontine away unharmed. With all the uproar there was on Salamis about Lycidas, the Athenian women heard what was happening. One woman passed the word to the next, and each brought another along with her, and on their own they went to Lycidas' house and stoned his wife and his children to death.

6. This is how the Athenians had come to cross over to Salamis. As long as they expected an army to come from the Peloponnese to help them, they stayed in Attica. But the Peloponnesians were very slow and kept delaying, and the invader was already said to be in Boeotia, so they moved everything out of harm's way and crossed over to Salamis themselves. At the same time they sent envoys to Sparta. The envoys were to reproach the Spartans for letting the invader into Attica instead of going with the Athenians to meet him in Boeotia, and to remind them how much the Persian had promised to give the Athenians if they changed sides. And they were told to warn the Spartans that if they did not help the Athenians, the Athenians would find some protection for themselves.

7. The Spartans, in fact, were holding a festival at this time, the Hyacinthia, their feast in honor of Apollo and his beloved Hyacinthus, and they thought nothing more important than doing what they owed the god. At the same time, the wall they had been building across the Isthmus was just then being finished with its battlements. When the envoys from Athens arrived at Sparta, bringing envoys from Megara and Plataea with them, they went before the ephors and said: "The Athenians have sent us to tell you this. The king of the Medes offers to give us back our land. He also wants to make us his allies on fair and equal terms, without trickery or treachery, and he is willing to give us another country besides our own, whichever we choose. But we respect Zeus, the god of all the Greeks, and we would not stoop to betray Greece. So we did not agree; we refused. We refused even though the other Greeks have treated us unjustly and left us to be destroyed, and even though we knew it would pay us better to make a treaty with the Persian than to go on fighting. Nor will we make a treaty in the future, if we have any say in it. That is how honestly we have done our duty by the Greeks. But you? Back then you were terrified that we would make a treaty with the Persian. Then you learned for certain what our spirit was, that we would never betray Greece, and your wall across the Isthmus is all but finished. So now you think nothing of the Athenians. You agreed with us to go to Boeotia and face the Persian there, and you have deserted us, and you let the invader into Attica besides. For now, then, the Athenians are angry with you, because you did not do what you ought to have done. And now they ask you to send out an army with us as fast as you can, so that we can meet the invader in Attica. Since we have missed our chance in Boeotia, the best place to fight in our own country is the Thriasian plain, the plain around Eleusis."

8. When the ephors heard this, they put off their answer to the next day, and then on the next day to the day after that. They kept this up for as many as ten days, putting the matter off from one day to the next, while all the Peloponnesians were working hard on the wall across the Isthmus and had it nearly finished. I can't say why, when Alexander the Macedonian came to Athens, they were so very anxious that the Athenians might go over to the Persians, and now they did not care at all. The only reason I can see is that their wall across the Isthmus was now built and they thought they had no more need of the Athenians, whereas when Alexander came to Attica the wall was not yet finished, and they were working on it in great fear of the Persians.

9. In the end, though, the answer was given and the Spartans marched out, and it happened like this. On the day before the envoys' last hearing was due, Chileus, a man of Tegea who had more influence at Sparta than any other foreigner, heard from the ephors everything the Athenians were saying. And he, it seems, said this to them: "This is how things stand, ephors. If the Athenians are not our friends but allies of the invader, then however strong a wall has been built across the Isthmus, a wide door has been opened for the Persian into the Peloponnese. So listen to them, before the Athenians decide on something else that will bring Greece down."

10. That was his advice, and they took his words to heart at once. Without saying anything to the envoys who had come from the cities, they sent out five thousand Spartans while it was still night, with no fewer than seven helots assigned to attend each man, and they appointed Pausanias son of Cleombrotus to lead them out. The command properly belonged to Pleistarchus son of Leonidas, but he was still a boy, and Pausanias was his guardian and his cousin. For Cleombrotus, Pausanias' father and the son of Anaxandrides, was no longer alive: after leading home from the Isthmus the army that had built the wall, he died not long afterward. The reason Cleombrotus led the army home from the Isthmus was this: while he was offering sacrifice for a battle against the Persian, the sun went dark in the sky. Pausanias chose as his fellow commander Euryanax son of Dorieus, a man of the same royal house.

11. So Pausanias and his army had left Sparta. When day came, the envoys, who knew nothing about the march, went before the ephors meaning to go home themselves, each to his own city. When they came in they said: "You Spartans are staying here celebrating this Hyacinthia of yours and enjoying yourselves, and you have left your allies to be destroyed. The Athenians, wronged by you and with no allies, will make peace with the Persians on whatever terms they can get. And once we have made peace, we will plainly become the king's allies, and so we will march with him against any land the Persians lead us to. Then you will find out what comes of all this for you." When the envoys said this, the ephors told them, and swore an oath to it, that by now they supposed the men were at Orestheum on their way against the strangers. ("Strangers" was what they used to call the non-Greeks.) The envoys did not understand and asked what this meant, and by asking they learned the whole truth. They were astonished, and they set off after the army as fast as they could. And five thousand picked hoplites of the Lacedaemonian "dwellers around," who were not Spartan citizens, did the same and went with them.

12. So they were hurrying toward the Isthmus. As soon as the Argives heard that Pausanias and his army had marched out of Sparta, they sent a herald to Attica, the best long-distance runner they could find. They did this because they had earlier promised Mardonius, of their own accord, that they would stop the Spartans from marching out. When the herald reached Athens, he said: "Mardonius, the Argives have sent me to tell you that the young men have marched out of Lacedaemon, and the Argives are not able to stop them. So, with this in mind, may you have the good fortune to plan well."

13. After saying this, the herald left and went back. Once Mardonius had heard the message, he had no wish at all to stay in Attica any longer. Before he heard it, he had been waiting there because he wanted to find out what the Athenians were going to do. He had not been damaging or ravaging the land of Attica, because he kept hoping they would make a treaty with him. But since he could not persuade them, and now knew the whole situation, he began to withdraw from the country before Pausanias' force reached the Isthmus. First, though, he set fire to Athens, and he knocked down and destroyed whatever was still standing of the walls, the houses and the temples. He marched away for these reasons. First, Attica was not country where cavalry could operate freely. And second, if he were beaten in a battle in Attica, the only way out was through a narrow pass, where a few men could stop his army. So he meant to fall back to Thebes and fight near a friendly city, in country where cavalry could move freely.

14. So Mardonius was withdrawing, and he was already on the road when a message reached him that another force, an advance guard of a thousand Lacedaemonians, had come to Megara. On hearing this he thought it over, wanting, if he could, to capture these men first. So he turned back and led his army toward Megara, and his cavalry, riding ahead of the rest, overran the land of Megara. That was the farthest point in Europe toward the setting sun that this Persian army ever reached.

15. After this a message reached Mardonius that the Greeks were gathered at the Isthmus. So he marched back by way of Decelea. The chiefs of Boeotia had sent for the Asopians who lived near his line of march, and these men guided him along the road to Sphendaleis and from there to Tanagra. He camped for the night at Tanagra, and the next day he turned toward Scolus, and so he was in Theban territory. There he began cutting down the trees on the Thebans' lands, even though they were on the Persian side. He did not do it out of any hostility toward them. He was driven by urgent need: he wanted to build a defense for his camp, and he was also making it a place of refuge in case the battle, when it came, did not go the way he wished. His army's camp stretched from Erythrae past Hysiae and reached down to the river Asopus. But he did not make the wall run as far as that; each side of it measured something like 6,000 feet, a little over a mile.

16. While the invaders were busy with this work, Attaginus son of Phyrnon, a Theban, made lavish preparations and invited Mardonius himself and fifty of the most important Persians to a banquet. They accepted, and the dinner was held at Thebes. What follows I heard from Thersander, a man of Orchomenus who was very highly respected there. Thersander said that he too was invited to this dinner by Attaginus, and that fifty Thebans were invited as well. Their host did not seat them nation by nation, each on separate couches, but put a Persian and a Theban on every couch. When dinner was over and they were drinking toasts to one another, the Persian who shared his couch asked him in Greek where he was from, and he answered that he was from Orchomenus. The Persian said: "Since you have now shared my table and my drink offering, I want to leave you something to remember my opinion by, so that you yourself may know ahead of time and be able to make whatever plans are best for you. Do you see these Persians feasting here, and the army we left camped by the river? A little while from now, of all these you will see only a very few still alive." As the Persian said this, he wept freely, so Thersander reported. Thersander was amazed at his words and said to him: "Surely, then, you ought to tell this to Mardonius, and to the Persians who rank next after him." To this the Persian said: "My friend, what is fated to come from heaven no man can turn aside. No one is willing to listen to advice, even when what he hears is sensible. Many of us Persians know well what I am telling you, and yet we go along, bound by necessity. The bitterest pain a man can have is this: to understand much and have power over nothing." This I heard from Thersander of Orchomenus, and this as well: that he told it to various people right away, before the battle at Plataea took place.

17. While Mardonius was camped in Boeotia, all the other Greeks living in those parts who had sided with the Persians were supplying troops, and they had joined in the invasion of Attica. Only the Phocians had not joined in the invasion. The Phocians too, I should explain, were now actively on the Persian side, though not willingly, but under compulsion. Not many days after Mardonius arrived at Thebes, however, a thousand of their hoplites came, led by Harmocydes, the most respected man among their citizens. When these too had come to Thebes, Mardonius sent horsemen and ordered the Phocians to take up a position by themselves on the plain. As soon as they had done so, the whole cavalry appeared. At that a rumor ran through the army of Greeks who were with the Persians that the cavalry was going to shoot the Phocians down with javelins, and the same report spread among the Phocians themselves. Then their commander Harmocydes encouraged them with these words: "Phocians, it is plain that these men mean to hand us over to a death we can clearly see coming, because the Thessalians have slandered us, I suspect. So now every one of you must prove himself a brave man. It is better to end our lives doing brave deeds and defending ourselves than to be destroyed by a shameful death, offering ourselves up to be slaughtered. Let each of them learn that they are barbarians, and that we, the men they have plotted to murder, are Greeks."

18. While he was encouraging them this way, the horsemen surrounded them and rode at them as if to destroy them. They were already aiming their missiles as if about to throw them, and some perhaps actually did throw. Meanwhile the Phocians stood facing them, gathered together and with their ranks closed up as tight as they could on every side. Then the horsemen turned and rode back. I can't say for certain which it was. Perhaps they came to destroy the Phocians at the Thessalians' request, and then, when they saw them turning to defend themselves, were afraid of taking losses themselves, and so rode away, because those were Mardonius' orders. Or perhaps he wanted to test them and see whether they had any fighting spirit in them. When the horsemen had ridden back, Mardonius sent a herald with this message: "Take heart, Phocians. You have shown yourselves to be brave men, and not what I was told you were. Now carry on with this war eagerly, and you will not outdo either me or the king in good turns." So much for the Phocians.

19. When the Lacedaemonians reached the Isthmus, they camped there. Hearing of this, the rest of the Peloponnesians, those who favored the better cause, and some also because they saw the Spartans marching out, did not think it right to be left behind by the Lacedaemonians in taking the field. So when the sacrifices turned out favorable, they marched out from the Isthmus all together and came to Eleusis. There they sacrificed again, and when the signs were favorable they marched on, and the Athenians with them, who had crossed over from Salamis and joined them at Eleusis. When they reached Erythrae in Boeotia, they learned that the invaders were camped on the Asopus. Seeing this, they drew themselves up facing them on the lower slopes of Cithaeron.

20. Then, since the Greeks would not come down into the plain, Mardonius sent all his cavalry against them. Their commander was Masistius (the Greeks call him Macistius), a man of reputation among the Persians, who rode a Nesaean horse with a golden bridle and fine trappings everywhere else too. When the horsemen rode up to the Greeks, they attacked them squadron by squadron, and with their attacks they did them a great deal of damage, and they jeered at them besides, calling them women.

21. It happened that the Megarians had been posted in the most exposed part of the whole position, where the cavalry could most easily get at them. So as the cavalry kept attacking, the Megarians, hard pressed, sent a herald to the Greek commanders. The herald came and said: "The Megarians say this: 'Allies, we cannot hold off the Persian cavalry by ourselves in the position where we were posted at the start. Even up to now we have held out against them only by endurance and courage, hard pressed as we are. And now, unless you send some others to take over our position from us, understand that we are going to leave it.'" That was the herald's report. At this Pausanias tested the Greeks, to see whether any others would volunteer to go to that place and take over the post from the Megarians. The rest did not want to go, but the Athenians took the job on: of the Athenians, the three hundred picked men whose captain was Olympidorus son of Lampon.

22. These were the men who took on the task and were posted at Erythrae, out in front of all the other Greeks who were there, and they chose to take the archers along with them. They fought for some time, and in the end the fighting finished like this. While the cavalry were attacking squadron by squadron, Masistius' horse, riding out ahead of the rest, was hit in the side by an arrow. In pain, it reared straight up and threw Masistius off. When he was down, the Athenians rushed at him at once. They took his horse, and they killed him as he fought back, though at first they could not manage it, because of the armor he wore. He had on a breastplate of golden scales underneath, and over the breastplate he had put on a crimson tunic. So their blows on the breastplate did nothing, until somebody saw what the trouble was and stabbed him in the eye. Then at last he fell and died. Somehow the other horsemen had not seen this happen. They had not seen him fall from his horse or seen him killed, because it happened while they were pulling back and wheeling round, and they did not notice what was going on. But when they halted their horses, they missed him at once, because there was no one giving them orders. When they realized what had happened, they called to one another and all rode in together, to try to recover the body.

23. When the Athenians saw that the cavalry were no longer coming at them squadron by squadron but all together, they shouted to the rest of the army to help them. While the whole body of the infantry was coming to their help, a fierce fight broke out over the body. As long as the three hundred were on their own, they had much the worse of it and were about to abandon the body. But when the main army came to help them, the horsemen could hold out no longer, and they did not manage to recover the body; and besides him they lost others of their own men as well. Then they pulled back about a quarter of a mile and talked over what to do. Since they had no commander, they decided to ride back to Mardonius.

24. When the cavalry reached the camp, Mardonius and the whole army mourned Masistius deeply. They cut off their own hair and the manes of their horses and pack animals, and they wailed without restraint, so that the sound of it filled all Boeotia, because a man had died who, after Mardonius, counted for most with the Persians and with the king.

25. So the invaders were honoring the dead Masistius in their own way. The Greeks, though, having stood up to the cavalry's attack and, after standing up to it, driven them back, took much greater heart. First they put the body in a cart and carried it along their lines. The body was well worth seeing for its size and its beauty, and that is why the men kept leaving their places in the ranks and coming one after another to look at Masistius. After this they decided to move down farther toward Plataea. The country around Plataea looked much better for a camp than the country around Erythrae, for other reasons and because it had better water. So they decided they must go to this country and to the spring of Gargaphia, which is there, and make camp in their separate positions. They took up their arms and went along the lower slopes of Cithaeron, past Hysiae, into the territory of Plataea. When they got there, they took up their positions nation by nation near the spring of Gargaphia and the sacred precinct of the hero Androcrates, on low hills and level ground.

26. Then, while the positions were being assigned, a long argument broke out between the Tegeans and the Athenians. Each claimed the right to hold the other wing of the army themselves, and each pointed to deeds both recent and ancient. The Tegeans said: "All the allies have always judged us worthy of this post, in every joint campaign the Peloponnesians have made before now, whether long ago or lately. It has been so ever since the sons of Heracles tried to return to the Peloponnese, which they claimed as their father's inheritance, after the death of Eurystheus, the king who had driven them out. We won this honor at that time through the following event. Together with the Achaeans and the Ionians, who were living in the Peloponnese then, we had gone out to the Isthmus to defend it, and we were camped facing the men who wanted to return. Then, it is said, Hyllus, the son of Heracles who led them, made a speech. He said it was not right for the two armies to risk everything by fighting a battle against each other, and he urged that the Peloponnesians choose whichever man of their army they judged the best, to fight him in single combat on terms agreed between them. The Peloponnesians decided that this should be done, and they swore an oath with one another on this condition: if Hyllus defeated the Peloponnesians' champion, the sons of Heracles would return to their father's inheritance; but if he was defeated, the sons of Heracles would go away and lead off their army, and not try to return to the Peloponnese for a hundred years. Out of all the allies, the man chosen, at his own offer, was Echemus son of Aeropus son of Phegeus, who was our commander and our king. He fought the single combat and killed Hyllus. Because of this deed we won from the Peloponnesians of that time many other great privileges, which we still have, and this one too: that we always lead the other wing of the army whenever a joint campaign is made. We do not oppose you, Spartans. We give you your free choice, and you may command whichever wing you want. But we say that the other wing is ours to lead, as it was in the past. And apart from the deed we have just told, we are more worthy of this post than the Athenians. We have fought many glorious contests against you, Spartans, and many against others as well. So it is right that we should have the other wing rather than the Athenians, because they have not done deeds like ours, either recent or ancient."

27. That is what they said, and the Athenians answered: "We know this gathering was assembled to fight the invader, not to make speeches. But since the man from Tegea has set us the task of speaking of things old and new, of the brave deeds each of our two peoples has done in all time, we must show you how it comes about that the first place belongs to us, who have always been brave men, as our inheritance, rather than to the Arcadians. First, the sons of Heracles, whose leader they say they killed at the Isthmus. Back then, they were fleeing slavery under the Mycenaeans and were driven away by every Greek people they came to, and we alone took them in. Together with them we broke the arrogance of Eurystheus, defeating in battle the people who lived in the Peloponnese at that time. Then again, when the Argives who marched against Thebes with Polynices had been killed and were lying unburied, we say that we led an army against the Cadmeans of Thebes, recovered the bodies and buried them in our own land, at Eleusis. We have another glorious deed to our name as well, against the Amazons, who once came from the river Thermodon and invaded Attica. And in the hard struggle at Troy we were second to none. But there is no use in bringing these things up. Men who were brave in those days might have become worthless now, and men who were worthless then might be better now. So enough about ancient deeds. Even if we had shown no other deed (and we have shown many, and glorious ones, as many as any Greek people), still, for what we did at Marathon alone we deserve this privilege and others besides. We alone of all the Greeks fought the Persian single-handed, and having taken on so great a task, we overcame him and defeated forty-six nations. Do we not deserve this post for that deed alone? But at a time like this it is not right to quarrel over positions. We are ready to do as you say, Spartans, and to stand wherever you think best, and opposite whomever you think best. Wherever we are posted, we will try to be brave men. Give us your orders, and we will obey." That was their answer. And the whole Lacedaemonian army shouted out that the Athenians were more worthy than the Arcadians to hold the wing. So the Athenians got the wing, and they won out over the Tegeans.

28. After this the Greeks were drawn up as follows, both those who kept arriving later and those who had come at the start. The right wing was held by 10,000 Lacedaemonians. Of these, the 5,000 who were Spartans were attended by 35,000 helots serving as light-armed troops, seven assigned to each man. Next to themselves the Spartans chose to place the Tegeans, both to honor them and because of their courage; there were 1,500 of these hoplites. After them stood 5,000 Corinthians, who had got permission from Pausanias to have the 300 men present from Potidaea in Pallene stand beside them. Next to these stood 600 Arcadians from Orchomenus, and next to them 3,000 Sicyonians. After these came 800 Epidaurians, and beside them 1,000 Troezenians. Next to the Troezenians were 200 Lepreans, next to these 400 men of Mycenae and Tiryns, and then 1,000 Phliasians. Beside these stood 300 Hermionians, and next to the Hermionians 600 Eretrians and Styrians. Next to these were 400 Chalcidians, and next to them 500 men of Ambracia. After these stood 800 Leucadians and Anactorians, and next to them 200 from Pale in Cephallenia. After these were 500 Aeginetans, beside them 3,000 Megarians, and next to these 600 Plataeans. Last, or first if you like, came the Athenians, holding the left wing, 8,000 strong, and their commander was Aristides son of Lysimachus.

29. All of these, except the men assigned to attend the Spartans, seven to each man, were hoplites, 38,700 in all. That was the whole number of hoplites gathered against the invader. The light-armed troops numbered as follows: in the Spartan division, 35,000 men, at the rate of seven for each Spartan, and every one of them was equipped for fighting; and the light-armed troops of the other Lacedaemonians and of the other Greeks, about one for each man, came to 34,500.

30. So the whole number of light-armed fighting men was 69,500, and the whole Greek force gathered at Plataea, counting both the hoplites and the light-armed fighting men, was 110,000 less 1,800. With the Thespians who were there, the full 110,000 was made up. For the Thespians who had survived were also present in the army, about 1,800 of them, and these too had no heavy armor. These, then, were drawn up in order and camped on the river Asopus.

31. Meanwhile, when the invaders with Mardonius had mourned Masistius enough, they learned that the Greeks were at Plataea, and they too came to the stretch of the Asopus that flows past there. When they arrived, Mardonius drew them up against the enemy as follows. Against the Lacedaemonians he posted the Persians. Since the Persians far outnumbered them, they were drawn up in deeper ranks, and even so their line stretched out in front of the Tegeans as well. He arranged them like this: he picked out all the strongest part of that force and posted it opposite the Lacedaemonians, and he set the weaker part beside it, opposite the Tegeans. He did this on the information and advice of the Thebans. Next to the Persians he posted the Medes, and these faced the Corinthians, Potidaeans, Orchomenians and Sicyonians. Next to the Medes he posted the Bactrians, and these faced the Epidaurians, Troezenians, Lepreans, Tirynthians, Mycenaeans and Phliasians. After the Bactrians he placed the Indians, and these faced the Hermionians, Eretrians, Styrians and Chalcidians. Next to the Indians he posted the Sacae, who faced the men of Ambracia, the Anactorians, Leucadians, Palians and Aeginetans. Next to the Sacae, opposite the Athenians, Plataeans and Megarians, he posted the Boeotians, Locrians, Malians, Thessalians, and the thousand Phocians. For not all the Phocians had gone over to the Persians. Some of them were even supporting the Greek cause, shut up on Parnassus, and from there they made raids and plundered Mardonius' army and the Greeks who were with him. He also posted the Macedonians and the peoples living around the borders of Thessaly opposite the Athenians.

32. These I have named were the greatest of the nations Mardonius drew up, by which I mean the most famous and important ones. But there were also men of several other nations mixed in among them in his army: Phrygians, Thracians, Mysians, Paeonians and the rest, and among them also some Ethiopians, and the Egyptians called Hermotybians and Calasirians, carrying knives, who are the only warriors among the Egyptians. These he had taken off the ships while he was still at Phalerum, where they had been serving as fighting men on board; for the Egyptians had not been assigned to the land army that came to Athens with Xerxes. Of the non-Greeks, then, there were 300,000, as I said before. But no one knows how many Greek allies Mardonius had, because they were never counted. As a guess, I judge that about 50,000 of them were gathered there. All these drawn up side by side were infantry; the cavalry was posted apart, in a separate body.

Chapter 49: The Seers, the Waiting Game, and the Night Retreat at Plataea

33. When everyone had been drawn up by nations and by divisions, both sides offered sacrifice on the next day. For the Greeks the man who sacrificed was Tisamenus son of Antiochus, since he was the seer who went with this army. He was an Elean by birth, of the family of the Iamids, a line of prophets, but the Spartans had made him one of their own people. This is how it happened. When Tisamenus went to Delphi to ask the oracle about having children, the Pythia answered that he would win five of the greatest contests. He missed the meaning of the oracle and took up athletics, thinking he was going to win athletic contests. He trained for the pentathlon, the "five contests," and came within one wrestling fall of winning at the Olympic games, where he was matched against Hieronymus of Andros. The Spartans, however, saw that the oracle given to Tisamenus was not about athletic contests but about contests of war. So they tried to hire him with money, to make him a leader in their wars alongside their kings, who were descended from Heracles. But he saw that the Spartans set great store on winning him over as a friend, and once he saw that, he raised his price. He let them know that he would do what they wanted if they made him a citizen of their state with full rights, but for no other payment. When the Spartans first heard this they were indignant and dropped their request altogether. But in the end, when great terror of this Persian army was hanging over them, they gave way and agreed. Then he, seeing that they had changed their minds, said that even this was no longer enough for him, not on these terms alone. His brother Hegias must also be made a Spartan citizen, on the same terms as he was.

34. In saying this he was following the example of Melampus, if one may compare a king's power with mere citizenship. For Melampus too made a demand. When the women of Argos had been seized by madness and the Argives tried to hire him to come from Pylos and cure their women of the disease, he asked as his payment for half of the royal power. The Argives would not allow this and went away. But later, when more of their women went mad, they finally accepted what Melampus had asked for and went to offer it to him. Then he, seeing that they had changed their minds, raised his demand. He said he would not do what they wanted unless they also gave his brother Bias a third share of the royal power. And the Argives, driven into a corner, agreed to this too.

35. In just the same way the Spartans, who needed Tisamenus very badly, agreed to everything he asked. And when they had agreed to this demand too, Tisamenus the Elean, now a Spartan, served them as their seer and helped them win five of the greatest contests. These two were the only men ever made fellow citizens of the Spartans. The five contests were these. The first was this one at Plataea. After it came the contest at Tegea, fought against the Tegeans and the Argives; then the one at Dipaea against all the Arcadians except the Mantineans; after that the contest with the Messenians at Ithome; and last of all the one at Tanagra against the Athenians and Argives. That was the last of the five contests to be won.

36. This Tisamenus, then, brought by the Spartans, was now acting as seer for the Greeks in the land of Plataea. For the Greeks the sacrifices were favorable if they only defended themselves, but not if they crossed the Asopus and started a battle.

37. Mardonius too was eager to start a battle, but he found the sacrifices unfavorable to that plan; for him too they were favorable only if he defended himself. He also sacrificed in the Greek manner, and his seer was Hegesistratus, an Elean and the most famous of the Telliads, another family of prophets. Some time before these events the Spartans had captured him and put him in chains, intending to put him to death, because he had done them a great deal of harm. In this desperate situation, knowing that he was running a race for his life and was likely to suffer a great deal of torture before he died, he did something that can hardly be believed. He was held fast in wooden stocks bound with iron. Somehow an iron blade had been smuggled in, and he got hold of it and at once carried out the bravest deed of any we know. First he worked out how much of his foot he would have to lose to get the rest of it out of the stocks, and then he cut off the front part of his own foot. After that, since he was still watched by guards, he broke through the wall and escaped to Tegea. He traveled by night, and by day he went into the woods and rested there. So although the Spartans searched for him with their whole force, he reached Tegea on the third night. The Spartans were filled with amazement, both at his courage, when they saw the piece of foot that he had cut off lying there, and at the fact that they could not find him. So he escaped them at that time and took refuge at Tegea, which was then on bad terms with the Spartans. When he was healed and had got himself a wooden foot, he became the Spartans' open enemy. In the end, however, his hatred of the Spartans did him no good. They caught him while he was working as a seer on Zacynthus, and put him to death.

38. But the death of Hegesistratus came later than the events at Plataea. Now he was at the Asopus, hired by Mardonius for no small sum, sacrificing and working hard for him, both because of his hatred of the Spartans and because of the money he was making. But the sacrifices were not favorable for a battle, either for the Persians themselves or for the Greeks on their side (these had a seer of their own, Hippomachus of Leucas). Meanwhile men kept streaming into the Greek camp, and the Greeks were growing in number. So Timagenides son of Herpys, a Theban, advised Mardonius to put a guard on the pass over Cithaeron. The Greeks, he said, were streaming in every day, and this way he would cut off large numbers of them.

39. By the time he gave Mardonius this advice, the two armies had been sitting facing each other for eight days. Mardonius saw that the advice was good, and when night came he sent the cavalry to the pass over Cithaeron that leads toward Plataea, which the Boeotians call the "Three Heads" and the Athenians the "Oak Heads." The cavalry did not go for nothing. They caught five hundred pack animals coming down into the plain, carrying provisions from the Peloponnese to the army, along with the men who were driving the carts. Having taken this prize, the Persians slaughtered them, sparing neither animal nor man. When they had had their fill of killing, they rounded up the rest and drove them into the camp to Mardonius.

40. After this they waited two more days, and neither side wanted to start a battle. The Persian army came forward as far as the Asopus to test the Greeks, but neither side would cross the river. Mardonius' cavalry, though, kept attacking and doing the Greeks harm. The Thebans, who were very strongly on the Persians' side, pushed the war hard and kept leading the cavalry on, right up to the point of fighting; from there the Persians and Medes took over and were the ones who showed their courage.

41. For ten days, then, nothing more happened than this. But on the eleventh day, with the two armies still facing each other at Plataea, the Greeks had by now grown much more numerous, and Mardonius was greatly annoyed at the delay. Then Mardonius son of Gobryas and Artabazus son of Pharnaces, whom Xerxes valued as he valued few other Persians, met to talk. As they discussed it, these were the opinions they gave. Artabazus thought they should move the whole army as quickly as possible and go to the walled city of Thebes, where great stores of grain had been brought in for them, and fodder for their animals. They should settle down there quietly and get the job done this way. They had, he said, great quantities of gold, both coined and uncoined, and of silver and of drinking cups. He advised them to send these around to the Greeks without holding back, especially to the leading men in each city. Those men, he said, would quickly hand over their freedom. And he advised them not to risk a battle. His opinion, then, was the same as the Thebans', since he too had some real foresight. But Mardonius' opinion was fiercer and more stubborn, and he was not at all inclined to give way. He said he thought their army was far stronger than the Greeks', and his advice was to fight as quickly as possible and not let the Greeks gather in still greater numbers than had gathered already. As for Hegesistratus' sacrifices, they should let them be and not try to force a good omen, but follow the Persian custom and fight.

42. When he gave his judgment this way, no one opposed him, and so his opinion carried the day, because it was he, not Artabazus, to whom the king had given command of the army. So he summoned the commanders of the divisions and the generals of the Greeks who were on his side, and asked whether they knew of any oracle about the Persians which said they would be destroyed in Greece. Those he had summoned said nothing, some because they did not know the oracles, others because they knew them but did not think it safe to speak. So Mardonius himself said, "Since you either know nothing or don't dare to speak, I will tell you, because I know very well. There is an oracle that says the Persians are destined to come to Greece, plunder the temple at Delphi, and after plundering it, die to the last man. Well, since we know this, we will not go to that temple and we will not try to plunder it, and for that reason we will not die. So all of you who wish the Persians well can be glad, as far as this goes, and rest assured that we will beat the Greeks." After he had spoken to them this way, he gave orders to prepare everything and put it all in order, because at dawn the next day there would be a battle.

43. Now this oracle that Mardonius said referred to the Persians was, as I know for my part, made about the Illyrians and the army of the Enchelians, and not about the Persians at all. But there is the oracle that Bacis made about this battle:

	When the Greeks gather together, and foreign voices cry out,
	where the Thermodon flows, by the banks of the grassy Asopus,
	there very many shall fall, before their fated time,
	the bow-carrying Medes, when the day of their doom comes near.

These sayings, and others like them composed by Musaeus, I know referred to the Persians. The river Thermodon flows between Tanagra and Glisas.

44. After the questions about the oracles and Mardonius' speech of encouragement, night came on and the guards were posted. Late in the night, when all seemed quiet throughout the camps and the men were in their deepest sleep, Alexander son of Amyntas, the commander and king of the Macedonians, rode his horse up to the Athenians' guard posts and asked to speak with their generals. Most of the guards stayed at their posts, but some ran to the generals. When they reached them, they said that a man had come riding on a horse out of the Persian camp. He would reveal nothing else, they said; he only named the generals and said he wanted to speak with them.

45. When the generals heard this, they went with the men to the guard posts at once. When they got there, Alexander spoke to them. "Athenians," he said, "I am leaving these words with you as a trust. I charge you to keep them secret and tell no one but Pausanias, or you will be my ruin. I would not be saying them if I did not care so much for the safety of all Greece, since I am a Greek myself by ancient descent and I would not want to see Greece enslaved instead of free. I tell you, then, that Mardonius and his army cannot get the sacrifices to come out the way they want; otherwise you would have fought long ago. But now he has decided to let the sacrifices be and to start a battle at dawn, because, I suspect, he is afraid you will gather in greater numbers. So get ready. And if after all Mardonius puts off the battle and does not start it, stay where you are and hold out patiently, because they have provisions for only a few more days. And if this war ends the way you hope, then every one of you ought to remember me too, and my own freedom, since for the sake of the Greeks I have done so dangerous a thing out of goodwill toward you, wanting to show you what Mardonius intends, so that the enemy will not fall on you before you are expecting them. I am Alexander the Macedonian." Having said this, he rode back to the camp and to his own position.

46. Then the Athenian generals went to the right wing and told Pausanias what they had heard from Alexander. At this news Pausanias was struck with fear of the Persians, and he said, "Since the battle is coming at dawn, it is right that you Athenians should take your stand facing the Persians, and we facing the Boeotians and the Greeks who are now posted opposite you. Here is why: you know the Medes and their way of fighting, since you fought them at Marathon, while we have had no experience of these men and know nothing about them. Not one of the Spartans has ever tried his strength against the Medes in battle, but we do have experience of the Boeotians and Thessalians. So it is right that you should take up your arms and come over to this wing of the army, and that we should go to the left wing." To this the Athenians answered, "From the very beginning, as soon as we saw the Persians being drawn up opposite you, it occurred to us to say the very thing you have now suggested before we could say it. But we were afraid our words might not please you. Since you have brought it up yourselves, know that your words have pleased us, and we are ready to do as you say."

47. Both sides were content with this, and as dawn broke they began to change places with each other. But the Boeotians noticed what was happening and reported it to Mardonius. When he heard it, he at once tried to change positions himself, moving the Persians over so that they would face the Spartans. When Pausanias learned that this was happening, he realized that his move had been seen, and he led the Spartans back again to the right wing. And Mardonius did the same on his left.

48. When they had been brought back to their original positions this way, Mardonius sent a herald to the Spartans, who said, "Spartans, the people here say you are very brave men. They admire you because you do not run away in war or leave your post, but stand your ground and either destroy your enemies or die yourselves. But none of this, it now seems, is true. Before we even joined battle and came to hand-to-hand fighting, we saw you running away already and leaving your post, wanting the Athenians to try us first, while you lined up against our slaves. These are not the actions of brave men at all. We were very much deceived in you. Because of your reputation we expected you to send us a herald, challenging us and wanting to fight the Persians alone. We were ready to do that, but we found you saying nothing of the kind; instead, you were cowering in fear. So since you did not make the offer first, we make it first. Why don't we fight right now, you for the Greeks, since you have the reputation of being the best of them, and we for the non-Greeks, with equal numbers on each side? If we decide that the others should fight too, let them fight afterward. If on the other hand we decide they should not, and that it is enough for us alone to fight, then let us fight it out to the end, and whichever of us wins, let that side be counted the winner for its whole army."

49. When the herald had said this, he waited for some time, and then, since no one gave him any answer, he left and went back. When he got back he reported to Mardonius what had happened to him. Mardonius was overjoyed and puffed up by this empty victory, and he sent the cavalry to attack the Greeks. The horsemen rode out against them and did harm to the whole Greek army, hurling javelins and shooting arrows at them, since they were mounted archers and therefore hard to come to grips with. They also churned up and choked the spring of Gargaphia, from which the whole Greek army drew its water. Only the Spartans were posted near this spring, and it was some distance from the rest of the Greeks, depending on where each happened to be posted, while the Asopus was close at hand. But when they were kept away from the Asopus, they would go back and forth to this spring, since the horsemen and archers would not let them fetch water from the river.

50. This, then, was the state of things. With the army cut off from its water and harassed by the cavalry, the Greek generals met to consult about this and other matters, coming to Pausanias on the right wing. For other things troubled them even more than what I have described. They had no more provisions, and their servants, who had been sent to the Peloponnese to get them, had been cut off by the cavalry and could not reach the camp.

51. The generals, conferring together, decided that if the Persians put off the battle for that day, they would move to the Island. This is about a mile from the Asopus and the spring of Gargaphia, where they were then camped, and it lies in front of the city of Plataea. If anyone asks how there can be an island on the mainland, this is how it is. Higher up, as the river flows down from Cithaeron to the plain, it splits into two, with about a third of a mile between its two channels, and then it joins up again into one stream. Its name is Oeroe, and the people who live there say she is the daughter of Asopus. That was the place they decided to move to, so that they could have plenty of water and the cavalry could not harm them as it did now, when they were right opposite it. They planned to move when the second watch of the night had come, so that the Persians would not see them setting out and send the cavalry after them to harass them. They also planned, once they had reached this place, around which, as I said, Oeroe the daughter of Asopus flows, splitting into two streams as she runs down from Cithaeron, to send half the army to Cithaeron that same night, to bring in their servants who had gone to fetch the provisions, since these were cut off up in Cithaeron.

52. After they had made this decision, they had endless trouble all that day, with the cavalry pressing on them. But when the day was ending and the cavalry's attacks had stopped, as night was falling and the agreed time for leaving their position had come, most of them set out and began to move off. They did not, however, have any intention of going to the place they had agreed on. On the contrary, once they had started moving, they gladly seized the chance to escape from the cavalry toward the city of Plataea, and in their flight they got as far as the temple of Hera. This temple stands in front of the city of Plataea, about two and a quarter miles from the spring of Gargaphia. When they arrived there, they halted in front of the temple.

53. So these were camping around the temple of Hera. Pausanias, seeing them leaving the camp, gave the word to the Spartans too to take up their arms and follow the others who had gone ahead, supposing that these were going to the place they had agreed to go to. Then, when all the other commanders were ready to obey Pausanias, Amompharetus son of Poliades, the commander of the Pitane division, said that he would not run from the foreigners, and that he would not, of his own free will, bring disgrace on Sparta. He was amazed at what he saw being done, since he had not been present at the earlier meeting. Pausanias and Euryanax were very upset that he would not obey them, and still more that, since he refused, they would be forced to leave the Pitane division behind. They were afraid that if they left it behind to carry out what they had agreed with the other Greeks, Amompharetus himself and the men with him would be left behind and destroyed. With this in mind they kept the Spartan army from moving, and meanwhile they tried to persuade him that he was wrong to act this way.

54. So they were urging Amompharetus, who alone of the Spartans and Tegeans had been left behind. Meanwhile the Athenians stayed quietly where they had been posted, because they knew the Spartan way of thinking, and that the Spartans tended to say one thing and mean another. When the army began to move, they sent one of their own horsemen to see whether the Spartans were trying to set out, or whether in fact they had no intention at all of pulling back, and they told him to ask Pausanias what they should do.

55. When the messenger came to the Spartans, he saw that they were still in their position and that their leaders had fallen into a quarrel. Euryanax and Pausanias had both been urging Amompharetus not to put himself and his men at risk by staying behind, alone of all the Spartans. They could not persuade him at all, and in the end they had come to an outright quarrel, just as the Athenian messenger arrived and stood beside them. In the heat of the argument Amompharetus picked up a rock in both hands and set it down at Pausanias' feet. With this pebble, he said, he was casting his vote not to run from the foreigners, by which he meant the Persian army. Pausanias called him a madman who was out of his mind. Then he told the Athenian messenger, who was asking what he had been sent to ask, to report how things stood with them. At the same time he asked the Athenians to come over toward the Spartans and to do as the Spartans did about the retreat.

56. So the messenger went back to the Athenians. When dawn found the Spartans still arguing with one another, Pausanias, who had stayed where he was all this time, gave the signal and led all the rest away over the low hills. He supposed that Amompharetus would not stay behind once the other Spartans had left, and in this he was in fact right. The Tegeans went with them too. Meanwhile the Athenians, following their orders, were moving in the opposite direction from the Spartans. The Spartans were keeping to the hills and the lower slopes of Cithaeron for fear of the cavalry, while the Athenians were marching below, toward the plain.

57. As for Amompharetus, at first he did not believe that Pausanias would ever dare to leave him and his men behind, and he insisted that they stay there and not abandon their post. But when Pausanias and his troops were well on their way, he saw that they really had left him behind. So he had his division take up their arms and led them at a walking pace toward the main body. The main body, after going about a mile, waited for Amompharetus' division, halting at the river Moloeis, at a place called Argiopium, where there is also a temple of Demeter of Eleusis. It waited there so that if Amompharetus and his division did not leave the place where they had been posted but stayed on, it could come back and help them. So Amompharetus and his men were coming up to join them, and at the same moment the enemy's cavalry began to attack in full force. For the horsemen did on this day what they had been in the habit of doing every day. Seeing the place empty where the Greeks had been posted on the days before, they kept riding farther and farther forward, and as soon as they caught up with the Greeks they began to attack them.

Chapter 50: The Battle of Plataea and Its Aftermath

58. When Mardonius learned that the Greeks had pulled out during the night, and saw their position empty, he called in Thorax of Larissa and his brothers Eurypylus and Thrasydeius. "Sons of Aleuas," he said, "what will you say now, when you see this place deserted? You live near these people, and you kept telling me that the Spartans never run from a battle, that they are the best fighters in the world. But first you saw these same men shifting from their post, and now we can all see that they ran away last night. They have shown plainly that when the time came to fight men who really are the best in the world, they were worth nothing after all. They had only been showing off their courage among Greeks, who are worthless themselves. As for you, you had no experience of the Persians, and since you praised these men because you knew some good of them, I for one was quite ready to excuse you. What amazed me far more was Artabazus. He was afraid of the Spartans, and in his fear he gave us that most cowardly advice: that we should break camp and go to the city of the Thebans, to be besieged there. The king will hear about that advice from me. But we will talk of these things another time. Right now we must not let them get away with this. We must chase them until we catch them, and make them pay us for everything they have done to the Persians in the past."

59. With these words he crossed the Asopus and led the Persians at a run on the track of the Greeks, believing that they were running away from him. He aimed his attack at the Spartans and the Tegeans alone, because the Athenians had marched off toward the plain, and the hills hid them from his sight. When the commanders of the other divisions of the king's army saw that the Persians had set off after the Greeks, they all at once raised the signals for battle and joined the chase, each as fast as he could, with no order and no ranks kept.

60. So they came on with shouting, in a disorderly crowd, expecting to make short work of the Greeks. And Pausanias, when the cavalry began its attack, sent a horseman to the Athenians with this message: "Athenians, the greatest contest of all lies before us. Its prize is the freedom or the slavery of Greece. And we have been deserted by our allies, we Spartans and you Athenians, because they ran away last night. So our course is decided: we must defend ourselves and protect one another as best we can. If the cavalry had attacked you first, we and the Tegeans, who stand with us and refuse to betray Greece, would have been bound to come to your help. But as it is, their whole force has come against us, so it is right for you to come and help the part of the army that is hardest pressed. If something has happened to you that makes it impossible to come to our help, then do us the favor of sending us your archers. We know that in this war you have been by far the most eager of all, so we know you will listen to us in this too."

61. When the Athenians heard this, they were eager to come to the rescue and give all the help they could. But they were already on their way when they were attacked by the Greeks on the king's side, who had been posted opposite them, and so they could no longer go to help the Spartans: the force attacking them gave them too much trouble. So the Spartans and the Tegeans were left alone. Counting their light-armed men, the Spartans numbered fifty thousand and the Tegeans three thousand, for the Tegeans never once separated from the Spartans. They began to sacrifice, meaning to give battle to Mardonius and the force that had come against them. But the sacrifices would not turn out favorable, and in the meantime many of them were being killed and many more wounded. For the Persians had made a barricade of their wicker shields and were shooting arrows in great numbers, without stinting. Pausanias saw that the Spartans were hard pressed and that the sacrifices still would not come out favorable. So he turned his eyes toward the temple of Hera at Plataea and called on the goddess for help, praying that they might not be cheated of their hope.

62. While he was still calling on her, the Tegeans rose up before the others and advanced against the enemy. And right after Pausanias' prayer, the sacrifices came out favorable for the Spartans. When this at last happened, they too advanced against the Persians, and the Persians put down their bows and came to meet them. The first fighting was around the wicker shields. When these had been knocked down, there was a fierce fight beside the temple of Demeter, and it went on for a long time, until at last it came to pushing and shoving, for the Persians would grab hold of the Greeks' spears and snap them off. In courage and in strength the Persians were not inferior. But they had no armor, and besides, they were untrained and no match for their opponents in skill. They would dash out one at a time, or in bunches of about ten, some more and some fewer, and throw themselves on the Spartans and die.

63. Mardonius himself was riding a white horse, with the thousand best men of the Persians, picked out from all the rest, around him. Where he was, they pressed their opponents hardest of all. As long as Mardonius was alive, they held their ground, and in defending themselves they brought down many of the Spartans. But when Mardonius was killed, and the men posted around him, who were the strongest part of the whole army, had fallen, then the rest also turned and gave way before the Spartans. What hurt them most was their dress, with no armor: in truth they were light-armed men fighting against hoplites.

64. So Mardonius paid the Spartans the price for the killing of Leonidas, as the oracle given to the Spartans had said he would, and Pausanias son of Cleombrotus son of Anaxandrides won the most glorious victory of any we know of. I have given the names of his earlier ancestors in the list for Leonidas, since as it happens they are the same for both. Mardonius was killed by Arimnestus, a man of standing in Sparta. Later, after the Persian Wars were over, this Arimnestus fought a battle at Stenyclerus with three hundred men against the whole army of the Messenians, who were then at war with the Spartans, and both he and the three hundred were killed.

65. When the Spartans had put the Persians to flight at Plataea, the Persians fled in disorder to their own camp and to the wooden fort they had built in Theban territory. And it amazes me that, although the fighting was beside the sacred grove of Demeter, not a single Persian was found to have gone into the sanctuary or to have died inside it. Most of the dead fell around the temple, on unconsecrated ground. My own guess, if one ought to guess at all about things divine, is that the goddess herself would not let them in, because they had burned her temple, the "palace," as it is called, at Eleusis.

66. That is how far the battle had gone. Now Artabazus son of Pharnaces had been unhappy from the start that Mardonius stayed behind after the king left. Afterward he kept raising objections and getting nothing done, always urging them not to fight a battle. And since he did not like what Mardonius was doing, this is what he did on his own account. He commanded no small force: it numbered as many as forty thousand men. When the fighting began, he knew well how the battle would end, and he led his men carefully. First he gave orders that they should all go wherever he led them, and at the same pace they saw him set. With these orders given, he led his troops out as if he were taking them into battle. But when he was well on his way, he saw the Persians already in flight. Then he no longer led his men in the same order as before. He set off at a run and fled by the quickest road, not to the wooden fort, nor to the walls of Thebes, but toward Phocis, wanting to reach the Hellespont as fast as he could.

67. That was the way they were heading. Meanwhile, the other Greeks on the king's side were deliberately slack in the fight, but the Boeotians fought the Athenians for a long time. The Thebans who had gone over to the Persians were very much in earnest. They fought hard and did not hold back, so that three hundred of them, their first and best, fell there at the hands of the Athenians. When these too were routed, they fled to Thebes, not to the same place as the Persians. And the great mass of the other allies fled without having fought anyone to the end or done anything brave.

68. This is further proof to me that everything on the king's side depended on the Persians: these men ran before they had even come to grips with the enemy, simply because they saw the Persians running. So everyone was in flight except the cavalry, the Boeotian cavalry included.
